book: The Art and Craft of Problem Solving
summary: Zeitz teaches college-level novices to solve mathematical problems through psychological and logical strategies, named tactics, and a tour of algebra, combinatorics, number theory, geometry and calculus.

unitSummaries.Preface: Zeitz explains what changed in the second edition and why he wrote a problem-solving book for college-level novices, drawing on his own contest background.
unitSummaries.Chapter 1: Separates exercises from problems, describes three levels of problem solving, offers a sampler of problems and gives advice on how to read the book.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: Psychological strategies, ways to get started, methods of argument (contradiction and induction) and further strategies such as drawing pictures and changing your point of view.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: Named tactics (symmetry, the extreme principle, pigeonhole, invariants) each shown with worked problems and the situations where it applies.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: Graph theory, complex numbers and generating functions as tools that carry problems across areas of mathematics.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: Sets, numbers and functions, algebraic manipulation, sums and products, series, polynomials and inequalities as problem-solving material.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: Counting methods: permutations, combinations, bijections, inclusion-exclusion and recurrences such as Fibonacci and Catalan.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: Primes, divisibility, congruence, number theoretic functions and Diophantine equations, with instructive examples.
unitSummaries.Chapter 8: Survival geometry, the power of elementary geometry and transformations, presented slowly for readers with little geometry background.
unitSummaries.Chapter 9: The fundamental theorem of calculus, convergence and continuity, differentiation and integration, power series and the idea of Eulerian mathematics.
unitSummaries.Whole book: How the strategies, tactics and area chapters fit together into one method for solving problems.

concepts.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
concepts.title: What the second edition adds, and why the problems matter
concepts.question: What changed in the second edition, and what should the reader do with the problems?

paragraphs: The second edition expands the first in three ways: a new chapter on geometry, a larger calculus chapter with many new problems, and more problems in several other chapters, especially easy ones. The geometry chapter, titled "Geometry for Americans", is an introduction for beginners, and the author expects experts to be dissatisfied with its pace and its omissions.

To make room, the problems now sit in two columns in a smaller font. Zeitz warns that the small print does not mean they matter less: as in the first edition, the problems are the heart of the book. A serious reader should at least read every problem statement and attempt as many as possible. The Hints appendix covers more problems and is now online.
card.rule: Treat the problems as the core of the book: read every statement and attempt as many as you can.
card.limits: Our reading: the preface asks for reading every statement and many attempts, not for solving every problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
concepts.title: Exercises versus problems
concepts.question: How does Zeitz separate a problem from an exercise, and why does he say problems matter?

paragraphs: Zeitz defines an exercise as a question that tests mastery of one narrow technique, usually one just covered in class. An exercise may be hard or easy, but it never puzzles: the path to the solution is always apparent, even when the technical work is heavy.

A problem is a question that cannot be answered immediately. It may be open-ended, paradoxical or even unsolvable, and it needs investigation before a solution comes close. What separates the two is whether the way forward is visible at the start, not how much work follows.
He adds that problems and problem solving are at the heart of mathematics, since research mathematicians do nothing but open-ended problem solving.
card.example: Solving ten equations of the type taught this morning is an exercise. Deciding whether a puzzling arrangement can exist at all, with no method signalled, is a problem.
card.rule: Ask whether the path to a solution is apparent from the start: if so, it is an exercise; if not, a problem.
card.limits: Our reading: the line depends on the solver, since a question that puzzles a novice can be routine for an expert; Zeitz writes for novices who have mostly done exercises.

concepts.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
concepts.title: The gym and the backpacking trip
concepts.question: What does the gym-versus-backpacking analogy claim about learning from exercises compared with learning from problems?

paragraphs: Zeitz likens the average math student to someone who goes to a gym three times a week for many repetitions with low weights on machines. The problem solver is like someone on a long, hard backpacking trip. Both people get stronger.

The backpacker gets hot, cold, wet, tired, hungry and lost, and gets blisters, but also reaches summits and views never imagined, with a joy amplified by the effort. At home the backpacker is energized and cannot stop talking about it. The gym-goer is steadily stronger but has had little fun and has little to share.
Our reading: this passage persuades rather than proves. A practical author tries to win the reader to the advice as well as to give it, and a vivid contrast is one way he does so.
card.rule: Notice where an author persuades with imagery, and ask what claim the image carries.
card.limits: Our reading: an analogy is an illustration, not evidence; the preface cites no study showing that problems build more strength than exercises.

concepts.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
concepts.title: The author's background and the problem-solving culture
concepts.question: What background does Zeitz bring to the book, and how should a reader weigh it as part of his case?

paragraphs: Zeitz describes an elite problem-solving culture. Its members were raised with math clubs and often took part in math contests, and they learned the folklore problems and ideas that most mathematicians take for granted. It is prevalent in parts of Eastern Europe and exists in small pockets in the United States.

He belongs to it. He grew up in New York City, captained his high school math team, and was on the first USA team at the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO). As a college professor he later coached several recent IMO teams.

He sets this beside his teaching of students who did not grow up in that culture and concludes that any bright math student can learn problem solving. He calls himself a missionary for the culture and the book his attempt to spread the gospel.
card.rule: When an author states his background and mission, treat it as a reason to listen and as persuasion to examine.
card.limits: Our reading: background shows the author knows the field, but it does not prove that problem solving can be learned; that claim rests on his teaching experience, which the preface reports without evidence.

concepts.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
concepts.title: The book's guiding principles and style
concepts.question: Which principles guide the book, and how do they shape its tone and structure?

paragraphs: Zeitz lists principles behind the book. Problem solving can be taught and learned. Success depends crucially on psychological factors such as confidence, concentration and courage. No-holds-barred investigation is at least as important as rigorous argument.

The non-psychological side is a mix of strategic principles, more focused tactical approaches and narrowly defined technical tools. And knowledge of folklore, such as the pigeonhole principle, is as important as mastery of technical tools.

The style follows. The book is organized like a standard textbook but is much less formal, playing a friendly coach that teaches by exposition, exhortation, example and challenge. Each section has exposition, examples and many problems of mixed difficulty.
card.rule: Expect the book to teach attitude, investigation and folklore as well as technique, in a coaching voice with many problems.
card.limits: Our reading: the principles are the author's stated beliefs, not claims the preface demonstrates; the book itself must show whether they hold.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.title: Exercises and problems
concepts.question: What makes the same question an exercise for one person and a problem for another?

paragraphs: The author separates exercises from problems. An exercise is a question you know how to settle at once: whether you get it right depends on how carefully you apply a specific technique, but you do not need to puzzle out which technique to use. A problem demands much thought and resourcefulness before the right approach is found.

The label depends on the solver. Take the sum \(\frac{1}{1\cdot 2}+\frac{1}{2\cdot 3}+\dots+\frac{1}{99\cdot 100}\). Anyone can add 99 fractions, but the first few partial sums, \(\frac12, \frac23, \frac34, \frac45\), suggest that the sum of the first \(n\) terms is \(\frac{n}{n+1}\). Proving that is routine for a reader who knows mathematical induction, a standard method of proof, and a problem for one who does not.
card.rule: A question is an exercise when you already know which technique to use, and a problem when you must first find the approach.
card.limits: Our reading: the label belongs to the question and the solver together, so it shifts with experience. An exercise can still be done wrongly, and a long calculation is not a problem if you know what to do.
card.example: Two readers meet the same sum. Reader A knows induction: she checks \(n=1\), shows that adding the next term turns \(\frac{n}{n+1}\) into \(\frac{n+1}{n+2}\), and is done. Reader B has never seen the method and must try approaches, perhaps many that fail. The question is identical; it is an exercise for A and a problem for B.

media.alt: A scanned fragment of a typeset sum of unit fractions with most numerals missing. Only fraction bars show, in two rows, and the single legible denominator is 1 times 2 under the lower-left bar. It belongs to the opening example about a sum of reciprocals of consecutive products.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.title: What makes a good problem
concepts.question: Why do beginners give up on problems, and what do experienced solvers do differently?

paragraphs: A good problem, the author says, is mysterious and interesting. It is mysterious because at first you do not know how to solve it. It is interesting enough that you will want to put a lot of time and effort into understanding it. Remove the mystery and you have an exercise; remove the interest and you will not think about it for long.

Beginners often give up quickly, for three reasons the author lists: they do not know how to begin; they make some early progress but cannot go further; or they try a few things, nothing works, and they stop. An experienced solver is rarely at a loss for how to begin and confidently tries several approaches.

The Census-Taker problem shows the mystery. A mother has three daughters whose ages are whole numbers with product 36. The census-taker says that is not enough. She adds that the sum of the ages would still leave him stumped, then that her oldest daughter likes dogs. On a first reading there seems to be no way to find the ages.
card.rule: Look for the mystery and the interest in a problem, and when you cannot see how to begin, try several approaches instead of stopping.
card.limits: The three reasons are the author's picture of inexperienced solvers, not a law. Interest is personal: a question that bores you will not hold your attention, however mysterious it looks.
card.example: List the age triples with product 36 and their sums. Only the sum 13 occurs twice, for (1, 6, 6) and (2, 2, 9); any other sum would have settled the question at once. So the sum is 13. The last clue says there is an oldest daughter, which rules out (1, 6, 6), where the two oldest are twins. The ages are 2, 2 and 9.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
concepts.title: Strategy, tactics and tools
concepts.question: What are strategy, tactics and tools, and how does each differ in focus?

paragraphs: The author says an experienced solver works at three levels. Strategy means mathematical and psychological ideas for starting and pursuing a problem. Tactics are diverse methods that work in many different settings. Tools are narrowly focused techniques and tricks for specific situations. These are the author's own labels, not standard definitions, so use them as he does.

He explains them with a mountain climb. Your first strategy might be to scout nearby peaks, then to try one ridge. Tactics deal with obstacles on that route: cross a snowfield early in the morning while the snow is hard, or scout the banks for the safest river crossing. Tools are the specific gear and tricks, such as a rope system and ice axes.

A test for the level: a short summary of the climb mentions the strategy and sometimes the tactics, but leaves out tool details, such as how the party kept their balance in the river. Those details are minor but essential.
card.rule: Strategy sets the plan, tactics meet obstacles on that plan in methods that work in many settings, and tools are narrow tricks for one situation.
card.limits: The three levels are the author's labels, and the lines blur: a tactic can be narrow, a tool can decide the climb, and some obstacles are only exercises.
card.example: Climbing by the south ridge is the strategy. Leaving at dawn, while the snow is hard, is a tactic for the snowfield. Roping up and carrying ice axes are tools.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
concepts.title: The crux move
concepts.question: What is a crux move, and at which level of a solution can it occur?

paragraphs: Climbers call the key obstacle on a route the crux move. The path to a summit may be easy walking except for one ten-foot section of steep ice; getting up that ice is the crux. The author borrows the term for mathematical problems.

Along a solution, some obstacles are mere exercises, though that depends on the solver's ability and experience. But one obstacle may be a small, difficult problem whose solution clears the way for everything else. That obstacle is the crux move.
A crux move may sit at any of the three levels: strategic, tactical or tool.
card.rule: Find the one obstacle whose solution makes the rest routine: that is the crux move, and it can sit at any level.
card.limits: Many problems have no crux move at all. What counts as one depends on the solver, since an obstacle that is an exercise for an expert can be a crux for a beginner.
card.example: A hike follows an easy trail for ten miles. A single stream with no bridge blocks it, and once it is crossed the rest is walking. Crossing the stream is the crux; the other stretches are exercises.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
concepts.title: Think strategically first
concepts.question: Why should a beginner think strategically before attacking a problem head on?

paragraphs: When a problem cannot be solved at once, you must start an investigation. One method, by no means a terrible one, is to try whatever comes into your head. With a fertile imagination, a good store of methods and plenty of time, you may eventually succeed. A beginner, the author says, does better to cultivate a more organized approach.

The organized approach begins with strategy. Do not try to solve the problem immediately. Think on a less focused level and look for a plan that may have barely any mathematical content but leads to an improved situation, as in the climber's thought: if we reach the south ridge, we should be able to reach the summit.
A strategy is only a vague outline of the work. The concrete tasks that carry out a strategic plan are done at the lower levels of tactic and tool.
card.rule: Before reaching for techniques, form a loose plan that improves your position, then carry it out with tactics and tools.
card.limits: Random trying can work for a gifted, well-equipped, unhurried solver, and a strategy alone does not finish the job: someone must still carry out the plan.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
concepts.title: The three levels in one proof
concepts.question: How do strategy, tactics and tools work together in the proof about four consecutive numbers?

paragraphs: The problem, from a 1926 Hungarian contest: prove that the product of four consecutive natural numbers is not the square of an integer. First comes orientation, a strategy. It asks for a proof, not a find, so split it into hypothesis (\(n\) is a natural number) and conclusion (\(f(n)=n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)\) is not a perfect square).

Looking at the penultimate step, the step just before the conclusion, fails: there is no easy test for when a number is not a square. The next strategy is numerical experiment. The values \(f(1),\dots,f(4)\) are 24, 120, 360 and 840, each one less than a square (25, 121, 361, 841). The conjecture: \(f(n)+1\) is always a perfect square.

That would finish the proof, because no two positive squares are consecutive integers. To prove it, factoring is the tactic. Pair \(n(n+3)\) with \((n+1)(n+2)\); both begin with \(n^2+3n\). Writing \(x=n^2+3n+1\) gives \((x-1)(x+1)+1\), and the difference of two squares, a tool, turns it into \(x^2\).

Looking back: the strategies were orientation, the failed penultimate step and numerical experiment; the tactic was factoring with a little symmetry; the tool was the difference of two squares. The crux was reaching the conjecture, a strategic step. After it the problem became an exercise that could be done in several ways.
card.rule: Read a solution in layers: strategies orient and find a conjecture, a tactic such as factoring proves it, and a tool finishes the algebra.
card.limits: Our reading: the levels are the author's labels for one solution, so another solver could place a step differently, and which step is the crux depends on the solver.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.title: Three families, two kinds
concepts.question: What are the book's three families of problems, and what two kinds sit within each?

paragraphs: The book's problems fall into three families: recreational, contest and open-ended. Within each family, following Polya, problems are of two basic kinds: problems to find ask for a specific piece of information, and problems to prove require a more general argument.

Recreational problems, also called brain teasers, use little formal mathematics. They rely on creative use of basic strategic principles, and no special knowledge is needed. The Census-Taker problem is one.

Contest problems are written for formal exams with time limits and often need specialized tools or ingenuity. The two kinds can blur: a party puzzle that asks how many hands the host's wife shook is a problem to find, yet its solution may need a very general argument.

Open-ended problems are sometimes vaguely worded and may have no actual solution, unlike the other two families. Often partial solutions are all you can get. One example asks you to discover as many patterns as you can in Pascal's Triangle and prove as much as possible.
card.rule: Name a problem's family and kind to know what to expect: a firm answer or not, and a specific result or a general argument.
card.limits: The line between find and prove is sometimes blurry. Partial solutions are acceptable even for a contest problem that has a complete solution.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.title: The contest ladder
concepts.question: How do the exams on the contest ladder differ in format, and who qualifies for each?

paragraphs: Contest problems come from a ladder of exams. High-school students take the AHSME, a multiple-choice test; roughly the top 2000 scorers qualify for the three-hour, 15-question AIME. Both are graded by machine, so both feature problems to find.

About the top 150 AIME participants sit the USAMO, a three-and-a-half-hour, five-question essay exam with mostly problems to prove. The top USAMO scorers go to a training program that picks the six-member US team for the IMO, a nine-hour, six-question essay exam spread over two days.
For American undergraduates the Putnam is the most important contest: twelve questions in six hours, taken each December. The median score is often zero.
Contest problems are very challenging. Solving even one, with no time limit, is a significant accomplishment.
card.rule: A machine-graded exam sets problems to find, an essay exam sets problems to prove, and each stage picks the top scorers of the one before.
card.limits: The details are the book's, from the 1990s. It notes that the AMC exams have replaced the AHSME, and that from 1996 the USAMO has six questions in two three-hour sessions.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.title: Reading the book non-linearly
concepts.question: How is the book organized, and in what order does the author expect you to read it?

paragraphs: The book is not meant to be read from start to finish but perused in a non-linear way. It serves two subjects at once, problem-solving method and specific mathematical ideas, and progress in one stimulates progress in the other.

Chapters 1 to 3 give an overview of strategies and tactics. Chapters 5 to 9 treat mathematical ideas at the tactic or tool level, one subject at a time, and depending on your interests and background you read all or some of them.

Chapter 4 is a bridge between the two: it covers three crossover tactics that connect branches of mathematics. Some of it is advanced, but it comes early to give a quick route to sophisticated ideas that apply very broadly.

Each section in the early chapters starts with simple examples and ends with sophisticated problems. Read the beginning of each section carefully, then skim or skip as the text gets harder. You can and should reread later: go back to skimmed sections as your mathematics grows, and read later chapters as your problem-solving skill grows.
card.rule: Read the start of each section closely, skim as it gets harder, and return to it as your mathematics and problem solving grow.
card.limits: Skimming and skipping are first-pass moves: the author wants you to come back. The skim-as-it-hardens advice is given for chapters 1 to 3; chapters 5 to 9 you choose by interest and background.

concepts.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
concepts.title: Reading actively, pencil in hand
concepts.question: What should you do before reading the solution to an example, and why does it matter?

paragraphs: Read with pencil and paper at your side, or write in the margins: mathematics is meant to be studied actively. The author asks for great restraint. Try to solve each example before reading its solution. At the very least, take a few moments to ponder the problem. The more actively you approach the material, the faster you master it, and the more fun you have.

Toward the end of a section there may be a classic problem, usually too hard for a beginner to solve alone in a reasonable time. Such classics are included on purpose, so pondering one is worthwhile even when you cannot solve it unaided.
The book's title joins art and craft. Most pages go to the craft, but the author reminds you that problem solving at its best is a passionate, aesthetic endeavor.

A few conventions help. New terms and the names of strategies, tactics and tools are in boldface. An important point is indented and in italics, which means pay attention. A filled-in square, the Halmos symbol, marks the end of a solution.
card.rule: Struggle with each example yourself before reading its solution.
card.limits: Our reading: for classic problems, which are usually too hard for a beginner alone, the aim shifts to pondering and then studying the solution, not solving unaided.

concepts.title: Two parts of every solution: investigate, then argue
concepts.question: What are the two jobs in solving any problem, and which one do polished write-ups hide?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat every solution as two jobs: investigate to find out what is going on, then argue to convince others of what you found.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To end with a result that you understand and that other people can check, instead of a guess or a lucky trick.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The authors say the investigation is almost always the heart of the work, but a tidy final solution hides its wrong turns. The argument is still needed, because a discovery that cannot be shown to others is not yet a solution.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the network-of-balls puzzle later in the chapter, spotting that one should push the count of two-coloured wires as high as possible was the investigation. The short reasoning that proves it works was the argument.

card.rule: Treat every solution as two jobs: investigate to find out what is going on, then argue to convince others of what you found.
card.limits: The two parts overlap: a hunch from the investigation may suggest which style of argument to use. A problem can also split into cases that each need a different kind of argument.

concepts.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse
concepts.title: Polya's mouse: try again, and vary the trials
concepts.question: What should you change between attempts when a problem resists you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When an attempt fails, try again, but vary the attempt so that you explore every side of the problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To find the one workable way in, which you cannot know in advance, instead of repeating the same failed push.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya argued that you cannot tell beforehand on which side the only practicable opening lies. Varying your trials makes sure you do not miss the few favourable possibilities.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A mouse in a cage trap threw itself against the bars, side after side, and finally squeezed through one slightly wider gap. Polya, watching, called this the way to solve problems.

card.rule: When an attempt fails, try again, but vary the attempt so that you explore every side of the problem.
card.limits: Varying is not the same as hitting the same wall harder. The authors add that a good solver also knows when to stop, at least for a while.

concepts.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse
concepts.title: Knowing when to stop, and why beginners stop too soon
concepts.question: When is giving up on a problem sensible, and what makes beginners quit too early?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not call a problem hopeless too soon; when you must stop, stop for now and plan to come back.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To avoid both banging your head on one wall and quitting at the first frustration.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Persistence alone is too simple an answer, because some problems cannot be solved today. The authors say knowing when to give up is part of the art, and that beginners give up early because they lack confidence and concentration.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A learner reads a problem, feels it is steep, and drops it after ten minutes. A solver who varies attempts, works past her frustration limit, and then sets it aside for later is using the same time better.

card.rule: Do not call a problem hopeless too soon; when you must stop, stop for now and plan to come back.
card.limits: This is a judgement call, not a formula: the authors give no number of minutes after which to stop.

concepts.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse
concepts.title: Building confidence and concentration with a rising load
concepts.question: How do you raise your confidence and how long you can concentrate at the same time?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Start with easy problems, then work on harder and harder ones that stretch you, so confidence and stamina rise together.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To lengthen the time you can stay on a hard problem, from minutes to hours, without needing deep changes in your personality.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each success on a problem you could solve with modest effort builds confidence. A gradually heavier load then lifts your frustration threshold, because interesting problems make longer stretches of work bearable.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A beginner burns out after 15 minutes of hard thinking. By adding slightly harder problems week after week, she can later work for hours and keep other problems simmering for days.

card.rule: Start with easy problems, then work on harder and harder ones that stretch you, so confidence and stamina rise together.
card.limits: It takes time, and keeping the toughness is a lifelong task. Easy here means solvable with modest effort, so drilling routine exercises does not count.

concepts.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse
concepts.title: Assume a problem can be solved before you call it impossible
concepts.question: What should you assume about a problem that looks impossible?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Begin optimistically, and try to prove a problem impossible only after several failed attempts.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To avoid dropping a solvable problem because it looked hopeless at first glance.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A problem that seems impossible may not be. The authors say a quick verdict feels good, but understanding a problem takes time, and no time pressure forces a snap decision.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A job-interview puzzle asks you to join each small box on top with its same-lettered box below, using paths that do not cross and stay inside a large box. At first look it seems impossible, and most people say so.

card.rule: Begin optimistically, and try to prove a problem impossible only after several failed attempts.
card.limits: If several honest attempts fail and you cannot prove impossibility, you have not settled the problem. Go back to it later.

media.alt: A large rectangle holding small boxes. Along the bottom wall, left to right, sit boxes C, B and A. Floating higher up are a box A at the upper left and a box C at the upper right, and a box whose letter is not visible hangs from the top wall in the middle. Same-letter boxes must be joined by paths that do not cross.

concepts.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse
concepts.title: Make the problem easier, then push back toward the original
concepts.question: If a problem is too hard, what easier problem can you solve first?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the given problem is too hard, solve an easier one, then try to move back to the original.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make progress and keep your confidence up when the hard part blocks you at the start.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Dropping the constraint that makes the problem hard lets you see the rest of it. If the easy version is close enough to the original, changing it back step by step can solve the original.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the box puzzle, two of the top boxes were in the wrong places. Moving them so that the paths became trivial gave an easy version, and sliding them back one at a time while bending the paths solved the original.

card.rule: If the given problem is too hard, solve an easier one, then try to move back to the original.
card.limits: The easier problem may not be equivalent to the original; the box puzzle worked because of a topological reason. At worst, the effort shows what the key difficulty is.

media.alt: The easier version of the box puzzle: the floating boxes have been moved so that every top box sits straight above its same-letter partner on the bottom wall. B hangs from the top wall in the middle, C and A sit above their partners, and three short straight vertical lines join the pairs without crossing.

Second stage of the box puzzle: box A has been pushed back to the upper left, near the top box. A's path leaves its right side in a wide arc down to the bottom-right A, B's path hooks around the left of A before dropping to the bottom B, and C is still joined by a short vertical line. No paths cross.

Final stage of the box puzzle: both floating boxes are back at their original spots, A at the upper left and C at the upper right. Winding non-crossing paths join each pair inside the frame: the A and B paths curve around the upper area before dropping to the bottom boxes, and the C path runs diagonally down to the bottom-left C.

concepts.title: Creativity as receptiveness to ideas in plain view
concepts.question: What does it mean to be creative in problem solving, if the solution is already there?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Stay open and receptive to ideas that are in plain view yet invisible to most people.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To notice the unexpected insight that makes a hard problem easy.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Most mathematicians are Platonists: they hold that the subject already exists and is discovered. For them, solving a problem means seeing a solution that is already there, so the good solver is the one who is receptive.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A monk climbs a mountain from 8AM to noon, sleeps at the summit, and descends the same route the next morning from 8AM to noon. Imagine a second monk who climbs up on the second morning exactly as the first did on the first day. The two monks must meet on the trail.

card.rule: Stay open and receptive to ideas that are in plain view yet invisible to most people.
card.limits: This is the authors' account of creativity, not a method you can run mechanically: the insight cannot be forced, only prepared for.

concepts.title: Shamelessly appropriate good ideas
concepts.question: How should you react when you see a beautiful solution you could not have found?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take beautiful ideas as your own, master them, and look for new places to use them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To build a stock of ideas that you can use and stretch, until you produce new ones.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Ideas are not patented. The reaction 'I could never have thought of that' shuts you down, while 'nice idea, it is like ones I have had; let me use it' keeps you working. A confident attitude is part of this.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After seeing the second-monk solution, you ask: where else might replaying one journey beside another help? You test it on a boat that crosses a lake twice, and on a runner who trains on the same loop on two days.

card.rule: Take beautiful ideas as your own, master them, and look for new places to use them.
card.limits: Copying an idea you do not understand will not help. You must master it and stretch it, applying it in situations the original never had.

concepts.title: Stay loose: use mental peripheral vision
concepts.question: What does it mean to look at a problem with peripheral vision?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Stay loose: do not lock onto one method, and let ideas arrive from the edges of your attention.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To spot the twists, turns and tricks that gazing straight at the problem hides.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the eye, receptors are packed most densely at the centre, but the most sensitive ones sit at the edge. In the dark, what you stare at vanishes while what you glance at appears. Starting a problem is being in the dark, so a relaxed, wide view helps.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a table of numbers with no pattern along any row, scan the whole table instead. Multiples of three appear in order along diagonals, then the primes along other diagonals; what is left is the Fibonacci numbers.

card.rule: Stay loose: do not lock onto one method, and let ideas arrive from the edges of your attention.
card.limits: The analogy is the authors' picture of attitude, not a procedure. Relaxing your vision does not replace the work of testing a pattern once you see it.

concepts.title: Drop restrictions you imposed on yourself
concepts.question: Which limits in a problem are real, and which did I add myself?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask whether you are imposing rules the problem does not impose, and drop or bend those.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To open up solutions that your own unnoticed limits were hiding.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: People often treat a picture's frame or a flat page as a boundary that the problem never stated. Once you see which limits are self-made, solutions that sat outside them become available.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Nine points sit in a 3 by 3 array, and you must link them with four connected straight lines. It is impossible while you stay inside the square the points seem to make, and easy once lines go past it.

card.rule: Ask whether you are imposing rules the problem does not impose, and drop or bend those.
card.limits: You cannot drop limits the problem really states. The skill is separating what the statement says from what you assumed.

media.alt: Nine dots arranged in a three-by-three array: three rows of three, evenly spaced, with nothing drawn between them. The puzzle is to join all nine with four connected straight lines.

Solution to the nine-dot puzzle: four connected straight segments, each ending in an arrowhead, pass through all nine dots. One runs along a diagonal, one up the right-hand column, one slants down to the left, and one runs along the bottom row. Three of the segments extend beyond the outline of the array, past the top right and the bottom left.

A cropped fragment of a typeset calculation: a square-root sign whose bar extends over the number one squared, with the rest of the expression cut off. It is the start of the length of the long diagonal of a one-metre cube in the sword example.

concepts.title: Who said they are numbers? Reinterpret the form
concepts.question: What if a sequence or table is not organised the way I first assumed?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Question the form you assume: a sequence may not be numbers, and a table's pattern may not lie along rows.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To find patterns that sit in a reading you did not try, such as letters, descriptions or diagonals.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A first reading is a habit, not a fact. Terms that look like numbers may be symbols describing earlier terms, and a pattern may run in a direction you did not scan.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The sequence O, T, T, F, F, S, S, E gives the first letters of one, two, three and so on, so the next letter is N for nine. The sequence 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221 has each term describing the previous one.

card.rule: Question the form you assume: a sequence may not be numbers, and a table's pattern may not lie along rows.
card.limits: A new reading must fit every given term, not just the last few. If it only fits some, it is a coincidence, not a pattern.

concepts.title: Find what really stays fixed
concepts.question: When a total seems to go missing, which quantity actually stays fixed?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When numbers do not add up, find the quantity that really stays fixed, instead of the sum you expected.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To dissolve a paradox by seeing that the expected total was never fixed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A puzzle can lead you to add two amounts whose sum means nothing. Naming the one quantity that must balance, and checking it, shows that nothing was lost.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Three women each pay $10 for a motel room advertised at $27. The real rate is $25, and the porter gives back $1 each and pockets $2. They spent $27 in all, which equals $25 to the desk plus $2 to the porter. Adding the porter's $2 to the $27 gives a meaningless $29.

card.rule: When numbers do not add up, find the quantity that really stays fixed, instead of the sum you expected.
card.limits: An invariant must be checked, not guessed: the quantity that balanced here need not be the one that a puzzle's wording points you to.

concepts.title: Pick the best configuration and show it cannot be flawed
concepts.question: How can choosing the best case prove that a good arrangement exists?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To show a good arrangement exists among finitely many, take the one that maximises a count, and show that any flaw would allow a better one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To prove existence without constructing the arrangement.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: With finitely many options, one of them gives the largest count. If that one had a flaw that a local change fixed while raising the count, it would not have been the largest, a contradiction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Colour balls joined by wires black or white, so that each ball has at least as many neighbours of the other colour as of its own. Choose the colouring with the most two-coloured wires. If some ball had more neighbours of its own colour, recolouring it would add two-coloured wires, which is impossible.

card.rule: To show a good arrangement exists among finitely many, take the one that maximises a count, and show that any flaw would allow a better one.
card.limits: This shows only that a maximising colouring is good. The reverse, that every good colouring maximises, is a separate question and need not hold.

media.alt: A network of six balls in three rows of two, joined by nine wires: a horizontal wire in each row, vertical wires down both sides, and a diagonal in each of the two squares, running from upper right to lower left. The top-left ball and the bottom-right ball are black; the other four balls are white.

A network of six balls in three rows of two, joined by nine wires: a horizontal wire in each row, vertical wires down both sides, and a diagonal in each of the two squares, running from upper right to lower left. The top-left, middle-right and bottom-left balls are black; the other three are white.

concepts.title: Toughen up, loosen up, and practice
concepts.question: What three habits turn a beginner into a stronger problem solver?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Toughen up by raising your problem load, loosen up by bending rules and welcoming ideas, and practice on many problems.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To become a solver who can work long, think freely and draw on a large stock of experience.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Toughness lets you stay on a problem; looseness lets you see new moves; practice supplies both. Failure is allowed, since several failed attempts are fine if you keep trying other approaches.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Lena raises the difficulty of her weekly set, tries an odd reading of each puzzle, and keeps several half-finished problems in the back of her mind. She does not need to solve them all quickly.

card.rule: Toughen up by raising your problem load, loosen up by bending rules and welcoming ideas, and practice on many problems.
card.limits: These are habits, not guarantees. The authors say they are not promising improved solving soon, only the ability to work, with improvement coming over time.

concepts.title: Cross-train, find your routine, then shatter it
concepts.question: What can you do outside problems to sharpen your problem solving, and what about routine?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Cross-train with other mental activities, find a thinking routine that works, and occasionally break it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To build concentration and flexibility that carry over to problems.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Word puzzles, strategic games, an instrument or a meditative sport train association and concentration. A routine gives your work a reliable time and place, and shattering it now and then tests that you can focus anywhere.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Someone who thinks best in a quiet morning room occasionally tries to concentrate on a problem during an evening concert. Another practises ciphers until she can solve them with little writing.

card.rule: Cross-train with other mental activities, find a thinking routine that works, and occasionally break it.
card.limits: This is advice for variety, not extra work: the authors still want most of your energy on math problems.

concepts.title: Mental squares: a concentration exercise
concepts.question: How can the identity for a difference of squares help you square numbers in your head?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To square a number x, choose a small y, compute (x - y)(x + y) by multiplying round numbers, and add y squared.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To force concentration and strengthen visual or auditory memory for harder problems.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Because x squared minus y squared equals (x - y)(x + y), x squared equals (x - y)(x + y) plus y squared. Choosing y so that one factor is round makes the product easy.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To square 87, take y = 3: 84 times 90 is 7560, and adding 3 squared, which is 9, gives 7569.

card.rule: To square a number x, choose a small y, compute (x - y)(x + y) by multiplying round numbers, and add y squared.
card.limits: It trains focus; it is not a way to solve problems. The authors also ask you first to memorise squares of small numbers.

concepts.title: Expect a winding investigation, and stimulate it
concepts.question: Why does a finished solution look easy when the work that produced it was not?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Expect the investigation to wind through wrong turns, and do whatever stimulates it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To stay with a problem long enough to be rewarded with the flash of insight.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The polished formal argument hides the investigation, which is almost always the heart of the solution. Looking back, you may wonder why it took so long, but the insight comes only after prolonged, sometimes fruitless toil.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student solves a counting problem after pages of false starts. Her final write-up is five lines and looks effortless, yet the five lines came out of the pages she does not show.

card.rule: Expect the investigation to wind through wrong turns, and do whatever stimulates it.
card.limits: Stimulating the investigation does not mean any activity will do: the aim is to learn what is going on in the problem.

concepts.title: Any progress is progress; never hurry
concepts.question: Is it a waste to spend time on a problem without solving it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat any progress as good progress, and never be in a hurry to solve.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep working, and to enjoy the process, even when no answer appears.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The authors say the process of investigation matters as much as the answer, and time spent thinking is time well spent even if you seem to make no progress.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the partial solutions of this chapter, the authors only build tables, spot patterns and form conjectures. They leave the proofs unfinished on purpose, and still count the tables and conjectures as real progress.

card.rule: Treat any progress as good progress, and never be in a hurry to solve.
card.limits: This does not license endless wandering: progress means learning something about the problem, such as a pattern, a simpler case or a failed idea.

concepts.title: Read the problem carefully for small details
concepts.question: Which small words in a problem statement can change the whole problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read the problem carefully, paying attention to details such as positive versus negative and finite versus infinite.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To solve the problem actually posed, not a nearby one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A single qualifier can change the answer: whether numbers may be negative, whether a set is finite, or whether a count includes zero. A careless first reading hides such details.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A problem asks for whole numbers n with n squared less than 10. If n may be negative, then -3 to 3 all work, which is 7 values. If n must be positive, only 1, 2 and 3 work.

card.rule: Read the problem carefully, paying attention to details such as positive versus negative and finite versus infinite.
card.limits: A careful first reading is not yet understanding: the authors want the reading repeated.

concepts.title: Classify the problem, and name hypothesis and conclusion
concepts.question: What kind of problem is this, and exactly what is given and what is wanted?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Decide whether the problem asks you to find or to prove, ask whether it resembles one you know, and identify the hypothesis and conclusion.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To know what you have and what you must reach before trying methods.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A to-find problem needs a value or object, a to-prove problem a justified claim. Naming hypothesis and conclusion tells you what you can use and what you must show; a similar known problem may offer a method.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Prove that if n is an odd positive integer, then n squared minus 1 is divisible by 8. This is a to-prove problem; the hypothesis is that n is odd, and the conclusion is that 8 divides n squared minus 1.

card.rule: Decide whether the problem asks you to find or to prove, ask whether it resembles one you know, and identify the hypothesis and conclusion.
card.limits: Classification is provisional: a problem can change type as you reformulate it. Treat it as a first sorting, not a final label.

concepts.title: Brainstorm quickly after reading
concepts.question: What quick ideas should I jot down before working in earnest?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Brainstorm briefly: pick convenient notation, ask whether a method of argument looks plausible, and watch for key words and concepts.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To give your first real attempt a direction.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A quick list costs little and may point to the method. Key words such as primes, perfect squares or infinite sequences often tell you which tools to bring.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A problem mentions consecutive integers and divisibility by 6. You write n, n+1, n+2 for the integers, note that divisibility suggests cases by remainder, and mark consecutive and 6 as key words.

card.rule: Brainstorm briefly: pick convenient notation, ask whether a method of argument looks plausible, and watch for key words and concepts.
card.limits: The brainstorm is a sketch. Its ideas are not commitments and may be dropped after a few minutes.

concepts.title: Go back and do it again: reread and restate
concepts.question: How does rereading and restating a problem uncover new information?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: After orienting, go back and do it again: reread the problem several times and restate its classification, hypothesis and conclusion.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To catch details and ideas that one reading misses.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Restating forces you to process, not just copy. A new notation or wording can expose structure that the original phrasing hid.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A sequence 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221 looks numerical. Reading it aloud as one, one-one, two-one, one-two-one-one reveals that each term describes the previous one.

card.rule: After orienting, go back and do it again: reread the problem several times and restate its classification, hypothesis and conclusion.
card.limits: Rereading must not become an excuse to avoid working; the authors want orientation kept short.

concepts.title: Fantasise an answer, then see why it fails
concepts.question: How can a made-up answer reveal the problem's constraints?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For a find problem, make up an answer, reread the problem with it in mind, and see why it is wrong.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To uncover constraints you had not noticed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A false answer tested against the statement fails somewhere, and the failing point shows a condition that matters.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Find two positive integers with sum 20 and product 101. Fantasise 10 and 10: the product is 100. That near miss shows the product cannot exceed 100, so no pair can reach 101.

card.rule: For a find problem, make up an answer, reread the problem with it in mind, and see why it is wrong.
card.limits: A fantasy answer is a probe, not a hypothesis; do not mistake it for a solution.

concepts.title: Orient briefly, then start investigating
concepts.question: How do I know my orientation is finished?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not spend too long on orientation: stop once you know what is asked and what is given.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep orientation from replacing the investigation.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Orientation is preparation. A clear idea of the question and the givens is all it must produce; guesses about answers or methods are welcome extras but should not be expected.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After two readings, Jo can say in one sentence what is asked and list the given facts. She has no idea yet how to proceed. She stops orienting and starts trying small cases.

card.rule: Do not spend too long on orientation: stop once you know what is asked and what is given.
card.limits: Rushing the first reading defeats the purpose: do not rush, but do not linger either.

concepts.title: The four startup strategies
concepts.question: Once oriented, which four strategies can I reach for to begin?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: After orienting, try the four startup strategies: get your hands dirty, find a penultimate step, use wishful thinking, and make the problem easier.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make a first move on a problem whose route you cannot yet see.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: These four strategies are simple, easy and often fun. They may not solve many problems at first, but they let you make encouraging progress and often prepare a later method.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Facing a puzzle about sums of consecutive numbers, you try several small sums by hand, ask what single step would give the claim, imagine the awkward condition away, and shrink the numbers to see the structure.

card.rule: After orienting, try the four startup strategies: get your hands dirty, find a penultimate step, use wishful thinking, and make the problem easier.
card.limits: These are starting moves, not a guarantee of a solution; some problems need a full strategic framework later.

concepts.title: Get your hands dirty: plug and chug
concepts.question: What do I do when I have no idea, except try numbers?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Stay loose, plug in lots of numbers, keep playing until you see a pattern, then try to explain why the pattern holds.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To discover patterns and conjectures that give the investigation a direction.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Concrete cases show what the general statement hides. The authors add that much high-level research starts with low-tech experiment. A pattern you do not understand is only a guess, so ask why it happens.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Add the first n odd numbers: 1, then 1 + 3 = 4, then 9, 16, 25. The totals are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, so you conjecture the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared, then look for the reason.

card.rule: Stay loose, plug in lots of numbers, keep playing until you see a pattern, then try to explain why the pattern holds.
card.limits: A pattern from a handful of cases is only a conjecture. The next lesson shows how patterns can mislead.

media.alt: Two drawings made of straight segments. The left is a rectangle made of a square with both diagonals drawn, joined to an empty square on its right. The right is a rectangle crossed by two parallel slanting lines running from top to bottom. Points where an odd number of segments meet number two in the left drawing and four in the right.

Two squares, each cut into equal pieces by straight lines. The left square is divided by one vertical line into two equal rectangles. The right square has both diagonals drawn, cutting it into four equal triangles that meet at the centre.

A cropped fragment of a fraction: the numeral 1 above a fraction bar, with only a small dot under the bar and the denominator missing. It belongs to the exercise about writing a reciprocal as a sum of two reciprocals.

Two solids drawn in perspective with straight edges. On the left, a flat rectangular box with 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces. On the right, an L-shaped block, like a box with one step, with 12 vertices, 18 edges and 8 faces. They are used to count parts of polyhedra and look for a pattern.

A typeset definition: q of n equals the whole part of n divided by the whole part of the square root of n, with floor brackets drawn around the whole fraction and again around the root. It defines a function whose values for small n can be tabulated.

concepts.title: Penultimate step: what yields the conclusion in one move?
concepts.question: Which single step would give me the conclusion, if I had it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Once you know the conclusion, ask what would yield it in a single step, and aim at that.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To turn a distant goal into a smaller, nearer one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Working backward by one step reduces the goal to a smaller target. For a claim that two expressions are equal you may show each is at least the other; for a claim that they differ you may show one is always even and the other always odd.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show that 2a is never equal to 2b + 1, notice that the left side is always even and the right side always odd. That single observation is the penultimate step.

card.rule: Once you know the conclusion, ask what would yield it in a single step, and aim at that.
card.limits: The search can fail, and a penultimate step may itself need other arguments to establish.

concepts.title: Wishful thinking: make the difficulty disappear
concepts.question: What makes this problem hard, and what if that part were not there?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask what makes the problem hard, and temporarily make that difficulty disappear.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To break the first impasse and learn what the difficulty really is.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: You may not be allowed to remove the hard part, but pretending you can lets you make progress and shows where the real trouble lies. Big ugly numbers can be made small, and awkward fractions or radicals dropped.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To find the last digit of 7 to the power 2024, shrink the exponent: the last digits of 7, 49, 343, 2401, 16807 are 7, 9, 3, 1, 7. The cycle of four reveals that 2024, a multiple of four, ends in 1.

card.rule: Ask what makes the problem hard, and temporarily make that difficulty disappear.
card.limits: Wishful thinking is a temporary device. The answer to the easy version must be linked back to the original before it counts.

concepts.title: Build up small values from a rule
concepts.question: How do I find the first values when a rule links terms in an unfamiliar way?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a rule links terms in a confusing way, plug in the smallest allowed indices to build up values one by one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To find enough terms to see a pattern and make a conjecture.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A rule with several indices can be hard to read. Choosing simple indices, such as zero, turns it into a short equation you can solve, and each new value helps to find the next.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A sequence has a_1 = 1 and satisfies a(m+n) + a(m-n) = half of a(2m) + a(2n), for m at least n. Putting m = n = 0 gives a_0 = 0. Putting n = 0 gives a(2m) = 4 a(m), so a_2 = 4 and a_4 = 16. Putting m = 2, n = 1 gives a_3 = 9.

card.rule: When a rule links terms in a confusing way, plug in the smallest allowed indices to build up values one by one.
card.limits: The values 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 suggest a_n = n squared. This is only a conjecture until proved, and the authors say it would probably be proved by induction.

concepts.title: Replace a specific number with a letter and tabulate
concepts.question: If a special number in the problem is just an example, what happens when I vary it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If a number in the problem looks arbitrary, replace it by a letter, tabulate several values, and look for a pattern.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To find the general pattern behind a specific case and then check it with algebra.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A special number may hide a pattern that a table across many values would show. Once a pattern appears, a little algebra tests whether it really holds.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Consecutive terms of 100 + n squared share a common factor; replace 100 by u and tabulate. For u = 1, 2, 3 the terms with the largest common factor are 5, 9, 13, which suggests 4u + 1. Algebra confirms that 4u + 1 divides both terms.

card.rule: If a number in the problem looks arbitrary, replace it by a letter, tabulate several values, and look for a pattern.
card.limits: Showing a common factor is not the same as showing the greatest common factor, nor that no pair can do better.

media.alt: An otherwise empty table grid with four rows and eight columns, laid out like a table of sequence values. The only visible entry is a bold 39 in the bottom row, seventh column. All other cells, including the headings, are blank.

concepts.title: Shrink, tabulate, conjecture, then restate
concepts.question: How can a small table lead to an equivalent, very different problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Shrink the problem, tabulate it, conjecture a pattern, then ask what causes each outcome and restate the problem in that form.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To convert a messy process into a clean question you can attack.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A table of a small case shows the pattern, and asking what decides each entry turns the process into a statement about divisors. Restating in the new terms can look unrecognisable yet remain equivalent.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: There are lockers numbered 1 to n, all closed. Person k, for k = 2, 3, 4, and so on, changes the state of lockers k, 2k, 3k, and so on. For 10 lockers, the closed ones at the end are 1, 4, 9. Locker m is changed once by each divisor k of m with k at least 2, so it ends closed exactly when it has an odd number of divisors in all.

card.rule: Shrink the problem, tabulate it, conjecture a pattern, then ask what causes each outcome and restate the problem in that form.
card.limits: A table supports a conjecture but does not prove it. Here the authors only restate the conjecture as: an integer has an odd number of divisors if and only if it is a perfect square.

media.alt: A mostly empty table frame: one vertical rule down the left side, two horizontal rules near the top, and the numeral 1 in the first row just right of the vertical rule. Everything else is blank; the table of locker states that belongs here is missing.

concepts.title: When a number looks special, test small cases of both parities
concepts.question: Does the claim depend on the number being odd or square, or not?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a number in the problem may be special, test small cases with different values, such as both odd and even, to see whether the claim depends on it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To learn which feature of the number the result truly needs.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A claim that fails for some small values shows what the number must satisfy. Trying an even and an odd case can show that a hidden condition, such as parity, matters.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Twenty-five people sit around a table, each with two cards; each number from 1 to 25 appears on exactly two cards. At each signal everyone passes the smaller card to the right. For two people holding 1 and 2 each, nothing ever changes and nobody holds a pair. For ten people, give each one card from 1 to 5 and one from 6 to 10: nobody ever holds a pair.

card.rule: When a number in the problem may be special, test small cases with different values, such as both odd and even, to see whether the claim depends on it.
card.limits: A counterexample for small even groups does not disprove the claim for 25, since 25 is odd; it shows only that oddness matters.

media.alt: A two-row, four-column table of card pairs for four people. The top row reads 1, 1, 2, 2 and the bottom row reads 3, 3, 4, 4. Each column is one person's two cards, so everyone holds one card from the set one to two and one from the set three to four.
