concepts.title: A false conjecture can still teach
concepts.question: What can I learn from a conjecture I know is not quite true?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Examine a conjecture even when you know it is false: it may show how the problem works and suggest a true version.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make partial progress, and to find the true statement that is nearby.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Wishful thinking asks you to look at what would help, even when it is not exactly true. Testing it shows where it works and where it breaks, and the break often points to the correct version.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Let f(n) be n plus the whole part of the square root of n. Tables suggest that if m is n squared plus b, then applying f twice b times reaches a perfect square. That works for b = 1 and 2, but fails for m = 7 (b = 3). The failed conjecture still led to the idea of measuring progress by the remainder b.

card.rule: Examine a conjecture even when you know it is false: it may show how the problem works and suggest a true version.
card.limits: A false conjecture is a tool, not a result: nothing is proved until a true version is established.

media.alt: An empty table with nine body rows and seven columns. Only the last five heading cells carry labels, naming the second through sixth repeated applications of a function f to m; the first two headings and every body cell are blank.

concepts.title: If you cannot reach one answer, search for the other
concepts.question: If I cannot find a last step for yes, can I find one for no?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For a yes-or-no question, if no penultimate step for one answer appears, hunt for one for the opposite answer.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To turn a hard-to-reach verdict into one with a manageable final step.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A property may be tough to establish yet easy to refute, or vice versa. Testing a different target keeps the investigation moving, and the authors treat a failed hunt as a normal part of working.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Let A and B be different n by n matrices with A cubed equal to B cubed and A squared times B equal to B squared times A. Can A squared plus B squared be invertible? Proving invertibility is hard, but disproving it needs only one nonzero vector v with Cv equal to zero.

card.rule: For a yes-or-no question, if no penultimate step for one answer appears, hunt for one for the opposite answer.
card.limits: There is no guarantee that the other direction is easier. The authors say only that you have no way of knowing until you investigate.

concepts.title: Simplify the worst part of the expression
concepts.question: Which part of the problem looks worst, and can I rewrite it more simply?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Find the ugliest part of the problem and transform it, for example by factoring or differentiating, into something simpler.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To reduce a daunting problem to a smaller question with the same core.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Naming the worst feature tells you what to remove or rewrite. A factoring pattern may collapse an expression to something simple, and a calculus tool may remove an integral.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Given a polynomial p with p - p' - p'' + p''' at least 0 everywhere, factoring the pattern 1 - x - x squared + x cubed as (1 - x)(1 - x squared) suggests writing the expression as (p - p'') - (p - p'')'. With q = p - p'' it becomes q - q', a much simpler question.

card.rule: Find the ugliest part of the problem and transform it, for example by factoring or differentiating, into something simpler.
card.limits: A simplified problem may not be equivalent to the original, so the result must be linked back. Here the authors reduce the original to a seemingly easier one rather than solving it outright.

media.alt: A curve on axes, with a tick marked 1 on the horizontal axis. It descends steeply from the upper left, levels off above the horizontal axis near the vertical axis, then falls through the horizontal axis once, a little to the right of the 1, and keeps plunging downward at the right.

concepts.title: Cautionary tales: patterns can mislead
concepts.question: How reliable is a pattern found from the first few cases?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat a pattern from a few cases as a conjecture to test and prove, not as a result.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To avoid the error of trusting experiment alone.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Experimenting and guessing is only part of mathematical investigation. A pattern that holds for many cases can still fail, and only an argument shows that it always holds.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The value n squared + n + 41 is prime for n = 1, 2, 3 and on up to 39, yet at n = 40 it equals 41 squared. Placing n points on a circle and joining them all gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 regions for n = 1 to 5, but 31 regions, not 32, for n = 6.

card.rule: Treat a pattern from a few cases as a conjecture to test and prove, not as a result.
card.limits: The warning is not against experiment. Experiment suggests conjectures; it cannot replace the argument that proves them.

concepts.title: Rigorous and clear, for the audience you have
concepts.question: How rigorous and clear must an argument be, and who decides?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make your argument free of glaring gaps and deliberate vagueness, and judge its clarity by who will read it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To convince the intended reader that the discovery is correct.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Rigor and clarity are partly subjective. A long chain of reasoning is harder to check than a short one, and what counts as clear depends more on the audience than on anything else.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Many professional mathematicians would accept the sentence 'Maximize balanced wires!' as a complete and clear solution to the network-colouring puzzle. A newcomer would need the full contradiction argument spelled out.

card.rule: Make your argument free of glaring gaps and deliberate vagueness, and judge its clarity by who will read it.
card.limits: Audience does not excuse logical gaps. The audience changes how much is said, not whether the reasoning is sound.

concepts.title: Three styles of argument
concepts.question: Which three styles of argument should I be able to use?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Be comfortable with direct deduction, argument by contradiction and mathematical induction, and pick the one that fits the claim.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To have a tool ready whenever an investigation suggests what to prove.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each style matches a shape of claim: a direct if-then, a claim that something cannot happen, and a statement indexed by the integers. Large arguments use one style overall, and smaller pieces may use others.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show there is no whole number whose square is between 2 and 3, you might assume there is one and reach a contradiction. To show that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared for every n, you would use induction. To show that an even number squared is even, you reason directly.

card.rule: Be comfortable with direct deduction, argument by contradiction and mathematical induction, and pick the one that fits the claim.
card.limits: A problem can break into cases or sub-problems, each needing a different style. The style is a choice you can revise.

concepts.title: Conventions for writing an argument
concepts.question: How should a clean written argument begin, flow and end?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Begin with the hypothesis and conclusion, write in complete sentences, display and label complicated equations, and mark the end.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make the argument easy to follow and easy to refer back to.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A clear start tells the reader what is assumed and what is to be shown. Sentences with verbs make the logic explicit, and a displayed, labelled equation can be cited later. An end mark says the argument is complete.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A proof begins: Hypothesis: n is odd. Conclusion: n squared minus 1 is divisible by 8. It then proceeds in sentences, labels a key identity (1), and ends with a box symbol.

card.rule: Begin with the hypothesis and conclusion, write in complete sentences, display and label complicated equations, and mark the end.
card.limits: These are conventions, not rules of logic; an argument can be sound without them but is harder to read.

concepts.title: TS, ISTS and the defining colon-equals
concepts.question: How do I mark a step I want to prove and introduce a new name?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Mark a penultimate step with TS or ISTS, and introduce a new name with a colon-equals sign.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To tell the reader what you are aiming at, and what is new.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: TS, to show, announces the target; ISTS, it is sufficient to show, announces a smaller target that would be enough. The colon-equals sign has the new name on its left and an expression of known quantities on its right.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To prove that n squared minus 1 is divisible by 8 for odd n, you might write: ISTS that (n - 1)(n + 1) is divisible by 8. Then define A := n - 1 to give a name to the first factor.

card.rule: Mark a penultimate step with TS or ISTS, and introduce a new name with a colon-equals sign.
card.limits: ISTS is only honest if the smaller target truly suffices. The colon-equals sign defines; the plain equals sign states something that may be false.

concepts.title: Without loss of generality, used honestly
concepts.question: When may I handle one case and claim the rest follow?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use WLOG to single out one illustrative case only when you can truly argue the specific case and prove the general one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To shorten an argument without making it false.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Many cases in a formal argument are logically similar. When they really are the same up to relabelling, proving one covers all. When they are not, a single case proves only itself.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show a statement symmetric in two numbers a and b, you may say: WLOG a is at most b, since swapping the labels changes nothing. But to prove that the sum of 1 through n is n(n+1)/2 for all n, saying WLOG n = 5 and checking it is wrong.

card.rule: Use WLOG to single out one illustrative case only when you can truly argue the specific case and prove the general one.
card.limits: WLOG is a promise to the reader that the other cases are the same. Break the promise and the proof fails.

concepts.title: Direct proof: if P, then Q
concepts.question: What is the shape of a direct argument, and where does the penultimate step fit?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a direct proof, assume the hypothesis P and reason step by step until you reach the conclusion Q.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To establish an if-then claim by the simplest route.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The form is P implies Q. If you have found a penultimate step, the problem reduces to showing that the truth of that step implies the conclusion, a simple deductive statement. Establishing the step itself may need other styles.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show that if n is even then n squared is divisible by 4: assume n is even, so n = 2k for an integer k. Then n squared = 4k squared, which is divisible by 4.

card.rule: In a direct proof, assume the hypothesis P and reason step by step until you reach the conclusion Q.
card.limits: Deduction here is not Sherlock Holmes: the word means a plain direct proof. The direct form is the overall shape only; the pieces may use other styles.

concepts.title: Converse versus contrapositive
concepts.question: Which restatement of if P then Q is equivalent, and which is not?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep track of the direction of implications: the contrapositive is equivalent to the original, while the converse is not.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To avoid proving the wrong direction, and to use the equivalent form when it is easier.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The converse, if Q then P, reverses the direction and may be false. The contrapositive, if not Q then not P, says the same thing as the original, so proving it proves the original.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If you are a dog then you are a mammal is true. Its converse, if you are a mammal then you are a dog, is false. Its contrapositive, if you are not a mammal then you are not a dog, is true.

card.rule: Keep track of the direction of implications: the contrapositive is equivalent to the original, while the converse is not.
card.limits: A statement and its converse may happen to both be true; then they are equivalent. That has to be proved separately.

concepts.title: Equivalence needs both directions
concepts.question: How do I prove that two statements say the same thing?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To prove that P and Q are equivalent, prove one direction and then its converse.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To show two statements are interchangeable.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Logical equivalence means each statement implies the other. One direction alone leaves the other open, so both are needed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show that a whole number n is even if and only if n squared is even: first prove that if n is even then n squared is even; then prove the converse, that if n squared is even then n is even.

card.rule: To prove that P and Q are equivalent, prove one direction and then its converse.
card.limits: Sometimes both directions can be handled in one chain of steps, but each step must itself be reversible.

concepts.title: Argument by contradiction
concepts.question: How do I prove something by assuming it is false?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Assume the statement is false, and show that this assumption leads to an absurd conclusion.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To prove that something cannot happen, when a direct route is hard to find.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If a false assumption forces an absurdity, the assumption cannot hold, so the statement is true. It works well for impossibility claims, because the assumption supplies a concrete object to work with.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Show that b squared + b + 1 equals a squared has no positive integer solutions. Suppose one exists. Then b is less than a, and (a - b)(a + b) = b + 1. But a - b is at least 1 and a + b is at least b + 2, so the product is at least b + 2, which exceeds b + 1. Contradiction.

card.rule: Assume the statement is false, and show that this assumption leads to an absurd conclusion.
card.limits: Contradiction proves a statement only if the absurdity truly follows from the assumption alone, with no other false step in between.

concepts.title: The classic proof that the square root of 2 is irrational
concepts.question: How does the smallest denominator lead to a contradiction?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Suppose the square root of 2 is a fraction a over b with the smallest possible b, and show that a and b would both be even.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To show that no fraction of whole numbers equals the square root of 2.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: From a over b equal to the root, a squared equals 2 b squared, so a squared is even and a is even. Writing a = 2t gives b squared = 2 t squared, so b is even too. Both even contradicts lowest terms.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Suppose the square root of 2 equals a over b, with positive whole numbers and b as small as possible. Then 2 b squared = a squared, so a is even. Put a = 2t. Then b squared = 2 t squared, so b is even. Both even contradicts the choice of b.

card.rule: Suppose the square root of 2 is a fraction a over b with the smallest possible b, and show that a and b would both be even.
card.limits: The proof uses facts about parity: a squared even forces a even. For other roots the same steps need adjusting.

concepts.title: Test the negation: does it give you something to work with?
concepts.question: When is contradiction a good choice for a positive statement?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask what happens if you negate the conclusion; if the negation gives something easy to work with, try contradiction.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To choose the argument style that makes the problem easiest.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Contradiction proves positive statements as well as impossibility ones. It helps when the negated conclusion supplies a concrete inequality or object. It will not always work, but the question costs little.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show the quartic ax^4 + bx^3 + cx^2 + dx + e has at least one real root, assume it has none. Then it is always positive or always negative, a handy inequality to play with against the hypothesis about a related quadratic.

card.rule: Ask what happens if you negate the conclusion; if the negation gives something easy to work with, try contradiction.
card.limits: Negation can make things worse, in which case drop it and try another style. The question is a test, not a guarantee.

concepts.title: Congruence modulo m
concepts.question: What does it mean to say a is congruent to b modulo m?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write a is congruent to b modulo m when a - b is a multiple of m; congruences can be added and multiplied.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To work with remainders and divisibility compactly.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Two numbers are congruent modulo m when they leave the same remainder, equivalently when their difference is a multiple of m. Sums and products respect congruence, so you may replace a number by any congruent one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 10 is congruent to 1 modulo 3, since 9 is a multiple of 3. 17 is congruent to 102 modulo 5, since their difference 85 is a multiple of 5. 32 is congruent to 0 modulo 8. If a is congruent to b and c to d modulo m, then a + c is congruent to b + d and ac to bd.

card.rule: Write a is congruent to b modulo m when a - b is a multiple of m; congruences can be added and multiplied.
card.limits: Congruence works only modulo a fixed positive integer m. Dividing both sides of a congruence by a number needs extra care.

concepts.title: Inverses modulo a prime, by contradiction
concepts.question: Why does every nonzero number have exactly one inverse modulo a prime?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To find an inverse of x modulo a prime p, show by contradiction that x, 2x, ..., (p-1)x are all different modulo p.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To prove that a multiplicative inverse exists and is unique.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Suppose two of the multiples agreed modulo p. Then p would divide (u - v) times x, but a prime that divides a product divides one of its factors, and neither factor is a multiple of p. So the multiples are different.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Modulo 7 the inverses of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are 1, 4, 5, 2, 3, 6. For x = 3, the multiples 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 leave remainders 3, 6, 2, 5, 1, 4 modulo 7, all different, and the remainder 1 occurs at 15, so the inverse of 3 is 5.

card.rule: To find an inverse of x modulo a prime p, show by contradiction that x, 2x, ..., (p-1)x are all different modulo p.
card.limits: The proof relies on p being prime. For a composite modulus, some nonzero numbers have no inverse.

concepts.title: Induction: base case and inductive step
concepts.question: What two things must I prove to establish a statement for every integer from a start?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To prove P(n) for all n from n0 onward, prove the base case P(n0), and then show that P(n) implies P(n+1) for an arbitrary n.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To prove a statement about infinitely many integers with two finite pieces of work.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The base case starts the chain, and the step passes truth from each case to the next, like dominoes that fall in turn. Neither piece is enough alone.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Let P(n) say that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared. Base case: for n = 1 the sum is 1, which is 1 squared. Step: if 1 + 3 + ... + (2n - 1) = n squared, adding the next odd number 2n + 1 gives n squared + 2n + 1 = (n + 1) squared.

card.rule: To prove P(n) for all n from n0 onward, prove the base case P(n0), and then show that P(n) implies P(n+1) for an arbitrary n.
card.limits: A correct step with no base case proves nothing. Starting at the wrong n0 can make the claim false.

media.alt: A row of upright dominoes drawn as tall narrow rectangles. An arrow from the left pushes the first domino, which is already tipping toward the others. The numbers 1 and 5 label the first and fifth dominoes, and dashed lines show the row continuing, with later dominoes still upright.

A polygon with eleven corners and several inward dents, three adjacent corners labelled v1, v2 and v3. A dashed segment joins v1 to v3, cutting off the triangle T at the left. The remaining polygon, labelled U, has ten corners.

concepts.title: Induction on an inequality: n factorial beats 2 to the n
concepts.question: How do I get from P(n) to P(n+1) in an inequality?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In an inequality induction, compare the hypothesis with the goal and find the operation, often multiplying both sides, that carries one to the other.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To pass the truth of the inequality from n to n + 1.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Both sides of the goal are the hypothesis's sides times a factor. Multiplying an inequality by a positive number keeps it true, and a final comparison finishes the step.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Prove n! > 2 to the power n for n at least 4. Base: 4! = 24 > 16. Step: from n! > 2 to the power n, multiply by n + 1 to get (n + 1)! > 2 to the power n times (n + 1), which exceeds 2 to the power n times 2, since n + 1 is bigger than 2.

card.rule: In an inequality induction, compare the hypothesis with the goal and find the operation, often multiplying both sides, that carries one to the other.
card.limits: The claim fails for small n, such as 1, 2 and 3, so the starting point matters.

concepts.title: Choose what to induct on
concepts.question: What if the statement does not mention an integer n at all?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a problem has no obvious integer, induct on something you can count, and look for a neat way to pass from n to n + 1.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To use induction where the index is hidden in the problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Experiments often add one object at a time, which suggests the index. The crux of an induction can be a clever choice of the index or a neat way of travelling between P(n) and P(n+1).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The plane is divided into regions by n straight lines. Show the regions can be coloured with two colours so adjacent regions differ. Induct on the number of lines. Add a new line and invert all colours on one side of it; regions that meet along the new line then differ.

card.rule: When a problem has no obvious integer, induct on something you can count, and look for a neat way to pass from n to n + 1.
card.limits: The choice of index is not forced. A poorly chosen index can leave the step stuck.

media.alt: A square cut by a vertical line, a horizontal line and a third slanting line from the top edge down to the right edge. The regions are grey or white like a checkerboard, so regions sharing a border segment always differ. Shades on the upper-right side of the slanting line were flipped; the lower-left quadrant stays white.

A square divided into four equal quadrants by one vertical and one horizontal line, shaded like a checkerboard: top-left and bottom-right grey, the other two white. A dashed slanting line from the upper edge to the right edge marks where a further line will be added.

A five-by-five grid of squares with four grey squares forming a zigzag: counting rows and columns from the top left, grey squares sit at row 2 column 2, row 3 column 2, row 3 column 3 and row 4 column 3. All other squares are white.

A five-by-five grid of squares with three grey squares in an L shape: counting rows and columns from the top left, grey squares sit at row 3 column 2, row 4 column 2 and row 4 column 3. All other squares are white.

concepts.title: Strong induction: use all earlier cases
concepts.question: When does one step need more than the previous case?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In strong induction, assume P holds for every case from the start up to n, and use any of them to prove P(n+1).

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To handle steps that depend on several earlier cases, not just the last.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Standard induction uses only P(n). If the next case depends on earlier ones, a stronger hypothesis is needed. Strong induction supplies all earlier cases; the base case is still required.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A sequence has a_1 = 1 and satisfies a rule linking terms. With a_0 = 0, a_1 = 1, and the rule giving a(u+1) = 2 a(u) + 2 - a(u-1), the term a(u+1) needs both a(u) and a(u-1). Knowing a_u = u squared and a_(u-1) = (u-1) squared gives a(u+1) = (u+1) squared.

card.rule: In strong induction, assume P holds for every case from the start up to n, and use any of them to prove P(n+1).
card.limits: Strong induction does not prove more than standard induction; it only gives a more convenient hypothesis. A base case is still needed.

media.alt: A blank white image with no visible drawing, text or labels; it appears to be an empty scanned page area with nothing to describe.

A cropped scan fragment of a formula: one over root five at the left, then two empty horizontal lines inside thick black bars, an artefact of scanning. It belongs to the closed formula for Fibonacci numbers in the exercises.

concepts.title: Three colours always suffice for a triangulation
concepts.question: Why can any triangulated polygon be coloured with three colours?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To prove a property of triangulated polygons by induction, pick any edge, split the polygon into smaller triangulated pieces, and use the hypothesis on each piece.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To colour the vertices of a triangulated polygon so no two adjacent vertices share a colour.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The triangle on the chosen edge divides the polygon into smaller triangulated parts. By the strong hypothesis each part has a three-colouring. Renaming colours in one part makes the shared vertices agree.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take a triangulated polygon with n + 1 vertices, a triangle T on some edge, and the left and right parts L and R. Colour L with three colours. T shares two vertices with L, now coloured. Colour R by the hypothesis, then rename its colours so the two shared vertices match.

card.rule: To prove a property of triangulated polygons by induction, pick any edge, split the polygon into smaller triangulated pieces, and use the hypothesis on each piece.
card.limits: The base case is the triangle. At least three colours are needed, since a single triangle needs three.

media.alt: Two copies of a nine-sided polygon, each cut into triangles by dashed diagonals joining its own corners. In the left copy many diagonals fan out from two corners; in the right copy the diagonals are arranged differently. They show two different triangulations of one kind of polygon.
A nearly blank white image with only a short double rule near the bottom right; no drawing, text or labels are visible.

A triangulated polygon split in three. A white triangle T has corners x and z on the upper edge and y below. A grey polygon L on its left contains x and y; a grey polygon R on its right contains y and z. L and R touch only at y. Dashed lines inside L and R show their own triangulations.

concepts.title: Strengthen the hypothesis when induction stalls
concepts.question: What do I do when the inductive step is false even though the statement is true?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the inductive step fails because the hypothesis is too weak, strengthen the statement you are proving and try again.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make the induction go through for a true statement.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A weak statement gives a weak hypothesis, which may be too little to reach the next case. A stronger statement is harder to prove at the base, but its hypothesis carries more power into the step.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To prove that the product of (2k - 1)/(2k) for k from 1 to n is at most 1 over the square root of 3n, the step needs a false inequality. Replacing 3n by 3n + 1 gives a statement that holds with equality at n = 1 and whose step works.

card.rule: If the inductive step fails because the hypothesis is too weak, strengthen the statement you are proving and try again.
card.limits: A stronger statement is not always provable; strengthening is a try. It must remain true.

media.alt: A displayed inequality: the product of the fractions one half, three quarters and so on, ending with the fraction two n minus one over two n, is at most one divided by the square root of three n.

A cropped fragment of an inequality: a large left bracket around a fraction with numerator two n minus something and denominator two n, then, at the right, one divided by the square root of three n plus one. The symbols between them are missing.
A bare square-root sign with an empty bar and nothing under it. It is a cropped fragment of an expression from the induction examples, and the contents under the root are missing from the picture.
A blank white image with no visible drawing, text or labels; it appears to be an empty scanned page area with nothing to describe.

concepts.title: Strategies that help at any stage
concepts.question: Which strategies stay useful after the start of an investigation?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep a few powerful strategies in the back of your mind through the whole investigation, not only at the start.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To have a way forward whenever you are stuck, at any stage.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Orientation and the startup strategies belong mostly to the beginning. Others, such as drawing a picture, recasting the problem or changing the point of view, can help in the middle or at the end. More advanced ones appear in later chapters.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A solver who has tried tables and small cases and is still stuck halfway through sketches the situation, recasts the numbers as a geometric figure, and looks at the situation from the object's side.

card.rule: Keep a few powerful strategies in the back of your mind through the whole investigation, not only at the start.
card.limits: Having many strategies is not a procedure for choosing among them. The choice remains a judgement.

concepts.title: Draw a picture: a graph of position against time
concepts.question: How can a simple graph settle a problem about two journeys?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Translate the situation into a picture; for journeys, plot position against time.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To see a relationship that words hide.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A picture can turn a puzzling claim into something visible. For two journeys, putting both on one position-time graph shows whether and where they meet.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the monk problem, draw time from 8AM to noon on one axis and position up the mountain on the other. The first day's path runs from the bottom at 8AM to the top at noon. The second day's path runs from the top at 8AM to the bottom at noon. Two such paths must cross.

card.rule: Translate the situation into a picture; for journeys, plot position against time.
card.limits: A picture shows what happens but is not itself an argument; the crossing must be justified, for example by continuity of the paths.

media.alt: A graph of height on a mountain, vertical axis from base at the bottom to summit at the top, against time of day on the horizontal axis. One curve climbs from the bottom left to the top right. A second, labelled as the second day's path, falls from the top left to the bottom right. The curves cross once, marked as a discovery.

concepts.title: Treat variables as coordinates
concepts.question: How can several algebraic variables become a picture?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a problem has several algebraic variables, ask whether some can be read as coordinates of a point or components of a vector.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To turn a count of solutions into a count of points you can see.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Pairs of numbers are points. If a combination of the variables is itself a pair, that pair can be treated as a point, and conditions on the variables become conditions on where the point lies.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Count pairs (s, t) with 0 < s, t < 1 for which 3s + 7t and 5s + t are both integers. Treat (3s + 7t, 5s + t) = s(3, 5) + t(7, 1) as a point. It lies inside the parallelogram with corners (0,0), (3,5), (7,1), (10,6). Both coordinates being integers means a lattice point inside, and there are 31.

card.rule: When a problem has several algebraic variables, ask whether some can be read as coordinates of a point or components of a vector.
card.limits: The picture is easier when the useful point is not the obvious one: here (s, t) itself did not help.

media.alt: A coordinate picture with dotted lattice lines. A parallelogram has one corner at the origin, one at the point (3, 5), one at (7, 1) and the far corner at (10, 6). Thick arrows run from the origin along two sides, scaled down, and thin dashed arrows add them to reach a point inside, drawn for s = 0.4 and t = 0.7.
Fragment of a sum term followed by a comma: the square root of the quantity 2k minus 1, squared, plus a with subscript k, squared. It has the form of a distance between two points.
Fragment of a formula: a large opening bracket, then the square root of 2 minus u squared, followed by a minus sign. The rest of the expression is missing; it comes from a minimum-value exercise.
Displayed equation: the sum for i from 1 to b minus 1 of the floor of a times i over b equals the sum for j from 1 to a minus 1 of the floor of b times j over a, followed by a comma.

concepts.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!
concepts.title: Recast a tiling problem as a count of colours
concepts.question: How can colouring turn a tiling question into a simple count?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Recast a covering problem by colouring the squares, and compare how many of each colour the pieces would need.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To replace many geometric cases by a single counting argument.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Colour the board like a chessboard. Every domino covers one square of each colour. A shape with unequal numbers of the two colours therefore cannot be tiled.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Remove two diagonally opposite corner squares from a chessboard; both are the same colour, leaving 32 squares of one colour and 30 of the other. Thirty-one dominoes would need 31 of each, so the tiling is impossible.

card.rule: Recast a covering problem by colouring the squares, and compare how many of each colour the pieces would need.
card.limits: The counting argument can only prove impossibility. Equal counts do not by themselves show that a tiling exists.

concepts.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!
concepts.title: Guarding a gallery with a three-colouring
concepts.question: How many guards does an n-sided gallery need, and why?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To guard an n-sided gallery, triangulate it, three-colour the vertices, and station guards at the vertices of the least-used colour.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To show that floor(n/3) guards always suffice.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Every triangle of the triangulation has a vertex of each colour, so guards on one colour see every triangle. The least-used colour is used at most floor(n/3) times, since otherwise the three colours would exceed n vertices.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a 15-sided gallery, triangulate and three-colour the 15 vertices. If the colours are used 6, 5 and 4 times, place 4 guards on the least-used colour. They see all triangles, so 4 guards suffice, and the argument gives at most 5 in the worst case.

card.rule: To guard an n-sided gallery, triangulate it, three-colour the vertices, and station guards at the vertices of the least-used colour.
card.limits: The argument gives an upper bound. To show that floor(n/3) guards can be necessary, a separate example gallery is needed.

media.alt: A six-sided gallery outline with dents, drawn as a jagged polygon that stretches out to a sharp point at the upper right. Two dots mark guard positions, each just inside next to one of the two inward dents. It illustrates a six-sided gallery that needs two guards.

An eight-cornered gallery outline shaped like the letter M: tall straight left and right edges, two sharp spikes at the bottom, and a V-shaped dip from the top. Two dots mark guard positions, one at each of the two inner peaks.

concepts.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!
concepts.title: A disguised trigonometry problem
concepts.question: How can an ugly algebra problem hide a trigonometry problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When the constants and square roots suggest a known triangle or angle formula, substitute a trigonometric quantity and let the formulas do the work.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To replace awkward radicals with sines and cosines.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The substitution x = cos t makes the square root of 1 - x squared equal sin t. The square roots of 1 plus or minus x become half-angle expressions. Sums of a cosine and a sine collapse into a single sine.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The equation 5(sqrt(1 - x) + sqrt(1 + x)) = 6x + 8 sqrt(1 - x squared) suggests 3-4-5 triangles. Put x = cos t. The authors obtain x = 24/25, which indeed works: the left side is 5(1/5 + 7/5) = 8 and the right side is 144/25 + 56/25 = 8.

card.rule: When the constants and square roots suggest a known triangle or angle formula, substitute a trigonometric quantity and let the formulas do the work.
card.limits: This is a tactic needing specialised knowledge, not a general strategy. Recasting is the strategy; the trigonometric formulas are the tool.
