concepts.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!
concepts.title: When geometry is really logic: the planets
concepts.question: What if a geometric problem is really a statement about logic?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If a geometric problem has a hidden duality, restate it as a logical statement about which items have a property.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To replace awkward solid geometry by a simple logical claim.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Private and public points are opposites. With a universal coordinate system for locations, one can ask for each location on which planets it is private, and a short argument shows it is private on at most one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take n equal spheres, not touching. A point on a planet is private if no other planet can see it. If a location is private on one planet, then every other planet lies on the far side, so the same location is visible on all the others. Hence each location is private on at most one planet.

card.rule: If a geometric problem has a hidden duality, restate it as a logical statement about which items have a property.
card.limits: The argument leaves a second claim, that each location is private on some planet, to be shown separately.

concepts.title: Change your point of view: the hat's frame
concepts.question: What viewpoint makes this problem simplest?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If a problem is hard from the obvious viewpoint, search for the natural point of view, for example that of a thing that is not moving.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To simplify a problem by removing a motion that does not matter.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Some problems are hard only because we choose an awkward viewpoint. In a river problem, the water is at rest from the hat's point of view, so the swimmer moves the same way before and after turning.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A swimmer dives from a bridge, swims upstream for 1 hour, turns, and swims downstream at the same speed through the water, catching her hat 1 mile downstream. From the hat's view, she swims away for 1 hour and returns in 1 hour. The hat drifted 1 mile in 2 hours, so the current is 1/2 mile per hour.

card.rule: If a problem is hard from the obvious viewpoint, search for the natural point of view, for example that of a thing that is not moving.
card.limits: The trick works because the speed relative to the water is the same before and after the turn. If it were different, the symmetry would be lost.

concepts.title: Tactics: narrow methods that find order
concepts.question: How does a tactic differ from a strategy, and what do this chapter's tactics try to find in a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a problem looks chaotic, reach for a named tactic and ask what order it could find or impose.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Simplify a problem enough that a focused tool can finish the job that a general strategy cannot.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, strategy alone rarely solves problems. Tactics are broadly applicable methods that often simplify them, and many work by finding order where parts seem missing or unconnected.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author's climbing tactic: push your rear out from the rock. Novices hug the rock, but leaning away raises the part of gravity pressing the feet into it, which adds friction. It feels unnatural and still works.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Chapter 2's strategies were mostly common sense. The tactics here are easy to use but less natural, since few people would think of them.

card.rule: Treat a tactic as a learned, non-obvious method that searches for order in a messy problem.
card.limits: A tactic often simplifies a problem but does not guarantee a solution; the author says specialised tools are often needed to finish.

media.alt: Cartoon stick figure with a smiling face and a large black oval body leaning out to the right; one hand and one foot touch a long wavy line that runs down the page like a rope or a rock edge.
Cartoon stick climber with a frowning face, hanging on a rope with the body held close to the rock, one foot against the rock and an arm reaching up to the rope.

concepts.title: What counts as a symmetry
concepts.question: What does it mean for an object to be symmetric, and why does the author keep the word 'action' vague?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Call an object symmetric if some non-trivial action leaves it unchanged, and let 'action' mean almost anything.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let you see symmetry in as many situations as possible, not only in pictures of shapes.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author is deliberately vague about the action. A broad meaning (reflect, rotate, shift, swap) widens what you notice, and the precise language of transformations is avoided on purpose.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A circle is unchanged by rotating through any angle. A square is unchanged by a 90-degree turn or by reflection in a diagonal. The endless list ... 3, 1, 4, 3, 1, 4 ... is unchanged by shifting everything three places.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Doing nothing is trivial and does not count. A loose definition names symmetry but does not yet say what it buys you.

card.rule: An object is symmetric when some non-trivial action, whatever its kind, leaves it unchanged; that action is a symmetry.
card.limits: The definition is informal on purpose. Spotting a symmetry is only the start; its value lies in the information it gives.

concepts.title: Symmetry gives free information
concepts.question: What can you learn about a symmetric object before doing any calculation?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When an object has a symmetry, examine one representative part and then the special point or line the symmetry leaves in place.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Cut the work of a problem by getting information you would otherwise have to compute.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author calls this free information. If an object is unchanged by a 90-degree turn about a point, one quarter shows the whole, and the centre of the turn is special and worth close study.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A design unchanged by every quarter turn about its centre: study one quarter, then the centre itself, instead of the whole design.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: symmetry only transfers what the action preserves. A quantity that the action changes, such as which corner is labelled A, is not shared by the copies.

card.rule: A symmetry means you need only study part of the object, plus the point or line it leaves fixed.
card.limits: Only features the action preserves carry over; check what the action actually preserves before you rely on the copies.

concepts.title: Look for symmetry even where it is only almost there
concepts.question: Where should you look for symmetry, and what should you do when a situation is almost, but not quite, symmetric?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look for symmetry in unlikely places, and if a situation is nearly symmetric, proceed as if it were.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find free information in problems that do not announce their order.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author links this to two Chapter 2 strategies: peripheral vision says look in unlikely places, and rule-breaking says do not worry if something is almost symmetric. Treating it as symmetric will probably teach you something useful.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author's informal second meaning of symmetry is harmony. If a change makes a problem more harmonious or more beautiful, even when you cannot define those words, you are often on the right track.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A pretend symmetry gives hints, not proof; any conclusion drawn from it must be checked against the real problem.

card.rule: Hunt for symmetry everywhere, and let an almost-symmetry guide you.
card.limits: Acting as if symmetry holds is a way to learn something, not a proof; check what you find against the actual problem.

concepts.title: Three questions to ask of a geometry problem
concepts.question: Which three questions should you ask about symmetry when you start a geometry problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask of a geometric problem: is symmetry present, if not can it be imposed, and how can it then be exploited? Check rotations and reflections first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a tangled figure into one with order that you can use.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, most geometric investigations profit from a look at symmetry. Rotation and reflection are the simplest symmetries, so checking whether either imposes order is cheap, and it often settles how to proceed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A shortest-route problem shows no symmetry at first sight. Question two asks whether you can impose some, for instance by reflecting one point in a line, and question three asks how to use it.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: a figure may offer no helpful rotation or reflection. The check is cheap, but the answer can be no.

card.rule: Ask of a figure: is symmetry present, can it be imposed, and how can it be used?
card.limits: A figure may offer nothing worth rotating or reflecting; the questions cost little but guarantee nothing.

concepts.title: Rotate to line things up: nested squares
concepts.question: How does turning the inner square show the ratio of the two squares' areas at a glance?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When one shape is inscribed in another, rotate or reflect it into the position where the touching points line up, then read off the answer.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Replace an algebra computation by one insight about the figure.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Turning or flipping a shape leaves its area unchanged, so you may choose any position. The hypothesis that the shapes are inscribed in one another tells you which position is worth choosing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A square sits inside a circle that sits inside a larger square. Turn the small square by 45 degrees: its corners now meet the points where the circle touches the large square, and it plainly has half the large square's area.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Notice the many symmetries. Use the inscribing hypothesis to pick the turn. Redraw the figure. Compare the shapes by eye.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A turn helps only if the hypotheses pick a useful position. A turn chosen at random reveals nothing.

card.rule: Turn the inner figure until its corners meet the points where the circle touches the outer figure.
card.limits: The turn must be chosen by the hypotheses; an arbitrary angle shows nothing, and a different arrangement needs a different turn.

media.alt: A large square with a circle inside touching all four of its sides, and a smaller square inside the circle with its four corners on the circle. The small square's sides are parallel to the large square's sides.

Large square with its inscribed circle; inside, a small square turned 45 degrees so each corner touches the circle at the midpoint of a side of the large square. Dotted horizontal and vertical lines through the centre join opposite corners of the small square.

concepts.title: Impose a reflection: the stream problem
concepts.question: Why does reflecting one cabin across the stream turn the shortest-route problem into a straight line?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a path must touch a line, reflect one end across the line so that the bent path becomes a straight one of the same length.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find the shortest route without calculus.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A route that touches the line has the same length as the route to the reflected point, and the shortest distance between two points is a straight line. So the best route is the straight one to the reflection.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Your cabin is 2 miles north of an east-west stream. Grandma's is 12 miles west and 1 mile further north. Reflect her cabin across the stream: the straight line is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 5 and 12, which is 13 miles.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Draw a picture. Spot the line begging for a reflection. Reflect one endpoint. Join the other endpoint to it. Fold the segment back to get the real route.

card.rule: To go via a line, reflect the destination across the line and travel straight to the reflection.
card.limits: The idea straightens a route that must touch the line once. It adds nothing when the two points already lie on opposite sides of the line.

media.alt: A horizontal line labelled Stream with points A and B on it. Y lies above the line on the right and Y' is its mirror image below; two unlabelled points at left are mirror images too. Thick route: Y to A to the upper-left point. Thin mirror route: Y' to A to the lower-left point. Dotted straight lines Y to lower-left and Y' to upper-left cross the stream at B.

Angle diagram: two line segments meet at a vertex on the left with the small angle beta between them; the upper one ends at A. A dotted ball path with arrowheads arrives from the right at angle alpha to the lower line and zigzags between the lines towards the vertex.

concepts.title: Study what the symmetry leaves fixed
concepts.question: What should you examine in a symmetric situation, apart from the repeated copies?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a situation is symmetric, spend a moment on the fixed objects that the symmetry leaves unchanged.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find the points and lines that carry the structure of the problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, if something is symmetric about a reflection axis, that axis is fixed and worthy of study. The same holds for the centre of a rotation. Fixed things are the ones the action does not disturb, so arguments can be anchored on them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the stream problem the stream, the axis of the reflection, is the fixed object: the whole argument is about reflecting across it.

card.rule: Ask what the symmetry leaves unchanged, and study that.
card.limits: A fixed object tells you where to look; it does not guarantee that looking there solves the problem.

concepts.title: Four bugs: a radial view of a rotating chase
concepts.question: How does tracking one line from the fixed centre reduce the four-bugs chase to a single shrinking length?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a rotationally symmetric chase, follow the line from the fixed centre to one chaser, and use only the part of its velocity that shrinks that line.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reduce a swirling motion to a question about one length.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The bugs keep the shape of a square as they shrink, so no bug is special. A bug that heads for its neighbour moves at 45 degrees to the line from the centre, so that line shrinks at the bug's speed times cos 45.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Four bugs start at the corners of a unit square, each chasing its counterclockwise neighbour at speed 1. The radial line starts at half the square root of 2 and shrinks at half the square root of 2 per minute, so they meet after 1 minute.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Spot the rotational symmetry. Find the fixed centre. Pick one bug and its line to the centre. Take the radial part of its speed. Divide length by speed.

card.rule: In a symmetric chase, track the distance from the fixed centre to one chaser, using its radial speed.
card.limits: The shortcut needs the symmetric shape to persist. If the starting shape is not symmetric, no single line stands for all the chasers.

media.alt: Partial picture of the four-bug chase: three thick curved arrows, each bending towards the next, surround a tilted dotted square with a dot at its centre. A short dotted line from the centre carries a cut-off label that begins radi.

concepts.title: Symmetry in a graph: an integral in your head
concepts.question: How can the mirror symmetry of two graphs give an integral without finding an antiderivative?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To evaluate an integral, draw the graphs, look for a mirror line that swaps your integrand with a partner, and use the partner's sum with it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Evaluate certain integrals mentally, as an example of drawing a picture together with symmetry.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: On the interval from 0 to pi/2 the graphs of sine and cosine are mirror images in the vertical line at pi/4. So the areas under cos squared and sin squared are equal, and since the two functions sum to 1, each area is half the interval's length.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The integral of cos squared x from 0 to pi/2 is half of the area pi/2 under the constant 1, which is pi/4.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The trick needs a mirror partner whose sum with the integrand is simple. Many integrands have none.

card.rule: Draw the graphs, find a mirror line that swaps two integrands, and use their sum.
card.limits: The trick needs a reflection that swaps the integrand with a partner whose sum is simple; most integrands lack one.

media.alt: Displayed equation: the integral from 0 to one-half pi of cosine squared x dx equals the integral from 0 to one-half pi of sine squared x dx, ending with a full stop.
Fragment of an integral: an integral sign with lower limit 0 and upper limit pi over 2, followed by a long horizontal fraction bar with nothing above or below it, so the integrand is missing.

concepts.title: Straighten a sum of lengths to prove an inequality
concepts.question: How can reflections turn a sum of several lengths into one chain to compare with a single straight segment?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To bound a sum of lengths, reflect parts of the figure so the sum becomes a broken path between two points, then compare it with the straight segment between them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove a geometric inequality by comparing a sum of lengths with a single length.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The shortest distance between two points is a straight line, so a broken path is at least as long as the segment joining its ends. Reflecting about the figure's line of symmetry helps the pieces line up end to end.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the book's hexagon problem from the 1995 IMO, reflect about the symmetry line BE. Two of the lengths merge into one by Ptolemy's theorem, and the five-length sum becomes a chain no shorter than the segment CF.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The segment gives only a lower bound. Equality needs every point of the chain to lie on that segment.

card.rule: Look for a way to compare a sum of several lengths with a single length, using reflections to chain them.
card.limits: The straight segment only bounds the chain from below; equality holds just when the chain's points all lie on it.

media.alt: A circle with four points on it: D at top left, A at top right, B at lower right and an unlabelled point on the left. Chords join D to A, A to B, B to the left point and the left point to D, and both diagonals, D to B and A to the left point, cross inside.

A network of straight segments with labelled points B at top centre, D at left, A at right, E at bottom centre, and G and H inside. G is joined to B, A and H; H to D and E. Four unlabelled outer corners at top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right complete triangles on the sides.

concepts.title: Symmetry beyond shapes: pairing things up
concepts.question: Where besides geometry can you look for symmetry, and what does it give you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In any situation where you can pair items up, look for symmetry and ask whether a clever pairing simplifies the problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Bring the benefits of symmetry to algebra, number lists and counting, not only to pictures.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, symmetry is not limited to physical or geometric objects. Sequences can have symmetry too, and thinking about symmetry almost always pays off, so a natural way of matching items is worth testing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author's example is a row of Pascal's triangle, which reads the same forwards and backwards. Matching each entry with its mirror entry is a pairing that you can use to check or extend a list.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author says almost always, not always. A pairing is worth testing, not guaranteed to exist or to help.

card.rule: Whenever things can be paired up, test whether the pairing exposes a symmetry that simplifies the problem.
card.limits: The author says symmetry almost always pays off, so some collections have no helpful pairing.

concepts.title: The Gaussian pairing tool for sums
concepts.question: How does pairing the first term with the last turn a long sum into a short product?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To add a run of evenly spaced numbers, pair the first with the last, the second with the second last, and so on; each pair has the same sum.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Replace a slow addition by a single multiplication.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In 1 + 2 + ... + 100 the pairs 1 and 100, 2 and 99, 3 and 98 each add to 101, and there are 50 of them. Equal pair sums turn the addition into 101 times 50.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The story is that the ten-year-old Gauss was set this sum as a punishment and answered 5,050 at once. The author notes that no one knows how true such stories are.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: If the number of terms is odd, one middle term is left without a partner. Count it separately or use a different method.

card.rule: Pair the ends of a run of numbers inward; equal pair sums make the total a product.
card.limits: With an odd number of terms the middle term has no partner, so the plain pairing needs an adjustment.

concepts.title: Write the sum forward and backward
concepts.question: How does adding a sum to its own reversal avoid the problem of an odd number of terms?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write the sum forward, write it again backward underneath, and add the two lines column by column.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get the total of an evenly spaced run whether the number of terms is odd or even.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each column adds to the same number, so twice the sum equals the number of columns times that number. Then you halve.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For S = 1 + 2 + ... + 100 written forward and backward, every column adds to 101, so 2S = 100 times 101 and S = 5050.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Write S forward. Write S backward. Add the columns. Count them. Halve the product.

card.rule: Add the sum to its own reversal; twice the sum is the column count times the common column sum.
card.limits: The method needs evenly spaced terms so that every column adds to the same total.

concepts.title: Pair each divisor with its partner
concepts.question: Why does a whole number have an odd number of divisors only when it is a perfect square?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To count the divisors of n, pair each divisor d with n/d; every divisor has a distinct mate unless d is the square root of n.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Settle the parity of the number of divisors, written d(n), without listing them all.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each divisor d has the mate n/d, which is also a divisor. Unmated divisors exist only when d equals n/d, that is when d squared is n. So the count is even except for perfect squares, where the square root is paired with itself.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The divisors of 28 are 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28, which pair as (1, 28), (2, 14), (4, 7): an even count. For 36 the pairs are (1, 36), (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9) and (6, 6), so the count is odd.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Pairing tells you the parity only. It does not say how many divisors a number has.

card.rule: Pair d with n over d; the number of divisors is odd exactly when n is a perfect square.
card.limits: The pairing decides odd or even, not the exact count of divisors.

concepts.title: Wilson's theorem by pairing inverses
concepts.question: How does pairing each number with its inverse evaluate the product (p - 1)! modulo a prime p?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To find (p - 1)! modulo a prime p, pair every factor with its multiplicative inverse; the products 1, and the leftover 1 and p - 1, give the answer.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Replace a huge product by a few easy factors, using 1 and -1.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Because p is prime, every factor from 1 to p - 1 has exactly one inverse among the same numbers, so factors pair off into products congruent to 1. The factors that are their own mates are 1 and p - 1, which is congruent to -1.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For p = 13 the pairs are (2, 7), (3, 9), (4, 10), (5, 8), (6, 11), with 1 and 12 alone. The pairs each give 1, so 12! is congruent to 12, which is -1 modulo 13.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: If the modulus is not prime, some nonzero factors have no inverse, and the pairing breaks down.

card.rule: Pair each factor with its inverse mod p; only 1 and p - 1 stand alone, so (p - 1)! is congruent to -1.
card.limits: The pairing needs every nonzero residue to have a unique inverse, which primality guarantees.

concepts.title: Raise the symmetry, then substitute
concepts.question: How do you use symmetric coefficients to bring a degree-4 equation down to a quadratic?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When an equation's coefficients read the same in both directions, divide by the middle power of x, collect x + 1/x terms, and substitute u = x + 1/x.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reduce a high-degree equation to a quadratic.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The coefficients are already symmetric; dividing makes the powers symmetric too, so terms pair as x^k + x^-k. Each pair is a polynomial in u, because x squared + 1/x squared = u squared - 2.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 = 0, divide by x^2 to get x^2 + 1/x^2 + x + 1/x + 1 = 0. With u = x + 1/x this is u^2 - 2 + u + 1 = 0, so u^2 + u - 1 = 0.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Check the coefficients are symmetric. Divide by x squared. Group like terms. Substitute u. Solve for u, then solve x + 1/x = u for x.

card.rule: Divide a symmetric-coefficient equation by the middle power of x and substitute u = x + 1/x.
card.limits: The trick needs symmetric coefficients. With uneven ones the terms do not pair, and u does not appear.

media.alt: Displayed formula from the symmetric-substitution step of the quartic equation: u squared equals x squared plus 2 plus the fraction one over x squared, followed by a comma.

Partly drawn formula: x equals a fraction whose numerator begins with u plus or minus the square root of u squared, with the bar running on and the rest of the radicand missing, ending in a full stop.

concepts.title: A symmetric inequality: factor, do not expand
concepts.question: How can symmetry under swapping variables help you prove an inequality without multiplying it out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When an inequality is unchanged by permuting its variables, prove a bound for one factor, then apply cyclic permutations and multiply.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove symmetric inequalities in a few lines without expanding.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author observes that permuting the variables gives the other factors from the first. One two-variable bound for a + b, repeated for b + c and c + a, multiplies out to the whole inequality.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To prove that (a + b)(b + c)(c + a) is at least 8abc for positive a, b and c, use a + b at least 2 times the square root of ab, repeat for the other two, and multiply the three bounds.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Notice the symmetry. Do not expand. Bound one factor. Permute cyclically (a to b to c to a). Multiply.

card.rule: Do not expand a symmetric product; prove one factor's bound and permute the variables.
card.limits: The bound for one factor must hold for positive values. Multiplying inequalities needs all sides positive.

media.alt: Inequality fragment: b plus c is at least 2 times the square root of bc, the two-variable arithmetic-geometric-mean bound, with the overbar of the root cut off at the right edge.

concepts.title: Cyclic sums and a symmetric factorisation
concepts.question: What does the cyclic-sum notation mean, and how does it help factor a symmetric cubic?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the cyclic-sum symbol to write expressions that repeat under cyclic permutation, and when factoring, keep every guess symmetric.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Save time and reduce errors when working with symmetric expressions.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A cyclic sum adds a term to the terms obtained by moving each variable one place along: x to y to z to x. Writing the pattern once shortens the algebra, and a symmetric guess for a factor keeps the leftover error terms symmetric too.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For variables x, y, z, the cyclic sum of x cubed is x^3 + y^3 + z^3, and the cyclic sum of x z^2 is x z^2 + y x^2 + z y^2.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Guess the simplest symmetric factor, a + b + c. Multiply by a symmetric partner. Compare with the target. Fix the error terms. Factor out again.

card.rule: Write symmetric expressions as cyclic sums, and keep factoring guesses symmetric.
card.limits: The notation shortens bookkeeping; it does not find the factor. The guess still has to be made.

concepts.title: The extreme principle: look at the largest and smallest
concepts.question: What does the extreme principle tell you to do with the elements of a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If possible, assume the elements of your problem are in order, and focus on the largest and smallest ones.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Tame a problem with many things to track by organising them and watching the ones that are constrained most.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author calls the order that this assumption gives free information. The largest and smallest elements may be constrained in interesting ways, because nothing lies beyond them. Putting elements in order is called monotonizing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: numbers sit round a circle, and each equals the average of its two neighbours. Look at the largest one. Its neighbours average to it and neither is larger, so both equal it. Repeating shows every number is equal.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the largest or smallest element must exist, and it may not constrain anything useful; the author adds that the principle can seem almost trite, yet it works wonders.

card.rule: Put the elements in order and study the largest and smallest.
card.limits: The extremes must exist and must be constrained by the problem. Infinite sets may have no extremes.

concepts.title: Minimal element plus contradiction
concepts.question: What is the typical shape of an extreme-principle proof, and how does the black and white points problem follow it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Assume the claim is false, take the smallest (or largest) example of the bad thing, and build a smaller (or larger) one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove a statement quickly by turning a hidden example into an impossible one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author calls this a typical structure: work by contradiction, assume what you want to prove is not true, then look at the minimal or maximal element and develop an argument that creates a smaller or larger element.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Finite sets of black and white points are such that every segment joining two points of one colour contains a point of the other colour. If the points were not all on one line, take the triangle of smallest area. Two vertices share a colour, so a point of the other colour lies between them and makes a smaller triangle, a contradiction.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Assume the opposite. Find the extreme object. Show a smaller (or larger) one exists. Conclude the opposite is impossible.

card.rule: Suppose the claim fails, take the extreme example, and derive a more extreme one.
card.limits: Our reading: the argument needs a smallest or largest example to exist, so it fits finite sets and positive integers best.

media.alt: A triangle with filled dots at its left vertex and bottom-right vertex and an open circle at its top-right vertex. A second open circle sits on the side joining the two filled vertices, and a dashed segment joins it to the top-right vertex.

concepts.title: When extremes exist: finite sets and well-ordering
concepts.question: When are you sure that a smallest or largest element exists?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before invoking an extreme, check that it exists: finite sets of reals have a smallest and largest member, and non-empty sets of positive integers have a least member.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep an extremal argument from resting on an element that may not exist.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A finite set of real numbers always has a minimum and a maximum. The Well-Ordering Principle gives a least element in every non-empty set of positive integers. Other infinite sets may have neither.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The infinite set 1, 2, 1/2, 2^2, 1/2^2, 2^3, ... has neither a minimum nor a maximum, since its entries get arbitrarily large and arbitrarily close to zero.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Beyond finite sets and positive integers, extremes can be missing, so the author tells you to be careful with infinite sets.

card.rule: Make sure an extreme exists: finite sets always have one, and so do non-empty sets of positive integers.
card.limits: In an infinite set of reals the smallest or largest element may not exist, so the argument needs extra care.

concepts.title: The largest triangle contains everything
concepts.question: How does taking the triangle of largest area bound a whole set of points inside a bigger triangle?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To bound a set of points by a triangle, take the largest triangle formed by the points and build the larger triangle whose midpoints are its vertices.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show that the whole set fits inside a figure with a known area.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If a point lay outside the enlarged triangle, joining it to two of the largest triangle's vertices would give a triangle of larger area, contradicting maximality. The enlarged triangle has four times the area of the largest.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Finitely many points have every triangle of area less than 1. Take the triangle ABC of largest area, and let LMN be the triangle whose midpoints are A, B, C. Then LMN has area less than 4, and all the points lie inside it.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The bound is not tight. The triangle LMN may be much larger than needed, and the argument needs finitely many points so that a largest triangle exists.

card.rule: Take the largest triangle ABC and build the triangle LMN that has ABC as its medial triangle.
card.limits: The result is a bound, not the smallest enclosing triangle, and it needs finitely many points.

media.alt: A large triangle with its top-right corner labelled N. Inside it is triangle ABC whose corners A, B, C are the midpoints of the large triangle's three sides (A left, C top, B right); the right side, through B, is parallel to AC. A point P outside the right side is joined to A and C by dotted segments.

concepts.title: The handshake party: investigate a smaller case
concepts.question: How do the people with the most and fewest handshakes reveal who is married to whom?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a problem looks intractable, work a smaller case, and look at the extremes: the person who shook the most hands must be partnered with the person who shook none.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find an unknown from a puzzle that seems to give too little information.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the small case the five answers are all different, so they are exactly 0 to 4. The person with 4 shook everyone but their partner, so everyone else has a nonzero number, and the person with 0 must be that partner.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The host invites 10 couples, asks everyone but himself how many hands they shook, and gets different answers from everyone. No one shook hands with their partner. The hostess shook exactly 10 hands.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Try the case with two couples. List the possible numbers. Pair the extremes. Remove them and repeat. The one left is the hostess.

card.rule: Make the problem small, then pair the person with the most handshakes with the one with none, and repeat.
card.limits: The method needs all the answers to be different; without that the extremes are not forced.

media.alt: Points P1, P2, P3, P4 and H. Solid segments join P4 to each of P1, P2, P3 and H. Dashed segments join P3 to P2 and P3 to H. P1 has only the one solid segment, to P4.

concepts.title: Strip off the extremes, then use induction
concepts.question: How does removing the extreme people from the handshake party lead to a proof by induction?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the extremes to strip a problem down to a smaller version of itself, then write the proof as an induction on the size.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn the handshake insight into a proof that holds for any number of couples.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The person who shook the most hands and the person who shook none are partners. Removing them lowers every other count by exactly one and leaves a party of the same kind with one fewer couple, so the induction hypothesis applies.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The statement P(n): at a party with n couples plus host and hostess, with no handshakes between partners and all other answers different, the hostess shook n hands. P(1) is checked by a diagram, and the step from n to n + 1 uses the removal.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Check the base case. Assume the statement for n couples. In the party with n + 1 couples find the two extreme people. Remove them. Apply the hypothesis. Put the hostess's handshake with the removed extreme back.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The induction needs the smaller party to satisfy the same conditions, which depends on the answers being different.

card.rule: Remove the extreme pair, show a smaller case of the same kind remains, and conclude by induction.
card.limits: The method works only if the removal leaves a problem satisfying the same hypotheses.

concepts.title: The blackboard of GCDs and LCMs
concepts.question: Why must replacing two numbers by their GCD and LCM eventually stop changing?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a process that evolves, watch the least and greatest elements: if one cannot go past a bound, find the stage where it settles and take it out of the picture.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove that an erase-and-replace process terminates.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Replacing a and b by GCD(a, b) and LCM(a, b) leaves them unchanged when a divides b, and otherwise lowers the smaller and raises the larger. So the least element never rises, stays at least the GCD of the originals, and only finitely many sequences are possible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Start with 10 and 15. They become 5 and 30, and since 5 divides 30 nothing more changes. With several numbers the process keeps going until a smallest-ever least element divides all the others.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Experiment with small lists. Track the least and greatest elements. Show the least cannot go up. Take the smallest least element that ever occurs, show it divides all others, ignore it and use induction.

card.rule: Track the least element; the smallest one that ever occurs divides the rest, so it can be set aside.
card.limits: The argument shows the process ends, but a separate step is needed to prove the final list is a chain of divisors.

concepts.title: An extreme on an infinite domain: show it exists
concepts.question: Why must you prove that a polynomial attains a minimum before arguing at the point where it is smallest?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before arguing at a minimum over an infinite domain, show that the minimum is actually attained.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make extremal arguments valid when the set of values is infinite.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A polynomial that is never negative has even degree and a positive leading coefficient, so it tends to plus infinity at both ends and has a lowest value. Without that check, the 'minimum point' may not exist.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If f(x) is a polynomial, never negative, of degree n, then g = f + f' + ... + f^(n) has the same leading term, so it too has a minimum. Suppose g is negative somewhere and look at its minimum point.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: For some functions, such as 1/x on the positive reals, the infimum is never reached, so there is no minimum point.

card.rule: On an infinite domain, prove that the extreme exists, for example by checking the behaviour at the ends.
card.limits: The check is needed; a function can be bounded below without ever attaining its lower bound.

concepts.title: Prove a stronger statement, then monotonize and pair
concepts.question: Why might you try to prove something stronger than the problem asks, and how do ordering and pairing help?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the goal is hard, experiment with small cases, guess a stronger and tidier statement such as pairing the terms, put the terms in order and argue by contradiction.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a proof for a difficult olympiad inequality by making the statement more specific.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author notes that part of the difficulty is working out the statement, and that sometimes stronger statements are easier to prove. Ordering the terms makes the pairing visible, and contradiction hands you a specific inequality to use.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the 1994 IMO problem about sequences of distinct numbers closed under small sums, the average of the terms is claimed to be at least (n + 1)/2. Experiments suggest pairing the smallest term with the largest, the second smallest with the second largest, each pair adding to at least n + 1.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Try easy values. Guess a stronger claim. Order the terms. Assume one pair sums to at most n. Use the closure property to force a contradiction.

card.rule: Guess a stronger, pairable statement, order the terms, and prove it by contradiction.
card.limits: A stronger statement may be false; check it against examples first.

concepts.title: The pigeonhole principle
concepts.question: What does the pigeonhole principle say, and why do mathematicians value so simple an idea?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you have more pigeons than pigeonholes, then at least one hole holds at least two pigeons.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove that something exists, such as a repeated colour or value, without finding which one it is.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author calls it a nearly vacuous observation: with more guests than spare rooms, some guests must share. Yet mathematicians revere it, since it is at least as powerful as the Gaussian pairing trick.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Thirteen people are in a room. There are twelve birth months, so at least two of them share a birth month. The principle does not say which two.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: It tells you that a crowded hole exists, not which one. With as many pigeons as holes, each hole can hold one.

card.rule: More pigeons than holes means some hole has at least two pigeons.
card.limits: The principle names no particular hole, and it gives nothing when pigeons do not outnumber holes.

concepts.title: Three parts of a pigeonhole solution
concepts.question: What three jobs does a solver have in a pigeonhole problem, and which is usually the crux?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a pigeonhole problem, recognise that the principle may apply, decide what the pigeons and the holes are, and plan for more work after the principle has been used.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Organise the search for a pigeonhole solution into three clear jobs.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, solving most pigeonhole problems is a three-part process. Working out what the pigeons and holes must be is frequently the crux move. The principle often yields only the penultimate step or an intermediate result, so a skilled solver plans for this.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show that among n + 1 integers two differ by a multiple of n, the holes are remainders on division by n and the pigeons are the integers. The principle gives the shared remainder; the multiple follows.

card.rule: Spot the pigeonhole, choose the pigeons and holes, and expect a finishing step.
card.limits: Choosing pigeons and holes can be hard, and the principle may supply only part of the argument.

concepts.title: Choose a small configuration: the two-coloured plane
concepts.question: How does the pigeonhole principle show two same-coloured points exactly a mile apart in a red-and-blue plane?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To force a repeat, pick a small configuration with more points than colours, in which every pair of points is the required distance apart.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Settle a statement about colouring the whole plane using only a few points.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The vertices of an equilateral triangle with side one mile are three points, any two a mile apart. Only two colours are available, so two vertices share a colour.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Every point of the plane is red or blue. Place an equilateral triangle of side one mile anywhere; two of its vertices have the same colour and are one mile apart.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: With more colours the same three points no longer force a repeat, so a larger configuration is needed.

card.rule: Choose points that are all the required distance from each other, with more points than colours.
card.limits: The configuration must have all pairs at the required distance; with more colours you need more cleverness.

concepts.title: Partition into regions: five points in a square
concepts.question: How can cutting a unit square into four pieces show that two of five points are close?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To show that two points are close, cut the region into as many small pieces as you have pigeons minus one, and use the largest distance inside a piece.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a distance bound for points in a region by pigeonhole.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Five points go into four pieces, so two points share a piece. Two points in one piece are no farther apart than the piece's longest distance, its diagonal.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Cut a unit square into four small squares of side 1/2. Each has diagonal the square root of 2 over 2, so two of any five points are at most that far apart.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The bound depends on the cut. With only four points they can sit at the four corners of the big square, a full unit apart.

card.rule: Cut the region into one fewer piece than there are points, and bound the distance inside a piece.
card.limits: With as many pieces as points the principle gives nothing; choose pieces whose largest distance is small.

concepts.title: Remainders as holes: a difference divisible by n
concepts.question: Why must some two of n + 1 integers differ by a multiple of n?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To find two numbers whose difference is divisible by n, let the n remainders be the holes and the numbers the pigeons.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get divisibility results from counting, and build a tool for later problems.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Two integers with the same remainder on division by n differ by a multiple of n. With n + 1 integers and only n remainders, two must share a remainder.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Among any 8 integers, two differ by a multiple of 7: there are 7 remainders and 8 integers.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: The author calls this the penultimate step: the shared remainder is the real aim, and the pigeonhole principle supplies it.

card.rule: Among n + 1 integers, two share a remainder mod n, so their difference is a multiple of n.
card.limits: With only n integers the remainders may all differ, so the result needs n + 1 numbers.

concepts.title: Subsets as pigeons: equal sums
concepts.question: How does counting subsets against possible sums show that two subsets of ten two-digit numbers have equal sums?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To show two collections share a total, make the collections the pigeons and the possible totals the holes, then fix any unwanted overlap afterwards.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove that equal sums occur without finding them.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Ten distinct two-digit numbers have 1024 subsets. Their sums lie between 10 and 945, which is 936 values. There are more subsets than values, so two subsets share a sum.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If the two subsets A and B overlap, remove the elements they have in common from both. The sums stay equal, and the two sets are now disjoint.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Choose subsets as pigeons. Count the subsets. Count the possible sums. Compare. Repair the overlap by removing common elements.

card.rule: Subsets are the pigeons and sums are the holes; more subsets than sums forces a repeat.
card.limits: The principle gives subsets that may overlap, so a repair step is needed when disjoint subsets are required.

concepts.title: The intermediate pigeonhole principle
concepts.question: If p pigeons go into h holes, how many must the fullest hole contain at least?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: With p pigeons and h holes, at least one hole contains at least \(\lceil p/h \rceil\) pigeons.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a guaranteed crowd size, not just a guaranteed repeat.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The ceiling \(\lceil x \rceil\) means the smallest integer at least x, so \(\lceil \pi \rceil = 4\). Our reading: if every hole held fewer than \(\lceil p/h \rceil\) pigeons, the total could not reach p. The author tells you to work examples until you see why it is true.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A hundred people have birthdays in 12 months. Since \(100/12\) is about 8.3, rounding up gives 9: some month contains at least 9 of them.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The ceiling is a guarantee, not a prediction. The fullest hole may contain far more, and the principle does not say which hole it is.

card.rule: At least one hole has \(\lceil p/h \rceil\) or more pigeons; always round up.
card.limits: It gives a lower bound on the fullest hole and no information on which hole it is.

concepts.title: Numbers that hint at pigeonhole
concepts.question: Which pattern in the numbers of a problem should make you suspect the pigeonhole principle?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a count is one more than a multiple of the number of holes, suspect pigeonhole and compute the ceiling to see what it promises.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spot a pigeonhole approach early and see how well it matches the goal.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author notices that 41 is one more than 4 times 10 and that the ceiling of 41 over 10 is 5, the number of rooks sought. That match is encouraging, though it is not a solution.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Forty-one rooks sit on a 10 by 10 board and five rooks that do not attack one another are wanted. With 10 rows, \(\lceil 41/10 \rceil = 5\).

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A neat numerical match is only a hint. It suggests probing carefully; it does not do the proof.

card.rule: A count that is one past a multiple of the number of holes is a sign to try pigeonhole.
card.limits: Numbers can match by coincidence, so the hint must be followed by a real argument.

concepts.title: Use pigeonhole repeatedly: 41 rooks
concepts.question: How can applying pigeonhole again and again to the leftover rows find five rooks that do not attack?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Apply the pigeonhole principle once, remove the part you used, and apply it again to what remains, extracting more information each time.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Build several nested facts when one application is not enough.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each application finds a row that is crowded. Removing that row takes away at most 10 rooks, so the principle applies again to the rows left, with fewer rows and a smaller guaranteed number.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Forty-one rooks on a 10 by 10 board: some row has at least 5. Removing it leaves at least 31 rooks in 9 rows, so some row has at least 4. Then 21 in 8 gives 3, then 11 in 7 gives 2, then 1 in 6 gives 1.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Find a crowded row. Remove it (at most 10 rooks). Count what is left. Repeat with one fewer row. Stop after five rows with 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 rooks at least.

card.rule: Pigeonhole, remove the crowded row, pigeonhole again, until you have a row of each size.
card.limits: Remove a row's worst-case number of rooks, not the number you found, or the counts will be too big.

concepts.title: From crowded rows to non-attacking rooks
concepts.question: Once you know five rows with at least 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 rooks, how do you choose the five rooks?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: After pigeonholing, build the object by taking the rows in increasing order of rooks: each row has a rook outside the columns already used.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn the pigeonhole information into an actual set of non-attacking rooks.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Two rooks attack only if they share a row or a column. The chosen rows are all different. A row with k rooks meets at most k - 1 columns already taken, so one of its rooks is in a new column.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take the rook from the row with at least 1 rook. In the row with at least 2, one rook avoids that column. In the row with at least 3, one avoids both columns used. Continue to the row with at least 5.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: If the rows are used in the wrong order, a row with few rooks may have all of them in columns already taken.

card.rule: Choose rooks from the rows in order of increasing rook count, picking one in a column not yet used.
card.limits: The order matters: starting with the crowded rows can leave the sparse rows with no free column.

concepts.title: Partial sums as pigeons
concepts.question: How do running totals make the differences of pigeons into sums of consecutive terms?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you need a sum of several given numbers to have a property, let the running totals be the pigeons, so that the difference of two pigeons is a sum of consecutive terms.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Create enough pigeons, and pigeons of the right kind, when the numbers themselves are too few or give the wrong differences.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: With numbers a1, a2, ..., an, let Pk = a1 + ... + ak. For i less than j, Pj - Pi = a(i+1) + ... + aj, a sum of several of the original numbers. Two running totals with the same remainder give such a sum divisible by n.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take the integers 6, 6, 9, 3, 9, with n = 5. The running totals 6, 12, 21, 24, 33 leave remainders 1, 2, 1, 4, 3. The first and third match, so 6 + 9 = 15 is a multiple of 5.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: In Chapter 3's earlier remainder problem the pigeons were the given numbers themselves; here they are the totals built from them.

card.rule: Let the running totals be the pigeons; the difference of two is a sum of consecutive given terms.
card.limits: With n numbers there are only n running totals, so another idea is needed to force a repeat of a remainder.

media.alt: Start of a column of displayed equations: p1 equals a1, comma; p2 equals a1 plus a2, comma; a vertical ellipsis; then an equals sign with the right side missing. They define running totals of a list of numbers.

concepts.title: Reduce the holes by splitting into cases
concepts.question: How does a case split give the n running totals one fewer hole to fall into?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you have n pigeons for n holes, split into cases: in one case you are done at once, and in the other a hole is removed, so a repeat is forced.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Rescue a pigeonhole argument when the pigeons only just fail to outnumber the holes.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: For n integers with running totals P1, ..., Pn, either some Pk leaves remainder 0 mod n, which is already a sum of several of the integers, or none does. Then the n totals fall into n - 1 non-zero remainders, so two share one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author's problem: among n integers, one is a multiple of n or some sum of several of them is. Case one: a total is divisible by n. Case two: no total is, so n totals and n - 1 holes.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The split works because one case ends the proof. If neither case is easy, the count is not rescued.

card.rule: Remove a hole by splitting off the case that finishes by itself, and apply pigeonhole to the rest.
card.limits: The saved case must really finish the argument, otherwise the split gains nothing.

concepts.title: Erdos's problem: the difficulty is in the holes
concepts.question: How do odd parts define pigeonholes so that two of n + 1 chosen numbers divide each other?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To force one number to divide another, make each hole a family of numbers with the same odd part, so any two in a hole divide one another.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove a divisibility fact by a clever choice of holes rather than of pigeons.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Every number from 1 to 2n can be written 2^r times an odd number q. Numbers with the same q form a hole, and in a hole the one with the smaller power of 2 divides the other. There are n odd numbers up to 2n, hence n holes.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For n = 100 and q = 11, the hole is 11, 22, 44, 88, 176. Choosing 101 numbers from 1 to 200 places two in one hole, and one divides the other.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: With only n chosen numbers they can sit one per hole, so the claim needs n + 1 numbers.

card.rule: Put numbers with the same odd part in the same hole; n holes force a divisor pair among n + 1 numbers.
card.limits: The bound n + 1 cannot be lowered: taking the numbers n + 1 to 2n avoids any divisor pair.

concepts.title: Design the holes backward from what you need
concepts.question: How can small cases and the property you want help you invent suitable pigeonholes?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Decide what property two numbers in the same hole must have, then experiment with small cases to build holes with that property.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a partition when no obvious pigeonholes are available.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the divisor problem each hole must be a family in which any two members divide one another. Such a family has a smallest element, so you pick seeds and multiply them up to cover everything.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For n = 5, take the seeds 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and keep doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8; then 3, 6; then 5, 10; then 7; then 9. These five families cover 1 to 10.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: State the property a hole needs. Try n = 5. Choose seeds. Multiply seeds by a fixed factor. Check all numbers are covered.

card.rule: State the property a hole must give, find seeds in a small case, then generalise the partition.
card.limits: A property that is too strong may allow no partition into few enough holes.

media.alt: Displayed inequality: zero is less than a plus b times the square root of 2, which is at most the fraction with numerator 1 plus the square root of 2 and denominator m plus 2, followed by a full stop.

concepts.title: Define a function, then pigeonhole its values
concepts.question: How can a function defined from the data turn a matrix problem into a pigeonhole problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If a family of objects depends on a parameter, define a function of the parameter, and use pigeonhole on its few possible values.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Convert a problem about many objects into one about a polynomial with few possible values.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: An integer matrix whose inverse also has integer entries has determinant 1 or -1. For 2 by 2 integer matrices A and B, f(t) = det(A + tB) is a quadratic polynomial with integer coefficients. If it takes only the values 1 and -1 at five inputs, some value repeats three times.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If f takes the same value at three different inputs, a quadratic polynomial must be constant. Then f(5) = 1 as well, so A + 5B is invertible with an integer inverse.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Find what values the objects force. Define the function. Count inputs against values. Pigeonhole. Conclude the function is constant.

card.rule: Define a function of the parameter, show it has few possible values, and pigeonhole to a constant.
card.limits: A quadratic that takes one value at three inputs must be constant; pigeonhole alone gives only the repeats.

concepts.title: Pigeonhole with area: a region that covers lattice points
concepts.question: How can stacking the pieces of a region on one unit square show it can cover n + 1 lattice points?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If a region has area greater than the whole number n, cut it into pieces on lattice squares and stack them on one unit square; some point lies under n + 1 pieces.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn an infinite pigeonhole problem, about points of a square, into an area argument.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Stack the pieces on a single unit square. If no point lay under n + 1 pieces, the total area would be at most n. The area exceeds n, so some point is under at least n + 1 pieces. Rebuilding the region and translating it puts those points on lattice points.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A region of area 1.36 sliced along the lattice lines gives five pieces. Stacked, a point lies under two of them. Slide the region so both of the corresponding points sit on lattice points.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: Cut the region along the lattice lines. Stack the pieces on one unit square. Find a point under n + 1 pieces. Rebuild the region and translate it so those points are lattice points.

card.rule: Region of area greater than n: stack its lattice pieces; a point under n + 1 pieces gives a translation covering n + 1 lattice points.
card.limits: The area must be greater than n; area exactly n does not force n + 1 lattice points.

concepts.title: Invariants: what stays the same
concepts.question: What is an invariant, and why does focusing on one help when many other things change?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look for an aspect of the problem, usually a number, that does not change while other properties do, and reason from it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reduce a messy, changing situation to one narrow aspect that holds still.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, invariants share the strategy of the extreme principle: extract key information from the chaos a problem first presents. A fixed quantity gives a fact true at every stage, however the rest evolves.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the motel room paradox, g - p - d is always zero, where g is what the guests spent, p what the porter pocketed and d what the desk received. For a polyhedron without holes, v - e + f is always 2.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: many quantities are invariant yet irrelevant to the question. Which one to use must be found by trying, not read off a recipe.

card.rule: Find a quantity that stays the same while other things change, and reason from it.
card.limits: An invariant helps only if it connects to what you must show; the formula for solids needs the solid to have no holes.

concepts.title: Symmetry is a kind of invariant
concepts.question: How is symmetry a kind of invariant, and what does the substitution u = x + 1/x have to do with it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: See a symmetry as an invariance: an object unchanged by a set of transformations, or a quantity unchanged when some roots are swapped.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Connect the first section of the chapter to the idea of invariants.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says symmetry is logically contained within invariants: a symmetric object is one that is unchanged by some transformations. The substitution u = x + 1/x worked because u is unchanged when some of the roots are permuted.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A square is invariant under rotations about its centre of 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees.

card.rule: A symmetry is an invariance under a set of transformations.
card.limits: Seeing symmetry as invariance adds no new technique; it only names what is conserved.

concepts.title: A divisibility invariant: n minus its digit sum
concepts.question: What does n minus the sum of its digits always leave on division by 9?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a quantity always leaves the same remainder on division by m, treat that remainder as an invariant.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Recast a property of numbers as a fixed fact you can use.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Let s(n) be the sum of the digits of n. Then n - s(n) is always divisible by 9. The author calls this a non-numeric invariant, but it can be recast numerically: the remainder of n - s(n) on division by 9 is always zero.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For n = 136, s(n) = 10 and n - s(n) = 126 = 9 times 14.

card.rule: n - s(n) is divisible by 9 for every positive integer n.
card.limits: The fact concerns division by 9 only; it says nothing about divisors such as 7 or 11.

concepts.title: Totals that share a remainder
concepts.question: If each step adds 1 or subtracts 2, what do all totals reachable at a given time share?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the possible changes at each step differ from one another by multiples of m, then all totals possible at a fixed time differ by multiples of m.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Rule out a target total by comparing remainders.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: From n people, one minute gives n + 1 or n - 2, which differ by 3. Over longer times any two possible totals still differ by a multiple of 3, so one reachable total fixes the remainder for all.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A room starts empty; each minute one person enters or two leave. After 3 to the power 1999 minutes, every reachable population is a multiple of 3, so 3 to the power 1000 plus 2 is not a valid population.

card.rule: Pick one reachable total, then rule out any target with a different remainder.
card.limits: Sharing the remainder rules targets out; it does not show a target with that remainder can be reached.

concepts.title: Parity: even or odd is often enough
concepts.question: When a problem involves integers, what can knowing only even or odd tell you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Sort integers into even and odd, and ask whether parity restricts the problem; experiment with other values if needed.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reduce an infinite set of integers to two classes when evenness or oddness is all the problem needs.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A sum is odd exactly when it has an odd number of odd terms. A product is odd exactly when it has no even factor. Zero counts as even.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The sum 3 + 5 + 8 + 11 + 14 has three odd terms, so it is odd; it equals 41.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: parity is crude. If the problem involves a quantity such as divisibility by 3, two classes cannot capture it.

card.rule: Ask of every integer problem whether even or odd restricts what can happen.
card.limits: Parity gives only two classes; when a problem is about 3, 5 or other moduli, a finer invariant is needed.

concepts.title: Counting twice: the number of odd counts is even
concepts.question: In any tournament or party, why must the number of people with an odd count be even?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If every event involves exactly two parties, add the per-party counts; the sum counts each event twice, so it is even.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show that the number of parties with an odd count is even, whatever the structure.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The problem fixes no structure, so the argument must work for every tournament. Each game has two players, so the sum of everyone's game counts counts every game twice and is even. A sum of 127 numbers is even only if an even number of them are odd.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Among 127 tennis players, the number who played an odd number of games is even; with no games played, it is zero.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Experiment with extreme structures, such as no games at all, to see that the claim is plausible.

card.rule: Two parties per event makes the total count even, so an even number of parties have odd counts.
card.limits: The count of two per event is essential; events that involve three parties break the evenness.

concepts.title: A product is even when a sum is zero
concepts.question: Why is the product (a1 - 1)(a2 - 2)...(an - n) even when n is odd?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To show a product is even, show one factor is even; the factors may sum to zero, which forces an even factor among an odd number of terms.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Settle a parity claim about a product by an argument that works for every arrangement.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Assume all n factors are odd. Then the sum of n odd numbers is odd for odd n. But the sum is (a1 + ... + an) - (1 + ... + n) = 0 for every arrangement, which is even, a contradiction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For n = 3 and the arrangement 2, 3, 1, the factors are 1, 1 and -2, which sum to 0, and the product is -2, which is even.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: For even n the claim is false: with n = 2 and the arrangement 2, 1, the product is 1 times -1 = -1.

card.rule: Make the factors sum to zero; an odd count of odd integers cannot sum to an even number.
card.limits: Odd n is required; for even n some arrangements give an odd product.

concepts.title: Alternating sides around a closed chain
concepts.question: Why can one line cross every segment of a closed chain of points only if the number of points is even?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a line crosses a segment, its endpoints lie on opposite sides; around a closed chain of n points the sides alternate, so n must be even.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Rule out a configuration by following a two-valued state around a loop.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Assume a line L crosses the interior of each segment P1P2, P2P3, ..., PnP1. Starting with P1 on the left, P2 is on the right, P3 on the left, and so on. For odd n, Pn is on the left like P1, so L cannot cross the segment PnP1.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With 7 points: P1 left, P2 right, P3 left, P4 right, P5 left, P6 right, P7 left; P7 and P1 are on the same side, so there is a contradiction.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Experiment with small numbers of points first to see which counts work.

card.rule: Follow the left-right state around the loop; an odd loop forces the start and end onto the same side.
card.limits: A contradiction arises only for an odd number of points; an even number allows the line.
