Seven points P1 to P7 joined by solid zigzag segments P1P2, P2P3 and so on to P6P7, each crossing a thick slanted line. P1, P3, P5 and P7 lie in the shaded region left of the line; P2, P4 and P6 lie right of it. A dotted segment joins P1 to P7.

concepts.title: Parity patterns of exponents as pigeonholes
concepts.question: How do parity patterns of prime exponents make two numbers multiply to a perfect square?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Record, for each number, the parity of every prime exponent; two numbers with the same parity pattern have a perfect-square product.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a product-is-a-square condition into a pigeonhole count of patterns.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A product of two numbers is a perfect square exactly when every prime has the same exponent parity in both. With 9 primes up to 23, each number gets a 9-tuple of parities, and there are 2 to the ninth, or 512, possible 9-tuples.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 12 = 2^2 times 3 and 27 = 3^3 have the same pattern for the primes 2 and 3, and 12 times 27 = 324 = 18 squared.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: This is the same pigeonhole idea as remainders: the patterns are the holes, and the numbers are the pigeons.

card.rule: Same parity pattern means the product is a perfect square; patterns are the pigeonholes.
card.limits: Two numbers give a square, not a fourth power; a further step is needed for fourth powers.

concepts.title: Counting lattice corners (Gnepp's tiling)
concepts.question: Why must a rectangle tiled by rectangles with an integer side also have an integer side?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Anchor the big rectangle's lower-left corner at a lattice point, so having an integral side means having an even number of lattice-point corners.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Convert a hard geometric condition into a parity count that adds up over the tiles.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A small rectangle has 0, 2 or 4 lattice corners, never 1 or 3, because it has an integral side. So the total S over all small rectangles is even. Counting the same corners by multiplicity gives S = w + 2g + 4b, so w = S - 2g - 4b is even, and w is the number of lattice corners of the big rectangle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the book's example, 10 small rectangles have 2 lattice corners each, so S = 20 = 1 times 2 + 2 times 7 + 4 times 1.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the argument needs every small rectangle to have an integral side; with one bad tile, S can be odd.

card.rule: Count lattice-point corners two ways: by tile (even total) and by corner multiplicity (w + 2g + 4b).
card.limits: Every tile must have an integral side, and the big rectangle must be placed with a corner on a lattice point.

media.alt: A rectangle 4 units wide and 2.5 tall cut into many small rectangles, drawn over a dotted unit lattice with its bottom-left corner on a lattice point. Eight filled circles mark lattice points at interior or side corners; two open circles mark the big rectangle's bottom corners.

concepts.title: Reduce to remainders modulo m
concepts.question: Why does a number leave the same remainder on division by 9 as its digit sum?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Reduce the infinite set of integers to the finite set of remainders modulo m, choosing m cleverly, and look for an invariant there.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove and use divisibility facts that parity is too crude to capture.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Since 10 is congruent to 1 modulo 9, 10 to the k is congruent to 1 for every nonnegative integer k. So n = 1000a + 100b + 10c + d is congruent to a + b + c + d modulo 9.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For 7384 the digit sum is 22, and both 7384 and 22 leave remainder 4 on division by 9.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the shortcut depends on 10 being congruent to 1; modulo 11, 10 is congruent to -1, and the digit sum alone gives the wrong remainder.

card.rule: Replace each number by its remainder modulo a well-chosen m, and track that.
card.limits: A modulus must be chosen to fit the problem; the digit-sum fact works for 9 and 3 because 10 is congruent to 1.

concepts.title: Population gaps modulo 3
concepts.question: How can population gaps that look chaotic be invariant modulo 3?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When counts change by amounts that differ by a multiple of m, the gaps between counts are invariant modulo m.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show a final configuration with some counts at zero cannot happen.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the bubble chamber with populations (x, y, z), an X-Z collision gives (x - 1, y + 2, z - 1). The X-Z gap is unchanged, and the X-Y and Z-Y gaps change by 3. So all gaps stay the same modulo 3.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Start with (10, 11, 111). The X-Y gap is 1, so it is always congruent to 1 modulo 3, so X and Y can never both reach zero. The same holds for the other pairs.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Experiment with a few collisions and record the gaps before guessing the modulus.

card.rule: Track the gaps between populations modulo 3; a gap that is not 0 modulo 3 can never close.
card.limits: A gap that is 0 modulo 3 is not ruled out by the invariant, and does not show the final state can be reached.

concepts.title: Colouring squares to rule out a tiling
concepts.question: How does a 12-colour pattern show that a 66 by 62 rectangle cannot be tiled by 12 by 1 strips?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Colour the squares so that every tile covers each colour once; a tiling then forces equal numbers of each colour.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove a tiling is impossible when the area test passes.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Colour cyclically along diagonals with 12 colours. Any 12 by 1 strip holds all 12 colours once, so a tiled region must be homogeneous, with each colour appearing equally often. Cutting 66 by 62 into 60 by 60, 60 by 2, 6 by 60 and 6 by 2 pieces, the first three have a side divisible by 12 and are homogeneous. The 6 by 2 piece is not.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The area 66 times 62 is 4092 = 12 times 341, so the area test passes, yet no tiling exists.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Experiment with smaller rectangles whose area is divisible by 12 but whose sides are not.

card.rule: Colour so every tile is balanced, then show the region is not.
card.limits: The area test is necessary only; the colouring argument needs a colouring that every tile balances.

A rectangle cut by one vertical and one horizontal line into four sub-rectangles: a big one at top left, a tall narrow one along the right, a short wide strip along the bottom, and a small one in the bottom-right corner. No lengths are marked.

concepts.title: Choosing the modulus
concepts.question: How do you decide which modulus or how many colours to use?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose the modulus so that the possible changes agree, or the number of colours to match the tile's length.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pick the finite world, 2, 3, 9, 12 or another number, in which the problem's invariant becomes visible.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A step that adds 1 or subtracts 2 changes totals by amounts that agree modulo 3, so 3 is the modulus. A 12 by 1 strip covers 12 colours, so 12 colours is the choice. Parity, with two values, is the crudest case.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Digit sums use 9, the room puzzle uses 3, and the tiling uses 12 colours.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: a poorly chosen modulus shows no obstruction; mod 2 does not separate adding 1 from subtracting 2 in the room puzzle.

card.rule: Pick m so that the allowed changes agree modulo m.
card.limits: No modulus is guaranteed to work; the right one comes from the problem's step sizes or tile sizes.

concepts.title: Monovariants: change in one direction only
concepts.question: What is a monovariant, and how does it count the games in an elimination tournament?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Find a quantity that may or may not change at each step, but when it changes does so in only one direction.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Analyse an evolving system by tracking one quantity that moves one way.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Because the quantity never reverses, its value at any time bounds what can have happened before or can happen next.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In an elimination tournament of n contestants, the number of people left drops by one with each game. It starts at n and ends at 1, so exactly n - 1 games are played.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: a quantity that sometimes rises and sometimes falls, such as the first card of a deck in the card problem, is not a monovariant.

card.rule: Track a quantity that moves in one direction only, and use where it starts and ends.
card.limits: The quantity must be monotone at every step; the argument says nothing if it can move both ways.

concepts.title: Card reversal: extreme value plus monovariant
concepts.question: Why does reversing the top k cards eventually put card 1 on top?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the extreme principle to pick the largest first-place value L1 that ever occurs; after it first occurs, the first card stays below L1.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove a process halts although the quantity you watch goes up and down.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The first-place number can repeat, so it is not itself monotone. After L1 reaches the top, the first L1 cards are reversed, placing L1 in the L1-th place; no later reversal is long enough to move it, and it cannot return to the top. The next largest value L2 is smaller, and so on.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the argument needs a finite deck, so that a largest first-place value exists.

card.rule: The successive largest first-place values form a strictly decreasing sequence, ending at 1.
card.limits: A largest value L must exist, which requires finitely many possible states; the top card alone does not decrease.

concepts.title: Finitely many states: repeat or halt
concepts.question: If a system has finitely many states, what must happen as it evolves?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If there are only finitely many states as something evolves, either a state will repeat or the evolution will eventually halt.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reduce a question about an endless process to the exclusion of repeats.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each step moves to a state; with finitely many available, a long enough run must revisit one unless it stops. To prove halting you must then rule out repeats, for instance by the extreme principle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the card problem the first-place numbers lie between 1 and n, so they either repeat or reach 1.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: With infinitely many possible states, a run need neither repeat nor halt.

card.rule: Finite states mean repeat or halt; rule out the repeat to show halting.
card.limits: The principle does not decide which of the two happens, and needs finitely many states.

concepts.title: Conway's checkers: a weighted sum as monovariant
concepts.question: How can weights on lattice points make a sum that never increases when checkers jump?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Give each position a weight so that moves toward the goal leave a total unchanged and moves away decrease it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show a target position can never be reached, by comparing the total at the start with the total if the target were occupied.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Let s = (-1 + sqrt 5)/2, so s squared plus s equals 1. A checker at distance d from the target C has weight s to the power d. A jump toward C removes weights s^d and s^(d-1) and adds s^(d-2); the net change is s^(d-2) times (1 - s - s squared), which is 0. A jump away from C lowers the sum.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The starting checkers fill the rows y at most 0 and have Conway sum 1. A checker on C alone would give weight 1, and the other checkers add a positive amount, so the sum would exceed 1.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: This is the same shape as the room puzzle: an inequality or a value fixed at the start rules out the target.

card.rule: Weight positions by s^distance; the sum starts at 1, never increases, but occupying C would force it above 1.
card.limits: The weights are tuned to one target row; for a nearer target the starting sum exceeds 1 and the argument shows nothing.

media.alt: Two groups of grey discs on a white page: on the left a block of eight discs in two rows of four; on the right a taller block of fifteen discs with a gap in the third column's upper two places and one disc sitting above the gap.

Eight grey discs on a dotted lattice, four in an upper row and four in a lower row. The four upper discs and the third lower disc have thick outlines; the other three lower discs are faint. A thick arrow leaves the third lower disc and curves up between the second and third upper discs to a point above the top row.

Part of a displayed algebra line from the Conway checkers calculation: a fraction with the book's curly weight symbol raised to the fifth power, plus two times a fraction with that symbol to the power five plus r, then an equals sign and one over one minus the symbol, times a bracket holding the fifth power times one minus the symbol plus two times the sixth power.

A tiny fragment of a displayed fraction from the checkers calculation: a plus sign above a horizontal fraction bar, with the book's curly weight symbol raised to the fourth power written below the bar.

concepts.title: Choosing and using a monovariant
concepts.question: What makes a quantity a usable monovariant, and what can it prove?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look for a quantity that moves one way each step, and use its start, its end or its bound.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Choose between a monovariant that shows a process stops and one that shows a target is unreachable.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If the quantity moves in steps of at least 1 and is bounded, the process halts. If it never increases and the target needs a bigger value than the start, the target cannot be reached.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The player count in a tournament moves down by 1; the Conway sum never increases.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A quantity that decreases by ever smaller amounts need not reach any final value.

card.rule: A bounded quantity moving in steps of at least 1 shows halting; a never-increasing quantity shows a larger value is unreachable.
card.limits: A real-valued quantity decreasing by shrinking amounts proves nothing about halting.

concepts.title: Graphs, neighbors and multigraphs
concepts.question: What do vertex, edge, neighbor, loop and multigraph mean?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A graph is a finite collection of vertices (dots) and edges (lines joining some pairs of vertices). Two vertices joined by an edge are neighbors. By the book's convention a graph has no multiple edges (two or more edges between the same pair) and no loops (an edge from a vertex to itself). If either appears, the object is called a multigraph.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book fixes the convention so that statements about graphs stay clean. Because every edge joins two different vertices, each edge is counted once at each of its two ends, which is why the book can state that the degrees of all vertices add up to twice the number of edges. Our reading: a loop or a repeated edge breaks this plain picture, since a loop touches only one vertex, so the book gives such objects a separate name, multigraph, rather than letting them blur the statements made for graphs.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Every later idea about degrees, paths and cycles is stated for these dots and lines, so the words must be exact: an edge always joins two different vertices, and each pair is joined at most once.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Four students, with a line between two students who study together. If Ana and Bo are joined once, it is a graph. A second Ana-Bo line, or a line from Ana to herself, would make it a multigraph.

card.rule: A graph is vertices and edges with no loops and no repeated edges; with either it is a multigraph.
card.limits: The no-loops, no-repeats rule is this book's convention. Once a loop or a repeated edge appears, the object is a multigraph, and a statement made for graphs need not carry over.

media.alt: Two small graphs side by side. Each has four dots at the corners of a square, the four sides, and one diagonal from top left to bottom right. The right-hand graph also has a curved edge bowing out beside its right side, giving a second edge between the two right-hand dots, so it has six edges and the left graph five.
A bipartite graph: four dots stacked in a left column and three dots in a right column. Every left dot is joined by a straight edge to every right dot, giving twelve edges that cross in the middle.

A bipartite graph with four dots in a left column and three in a right column, with only some left-to-right edges, six in all. The top right dot has three edges, the bottom right dot has two, and the middle right dot has one.

concepts.title: Recasting a problem as a graph
concepts.question: How do you turn a problem about people or things into a problem about dots and lines?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Any situation with objects and relationships between them can be recast as a graph. Each object becomes a vertex, and two vertices are joined by an edge when the corresponding objects are related.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The graph keeps only who is related to whom. Handshakes, networks of pipes and colouring puzzles then become the same kind of problem, so one set of tools serves many settings.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the handshake problem the people are vertices and each handshake is an edge. A room where every pair has shaken hands once gives a graph with one edge per pair of people.

blocks.label: Common slip
blocks.text: The hard step is deciding what the vertices and edges are. The obvious objects are not always the useful ones.

card.rule: Objects become vertices; join two vertices when their objects are related.
card.limits: The recasting helps only if the chosen relation carries what the question asks. A poor choice of vertices or edges can leave the problem as hard as before or lose the question.

media.alt: A domino drawn as a rectangle split into two squares by a vertical line. The left square holds one dot in its centre and the right square holds three dots along a diagonal.

concepts.title: The sleeping mathematicians as a graph
concepts.question: When five mathematicians each nap twice and every pair overlaps, what are the vertices and the edges?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: During a lecture each of five mathematicians sleeps exactly twice, and every two mathematicians are asleep at the same moment at some time. Prove that at some moment three are asleep together (USAMO 1986). The graph has one vertex for each nap interval, ten in all, and an edge between two naps that overlap.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The ten pairs of mathematicians each give an overlapping pair of naps, so the graph has at least ten edges. Two naps of one mathematician are separate, so they are never joined.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Suppose the overlaps give a loop of four naps: C1 meets A1, A1 meets E2, E2 meets B2 and B2 meets C1. Stack the intervals in time. If B2 and A1 do not meet inside C1, a gap separates them, and E2 must stretch across that gap. Then C1, B2 and E2 overlap, or C1, E2 and A1 do.

card.rule: Make the naps the vertices and join overlapping naps; a closed loop of overlaps forces three naps to overlap.
card.limits: Only a closed loop forces the triple overlap. A chain of overlaps that never closes does not: the first and last naps in the chain may miss each other.

media.alt: Graph on ten dots labelled A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2, D1, D2, E1, E2, two naps for each of five mathematicians. Its ten edges join A1 to E2, A1 to C1, A2 to B2, A2 to D1, B1 to D1, B2 to E2, B2 to C1, C2 to D1, C2 to E1 and D2 to E1. A closed loop runs C1, A1, E2, B2 and back to C1.

Five horizontal bars stacked, time running left to right, labelled top to bottom C1, B2, E2, A1 and C1 again, the first and last being the same long interval. B2 starts left of C1 and ends under it. E2 lies entirely within C1's span and overlaps both B2 and A1. A1 starts later and ends beyond C1's right end. B2 and A1 do not overlap.

concepts.title: Degree and the handshake lemma
concepts.question: How does the total of all vertex degrees relate to the number of edges?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The degree of a vertex x, written \(d(x)\), is the number of edges coming out of it. Handshake lemma: in any graph, the sum of the degrees of all vertices equals twice the number of edges.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each edge has two ends. It adds one to the degree of each end, so adding up all degrees counts every edge exactly twice.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A graph has 5 vertices with degrees 1, 2, 2, 3, 4. The degrees add to 12, so it has 6 edges. Check: each of the 6 edges was counted at both of its ends.

card.rule: The degree sum is \(2e\), where \(e\) is the number of edges.
card.limits: The lemma counts degrees, not vertices, and it needs an actual graph. A list of degrees whose sum is odd cannot come from any graph.

media.alt: A graph with ten dots and eleven edges in two separate pieces. One piece has four dots: a triangle with a fourth dot hanging off one corner. The other has six dots: two triangles sharing an edge, with one extra dot hanging off each of two corners. Three dots have one edge, three have two, three have three, one has four.

concepts.title: Connected graphs, cycles, trees and forests
concepts.question: What makes a graph connected, and what turns a connected graph into a tree?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A graph is connected if every pair of vertices has a path between them. A graph that is not connected falls apart into connected components. A cycle is a closed path that travels along edges. A tree is a connected graph that contains no cycles.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book argues that a tree is poor in edges. Take a longest path in a tree: if its end vertex had a second neighbour, that neighbour would either lie on the path, which creates a cycle, or extend the path, which contradicts that it is longest. So the ends have degree 1, and every tree with two or more vertices has at least two leaves. Removing a leaf and its edge leaves a graph that is still connected and still has no cycle, so induction on the number of vertices shows that a tree with v vertices has exactly \(v - 1\) edges. Connectedness is what guarantees the paths exist and cycle-freeness is what stops them folding back, which is why both conditions are needed.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Connectedness and cycles are the two properties the rest of the section counts against vertices and edges.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Five vertices in a line, joined one after the other, form a tree. Join the last vertex back to the first and a cycle appears, so it is no longer a tree. Two separate lines are not connected, so neither combination is a tree.

card.rule: A tree is a graph that is both connected and cycle-free.
card.limits: Both conditions are needed. A connected graph with a cycle is not a tree, and a cycle-free graph in several pieces is not a tree either.

media.alt: A tree with eight dots. A leftmost dot is joined to a branching dot, which splits into an upper and a lower branching dot, and each of those has two further dots as its ends. It has seven edges and five end dots, each of which touches just one edge.

concepts.title: Every tree has at least two leaves
concepts.question: Why must every tree with two or more vertices have at least two vertices of degree 1?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A leaf is a vertex of degree 1 in a tree. Every tree with two or more vertices has at least two leaves.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Look at a longest path in the tree, \(x_1 x_2 \ldots x_n\). Suppose \(x_1\) had a second neighbor \(y\). Then \(y\) is not on the path, since that would close a cycle, and so \(y x_1 \ldots x_n\) is a longer path, which is impossible. So \(x_1\) has degree 1. The same argument gives \(x_n\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a path of five vertices the two ends are the leaves. In a star with one centre and four others, the four outer vertices are leaves.

card.rule: Both ends of a longest path in a tree are leaves, so a tree has at least two.
card.limits: Without the no-cycle property the proof breaks: the extra neighbor \(y\) could lie on the path. A ring of vertices, where every vertex has degree 2, has no leaves.

concepts.title: A tree has one fewer edge than vertices
concepts.question: How many edges does a tree with v vertices have, and how is it proved?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A tree with \(v\) vertices has exactly \(v - 1\) edges.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Induction on \(v\). For \(v = 2\) the tree is one edge. Assume every tree with \(v\) vertices has \(v - 1\) edges. Take a tree with \(v + 1\) vertices, pick a leaf (one exists) and remove it with its edge. What is left is a tree on v vertices, so it has v - 1 edges, and putting the leaf back gives v.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A tree with 8 vertices has 7 edges. Trees are poor in edges: a connected graph with more than \(v - 1\) edges has to contain a cycle.

card.rule: A tree on \(v\) vertices has \(v - 1\) edges.
card.limits: The count holds only for trees. A connected graph can have more edges, and a graph without connectedness can have fewer. The proof needs a leaf to exist, which is why the leaf theorem comes first.

concepts.title: Enough edges force a cycle
concepts.question: How many edges, compared with vertices, guarantee that a graph has a cycle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If a graph has \(e\) edges and \(v\) vertices with \(e \ge v\), then it contains a cycle. The graph need not be connected.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A graph with no cycles is a forest, and a tree on \(n\) vertices has \(n - 1\) edges. Adding over the components, a cycle-free graph has fewer edges than vertices. So \(e \ge v\) rules out cycle-free graphs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A graph with 10 vertices and 10 edges must contain a cycle. So must one with 7 vertices and 9 edges, even if it falls into several pieces.

card.rule: If \(e \ge v\), a cycle exists.
card.limits: The test is one-way. Fewer edges than vertices does not rule a cycle out: a triangle plus three isolated vertices has 6 vertices, 3 edges and a cycle.

concepts.title: Finishing the sleeping mathematicians
concepts.question: How do the edge count and the cycle criterion together finish the proof about the napping mathematicians?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The nap graph has 10 vertices and at least 10 edges. By the cycle criterion it contains a cycle, and a cycle of overlapping naps forces three naps to overlap at one moment. So at some moment three mathematicians are asleep together.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The recasting reduces the problem to a pure graph question: must a graph with 10 vertices and 10 edges contain a cycle? The answer is yes whether or not the graph is connected, so the overlap pattern cannot avoid a cycle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Six scientists each take exactly two shifts, and every two scientists have overlapping shifts. There are 12 shift vertices and at least \(\binom62 = 15\) edges, so a cycle exists and three shifts overlap.

card.rule: Count vertices and edges of the overlap graph; if edges are at least vertices, a cycle forces a triple overlap.
card.limits: The count must reach the vertex number. With more naps per person, the graph has more vertices while the number of required overlaps stays fixed, and the criterion no longer applies.

concepts.title: Odd-degree vertices and Eulerian paths
concepts.question: Why must an odd-degree vertex be the start or the end of any Eulerian path?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: An Eulerian path travels along a graph so that it uses every edge exactly once. Eulerian paths are named after Euler, the 18th-century mathematician who first studied graphs formally.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Look at a vertex v of odd degree. Each time the path passes through v it comes in along one edge and leaves along another, using two edges. With an odd number of edges, one edge is left over, so the path must begin or end at v.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Four junctions, each with three roads meeting (a square with both diagonals): all four have odd degree, so no walk can use every road once. A path of three vertices in a line has two odd vertices, its ends, and walking from one end to the other uses both edges.

card.rule: In an Eulerian path every vertex that is not the start or end has even degree, so odd vertices are the ends.
card.limits: This shows what is necessary, not that a path exists. Whether a graph with few odd vertices really has an Eulerian path, and what happens when the graph is disconnected, is the next idea.

media.alt: A rectangle made of two squares side by side, sharing a vertical middle side. The left square has both diagonals drawn, crossing at its centre, and the right square has none. Vertices are the corners and the crossing point. Exactly two vertices, the far-left corners, have odd degree, so this drawing can be traced once through every segment.

A rectangle crossed by two parallel diagonals. One runs from the top-left corner to a point on the bottom side, the other from a point on the top side to the bottom-right corner. Four vertices have odd degree: the top-left corner, the bottom-right corner, and the two points where a diagonal meets the top or bottom side.

concepts.title: Euler's condition for an Eulerian path
concepts.question: Which connected graphs have an Eulerian path, and where does the path start and end?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A connected graph (or multigraph) has an Eulerian path if and only if it has zero or exactly two vertices of odd degree. With zero odd vertices the path is closed. With two, it must begin and end at them.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Necessity is the parity argument: odd vertices can only be ends. Sufficiency is shown by an algorithm that builds the path, described in the next idea.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A ring of five vertices has all degrees 2, so a closed Eulerian path goes around once. A line of four vertices has two odd ends and the Eulerian path runs from one end to the other.

card.rule: Connected, with 0 or 2 odd-degree vertices, means an Eulerian path exists.
card.limits: Connectedness is required. Two separate triangles have only even degrees but no single path can use all six edges.

concepts.title: Building an Eulerian path step by step
concepts.question: How can you construct an Eulerian path in a connected graph with exactly two odd vertices?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In a connected graph with exactly two odd-degree vertices s and f, an Eulerian path from s to f can be built by a recipe. This algorithmic proof shows the path exists by constructing it.

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: 1. Start at s and travel along untraveled edges until stuck; the only place you can get stuck is f. 2. Remove the traveled edges. If edges remain, they form a subgraph with all degrees even that meets the path at some vertex u. 3. From u travel that subgraph until stuck; you can only stop back at u. 4. Splice this closed trip into the path at u. 5. Repeat while edges remain.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Entering an even-degree vertex always leaves an unused edge to leave by, unless the vertex is exhausted. The traveled path uses an even number of edges at every vertex except s and f, so the leftover degrees stay even, and the graph is finite.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Edges s-a, a-b, b-c, c-f and a triangle b-d, d-e, e-b. The walk s, a, b, c, f is stuck at f with the triangle unused. The triangle meets the walk at b, so splice it in: s, a, b, d, e, b, c, f.

card.rule: Travel until stuck, then splice closed trips of the leftover edges into the path.
card.limits: Travelling at random without the repair step can leave edges unused, so the repair is part of the method. The recipe also needs the graph to be connected, or the leftover edges may not touch the path.

media.alt: A connected multigraph with eight dots and edges lettered. A leftmost dot hangs off a vertex on the left side of a rectangular outline running along the top and bottom to the right side. A vertical edge joins the top and bottom of the outline, and three curved extra edges run beside the top-right, right and bottom-right. Vertex u, on the top edge, has four edges. Only two vertices have odd degree: the far-left dot and the left-side vertex with three edges.

A graph with eleven dots, ten of them on one horizontal line. Several circles centred on that line nest inside one another in two groups, with one small circle between the groups, each circle meeting the line at two dots. The eleventh dot sits on the lower right of the right-hand circle and is joined by a long arc swinging under the picture to the leftmost dot.

concepts.title: Hamiltonian paths and cycles
concepts.question: How does a Hamiltonian path differ from an Eulerian path?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A Hamiltonian path visits each vertex exactly once. If the path is closed it is a Hamiltonian cycle. It is the dual of an Eulerian path: vertices take the place of edges.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book calls the Hamiltonian path the dual of the Eulerian path, and the reason it is harder is that the Eulerian case has a complete theory, while for Hamiltonian paths the necessary and sufficient conditions are unknown. What the book does give is a weak sufficient condition: a graph (not a multigraph) on \(v\) vertices in which every vertex has degree at least \(v/2\) has a Hamiltonian cycle. It calls this weak because the hypothesis is so strong (50 vertices would need every degree at least 25). Our reading: the example below fails for a plain reason, because the centre is the only link among the outer vertices, so a path must pass through it twice.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Many practical problems are Hamiltonian-path searches. To seat people around a table so nobody sits beside someone disliked, make people vertices and join friends; a Hamiltonian cycle is a seating plan. Scheduling and network routes can also be recast this way.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Friends a-b, b-c, c-d, d-a form a cycle through all four, so they can sit around a table. A centre b joined to a, c, d has no Hamiltonian path: after visiting two of the outer vertices the path cannot reach the third without returning to b.

card.rule: Eulerian: every edge once. Hamiltonian: every vertex once.
card.limits: Existence of a Hamiltonian path must be settled graph by graph. The odd-degree test that settles Eulerian paths does not carry over.

concepts.title: A sufficient condition for a Hamiltonian cycle
concepts.question: If every vertex has high enough degree, does a Hamiltonian cycle exist?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(G\) be a graph (not a multigraph) with \(v\) vertices. If every vertex has degree at least \(v/2\), then \(G\) has a Hamiltonian cycle.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book leaves the proof to the reader. Its first hint: the degree hypothesis forces G to be connected, since no vertex can be cut off from the rest.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A graph with 6 vertices where every vertex has degree at least 3 has a Hamiltonian cycle. With 50 vertices, every vertex would need degree at least 25.

card.rule: Every degree at least \(v/2\) guarantees a Hamiltonian cycle.
card.limits: The condition is sufficient, not necessary. The book calls it weak because the hypothesis is so strong: a 50-vertex ring has a Hamiltonian cycle with every degree equal to 2.

concepts.title: Recasting the Two Men of Tibet
concepts.question: How can the Two Men of Tibet be turned into a question about paths in a graph?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Two men stand at opposite ends of a mountain range, at the same elevation, and the range never drops below that elevation. Can they walk, backward steps allowed, always at the same elevation, until each reaches the other's starting place?

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Label the interesting locations, those at the elevations of peaks and troughs, and call the set I. A configuration is an ordered pair (x, y) of locations in I at the same elevation. Make each configuration a vertex of a graph, and join two when the men can move from one to the other in one step. A walk of both men is a path in this graph.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A range with one hill: left foot L, peak P, right foot R, feet at the start elevation. From (L, R) both men climb to (P, P), then descend to (R, L). That path swaps their places.

card.rule: Let vertices be equal-height pairs of positions; look for a path from start to swapped positions.
card.limits: The graph also contains configurations the men can never reach. The question is not whether the graph is connected, but whether a path joins the start to the swapped configuration.

media.alt: A side view of a jagged mountain range drawn as a zigzag line over a flat ground line. A filled dot marks the left foot and an open dot the right foot, both at ground level. The line has four peaks, the second tallest of all, separated by three valleys, and never drops below ground level.

concepts.title: Counting degrees in the Tibet graph
concepts.question: Which vertices of the Tibet configuration graph have odd degree?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In the configuration graph, the start pair and the swapped pair are the only vertices of degree 1. Every other vertex has degree 0, 2 or 4: a (peak, peak) pair has degree 4, a (peak, slope) or (slope, slope) pair has degree 2, and a (peak, trough) pair has degree 0 (isolated).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The degree counts joint one-step moves that keep the men level. Each man steps to the next interesting location up or down his side, and both must land at the same height.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Both men on peaks at one height: each can step down either side, giving \(2 \cdot 2 = 4\) moves. A man on a peak with the other on a slope: the peak man must go down (2 ways), so the slope man must go down (1 way): 2 moves. A man on a peak with the other in a trough: one must go down and the other up, so no joint move exists.

card.rule: Only the start and swapped pairs have odd degree; every other vertex has degree 0, 2 or 4.
card.limits: The facts rely on the book's assumption that the range never drops below the starting elevation. They describe which pairs are legal moves, not a path.

media.alt: The jagged mountain range with its peaks, valleys and other points labelled by letters, from a at the filled left foot to s at the open right foot. Dashed horizontal lines join points of equal height, linking positions on one side of the range with positions on the other at the heights of the peaks and valleys.

concepts.title: Parity finishes the Tibet proof
concepts.question: How does the handshake lemma show that the men can swap places?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Look at the connected component of the configuration graph that contains the start pair. By the handshake lemma, the degrees in that component add to an even number. Only the start pair and the swapped pair have odd degree anywhere, so the swapped pair must be in the same component. That gives a path from start to swapped pair, so the men can swap.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A part of a graph cannot contain exactly one vertex of odd degree, because degrees would then add to an odd number, which twice the number of edges never is.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The component of the start pair has degrees 1, 2, 4, 2, 2 and one more odd vertex. That vertex must be the swapped pair, since the start pair is the only other vertex of degree 1.

card.rule: A component with exactly one odd vertex is impossible, so the start's component also contains the swapped pair.
card.limits: The argument uses the component of the start, not the whole graph, which has isolated vertices. It also needs the facts about degrees, which hold only when the range never drops below the start.

concepts.title: A complex number as a point and a vector
concepts.question: In what two ways can the complex number \(a + bi\) be pictured on the plane?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A complex number is \(z = a + bi\) with \(a, b\) real and \(i^2 = -1\). In the Gaussian (Argand) plane the horizontal axis is the real axis and the vertical axis is the imaginary axis. The number \(z\) is the point \((a, b)\) and also the vector from the origin to \((a, b)\). Its real part is \(\mathrm{Re}\,z = a\) and its imaginary part is \(\mathrm{Im}\,z = b\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book gets the two pictures from how the numbers behave. Complex numbers add componentwise, \((a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i\), which is exactly how the vectors \((a, b)\) and \((c, d)\) add, and the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram (the parallelogram rule). All other algebra follows the usual rules with \(i^2 = -1\). So the pair of real numbers \((a, b)\) carries the whole number, and reading it as a point or as an arrow from the origin is only a change of view.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Complex numbers are both algebraic and geometric. Being able to switch between the two pictures lets a geometry problem be solved by algebra and an algebra problem by drawing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The number \(3 - 2i\) is the point \((3, -2)\). Its real part is 3 and its imaginary part is \(-2\), a real number, not \(-2i\).

blocks.label: Common slip
blocks.text: Writing \(\mathrm{Im}\,z = bi\). The imaginary part is the real number \(b\).

card.rule: Read \(a + bi\) as the point \((a, b)\) or the vector from the origin to it.
card.limits: A point and a vector are two pictures of the same number, and which one helps depends on the problem. The imaginary part is a real number, so it never contains the symbol \(i\).

concepts.title: Magnitude, argument and polar form
concepts.question: How do the length and the direction of \(a + bi\) give a second way to write it?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The magnitude of \(z = a + bi\) is \(|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\), the length of its vector. The argument \(\arg z\) is the angle the vector makes with the real axis, measured counterclockwise. With \(r = |z|\) and \(\theta = \arg z\), the polar form is \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\), abbreviated \(r\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\theta\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The vector to \((a, b)\) has length \(\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\) by the Pythagorean theorem, and its direction is the counterclockwise angle \(\theta\) from the real axis. With \(r\) the length, the horizontal and vertical parts of the vector are \(a = r\cos\theta\) and \(b = r\sin\theta\), so \(a + bi = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\). Check: for \(1 + i\), \(r = \sqrt{2}\) and \(\theta = \pi/4\) give \(\sqrt{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 1\) for each part. Our reading: the angle is chosen from the quadrant of the point, which is why the tangent alone is not enough.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Length and angle describe the vector as well as the coordinates do, and they are the data that multiplication acts on. Angles are in radians.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(1 + i = \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/4)\), and \(-12i = 12\,\mathrm{Cis}(3\pi/2)\), and \(57 = 57\,\mathrm{Cis}\,0\).

blocks.label: Common slip
blocks.text: Taking \(\arctan(b/a)\) as the argument without checking the quadrant of the point.

card.rule: \(z = r\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\theta\) with \(r = |z|\) and \(\theta\) the counterclockwise angle from the real axis.
card.limits: The argument of a point is fixed only up to whole turns, and the tangent of the angle cannot tell opposite quadrants apart. Always place the point first, then choose the angle.

concepts.title: The conjugate and the product \(z\bar z\)
concepts.question: What is the conjugate of a complex number, and what is \(z\bar z\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The conjugate of \(z = a + bi\) is \(\bar z = a - bi\). Geometrically \(\bar z\) is the reflection of \(z\) in the real axis.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Multiplying out, \(z\bar z = (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 + b^2\), because the cross terms cancel and \(-(bi)^2 = b^2\). So \(z\bar z = |z|^2\), a real number.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(z = 3 + 4i\), \(\bar z = 3 - 4i\) and \(z\bar z = 25 = 5^2\), matching \(|z| = 5\).

card.rule: \(\bar z\) reflects \(z\) in the real axis, and \(z\bar z = |z|^2\).
card.limits: The reflection is in the real axis, not the imaginary axis. The product \(z\bar z\) is a real number, not a complex one with an imaginary part.

concepts.title: Adding and subtracting complex numbers
concepts.question: How do sums and differences of complex numbers look as vectors?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Complex numbers add component by component: \((a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i\). As vectors, \(z + w\) is the diagonal of the parallelogram with sides \(z\) and \(w\) (the parallelogram rule). The difference \(z - w\) has the same magnitude and direction as the vector that starts at \(w\) and ends at \(z\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Adding components is adding vectors. For the difference, \(w + (z - w) = z\), so \(z - w\) is the arrow that carries \(w\) to \(z\). So \(|z - w|\) is the distance between the points \(z\) and \(w\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \((3 + 2i) + (1 - 5i) = 4 - 3i\). The midpoint of the segment joining \(z\) and \(w\) is \((z + w)/2\), half of the parallelogram diagonal.

card.rule: Sum is the parallelogram diagonal; \(z - w\) points from \(w\) to \(z\), and \(|z - w|\) is their distance.
card.limits: The vector \(z - w\) is not the same as \(w - z\): it points the other way. The parallelogram rule applies to vectors drawn from a common starting point.

media.alt: Two vector pictures in the complex plane. Above, arrows z and w start at the origin and a dashed parallelogram is completed on them; its diagonal from the origin is labelled z plus w. Lower right, five arrows z1 to z5 are laid head to tail around a closed five-sided polygon.

concepts.title: Lengths multiply and angles add
concepts.question: What happens to the length and the angle when two complex numbers are multiplied?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(z = r\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\alpha\) and \(w = s\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\beta\), then \(zw = rs\,\mathrm{Cis}(\alpha + \beta)\). The length of \(zw\) is the product of the lengths, and the angle of \(zw\) is the sum of the angles.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Multiply out \((\cos\alpha + i\sin\alpha)(\cos\beta + i\sin\beta)\) and use the angle-sum identities for cosine and sine. The book calls this a good exercise but not illuminating; the geometric reason comes in the next idea.

card.rule: In a product, multiply the lengths and add the angles.
card.limits: Add angles as angles: a sum beyond a full turn is reduced by whole turns. Do not add the lengths or multiply the angles.

concepts.title: Multiplication as rotating and stretching
concepts.question: What does multiplying by a complex number do to the plane?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Multiplication by \(i\) rotates by \(\pi/2\) counterclockwise. Multiplication by a real number \(a\) stretches by the factor \(a\). Multiplication by \(r\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\theta\) is a counterclockwise rotation by \(\theta\) followed by stretching by the factor \(r\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Since \(i(a + bi) = -b + ai\), multiplying by \(i\) turns the vector a quarter turn. To multiply \(z\) by \(3 + 4i\) write \((3 + 4i)z = 3z + 4iz\): the vector \(z\) stretched by 3, plus \(z\) turned a quarter turn and stretched by 4. The sum has length \(5|z|\) and angle \(\theta + \arg z\), where \(\theta = \arctan(4/3) \approx 0.93\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(i(3 + i) = 3i + i^2 = -1 + 3i\). The vector \((3, 1)\) has turned to \((-1, 3)\), a quarter turn counterclockwise.

card.rule: Multiplying by \(r\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\theta\) rotates by \(\theta\) and stretches by \(r\).
card.limits: Rotation and stretch commute, so the order does not matter. The rotation is about the origin, not about the vector's own starting point.

concepts.title: Dividing complex numbers
concepts.question: How do the lengths and angles of \(z\) and \(w\) combine in \(z/w\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(z = r\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\alpha\) and \(w = s\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\beta\), then \(z/w = (r/s)\,\mathrm{Cis}(\alpha - \beta)\). Geometrically, dividing by \(s\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\beta\) is a clockwise rotation by \(\beta\) followed by stretching by \(1/s\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Let \(v = z/w = t\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\gamma\). Then \(vw = z\), so by the multiplication rule \(ts = r\) and \(\gamma + \beta = \alpha\). Hence \(t = r/s\) and \(\gamma = \alpha - \beta\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \((6\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\pi)/(2\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/3)) = 3\,\mathrm{Cis}(2\pi/3)\).

card.rule: Divide the lengths and subtract the angles.
card.limits: The divisor must be nonzero. Dividing undoes multiplication, so the angle is subtracted, not added.

concepts.title: De Moivre's theorem
concepts.question: What is \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n\), and why?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: De Moivre's theorem: \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\) for every positive integer \(n\) and real \(\theta\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each factor has length 1 and angle \(\theta\). Multiplying \(n\) of them multiplies the lengths (\(1^n = 1\)) and adds \(n\) copies of \(\theta\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^2 = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta + 2i\sin\theta\cos\theta\), so \(\cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta\) and \(\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\). Also \((1 + i)^6 = (\sqrt2)^6\,\mathrm{Cis}(6\pi/4) = -8i\).

card.rule: Raising \(\mathrm{Cis}\,\theta\) to the power \(n\) gives \(\mathrm{Cis}\,n\theta\).
card.limits: The base must have length 1; otherwise the length is raised to the power as well. Comparing real and imaginary parts of the two sides yields identities for \(\cos n\theta\) and \(\sin n\theta\).

concepts.title: Exponential form and Euler's formula
concepts.question: Why can \(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta\) be written as \(e^{i\theta}\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Euler's formula: \(\mathrm{Cis}\,\theta = e^{i\theta}\), where \(e = 2.71828\ldots\) is the base of natural logarithms. This exponential form is a shorter notation for polar form: \(z = re^{i\theta}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Under multiplication angles add and under division they subtract, just as exponents do for powers. So \(\mathrm{Cis}\) behaves like an exponential function. The usual proof by power series works but gives little insight, and a deeper explanation is beyond the book's scope.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(e^{i\pi} = \mathrm{Cis}\,\pi = -1\) and \(e^{i\pi/2} = \mathrm{Cis}(\pi/2) = i\). Also \(e^{i\alpha}e^{i\beta} = e^{i(\alpha + \beta)}\).

card.rule: \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\), so \(re^{i\theta}\) has length \(r\) and angle \(\theta\).
card.limits: The formula links a complex exponential to angles for real \(\theta\). The angle is in radians, and \(e^{i\theta}\) always has length 1 when \(\theta\) is real.

concepts.title: Chord lengths on the unit circle
concepts.question: How far apart are \(1\) and a point \(z\) on the unit circle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(|z| = 1\) and \(\theta = \arg z\) with \(0 \le \theta \le 2\pi\), then \(|1 - z| = 2\sin(\theta/2)\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The points \(0\), \(1\) and \(z\) form an isosceles triangle with two sides of length 1 and apex angle \(\theta\) at the origin. Dropping the perpendicular from the origin to the base bisects it, so half the base is \(\sin(\theta/2)\). The base is \(|1 - z|\).

card.rule: On the unit circle, \(|1 - z| = 2\sin(\theta/2)\) with \(\theta = \arg z\).
card.limits: The formula needs \(|z| = 1\) and the angle taken between \(0\) and \(2\pi\). It uses half the angle, not the whole angle.

media.alt: Typeset fraction with the argument of z on top and 2 below, inside large parentheses: half the argument of z, the angle inside a sine in an exercise about the length of one minus z for z on the unit circle.

concepts.title: Zeros of real polynomials come in conjugate pairs
concepts.question: If a polynomial with real coefficients has a non-real zero, what else must be a zero?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(P(x)\) be a polynomial with real coefficients. If \(z\) is a zero of \(P\), then \(\bar z\) is also a zero. Non-real zeros come in complex-conjugate pairs.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Conjugation respects sums and products, and real coefficients are their own conjugates. So \(\overline{P(z)} = P(\bar z)\). If \(P(z) = 0\) then \(P(\bar z) = \overline{0} = 0\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(x^2 - 2x + 5\) has zeros \(1 + 2i\) and \(1 - 2i\), a conjugate pair, since \(x = 1 \pm \sqrt{-4}\).

blocks.label: Common slip
blocks.text: Forgetting that the coefficients must be real. \(x - i\) has the zero \(i\) but not \(-i\).

card.rule: For real coefficients, a zero \(z\) brings its conjugate \(\bar z\).
card.limits: The statement needs real coefficients. A polynomial with a coefficient like \(i\) can have a lone non-real zero.

concepts.title: A map that turns a line into a circle
concepts.question: What does \(f(z) = z/(z - 1)\) do to the imaginary axis?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The function \(f(z) = z/(z - 1)\) sends the imaginary axis onto the circle with centre \(\tfrac12\) and radius \(\tfrac12\). It is an example of a Mobius transformation, and it turns the rectangular grid into circles all tangent at 1, though 1 itself is never reached.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Algebraically, put \(z = it\). Then \(f(it) = \dfrac{t^2 - it}{t^2 + 1} = x + yi\) with \(x = \dfrac{t^2}{t^2+1}\) and \(y = \dfrac{-t}{t^2+1}\), and \((x - \tfrac12)^2 + y^2 = \tfrac14\). Geometrically, \(f\) is four steps: reciprocate, negate, add 1, reciprocate.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(f(i) = \dfrac{i}{i - 1} = \dfrac{1 - i}{2}\). Its distance from \(\tfrac12\) is \(\left|-\tfrac{i}{2}\right| = \tfrac12\), so it lies on the circle.

card.rule: The imaginary axis goes to the circle centre \(\tfrac12\), radius \(\tfrac12\) under \(z/(z - 1)\).
card.limits: The point 1 is on the circle's edge but is not an image of any \(z\). The proof uses the imaginary axis; other lines go to other circles.

media.alt: A cropped fragment of a typeset fraction: the letter z above a short horizontal bar, followed by a full stop, the numerator of the map z over z minus one considered in the exercise.

Computer-drawn plot of the complex plane with axis ticks from minus four to four. Two families of circles and circular arcs cross in a net that grows very dense around the point 1 on the real axis, where a small peanut-shaped blank region is left empty. concepts.title: A map that turns a circle into a line
concepts.question: Where does \(z/(z - 1)\) send the unit circle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The map \(f(z) = z/(z - 1)\) sends the unit circle onto the vertical line with real part \(\tfrac12\). In fact \(f(e^{i\theta}) = \tfrac12 - \tfrac{i}{2}\cot(\theta/2)\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Multiply top and bottom of \(e^{i\theta}/(e^{i\theta} - 1)\) by \(e^{-i\theta/2}\) to get \(e^{i\theta/2}/(e^{i\theta/2} - e^{-i\theta/2}) = e^{i\theta/2}/(2i\sin(\theta/2))\). Splitting cosine and sine gives \(\tfrac12 - \tfrac{i}{2}\cot(\theta/2)\), so the real part is always \(\tfrac12\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(f(-1) = \dfrac{-1}{-2} = \tfrac12\). As \(z\) moves counterclockwise from \(-1\) toward \(1\), the image climbs the line upward without bound.

card.rule: The unit circle goes to the line \(\mathrm{Re} = \tfrac12\).
card.limits: The point \(z = 1\) has no image because the denominator is zero. The earlier idea sent a line to a circle; this one sends a circle to a line.

concepts.title: The \(n\)th roots of unity
concepts.question: Which complex numbers satisfy \(z^n = 1\), and where do they sit?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The zeros of \(x^n = 1\) are the \(n\)th roots of unity. There are \(n\) of them: \(1, \zeta, \zeta^2, \dots, \zeta^{n-1}\), where \(\zeta = \mathrm{Cis}(2\pi/n)\). Geometrically they are the vertices of a regular \(n\)-gon inscribed in the unit circle, with one vertex at 1.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: By De Moivre, \(\zeta^k = \mathrm{Cis}(2\pi k/n)\), and \((\zeta^k)^n = \mathrm{Cis}(2\pi k) = 1\). These \(n\) numbers have length 1 and equally spaced angles, so they are distinct.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The 4th roots are \(1, i, -1, -i\), the corners of a square. The cube roots are \(1, \omega, \omega^2\) with \(\omega = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\), the corners of an equilateral triangle.

card.rule: The \(n\)th roots of unity are \(\zeta^k\) with \(\zeta = \mathrm{Cis}(2\pi/n)\), \(k = 0, \dots, n-1\), equally spaced on the unit circle.
card.limits: The roots of \(x^n = 1\) always include 1. A regular polygon rotated so that no vertex is at 1 is not the set of \(n\)th roots of unity.

media.alt: A dashed circle around the origin with six spokes to equally spaced points on it. Going counterclockwise from the point on the right, labelled zeta to the sixth equals 1, the spokes end at an unlabelled point in the upper right, then at zeta squared, zeta cubed on the left, zeta to the fourth and zeta to the fifth.

concepts.title: Factoring \(x^n - 1\)
concepts.question: How does \(x^n - 1\) factor over the complex numbers?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: With \(\zeta = \mathrm{Cis}(2\pi/n)\), for every complex \(x\): \(x^n - 1 = (x - 1)(x - \zeta)(x - \zeta^2)\cdots(x - \zeta^{n-1})\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each of \(1, \zeta, \dots, \zeta^{n-1}\) is a zero of \(x^n - 1\). There are \(n\) distinct zeros, the degree is \(n\), and the leading coefficient is 1, so these account for the whole polynomial.

card.rule: \(x^n - 1\) is the product of \(x - \zeta^k\) over the \(n\)th roots of unity.
card.limits: There are exactly \(n\) factors, with exponents \(0\) to \(n - 1\). Including \(\zeta^n\) would repeat the factor \(x - 1\).

concepts.title: The roots of unity add up to zero
concepts.question: Why do all the \(n\)th roots of unity add up to 0, without using the geometric series?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For \(n \ge 2\), \(1 + \zeta + \zeta^2 + \dots + \zeta^{n-1} = 0\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Let \(S\) be the sum. Multiplying by \(\zeta\) turns each root into the next one around the circle, so \(\zeta S\) is the same list of numbers, and \(\zeta S = S\). Since \(\zeta \ne 1\), \(S = 0\). Geometrically, the arrows to the vertices of a regular polygon balance about its centre.

card.rule: The \(n\)th roots of unity sum to 0 for \(n \ge 2\).
card.limits: It needs \(n \ge 2\): for \(n = 1\) the only root is 1. The arrows add to zero as vectors, not as lengths.

concepts.title: A trig identity from squaring \(1 + it\)
concepts.question: How can squaring a complex number give a formula for \(\tan 2\alpha\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: 1. Let \(t = \tan\alpha\) and \(z = 1 + it\), so \(\arg z = \alpha\). 2. Square or power \(z\) by algebra. 3. Use \(\tan(\arg(x + iy)) = y/x\) on the result. 4. The argument of \(z^2\) is \(2\alpha\), so the ratio gives \(\tan 2\alpha\).

blocks.label: When to use
blocks.text: You want a trigonometric identity for a multiple of an angle, and the tangent or the pair (cosine, sine) can be read off a complex number.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Squaring doubles the argument, and for \(x + iy\) the tangent of the argument is \(y/x\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(z^2 = (1 + it)^2 = 1 - t^2 + 2it\), so \(\tan 2\alpha = \dfrac{2t}{1 - t^2} = \dfrac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^2\alpha}\). If \(\tan\alpha = \tfrac13\), then \(\tan 2\alpha = \tfrac34\).

card.rule: Build \(1 + it\), power it, and read the tangent of the new argument.
card.limits: The formula fails where the denominator is zero (\(\tan^2\alpha = 1\), so \(z^2\) is purely imaginary). Check the quadrant if the angle is large.

concepts.title: The midpoint locus of two circles
concepts.question: What shape do the midpoints of segments between points of two circles fill?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Putnam 1996: circles with centres \(a, b\) (complex) and radii \(u, v\), with \(v\) bigger. The locus of midpoints \(M\) of segments \(XY\), with \(X\) on the first and \(Y\) on the second, is an annulus (a ring) centred at \(c = (a + b)/2\) with inner radius \((v - u)/2\) and outer radius \((v + u)/2\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Write \(X = a + ue^{it}\) and \(Y = b + ve^{is}\). Then \(M = \dfrac{a + b}{2} + \dfrac{ue^{it} + ve^{is}}{2}\). For fixed \(s\), \(ve^{is}\) is a point \(P\) on the circle of radius \(v\) about 0, and adding \(ue^{it}\) traces a circle of radius \(u\) about \(P\). As \(s\) varies this circle sweeps out the ring \(v - u \le |z| \le v + u\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Circles with centres 10 apart and radii 1 and 3: the locus is the ring with radii \((3 - 1)/2 = 1\) and \((3 + 1)/2 = 2\) about the midpoint of the centres.

card.rule: Midpoints fill a ring centred midway between the centres, with radii \((v \mp u)/2\).
card.limits: The ring shape needs \(s\) and \(t\) to vary independently. If the radii are equal, the inner radius is 0 and the ring fills a disc.

A segment joins X on the small circle to Y on the large circle, with its midpoint M marked. Angle t at a runs from the horizontal radius to X, and angle s at b from the horizontal radius to Y.
