concepts.title: Cube roots of unity and a triangle
concepts.question: How do the cube roots of unity show that three distances always form a triangle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Putnam 2003: \(A, B, C\) are equally spaced points on a unit circle centred at \(O\), and \(P\) is any interior point with distances \(a, b, c\) to \(A, B, C\). Show that a triangle with sides \(a, b, c\) exists and that its area depends only on the distance \(OP\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Three lengths need not form a triangle (1, 1 and 10 do not). Lemma: if complex numbers \(z_1, z_2, z_3\) have lengths \(a, b, c\) and \(z_1 + e^{i\alpha}z_2 + e^{i\beta}z_3 = 0\), rotating the second and third vectors and placing all three end to end gives a triangle. Now take \(O = 0\), \(A = 1\), \(B = \omega\), \(C = \omega^2\), \(P = z\) with \(|z| < 1\).

blocks.label: Steps
blocks.text: The vectors \(z - 1\), \(\omega(z - \omega)\), \(\omega^2(z - \omega^2)\) have lengths \(a, b, c\) because \(|\omega| = 1\). Their sum is \(z(1 + \omega + \omega^2) - (1 + \omega^2 + \omega) = 0\). By the lemma the triangle exists. The area is then computed and depends only on \(|z|\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If \(P\) is the centre \(O\), then \(a = b = c = 1\), and the triangle is equilateral with side 1.

card.rule: Rotating the three distance vectors by cube roots of unity makes them add to zero, so they close up into a triangle.
card.limits: The lemma only asks for some rotations making the sum zero. The area formula is left for the reader in the book, and the argument needs \(P\) inside the circle.

concepts.title: Products of sums of two squares
concepts.question: If \(m\) and \(n\) are sums of two squares, why is \(mn\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If integers \(m\) and \(n\) can each be written as a sum of two perfect squares, so can \(mn\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Write \(m = a^2 + b^2\) and \(n = c^2 + d^2\) with integers \(a, b, c, d\), and let \(z = (a + bi)(c + di)\). Then \(|z|^2 = |a + bi|^2\,|c + di|^2 = mn\). But \(|z|^2 = (\mathrm{Re}\,z)^2 + (\mathrm{Im}\,z)^2\), and both parts are integers.

card.rule: Multiply \(a + bi\) by \(c + di\); the squares of the real and imaginary parts add to \(mn\).
card.limits: Everything is integer arithmetic, so the argument works only because \(a, b, c, d\) are integers. It says nothing about numbers that are not products of such sums.

media.alt: Typeset expression: the square root of the product of a squared plus b squared and c squared plus d squared, followed by a full stop, the length of the product of the complex numbers a plus b i and c plus d i.

concepts.title: Roots of unity as an invariant
concepts.question: How can a sum of roots of unity prove that a lights puzzle cannot be solved?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Jim Propp's puzzle: \(n\) lights stand in a circle, exactly one on. A move picks a divisor \(d\) of \(n\) with \(d < n\); if the \(n/d\) lights at positions \(a, a + d, a + 2d, \dots\) are all in the same state, flip them all. Can every light be turned on? For \(n \ge 2\) the answer is no.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Put the lights at the roots of unity \(\zeta^k\) and let \(S\) be the sum of the roots at lights that are on. A move changes \(S\) by \(\pm\zeta^a(1 + \zeta^d + \dots + \zeta^{(n/d - 1)d}) = \pm\zeta^a\dfrac{1 - \zeta^n}{1 - \zeta^d} = 0\), since \(\zeta^d \ne 1\). So \(S\) never changes.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The start has only the light at 1 on, so \(S = 1\). With all lights on, \(S = 1 + \zeta + \dots + \zeta^{n-1} = 0 \ne 1\), so that arrangement is unreachable.

card.rule: Moves leave \(S\), the sum of the roots at lit lights, unchanged; \(S = 1\) at the start and \(0\) when all are on.
card.limits: The proof shows all lights on is unreachable, not that every other arrangement is. For \(n = 1\) there is no legal move and the single light is already on.

media.alt: Two typeset fractions, each two pi over n, side by side with a gap between them and a full stop at the end: the angle in the cosine and sine that define the nth root of unity zeta.

concepts.title: What a generating function is
concepts.question: How does a sequence become a polynomial or power series, and why is that useful?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The generating function of a sequence \(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots\) is \(a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + \cdots\). The sequence may be finite or infinite, and the number \(a_k\) is the coefficient of \(x^k\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book gives two facts. First, \(x^n \cdot x^m = x^{n+m}\): when two polynomials are multiplied, exponents add, so a term of the product comes from pairing one term of each factor whose exponents sum to the target. This ties adding numbers to multiplying polynomials. Second, the generating function is one function \(f(x)\) whose coefficients are the sequence, so what you know locally about the coefficients tells you globally about \(f\), and what you know globally can be read back as facts about the coefficients, for example by plugging in values such as \(x = 1\) or \(x = -1\), or by differentiating. For \(1, 1, 1, \dots\) the geometric series gives \(\dfrac{1}{1 - x}\) when \(|x| < 1\), though the book does not worry much about convergence.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Two facts give the tactic its power. First, \(x^n \cdot x^m = x^{n+m}\), so adding numbers (the exponents) becomes multiplying polynomials. Second, local knowledge of the coefficients often gives global knowledge of the function \(f(x)\), and the reverse.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The sequence \(2, 0, 5\) has generating function \(2 + 5x^2\). The sequence \(1, 1, 1, \dots\) has \(1 + x + x^2 + \cdots\).

card.rule: A sequence's generating function holds \(a_k\) as the coefficient of \(x^k\).
card.limits: The generating function is a bookkeeping device, so the position of each number is carried by its power of \(x\). Do not sum the sequence's terms and call the sum its generating function.

concepts.title: The geometric series tool
concepts.question: How does \(1/(1 - x)\) turn into a series, and a series into a fraction?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The sequence \(1, 1, 1, \dots\) has the generating function \(1 + x + x^2 + \cdots = \dfrac{1}{1 - x}\) for \(|x| < 1\). The book calls this the geometric series tool, and it appears everywhere in generating functions. More generally \(\dfrac{1}{1 - cx} = 1 + cx + c^2x^2 + \cdots\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Multiply \(1 + x + x^2 + \cdots\) by \(1 - x\) and everything cancels except the leading 1, so the series times \((1 - x)\) is 1.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(\dfrac{1}{1 - 3x} = 1 + 3x + 9x^2 + 27x^3 + \cdots\), so the coefficient of \(x^n\) is \(3^n\). Substituting \(-2x\) for \(x\) gives \(\dfrac{1}{1 + 2x} = 1 - 2x + 4x^2 - 8x^3 + \cdots\).

card.rule: \(\dfrac{1}{1 - x} = 1 + x + x^2 + \cdots\), and replacing \(x\) by \(cx\) or \(x^k\) gives other series.
card.limits: The identity needs \(|x|\) small enough for the series to converge, but for coefficient work this rarely matters. Substituting means replacing every \(x\), including inside powers.

media.alt: A cropped fragment of a typeset fraction: the number one above a horizontal bar followed by a comma, with the denominator not visible, from the discussion of the geometric series tool for generating functions.

concepts.title: Plugging in values: the binomial theorem
concepts.question: What does substituting a number for \(x\) in \((1 + x)^n\) tell us about the coefficients?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The sequence \(a_k = \binom{n}{k}\) for \(k = 0, \dots, n\) has generating function \((1 + x)^n\), by the binomial theorem. Putting \(x = 1\) gives \(\sum_k \binom{n}{k} = 2^n\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The function \((1 + x)^n\) is a simple global object, so any value of \(x\) may be substituted. Each substitution gives a statement about the coefficients (the local information), so moving between the function and its coefficients yields results.

card.rule: Plug a value into the generating function to get an identity about its coefficients.
card.limits: The identity concerns the coefficients of one generating function, and only the chosen values of \(x\) help. Substituting \(x = 0\) gives only the first coefficient.

media.alt: A large summation sign with the index j equals 0 below it and the upper limit k above it; the expression being summed is missing from the picture.

concepts.title: Differentiating a generating function
concepts.question: What identity appears if we differentiate \((1 + x)^n\) and then substitute?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Differentiate \((1 + x)^n = \sum_k \binom{n}{k}x^k\) to get \(n(1 + x)^{n-1} = \sum_k k\binom{n}{k}x^{k-1}\). Putting \(x = 1\) gives \(\sum_k k\binom{n}{k} = n\,2^{n-1}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Differentiation is another global operation on the function, and it multiplies the coefficient of \(x^k\) by \(k\). The simple closed form \((1 + x)^n\) is easy to differentiate.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(n = 4\): \(1\cdot4 + 2\cdot6 + 3\cdot4 + 4\cdot1 = 32 = 4 \cdot 2^3\).

card.rule: Differentiate the closed form, then plug in a value to get \(\sum k\binom nk = n2^{n-1}\).
card.limits: Substitute after differentiating, not before: substituting first turns the function into a constant, and its derivative is 0.

concepts.title: Solving a recurrence with the shift trick
concepts.question: How does multiplying a generating function by \(x\) help solve a recurrence?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: 1. Let \(f(x) = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + \cdots\). 2. Form \(xf(x)\), which is the shifted sequence: the coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(xf(x)\) is \(a_{n-1}\). 3. Subtract using the recurrence so the unknown coefficients cancel: \(f(x) - 3xf(x) = 1 + 2(x + x^2 + \cdots) = 1 + \dfrac{2x}{1 - x}\). 4. Solve for \(f(x)\). 5. Read the coefficients off \(f(x)\).

blocks.label: When to use
blocks.text: A sequence is given by a recurrence such as \(a_0 = 1\), \(a_n = 3a_{n-1} + 2\), and you want a formula for \(a_n\) that guessing will not reliably give.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Since \(a_n - 3a_{n-1} = 2\) for every \(n \ge 1\), subtracting \(3xf(x)\) replaces the whole unknown sequence by a known one.

card.rule: Multiply by \(x\) to shift the sequence, subtract using the recurrence, and solve for \(f(x)\).
card.limits: The method is much more laborious than guessing for this particular recurrence. It earns its keep where the pattern is not easy to guess.

concepts.title: Recovering coefficients with partial fractions
concepts.question: How do you get a formula for \(a_n\) from \(f(x) = \dfrac{1 + x}{(1 - x)(1 - 3x)}\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Split \(f(x)\) into simple fractions, apply the geometric series tool to each, and read the coefficients: \(f(x) = \dfrac{1 + x}{(1 - x)(1 - 3x)} = \dfrac{2}{1 - 3x} - \dfrac{1}{1 - x}\), so \(a_n = 2\cdot3^n - 1\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Combining the two fractions over \((1 - x)(1 - 3x)\) gives numerator \(2(1 - x) - (1 - 3x) = 1 + x\). Then \(\dfrac{2}{1 - 3x} = 2(1 + 3x + 9x^2 + \cdots)\) and \(\dfrac{1}{1 - x} = 1 + x + x^2 + \cdots\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The sequence is \(1, 5, 17, 53, 161, \dots\), matching \(2\cdot3^n - 1\) for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\).

blocks.label: Author's verdict
blocks.text: For this recurrence, working out terms and guessing \(a_n = 2\cdot3^n - 1\), then proving it by induction, is far more efficient. Generating functions pay off where guessing fails.

card.rule: Partial fractions plus the geometric series tool turn \(f(x)\) into a formula for \(a_n\).
card.limits: The method is technically messy and uses partial fractions and the geometric series tool repeatedly. It is worth it where inspired guessing does not work.

media.alt: A cropped typeset fragment of a fraction: x plus 1 on top, and below it the end of one factor, minus x, then the start of another beginning with 1 minus. It is part of a generating function being split by partial fractions.

concepts.title: Coefficients of a product count pairings
concepts.question: How do you read the coefficient of \(x^k\) in a product of two polynomials?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In a product \(A(x)B(x)\), the coefficient of \(x^k\) comes from all pairings of one term from \(A\) and one term from \(B\) whose exponents add up to \(k\). Multiply each pair and add.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each term of the product is a term of \(A\) times a term of \(B\), and \(x^i \cdot x^j = x^{i+j}\). So the terms that produce \(x^k\) are exactly those with \(i + j = k\).

card.rule: The coefficient of \(x^k\) in \(A(x)B(x)\) adds up the products of coefficients over all exponent pairs with sum \(k\).
card.limits: Only the exponents decide which terms combine; a coefficient of 3 stands for three equal terms. Combining must be by exponent sum, not by position in the factor.

media.alt: Two small black dots on a white background, one near the top left and one near the bottom right, with nothing drawn between them.

concepts.title: Counting solutions of \(2a + 5b = n\)
concepts.question: How can a product of two series count the solutions of \(2a + 5b = n\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(u_n\) be the number of pairs \((a, b)\) of non-negative integers with \(2a + 5b = n\). Then \(A(x)B(x)\) is the generating function of \(u_n\), where \(A(x) = 1 + x^2 + x^4 + \cdots = \dfrac{1}{1 - x^2}\) and \(B(x) = 1 + x^5 + x^{10} + \cdots = \dfrac{1}{1 - x^5}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each term of \(A\) is \(x^{2a}\) and each term of \(B\) is \(x^{5b}\), so every term of the product is \(x^{2a + 5b}\). Each solution \((a, b)\) of \(2a + 5b = n\) produces one copy of \(x^n\), so the coefficient of \(x^n\) is \(u_n\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The pairs for \(n = 20\) are \((10, 0)\), \((5, 2)\), \((0, 4)\), so \(u_{20} = 3\). The book computes \(u_{100} = 11\) by working out values step by step.

card.rule: Give each variable a series with its own step size; the product's coefficients count the solutions.
card.limits: The product gives a generating function, not the answer: one still has to extract the coefficient. The exponents must match the equation's coefficients (2 and 5), not the variables' own values.

concepts.title: Weighing with powers of 3
concepts.question: Why can every whole number of grams be weighed in exactly one way with the weights \(1, 3, 9, 27, \dots\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: With weights \(1, 3, 3^2, \dots\) grams placed on either pan, every positive integer \(n\) can be weighed in exactly one way. Equivalently \(n\) is a sum or difference of distinct powers of 3 in exactly one way.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Let \(h_r(x) = (1 + x + x^{-1})(1 + x^3 + x^{-3})\cdots(1 + x^{3^r} + x^{-3^r})\). Each factor offers 'omit, add or subtract' that weight. Using \(u^3 - 1 = (u - 1)(u^2 + u + 1)\) on each factor, the product telescopes to \(x^{-a}(x^{3^{r+1}} - 1)/(x - 1)\) with \(a = (3^{r+1} - 1)/2\). So \(h_r = x^{a} + \cdots + x + 1 + x^{-1} + \cdots + x^{-a}\), every coefficient 1.

card.rule: Each integer from \(-a\) to \(a\) appears once in \(h_r\), so it is weighed in exactly one way.
card.limits: It is like base 3 with the digit \(-1\) in place of 2. That is why uniqueness is hard to see without the generating function; and the range grows with each new weight.

media.alt: A typeset product of three bracketed fractions: x squared plus x plus 1 over x; x to the sixth plus x cubed plus 1 over x cubed; x to the eighteenth plus x to the ninth plus 1 over x to the ninth. Below are four short bars from the next line of working, with their contents missing.
A bracketed fraction with x to the 27th power and a one in its numerator, the sign between them lost, beside a long fraction bar: part of the working that cancels factors in the product.

Typeset line defining f3 of x as f2 of x times the bracket one plus x to the power 3 cubed plus x to the power minus 3 cubed. Below it the working continues with a bracketed fraction with x to the power 2 times 27 and a one in its numerator, and several fraction bars whose parts are missing.

Typeset identity: the infinite product, over n from 0 to infinity, of one plus x to the power three-to-the-n plus x to the power minus three-to-the-n, equals the sum over all integers n, from minus infinity to infinity, of x to the n.

concepts.title: Generating functions for partitions
concepts.question: How does a factor \((1 + x^k + \cdots)\) control how often the part \(k\) can be used?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A partition of \(n\) is a way of writing \(n\) as a sum of positive integers, order ignored (parts are listed in increasing order). For example \(1 + 1 + 3\) and \(1 + 1 + 1 + 2\) are two partitions of 5.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: When the factors are multiplied out, each term of the product comes from picking exactly one term from every factor and adding the exponents. In \((1 + x^k + x^{2k} + \cdots)\) the chosen exponent \(jk\) records using the part \(k\) exactly \(j\) times, so a term \(x^n\) in the product is one way of writing \(n\) as a sum of allowed parts, and the coefficient of \(x^n\) counts those ways. A factor \(1 + x^k\) cannot give \(x^k \cdot x^k\), so the generating function prevents repeated parts. The geometric series tool turns \(1 + x^k + x^{2k} + \cdots\) into \(1/(1 - x^k)\). The book checks \(n = 6\) for unequal parts: \(x\cdot x^5 + x\cdot x^2\cdot x^3 + x^2\cdot x^4 + x^6 = 4x^6\).

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Build one factor per allowed part \(k\): it holds \(x^{0}, x^k, x^{2k}, \dots\) for using \(k\) zero, one, two, ... times. The factor \(1 + x^k\) allows \(k\) at most once; \(1 + x^k + x^{2k} + \cdots = \dfrac{1}{1 - x^k}\) allows it any number of times. The coefficient of \(x^n\) in the product counts the partitions.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(U(x) = (1 + x)(1 + x^2)(1 + x^3)\cdots\) counts partitions into unequal parts. \(V(x) = \dfrac{1}{(1 - x)(1 - x^3)(1 - x^5)\cdots}\) counts partitions into odd parts. For \(n = 6\) there are four of each.

card.rule: Choose one factor per allowed part: \(1 + x^k\) for at most once, \(1/(1 - x^k)\) for any number of times.
card.limits: The product prevents repeated parts only because each part has its own single factor. Parts that are not allowed simply have no factor.

media.alt: The outline of an empty table: a horizontal rule across the top, two vertical lines forming a narrow first column and a narrow second column, and the number 1 at the start of the first row below the rule. No other entries are visible.

concepts.title: Unequal parts equal odd parts
concepts.question: Why do partitions into unequal parts and into odd parts have the same count for every \(n\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For every positive integer \(n\), the number of partitions of \(n\) into unequal parts equals the number of partitions of \(n\) into odd parts. For \(n = 6\): unequal parts \(1+5\), \(1+2+3\), \(2+4\), \(6\); odd parts \(1+1+1+1+1+1\), \(1+1+1+3\), \(1+5\), \(3+3\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Show \(U(x) = V(x)\). Write \(1 + x^k = \dfrac{1 - x^{2k}}{1 - x^k}\), so \(U(x) = \dfrac{1 - x^2}{1 - x}\cdot\dfrac{1 - x^4}{1 - x^2}\cdot\dfrac{1 - x^6}{1 - x^3}\cdots\). Each numerator with an even exponent cancels the denominator with the same even exponent, leaving \(\dfrac{1}{(1 - x)(1 - x^3)(1 - x^5)\cdots} = V(x)\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Both counts are the coefficient of \(x^6\) in the same series, which is 4.

card.rule: Equal generating functions have equal coefficients, so the two partition counts agree.
card.limits: The identity says the counts are equal, not that the partitions themselves match one for one in this proof. It holds for every \(n\) at once.

concepts.title: Number systems and closure
concepts.question: Which operations keep us inside N, Z, Q, R and C, and why was each larger set invented?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The natural numbers N are 1, 2, 3, ...; the integers Z add 0 and the negatives; the rationals Q are quotients of integers; the reals R fill the whole number line, including numbers like \(\sqrt{2}\); the complex numbers C are numbers \(a+bi\) with \(i^2=-1\). A set is closed under an operation when the result always stays in the set.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each set fixes a failure of the one before it. The complex numbers have the property of algebraic closure: any finite chain of additions, subtractions, multiplications, divisions (never by zero) and root extractions, applied to a complex number, gives another complex number. None of N, Z, Q or R has this property.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Starting inside N, the step \(3-5\) leaves it. Starting inside Z, the step \(1\div 2\) leaves it. Starting inside R, the step \(\sqrt{-9}\) leaves it, but the answer \(3i\) is still a complex number.

card.rule: Each larger number system repairs a failure of closure in the smaller one, and only C survives every operation on the list.
card.limits: Closure always refers to a stated list of operations: Z is closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, so being 'not closed' needs a named operation that fails.

concepts.title: Elements, union, intersection and subsets
concepts.question: What do the symbols for membership, union, intersection and subset say, and which sets are subsets of every set?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A set is a collection of elements; \(x\in A\) says x belongs to A. The empty set \(\emptyset=\{\}\) has no elements. The union \(A\cup B\) holds everything in A or in B (or both); the intersection \(A\cap B\) holds everything in both. A is a subset of B, written \(A\subset B\), when every element of A is in B.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Subset only demands that no element of A be missing from B. A set meets this test against itself, so \(A\subset A\). The empty set has no element that could be missing, so \(\emptyset\subset A\) for every A.

card.rule: Union keeps what is in either set, intersection keeps what is in both, and every set contains itself and the empty set as subsets.
card.limits: The empty set and the set holding it are different: \(\emptyset\) has no elements, while \(\{\emptyset\}\) has exactly one.

concepts.title: Set difference and complement
concepts.question: What does A minus B contain, and why does a complement need a universal set?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The difference \(A-B\) is the set of elements of A that are not in B. A universal set U holds all sets under discussion (usually Z, R or C for numbers). The complement of A, written with a bar over the A, is \(U-A\): everything in U that is not in A.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A complement has no meaning on its own, because 'not in A' could include anything at all. Once U is fixed, the question has a definite answer, and changing U changes the complement.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With U = Z and A the even integers, the complement of A is the odd integers.

card.rule: A minus B removes B from A, and a complement is always taken inside a named universal set U.
card.limits: In \(A-B\), elements of B that are not in A change nothing; B need not be a subset of A.

concepts.title: Set-builder notation and intervals
concepts.question: How do you read a set written with 'such that', and what do square and round brackets mean in intervals?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The notation \(\{x : \text{condition}\}\) means the set of x for which the condition holds; the colon or a bar abbreviates 'such that'. For example \(\mathbb{Q}=\{a/b : a,b\in\mathbb{Z},\ b\neq 0\}\). The closed interval \([a,b]\) is \(\{x\in\mathbb{R} : a\le x\le b\}\); the open interval \((a,b)\) uses strict inequalities; \([a,b)\) and \((a,b]\) are hybrids.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The part before the colon names what kind of thing x is; the part after filters. A square bracket keeps its endpoint because the inequality is non-strict, a round bracket drops it because the inequality is strict.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The interval \([2,5)\) contains 2 but not 5. The real number \(\sqrt{2}\) is in R but not in Q, because it is not a quotient of integers.

card.rule: Read braces with a colon as 'the x such that', and read square brackets as keeping the endpoint and round brackets as dropping it.
card.limits: The condition \(b\neq 0\) is part of the definition of Q; without it the quotients \(a/b\) would include a division by zero.

concepts.title: The Cartesian product
concepts.question: What does A times B contain, and how many elements does it have?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The Cartesian product \(A\times B\) is the set of all ordered pairs \((a,b)\) with \(a\in A\) and \(b\in B\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The pairs are ordered: the first entry comes from A and the second from B, so \((a,b)\) and \((b,a)\) are different pairs. Each of the \(|A|\) choices for the first entry can be combined with each of the \(|B|\) choices for the second, giving \(|A|\cdot|B|\) pairs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With \(A=\{1,2,3\}\) and \(B=\{\text{Paris},\text{London}\}\), the product has \(3\cdot 2=6\) pairs: (1, Paris), (2, Paris), (3, Paris), (1, London), (2, London), (3, London).

card.rule: A times B lists every ordered pair with the first entry from A and the second from B, so it has |A| times |B| elements.
card.limits: Order matters: \(A\times B\) and \(B\times A\) contain different pairs unless A and B are equal (or one is empty).

concepts.title: What a function is
concepts.question: What makes a set of pairs a function, and how do domain, range and image fit in?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A function \(f:A\to B\) is a subset of \(A\times B\) in which every \(a\in A\) appears in exactly one pair \((a,b)\). The set A is the domain; the values lie in B; we write \(f(a)\) for the b paired with a. Informally, f is a rule that gives every input one output.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: 'Exactly one' is what makes \(f(a)\) a well-defined single value. Two inputs may share an output, but one input must not have two. The set of pairs and the rule are two descriptions of the same thing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The pairs (1, Paris), (2, Paris), (3, London) form a function from {1,2,3} to {Paris, London}. Adding (1, London) would break it, since 1 would then have two outputs.

card.rule: A function gives every input exactly one output, and different inputs are allowed to share an output.
card.limits: Not every element of B must be used as an output. The set of outputs actually reached can be smaller than B.

concepts.title: Range and inverse image: squaring
concepts.question: For the squaring function, what are its range and the inverse image of 9?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on the reals, the range is the non-negative reals only, not all of R. The inverse image of a value y, written \(f^{-1}(y)\), is the set of all inputs x with \(f(x)=y\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The equation \(x^2=9\) has two solutions, 3 and -3, so \(f^{-1}(9)=\{3,-3\}\). An inverse image is a set rather than a single element, because several inputs may share one output, or none may.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(f^{-1}(9)=\{3,-3\}\), \(f^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\), and \(f^{-1}(-4)\) is the empty set, since no real number squares to -4.

card.rule: The inverse image of y is the set of all inputs that give y, and it may have many elements or none.
card.limits: The symbol \(f^{-1}(y)\) does not promise an inverse function exists; it only names a set.

concepts.title: Onto, 1-to-1 and bijections
concepts.question: When is a function onto, when is it 1-to-1, and what is a bijection?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A function \(f:A\to B\) is onto when its range is all of B (every value is hit). It is 1-to-1 when every inverse image has at most one element, so different inputs never share an output. A function that is both is a bijection.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Onto is about the output side (nothing in B is missed); 1-to-1 is about the input side (no two inputs collide). Cubing on the reals is a bijection: every real has exactly one real cube root, because cube roots of positives are positive and of negatives are negative.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(x\mapsto x^3\) on R is onto and 1-to-1. \(x\mapsto x^2\) is neither. \(x\mapsto b^x\) (b positive, not 1) is 1-to-1 but not onto R, since it never reaches 0 or negatives.

card.rule: Onto means every output is reached, 1-to-1 means no two inputs share an output, and a bijection is both.
card.limits: Whether a function is onto depends on the target set B you name: squaring on R is not onto R but is onto the non-negative reals.

concepts.title: Exponentials and logarithms as functions
concepts.question: Why is the logarithm well defined, and what are the range and domain of the exponential and the logarithm?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Fix a positive real \(b\neq 1\) and let \(h(x)=b^x\). Its range is the positive reals, so it is not onto R, but it is 1-to-1. For \(y>0\) the unique solution x of \(b^x=y\) is called \(\log_b y\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Because h is 1-to-1 and reaches every positive y, each positive y has exactly one preimage, and that preimage gets a name. A function that is not 1-to-1 would make the name ambiguous.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(\log_3 81=4\), since \(3^4=81\) and 4 is the only solution of \(3^x=81\).

card.rule: The logarithm is the unique exponent that gives y, and it exists only for positive y because powers of b are positive.
card.limits: If complex numbers are allowed, the solution of \(b^x=y\) is no longer unique, so the clean definition belongs to real exponents.

media.alt: A summation with the index k starting at 2 beneath the sum sign. The summand is built from the logarithm of u to the base k. A fraction bar sits above the logarithm, but its numerator is missing from the cropped picture.

concepts.title: Floor and ceiling
concepts.question: What do the floor and ceiling of a real number give, especially for negative numbers?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The floor \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) is the greatest integer less than or equal to x. The ceiling \(\lceil x\rceil\) is the smallest integer greater than or equal to x. Both have domain R and take integer values.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Floor walks down to the nearest integer at or below x; ceiling walks up to the nearest integer at or above x. For negatives, 'down' means more negative, so \(\lfloor -2.4\rfloor=-3\), not -2.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(\lfloor 3.7\rfloor=3\), \(\lfloor 2\rfloor=2\), \(\lfloor -2.4\rfloor=-3\), \(\lceil 3.1\rceil=4\), \(\lceil -1.2\rceil=-1\). Floors also appear in sums over fractions of the form \(\frac{n+2^{k-1}}{2^k}\) for k = 1, 2, 3, ...; the pictures on this card show those fractions.

card.rule: Floor rounds down to the integer at or below x, ceiling rounds up to the integer at or above x, and negatives follow the same rule.
card.limits: Floor is not 'drop the decimals': that works for positives but gives the wrong integer for negatives.

media.alt: Three fractions side by side. Each has a numerator of n plus a power of two and a denominator equal to the next power of two: n plus 2 to the 0 over 2 to the 1, then n plus 2 to the 1 over 2 to the 2, then n plus 2 squared over 2 cubed. The exponents rise by one from each fraction to the next.

A single fraction. Its numerator is n plus 2 raised to the power n minus 1, and its denominator is 2 raised to the power n. It has the same form as the fractions with a power of two added to n over the next power of two, written for a general position n.

concepts.title: Sequences as functions
concepts.question: How is a sequence a function, and how can its domain differ from the natural numbers?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A function whose domain is the natural numbers has values \(f(1),f(2),f(3),\dots\). Written \(f_1,f_2,f_3,\dots\), the function is called a sequence. An infinite sequence may be written \((f_i)\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The subscript is the input: \(f_n\) is just \(f(n)\) in a different notation. The conventional letters for the subscript are i, j, k, l, m, n because they stand for integers.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The sequence \(f_n=n^2-1\) begins 0, 3, 8, 15, 24, and \(f_5=24\).

card.rule: A sequence is a function on the positions 1, 2, 3, ..., and its subscript is the input.
card.limits: Positions need not start at 1 and need not go on forever; a sequence may start at zero or be finite.

concepts.title: Indicator functions
concepts.question: What does an indicator function record, and what do products and sums of indicators do?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For a set A inside a universal set U, the indicator function \(1_A\) has domain U and range \(\{0,1\}\): \(1_A(x)=1\) if \(x\in A\) and \(1_A(x)=0\) if \(x\notin A\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Multiplying two indicators gives 1 only when both are 1, i.e. only when x is in both sets, so \(1_A\cdot 1_B=1_{A\cap B}\). Subtracting from 1 flips every 0 and 1, so \(1-1_A\) is the indicator of the complement of A.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With \(U=\mathbb{N}\) and A the primes, \(1_A(9)=0\) and \(1_A(17)=1\).

card.rule: An indicator function marks membership with 1 and non-membership with 0; products give intersections and 1 minus it gives the complement.
card.limits: The complement identity needs a universal set U; and the sum \(1_A+1_B\) is not the indicator of the union, because overlap gives 2.

media.alt: The sum over all x in U of the indicator function of A evaluated at x equals the number of elements of A, written as the set A between absolute value bars. Each member of A contributes 1 and every other element contributes 0.

concepts.title: Keeping a light touch in algebra
concepts.question: Why look for an elegant route instead of solving for every unknown and substituting?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Algebra is not only computation. The book advises a light touch: before grinding through messy manipulation, choose the final target and ask what simple expression leads to it. This is wishful thinking applied to algebra.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Goals often depend only on symmetric combinations such as \(x+y\) and \(xy\), which are already given. The identity \(x^3+y^3=(x+y)^3-3xy(x+y)\) turns those two numbers directly into the target, with no need to find x and y.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If \(x+y=xy=3\), then \(x^3+y^3=3^3-3\cdot3\cdot3=0\). Solving the system by the quadratic formula would give complex x and y and a tedious check.

card.rule: Pick the target, find the penultimate step, and use the symmetric quantities you are given instead of solving for the unknowns.
card.limits: A light touch is a first resort, not a guarantee; some problems do need a slog, but the book says these occasions are pretty rare.

media.alt: A cropped piece of a typeset answer: a large opening parenthesis, then a fraction whose numerator reads 3 plus i times the square root of 3, with a horizontal line continuing to the right where a second, empty fraction bar begins. The rest of the ordered pair is not visible in this picture.

concepts.title: Factor relentlessly
concepts.question: Which factorisation formulas should you know actively, and when does the sum-of-powers formula apply?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Multiplication rarely simplifies; factoring does. Know these actively: \(x^2-y^2=(x-y)(x+y)\), \(x^3+y^3=(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2)\), \(x^3-y^3=(x-y)(x^2+xy+y^2)\), and the squares \((x\pm y)^2\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each formula is checked by multiplying the right side out; the cross terms cancel in pairs. Knowing them actively means you recognise their shape inside a problem instead of looking them up.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(3^6-1=(27-1)(27+1)=26\cdot28=728\), which shows at a glance that 13 and 7 divide it.

card.rule: Whenever an expression looks like a difference of squares or a sum or difference of cubes, factor it before doing anything else.
card.limits: These formulas are special cases; a general sum or difference of powers needs the longer pattern with n terms in the second factor.

media.alt: A fraction whose denominator is the single letter y. Its numerator shows the quantity y minus 1 raised to the 18th power; anything that may follow the power is cut off. The shape is an 18th power of a shifted variable divided by that variable.

A displayed line: the coefficient a sub 2 equals the binomial coefficient 18 choose 15, which equals the binomial coefficient 18 choose 3, which equals 816. The middle step swaps the lower number 15 for 18 minus 15.

concepts.title: Adding zero creatively
concepts.question: How can adding and subtracting the same term turn x^4+4 into a difference of squares?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To factor an expression that is not quite a difference of squares, add zero creatively: add a term and subtract it again so that a perfect square appears. This is wishful thinking applied to factoring.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Adding and subtracting the same term leaves the value unchanged, so you can choose it freely. Choose the term that completes a square, then the leftover subtracted term is hoped to be a square as well.

card.rule: To factor, look for perfect squares and create them by adding and subtracting a suitable term.
card.limits: Adding zero is trial and error: the term must make both parts squares; if the leftover is not a square, try another choice.

concepts.title: Squares of sums with more terms
concepts.question: What is the square of a three-term sum, and why do cross terms matter?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: \((x+y+z)^2=x^2+y^2+z^2+2xy+2xz+2yz\). With four terms, \((x+y+z+w)^2\) adds \(w^2\) and the cross terms \(2xw,\,2yw,\,2zw\). Learn these actively and know how to create and recognise perfect squares.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Multiplying the sum by itself gives every term times every term. Each square appears once; each product of two different terms appears twice, once in each order.

card.rule: Squaring a sum gives every square once and every pair product twice.
card.limits: The cross terms are not optional: leaving them out is the most common slip when squaring.

concepts.title: Completing the square
concepts.question: How does adding and subtracting (a/2)^2 turn x^2+ax into a square minus a constant?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: \(x^2+ax=\left(x+\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2-\left(\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2\). Completing the square means adding the number \((a/2)^2\) so a perfect square appears, and subtracting it to keep the value.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The square \((x+a/2)^2=x^2+ax+a^2/4\) already contains \(x^2+ax\) plus the extra \(a^2/4\), so you subtract that extra. It is adding zero creatively with a chosen term.

card.rule: Half the coefficient of x, squared, is the term to add and subtract.
card.limits: The pattern is cleanest when the coefficient of x squared is 1; otherwise factor it out first.

concepts.title: Square identities that generate triples
concepts.question: How does (x-y)^2+4xy=(x+y)^2 produce Pythagorean triples?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The identity \((x-y)^2+4xy=(x+y)^2\) holds for all x and y. Replacing x and y by their squares gives \((x^2-y^2)^2+(2xy)^2=(x^2+y^2)^2\), so \((a,b,c)=(x^2-y^2,\,2xy,\,x^2+y^2)\) satisfies \(a^2+b^2=c^2\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Expanding \((x+y)^2-(x-y)^2\) leaves exactly \(4xy\). Substituting x squared and y squared turns the product term into \(4x^2y^2=(2xy)^2\).

card.rule: Any two integers x > y give a Pythagorean triple (x^2 - y^2, 2xy, x^2 + y^2).
card.limits: The formula produces triples, but a triple may not be in lowest terms (x = 3, y = 1 gives 8, 6, 10).

concepts.title: Products of sums of two squares
concepts.question: If two integers are each a sum of two squares, why is their product also one?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: \((x^2+y^2)(a^2+b^2)=(xa-by)^2+(ya+bx)^2\). So the product of two integers that are each a sum of two squares is again a sum of two squares.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Expand both squares on the right: the terms \(\pm 2abxy\) cancel, leaving \(x^2a^2+y^2b^2+y^2a^2+x^2b^2\), which is the product on the left. The book notes that this explains how, not why.

card.rule: A product of two sums of two squares is a sum of two squares, with parts xa - by and ya + bx.
card.limits: Both factors must themselves be sums of two squares; 3 is not, so 3 times 5 is not covered.

concepts.title: Simplify toward symmetry, not mechanically
concepts.question: When is combining terms the right way to simplify, and what should guide your choice?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Simplification means moving an expression toward greater simplicity, symmetry or beauty, which are often the same thing. Avoid mindless combinations of terms unless they make the expression simpler.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The goal decides the move. Fractions invite long mechanical work, but a task-oriented approach asks what form makes the next step easy, such as a difference of squares or a symmetric pair.

card.rule: Choose each rewriting by whether it brings you closer to the goal, not by habit.
card.limits: Sometimes you should make an expression uglier because it reveals more, as when 1998/1999 is rewritten as 1 minus 1/1999.

concepts.title: Substituting to remove a radical
concepts.question: How does naming a square root as a new variable simplify an equation, and what must you check afterwards?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: When a square root is the only obstacle, name it: put \(y=\sqrt{\cdots}\). The equation becomes a polynomial in y. Solve for y, discard values that violate \(y\ge 0\), then substitute back to find x.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A square root of a real number is never negative, so any negative root found for y is spurious. The back-substitution turns \(y\) into an equation in x, where the relation between zeros and coefficients gives sums and products of roots.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(x^2+18x+30=2\sqrt{x^2+18x+45}\), let \(y=\sqrt{x^2+18x+45}\). Then \(y^2-15=2y\), so \((y-5)(y+3)=0\); keep \(y=5\), giving \(x^2+18x+20=0\), whose roots have product 20.

card.rule: Name the troublesome radical y, solve for y, keep only y at least 0, then solve for x.
card.limits: The new equation can hide extra roots that fail the original equation, so always apply the condition on y (and check in the original).

media.alt: A cropped formula piece: the number 2 followed by a square root sign whose radicand begins with x squared. The remainder of the radicand is cut off, so only the start of a square root of a quadratic expression, multiplied by 2, can be read.

A cropped formula piece: a square root sign whose radicand begins with x squared. The rest of the radicand is cut off, so only the start of the square root of a quadratic expression can be read, with no coefficient in front of the root.

concepts.title: Pairing factors to cancel radicals
concepts.question: How can you multiply a product of radical factors without expanding every term?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To simplify a product of several radical factors, pair factors so that each pair is a difference of squares: \((u+v)(u-v)=u^2-v^2\). The pair then contains fewer radicals.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Multiplying all the terms out is long and error-prone. A good pair leaves only one radical, and multiplying the pairs gives a difference of squares again that clears the last radical.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \((\sqrt5+\sqrt6+\sqrt7)(\sqrt5+\sqrt6-\sqrt7)=4+2\sqrt{30}\), the last two factors give \(-4+2\sqrt{30}\), and their product is \(120-16=104\).

card.rule: Pair the factors so each pair is a difference of squares, then pair the results again.
card.limits: Pairing does not always remove every radical; choose pairs by their structure and be ready to try another pairing.

concepts.title: Adding equations to symmetrize a system
concepts.question: When a system is nearly symmetric, what single move reveals the total of the unknowns?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If every equation has the same total of the unknowns plus one extra copy of its own variable, add all the equations. The coefficients become symmetric, and the sum of the unknowns can be read off at once.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Adding \(n\) such equations counts every variable the same number of times, so one equation of the form \(c\,(x_1+\dots+x_n)=\text{total of the right sides}\) remains. Then the individual equations give each variable.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the book's five-equation system with right sides 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, adding gives \(6S=6\cdot31\), so \(S=31\).

card.rule: Look for symmetry, add the equations to symmetrize, and then isolate each unknown.
card.limits: The trick needs the right shape: each variable must appear with the same total weight across the equations.

concepts.title: Define a function and use the factor theorem
concepts.question: How can replacing one variable by x and finding zeros prove an identity without expanding?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To prove an identity without multiplying out, replace one variable by x to define a function \(f(x)\). If \(f(b)=0\) and \(f(c)=0\), then \(x-b\) and \(x-c\) are factors of the numerator. Symmetry gives the remaining factors, and a constant is fixed by plugging in numbers.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The factor theorem says a zero a of a polynomial gives a factor \(x-a\). If the numerator has degree 3 and two factors are known, the third is a linear factor, and the identity is determined up to a constant.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(\frac{b-c}{a}+\frac{c-a}{b}+\frac{a-b}{c}\), setting \(a=b\) or \(a=c\) gives 0, and plugging in \(a=1,b=2,c=3\) fixes the constant: the sum equals \(\frac{(a-b)(b-c)(a-c)}{abc}\).

card.rule: Find where a function vanishes, use zeros to read off factors, and fix the constant by a single substitution.
card.limits: The method needs the degree to be small enough that the known factors leave only a constant unknown.

concepts.title: Cubing to remove cube roots
concepts.question: How do you turn an equation containing cube roots into a polynomial equation?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(x=u+v\) with \(u^3\) and \(v^3\) known, cube both sides using \((u+v)^3=u^3+v^3+3uv(u+v)\). The sum \(u+v\) on the right can be replaced by x itself, which removes the radical from the right side.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The identity expresses the cube of a sum through the cubes and the product. Because \(uv\) is often a simple number or one remaining radical, substituting \(u+v=x\) keeps the equation in x.

card.rule: Isolate the radicals, cube with the sum-of-cubes identity, and replace u + v by the known expression.
card.limits: If the product uv is itself a radical, the first cubing leaves one radical and a second cubing is needed.

concepts.title: Sums of squares and cyclic symmetry
concepts.question: How can a sum of squares that must be at most zero pin down every variable?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A sum of squares of real numbers is non-negative, and equals zero only when every square is zero. So if a symmetric system of inequalities forces such a sum to be \(\le 0\), every term is zero.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A real square is never negative, so a total of squares cannot be below zero. If it is not above zero either, no square can be positive.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: From \(x^2+y^2\le 2xy\) we get \((x-y)^2\le 0\), so \(x=y\). The book applies this to five cyclic inequalities and finds \(x_1=\dots=x_5\).

card.rule: Add the inequalities, write the total as half a sum of squares, and conclude all squares vanish.
card.limits: The conclusion only gives equalities among variables; it does not tell you the common value, which stays free.

media.alt: A cropped piece of a formula: a fraction bar with a 2 below it, followed by a large summation sign with index i running from 1 up to 5. The quantity being summed is cut off, so only the half factor and the limits of the sum can be read.

concepts.title: Substituting reciprocals when abc = 1
concepts.question: How does x=1/a, y=1/b, z=1/c simplify a fraction inequality under abc=1?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: When \(abc=1\) and the problem has ugly fractions, substitute \(x=1/a,\ y=1/b,\ z=1/c\). The condition becomes \(xyz=1\), and the fractions lose their cubes.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: \(\frac{1}{a^3(b+c)}=\frac{x^3}{1/y+1/z}=\frac{x^3\,yz}{y+z}=\frac{x^2}{y+z}\), using \(xyz=1\). Each fraction has a simpler denominator.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book turns the 1995 IMO inequality into \(\frac{x^2}{y+z}+\frac{y^2}{z+x}+\frac{z^2}{x+y}\ge\frac32\), which is easier to attack.

card.rule: If a condition and an expression are awkward in a, b, c, try the reciprocals as new variables.
card.limits: The substitution only simplifies the problem; it does not solve it, and the new inequality still needs another idea.

concepts.title: Sigma and pi notation
concepts.question: How do you read a sum or product with an index, and how many terms does a condition like i<j give?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=x_1+\dots+x_n\) and \(\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i=x_1x_2\cdots x_n\). The index i is a dummy variable with any name and any limits, even infinite. Indices can be given by a condition: \(\sum_{d\mid 10}d^2=1^2+2^2+5^2+10^2\), where d runs over the divisors of 10.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The condition under the sign says which values of the index are used. For \(\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\), each unordered pair of different indices occurs once, so it has \(\binom n2\) terms.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(\sum_{3\le i<j\le5}f(i,j)=f(3,4)+f(3,5)+f(4,5)\), and for n = 3 the square \((x_1+x_2+x_3)^2\) is the sum of squares plus \(2\sum_{1\le i<j\le3}x_ix_j\).

card.rule: Read the condition under the sign to see which indices appear; the pair condition i < j gives n(n-1)/2 terms.
card.limits: Informal writing without limits is acceptable when context is clear, but it is technically incomplete; check small cases when in doubt.

media.alt: An identity for the square of a sum: the sum of x sub i for i from 1 to n, all squared, equals the sum of x sub i squared for i from 1 to n, plus twice a second sum of the products x sub i times x sub j taken over all index pairs with 1 at most i less than j at most n.

A summation sign with the index condition d divides 10 written underneath, meaning that d runs over the divisors of 10. The expression being summed is not part of the picture, so only the way the index is specified is visible.

An infinite product with the index n starting at 2 and running up without bound. Each factor is a fraction: n cubed minus 1 in the numerator and n cubed plus 1 in the denominator, followed by a full stop.

concepts.title: Gaussian pairing for arithmetic series
concepts.question: Why does an arithmetic series equal the number of terms times the average of first and last?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: An arithmetic sequence has a constant difference d: \(a,\ a+d,\ a+2d,\dots\). Its sum with n terms, first term a and last term f is \(S=\frac{n(a+f)}{2}\): the number of terms times the average of the first and last.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Write the sum twice, once reversed. Each vertical pair adds to \(a+f\), and there are n pairs, so \(2S=n(a+f)\).

card.rule: Write the sum forwards and backwards; each pair adds to first plus last.
card.limits: The pairing needs terms equally spaced: if consecutive terms do not differ by a constant, the vertical sums are not equal.

media.alt: The formula S equals n times the fraction a plus l over 2. It says the sum S of an arithmetic series is the number of terms n times the average of the first term a and the last term l.

concepts.section: Geometric Series and the Telescope Tool
concepts.title: Summing a geometric series
concepts.question: How does subtracting rS from S sum a geometric series?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A geometric sequence has a common ratio r: \(a,\ ar,\ ar^2,\dots\). For n terms, \(S=a+ar+\dots+ar^{n-1}=\frac{a-ar^n}{1-r}\) when \(r\neq1\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Write S and rS. They are nearly identical, so \(S-rS\) cancels everything except the first term a and the last \(ar^n\): \(S(1-r)=a-ar^n\). This cancelling of a chain is the telescope tool.

card.rule: Subtract r times the sum from the sum: all middle terms cancel and S = (a - ar^n)/(1 - r).
card.limits: The division by 1 - r fails when r = 1; then every term is a and the sum is simply na.

concepts.section: Geometric Series and the Telescope Tool
concepts.title: Telescoping a sum of fractions
concepts.question: How can writing each fraction as a difference make a long sum collapse?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Write each term as a difference of consecutive pieces so that most pieces cancel. The key identity is \(\frac1{k(k+1)}=\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: In \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}\right)\) the \(-\frac1{k+1}\) of one term cancels the \(+\frac1{k+1}\) of the next, leaving \(1-\frac1{n+1}\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(\frac1{1\cdot2}+\frac1{2\cdot3}+\dots+\frac1{99\cdot100}=1-\frac1{100}=\frac{99}{100}\).

card.rule: Find a way to write each term as a difference u(k+1) - u(k), then the sum is the last minus the first.
card.limits: Finding the right difference is the hard part, and the attempt will not always work perfectly; it may only reduce the complexity.

concepts.section: Geometric Series and the Telescope Tool
concepts.title: Telescoping to sum the first n squares
concepts.question: How do you choose a sequence whose differences look like k^2?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To sum \(k^2\), look for a sequence \(u_k\) with \(u_{k+1}-u_k\) close to \(k^2\). Then the sum collapses to \(u_{n+1}-u_1\). The guess \(u_k=k^3\) gives \((k+1)^3-k^3=3k^2+3k+1\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Summing the differences telescopes to \((n+1)^3-1\). Since \(\sum(3j+1)\) is an arithmetic series we already know, the sum of squares can be solved for.

card.rule: Pick u_k of one degree higher so differences have the right leading term, then solve for the unknown sum.
card.limits: An exact telescope is not required: any sequence whose differences are close to what you want reduces the problem.

media.alt: An equation: three times the sum of j squared for j from 1 to n, plus the sum of 3j plus 1 for j from 1 to n, equals n cubed plus 3 n squared plus 3 n. The right side is the total left after a sum of cube differences collapses.

concepts.section: Geometric Series and the Telescope Tool
concepts.title: The catalyst tool
concepts.question: How can multiplying by one new factor make a product collapse?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Sometimes telescoping fails on what you start with, but introducing a single new term transforms the problem. This is the catalyst tool. For \(P=\left(1+\frac1a\right)\left(1+\frac1{a^2}\right)\left(1+\frac1{a^4}\right)\cdots\left(1+\frac1{a^{2^n}}\right)\), multiply by \(1-\frac1a\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each step is a difference of squares \((1-x)(1+x)=1-x^2\), which doubles the exponent and absorbs the next factor. After all factors, \(\left(1-\frac1a\right)P=1-\frac1{a^{2^{n+1}}}\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With a = 2 and three factors, \(P=\frac{1-1/2^8}{1-1/2}=\frac{255}{128}\).

card.rule: Look for a factor that makes each product a difference of squares, and the whole product telescopes.
card.limits: The catalyst is found by recognising the pattern; it does not exist for every product.

media.alt: A column of equalities. It starts with the quantity 1 minus 1 over a, times P, written as the product of 1 minus 1 over a, 1 plus 1 over a, 1 plus 1 over a squared, and so on up to 1 plus 1 over a to the power 2 to the 100. Each next line pairs the leading difference with the next sum, giving 1 minus 1 over a squared, then a to the 4th, and so on, ending at 1 minus 1 over a to the power 2 to the 101.

concepts.title: Infinite geometric series
concepts.question: When does an infinite geometric series have a finite sum, and what is it?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: An infinite series converges if its sum is finite and diverges if it is infinite. The infinite geometric series \(a+ar+ar^2+\cdots=\frac{a}{1-r}\) converges exactly when \(|r|<1\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: When \(|r|\ge1\) the terms do not shrink, so no finite total can result. When \(|r|<1\) the \(ar^n\) in the finite formula tends to zero, leaving \(a/(1-r)\).

card.rule: An infinite geometric series sums to a/(1 - r) exactly when the ratio is smaller than 1 in size.
card.limits: The formula applies only for |r| < 1; with |r| at least 1 the series diverges and the expression a/(1 - r) means nothing.

concepts.title: Comparing series
concepts.question: How can a known series settle the convergence of an unknown one?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(\sum a_k\) converges and \(a_k\ge b_k\ge0\) for all but finitely many k, then \(\sum b_k\) converges. If \(\sum a_k\) diverges and \(b_k\ge a_k\) for all but finitely many k, then \(\sum b_k\) diverges.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A series smaller termwise than one with a finite total cannot exceed that total; one larger termwise than an infinite series is itself infinite. Finitely many exceptions change the sum by a finite amount only.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(\sum\frac1{2^k+k}\) converges, because \(\frac1{2^k+k}\le\frac1{2^k}\) and \(\sum\frac1{2^k}\) is finite.

card.rule: To decide an unknown series, compare it term by term with a known one, in the correct direction.
card.limits: The inequality has to point the right way: a smaller series says nothing if the bigger one diverges.

concepts.title: Why the harmonic series diverges
concepts.question: How does grouping terms and replacing each by a smaller one show the harmonic series is infinite?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The harmonic series \(1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots\) diverges. Group the terms in blocks of lengths 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., and replace every term in a block by the smallest term of that block.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The block from \(\frac1{2^n+1}\) to \(\frac1{2^{n+1}}\) has \(2^n\) terms, each at least \(\frac1{2^{n+1}}\), so the block sums to at least \(\frac12\). Infinitely many blocks each at least \(\frac12\) give an infinite total.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(\frac13+\frac14\ge\frac14+\frac14=\frac12\) and \(\frac15+\cdots+\frac18\ge4\cdot\frac18=\frac12\).

card.rule: Replace a complicated denominator by a larger, simpler one; the sum of the smaller terms already diverges.
card.limits: Terms going to zero does not make a series converge; the harmonic series is the standard counterexample.

media.alt: A mostly empty cropped layout: three short horizontal rules across the top, the fraction 1 over 2 to the power n plus 1 followed by a full stop at the right, and a lone comma lower down. The surrounding terms have been lost, so only these few marks can be read.

concepts.title: Shifting the index and the zeta series
concepts.question: How do you show that the sum of 1/k^s converges for s at least 2?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The zeta function is \(\zeta(s)=\frac1{1^s}+\frac1{2^s}+\frac1{3^s}+\cdots\). It converges for every \(s\ge2\). It suffices to show \(\zeta(2)<\infty\), because for \(s\ge2\) each term \(\frac1{k^s}\le\frac1{k^2}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Compare \(\frac1{k^2}\) with the telescoping series \(\sum\frac1{k(k+1)}\): the inequality goes the wrong way. Shifting the index, \(\frac1{k^2}\le\frac1{k(k-1)}\) for \(k\ge2\), and \(\sum_{k\ge2}\frac1{k(k-1)}=1\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: So \(\zeta(2)\le1+1=2<\infty\).

card.rule: Bound the terms by a telescoping series after shifting the index so that the inequality points the right way.
card.limits: Comparison only gives an upper bound, not the exact value of the sum.

concepts.title: Polynomial vocabulary
concepts.question: What do degree, leading coefficient, monic and constant term mean for a polynomial?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For a set A of numbers closed under addition and multiplication, \(A[x]\) is the set of polynomials \(a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n\) with every \(a_i\in A\). The usual coefficient sets are Z, Q, R and C. Each \(a_ix^i\) is a term or monomial. The degree is the highest exponent whose coefficient is not zero; that coefficient is the leading coefficient. A polynomial is monic if its leading coefficient is 1, and \(a_0\) is the constant term.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Naming the coefficient of \(x^i\) as \(a_i\) consistently keeps long manipulations clear. The coefficient set matters: \(\tfrac12 x\) lies in Q[x] but not in Z[x].

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(5x^3-2x+7\) has degree 3, leading coefficient 5 and constant term 7; \(x^2+3x+1\) is monic.

card.rule: Degree is the largest exponent with a non-zero coefficient, and monic means that coefficient is 1.
card.limits: A zero coefficient does not count toward the degree: 3x^4 + 0x^5 + 2 has degree 4.

concepts.title: Multiplying polynomials by coefficient
concepts.question: How is each coefficient of a product built from the coefficients of the factors?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(A(x)=\sum a_ix^i\), \(B(x)=\sum b_ix^i\) and \(C(x)=A(x)B(x)=\sum c_ix^i\), then \(c_j=a_0b_j+a_1b_{j-1}+\dots+a_jb_0=\sum_{s+t=j,\ s,t\ge0}a_sb_t\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The term \(x^j\) in the product comes from multiplying an \(x^s\) of A by an \(x^t\) of B with \(s+t=j\). Collecting all such pairs gives \(c_j\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \((1+2x)(3+x)=3+7x+2x^2\): the coefficient of x is \(1\cdot1+2\cdot3=7\).

card.rule: The coefficient of x^j in a product is the sum of a_s b_t over all s and t adding to j.
card.limits: The formula needs a_s = 0 when s is beyond the degree of A, and likewise for B.

concepts.title: The polynomial division algorithm
concepts.question: What do quotient and remainder mean for polynomials, and how can division test divisibility?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If f and g are polynomials with coefficients in Z, Q, R, C or \(\mathbb{Z}_n\) (g non-zero), then \(f(x)=Q(x)g(x)+R(x)\), where \(R\) is zero or has degree less than the degree of g. Q is the quotient and R the remainder.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Like integer division, you repeatedly subtract a multiple of g that cancels the leading term, until what is left has smaller degree than g. Degree plays the role of size.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(x^3+x^2+7=(x^2+3)(x+1)+(-3x+4)\), so the quotient is \(x+1\) and the remainder is \(-3x+4\).

card.rule: Dividing f by g leaves a remainder of smaller degree than g; g divides f exactly when the remainder is zero.
card.limits: For integer-coefficient polynomials the quotient may leave Z[x] unless the divisor is monic.

media.alt: The fraction 900 over n plus 10, with 900 in the numerator and the sum n plus 10 in the denominator. It is the leftover term when a cubic expression is divided by n plus 10.

A cropped layout of three stacked rows. Each row begins at the left with a double horizontal bar like an equals sign, followed by three dots; only the top row also has a double bar at the far right. No other symbols are visible.

concepts.title: The quadratic formula comes from completing the square
concepts.question: Why remember how the quadratic formula is derived instead of just the formula?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The quadratic formula says that \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) has solutions \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\). The book says it is far more important to remember how it is derived: by the complete-the-square tool.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Completing the square reduces any quadratic to \((x+h)^2=k\), which is solved by a square root. The method works for any numbers, while the formula is one result of it.

card.rule: To solve a quadratic, complete the square; the formula is only a record of that method.
card.limits: Complete the square handles quadratics; formulas for zeros do not exist in elementary form for general polynomials of degree 5 or more.

media.alt: The top of the quadratic formula: negative b, plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4 a c, above a fraction bar. The denominator below the bar is cut off, and a full stop ends the line.

concepts.title: The remainder theorem
concepts.question: What remainder does P(x) leave when divided by x - a, and why?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If a polynomial \(P(x)\) is divided by \(x-a\), the remainder is \(P(a)\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Division gives \(P(x)=Q(x)(x-a)+r\) with r a constant. This is an identity true for all x, so substitute the convenient value \(x=a\): \(P(a)=r\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Dividing \(x^3-2x+3\) by \(x+2\) leaves remainder \(P(-2)=-8+4+3=-1\).

card.rule: To find a remainder on division by x - a, just evaluate the polynomial at a.
card.limits: The divisor must be linear, of the form x - a; for x + 2 use a = -2.

media.alt: A fraction whose numerator is missing and whose denominator is x plus 2, followed by an equals sign and x squared. Only the denominator and the right side of the equation can be read in this cropped picture.

concepts.title: The factor theorem
concepts.question: If a is a zero of P, what must be a factor of P?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If a is a zero of \(P(x)\), then \(x-a\) is a factor: \(P(x)=(x-a)Q(x)\) for some polynomial Q.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: By the remainder theorem, dividing by \(x-a\) leaves the remainder \(P(a)=0\), so the division is exact.

card.rule: A zero a gives the factor x - a, and a known factor x - a means P(a) = 0.
card.limits: The theorem finds linear factors from zeros; it does not guarantee any zero exists (that is a separate theorem).

concepts.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and multiplicity
concepts.question: How many zeros does a polynomial of degree n have, counting multiplicity?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Every polynomial in C[x] (of degree at least 1) has at least one complex zero. Hence a polynomial of degree n has exactly n complex zeros counted with multiplicity: \(a_nx^n+\dots+a_0=a_n(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_n)\). A zero that appears k times has multiplicity k.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The theorem itself is deep and its proof is beyond the book. Given one zero, the factor theorem removes one linear factor, leaving a polynomial of degree one lower, and repeating gives n factors.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \((x-1)(x-2i)(x+2i)(x-7)^3(x+6)^2\) has degree 8, so 8 zeros with multiplicity, but only 5 distinct ones.

card.rule: A polynomial of degree n has n complex zeros if you count each as often as its multiplicity.
card.limits: Over the real numbers a polynomial may have no zeros at all (x^2 + 1), so the guarantee is for complex zeros.

concepts.title: To know the zeros is to know the polynomial
concepts.question: How do you handle a problem about a polynomial whose zeros you do not know?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A reinterpretation of the factor theorem: to know the zeros of a polynomial is to know the polynomial (up to a constant). If a problem does not show the zeros, find them or shift focus to a related polynomial whose zeros are apparent.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Given \(P(k)=\frac{k}{k+1}\) for \(k=0,\dots,n\), the values say nothing about zeros of P. But \(Q(x)=(x+1)P(x)-x\) has zeros 0, 1, ..., n, so \(Q(x)=Cx(x-1)\cdots(x-n)\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Putting \(x=-1\) (which kills the term \((x+1)P(x)\)) gives \(C=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\). Then \(P(n+1)=\frac{n+1+(-1)^{n+1}}{n+2}\).

card.rule: If you cannot see zeros, build a new polynomial that has them, then fix the constant with a convenient value.
card.limits: The constant C needs one convenient substitution, and the substitute value must not make both sides zero.

concepts.title: Relations between zeros and coefficients
concepts.question: How do the coefficients of a monic polynomial relate to sums and products of its zeros?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For a monic polynomial with zeros \(r_1,\dots,r_n\): \(x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+a_0=(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_n)\). Then \(a_{n-k}=(-1)^k\) times the sum of all products of k different zeros. So \(a_{n-1}=-\)(sum of zeros) and \(a_0=(-1)^n\)(product of zeros).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Expanding the product, each term picks x or minus a zero from every factor. Choosing k zeros and x from the rest gives a term of degree n - k with coefficient \((-1)^k\) times the product of those k zeros.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With zeros 1, 2, 3, 4: \(x^4-10x^3+35x^2-50x+24\); the \(x^2\) coefficient 35 is the sum of the six pair products.

card.rule: Coefficients are plus or minus the sums of products of zeros taken k at a time, alternating in sign.
card.limits: The formulas are for monic polynomials; divide by the leading coefficient first when it is not 1.

concepts.title: Using the coefficient relations strategically
concepts.question: How do you find a coefficient from partial information about the zeros without finding the zeros?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: When a problem asks for a coefficient, use the relations between zeros and coefficients directly, and compute only what is needed. Introduce combined quantities such as \(u=a+b\) and \(v=c+d\) rather than the individual zeros.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The penultimate step toward the target is often factorable: \(ac+ad+bc+bd=(a+b)(c+d)\). That reduces the unknowns to two sums that satisfy two linear equations.

card.rule: Name the quantity you need, find the step before it, and use sums and products of pairs instead of single zeros.
card.limits: This works when the information given (a pair product) splits the zeros into two groups; it does not solve arbitrary systems.

concepts.title: The rational roots theorem
concepts.question: What do the numerator and denominator of a rational zero have to divide?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(P(x)\) has integer coefficients and a rational zero \(\frac ab\) in lowest terms, then the leading coefficient is a multiple of b and the constant term is a multiple of a.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: By the factor theorem and Gauss's Lemma, \(P(x)=(bx-a)Q(x)\) with Q having integer coefficients. The leading coefficient of P is b times that of Q, and the constant term is -a times that of Q.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A zero of \(x^2-2\) of the form \(\frac ab\) needs \(b\mid1\) and \(a\mid2\), so the only candidates are \(\pm1,\pm2\). None works, so \(\sqrt2\) is irrational.

card.rule: List the candidates a/b with a dividing the constant term and b dividing the leading coefficient, then test them.
card.limits: The theorem only lists candidates; each must still be checked, and it needs integer coefficients.

concepts.title: Monic polynomials and irrational numbers
concepts.question: How can you prove a number irrational using a monic polynomial?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Any rational zero of a monic polynomial with integer coefficients must be an integer. Conversely, a number that is not an integer but is a zero of a monic integer polynomial must be irrational.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The rational roots theorem says the denominator of a rational zero divides the leading coefficient 1, so the denominator is 1.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The number \(\sqrt2+\sqrt3\approx3.146\) satisfies \(x^4-10x^2+1=0\) and lies between 3 and 4, so it is irrational.

card.rule: Show the number is not an integer and that it solves a monic integer polynomial.
card.limits: Both parts are needed: a number between integers is irrational only if it is also a zero of a monic polynomial.

concepts.title: Basic arithmetic of inequalities
concepts.question: How do addition, multiplication by a negative number and reciprocals change an inequality?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(x\ge y\) and \(a\ge b\), then \(x+a\ge y+b\). If \(x\ge y\) and \(a\ge0\), then \(ax\ge ay\); if \(a<0\), then \(ax\le ay\). If \(x\ge y\) and x, y have the same sign, then \(\frac1x\le\frac1y\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Adding keeps order because both sides move up by non-negative amounts. Multiplying by a negative number reflects the number line, reversing the order. Taking reciprocals of two positive numbers makes the bigger one smaller; mixed signs break the rule.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Since \(2\le5\), \(-3\cdot2=-6\ge-15=-3\cdot5\), and \(\frac12\ge\frac15\).

card.rule: Adding keeps the direction; multiplying by a negative reverses it; reciprocals reverse it when the signs match.
card.limits: Reciprocals need both numbers non-zero with the same sign: for -2 < 3 the reciprocals -1/2 and 1/3 stay in the same order.

concepts.title: The hierarchy of growth rates
concepts.question: Which of logarithms, powers and exponentials eventually dominates which?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A function f eventually dominates g if \(f(x)>g(x)\) for all large enough x. The hierarchy, from slowest to fastest, is logarithms, powers, exponentials. A quadratic eventually dominates any linear function, \(x^a\) eventually dominates \(x^b\) when \(a>b>0\), and \(c^x\) with \(c>1\) eventually dominates any power.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The 'eventually' matters: \(0.001x^2>100000x+20000000\) only once x is large (it holds for \(x>10^9\)). Graphs show the crossing points; beyond them the faster growth wins.

card.rule: For large enough x, logarithms are beaten by powers and powers are beaten by exponentials.
card.limits: Domination is only eventual, so a faster-growing function can be far smaller at moderate x.

concepts.title: Proving inequalities by equivalent steps
concepts.question: How do you prove an inequality by turning it into simpler equivalent ones?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To compare two quantities, replace the alleged inequality by logically equivalent simpler ones until the truth is obvious. Squaring both sides is allowed when both sides are positive. Taking reciprocals reverses the direction.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each step is reversible, so the last (obviously true or false) inequality is equivalent to the first. A mistake enters only if a step silently changes direction or is not reversible, as squaring sides of unknown sign is.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To compare \(\sqrt{19}+\sqrt{99}\) with \(\sqrt{20}+\sqrt{98}\), square both: this reduces to \(19\cdot99\) versus \(20\cdot98\), i.e. 1881 < 1960. So the first is smaller.

card.rule: Keep each step equivalent, watch for direction reversals, and square only positive quantities.
card.limits: An irreversible step proves nothing: squaring numbers of unknown sign can turn a false claim true.

media.alt: Two displayed comparisons with a question mark where the sign belongs. The first compares 19 plus 2 times the root of 19 times 99 plus 99 with 20 plus 2 times the root of 20 times 98 plus 98. The second, below it, compares the root of 19 times 99 with the root of 20 times 98.

concepts.title: Comparing by a monotone function
concepts.question: How can defining a function show that consecutive fractions increase?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To compare \(\frac{1998}{1999}\) with \(\frac{1999}{2000}\), define \(f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}\). Then the question compares \(f(1998)\) with \(f(1999)\). Rewrite \(f(x)=\frac1{1+1/x}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: As x grows, \(1/x\) decreases, so the denominator \(1+1/x\) decreases, so the fraction increases. Thus f is increasing for positive x, and \(f(1998)<f(1999)\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Likewise \(\frac78<\frac89\), since \(f(7)<f(8)\).

card.rule: Turn a comparison of two numbers into a comparison of one function at two inputs, then show the function is monotone.
card.limits: Rewriting may make the expression uglier, but the new form shows the behaviour.

concepts.title: AM-GM for two numbers
concepts.question: Why is the arithmetic mean of two positive numbers at least their geometric mean?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For positive x and y, \(\frac{x+y}{2}\ge\sqrt{xy}\), with equality only if \(x=y\). The left side is the arithmetic mean and \(\sqrt{xy}\) the geometric mean. Equivalent: for a fixed sum, the product is greatest when the numbers are equal.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The inequality is equivalent to \((x+y)^2\ge4xy\), which is equivalent to \(x^2-2xy+y^2\ge0\), i.e. \((x-y)^2\ge0\). A square is never negative, and is zero only when \(x=y\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If \(x+y=10\), then \(xy\le25\), with the maximum at \(x=y=5\).

card.rule: Arithmetic mean at least geometric mean for positives, with equality only when the numbers are equal.
card.limits: The numbers must be positive; for negatives the geometric mean may be undefined or the inequality fails.

media.alt: The fraction x plus y, in parentheses and squared, over 4. It is the square of the arithmetic mean of x and y.
The fraction x plus y over 2, which is the arithmetic mean of the two numbers x and y.
