concepts.title: Triangulations and the Catalan recurrence
concepts.question: How does fixing one side of a polygon give a recurrence for triangulations?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A triangulation of a convex n-gon cuts it into triangles by non-crossing diagonals. Let t(n) be their number. Experiments give t(3) = 1, t(4) = 2, t(5) = 5. Fixing a base side, the triangle on that base has its third vertex at one of n - 2 places, and this partitions the triangulations. The result is t(n) = t(2) t(n-1) + t(3) t(n-2) + ... + t(n-1) t(2), where t(2) = 1 by convention.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The triangle on the base splits the rest of the polygon into two smaller polygons, one on each side (a side may be degenerate, a 2-gon, which gives no new choices). The two sides are triangulated independently, so their counts multiply; the different positions of the third vertex are disjoint classes, so those products add.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For a hexagon the four positions give t(5) + t(4) + t(4) + t(5) = 5 + 2 + 2 + 5 = 14. For a heptagon the five positions give 14 + 5 + 2 x 2 + 5 + 14 = 42.

card.rule: Triangulations of an n-gon: add, over the position of the third vertex, the product of the counts for the two sub-polygons.
card.limits: The sum has products, not sums, of earlier terms, so the recurrence is not the Fibonacci one. The convention t(2) = 1 is needed to treat degenerate sides uniformly.

media.alt: Four copies of a convex hexagon, each with its bottom side drawn thick as a fixed base. In each, a dashed triangle on that base reaches a different one of the other four vertices: the first and last copies show one dashed segment each, the two middle copies show two dashed segments each.

Five copies of a convex pentagon, each cut into three triangles by two dashed diagonals from a shared vertex. The five pictures differ in which vertex the two diagonals leave, so they show five different triangulations.

Five copies of a convex heptagon, each with its bottom side drawn thick as the fixed base. Dashed segments make a triangle on that base whose third vertex moves along the other five vertices from picture to picture, splitting the rest of the heptagon into smaller polygons.

concepts.title: The Catalan numbers and their closed form
concepts.question: What closed form do the Catalan numbers have, and how does a generating function find it?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The Catalan numbers \(C_0,C_1,C_2,\dots\) are 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, ... and the triangulations of a convex n-gon number \(t_n=C_{n-2}\). Their closed form is \(C_n=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\dbinom{2n}{n}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Let \(f(x)=C_0+C_1x+C_2x^2+\cdots\). The recurrence is a sum of products over indices that add to a constant, exactly the shape of multiplying polynomials, so \(f(x)^2\) has coefficients \(C_1,C_2,\dots\) and \(xf(x)^2=f(x)-1\). Solving this quadratic and expanding with the generalized binomial theorem gives \(C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(C_4=\frac15\binom84=\frac{70}{5}=14\) and \(C_5=\frac16\binom{10}{5}=\frac{252}{6}=42\), matching the table.

card.rule: C_n = C(2n, n) / (n + 1), and a generating function turns the recurrence into a quadratic equation.
card.limits: The generating-function derivation is algebraic; the book mentions a purely combinatorial derivation in its references. The index shift t_n = C_(n-2) depends on starting the Catalan numbers at 0.

concepts.title: Divisibility, primes and composites
concepts.question: What does it mean for one integer to divide another, and which numbers count as prime?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: We say \(b\) divides \(a\), written \(b \mid a\), when \(a = bm\) for some integer \(m\). A number \(n\) is prime when its only divisors are 1 and \(n\); otherwise it is composite. By convention 1 is neither prime nor composite. In this chapter every letter is an integer, and \(p\) and \(q\) always name primes.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Writing \(a = bm\) turns 'divides' into a statement about whole-number multiples, so no fractions are needed. The exclusion of 1 is a convention the book adopts, not a theorem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(6 \mid 42\) because \(42 = 6 \cdot 7\). But 5 does not divide 42, since no integer \(m\) gives \(42 = 5m\). And \(91 = 7 \cdot 13\) is composite even though it is odd and does not end in 5.

card.rule: \(b \mid a\) means \(a = bm\) for an integer \(m\); a prime has no divisors besides 1 and itself, and 1 is not counted as prime.
card.limits: Divisibility is about integers only: 2 does not divide 7 although 7/2 exists as a fraction. Not being divisible by 2, 3 or 5 does not make a number prime.

concepts.title: There are infinitely many primes
concepts.question: Why can no finite list of primes contain every prime?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: There are infinitely many primes. Euclid's proof is by contradiction: assume every prime is on the finite list \(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_N\), and form \(Q = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_N + 1\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: \(Q\) is not divisible by any listed prime. If \(Q\) is prime it is new, since it exceeds every \(p_i\). If \(Q\) is composite it has a prime divisor, which is not on the list either. Both cases contradict completeness.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the list 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 we get \(Q = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509\). Q is composite, yet 59 and 509 are primes missing from the list.

card.rule: Multiply any finite list of primes and add 1: the result has a prime divisor outside the list, so the list was not complete.
card.limits: Q need not be prime itself, and the proof does not say that product plus one is always prime. It also uses, without proof, that a composite Q has a prime divisor; the book flags this as a small gap.

concepts.title: Every number above 1 factors into primes
concepts.question: Why must every integer greater than 1 be a product of primes?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Every natural number greater than 1 can be factored completely into primes. For example \(360 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5\). Euclid's proof relies on this when it says a composite \(Q\) has at least one prime divisor.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book suggests strong induction. If \(n\) is prime it is its own factorization. If not, \(n = ab\) with both factors between 1 and \(n\); each is smaller, so by hypothesis each already factors into primes, and joining them factors \(n\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(84 = 4 \cdot 21\). Neither 4 nor 21 is prime, so continue: \(4 = 2 \cdot 2\) and \(21 = 3 \cdot 7\). Hence \(84 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7\), with every factor prime.

card.rule: Every natural number greater than 1 is a product of primes, found by splitting composites until only primes remain.
card.limits: This is existence only: it does not say the factorization is the only one. Uniqueness is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. The number 1 is excluded.

concepts.title: Unique factorization and the PPF
concepts.question: What does the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic say, and what is a prime-power factorization?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (FTA): every natural number above 1 factors into primes in exactly one way, apart from the order of the factors. Grouping equal primes gives the prime-power factorization (PPF), written \(n = p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \cdots p_t^{e_t}\) with distinct primes \(p_i\) and exponents \(e_i\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The proof comes later in the chapter, from the division algorithm and the gcd. For now note what it buys: two numbers are equal only if their PPFs agree prime by prime.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(360 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5\). The lists \(2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot3\cdot5\) and \(5\cdot3\cdot2\cdot3\cdot2\cdot2\) count as the same factorization, only reordered.

card.rule: Every natural number above 1 has one and only one prime-power factorization, up to the order of the factors.
card.limits: Uniqueness is a special property of the integers. Some number systems have it and others do not, so it cannot be assumed whenever one 'factors' numbers.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: n equals p sub 1 to the power alpha sub 1, then dots, then p sub k to the power alpha sub k; a prime factorization written in general form.

concepts.title: Why the 'obvious' needs the FTA
concepts.question: Why does an obvious-looking statement such as 5x = 3y implying 3 divides x depend on the FTA?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If integers \(x, y\) satisfy \(5x = 3y\), then \(3 \mid x\) and \(5 \mid y\). This seems obvious, yet proving it uses the FTA: 5x is a multiple of 3, 3 and 5 are different primes, so the 3 must come from the PPF of x.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: With unique factorization, the prime 3 in the PPF of \(5x\) cannot come from 5, so it lies in \(x\). If factorization were not unique, \(5x\) could have one factorization containing a 5 and no 3, and another containing a 3 and no 5.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take E, the even integers. The numbers 2, 6, 10 and 30 cannot be factored inside E, and \(60 = 2 \cdot 30 = 6 \cdot 10\). So E has two different factorizations of 60.

card.rule: Statements that look obvious about divisibility may rest on unique factorization, which holds in the integers but not everywhere.
card.limits: The FTA is not needed for every divisibility fact; the book proves some, such as gcd facts, without it. And the statement holds in the integers, so this idea cannot be used to doubt it.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: GCD, LCM and relatively prime
concepts.question: What are the greatest common divisor and the least common multiple of two numbers, and when are they relatively prime?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The greatest common divisor \((a,b)\), also written GCD(a, b), is the largest integer dividing both \(a\) and \(b\). If \((a,b) = 1\) the numbers are relatively prime. The least common multiple \([a,b]\), or LCM(a, b), is the least positive integer that is a multiple of both.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: These are definitions, not theorems: each picks one extreme member of a set of common divisors or common multiples. For two different primes, the only shared divisor is 1, so \((p,q) = 1\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \((66,150) = 6\), \((84,90) = 6\) and \((4096,999) = 1\), so 4096 and 999 are relatively prime although neither is prime.

card.rule: The GCD is the largest shared divisor, the LCM the smallest positive shared multiple, and GCD 1 means relatively prime.
card.limits: Relatively prime does not mean prime: 4096 and 999 are both composite. And the notation (a, b) here means the gcd, not an ordered pair.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: GCD and LCM from prime factorizations
concepts.question: How do the exponents in two PPFs give the GCD and LCM, and how are they related to the product?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Write \(a = p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_t^{e_t}\) and \(b = p_1^{f_1}\cdots p_t^{f_t}\), allowing zero exponents. Then \((a,b) = \prod p_i^{\min(e_i,f_i)}\) and \([a,b] = \prod p_i^{\max(e_i,f_i)}\). Also \((a,b)\,[a,b] = ab\) for all positive integers.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: For each prime, the smaller exponent is the most both numbers can share, and the larger is the least a common multiple needs. Since \(\min + \max = e + f\) for each prime, the exponents of the gcd and lcm add up to those of \(ab\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(360 = 2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5\) and \(1597050 = 2\cdot3^3\cdot5^2\cdot7\cdot13^2\). Taking smaller exponents: \(2^1\cdot3^2\cdot5^1 = 90\).

card.rule: GCD takes the smaller exponent of each prime, LCM the larger, and \((a,b)\,[a,b] = ab\).
card.limits: The min and max rule needs the PPFs, so it presumes unique factorization, though the product rule can also be proved from the definitions alone. A prime missing from one number counts with exponent 0.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: Linear combinations and the GCD
concepts.question: What follows if g divides a and b, and how can a combination ax + by show numbers are relatively prime?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A quantity \(ax + by\) with integers \(x, y\) is a linear combination of \(a\) and \(b\). If \(g \mid a\) and \(g \mid b\), then \(g \mid ax + by\) for all integers \(x, y\). Consequences: consecutive integers are relatively prime, and if \(ax + by = 1\) has integer solutions then \(a\) and \(b\) are relatively prime.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Write \(a = gm\) and \(b = gn\). Then \(ax + by = g(mx + ny)\), a multiple of \(g\). A common divisor of \(a\) and \(b\) then divides 1 whenever \(ax + by = 1\), so it can only be 1.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(7\cdot(-3) + 11\cdot 2 = 1\), so 7 and 11 are relatively prime. Any common divisor of 15 and 16 divides \(16 - 15 = 1\).

card.rule: A common divisor of a and b divides every combination ax + by, so a combination equal to 1 proves the numbers are relatively prime.
card.limits: The coefficients x and y may be negative; if they had to be positive the result could fail. The fact runs one way: a combination equal to 1 forces gcd 1, and the converse needs a separate argument.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: The division algorithm
concepts.question: What does the division algorithm guarantee, and why is the remainder strictly smaller than the divisor?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be positive integers with \(b \ge a\). Then there are integers \(q \ge 1\) and \(r\) with \(0 \le r < a\) such that \(b = qa + r\). Here \(q\) is the quotient and \(r\) the remainder.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book suggests the extreme principle: among the non-negative numbers of the form \(b - ka\), take the smallest. If it were at least \(a\), subtracting one more \(a\) would give a smaller one, a contradiction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Dividing 333 by 51: \(333 = 6\cdot 51 + 27\), with quotient 6 and remainder 27, and \(0 \le 27 < 51\).

card.rule: For positive \(a \le b\) there are integers \(q \ge 1\) and \(0 \le r < a\) with \(b = qa + r\).
card.limits: The proof uses the well-ordering of the integers and the integer 1. In a system lacking them, such as the even integers E, no such quotient and remainder need exist.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: The GCD as the smallest positive combination
concepts.question: Why is the gcd of a and b the smallest positive value of ax + by?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The greatest common divisor of \(a\) and \(b\) is the smallest positive linear combination of \(a\) and \(b\). For example \((8,10) = 2\): the smallest positive value of \(8x + 10y\) is 2, reached at \(x = -1, y = 1\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Let \(u\) be the smallest positive combination and \(g = (a,b)\). Since \(g\) divides every combination, \(g \le u\). If \(u\) did not divide \(a\), then \(a = ku + r\) with \(0 < r < u\), and \(r = a - ku\) would be a smaller positive combination. So \(u\) divides \(a\) and \(b\), hence \(u \le g\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \((7, 11) = 1\) because \(7(-3) + 11(2) = 1\). No smaller positive value exists, so the gcd is 1.

card.rule: The gcd is the smallest positive value that ax + by takes as x and y range over the integers.
card.limits: The proof uses the extreme principle and the division algorithm, not prime factorizations. It describes the value, not how to find x and y; for that see the Euclidean algorithm.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: A prime dividing a product
concepts.question: If a prime divides a product ab, why must it divide a or b?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(p\) is prime and \(p \mid ab\), then \(p \mid a\) or \(p \mid b\). The book proves this without using the FTA, and then uses it as the key to the FTA.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Suppose \(p\) divides neither. Then \(p\) is relatively prime to \(a\), so \(px + ay = 1\) for some integers. Multiply by \(b\): \(pxb + aby = b\). Both terms are multiples of \(p\) (since \(p \mid ab\)), so \(p \mid b\), a contradiction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(7 \mid 14 \cdot 9 = 126\) and indeed \(7 \mid 14\). But 6 divides \(4\cdot 9 = 36\) while 6 divides neither 4 nor 9.

card.rule: A prime that divides a product divides at least one of the factors.
card.limits: Primality is essential: 6 divides 4 · 9 but neither factor. The conclusion is 'or', not 'and', and a non-prime modulus needs different reasoning.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: Why factorization is unique
concepts.question: How does the lemma that a prime dividing a product divides a factor prove unique factorization?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Uniqueness in the FTA follows from the lemma 'if \(p \mid ab\) then \(p \mid a\) or \(p \mid b\)'. The book shows the idea on \(n = 2^3\cdot 7^6\) and says it generalizes.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: First, no other prime \(q\) can divide \(n\): repeated use of the lemma would force \(q\) to divide 2 or 7, impossible for a different prime. Second, suppose also \(n = 2^8\cdot 7^3\). Cancelling common powers leaves \(7^3 = 2^5\), which again would make 7 divide 2.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If \(3^2\cdot 5^7 = 3^6\cdot 5^3\) were true, cancelling \(3^2\cdot 5^3\) would leave \(5^4 = 3^4\); then 5 would divide 3, which is impossible.

card.rule: Two factorizations of one number would, after cancelling common powers, make a power of one prime equal a power of another, which the lemma forbids.
card.limits: The book argues one concrete case and asks the reader to check that it generalizes. It also needs the division algorithm; in a system without it, uniqueness can fail.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: Rational zeros of monic polynomials
concepts.question: Why must a rational zero of a monic integer polynomial be an integer?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A polynomial with integer coefficients is monic if its highest-degree term has coefficient 1. If a monic polynomial has a rational zero, that zero is an integer.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Write the zero as \(u/v\) in lowest terms and clear fractions. The equation becomes \(u^n = -v(\ldots)\), so \(v\) divides \(u^n\). But \(v\) shares no factor with \(u^n\), so \(v = \pm 1\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The monic polynomial \(x^2 - x - 6\) has zeros 3 and \(-2\), both integers. The polynomial \(2x - 1\) is not monic and has the non-integer zero \(1/2\).

card.rule: A monic integer polynomial cannot have a fractional rational zero.
card.limits: The argument needs the coefficient of the top term to be 1; otherwise zeros like 1/2 are possible. It also needs lowest terms, so that u and v share no factor.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: Bounding a GCD by a linear combination
concepts.question: How can a clever linear combination of two terms bound their gcd, whatever n is?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For \(a_n = u + n^2\) let \(d_n = (a_n, a_{n+1})\). A combination of \(a_n\) and \(a_{n+1}\) that cancels \(n\) shows \(d_n \mid 4u + 1\) for every \(n\), so \(d_n \le 4u+1\). The bound is reached at \(n = 2u\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: With \(a = a_n\), \(b = a_{n+1}\): \(b - a = 2n+1\) and \(2a - n(b-a) = 2u - n\). Then \(2(2u-n) + (2n+1) = 4u+1\), a combination of \(a\) and \(b\) with no \(n\) left.

card.rule: To bound a gcd, build a linear combination of the two terms that is independent of n; the gcd divides it.
card.limits: Showing a gcd divides a number only gives an upper bound. To say the bound is the maximum you must also exhibit a case that reaches it. Experimentation, not clairvoyance, finds the combination.

concepts.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
concepts.title: The Euclidean algorithm
concepts.question: How does repeated division with remainder compute the gcd of two numbers?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Divide the larger number by the smaller, then divide the previous divisor by the remainder, and keep going until the remainder is 0. The last non-zero remainder is the gcd.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each step replaces \((b, a)\) by \((a, r)\) where \(b = qa + r\). Any common divisor of \(b\) and \(a\) divides \(r = b - qa\), and any common divisor of \(a\) and \(r\) divides \(b\), so the gcd never changes. The remainders shrink to 0.

card.rule: Repeat division with remainder; the last non-zero remainder is the gcd.
card.limits: The algorithm gives the gcd but does not itself show how to write it as ax + by; that requires working the steps backwards. The remainders must shrink, so the quotients need the division algorithm.

concepts.title: Congruence and residues
concepts.question: What does a ≡ b (mod m) mean, and how does it relate to remainders?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: We write \(a \equiv b \pmod m\) when \(a - b\) is a multiple of \(m\), equivalently \(a = b + mk\) for some integer \(k\). Dividing \(a\) by \(b\) and getting remainder \(r\) means \(a \equiv r \pmod b\). Only \(m\) integers are different modulo \(m\), namely the remainders \(0, 1, \ldots, m-1\); the set is called \(\mathbb{Z}_m\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: \(a - b = mk\) and \(a = b + mk\) say the same thing. A remainder \(r\) from \(a = qm + r\) gives \(a - r = qm\), a multiple of \(m\). Every integer is congruent to exactly one remainder, so there are only \(m\) classes.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(38 \equiv 3 \pmod 7\) since \(38 - 3 = 35 = 5\cdot 7\). The numbers 7 and 3 are different residues modulo 5 but equal residues modulo 4.

card.rule: \(a \equiv b \pmod m\) means \(m \mid a - b\); modulo \(m\) there are only \(m\) different values, the remainders \(0, \ldots, m-1\).
card.limits: Congruence depends on the modulus: numbers congruent modulo one m need not be congruent modulo another. And a ≡ b (mod m) means the difference is a multiple of m, not that the difference equals m.

concepts.title: Adding and multiplying congruences
concepts.question: How can congruences be added and multiplied to find a remainder of a huge power?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(a \equiv b\) and \(c \equiv d \pmod m\), then \(a + c \equiv b + d\) and \(ac \equiv bd \pmod m\). So you may replace numbers by congruent ones before adding or multiplying, and raise both sides of a congruence to a power.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Write \(a = b + mk\) and \(c = d + ml\). Then \(a + c = b + d + m(k+l)\) and \(ac = bd + m(\ldots)\), where everything in the bracket is an integer.

card.rule: Congruent numbers can be swapped for each other inside sums, products and powers.
card.limits: Division is not covered: you cannot divide both sides freely, and exponents must be real exponents, not reduced modulo m. Only the base is reduced, not the exponent.

concepts.title: Digit sums and divisibility by 9 and 3
concepts.question: Why is a number congruent to its digit sum modulo 9 and modulo 3?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In base 10, a number is congruent to the sum of its digits modulo 9 and modulo 3. So a number is divisible by 9 exactly when its digit sum is, and likewise for 3.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Since \(10 \equiv 1 \pmod 9\), every power \(10^k \equiv 1\). A number \(d_k 10^k + \cdots + d_0\) is therefore congruent to \(d_k + \cdots + d_0\). The same works modulo 3, because \(10 \equiv 1 \pmod 3\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(7812\) has digit sum \(7+8+1+2 = 18\), which is a multiple of 9, so \(9 \mid 7812\) (indeed \(7812 = 9 \cdot 868\)).

card.rule: Replace a base-10 number by its digit sum when working modulo 9 or modulo 3.
card.limits: The rule gives the remainder modulo 9 or 3 only; it says nothing directly about other moduli such as 4 or 11. A digit sum divisible by 3 gives divisibility by 3, not necessarily by 9.

concepts.title: Simplify first: primes and primitive solutions
concepts.question: Why does the book advise assuming primes, or numbers without common factors, at the start?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: When beginning a number theory investigation, assume the variables are prime or at least relatively prime; the general case often follows with a few technical details. Applied to \(x^n + y^n = z^n\): we may assume \(n\) is prime, and that \(x, y, z\) have no common factor (a primitive solution).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A common factor \(g\) can be removed: if \(x = ga,\, y = gb,\, z = gc\), dividing the equation by \(g^n\) gives \(a^n + b^n = c^n\). For the exponent, \(n = km\) lets us write \(x^{km} = (x^k)^m\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If \(x^3 + y^3 = z^3\) had no non-zero integer solutions, then neither would \(x^{12} + y^{12} = z^{12}\), since it equals \((x^4)^3 + (y^4)^3 = (z^4)^3\).

card.rule: Reduce to the simplest case, primes or relatively prime variables, before attacking the general problem.
card.limits: The reduction shifts work to the technical details, which are not free. The book states it for Fermat's Last Theorem, where it was a first step toward a proof that took until 1995.

concepts.title: Multiplicative inverses modulo a prime
concepts.question: Why do all non-zero elements of Z_p have multiplicative inverses when p is prime?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A multiplicative inverse of \(x\) modulo \(m\) is a number \(y\) with \(xy \equiv 1 \pmod m\). If \(p\) is prime and \(x\) is not a multiple of \(p\), there is a unique \(y \in \{1, \ldots, p-1\}\) with \(xy \equiv 1 \pmod p\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book proved this earlier (Example 2.3.4); the key step is that the multiples \(x, 2x, \ldots, (p-1)x\) are all different modulo \(p\), so exactly one of them equals 1.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In \(\mathbb{Z}_7\) the inverses of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are 1, 4, 5, 2, 3, 6. In \(\mathbb{Z}_6\), \(5 \cdot 5 \equiv 1\), so 5 is its own inverse.

card.rule: Modulo a prime p, every residue other than 0 has exactly one multiplicative inverse.
card.limits: The guarantee needs p prime. Modulo a composite number such as 6, some non-zero residues have no inverse, so division is not generally available.

concepts.title: Multiples of x run through all non-zero residues
concepts.question: Why are the multiples x, 2x, …, (p−1)x all different modulo a prime?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(p\) is prime and \(x \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\), then \(x, 2x, \ldots, (p-1)x\) are distinct in \(\mathbb{Z}_p\). Equivalently, as sets, \(\{x, 2x, \ldots, (p-1)x\} = \{1, 2, \ldots, p-1\}\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_p\): the multiples are a rearrangement of the non-zero residues.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Suppose \(ix \equiv jx\) for some \(1 \le i < j \le p-1\). Then \(p \mid (j-i)x\). A prime dividing a product divides a factor, but \(0 < j - i < p\) and \(p \nmid x\). That is a contradiction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With \(p = 7\) and \(x = 4\): \(4\cdot1, 4\cdot2, \ldots, 4\cdot6\) give \(4, 1, 5, 2, 6, 3\) modulo 7, a permutation of 1 to 6.

card.rule: Multiplying 1, 2, …, p − 1 by a non-zero x modulo a prime p only rearranges them.
card.limits: Primality is essential. Modulo 6 the multiples of 2 are 2, 4, 0, 2, 4, with repeats and a zero. And x must not be a multiple of p, or every multiple is 0.

concepts.title: Fermat's little theorem
concepts.question: Why is a^(p−1) congruent to 1 modulo a prime p when p does not divide a?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Fermat's little theorem: if \(p\) is prime and \(p \nmid a\), then \(a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p\). (The word 'little' separates it from Fermat's Last Theorem.)

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The sets \(\{a, 2a, \ldots, (p-1)a\}\) and \(\{1, 2, \ldots, p-1\}\) are equal in \(\mathbb{Z}_p\), so their products agree: \(a^{p-1}(p-1)! \equiv (p-1)!\). Since \((p-1)!\) is relatively prime to \(p\), it can be cancelled.

card.rule: For a prime p not dividing a, \(a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p\).
card.limits: The hypothesis p ∤ a is needed: if p divides a, then a^(p−1) is 0 modulo p. And p must be prime: for the composite modulus 9, 2⁸ leaves remainder 4, not 1.

concepts.title: Using Fermat to force composites
concepts.question: How does Fermat's little theorem produce infinitely many composite terms in a sequence?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For \(x_0 = 1\), \(x_{n+1} = a x_n + b\) with positive integers \(a, b\), the sequence has infinitely many composite terms. Idea: if \(x_n = p\) is a prime not dividing \(a\) or \(a-1\), then \(x_{n+p-1}\) is a multiple of \(p\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: By induction \(x_{n+k} = a^k p + b\,\dfrac{a^k - 1}{a-1}\). Take \(k = p - 1\): Fermat gives \(a^{p-1} \equiv 1\), so \(p\) divides the numerator \(a^{p-1}-1\), and \(p \nmid a-1\) keeps the factor \(p\) after the division.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(a = 2,\, b = 3\) the terms 1, 5, 13, 29, 61, 125, … include 5 at the second place; four steps later 125 is again a multiple of 5.

card.rule: If a term is a prime p, Fermat's theorem forces the term p − 1 places later to be a multiple of p.
card.limits: The argument excludes the finitely many primes dividing a or a − 1, and works by contradiction: assume only finitely many composites, so eventually all terms are primes. If a and b are both odd another route (parity) gives composites.

concepts.title: Multiplicative functions
concepts.question: What is a multiplicative function, and why do its values at prime powers determine everything?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A function \(f\) defined on the natural numbers is multiplicative if \(f(ab) = f(a)f(b)\) whenever \(a\) and \(b\) are relatively prime. Then \(f(1) = 1\), and \(f\) is fixed by its values \(f(p^r)\) at prime powers.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The PPF \(n = p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_t^{e_t}\) splits \(n\) into pairwise relatively prime factors \(p_i^{e_i}\), so \(f(n) = f(p_1^{e_1})\cdots f(p_t^{e_t})\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Let \(d(n)\) count the divisors of \(n\). Then \(d(4) = 3\), \(d(3) = 2\) and \(d(12) = 6 = 3\cdot 2\), because 4 and 3 are relatively prime.

card.rule: A multiplicative function turns a product of coprime numbers into a product of values.
card.limits: The product rule needs a and b relatively prime: d(2 · 6) is not d(2) d(6). Not every natural function is multiplicative; for instance n + 1 gives 2 · 3 + 1 = 7 against 3 · 4 = 12.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: only a large summation sign with the condition p to the power e, then a double vertical bar, then n, written underneath it. No summand is visible.

concepts.title: Sums of powers of divisors and counting divisors
concepts.question: How is the number of divisors of n read off from its prime-power factorization?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Define \(\sigma_r(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d^r\), the sum of the \(r\)th powers of the divisors of \(n\). With \(r = 0\) this counts divisors: \(d(n) = \sigma_0(n)\). If \(n = p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_t^{e_t}\), then \(d(n) = (e_1+1)(e_2+1)\cdots(e_t+1)\), and \(d\) is multiplicative.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A divisor of \(n\) picks, for each prime \(p_i\), an exponent from \(0, 1, \ldots, e_i\), that is \(e_i + 1\) independent choices; by unique factorization different choices give different divisors.

card.rule: The number of divisors is the product of (exponent + 1) over the primes in the PPF.
card.limits: The product formula for d(ab) needs a and b relatively prime: for shared primes, d(ab) is smaller than d(a) d(b). In practice only r = 0 and r = 1 are used often, though r can be any integer.

media.alt: The definition of the divisor-power sum: sigma with subscript r applied to n equals the sum, over every divisor d of n, of d raised to the power r, followed by a comma.

concepts.title: The sum of divisors σ(n)
concepts.question: How do you compute the sum of the divisors of a prime power and of a product of two primes?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The sum of divisors is \(\sigma(n) = \sigma_1(n)\). For a prime power \(\sigma(p^r) = \dfrac{p^{r+1}-1}{p-1}\), and for distinct primes \(p, q\): \(\sigma(pq) = (p+1)(q+1)\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The divisors of \(p^r\) are \(1, p, \ldots, p^r\), a geometric series. The divisors of \(pq\) are \(1, p, q, pq\), and \(1 + p + q + pq = (1+p)(1+q)\).

card.limits: The formula (p+1)(q+1) is for distinct primes only; for p = q it would not give the divisors of p². Also σ(n) is the sum of divisors, not their count.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: the sum over divisors d of n of the quantity minus one raised to the power n over d, multiplied by d, ending with a full stop.

concepts.title: Pairing divisors of coprime factors
concepts.question: If n = ab with a and b relatively prime, how do divisors of n split into divisors of a and b?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(n = ab\) with \(a\) and \(b\) relatively prime. Every divisor \(d\) of \(n\) can be written \(d = uv\) with \(u \mid a\) and \(v \mid b\), and this is a one-to-one correspondence: different pairs \((u,v)\) give different divisors.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Since \(a\) and \(b\) share no prime, each prime power in \(d\) lies in \(a\) or in \(b\) and cannot be shared. So \(d\) splits uniquely into a part dividing \(a\) and a part dividing \(b\).

card.rule: For coprime a and b, divisors of ab correspond one-to-one to pairs (u, v) with u dividing a and v dividing b.
card.limits: Coprimality is essential: with a = b = 2 there are four pairs (u, v) but the product 4 has only three divisors, as 1·2 and 2·1 coincide.

concepts.title: Summing a multiplicative function over divisors
concepts.question: If f is multiplicative, why is F(n), the sum of f over the divisors of n, multiplicative too?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For a function \(f\), let \(F(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)\). If \(f\) is multiplicative, then so is \(F\). Taking \(f(n) = n^r\) gives \(F = \sigma_r\), and \(f(n) = 1\) gives \(F = d\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: For \(a\) and \(b\) coprime, divisors of \(ab\) are the products \(uv\), so \(F(ab) = \sum f(uv) = \sum f(u)f(v) = \big(\sum f(u)\big)\big(\sum f(v)\big) = F(a)F(b)\).

card.rule: A sum of a multiplicative function over the divisors is multiplicative.
card.limits: The hypothesis that f is multiplicative is needed. The function n + 1 has f(1) = 2, so it is not multiplicative, and the divisor sum of it fails to multiply on coprime arguments.

concepts.title: Euler's phi function by inclusion-exclusion
concepts.question: How does counting the complement with inclusion-exclusion give φ(n)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: \(\varphi(n)\) is the number of positive integers up to \(n\) that are relatively prime to \(n\). For a prime \(p\), \(\varphi(p) = p - 1\). Example: \(\varphi(12) = 4\), because 1, 5, 7 and 11 are the numbers up to 12 relatively prime to 12.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Only the primes dividing \(n\) matter: a number shares a factor with \(n\) exactly when a prime divisor of \(n\) divides it. For 12, count multiples of 2 or 3 by inclusion-exclusion and subtract from 12.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(|M_2 \cup M_3| = |M_2| + |M_3| - |M_6| = 6 + 4 - 2 = 8\), so \(\varphi(12) = 12 - 8 = 4\), where \(M_k\) is the set of multiples of \(k\) up to 12.

card.rule: φ(n) counts the integers up to n that share no factor with n, found by counting the complement.
card.limits: Inclusion-exclusion lists one term per subset of the primes dividing n, so it grows long for many primes. And M_2 ∩ M_3 = M_6 uses that 2 and 3 are relatively prime.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: the letter M with subscript k equals the floor of n divided by k, meaning the fraction n over k inside floor brackets, followed by a comma.
Cropped formula piece: two stray fractions from a longer formula, 2 pi over p at the upper right and 2 pi over n followed by a comma at the lower left.

concepts.title: The product formula for φ
concepts.question: How does φ(n) factor into a product over the primes dividing n?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: \(\varphi(p^r) = p^r - p^{r-1}\), \(\varphi(pq) = (p-1)(q-1)\), and in general \(\varphi(n) = n\prod_{p \mid n}\left(1 - \dfrac1p\right)\). The function \(\varphi\) is multiplicative.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Inclusion-exclusion over the primes dividing \(n\) gives \(n - \sum \frac np + \sum \frac n{pq} - \cdots\), which factors as \(n\prod(1 - \frac1p)\). Then \(\varphi(p^r) = p^r(1 - \frac1p) = p^{r-1}(p-1)\), so the formula is a product of prime-power values.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(\varphi(360) = 360\left(1-\tfrac12\right)\left(1-\tfrac13\right)\left(1-\tfrac15\right) = 360\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac45 = 96\).

card.rule: \(\varphi(n) = n\prod_{p \mid n}(1 - 1/p)\), and \(\varphi\) is multiplicative.
card.limits: The product runs over the distinct primes dividing n, not over prime factors with repetition. The quick argument (half odd, two-thirds of those not multiples of 3, …) assumes divisibility by different primes is independent, which needs justification.

concepts.title: The Möbius function μ
concepts.question: How is μ(n) defined, and why does its sign depend on the number of prime factors?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: \(\mu(1) = 1\); \(\mu(n) = 0\) if \(p^2 \mid n\) for some prime \(p\); and \(\mu(n) = (-1)^r\) if \(n = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r\) is a product of \(r\) distinct primes. The function \(\mu\) is multiplicative.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The definition is built to encode inclusion-exclusion: each squarefree divisor contributes a sign that alternates with the number of primes, and any repeated prime kills the term.

card.rule: μ(n) is 0 if a prime square divides n, else (−1)^r for r distinct primes.
card.limits: μ is zero on every number divisible by a prime square, even if it has many other primes. A sign of −1 does not mean one prime factor: it means an odd number of distinct primes.

concepts.title: Σμ(d) over divisors is 0, and a formula for φ
concepts.question: Why does the sum of μ over the divisors of n equal 0 for n > 1?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: \(\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d) = 1\) if \(n = 1\) and \(0\) if \(n > 1\). Consequently \(\varphi(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)\,\dfrac nd\): the Möbius function filters out terms of inclusion-exclusion.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: \(\mu\) is multiplicative, so the divisor sum \(F(n)\) is multiplicative. For a prime power, \(F(p^r) = 1 + (-1) + 0 + \cdots = 0\). Hence \(F(n) = 0\) as soon as \(n\) has a prime factor.

card.rule: The Möbius function sums to 0 over the divisors of any n > 1.
card.limits: The sum is 1 for n = 1, so the statement is about n > 1. And terms with a repeated prime vanish, so only squarefree divisors matter.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: phi of n equals the sum, over all divisors d of n, of mu of d multiplied by the fraction n over d, ending with a full stop.

concepts.title: Möbius inversion
concepts.question: If F(n) is the sum of f over the divisors of n, how do you recover f from F?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(F(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)\), then \(f(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)\,F\!\left(\dfrac nd\right)\). This 'solves' the divisor-sum equation for \(f\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Substituting the definition of \(F\) into the right side gives a double sum in which the coefficient of each \(f(k)\) is \(\sum \mu(u)\) over the divisors of \(n/k\). That sum is 0 unless \(k = n\), so only \(f(n)\) survives.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A word of length \(n\) over 26 letters is prime if it is not a repetition of a smaller word. The number of prime words is \(p(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)\,26^{n/d}\); for example \(p(2) = 26^2 - 26 = 650\).

card.rule: Möbius inversion recovers f(n) as a signed sum of F over the divisors of n.
card.limits: The identity needs F to be the divisor sum of f exactly. For squares of primes and higher, terms with μ = 0 drop out, so only squarefree divisors matter in the sum.

concepts.title: Euler's extension of Fermat's little theorem
concepts.question: Why does a^φ(m) ≡ 1 (mod m) when a and m are relatively prime?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Euler's extension of Fermat's little theorem: if \(m\) is any natural number (prime or not) and \(a\) is relatively prime to \(m\), then \(a^{\varphi(m)} \equiv 1 \pmod m\). For \(m = p\) prime this is Fermat's theorem, since \(\varphi(p) = p - 1\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Emulate Fermat's proof. Multiply the \(\varphi(m)\) residues relatively prime to \(m\) by \(a\); this only rearranges them. Equating the products gives \(a^{\varphi(m)}P \equiv P\), and \(P\) is relatively prime to \(m\), so it can be cancelled.

card.rule: If a is relatively prime to m, then \(a^{\varphi(m)} \equiv 1 \pmod m\).
card.limits: The hypothesis gcd(a, m) = 1 is needed: powers of 4 modulo 10 are 4, 6, 4, 6, never 1. The exponent is φ(m), not m − 1, when m is composite.

concepts.title: Linear diophantine equations
concepts.question: When does ax + by = c have integer solutions, and how are all of them found?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A diophantine equation is an equation whose variables are integers. The linear equation \(ax + by = c\) has solutions exactly when \(\gcd(a,b)\) divides \(c\). If \((x_0, y_0)\) is one solution, all solutions are \(x = x_0 + \frac{b}{g}t,\; y = y_0 - \frac{a}{g}t\) for integers \(t\), where \(g = \gcd(a,b)\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The values of \(ax + by\) are exactly the multiples of \(g\), the smallest positive combination. Adding \(b/g\) to \(x\) and subtracting \(a/g\) from \(y\) leaves \(ax + by\) unchanged, and these are all the changes possible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(3x + 21y = 19\) has no solution, since \(\gcd(3,21) = 3\) does not divide 19. But \(3x + 19y = 4\) has \(x = -24 + 19t,\; y = 4 - 3t\).

card.rule: ax + by = c is solvable in integers exactly when gcd(a, b) divides c, and one solution generates them all.
card.limits: This complete theory is special to linear equations; most higher-degree diophantine equations have none. Solvability concerns integers: 3x + 21y = 19 has real solutions.

concepts.title: Four questions for a diophantine equation
concepts.question: Which four questions should you ask about any diophantine equation?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For any diophantine equation, ask: (1) Is it in simple form? Divide out common factors or assume the variables share none. (2) Do solutions exist? (3) Are there no solutions? (4) Can we find all solutions? The book notes the third is quite frequently the first to ask.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: These are a plan, not a theorem. Each question closes a different gap: simplify the setting, show something exists, rule the whole equation out, or describe the complete set and prove it is complete.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(x^2 + y^2 = 1000003\) has no solutions (modulo 4). \(3x + 21y = 19\) has none (gcd). And \(x^2 + y^2 = z^2\) has a complete description of its primitive solutions.

card.rule: Simplify the equation, then ask whether solutions exist, whether none exist, and whether you can list them all.
card.limits: The questions guide an investigation but do not decide it: most higher-degree equations have no complete theory. Finding one solution does not answer the fourth question, which asks that the whole set be shown complete.

concepts.title: The factor tactic
concepts.question: How can you rewrite a diophantine equation as a product equal to a constant?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Factoring is an essential tactic: rewrite the equation so one side is a product of integer expressions and the other a constant. Then only finitely many factor pairs need checking. Book example: right triangles with integer sides whose area equals perimeter.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: After clearing the radical and fraction the area-perimeter equation becomes \(xy - 4x - 4y + 8 = 0\). Adding 8 to both sides gives \((x-4)(y-4) = 8\), since the left side almost factored already.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The factor pairs of 8 give \((x,y) = (6,8), (8,6), (5,12), (12,5)\), so just two triangles: 6-8-10 and 5-12-13.

card.rule: Add a constant to make the equation factor, then list the factor pairs of the constant.
card.limits: The factorization is only useful when the right side is a fixed non-zero constant, so the number of integer factor pairs is finite. Squaring to clear a radical can add solutions, so check them in the original equation.

concepts.title: Filtering modulo n
concepts.question: How can looking at an equation modulo n show that it has no solutions?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Reduce the equation modulo a well-chosen \(n\) and list the possible residues. If the two sides cannot match, there are no integer solutions. Example: squares leave remainder 0 or 1 modulo 4, so \(x^2 + y^2\) leaves 0, 1 or 2, never 3.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: \(0^2 = 0,\ 1^2 = 1,\ 2^2 \equiv 0,\ 3^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4\). Since \(1000003 \equiv 3 \pmod 4\), the equation \(x^2 + y^2 = 1000003\) has no integer solutions. In general \(x^2 + y^2 = n\) fails whenever \(n \equiv 3 \pmod 4\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book's example is \(x^2 + y^2 = 1000003\): \(1000003 = 4\cdot 250000 + 3\), so no pair of integers works.

card.rule: If the residues on the two sides never match modulo n, the equation has no integer solutions.
card.limits: The filter can only exclude: a residue that is possible does not prove a solution exists (21 ≡ 1 mod 4 but is not a sum of two squares). Choose n well; parity is the case n = 2.

concepts.title: Primitive Pythagorean triples: setup
concepts.question: Why can a Pythagorean solution be assumed to have pairwise relatively prime entries, with exactly one even leg?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For \(x^2 + y^2 = z^2\) assume positive entries and a primitive solution (no common factor). A common divisor of any two of \(x, y, z\) divides the third, so the entries are pairwise relatively prime. Then exactly one of \(x, y\) is even.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: If \(d \mid x\) and \(d \mid y\), then \(d^2 \mid z^2\), so \(d \mid z\). Parity: both even contradicts relative primality; both odd gives \(z^2 \equiv 2 \pmod 4\), impossible for a square.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (3, 4, 5) is primitive. (6, 8, 10) is not, and neither are the multiples (9, 12, 15), …, which all come from (3, 4, 5).

card.rule: A primitive Pythagorean triple has pairwise coprime entries, and exactly one of its legs is even.
card.limits: Primitivity is an assumption justified by dividing out the gcd, which loses no solutions up to scaling. It holds for squares of integers; the parity argument leans on squares being 0 or 1 modulo 4.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: the equation x squared plus y squared equals z squared, written on one line and ending with a full stop. Nothing else is shown.

concepts.title: All primitive Pythagorean triples
concepts.question: How do GCD analysis and perfect squares produce every primitive Pythagorean triple?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: All primitive solutions of \(x^2 + y^2 = z^2\) (with \(x\) even) are \(x = 2rs,\ y = r^2 - s^2,\ z = r^2 + s^2\), where \(r\) and \(s\) are relatively prime and one is odd, one even.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: \(x^2 = (z-y)(z+y)\) is a square. The gcd of \(z-y\) and \(z+y\) divides \(2z\) and \(2y\), and \(y \perp z\), so it is 2. A product of two numbers with gcd 2 that is a square gives \(z+y = 2r^2\), \(z-y = 2s^2\), with \(r \perp s\).

card.rule: Primitive Pythagorean triples are exactly (2rs, r² − s², r² + s²) for coprime r and s of opposite parity.
card.limits: If r and s are both odd, y and z are even and the triple is not primitive. Also a product being a square does not make each factor a square unless the factors are relatively prime; 6² = 3 · 12 is the book's counterexample.

concepts.title: Comparing exponents of 2: the Putnam 1992 problem
concepts.question: How can the greatest power of 2 dividing each side of (x²+y²)^m = (xy)^n settle the equation?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Putnam 1992: for given \(m\), find positive \((n, x, y)\) with \(n\) relatively prime to \(m\) and \((x^2+y^2)^m = (xy)^n\). Write \(p^t \,\|\, N\) when \(p^t\) is the exact power of \(p\) dividing \(N\) (for example \(3^2 \,\|\, 360\)). Result: no solutions for odd \(m\); for even \(m\), only \(n = m+1,\ x = y = 2^{m/2}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: AM-GM gives \(n > m\); parity forces \(x, y\) even. Take \(2^r \,\|\, x\), \(2^s \,\|\, y\). If \(r < s\), the left side has \(2^{2rm}\) and the right \(2^{nr+ns}\), impossible since \(n > m\). The same holds for every prime, so \(x = y\).

card.rule: Compare exponents of each prime on both sides: unequal valuations of x and y are impossible, so x = y.
card.limits: The argument that parity can be repeated forever is avoided by the extreme principle. The case r = s needs extra care because a² + b² of two odd numbers has exactly one factor of 2.

concepts.section: Can a Polynomial Always Output Primes?
concepts.title: No integer polynomial outputs only primes
concepts.question: Why can no polynomial with integer coefficients be prime at every positive integer?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Euler's \(f(x) = x^2 + x + 41\) is prime for \(x = 0, \ldots, 39\) but \(f(41) = 41\cdot 43\). In general, for a polynomial \(f\) with integer coefficients, \(f(u + f(u))\) is a multiple of \(f(u)\), so no such polynomial (with constant term \(\pm 1\)) gives only primes.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: If \(f(u) = p\), then \(u + p \equiv u \pmod p\), so \((u+p)^k \equiv u^k\) and \(f(u+p) \equiv f(u) \equiv 0 \pmod p\). So \(p\) divides \(f(u+p)\); that value is composite unless it equals \(\pm p\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x) = x^3 + x + 1\): \(f(1) = 3\), \(f(4) = 69 = 3\cdot 23\), \(f(7) = 351 = 3^3\cdot 13\), \(f(10) = 1011 = 3\cdot 337\). Every third input gives a multiple of 3.

card.rule: If f(u) = p then p divides f(u + kp) for every integer k, so a polynomial cannot be prime at every input.
card.limits: A polynomial can give many primes in a row, as Euler's gives 40. The proof must also handle the finitely many inputs where f equals p itself, by moving to u + 2p, u + 3p, and so on.

concepts.section: If You Can Count It, It's an Integer
concepts.title: A product of k consecutive integers is divisible by k!
concepts.question: Why is the product of k consecutive integers a multiple of k!?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The product of \(k\) consecutive integers is divisible by \(k!\). The pure number-theory proof is possible but a counting view is easier: the quotient is a binomial coefficient, hence an integer.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: \(m(m+1)(m+2)\cdots(m+k-1) = k!\binom{m+k-1}{k}\), and binomial coefficients count subsets, so they are integers. The moral: keep your point of view flexible, since anything involving integers is fair game for combinatorial reasoning.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(7\cdot8\cdot9\cdot10\cdot11 = 55440 = 5!\cdot\binom{11}{5} = 120\cdot462\).

card.rule: A product of k consecutive integers equals k! times a binomial coefficient, so k! divides it.
card.limits: The factorial is k!, matching the number of consecutive factors; a larger factorial need not divide the product. For instance 4 · 5 = 20 is not a multiple of 3! = 6 (it is of 2!).

concepts.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
concepts.title: Words, shifts and sororities
concepts.question: How does shifting the letters of a word split all words of length p into groups?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: With an alphabet of \(a\) letters there are \(a^p\) words of length \(p\). The shift \(s\) moves the last letter to the front: \(s(\text{fermats}) = \text{sfermat}\). Words are sisters if finitely many shifts turn one into the other; a word's sisters form its sorority. Words with all letters equal are boring.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Any word is its own sister, so every word lies in a sorority. If \(s(u) = u\), the last letter equals the first, and each letter equals its neighbour, so \(u\) is boring. There are exactly \(a\) boring words.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With 26 letters and \(p = 7\), the sorority of integer has the seven words integer, rintege, erinteg, gerinte, egerint, tegerin, ntegeri.

card.rule: The shift groups the a^p words of length p into sororities, and the a boring words are the ones fixed by the shift.
card.limits: Counting sororities needs a prime length. For p = 4, the word abab is not boring yet s²(abab) = abab, so the argument that only boring words repeat fails.

concepts.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
concepts.title: Sororities have 1 or p members
concepts.question: Why does grouping non-boring words into sororities of size p prove Fermat's little theorem?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For prime \(p\), every sorority has exactly 1 member (a boring word) or exactly \(p\) members. So the \(a^p - a\) non-boring words fall into groups of \(p\), and \(p \mid a^p - a\). That is Fermat's little theorem, \(a^p \equiv a \pmod p\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: If \(s^r(u) = u\) for some \(0 < r < p\), then \(u\) is boring, because \(p\) is prime. So a non-boring word returns to itself only after \(p\) shifts, and its \(p\) shifts are all different.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With \(a = 2\) and \(p = 5\) there are \(32 - 2 = 30\) non-boring words, forming \(30/5 = 6\) sororities of five words each.

card.rule: Count words two ways: a^p − a non-boring words are partitioned into groups of p, so p divides a^p − a.
card.limits: The argument breaks for a composite length: with p = 6 and a = 2, the word 010101 returns after two shifts, so sororities of size 2 and 3 exist and 2⁶ − 2 = 62 need not split into groups of 6.

concepts.title: Which primes are sums of two squares?
concepts.question: Which primes p can be written as x² + y², and what does experiment suggest?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For \(x^2 + y^2 = p\): there are no solutions if \(p \equiv 3 \pmod 4\) (the modulo-4 filter), and \(p = 2 = 1^2 + 1^2\) is boring. That leaves primes \(p \equiv 1 \pmod 4\), where experiments suggest a solution always exists.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The no-solution part is proved by residues of squares modulo 4. The existence part is only a conjecture from data at this point, which the rest of the section proves.

card.rule: A prime with remainder 3 modulo 4 is never a sum of two squares; the experiments suggest every prime with remainder 1 is.
card.limits: Numerical experiments only suggest the truth; the book says it still has to prove the claim. The result concerns primes: not every number with remainder 1 modulo 4 is a sum of two squares, as 21 shows.

concepts.title: Factoring x² + y² using a square root of −1
concepts.question: How does a square root of −1 modulo p let x² + y² factor?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(u^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p\), then \(x^2 + y^2 \equiv (x - uy)(x + uy) \pmod p\). So every pair \(y = k,\ x = uk\) makes \(x^2 + y^2\) a multiple of \(p\). If \(x\) and \(y\) are both below \(\sqrt p\), then \(x^2 + y^2 < 2p\) and it equals \(p\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Over the integers \(x^2 + y^2\) does not factor, but modulo \(p\) the number \(i\) makes sense as \(u\). The two hurdles: a square root of \(-1\) must exist, and the values must be small.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(p = 13\), \(u = 5\) since \(25 \equiv -1\). The pair \((x, y) = (5, 1)\) gives 26, a multiple of 13. Reducing \(y = 3,\, x = 15\) to \(x \equiv 2\) gives \(4 + 9 = 13\).

card.rule: Modulo p, a square root u of −1 factors x² + y², giving pairs with x² + y² divisible by p.
card.limits: A multiple of p need not equal p: (5, 1) gives 26 = 2 · 13. The method also needs the square root of −1 to exist and a small enough pair, the two hurdles the rest of the section removes.

concepts.title: The pigeonhole step: making x and y small
concepts.question: How does the pigeonhole principle guarantee a small pair (x, y) with x² + y² = p?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(u^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p\), with \(u > \sqrt p\), and \(t = \lfloor \sqrt p\rfloor\). Among \(u, 2u, \ldots, tu\) reduced modulo \(p\), some \(ku\) has absolute value below \(\sqrt p\). Then \(y = k\) and \(x = ku\) reduced are both below \(\sqrt p\), so \(x^2 + y^2 = p\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The \(t\) values \(u, \ldots, tu\) are distinct modulo \(p\). Mark \(\sqrt p, 2\sqrt p, \ldots, t\sqrt p\) on the line from 0 to \(p\). If a value lands left of the first mark or right of the last, we are done. Otherwise \(t\) values lie in \(t - 1\) gaps, so two share a gap.

card.rule: Among the multiples u, 2u, …, tu one reduces to a value smaller than √p, by the pigeonhole principle.
card.limits: The marks √p, 2√p, … are irrational positions, so no value lands exactly on one. The method needs a square root u of −1 modulo p to already be available, which the next idea supplies.

concepts.title: A square root of −1 from Wilson's theorem
concepts.question: How does Wilson's theorem produce an explicit square root of −1 when p ≡ 1 (mod 4)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(p\) is prime and \(p \equiv 1 \pmod 4\), then \(\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!^{\,2} \equiv -1 \pmod p\). So \(u = \left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!\) is an explicit square root of \(-1\). This finishes the proof that \(x^2 + y^2 = p\) is solvable when \(p \equiv 1 \pmod 4\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Wilson's theorem: \((p-1)! \equiv -1\). Pair \(k\) with \(p - k \equiv -k\): \((p-1)! \equiv \prod k(-k) = (-1)^{(p-1)/2}\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!^2\). Since \((p-1)/2\) is even, the sign is plus.

card.rule: For a prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4), ((p − 1)/2)! squared is −1 modulo p.
card.limits: It needs p ≡ 1 (mod 4) so that (p − 1)/2 is even and the minus signs cancel. For p ≡ 3 (mod 4) the sign is −1 and the same product gives +1, not −1.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: a fraction bar with the number 2 below it. The numerator is blank or too faint to read in this crop, so only the denominator is certain.

concepts.title: The two parts of a geometry problem
concepts.question: What are the two parts of a typical geometry problem, and what does the second part ask for?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A typical geometry problem has two parts. First a diagram is described, usually in words, and you must draw it correctly. Then you are asked to prove a rigidity statement: a property that does not change however the diagram is drawn.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Drawing the diagram is harder than it looks, and beginners often spend too little effort on it. The authors urge good drawing tools, or a dynamic geometry program, because accurate pictures that can be modified make investigation easier.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Draw a circle and a point P. Any line through P that cuts the circle at two points X and Y gives a product PX times PY. The claim to prove is that the product is the same for every such line.

card.rule: Draw the described diagram carefully first, then look for the property that stays the same however the diagram is drawn.
card.limits: One accurate drawing shows the property in one case only; the claim to prove covers every way the diagram can be drawn.

concepts.title: The power of a point
concepts.question: What number stays the same when a line is turned about a fixed point P and cuts a fixed circle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Fix a point P and a circle. A line through P meets the circle at X and Y. The power of P is the product PX times PY. The Power of a Point theorem (POP) says this product does not depend on which line is drawn.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Two lines through P give two triangles sharing the angle at P. Equal inscribed angles make them similar, and cross-multiplying their side ratios gives the equal products. The full proof comes in the solutions section.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take a circle of radius 5 and a point P outside it, 13 from the centre. The line through the centre meets the circle at distances 8 and 18 from P, so the power is 144. Every other line through P gives 144 as well.

blocks.label: If-then
blocks.text: There are three cases: P outside, inside or on the circle. On the circle one of the two points is P itself, so the product is zero.

card.rule: For a fixed point and circle, PX times PY is the same for every line through P that cuts the circle.
card.limits: The product uses distances from P to each cutting point, not the chord length XY. The statement concerns lines that cut the circle at two points.

media.alt: A circle with a point P outside it at the upper right. Two lines from P each cross the circle twice: the upper line meets it first at X and then at Y, the lower line first at X' and then at Y'.

concepts.title: The angle bisector theorem
concepts.question: In what ratio does the bisector of an angle of a triangle cut the opposite side?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In triangle ABC the bisector of angle A meets side CB at D. Then CD divided by DB equals AC divided by AB. In words: the two pieces of the opposite side are in the same ratio as the two sides next to the bisected angle.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book gives two proofs. One makes similar triangles by adding a point on the bisector; the other compares the areas of the two triangles that the bisector creates.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Let AC = 6, AB = 4 and CB = 10. The ratio is 6 to 4, so CD = 6 and DB = 4.

blocks.label: If-then
blocks.text: The converse holds too: if D on CB satisfies the ratio, then AD bisects angle CAB.

card.rule: The bisector of angle A splits the opposite side so that CD/DB = AC/AB.
card.limits: It concerns an interior angle bisector reaching the opposite side; the longer neighbouring side gets the longer piece, so match each piece with the side that meets it at that end.

media.alt: A triangle with an unlabelled apex at the upper left and a base with points C, D and B in that order from left to right. Segments run from the apex to C, to D and to B.

concepts.title: Medians and the centroid
concepts.question: Where do the three medians of a triangle meet, and how is each median cut there?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A median is a segment from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The Centroid Theorem says the three medians of a triangle meet in one point G, and G cuts every median in the ratio 2 to 1: the part next to the vertex is twice the part next to the midpoint.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Two medians are shown to cut each other in 1 to 2 pieces by similar triangles built on the line joining two midpoints; a phantom point then shows the third median passes through the same point. The proof is in the solutions section.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A median is 18 long. The centroid is 12 from the vertex and 6 from the midpoint.

card.rule: The medians are concurrent at the centroid, which lies two thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.
card.limits: The 2 to 1 ratio is measured from the vertex; it describes medians only, not altitudes or angle bisectors.

media.alt: A triangle with vertices C at lower left, B at lower right and an unlabelled top vertex. Three segments join each vertex to a point on the opposite side, namely D, E and F, and cross at one point G inside; these are the medians.

concepts.title: What you may assume
concepts.question: Which results may you use without proof, and which are left for you to prove?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Strict Euclidean geometry starts from undefined objects such as points and lines, and from postulates. To save time the book hands you a larger stock of results labelled Fact, which you may assume. A result with no label is an exercise you should prove yourself.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Survival geometry is meant to be lean but enough to start most problems. Doing the unlabelled exercises actively, and not reading passively, is what prepares you for tricky questions.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Congruence conditions and the triangle inequality are labelled facts. That vertical angles are equal carries no label, so it is an exercise.

card.rule: Assume what is labelled Fact; prove what is unlabelled, and do not read passively.
card.limits: The facts are granted for speed. Some rest on deeper postulates, so a label means 'assume here', not 'needs no proof anywhere'.

media.alt: Five small drawings of a long strip of paper show stages of a folding procedure: a strip with one slanted crease, a strip with a corner folded over in black, a larger folded piece, and strips with one or two creases.

concepts.title: Notation for lines, rays, segments and angles
concepts.question: How do the symbols for a line, ray, segment, length and angle differ, and which letter is the vertex?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A line through A and B extends forever in both directions. A ray starts at A and passes through B. A segment begins at A and ends at B. The length of the segment is a number, also written AB. Angle ABC has its vertex at the middle letter B; its measure is written m angle ABC.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Precise symbols avoid confusion, but in practice the authors write AB loosely and rely on context. In a simple, uncluttered figure a single letter can name an angle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In triangle ABC, extend side BC past C to a point D. The interior angle at C is angle ACB, and the exterior angle is angle ACD.

card.rule: The middle letter is the vertex; use three letters for an angle when a figure is crowded.
card.limits: Loose notation is acceptable only when context decides whether AB means a line, segment or length, and a single letter can name an angle only if no other angle shares that vertex.

media.alt: A triangle with an unlabelled apex at the top left and unlabelled lower vertices. The base is extended to the right past the second vertex to a point D, so an exterior angle appears there.

concepts.title: Straight, right, complementary and supplementary angles
concepts.question: How are straight, right, complementary and supplementary angles related in measure?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A straight angle is formed by three points on a line and measures 180 degrees, or pi radians. A right angle is half of that, 90 degrees; perpendicular lines make four. Two angles are complementary if they sum to a right angle and supplementary if they sum to 180 degrees.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: These are definitions, built from the straight angle. Degrees and radians are used interchangeably, whichever is convenient.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An angle of 37 degrees has complement 53 degrees and supplement 143 degrees.

card.rule: Complementary angles sum to 90 degrees; supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees.
card.limits: The names apply to a pair of angles by their sum, wherever the angles lie; they need not be adjacent.

concepts.title: Congruence conditions
concepts.question: Which triples of equal measurements are enough to show that two triangles are congruent?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Two triangles are congruent if one can be moved onto the other, so that all corresponding angles and lengths are equal. Going round a triangle, you meet side, angle, side and so on. Equal records of side-angle-side (SAS), ASA, SSS or AAS show congruence.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: These are granted as a fact. Each recorded triple pins down the triangle so that only one shape and size fits.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two triangles each have angles of 40 and 60 degrees and a side of 7 opposite the 80-degree angle. Two angles and a side not between them is AAS, so they are congruent.

blocks.label: Counterexample
blocks.text: Side-side-angle (ASS) fails in general. With angle 30 degrees, adjacent side 10 and opposite side 6, two different triangles fit. It is safe when the angle is at least 90 degrees or the second side is longer than the first. AAA gives only similarity.

card.rule: SAS, ASA, SSS and AAS prove congruence; ASS and AAA do not by themselves.
card.limits: Matching the right kind of triple is essential: the angle must sit in the right place relative to the sides, and equal angles alone fix only the shape.

concepts.title: Inequalities in triangles
concepts.question: How do side lengths and angle sizes of a triangle limit each other?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Triangle inequality: the sum of any two sides of a triangle is strictly greater than the third side. Angle inequality: in triangle ABC, if angle A is greater than angle B then side BC is longer than side AC, and conversely. The larger angle faces the longer side.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: These are granted as facts. In the first, going directly between two points is shorter than any detour, and equality would make the three points lie on one line.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Sticks of length 3, 4 and 8 cannot form a triangle because 3 + 4 is less than 8. In a triangle with sides 7, 9 and 5, the longest side 9 faces the largest angle.

card.rule: Two sides together must exceed the third, and the longest side faces the largest angle.
card.limits: The inequality is strict: sides 4, 6 and 10 collapse into a flat segment. Angle inequalities compare an angle with the side opposite it, not an adjacent one.

concepts.title: Vertical angles
concepts.question: When two lines cross, which of the four angles are equal?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: When two lines meet in a point, four angles are formed, in two pairs of opposite angles. Opposite angles are called vertical angles, and vertical angles are equal.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book leaves this as an easy exercise. Each of the two vertical angles together with their common neighbour forms a straight angle, so both equal 180 degrees minus the same angle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two lines cross and one angle is 65 degrees. The opposite angle is also 65 degrees, and the two neighbours are each 115 degrees.

card.rule: Opposite angles at a crossing of two lines are equal.
card.limits: Vertical angles are equal; angles that sit side by side at a crossing are supplementary, not equal unless each is 90 degrees.

media.alt: Two lines cross at point C. One passes through B, C and D, the other through A, C and E, with arrowheads at both ends. B and E are on opposite sides of C, as are A and D.

concepts.title: Alternate interior angles and parallel lines
concepts.question: What do parallel lines and a crossing transversal tell you about the angles at the two crossings?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A line that crosses two parallel lines is a transversal. Fact 8.2.6: alternate interior angles cut by a transversal of parallel lines are equal. The converse also holds: if two lines are cut by a third and the alternate interior angles are equal, the two lines are parallel.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book grants this as the critical fact about parallel lines, the source of many lemmas. It rests on Euclid's parallel postulate; other geometries change that postulate.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Lines AB and CD are parallel and BC crosses both. Then angle BCD equals angle ABC. If angle ABC is 70 degrees, so is angle BCD.

blocks.label: If-then
blocks.text: The statement assumes the lines are parallel. The converse is the tool for proving that lines are parallel from equal angles.

card.rule: Parallel lines give equal alternate interior angles, and equal alternate interior angles give parallel lines.
card.limits: The equality needs the lines to be parallel; for lines that are not, the alternate angles differ. Alternate means on opposite sides of the transversal and between the two lines.

media.alt: Two horizontal parallel lines with arrowheads, A and B on the upper one and C and D on the lower. A slanted transversal crosses both at B and C. A small arc marks the angle at B and another marks the angle at C on opposite sides of the transversal.

concepts.title: Angle sum and exterior angle of a triangle
concepts.question: Why do the angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees, and what does an exterior angle equal?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The interior angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees. An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles at the other vertices.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Through vertex A of triangle ABC, draw a line parallel to BC. Alternate interior angles equal the angles at B and C, and the three angles at A form a straight angle. The exterior angle follows because it is supplementary to the interior angle next to it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A triangle has angles 50 and 60 degrees, so its third angle is 70 degrees. The exterior angle at that vertex is 110 degrees, which equals 50 plus 60.

card.rule: The angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two far interior angles.
card.limits: The sum rule holds in Euclidean geometry because it rests on the parallel-lines fact; the exterior angle statement refers to the two interior angles that are not adjacent to it.

concepts.title: Properties of a parallelogram
concepts.question: What can be proved about the sides, angles and diagonals of a parallelogram?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite edges are parallel. Its opposite sides are equal, its opposite angles are equal, adjacent angles are supplementary, and its diagonals bisect each other.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Draw a diagonal. It is a transversal of both pairs of parallel sides, so alternate angles are equal; it is also a shared side. ASA then makes two triangles congruent, which gives equal opposite sides. The other diagonal and vertical angles give the bisecting diagonals.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A parallelogram has diagonals 10 and 14. They cross at their midpoints, so the crossing is 5 from the ends of the short diagonal and 7 from the ends of the long one.

card.rule: Opposite sides and angles of a parallelogram are equal, adjacent angles add to 180, and the diagonals bisect each other.
card.limits: These hold for every parallelogram; they do not say the diagonals are equal or perpendicular, which happens only in special cases such as rectangles and rhombuses.

media.alt: A parallelogram with A at the top left, B at the top right, C at the bottom and D at the bottom right. AB and CD are the two horizontal sides, AC and BD the two slanted sides. No diagonal is drawn.
The same four-point parallelogram with A top left, B top right, C bottom left and D bottom right, now with the diagonal BC drawn. It splits the figure into triangle ABC and triangle DCB.

concepts.title: Drawing auxiliary objects
concepts.question: How do you decide what to add to a figure so that a proof can start?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The most productive technique in this chapter is drawing an auxiliary object: a line, circle or triangle added to the figure. Ask what the penultimate step of the proof must be, and add the objects that step needs.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: If the only tool for equal lengths is congruent triangles, triangles must exist, so you force them into existence by drawing a diagonal. The goal tells you what is missing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, draw a diagonal. The diagonal creates two triangles that can be shown congruent.

blocks.label: Common slip
blocks.text: Adding too many objects makes the figure hopelessly confused. Look for natural entities: triangles, circles, symmetry.

card.rule: Let the penultimate step of the proof tell you which auxiliary object to draw, and add few.
card.limits: Finding the right object takes skill, experience and luck; no rule guarantees it, and each added object must earn its place.

concepts.title: Base angles of an isosceles triangle
concepts.question: What can you say about the angles of a triangle that has two equal sides?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A triangle is isosceles if two sides are equal. The angles opposite the equal sides, the base angles, are equal. The angle between the equal sides is the vertex angle.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Drawing the segment from the vertex to the midpoint of the base creates two triangles congruent by SSS, so the base angles match. The book leaves the proof as an easy exercise.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In triangle ABC with AB = AC and vertex angle 40 degrees, the base angles B and C are equal, and each is (180 - 40)/2 = 70 degrees.

card.rule: Equal sides of a triangle have equal angles opposite them.
card.limits: It is a statement about triangles with two equal sides. A triangle whose angles are equal in some other way has to be shown isosceles by a separate argument.

concepts.title: Joining midpoints and the phantom point method
concepts.question: How does a phantom point help prove that joining the three midpoints cuts a triangle into four congruent triangles?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In triangle ABC, let D, E, F be the midpoints of BC, AC, AB. Lines DE, EF, FD cut the triangle into four congruent triangles. The proof uses a phantom point: invent a point with a desired property, then show it coincides with the intended point.

blocks.label: Why it is true
