blocks.text: Draw through F a line parallel to BC and call its meeting with AC by the name E-prime. Draw through F a parallel to AC meeting BC at D-prime. Congruent triangles give BD-prime equal D-prime C and CE-prime equal E-prime A, so the phantoms are the midpoints D and E.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A triangle with sides 6, 8, 10 has a medial triangle with sides 3, 4, 5, and each of the four small triangles has area one quarter of the whole.

blocks.label: Used for
blocks.text: The phantom point plays the part of a contrary assumption in proof by contradiction: a concrete object to work with that disappears once it has done its job.

card.rule: To prove a point has a property, build a phantom point that has it, then show the phantom equals the real point.
card.limits: A phantom point is only a device: the proof is complete only after the phantom is shown to coincide with the intended point.

media.alt: A triangle with vertex B at the lower left and unlabelled top and lower-right vertices. F is on the left side, E' on the right side, joined by a horizontal segment. D' is on the base, and F is joined to D' by a slanted segment.

concepts.title: Circle vocabulary
concepts.question: What do centre, chord, arc, central angle, inscribed angle and tangent mean?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In a circle with centre O, a chord joins two points of the circle; an arc is the part of the circle between two points. A central angle has its vertex at O, and its measure defines the measure of the arc it cuts off. An inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle. A tangent meets the circle in exactly one point.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: These are definitions. Arc BC is read counterclockwise from B to C, so the convention tells you which of the two arcs between B and C is meant.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If central angle COB is 110 degrees, the arc from B to C that it cuts off measures 110 degrees. An inscribed angle at A that cuts off the same arc is said to subtend it.

card.rule: Arcs are measured by their central angles; inscribed angles have vertices on the circle.
card.limits: An arc is ambiguous between two choices of path, so the counterclockwise convention matters; a chord is a segment while an arc is part of the circle.

media.alt: A circle with centre O and three points A, B and C on it, joined into triangle ABC. O is joined to B and to C. A straight line through D and B touches the circle only at B.

A right triangle on a horizontal base with angle theta marked at the left vertex. A slanted side rises to the upper right. A circular arc centred at the left vertex runs from a point D on the slanted side down to a point B on the base. A vertical segment from D meets the base at E, and another rises at B.

concepts.title: Chords, radii and the three for two sale
concepts.question: If a line has two of three features relating it to a chord and a circle, what follows?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Take a line, a circle and a chord. Three statements: the line passes through the centre; the line passes through the midpoint of the chord; the line is perpendicular to the chord. If any two are true, all three are true.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The centre is equally far from both ends of the chord, so triangle formed by the centre and the two ends is isosceles; its median, altitude and symmetry line coincide.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A chord of length 16 lies in a circle of radius 10. The perpendicular from the centre bisects it, so the distance from the centre to the chord is 6.

card.rule: Through the centre, through the midpoint, perpendicular to the chord: any two imply the third.
card.limits: One statement alone is not enough. Our reading: if the chord is a diameter, its midpoint is the centre, so the first two statements coincide and do not force the third.

media.alt: A circle with two diameters AB and CD crossing near the centre. A point P on the circle, at the top, has perpendiculars dropped to the two diameters, meeting them at X on AB and Y on CD, with right-angle marks. The segment XY joins the two feet.

concepts.title: Tangents and radii
concepts.question: How is a tangent related to the radius at the point where it touches, and how do two tangents from one point compare?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency. From a point A outside a circle, the two tangent segments AX and AY are equal in length.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Right triangles OXA and OYA share the hypotenuse OA, and OX equals OY as radii, so they are congruent and AX equals AY.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A point 13 from the centre of a circle of radius 5 has tangent length 12, since 5, 12, 13 is a right triangle.

card.rule: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and tangent segments from an outside point are equal.
card.limits: Equal tangent segments are measured from the external point to the points of contact; the statement does not hold for lines that cut the circle twice.

concepts.title: The inscribed angle theorem
concepts.question: How does the size of an inscribed angle compare with the arc it cuts off?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The measure of an arc is twice the measure of the inscribed angle that subtends it. Equivalently, the angle subtended at the centre is twice the angle subtended at the circle. So wherever A is placed on the circle, angle CAB stays half the central angle COB.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Draw the segment AO. Triangles AOB and AOC are isosceles because OA, OB, OC are radii. Chase angles: the base angles of each give CAB as half of angle COB, with two variables cancelling at the end.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A central angle COB of 80 degrees means every inscribed angle on the same arc is 40 degrees.

card.rule: An inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc.
card.limits: The comparison is with the arc that the angle subtends; inscribed angles on the other arc of the same chord are measured by that other arc.

concepts.title: Angle chasing
concepts.question: How do you compute many angles in a figure without drowning in variables?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Angle chasing means computing as many angles as possible, keeping the number of variables down. In the inscribed angle proof the book used just two variables, and one cancelled at the end.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each triangle, straight line or isosceles pair yields an equation among angles; fewer variables keep the system simple.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In triangle ABC with AB = AC and angle B = 70, take D on AC with BD = BC. Then A = 40, C = 70, angle BDC = 70, DBC = 40, so angle ABD = 30.

blocks.label: Common slip
blocks.text: Many students use angle chasing, perhaps with trigonometry and algebra, to the exclusion of more elegant tactics. Learn when to transcend it.

card.rule: Compute as many angles as you can with as few variables as possible, but do not rely on angle chasing alone.
card.limits: Some figures give little angular information, for example those built on medians, and then angle chasing is doomed.

concepts.title: Inscribed right triangles
concepts.question: When is the angle at a point of a circle subtended by a diameter a right angle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let AB be a diameter of a circle and C any other point on the circle. Then angle BCA is 90 degrees. Conversely, if AB is a diameter and angle BCA is 90 degrees, then C lies on the circle.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A diameter subtends a central angle of 180 degrees, so by the inscribed angle theorem the angle at C is half of that, 90 degrees.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A right triangle has hypotenuse 10, so the circle on the hypotenuse as diameter has radius 5 and passes through the right-angle vertex.

card.rule: A point lies on the circle with diameter AB exactly when it sees AB at a right angle.
card.limits: The converse concerns the circle on that diameter; a right angle elsewhere in the figure says nothing about this circle.

media.alt: A circle with a chord through its centre as a diameter, ending at B on the right and at an unlabelled point on the left. C lies on the circle above, joined to both ends; a small square marks the right angle at C.

concepts.title: Cyclic quadrilaterals
concepts.question: What conditions show that four points lie on one circle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A quadrilateral is cyclic if its vertices lie on a circle; the four points are concyclic. Two tests: a quadrilateral is cyclic if and only if a pair of opposite angles are supplementary. Points A, B, C, D are concyclic if and only if angle ACB equals angle ADB.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Opposite angles subtend arcs that together make the whole circle, so the inscribed angles add to 180. Equal angles on the same side of a chord mean the same arc.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = 80 degrees, so opposite angle C = 100 degrees.

blocks.label: Used for
blocks.text: With cyclic quadrilaterals you get circles and pairs of equal angles for free; get in the habit of finding or creating them.

card.rule: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary; equal angles on one side of a segment put two points on a common circle.
card.limits: The equal-angle test needs the two points on the same side of the segment; opposite angles sum to 180 only when all four points are concyclic.

media.alt: A quadrilateral inscribed in a circle with both diagonals drawn; D is the top vertex, A the right one, the other two are unlabelled. Two small arcs mark the angle at D and the angle at the left vertex, both facing the chord from A to the bottom vertex.

A circle with points D, C, B and an unlabelled top vertex on it, forming a quadrilateral. The diagonals from the top vertex to C and from D to B cross at E. A dashed segment drops from the top vertex to F on DB with a right-angle mark, and a small arc marks the angle at the top vertex.

concepts.title: The circumcircle and circumcentre
concepts.question: Where is the centre of the circle through a triangle's three vertices?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A triangle inscribed in a circle has that circle as its circumscribed circle or circumcircle. Its centre is the circumcentre and its radius the circumradius. The circumcentre is the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides, and all three bisectors meet in one point.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Any point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equally far from that side's ends. The intersection of two bisectors is equally far from all three vertices, so it is the centre of a circle through them; the third bisector then passes through it as well.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the triangle with vertices (0,0), (10,0) and (0,24), the perpendicular bisectors meet at (5,12), and the circumradius is 13.

card.rule: The circumcentre is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet, equidistant from the three vertices.
card.limits: The book shows a triangle always has a circumcircle, and it is unique; the circumcentre may lie outside the triangle, and the claim concerns perpendicular bisectors, not angle bisectors.

concepts.title: The incircle and incentre
concepts.question: Where is the centre of the circle that touches all three sides of a triangle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A circle inscribed in a triangle is tangent to each side. It is the incircle; its centre is the incentre and its radius the inradius. Every triangle has a unique incircle, and its centre is the intersection of the three angle bisectors.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A point inside an angle is equally far from the two sides exactly when it is on the bisector. The intersection of two angle bisectors is equally far from all three sides, so it is the centre of a circle tangent to all of them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a triangle with angle A = 60 degrees, the incentre lies on the bisector of A, which makes 30 degrees with each side at A.

card.rule: The incentre is where the angle bisectors meet, equidistant from the three sides.
card.limits: Incircle and circumcircle are different circles with different centres; the incentre is always inside the triangle, while the incircle touches sides, not vertices.

media.alt: A triangle ABC inside a large circle Gamma 1 through A, B and C, with a smaller circle Gamma 2 inside touching all three sides. I is the small circle's centre, joined to D on side CB. O, the large circle's centre, is joined to A.

Two circles touching the sides of an angle with vertex A on the right. The small circle with radius r sits inside triangle ABC and touches all three sides. The large circle with radius r-sub-a lies beyond side BC, touching BC and the extensions of AB and AC. Radii to the tangent points are drawn.

concepts.title: Assume it exists, then verify
concepts.question: How can you prove that a circle with a given property exists and is unique?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To prove a triangle has an incircle (or circumcircle) and that it is unique, first assume it exists and explore its properties. This pins the centre down to an intersection of special lines. Then show the converse: the intersection really is the centre of such a circle.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Assuming existence tells you where to look; checking the converse proves the point works; uniqueness follows because the centre is forced to be one specific point.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the incircle, if it exists its centre lies on two angle bisectors. Conversely, any two angle bisectors meet at a point equidistant from all three sides, so the circle exists and is unique.

card.rule: Assume the object exists, deduce where it must be, then verify that this place works.
card.limits: The tricky part is uniqueness and existence; deducing necessary properties alone does not prove the object exists, so the converse check cannot be skipped.

concepts.title: Altitudes and the orthocentre
concepts.question: Why do the three altitudes of any triangle meet in a single point?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: An altitude is a line through a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side (extended if necessary); its foot is where it meets that side. The three altitudes of any triangle are concurrent, at the orthocentre. Altitudes may lie outside the triangle.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Draw through each vertex a line parallel to the opposite side; these form a larger triangle. Each original vertex is the midpoint of a side of the large triangle, since it forms parallelograms. The altitudes of the small triangle are the perpendicular bisectors of the large triangle's sides, so they meet at its circumcentre.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If side AC of triangle ABC has length 7, then the large triangle's side through B has length 14, since B is the midpoint.

card.rule: Altitudes are the perpendicular bisectors of a larger triangle, so they all pass through its circumcentre.
card.limits: Altitudes are lines, not segments; in an obtuse triangle they meet outside, and the trick works for any triangle.

media.alt: A triangle with an unlabelled apex at the upper left and vertices B and C. D lies on the long side from the apex to C, and BD meets it at a right angle, marked with a small square. Short dashed lines run down from B and from C.

A triangle ABC inside a larger triangle DEF, with D at left, F at top and E at lower right. A lies on DF, B on DE and C on FE. A line m through B meets AC at a right angle, marked with a small square, and runs on past B.

A triangle ABC with C at lower left, B at lower right and A at top. Point H lies inside near side AC. Two more points, H2 left of AC and H3 beyond AB, sit on dashed lines from H, and another dashed line runs down from H.

concepts.title: Area as a function
concepts.question: What rules does area obey, and how is the area of overlapping pieces found?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Area is a function, not an object: it assigns a non-negative number to each geometric figure. Congruent figures have equal area. Non-overlapping parts add. If two parts overlap, the area of the union is the sum minus the area of the overlap. The area of a rectangle is base times height. The area of figure XYZ is written [XYZ].

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: These are axioms that anyone who has cut construction paper has internalised. The overlap rule is the geometric version of the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two overlapping paper rectangles have areas 20 and 15, and the overlapping region has area 6. The covered region has area 20 + 15 - 6 = 29.

card.rule: Areas of non-overlapping parts add; for overlapping parts, subtract the overlap once.
card.limits: These rules treat area intuitively, as an undefined notion like points and lines; the rectangle rule is what actually fixes the numbers.

concepts.title: Shearing leaves area unchanged
concepts.question: Why do two parallelograms with the same base between the same two parallel lines have the same area?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Two parallelograms that share the same base, with their opposite sides on the same line, have equal area. Sliding the top side along its line, a shear, changes the shape but not the area. So a parallelogram has area base times height.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Write each area as a common triangle plus a congruent triangle minus the shared overlap. The two extra triangles are congruent, so the areas match. Intuitively the figure is a stack of lines of constant length, and sliding the stack leaves the total unchanged.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A parallelogram has base 12 and height 5. Shear it into a rectangle 12 by 5; its area is 60 however far it leans.

card.rule: Area depends on base and height only: sliding the top of a parallelogram along its line does not change it.
card.limits: Height means the perpendicular distance between the lines, not the length of the slanted side.

media.alt: Two parallelograms share the bottom side AB. Points F, E, D and C lie left to right on one line above it. FA and CB slant down to A and B. Segments from A up to D and from B up to E cross at G, and the dark triangle ABG is where the parallelograms overlap.
A neat stack of seventeen thick horizontal bars of equal length, lined up exactly one above another with equal gaps, like a deck of cards seen from the side.

The same kind of stack of seventeen equal-length horizontal bars, but each bar is shifted sideways by a different amount, so the left and right edges of the stack are ragged, leaning one way and then the other.

A horizontal line with arrowheads at both ends and four points marked on it. Two lower points are joined by a short horizontal segment. One parallelogram leans to the left and another stands almost upright, overlapping it. Both have that same bottom side and their top sides lie on the line.

concepts.title: Area of a triangle and ratios of areas
concepts.question: How is a triangle's area found, and what do triangles sharing a vertex have in common?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The area of a triangle is half base times height. If two triangles share a vertex and their bases lie on the same line, the ratio of their areas equals the ratio of their bases.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Two copies of a triangle glue into a parallelogram, giving the half. Triangles with a common vertex have the same height to the line, so only their bases differ.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: D lies on BC with BD = 4 and BC = 15. Then triangle ABD has 4/15 of the area of triangle ABC; if [ABC] is 90, then [ABD] is 24.

card.rule: Triangles sharing a vertex with bases on one line have areas in the ratio of their bases.
card.limits: The triangles must share the same height, which they do only when the apex is common and the bases lie on one line.

media.alt: A triangle with one vertex labelled A at the top and a base along the bottom. A segment runs from A down to a point on the base, splitting the triangle into two smaller triangles that share vertex A and have bases on the same line.

A trapezoid whose top side AD is parallel to its bottom side, with B at the lower left and an unlabelled lower right vertex. Both diagonals are drawn and cross at E. The two triangles touching the slanted sides, ABE on the left and the one on the right with D, are shaded black; top and bottom triangles are white.

concepts.title: The Pythagorean theorem by shearing
concepts.question: How can shearing prove that the squares on the legs sum to the square on the hypotenuse?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In a right triangle the sum of the squares of the legs equals the square of the hypotenuse. Recast as areas: the two smaller squares together have the area of the largest square.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: An equation of lengths times lengths is about area, the only concept so far for products. Draw through the right-angle vertex a line perpendicular to the hypotenuse; it splits the big square into two rectangles. Shear each rectangle and the matching leg square to congruent parallelograms.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A right triangle with legs 9 and 12 has hypotenuse 15 since 81 + 144 = 225.

blocks.label: Common slip
blocks.text: The picture is not rigorous by itself: proving the sheared parallelograms congruent needs angle chasing to find copies of the original triangle.

card.rule: Turn the equation into areas, split the hypotenuse square by the perpendicular from the right angle, and shear.
card.limits: Shearing preserves area only for parallelograms with a common base between the same parallels; the final congruence still needs a proof.

media.alt: A right triangle ABC with its right angle at B; A is above B and C is to the right of B. A square is drawn outward on each of the three sides: on AB to the left, on BC below, on the hypotenuse AC at the upper right.

Right triangle ABC with the right angle at B, with a square drawn on each side. A line m through B is perpendicular to hypotenuse AC and meets it at R, cutting the hypotenuse square AIHC into rectangles RSIA and RCHS. Small arrows show the segment RS and the leg-square edges FG and DE sliding.

A line with arrowheads at both ends running from lower left to upper right. Several parallelograms and a small right triangle are arranged along and above it, with tall vertical edges rising from the line. It is the shearing step, where squares and rectangles have been slid along the line into parallelograms.

concepts.title: A dissection proof of the Pythagorean theorem
concepts.question: How can cutting and pasting two equal squares prove that a squared plus b squared equals c squared?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The dissection proof comes from ancient India and uses only cutting and pasting. Take two congruent squares, each of side a + b. One is cut into a square of side a, a square of side b, and four copies of the right triangle. The other is cut into a square of side c and four copies of the same triangle.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The two big squares are congruent, so their areas are equal. Removing the four equal triangles from each leaves a squared plus b squared on one side and c squared on the other.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With legs 3 and 4, the big square has side 7 and area 49. Four triangles take 4 times 6 = 24, leaving c squared = 25, so c = 5.

card.rule: Equal big squares minus the same four triangles leave a squared plus b squared equal to c squared.
card.limits: The proof needs the pieces to fit exactly, which the picture shows; the book gives it as a quick, visual proof.

media.alt: Three panels. On the left a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c. In the middle a large square cut into a square a squared, a square b squared and two copies of the triangle. On the right an equal large square holding a tilted inner square c squared and four triangles in its corners.

A square-based outline with a right triangle attached at its upper right. Slanted lines and horizontal and vertical lines cut it into triangles, small rectangles and a tilted quadrilateral in the middle. It is a diagram for a cut-and-rearrange proof of the Pythagorean theorem, and no labels are visible.

concepts.title: Similar triangles
concepts.question: What does it mean for two triangles to be similar, and how are corresponding parts matched?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Triangles ABC and DEF are similar if their respective angles are equal and their respective sides are proportional: angle A = D, B = E, C = F, and AB/DE = AC/DF = BC/EF. They have the same shape, and the common ratio is the ratio of similitude.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: This is a definition. Similarity extends congruence: congruent triangles are similar with ratio 1.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Triangle ABC with sides 3, 4, 5 is similar to triangle DEF with sides 6, 8, 10, with ratio 1 to 2. The order of the letters matters: A matches D, B matches E, C matches F.

card.rule: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.
card.limits: Equal ratios of some sides are not enough unless every pair of corresponding sides has the same ratio; the order of the letters tells which parts correspond.

concepts.title: Tests for similarity
concepts.question: Which minimal pieces of information are enough to show two triangles are similar?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Fact 8.3.8: two triangles are similar if (a) their angles are respectively equal (AA is enough), or (b) their sides are respectively proportional, or (c) two sides are in proportion and the angles between them are equal (proportional SAS).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Two equal angles force the third to be equal since angles sum to 180. Proportional sides or two proportional sides with an equal included angle fix the shape.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Triangle with sides 4 and 6 enclosing a 50 degree angle, and one with sides 6 and 9 enclosing 50 degrees: ratio 3/2 both times, so similar by proportional SAS.

blocks.label: Common slip
blocks.text: Whenever two triangles share an angle, a single further pair of equal angles is enough.

card.rule: Equal angles, proportional sides, or proportional sides around an equal included angle each prove similarity.
card.limits: In proportional SAS the equal angle must lie between the two proportional sides; an angle elsewhere is not enough.

media.alt: A single triangle drawn with dots at its three vertices, a long side running from lower left to the upper right vertex and a short base along the bottom. A small arc marks the angle at the upper right vertex, between the long side and the right-hand side.

concepts.title: A line parallel to a side
concepts.question: What triangle does a line drawn parallel to one side cut off?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In triangle ABC, let a line parallel to BC meet AB at D and AC at E. Then triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC. Conversely, if D and E divide AB and AC in the same ratio (AD/AB = AE/AC), then DE is parallel to BC.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Alternate or corresponding angles at D and E equal those at B and C, and the angle at A is shared, so AA gives similarity. The converse follows from proportional SAS.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: AD = 3 and AB = 9 give ratio 1/3, so AE = 4 means AC = 12 and DE = BC/3.

card.rule: A parallel to one side cuts off a triangle similar to the whole, and proportional division implies parallelism.
card.limits: The line must cross the two other sides (or their extensions) in the same ratio from the vertex A; ratios measured from different ends do not match.

media.alt: A triangle with its base along the bottom and its apex at the top. A dashed line m, with arrowheads at both ends, runs horizontally across the triangle parallel to the base, meeting the left side at a point D and the right side at a point E.

concepts.title: The altitude to the hypotenuse
concepts.question: How do the two small triangles cut off by the altitude to the hypotenuse relate to the large one?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, drop a perpendicular of length h from the right angle to the hypotenuse, dividing it into x and y. The two small triangles are similar to each other and to the large one. Moreover h is the square root of xy, and c x = a squared, c y = b squared.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each small triangle shares an acute angle with the large one and has a right angle, so AA gives similarity. The proportional sides give the three relations.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Legs 3 and 4, hypotenuse 5. The segments are x = 9/5 and y = 16/5, and h = 12/5, with h squared = xy = 144/25.

card.rule: The altitude to the hypotenuse makes three similar right triangles, with h squared = xy and c x = a squared.
card.limits: x pairs with the leg that touches it: cx = a squared only when a is the leg adjacent to x.

media.alt: A right triangle with its right angle at the top, a small square marking it. The legs are labelled a on the left and b on the right. The altitude h drops from the right angle to the hypotenuse along the bottom and splits it into x on the left and y on the right.

concepts.title: Looking for similar triangles
concepts.question: When a problem involves ratios, what should you look for?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If a geometry problem involves ratios, it is almost certain to need similar triangles. Look for them; if they are not visible, produce them with auxiliary lines such as parallels or perpendiculars.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Similar triangles turn equal angles into equal ratios of sides. Auxiliary parallel lines create equal angles and so create similarity.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To prove the Power of a Point equality of products, join the cutting points to form two triangles that share an angle and have a pair of equal inscribed angles.

card.rule: For ratio problems, hunt for similar triangles, and create them with parallels or perpendiculars when needed.
card.limits: Similarity is not the only route; areas also turn ratios of lengths into ratios of areas, and the pairing of vertices must be right.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: the square root of a squared plus b squared, with a horizontal line along its top edge, probably the edge of a larger fraction that the crop cut off. Nothing else from the surrounding formula is visible.

Coordinate axes with a slanted line running down to the right, labelled with the equation a x plus b y plus c equals 0. A point (u, v) lies above it. A horizontal segment w and a vertical segment h from the point reach the line, and a shorter perpendicular d from the point meets the line, forming a small right triangle.

Right triangle ACB with the right angle at C at the top, A at lower left and B at lower right. Points F and D lie on AB, F nearer A. E is on side CB, with segments CD, DE and FE drawn. A right angle is marked at E, and the angle at A and the angle CDE at D carry the same mark.

concepts.title: Proving the power of a point
concepts.question: Which similar triangles prove that PX times PY does not depend on the line?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let P be outside the circle. One line through P meets it at X (near) and Y (far); another meets it at U (near) and V (far). Draw the segments YU and VX. Triangles PYU and PVX are similar, so PY/PV = PU/PX and cross-multiplying gives PX times PY = PU times PV.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The two triangles share the angle at P. Angles at Y and V subtend the same arc XU, so they are equal. Two equal angles give similarity. The order of the points matters: P, Y, U goes with P, V, X.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: PX = 3, PY = 10 and PU = 5 give PV = 30/5 = 6.

blocks.label: If-then
blocks.text: If P is on the circle, one of the points coincides with P and the products are zero. If P is inside, two other auxiliary lines give similar triangles in the same way.

card.rule: An equality of products becomes an equality of ratios from two similar triangles sharing the angle at P.
card.limits: The pairing of vertices is essential, and the argument as given covers P outside; the inside case needs its own diagram.

media.alt: A circle with a point P outside, upper right. One line from P passes through X and then Y on the circle; another passes through X-prime and then Y-prime. Two auxiliary chords are drawn, from Y to X-prime and from X to Y-prime, crossing inside the circle, so that triangles sharing the angle at P appear.

concepts.title: Angle bisector theorem: the similar triangles proof
concepts.question: How can an auxiliary point on the bisector create the similar triangles that prove the theorem?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Given angle CAD = angle DAB = alpha, choose a point E on AD with angle ACE = angle ABC (call it beta). Then triangles ACE and ABD are similar, giving AC/AB = CE/DB. It remains to show CE = CD.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The exterior angle CDE of triangle ABD equals alpha + beta, and the angle CED of triangle ACE also equals alpha + beta. Triangle CED is therefore isosceles with CE = CD, so CD/DB = AC/AB.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If AC = 6 and AB = 4 with CB = 10, the proof shows CD/DB = 6/4, which gives CD = 6.

card.rule: Create the missing equal angle with an auxiliary point, then turn the ratio into the one you want using an isosceles triangle.
card.limits: The proof needs the new point to be constructed with the right angle; it is a trick of creating similar triangles out of thin air.

media.alt: A triangle with apex at upper left, vertex C at lower left and another vertex at lower right, and a point D on the base. The bisector from the apex passes through D, with an angle alpha marked on each side of it. A point E on it is joined to C, and an angle beta is marked at C and at the lower right vertex.

concepts.title: Angle bisector theorem: the area proof
concepts.question: How does comparing areas of two triangles with a common vertex prove the bisector theorem?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let CD/DB = x/y. Triangles ACD and ADB share vertex A, so x/y = [ACD]/[ADB]. Compute the areas another way with the altitudes u = CF and v = DG: [ACD]/[ADB] = (1/2 u m)/(1/2 v c) = um/vc, where m is AD.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Right triangles CAF and DAG have equal angles at A, so they are similar and u/v = b/m. Substituting gives x/y = b/c.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With b = AC = 6 and c = AB = 4, the pieces satisfy x : y = 6 : 4.

card.rule: Write a length ratio as an area ratio, recompute the areas with altitudes, and use a pair of similar right triangles.
card.limits: The proof uses the bisected angle only to make the right triangles similar; the converse is left as a problem.

media.alt: Triangle with apex A at upper left, C at lower left, and the third vertex at lower right. Point D lies on the base CB, splitting it into x and y. Segment AD has length m, AC is b and AB is c. From C a perpendicular of length u meets AD at F, and from D a perpendicular of length v meets AB at G.

Cropped formula piece: a displayed line of algebra in which a fraction with u and m over v and c is written as the product of two fractions, b over m and m over c, and then as b over c. It is a fragment, not a diagram.

concepts.title: Proving the centroid theorem
concepts.question: How can two medians and a midline prove the 2 to 1 ratio, and a phantom point the concurrency?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let D, E, F be the midpoints of BC, CA, AB. Set aside median CF and look at medians AD and BE, which meet at G. The midline DE is parallel to AB and half as long, so triangles DEG and ABG are similar with ratio 1 : 2. Hence DG : GA = EG : GB = 1 : 2.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Nothing special was used about the pair AD, BE, so any two medians meet in a point dividing both 1 : 2. The third median CF meets AD at some point G-prime with DG-prime : G-prime A = 1 : 2. Only one point divides AD that way, so G-prime = G.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If a median is 30 long, its centroid is 20 from the vertex and 10 from the midpoint.

blocks.label: Used for
blocks.text: This phantom-point step shows that the intersection point is unique, and so that the three medians are concurrent.

card.rule: Two medians meet in a 2 to 1 point by a midline and similar triangles, and a phantom point shows the third median passes through it.
card.limits: The argument closes because a given 1 : 2 division point on a segment is unique; without that, the third median could meet AD elsewhere.

media.alt: Triangle with the apex unlabelled at top right and base vertices C at lower left and B at lower right. D is on the left side, E on the right side and F on the base. Two segments run from C to E and from the apex to F, crossing at G, and segment EF is drawn between the two side points.

concepts.title: The eight-point geometry checklist
concepts.question: What are the eight items the book lists for attacking a geometry problem?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: 1. Draw a careful diagram. 2. Draw auxiliary objects, but sparingly. 3. Start with angle chasing, but do not rely on it for everything. 4. Seek out your best friends: right triangles, parallel lines, concyclic points. 5. Compare areas. 6. Relentlessly exploit similar triangles. 7. Look for symmetry and distinguished points or lines. 8. Create a phantom point with a desired property and show it coincides with an existing point.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The list collects the strategies, tactics and tools of the previous sections, to help a beginner get organised. It is by no means complete.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A problem about perpendicular lines: use the best friends (right triangles inscribed in circles) and ask for concyclic points before reaching for angle chasing.

card.rule: Draw carefully, add objects sparingly, chase angles but not only that, and use right triangles, parallels, circles, areas, similarity, symmetry and phantom points.
card.limits: The list is a good start for beginners, not a complete recipe; items 1 to 3 are restatements of the obvious.

concepts.title: Five ways to prove four points are concyclic
concepts.question: What are the options for showing that four given points lie on one circle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To show M, N, P, Q lie on a circle the book lists options in increasing order of sophistication: (1) find a likely centre and show all four points are equally far from it; (2) show angles QMP and QNP are supplementary; (3) show angle QPM equals angle QNM; (4) use the converse of Power of a Point; (5) use the converse of Ptolemy's theorem.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Options 2 and 3 use the cyclic quadrilateral test. Option 4 needs the intersection X of the chords and QX times XP equal to MX times XN. Option 5 needs QM NP + MP NQ = QP MN.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Chords QP and MN meet at X with QX = 2, XP = 9, MX = 3, XN = 6. Since 2 times 9 = 3 times 6 = 18, the converse of POP says the four points are concyclic.

card.rule: Pick the test whose needed lengths or angles the figure already offers: a centre, supplementary angles, equal angles, equal chord products, or Ptolemy's sum.
card.limits: Options 2 and 3 can demand many more lines, which clutter the figure, and option 5 looks complicated; the book weighs these costs before choosing.

concepts.title: Concyclic points: the centre method
concepts.question: How can you show four points are concyclic by locating a likely centre?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In acute triangle ABC, the circle on diameter AB meets altitude CC-prime at M and N, and the circle on diameter AC meets altitude BB-prime at P and Q. To show M, N, P, Q concyclic, guess the centre is A and show AM = AN = AP = AQ.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: MN lies on the altitude, perpendicular to AB, and is a chord of the circle on AB, so AB is its perpendicular bisector and AM = AN. Likewise AC bisects PQ, so AP = AQ. Right triangles give AM squared = AC-prime times AB and AP squared = AB-prime times AC.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With AC-prime = AC cos A and AB-prime = AB cos A, both squares equal AB times AC times cos A, so AM = AP and the centre is A.

card.rule: Chords that share a perpendicular bisector point to a common centre; check that centre is equally far from all points.
card.limits: The method works because the figure already offered a natural candidate for the centre; with no such candidate the other options may be easier.

media.alt: Triangle ABC with two overlapping circles, omega 1 and omega 2, meeting at A and at A-prime on side BC. The altitude from C meets AB at C-prime, with points M and N on its line, and the altitude from B meets AC at B-prime, with points P and Q on its line. Right angles are marked at B-prime and C-prime.

Triangle with an unlabelled apex at the top, C at lower left and an unlabelled vertex at lower right. B-prime lies on the left side and C-prime on the right side, with right-angle marks. Altitudes from C and from the lower right vertex carry M and P. Dashed segments join the apex to M and to P, and the base corners to M and P.

concepts.title: Concyclic points: the Power of a Point method
concepts.question: How can two applications of Power of a Point, on two circles sharing a chord, prove four points concyclic?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let X be the intersection of QP and MN; it is the orthocentre of ABC. The foot A-prime of the altitude from A lies on both circles, since AA-primeB and AA-primeC are right triangles. Chord AA-prime passes through X and belongs to both circles.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: POP in the circle on AC gives AX times XA-prime = QX times XP. POP in the circle on AB gives AX times XA-prime = MX times XN. Hence QX times XP = MX times XN, and the converse of POP finishes.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If AX times XA-prime is 12 and QX = 3, then XP = 4.

card.rule: A chord shared by two circles lets one product serve both: equate the two POP products to link chords that live in different circles.
card.limits: The four segments QX, XP, MX, XN do not live in a single circle, so POP cannot be applied to them directly; the common chord AA-prime is what links them.

media.alt: The two-circle figure with triangle ABC, omega 1 and omega 2, the altitudes carrying M, N, P and Q, and right angles at the feet B-prime and C-prime. A new point X is where the two altitudes cross, and a dashed vertical line runs from A through X down to A-prime, a chord shared by both circles.

concepts.title: Finding the crux object
concepts.question: How does the symmetry of a problem hint at the key object?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In both solutions the proof hinged on a crux object: the point A in the first, the line AA-prime in the second. The problem was set up symmetrically with diameters AB and AC, so objects through A were the natural candidates.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The crux is found by reading the setup: what does it single out, and what do all the data share? This takes peripheral vision and wishful thinking, more art than craft.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two circles on diameters AB and AC share the point A and the point A-prime, so the line AA-prime, a chord of both, becomes the crux.

card.rule: Ask what object the setup singles out, and build the proof around it instead of adding random constructions.
card.limits: No rule produces the crux object; guided search beats random lines, but it can still fail.

concepts.title: Cevians and area ratios
concepts.question: How do area ratios turn a cevian figure into segment ratios?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A cevian is a segment joining a vertex of a triangle with a point on the opposite side (extended if necessary). Two triangles that share a vertex, with bases on one line, have areas in the same ratio as their bases; this turns cevian figures into area bookkeeping.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Give small regions letters, use known base ratios to chain relations, and then read segment ratios back from areas. Letting one area be 2y instead of y avoids fractions.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the trisection figure, [FIA] = x forces [FBI] = 2x because AF : FB = 1 : 2. Using triangles CIA and CID with bases on AD gives AI : ID = 3 : 4.

card.rule: Name small areas, chain base ratios through shared vertices, and read segment ratios back from area ratios.
card.limits: Area ratios apply only to triangles sharing a vertex with bases on one line; each step must satisfy that condition.

media.alt: A triangle with an unlabelled top vertex, C at lower left and B at lower right. A segment from the top vertex passes through D and ends at F inside the triangle. From D another segment passes through E and ends at B, and a segment from C passes through F and ends at E.
Cropped formula piece: a displayed equation saying the sum of three ratios, GD over AD, GE over BE and GF over CF, equals 1. It is a fragment of a formula with no diagram.

concepts.title: The trisection puzzle
concepts.question: What fraction of a triangle's area is the small triangle formed by cevians to the first trisection points?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Points D, E, F are the first trisection points of BC, CA, AB, so AF = AB/3, DB = BC/3, CE = CA/3. The cevians AD, BE, CF form a small triangle GHI. If the area of ABC is 1, the area of GHI is 1/7.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Area ratios show each cevian is cut in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3, and the vertices G, H, I bisect the segments HB, CI, AG. This dissects the large triangle into seven triangles of equal area.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If [ABC] = 70, then [GHI] = 10.

card.rule: The three cevians to first trisection points cut each other in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3, and the inner triangle has one seventh of the area.
card.limits: The result belongs to first trisection points measured consistently around the triangle; other division ratios give other fractions.

media.alt: Triangle ABC with a point D on side BC, E on side CA and F on side AB. Three cevians AD, BE and CF are drawn. They cross pairwise at points G, H and I, and the small triangle they form in the middle, with vertices H, G and I, is shaded black.

Triangle ABC with cevians AD and CF crossing at I, plus a dashed segment from I to B. The small regions are labelled by area. Triangle AIF is x, triangle FIB is 2x, triangle DIB is 2y, and triangle CID is 4y, so the labels show the ratios of the areas.

A triangle with a shaded black triangle in its middle. Solid and dashed segments join the corners of the shaded triangle to the corners of the large triangle, dissecting the large one into several smaller triangles. No labels or numbers are visible in this picture.

concepts.title: Ceva's theorem
concepts.question: What product of three ratios is 1 exactly when three cevians are concurrent?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Cevians AD, BE, CF of triangle ABC (D on BC, E on CA, F on AB) are concurrent if and only if (AF/FB) times (BD/DC) times (CE/EA) = 1.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The ratios are expressed by areas; when the cevians meet at G, the areas cancel in the product. The converse is proved by contradiction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For three medians every ratio is 1, so the product is 1. For the trisection cevians each ratio is 1/2, the product is 1/8, so they are not concurrent, as the small triangle GHI shows.

blocks.label: Common slip
blocks.text: The ratios must go around the triangle in one direction, vertex to point to next vertex.

card.rule: Three cevians concur exactly when the product of the three ratios around the triangle equals 1.
card.limits: The theorem is about cevians, one through each vertex, and uses ratios of lengths, not areas; a mix-up of the order of the points gives a wrong product.

media.alt: Triangle ABC with a long line m with arrowheads at both ends cutting across it. The line meets side AC at D, side BC at F and the extension of AB beyond B at E, with A, B and E on the base line.

concepts.title: Proving Ceva's theorem
concepts.question: How does an algebra lemma about proportions turn area ratios into Ceva's product?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Lemma: if x/y = a/b, then x/y = (x + a)/(y + b) = (x - a)/(y - b). With cevians concurrent at G, express AF/FB, BD/DC, CE/EA as ratios of areas of the small triangles.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each length ratio equals a ratio of two small areas, which the lemma rewrites as a ratio of sums such as (x + z)/(u + v). The three ratios cancel in the product to give 1.

blocks.label: If-then
blocks.text: The converse (product 1 implies concurrent) is left as an exercise, with the hint: proof by contradiction.

card.rule: Write each ratio as a ratio of areas, add or subtract them with the proportion lemma, and the product cancels to 1.
card.limits: The lemma works only when the two added fractions are equal; adding unequal numbers to numerator and denominator changes a fraction.

media.alt: Triangle with cevians AD, BE and CF meeting at G, with D on the base CB, E on the left side and F on the right side. The six small regions around G are labelled with areas: x and y near the top, z on the left, w on the right, and u and v along the base on either side of AD.

concepts.title: The method of weights
concepts.question: How can weights placed at the vertices give segment ratios without computing areas?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Imagine weights at the vertices of a triangle. A segment balances at a point where weight times distance from the balance point is equal on both ends. Two weights act like a single weight, their sum, at the balance point.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: It uses informal physical intuition about levers. The book says the method seems like magic and asks you to prove rigorously that it works.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the trisection figure put 2 at B and 4 at A, so F balances AB. F then carries 6. With D balancing CB, C gets 1 and D carries 3. On AD the weights 4 and 3 give AI : ID = 3 : 4.

card.rule: Choose weights so each cevian foot balances, then read ratios along each cevian from the weights.
card.limits: It is an intuitive device; the book poses the rigorous justification as a problem and also asks whether it can prove Ceva's theorem.

media.alt: Triangle ABC with a cevian from A to D on BC and a cevian from C to F on AB, crossing at I. Circled weights are written at the points: 4 at A, 2 at B, 1 at C, 3 at D and 6 at F, each cevian balancing at I like a lever.

concepts.title: Proving perpendicular lines
concepts.question: What is a good penultimate step for showing two lines are perpendicular?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Example 8.4.4: ABC is isosceles with AB = AC; D is the foot of the perpendicular from A to BC; E the foot from D to AC; F the midpoint of ED. Prove AF is perpendicular to BE. Angle chasing is doomed here because AF is a median of triangle AED.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: For perpendicular lines the penultimate step is often an inscribed right triangle. Triangle ADB is right-angled and inscribed in the circle with diameter AB. If the intersection G of AF and BE is on this circle, then AGB is also a right angle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: So it suffices to show A, G, D, B are concyclic, that is, angle GAD = angle GBD.

card.rule: To prove two lines perpendicular, try to make them the legs of a right triangle inscribed in a circle with a known diameter.
card.limits: The reduction only moves the work: you still need a reason for the equal angles, and a median gives no angular information by itself.

concepts.title: Wishful thinking and similar subtriangles
concepts.question: How can wishing for a midline lead to an auxiliary line and similar subtriangles?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To show angle GAD = angle GBD, the solution needs another triangle that interacts with a midpoint, as AF does in triangle AED. D is the midpoint of BC, and the solver wishes DE were a midline. Wishful thinking draws BH parallel to DE.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: BHC is a right triangle with midline DE and median BE, and it is similar to triangle AED. Similar subtriangles then give FAD similar to EBC, which supplies the equal angles.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Similar subtriangles: if ABC is similar to DEF and X, Y divide AB and DE in the same ratio, then triangle AXC is similar to DYF.

card.rule: When a missing midline would help, draw the parallel that makes it exist; matching points in similar triangles give similar subtriangles.
card.limits: Wishful thinking only suggests a construction; the new triangles must still be proved similar, and the correspondence must follow the matching points.

media.alt: An isosceles-style triangle with its apex at top and B and C on the base. The altitude from the apex lands at D on the base, with a right-angle mark. From D a perpendicular meets the right side at E. F is a point on segment DE. Segments BE and the apex to F cross at G.

The same triangle with apex A, base BC, altitude AD, point E on AC with DE perpendicular to AC, F on DE and G where BE crosses AF. A new dashed segment joins B to a point H on AC, above E, added as a construction line.

concepts.title: The Euler line
concepts.question: Which three centres of a triangle lie on one line, and how does the centroid split the segment between two of them?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In any triangle the orthocentre H, the centroid M and the circumcentre K are collinear. The centroid divides HK in the ratio 2 : 1, with HM twice MK. The line through them is the Euler line.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The proof uses the medial triangle: the circumcentre of ABC is the orthocentre of the medial triangle, and the two triangles are similar with ratio 1 : 2 and the same centroid.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Triangle with vertices (0,0), (6,0), (0,8): H = (0,0), circumcentre K = (3,4), centroid M = (2, 8/3). M is two thirds of the way from H to K.

card.rule: H, the centroid and K lie on a line, and the centroid is twice as far from H as from K.
card.limits: The theorem holds for every triangle but the line is determined only if the points are distinct; in a very symmetric triangle they may coincide.

concepts.title: Proving the Euler line
concepts.question: Which auxiliary triangle makes the collinearity of H, M and K provable?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The crux move is the medial triangle EGI. K, the circumcentre of ABC, is the orthocentre of the medial triangle, which is similar to ABC with ratio 1 : 2 and has the same centroid M.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: AD and EK are both perpendicular to BC, so they are parallel and angle HAM = angle KEM. EK/AH = 1/2 by similarity and EM/MA = 1/2 by the centroid theorem. Proportional SAS gives triangle HAM similar to triangle KEM, so H, M, K are collinear.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If AH = 10 then EK = 5, and if the median AE has length 18, then EM = 6.

card.rule: The medial triangle links H and K as sister points of similar triangles; proportional SAS shows the two triangles are similar, hence collinearity.
card.limits: The proof needs the angle equality from parallel lines and both ratios 1 : 2; if either failed, similarity would not follow.

media.alt: Triangle ABC with its apex A at top, B at lower left and C at lower right. Two altitudes, AD and the one from B to F, meet at H. The midpoints I, G and E of the sides are joined to form the medial triangle. Points M and K lie inside, unconnected.

Triangle with its medial triangle drawn in heavy lines, with midpoints I, G and E. A dashed altitude from the apex reaches the base at D, and a dashed vertical rises from E through K to segment IG. A thin line runs from the apex through M to E, and the line from H through M to K shows three collinear points.

concepts.title: Three circles and three common chords
concepts.question: What do the common chords of three pairwise intersecting circles have in common?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Place three circles so that each pair meets in two points. Each pair gives a common chord. The three chords are concurrent: they meet in one point.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Ceva needs a triangle, and the picture is too crowded for auxiliary lines, so the book copies the centroid proof: study two chords first, then show the third passes through their meeting point by a phantom argument.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Chords AB and CD of the first and second pair meet at X. They are both chords of the third circle, so POP gives AX times XB = CX times XD.

card.rule: Common chords of three pairwise intersecting circles are concurrent.
card.limits: The circles must meet pairwise in two points; the generalisation to non-intersecting circles uses the radical axis.

media.alt: Three overlapping circles omega 1, omega 2 and omega 3, each pair meeting in two points. The three common chords AB, CD and EF are drawn inside the figure, and they appear to cross at one point near the centre where all three circles overlap.

concepts.title: Phantom points in a proof by contradiction
concepts.question: How do two phantom points show that a third chord must pass through the meeting point of the first two?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Remove chord EF and let X be the intersection of chords AB and CD. Suppose the third chord does not pass through X. Draw a false line from F through X; it meets the two circles again at phantom points E1 and E2 instead of E.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: POP in the first circle gives FX times XE1 = AX times XB; in the second, FX times XE2 = CX times XD. Since AX times XB = CX times XD, we get XE1 = XE2, so E1 = E2. A common point of the two circles is a point of intersection, so E1 = E2 = E.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If AX times XB = CX times XD = 12 and FX = 4, then XE1 = XE2 = 3.

card.rule: Assume the third chord misses X, build phantom points on a line through X, and POP forces them to coincide with the real intersection point.
card.limits: The two ways to draw a false line are not equally easy: a false line that misses X yields equations with no easy contradiction, so choose the one that goes through X.

media.alt: The three-circle figure with chords AB and CD crossing at X. A dashed path runs from F through X and ends at E2, passing E1 on the way, so it misses the true intersection point E of the circles. E1 and E2 are two separate points beside E, one on each circle.

concepts.title: Rearranging a figure to gain symmetry
concepts.question: How can rearranging parts of a problem into a more symmetric shape make it easy?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A problem that is not symmetric may become so after a rearrangement that keeps the data intact. Writing 1 + 2 + ... + 100 and its reverse beneath it makes every column sum the same. A hexagon inscribed in a circle with sides 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1 can be rearranged to alternate 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each side is the base of an isosceles triangle with apex at the centre and two radii as legs. The six triangles can be reordered without changing the circle. In the alternating hexagon a third of it, quadrilateral XOZY, has angle XOZ = 120 and angle XYZ = 120.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With XY = 1 and YZ = 2, the law of cosines gives XZ squared = 1 + 4 + 2 = 7. Triangle XOZ has apex 120 degrees and legs r, so XZ squared = 3 r squared. Therefore r squared = 7/3.

card.rule: If a rearrangement leaves the essential data unchanged but makes the figure symmetric, solve the symmetric version.
card.limits: The rearranged figure must keep everything the question depends on, here the circle and the six chords; a rearrangement that changes the data solves a different problem.

media.alt: A completely blank white image. Nothing is drawn in it.

A hexagon ABCDEF inscribed in a circle with centre O, with radii drawn to all six vertices. Six triangles surround O. The three triangles ODE, OEF and OFA are shaded grey, and the other three, OAB, OBC and OCD, are white.

A circle with centre O and an inscribed hexagon whose sides alternate short and long: side XY is labelled 1 and side YZ labelled 2. Radii r join O to the vertices. The six triangles around O alternate shaded grey and white, and a dashed segment joins X to Z.

concepts.title: The transformational viewpoint
concepts.question: Why do transformations and their invariants shed light on geometry, and which transformations keep lengths?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A transformation is a mapping from the points of the plane to itself. Felix Klein proposed in 1872 that studying the algebraic properties of transformations sheds light on geometry. Rigid motions preserve length. There are four types: translations, reflections, glide reflections and rotations.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The composition of any two of these four is again one of the four. Beyond rigid motions come transformations that keep angles but change distances, such as the similarities and inversion.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Reflecting a figure keeps all its distances, so it is rigid. Doubling all distances from a centre keeps shapes, but is not rigid.

card.rule: Rigid motions keep every distance; they are translations, reflections, glide reflections and rotations.
card.limits: Transformations help most when used selectively, transforming only the symmetric part of a diagram and leaving the rest alone.

concepts.title: Translations and relative motions
concepts.question: How can the same translation be written with coordinates, complex numbers, vectors and words?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A translation moves every point by a fixed vector. It can be written T(x, y) = (x + 2, y - 1), or z becomes z + a with a = 2 - i, or by a vector of magnitude square root of 5, or in words: two units right and one down. Vectors are relative motions with no fixed starting point.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Think of translations as actual motions. To use points as vectors, choose an origin O; then A, B, C name the motions from O to those points, and the motion from B to C is C - B.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: T(3, 5) = (5, 4). With B = (1, 2) and C = (4, 6), the motion from B to C is (3, 4), of length 5.

card.rule: A translation adds a fixed vector to every point; the vector from B to C is C minus B.
card.limits: Position vectors depend on the chosen origin; relative motions do not. A translation by the zero vector is the identity, and other translations have no fixed point.

media.alt: A completely blank white image with only a few tiny specks. Nothing is drawn in it.

Two congruent grey triangles with the same orientation, one at lower left and one at upper right, the upper a copy of the lower shifted up and right. The lower triangle has its top vertex labelled E, and the upper one has vertices labelled F-prime and G-prime. Black rectangles at the edges are scan artifacts.

A triangle drawn with solid lines, with the side vector BC marked by an arrow. Dashed arrows from a common origin at the lower left point to the triangle vertices, labelled A and C. Black rectangles at the edges are scan artifacts, hiding parts of the picture.

concepts.title: Adding vectors and midpoints
concepts.question: What does a vector sum mean, and what is the vector position of a midpoint?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The vector sum X + Y means: do the motion X, followed by the motion Y. The vector sum along the sides of a closed polygon is zero. Since the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, the midpoint of AB has position vector (A + B)/2.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Composition of motions follows the parallelogram rule. Going round a closed polygon returns you to the start. Writing AB as B - A makes every term cancel.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For A = (1, 2) and B = (5, 6) the midpoint is (3, 4). For triangle ABC, AB + BC + CA = 0.

card.rule: A vector sum is a composition of motions; the sum around a closed polygon is zero; the midpoint of AB is (A + B)/2.
card.limits: The midpoint formula holds for vector positions measured from any one origin; the closed-polygon sum uses relative motions and does not depend on the origin.

concepts.title: The centroid as centre of mass
concepts.question: Why is the centroid of a triangle the average of its three vertices?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The centre of mass of n equal point masses at positions X1, X2, ..., Xn is (X1 + X2 + ... + Xn)/n. The centroid of triangle ABC is (A + B + C)/3, so it is the centre of mass of its vertices.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Let M be the midpoint of AB. By the centroid theorem the centroid K is one third of the way from M to C, so K = M + (1/3)(C - M) = (2M + C)/3. With M = (A + B)/2 this becomes (A + B + C)/3.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For A = (1, 2), B = (5, 2), C = (3, 8) the centroid is (3, 4).

card.rule: The centroid is the average of the vertex positions.
card.limits: The average gives the centre of mass for equal masses at the vertices; unequal masses would shift the point toward the heavier vertex.

media.alt: Triangle with its apex at top and base vertices A at lower left and B at lower right. M is a point on the base AB, and a segment joins the apex to M. A point K lies on that segment, between the apex and M, nearer to M.

Cropped formula piece, not a diagram: an equals sign, then the point M plus one third times the vector MC, written with an arrow drawn over the letters M and C. It is one line of a longer vector calculation.

concepts.title: A finite set has one centre of symmetry
concepts.question: How can vector sums show that a finite point set cannot have two different centres of symmetry?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A centre of symmetry of a set S is a point O, not necessarily in S, such that for every point A in S there is another point B in S with O the midpoint of AB. A finite set S cannot have more than one such centre.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: If P is a centre, the vectors from P to the points of S cancel in pairs, so they sum to zero. The same holds for a second centre Q. Subtracting the two sums leaves n times the vector QP equal to zero, so Q = P.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The four corners of a square have the centre of the square as their only centre of symmetry.

card.rule: If the vectors from a centre to all points sum to zero, two centres would force n times their difference to be zero.
card.limits: The count of points must be finite: a sum over infinitely many points is not defined, and an infinite pattern such as all integers on a line has many centres.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece, not a diagram: the vector from P to A with subscript k, plus the vector from P to B with subscript k, equals the zero vector. Each vector has an arrow over its letters.

Two overlapping triangles forming a six-pointed star around a dot M at the centre. One triangle has vertices C, B and an unlabelled top vertex; the other has B', C' and an unlabelled bottom vertex. Each looks like the other turned half a turn about M.

concepts.title: The dot product
concepts.question: What does the dot product tell you about lengths and perpendicularity?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The dot product of vectors A and B satisfies A . B = |A| |B| cos theta, where theta is the angle between them. It is commutative and distributive. A . A = |A| squared. A is perpendicular to B if and only if A . B = 0.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: These properties let you replace angle information by algebra without coordinates, which the book recommends avoiding when possible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (3, 4) . (4, -3) = 12 - 12 = 0, so these vectors are perpendicular. (3, 4) . (3, 4) = 25 = 5 squared.

card.rule: A dot B is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular, and A dot A is the squared length.
card.limits: The vector must be nonzero for zero dot product to mean perpendicular in the usual sense, and the dot product is a number, not a vector.

concepts.title: Reflections, glide reflections and rotations
concepts.question: How do reflections, glide reflections and rotations differ in what they fix?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A reflection across a line l sends X to X' so that l is the perpendicular bisector of XX'; every point of l is fixed. A glide reflection along l is a reflection across l followed by a translation parallel to l; it has no fixed point, but the line l is mapped to itself. A rotation about C by angle theta turns every point counterclockwise about C; its only fixed point is C.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: In complex form the rotation is z becomes c + (z - c) e to the i theta, since multiplying by e to the i theta rotates.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Rotating (3, 0) about (1, 0) by 90 degrees gives (1, 2).

card.rule: Reflections fix a whole line, translations and glide reflections fix no point, and a rotation fixes exactly its centre.
card.limits: A glide reflection with zero translation is an ordinary reflection; a rotation by 0 degrees is the identity, which fixes every point.

concepts.title: Composing two reflections
concepts.question: What single motion results from reflecting in one line and then in another?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let T1 and T2 be reflections across lines l1 and l2. If l1 = l2, the composition is the identity. If l1 and l2 are parallel, it is a translation by twice the vector from l1 to l2, perpendicular to both. If they meet at a point C, it is a rotation about C by twice the angle from l1 to l2.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: In the parallel case the point moves twice the distance between the lines. In the crossing case, C is fixed by both reflections, and angle chasing shows the rotation angle is 2 theta.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Reflect (1, 5) in x = 0 and then in x = 3: the image is (7, 5), a shift of 6, twice the distance 3.

card.rule: Two reflections make a translation if the mirrors are parallel, and a rotation by twice the angle if they cross.
card.limits: The order matters for the direction of the result, and the result is always a translation (possibly identity) or a rotation, never a reflection.

media.alt: Two parallel lines l1 (lower) and l2 (upper), tilting gently downward to the right, each with arrowheads at both ends. Point A is on l1 and B on l2, joined by a short segment with an arrow pointing from A up to B, perpendicular to both lines. Three dots run up the left side: an unlabelled one below l1, X' between the lines and X'' above l2.

Two lines l1 and l2 cross at point C, l1 rising to the right and l2 falling to the right, both with arrowheads at each end. A small arc on the left of C marks the angle theta between them. Three dots lie to the left: X below, X' beside C and X'' above.

concepts.title: Rotating part of a figure
concepts.question: How can rotating one line about a vertex locate the other vertices of an equilateral triangle?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Lines l1, l2, l3 are parallel, with A on l1. Find B on l2 and C on l3 so that ABC is equilateral. Rotating clockwise by 60 degrees about A takes AC to AB, and the image of l3 meets l2 at B. Rotate l3 by 60 degrees and read off B.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The rotation about A by 60 degrees takes C to B, so the image of l3 passes through B; since B is on l2 it is the meeting point of l2 with the image of l3. Rotating a line by theta makes an angle theta with the original.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take l1: y = 0, l2: y = 1, l3: y = 2 and A = (0, 0). Then B = (square root of 3, 1), C = (0, 2), and the side length is 2.

card.rule: Rotate the part of the figure that must move with the triangle, here the third line, so the vertex falls on a known line.
card.limits: A coordinate solution also works but is ugly; the rotation helps only because an equilateral triangle has 60 degree symmetry about each vertex.

media.alt: Three horizontal parallel lines l1 (bottom), l2 (middle) and l3 (top), each with arrowheads at both ends. A triangle ABC is drawn with A on l1, B on l2 and C on l3, so it spans all three lines. It stands for the equilateral triangle the problem asks for.

Three horizontal parallel lines l1, l2 and l3 from bottom to top, crossed by a thick steep line l4 sloping down to the right. A is on l1 and B is where l4 meets l2. A dashed vertical rises from A to l3 and a dashed segment runs from A through B; a 60 degree arc is marked between these two dashed lines.

Two triangles form a bow-tie meeting at C: one segment from an unlabelled top vertex to X, and another from B to Y, cross at C; short sides join the top vertex to Y and B to X. A third triangle with apex Z is attached on the left, joining Z to the top vertex and to B.

concepts.title: Composing rotations
concepts.question: What is the composition of two rotations, and where is its centre?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A rotation by alpha followed by a rotation by beta, possibly about a different centre, is a rotation by alpha + beta if alpha + beta is not 360 degrees. If the sum is 360 and the centres differ, it is a translation; if the centres coincide, the identity. A rotation followed by a translation is a rotation by the same angle about a different centre.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Write each rotation as two reflections and cancel the shared mirror. To find the centre of R(B, beta) after R(A, alpha), draw rays from A and B making angles alpha/2 and beta/2 with AB; they meet at the centre.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A 90 degree rotation followed by a 150 degree rotation is a rotation by 240 degrees. A 200 degree rotation followed by a 160 degree rotation about a different centre is a translation.

card.rule: Angles of rotations add; if they total 360 degrees the result is a translation or the identity.
card.limits: The centres matter: the angle of the composition is the sum, but its centre is not either original centre unless they coincide.

media.alt: Two lines cross at point P: a thicker line l running from upper left to lower right, and a thinner line l' rising gently to the right. X is a dot on l and Y a dot on l', both on the upper-left side of P. Small right-angle marks with short dashed stubs sit near P on each line.

concepts.title: Recovering triangle vertices from apexes
concepts.question: How can composing three rotations locate the vertices of a triangle from the apexes of isosceles triangles on its sides?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Erect exterior isosceles triangles on sides XY, YZ, XZ with apex A (angle 60), B (angle 120) and C (angle 90). Given only A, B, C, find X, Y, Z. Let R_A, R_B, R_C be the rotations about the apexes by these angles. Then R_A(X) = Y, R_B(Y) = Z, R_C(Z) = X.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: So the composition R_C . R_B . R_A sends X to itself. It is a rotation by 60 + 120 + 90 = 270 degrees, and a rotation has exactly one fixed point, its centre. So X is the centre, which Fact 8.5.8 locates.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With apex angles 60, 120 and 90 the composite angle is 270, not 360, so the centre exists.

card.rule: Make the unknown a fixed point of a composition of known rotations, then find that composition's centre.
card.limits: The method needs the total angle not to be 360 degrees; with 360 the composition is a translation or the identity and has no unique centre.

media.alt: A scalene triangle in heavy lines with one vertex labelled X at left; the other two vertices, at the top and at the far lower right, are unlabelled. Thin dashed segments stick out from the vertices, hinting at an unfinished construction, and one stray dot sits at the far upper left on a dashed line.

concepts.title: Homothety
concepts.question: What does a homothety with a given centre and ratio do to a point and to a figure?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A similarity is a transformation that preserves ratios of distances. The simplest are homotheties, or central similarities. A homothety with centre C and ratio k sends each point X to the point X-prime on ray CX with CX-prime divided by CX equal to k.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: It is a transformational way of thinking about similarity. Every homothety is a similarity, but not every similarity is a homothety. A homothety has exactly one fixed point, the centre.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With centre at the origin and k = 3, the point (2, 1) goes to (6, 3). With k = 1/2, the point (8, 4) goes to (4, 2).

card.rule: A homothety with centre C and ratio k multiplies every distance from C by k, along the same ray.
card.limits: The book takes the ratio k positive; for a point at C the image is C, and a homothety with k = 1 is the identity.

media.alt: A hinged linkage of straight bars. Two bars rise from filled dots at the lower left and lower right to meet at hinge B at the top. A is a hinge on the left bar and C on the right bar. Two shorter bars from A and C slope down and meet at an unlabelled hinge at the bottom, closing a diamond.

concepts.title: Properties of homotheties
concepts.question: What does a homothety do to lines and angles, and what does it say about concurrence?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Fact 8.5.11: homotheties map lines to parallel lines, so they preserve angles. Conversely, if two figures are directly similar, not congruent, and corresponding sides are parallel, they are homothetic. So the lines joining corresponding points of such figures concur at the centre of the homothety.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each point moves along its ray from the centre by the same ratio, so a segment and its image are in the ratio k and parallel, by the similar triangles fact.

blocks.label: Example
