blocks.text: Whenever a problem involves midpoints, look for a homothety with ratio 1/2.

card.rule: Homotheties keep directions: corresponding sides are parallel and the joining lines meet at the centre.
card.limits: The converse needs figures that are directly similar, with the same orientation, and not congruent; a reflected figure is oppositely similar.

concepts.title: A locus of midpoints by homothety
concepts.question: Where do the midpoints of segments joining a point on one circle to a point on another lie?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Circles C1 and C2 have centres 10 apart and radii 1 and 3. Find the locus of midpoints M of segments XY with X on C1 and Y on C2. The locus is an annulus (ring) centred halfway between the centres, with inner radius 1 and outer radius 2.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Fix X. M is the image of Y under the homothety of centre X and ratio 1/2, so M traces a circle of radius 3/2 centred at the midpoint of BX, where B is the centre of C2. As X moves on C1, these centres trace the image of C1 under the homothety with centre B and ratio 1/2, a circle of radius 1/2.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The distance from the ring's centre to M ranges from (3 - 1)/2 = 1 to (3 + 1)/2 = 2.

card.rule: Use a homothety of ratio 1/2 twice: first fixing one endpoint, then moving it.
card.limits: The annulus answer needs the circles not to meet and the radii to differ; with intersecting or equal circles the shape of the region changes.

media.alt: Two circles of very different size: a small one with centre A at the left and a large one with centre B at the right. A straight segment runs from X on the small circle, through the gap between the circles, to Y on the large circle. Its midpoint M lies in the gap, outside both circles.

concepts.title: Inversion in a circle
concepts.question: How is the inverse of a point defined, and how is it constructed?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Inversion with centre O and radius r sends a point X different from O to the point X-prime on ray OX with OX times OX-prime equal to r squared. It is also called inversion with respect to the circle with centre O and radius r. It acts like a homothety whose ratio varies inversely with the distance to the centre.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: For X inside the circle, draw the chord through X perpendicular to OX; the tangents at its ends meet at X-prime. For X outside, draw the two tangents; the midpoint of the chord of contact is X-prime. Similar triangles give OX times OX-prime = OB squared = r squared.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With r = 6 and OX = 4, the inverse is 9 away from O along the same ray.

card.rule: The inverse of X lies on ray OX at distance r squared divided by OX.
card.limits: The centre O has no inverse (it goes to the point at infinity), and applying inversion twice returns the original point.

media.alt: Circle omega with centre O on its left. A horizontal ray from O passes through X inside the circle and A on the circle, then continues to a dot outside and on with an arrowhead. A vertical chord BC through X is perpendicular to the ray, with B at the top. Radius OB is drawn, and the tangent at B, marked with a right angle, meets the ray at the outside dot.

concepts.title: Basic facts about inversion
concepts.question: Which points, rays and circles does inversion leave in place, and how does it exchange inside and outside?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let T be inversion in the circle w with centre O. Points of w are fixed, so T(w) = w. T exchanges the inside and outside of w. As X goes to O, T(X) goes off to infinity, and conversely. A ray OX maps to itself. A circle concentric with w of radius t maps to a concentric circle of radius r squared divided by t.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: All follow from OX times OX-prime = r squared. A point on w has OX = r, so OX-prime = r too.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With r = 6, the circle of radius 4 about O maps to the circle of radius 9, and the circle of radius 9 maps back to radius 4.

card.rule: Points on the circle stay put, inside and outside swap, and concentric circles of radius t go to concentric circles of radius r squared over t.
card.limits: These facts concern O and the circle w; the centre O itself has no ordinary image, and lines not through O do not map to themselves.

concepts.title: The point at infinity and generalised circles
concepts.question: How does adding a point at infinity let lines count as circles?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The image of a point tending to the centre O goes off to infinity in all directions at once. Add one point at infinity, written infinity, with T(O) = infinity and T(infinity) = O. A line is then a circle through infinity, of infinite radius and zero curvature.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Three points determine a circle; a line is determined by two points on it plus infinity. Calling both ordinary circles and lines circles, two lines are tangent exactly when they coincide or are parallel, tangent at infinity.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two parallel lines are two circles touching at infinity.

card.rule: Treat lines as circles through the point at infinity; inversion then sends circles to circles.
card.limits: The point at infinity is an informal device here, made rigorous in projective geometry; it is not an ordinary point of the plane.

concepts.title: Fundamental properties of inversion
concepts.question: What does inversion do to distances and to circles?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Fact 8.5.14: (a) for points X and Y, triangles OXY and OY-prime X-prime are oppositely similar. (b) The distance X-prime Y-prime equals XY times r squared divided by (OX times OY). (c) The image of any circle (line or circle) is a circle. (d) The image of an ordinary circle not meeting O is the image of that circle under a homothety centred at O.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: (a) and (b) follow from similar triangles, because OX times OX-prime = OY times OY-prime = r squared. (d) is a simple consequence of (c).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With r = 4, X = (2, 0) and Y = (0, 4): X-prime = (8, 0) and Y-prime = (0, 4). The distance X-prime Y-prime = 2 times XY.

card.rule: Inversion changes distances by a factor depending on OX and OY, but sends circles and lines to circles and lines.
card.limits: Lines and circles through the centre are exceptional: they map to lines and the property (c) is stated with generalised circles.

concepts.title: A circle through the centre inverts to a line
concepts.question: What is the image of a circle through the centre of inversion?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Example 8.5.15: let w have centre O, and let a circle gamma pass through O and meet w at A and B. Under inversion in w, the image of gamma is the line AB.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Take X on gamma outside w. Draw the tangents from X to w, touching at C and D; the midpoint of CD is the image X-prime. The circle with diameter OX meets w at C and D. The chords CD (of w and that circle), OX (of that circle and gamma) and AB (of w and gamma) are the three common chords of three circles, and are concurrent by Example 8.4.6.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Since the chords meet in one point, and X-prime lies on CD and on OX, X-prime is on AB.

card.rule: A circle through the centre of inversion becomes a line through its other intersections with the inversion circle.
card.limits: The proof as given handles X outside w; the case with X inside w puts the image on line AB but outside the segment, and the book leaves it to you.

media.alt: A small circle omega with centre O and a larger circle gamma through O cross at A (top) and B (bottom), joined by a dashed vertical line. X is on gamma, outside omega, far to the upper right. Lines from X reach C and D on omega; segment CD is crossed at X' by line OX. A dashed circle passes through O, C, X and D.

concepts.title: Using inversion to simplify a figure
concepts.question: How can inversion about a well-chosen point turn circles into lines and reveal a hidden structure?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Strategy: find a point where several circles meet and invert about it, turning those circles into lines and making the figure simpler. Example 8.5.16: circles C1, C2, C3, C4 are tangent cyclically (C1 to C2, C2 to C3, C3 to C4, C4 to C1). Prove the four points of tangency are concyclic.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Invert about C, the tangency point of C4 and C1. The images of C1 and C4 are parallel lines, because tangency at the centre goes to tangency at infinity; the images of C2 and C3 are circles between those lines, tangent to them and to each other. Angle chasing shows the three finite tangency points are collinear, and the fourth is infinity.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The images of the four points lie on a line, which is a generalised circle. Inverting again, the original four points are concyclic, since they cannot be collinear.

card.rule: Invert about a point shared by many circles; lines are simpler than circles, and tangency is preserved.
card.limits: The new picture must be easier than the old one; the result is concyclic or collinear, so a separate argument is needed to exclude collinear.

media.alt: Four circles in a ring, each touching the next: c1 (upper left) touches c2 (left) at D, c2 touches c3 (bottom) at A, c3 touches c4 (large, right) at B, and c4 touches c1 at C. A dashed circle omega, centred at C, overlaps c1 and c4 and passes near B.

Picture after inversion: two parallel thick lines c'1 (left) and c'4 (right), leaning slightly from vertical. Between them, small circles c'2 and c'3 touch each other at A'. Circle c'2 touches the left line at D' and c'3 touches the right line at B'. A thick segment runs from D' through A' to B'. A dashed circle omega surrounds the lower part.

concepts.title: The fundamental theorem of calculus
concepts.question: How can an area under a curve be found from an antiderivative, when area and slope seem unrelated?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a,b]\) and let \(F\) be any antiderivative of \(f\), meaning \(F'(x)=f(x)\). Then \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b)-F(a)\). The left side is the area between the graph of \(f\), the x-axis and the lines \(x=a\) and \(x=b\). The right side comes from differentiation, the slope of tangent lines.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The surprise is that an area and a slope seem to have nothing in common. The theorem does not say that area equals slope. It says area equals the change in a function whose slope at each point is the height of the graph. The next ideas show why that link holds.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=2x\) on \([1,3]\), take \(F(x)=x^2\). Then \(F(3)-F(1)=9-1=8\), and the trapezoid under the graph (heights 2 and 6, width 2) also has area 8.

card.rule: A definite integral of a continuous function equals the change F(b) - F(a) in any antiderivative of that function.
card.limits: The theorem is stated for a continuous f. Used as a procedure, it says what to compute, but it does not by itself say why area and antiderivatives are linked.

concepts.title: The define-a-function tool
concepts.question: How can a single definite integral be turned into a function that can be differentiated?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Given a continuous \(f\) on \([a,b]\), define \(g(t):=\int_a^t f(x)\,dx\). The upper limit is now the variable \(t\), and \(g(t)\) is the area under the graph from \(a\) to \(t\). As \(t\) increases, the region sweeps to the right, like a moving curtain.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A definite integral with fixed limits is one number, and a number has no rate of change. Letting the upper limit vary gives a function of t. A function can be differentiated, so questions about how fast the area grows can now be asked.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=2x\) and \(a=1\), \(g(t)=t^2-1\). Then \(g(3)=8\), the area found earlier, and \(g'(t)=2t\), the height of the graph at \(t\).

card.rule: Make the upper limit a variable to turn a fixed area into a function of t that you can differentiate.
card.limits: The function g depends on the starting point a. Changing a changes g by a constant, so the tool is a way of seeing the integral, not a new way to compute it.

media.alt: A completely blank white image with no visible drawing, text or marks.

Graph on x and y axes: a wavy curve y equals f of x runs across the plane. The region under it between two vertical lines is shaded grey, like a curtain. Four short arrows just right of its right edge point rightward, showing that edge moving along the x-axis.

concepts.title: How fast the curtain grows
concepts.question: How fast does the curtain's area grow, compared with the height of its leading edge?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For the moving curtain \(g(t)=\int_a^t f(x)\,dx\), the rate of change of the area is \(g'(t)=f(t)\): the speed at which the area grows equals the height of the leading edge at time \(t\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: When the leading edge is tall, the area grows fast. When it is short, the area grows slowly. So the speed of growth is the height itself. The book calls this intuitive and returns to it later for a careful treatment.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=2x\), \(g(t)=t^2-1\) and \(g'(t)=2t=f(t)\). At \(t=3\) the leading edge is 6 tall, and the area grows at 6 units per unit of time.

card.rule: The rate at which swept area grows equals the height of the leading edge: g'(t) = f(t).
card.limits: This is a picture-based argument. The exact growth over a time step is not simply height times step, so the equation still needs the careful treatment in the next idea.

media.alt: A wavy curve above a horizontal axis, with t marked below the axis. A tall double-headed arrow at t, labelled f of t, spans from axis to curve. A second vertical line stands a short distance to the right, and a small horizontal double arrow between the two verticals marks the narrow strip.

concepts.title: From the curtain to the theorem
concepts.question: How does the equation g'(t) = f(t) turn into the fundamental theorem?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(g'(t)=f(t)\), then for any constant \(C\) the function \(F(t):=g(t)+C\) also has \(F'(t)=f(t)\), and \(F(b)-F(a)=g(b)-g(a)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). That is the fundamental theorem.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Adding a constant does not change a derivative, so F is an antiderivative of f. In the difference F(b) - F(a) the constants cancel. Since g(a) = 0, what is left is g(b), the area from a to b.

card.rule: Speed of area equals edge height gives an antiderivative F = g + C, and F(b) - F(a) is the area from a to b.
card.limits: The argument is only as strong as g'(t) = f(t), which so far rests on a picture. It builds the antiderivative as g plus a constant, and it needs f continuous to be made careful.

concepts.title: The error term in the proof
concepts.question: What must still be shown to turn the curtain picture into a rigorous proof?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The curtain's exact growth is \(\int_t^{t+\Delta t} f(x)\,dx=f(t)\Delta t+E(t)\), where \(E(t)\) is the area of the thin error region between the curve and a rectangle of height \(f(t)\). The equation \(g'(t)=f(t)\) holds when \(\lim_{\Delta t\to 0} E(t)/\Delta t=0\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The difference quotient of g is \((g(t+\Delta t)-g(t))/\Delta t = f(t)+E(t)/\Delta t\). If the error ratio goes to 0, the quotient goes to f(t). E(t) itself tends to 0 for any reasonable f, so what matters is that it shrinks faster than \(\Delta t\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Let \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(t=1\). For \(\Delta t=0.1\), the exact growth is 0.11033 and the rectangle gives 0.1, so \(E=0.01033\) and \(E/\Delta t=0.103\). For \(\Delta t=0.01\), \(E/\Delta t\approx 0.010\).

card.rule: The curtain proof is complete when the error E(t) shrinks faster than the time step: E(t) / Delta t tends to 0.
card.limits: A small \(E(t)\) alone is not enough, since the rectangle's own area also shrinks with \(\Delta t\). What decides the matter is the ratio, and showing that it tends to 0 needs more than the picture.

media.alt: A completely blank white image with no visible drawing, text or marks.

A wavy curve above a horizontal axis with t marked below. A tall double arrow at t is labelled f of t, and a horizontal double arrow labelled delta t spans the strip to a second vertical line on the right. A dashed rectangle top at height f of t leaves a small grey sliver between it and the falling curve.

concepts.title: Convergence of sequences as the foundation
concepts.question: Which one idea underlies limits, continuity, differentiation and integration?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Almost everything in rigorous calculus stems from one idea: convergence of sequences. If you understand it, you can handle limits, continuity, differentiation and integration. The book treats it as the theoretical foundation of calculus.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each of those notions says that some sequence of numbers settles down. A derivative is the limit of difference quotients, an integral the limit of sums, and an infinite series the limit of its partial sums. Learning to prove convergence therefore pays off everywhere.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=x^2\) at 3, the quotients \(\frac{f(3+1/n)-f(3)}{1/n}=6+\frac1n\) form a sequence that settles at 6, the derivative.

card.rule: To handle a limit, derivative or integral rigorously, ask which sequence is converging and to what.
card.limits: An intuitive feel for limits is not enough for interesting problems, and the book calls for a more rigorous kind of wisdom. Convergence itself rests on the real numbers, whose foundations are treated elsewhere.

concepts.title: The formal definition of convergence
concepts.question: What does it mean, precisely, for a sequence to converge to a limit L?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A real sequence \((a_n)\) converges to \(L\), written \(\lim a_n=L\) or \(a_n\to L\), if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an integer \(N\) such that \(|a_n-L|<\varepsilon\) for all \(n\ge N\). Here \(\varepsilon\) is the distance you demand and \(N\) is the index after which the terms stay that close.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Think of epsilon as a tiny distance chosen by a challenger. You reply with a huge N: from that term on, every term lies within epsilon of L. The key phrase is eventually, and forever after. Getting close once is not enough.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take \(a_n=1/n\) and \(L=0\). For \(\varepsilon=0.01\), we need \(1/n<0.01\), which holds for all \(n\ge 101\). So \(N=101\) answers that challenge.

card.rule: a_n tends to L when, for any tolerance, all terms after some index stay within that tolerance of L.
card.limits: A sequence that comes within \(\varepsilon\) of \(L\) sometimes, but leaves again, does not converge. For example, \(1,-1,1,-1,\ldots\) never stays close to any one number.

concepts.title: Draw a picture, guess the limit
concepts.question: How can a picture and a guess help prove that a sequence converges?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Two first methods for showing that a sequence converges: draw a picture to find the key idea, or guess the limit \(L\) and then show that the terms get arbitrarily close to \(L\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Pictures rarely supply rigor, but they often supply the idea that makes an argument lucid and correct. Once L is guessed, the definition becomes a concrete check: show that the distance |a_n - L| can be made smaller than any tolerance by going far enough along.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Let \(a_n=\frac{3n+1}{n}\). Guess \(L=3\). Then \(|a_n-3|=\frac1n\), which is below any \(\varepsilon\) once \(n>1/\varepsilon\). So \(a_n\to 3\).

card.rule: Guess the limit with a picture or a table, then prove it by making the distance from the guess as small as you like.
card.limits: A picture or table is evidence for a guess, not a proof. A wrong guess fails at the second step, because the distance to it will not shrink to 0.

concepts.title: The Cauchy property
concepts.question: Can you show that a sequence converges without knowing its limit?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A sequence \((a_n)\) has the Cauchy property if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an \(N\) such that \(|a_m-a_n|<\varepsilon\) for all \(m,n\ge N\). A real sequence with this property converges.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The terms are compared with each other, not with a limit. If they eventually crowd together as closely as you like, they must be heading to one place. That a place exists is one of the foundational facts about the real numbers, which the book does not prove and instead cites.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(a_n=3+\frac1{2^n}\), any two terms with indexes beyond \(N\) differ by less than \(1/2^N\). So the sequence is Cauchy, and it converges.

card.rule: If the terms eventually stay within epsilon of each other for every epsilon, the real sequence converges.
card.limits: The property must hold for every pair of later terms, not just neighbours. Terms that move only a little at each step can still wander off, as with the sequence of logarithms of 1, 2, 3, and so on.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece, not a diagram: the label (b), then the limit as n goes to infinity of the sum from k equals n to infinity of a with subscript k, equals zero.

concepts.title: Bounded monotonic sequences
concepts.question: When must a sequence converge just because it only moves one way and cannot escape?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A sequence \((a_n)\) is bounded if there is a finite \(B\) with \(|a_n|\le B\) for all \(n\), and monotonic if it is non-decreasing or non-increasing. Every bounded monotonic real sequence converges.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A monotonic sequence moves in only one direction, and a bound stops it from running off. Our reading of the book's argument: if it did not converge, it would lack the Cauchy property, and one-way motion would then force jumps of a fixed size that the bound cannot allow.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The sequence \(a_n=1-\frac1n\) increases and never exceeds 1. So it is bounded and monotonic, and it converges.

card.rule: A sequence that moves in only one direction and stays bounded must converge.
card.limits: Both hypotheses are needed. A bounded sequence that is not monotonic, such as 1, -1, 1, -1, may fail to converge, and a monotonic one that is not bounded, such as 1, 2, 3, may run off to infinity.

concepts.title: The squeeze principle
concepts.question: How can two simpler sequences trap a harder one and force its limit?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If the terms of \((a_n)\) lie between the terms of two convergent sequences that converge to the same limit \(L\), then \(a_n\to L\). The book's example: \(0<x_n<(0.9)^n\) forces \(x_n\to 0\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A trapped sequence has nowhere else to go. Whatever tolerance you pick, both bounding sequences are within it from some point on, and a sequence between them is within it too. The bounds must close in on the same limit.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(a_n=\frac{\sin n}{n}\), we have \(-\frac1n\le a_n\le\frac1n\). Both bounds tend to 0, so \(a_n\to 0\), even though \(\sin n\) itself has no limit.

card.rule: A sequence squeezed between two sequences with the same limit L has limit L.
card.limits: A bound that does not tend to the same limit gives no conclusion. If one of the two bounds stays far from the other, the sequence between them may do anything.

concepts.title: Big-Oh and little-oh
concepts.question: How do big-Oh and little-oh describe growth rates without tracking every constant?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) (\(f\) is big-Oh of \(g\)) means there is a constant \(C\) with \(|f(x)|\le C|g(x)|\) for all sufficiently large \(x\). \(f(x)=o(g(x))\) (little-oh) means \(f(x)/g(x)\to 0\) as \(x\to\infty\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Big-Oh gives an upper bound on growth, up to a constant. Little-oh says that f grows fundamentally slower than g. The notation keeps the parts of a function that matter and hides the rest.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=5x^3+100x^2\): \(f=O(x^3)\), since \(f\le 105x^3\) for \(x\ge1\). But \(f\) is not \(o(x^3)\), because \(f/x^3\to 5\). Also \(x^2=o(x^3)\), since \(x^2/x^3=1/x\to 0\).

card.rule: O(g) is a bound by a constant multiple of g; o(g) means the ratio to g tends to 0.
card.limits: Big-Oh is only an upper bound: x squared is O(x cubed) even though it is far smaller. Little-oh is the stronger statement, and o implies O but not the other way round.

concepts.title: Bounds for an infinite product
concepts.question: How can you trap the limit of an infinite product between two simple bounds?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For \(0<x<1\), let \(S(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+x)(1+x^2)\cdots(1+x^n)\). Then \(\frac{1}{1-x}<S(x)<e^{x/(1-x)}\). For the product \((1+\frac12)(1+\frac14)\cdots\), this gives bounds 2 and \(e\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Lower bound: multiply out. Every power of x appears at least once with coefficient at least 1, so S is at least 1 + x + x squared + ..., a geometric series. Upper bound: each factor 1 + t is less than e to the t, so S is less than e to the sum x + x squared + ..., which is x/(1-x).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(x=\frac12\), the product \(\left(1+\frac12\right)\left(1+\frac14\right)\left(1+\frac18\right)=2.11\) already exceeds the lower bound 2 after three factors. The limit is about 2.38, between 2 and \(e\approx 2.72\).

card.rule: Bound a product below by multiplying out and above by comparing each factor 1 + t with e to the t.
card.limits: The bounds are estimates, not the value. The book asks whether they can be improved, so a bound should never be reported as the limit itself.

concepts.title: Averaging toward a square root
concepts.question: Why does the averaging sequence \(x_{n+1}=\frac12(x_n+a/x_n)\) have to converge?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Fix \(a>1\) and let \(x_0=a\) and \(x_{n+1}=\frac12\left(x_n+\frac{a}{x_n}\right)\). The sequence is non-increasing and every term is at least \(\sqrt a\). So it is bounded and monotonic, and it converges.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Monotone: \(x_n-x_{n+1}=\frac{x_n^2-a}{2x_n}\ge 0\) whenever \(x_n^2\ge a\). Bounded: each term is the average of \(x_n\) and \(a/x_n\), and an average is at least the geometric mean \(\sqrt{x_n\cdot a/x_n}=\sqrt a\) (the AM-GM inequality).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(a=5\): \(x_0=5\), \(x_1=3\), \(x_2=\frac73\approx2.333\), \(x_3=\frac{47}{21}\approx2.238\). The values fall steadily toward \(\sqrt5\approx2.236\).

card.rule: Prove monotonic convergence by showing the terms never increase and stay above a bound, with AM-GM giving the bound.
card.limits: Monotone alone is not enough. A decreasing sequence with no lower bound can run off to minus infinity, so the lower bound sqrt(a) is essential. The argument shows convergence, not yet the value of the limit.

concepts.title: Showing the error tends to zero
concepts.question: How does the error ratio \(E_{n+1}/E_n\) prove that the averaging sequence converges to \(\sqrt a\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(E_n=x_n-\sqrt a\ge0\) be the error. A short algebra computation gives \(E_{n+1}=\dfrac{E_n^2}{2x_n}\), so \(\dfrac{E_{n+1}}{E_n}=\dfrac{E_n}{2x_n}<\dfrac12\). A positive ratio below one half forces \(E_n\to0\), so \(x_n\to\sqrt a\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Since E_n is less than x_n, the ratio is less than 1/2: each error is under half the previous one. So the error is squeezed between 0 and a halving sequence, and the squeeze principle sends it to 0.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(a=5\): \(E_0=2.764\), \(E_1=0.764\) (ratio 0.28), \(E_2=0.0973\) (ratio 0.13), \(E_3=0.00203\) (ratio 0.021). The ratios stay below one half and keep falling.

card.rule: Prove convergence to a target by showing that the error is positive and shrinks by a factor below one.
card.limits: The ratio bound shows only that the error tends to 0; it does not show how many steps are needed. Here the ratio itself shrinks, so convergence is much faster than halving.

concepts.title: The solve-for-the-limit tool
concepts.question: How can a recursive formula reveal its limit before you know the limit exists?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(x_{n+1}=h(x_n)\) and \(x_n\to L\), then both \(x_n\) and \(x_{n+1}\) approach \(L\) for large \(n\). Taking the limit of the recurrence gives \(L=h(L)\). Solving this equation shows what the limit must be, if the limit exists.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: For large n, the term x_n and the next term are both very nearly L, so the recurrence collapses into an equation in L alone. The tool does not prove existence. It narrows the candidates for the limit.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(x_{n+1}=\frac12(x_n+a/x_n)\), the equation is \(L=\frac12(L+a/L)\). Simplifying gives \(L^2=a\), so \(L=\sqrt a\) for positive terms.

card.rule: Replace x_n and x_{n+1} by L in the recurrence and solve; do this only after (or alongside) showing that a limit exists.
card.limits: The equation may have solutions that are not limits. For \(x_{n+1}=2x_n\) with \(x_0=1\), the tool gives \(L=0\), but the terms 1, 2, 4, 8 grow without bound.

concepts.title: Differences of cube roots
concepts.question: Can differences \(\sqrt[3]{n}-\sqrt[3]{m}\) of cube roots get arbitrarily close to \(\sqrt2\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Yes. Outline: (1) show \(\sqrt[3]{n+1}-\sqrt[3]{n}=O(n^{-2/3})\), so consecutive cube roots get closer together; (2) fix \(m\), so that \(\sqrt[3]{n}-\sqrt[3]{m}\) climbs by tiny steps as \(n\) grows; (3) make this rigorous and general for any target.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: For large integers, cube roots crowd together, so subtracting a fixed cube root leaves a ladder of values with small steps. A target such as the square root of 2 must lie between two neighbouring rungs. Starting from a bigger cube makes the steps finer.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book writes 3 as \(\sqrt[3]{1000}-\sqrt[3]{343}=10-7\) and continues with \(\sqrt[3]{1001}-7,\ \sqrt[3]{1002}-7,\dots\). The first step is \(\sqrt[3]{1001}-10\approx0.0033\), finer than the gap \(\sqrt[3]{28}-3\approx0.037\) of the earlier sequence.

card.rule: Show that the gaps between candidate values tend to 0, then place the target between two neighbours.
card.limits: The outline shows only the idea, as the book says it is a partial solution. Making it rigorous needs an explicit estimate for the gap and a choice of m for each target accuracy.

concepts.title: Continuity through sequences
concepts.question: What does it mean for a function to be continuous at a point, using sequences?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) and \(a\in D\). Then \(f\) is continuous at \(a\) if \(\lim_{n\to\infty}f(x_n)=f(a)\) for every sequence \((x_n)\) in \(D\) with limit \(a\). It is continuous on \(D\) if it is continuous at every point of \(D\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Informally, the graph can be drawn without lifting the pencil. In the sequence form, however you creep up on a, the outputs must creep up on f(a). The book picks this form from many equivalent definitions because it is one of the easiest to use.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Let \(f(x)=0\) for \(x<1\) and \(f(x)=1\) for \(x\ge1\). For \(x_n=1-\frac1n\), \(f(x_n)=0\) for every \(n\), but \(f(1)=1\). So \(f\) is not continuous at 1.

card.rule: f is continuous at a when every sequence approaching a is sent by f to a sequence approaching f(a).
card.limits: The test is about every sequence, so a single sequence that fails is enough to show a function is not continuous. The definition also says nothing about points outside the domain D.

concepts.title: Which functions are continuous
concepts.question: Which familiar functions are continuous, and where does a function like 1/x stand?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: All elementary functions are continuous at every point of their domains. These are finite combinations of polynomials, rational functions, trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions, exponentials, logarithms and radicals.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Continuity is a condition you probably take for granted, since virtually every function with a simple formula has it. Continuous at all points of the domain is a statement about points where the function is defined. A point missing from the domain is not a point of discontinuity.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The function \(\frac1x\) is continuous at every point of its domain, all \(x\ne0\), even though it has no value at 0. Polynomials and \(\sin x\) are continuous at every real number.

card.rule: Elementary functions are continuous at every point where they are defined.
card.limits: Continuous on its domain does not mean continuous on a larger interval. A function that is not elementary, or that is built piece by piece, needs to be checked with the definition.

concepts.title: The intermediate value theorem
concepts.question: If a continuous function takes two values, must it take every value in between?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a,b]\), then \(f\) takes every value between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\): for each \(y\) between them there is an \(x\in[a,b]\) with \(f(x)=y\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Following the graph from one end to the other without lifting the pencil, you cannot jump past a height. The book calls this obvious, and says a rigorous proof is built by repeated bisection, narrowing the interval in which the value must lie.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Let \(f(x)=x^3-x-1\) on \([1,2]\). Then \(f(1)=-1\) and \(f(2)=5\). The value 0 lies between them, so \(f\) has a zero in \([1,2]\).

card.rule: A continuous function on a closed interval takes every value between its end values.
card.limits: Both hypotheses matter. The function \(1/x\) on \([-1,1]\) has end values -1 and 1 but never takes the value 0, because it is not defined and not continuous at 0.

media.alt: Cropped formula layout: f of one tenth, a minus sign, then plus f of nine tenths on the top line; the bracketed fractions one tenth, two tenths and nine tenths are lined up beneath. It is a piece of a sum of function values, not a figure.

concepts.title: The extreme value theorem
concepts.question: When must a continuous function reach a largest and a smallest value?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a,b]\), then there are points \(u,v\in[a,b]\) with \(f(u)\le f(x)\) and \(f(v)\ge f(x)\) for all \(x\in[a,b]\). So \(f\) attains a minimum and a maximum on the interval.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The theorem seems almost without content, but its hypotheses matter. The interval has to be closed, so that the endpoints are included and the function cannot creep toward a value it never reaches.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([-1,2]\), the minimum is \(f(0)=0\) and the maximum is \(f(2)=4\). Both are attained at points of the interval.

card.rule: A continuous function on a closed interval attains a minimum and a maximum.
card.limits: The extremes may be at the endpoints, and the theorem does not say where they are. It does not apply on an interval that leaves out an endpoint, nor to a function that is not continuous.

concepts.title: A fixed point from the intermediate value theorem
concepts.question: Why must a continuous map of [0,1] into itself have a point it leaves unmoved?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) is continuous, then there is \(u\in[0,1]\) with \(f(u)=u\). Proof: let \(g(x)=f(x)-x\). It is continuous, \(g(0)=f(0)\ge0\) and \(g(1)=f(1)-1\le0\), so by the intermediate value theorem \(g(u)=0\) for some \(u\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A fixed point is a place where the graphs of y = f(x) and y = x meet. The difference g measures how far the first graph is above the second. It starts at or above 0 and ends at or below 0, so it must cross 0.

card.rule: To show two graphs meet, apply the intermediate value theorem to the difference of the functions.
card.limits: The argument needs f to map [0,1] into [0,1], so that the signs of g at the ends are known, and it needs a closed interval. It proves existence only; it does not locate the fixed point.

concepts.title: Uniform continuity
concepts.question: What is uniform continuity, and how does it differ from continuity at each point?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A function \(f:A\to B\) is uniformly continuous on \(A\) if for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x_1-x_2|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|<\varepsilon\) for all \(x_1,x_2\in A\). The \(\delta\) depends only on \(\varepsilon\), not on the \(x\)-values.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Informally, the amount of wiggle in the graph is limited in the same way throughout the domain. For each ε challenge, a single δ response works everywhere. A function that wiggles faster in some places than others would need smaller δ there.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=2x+1\), \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|=2|x_1-x_2|\). Choose \(\delta=\varepsilon/2\). Then any two inputs closer than \(\delta\) have outputs closer than \(\varepsilon\), wherever on the line they are.

card.rule: In uniform continuity, one δ per ε works for the whole domain.
card.limits: Uniform continuity is a property of a function on a set, not at a point. A function can be continuous at every point of a set without being uniformly continuous on it.

concepts.title: Square function on a closed interval
concepts.question: How can a single \(\delta\) be found for \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([-3,3]\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The function \(f(x)=x^2\) is uniformly continuous on \([-3,3]\): if \(|x_1-x_2|<\delta\) then \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|<\varepsilon\) for \(\delta=\varepsilon/6\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Factor: \(|x_1^2-x_2^2|=|x_1+x_2|\cdot|x_1-x_2|\). On \([-3,3]\), \(|x_1+x_2|\le6\). So the output difference is at most \(6|x_1-x_2|\), which is below \(\varepsilon\) once \(|x_1-x_2|<\varepsilon/6\).

card.rule: Bound the factor that varies, then divide the tolerance by that bound.
card.limits: The constant 6 comes from the interval. On a larger interval the bound on |x_1 + x_2| grows and δ shrinks. The method gives a sufficient δ, not necessarily the largest one.

concepts.title: Reciprocal on an open and a closed domain
concepts.question: Why is \(1/x\) not uniformly continuous on \((0,\infty)\), yet uniformly continuous on \([2,1000]\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The function \(f(x)=1/x\) on \((0,\infty)\) is not uniformly continuous: near 0 it changes too fast, so for a given \(\varepsilon\) no single \(\delta\) works for \(x\)-values close enough to 0. On \([2,1000]\) it is uniformly continuous, with \(\delta=4\varepsilon\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Compute \(\left|\frac1{x_1}-\frac1{x_2}\right|=\frac{|x_1-x_2|}{x_1x_2}\). On \([2,1000]\), \(x_1x_2\ge4\), so the difference is at most \(\frac14|x_1-x_2|\). Near 0 the product \(x_1x_2\) is tiny and the quotient is huge.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take \(x_1=\delta/2\) and \(x_2=\delta/4\) with \(\delta\le1\). They differ by \(\delta/4<\delta\), but \(1/x_1-1/x_2=2/\delta-4/\delta\) has size \(2/\delta\ge2\). No \(\delta\) can keep outputs within 1.

card.rule: A function that speeds up near an excluded point cannot be uniformly continuous up to that point.
card.limits: Continuity at each point of (0, infinity) does not give a single δ. Removing the troublesome end by working on a closed interval away from 0 restores uniform continuity.

concepts.title: Finishing the fundamental theorem
concepts.question: How does uniform continuity show that the error \(E(t)/\Delta t\) tends to 0?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Since \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a,b]\), it is uniformly continuous. Given \(\varepsilon>0\), pick \(\Delta t\) so small that \(|f(x)-f(t)|<\varepsilon\) whenever \(x\) is within \(\Delta t\) of \(t\), for every \(t\). Then \(|E(t)|\le\varepsilon\,\Delta t\), so \(|E(t)/\Delta t|<\varepsilon\), and the limit is 0.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The error region is a sliver between the curve and a rectangle of height f(t). Its height is at most epsilon at every point of the strip, and its width is the time step. Area is at most height times width.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,1]\), \(|f(x)-f(t)|\le2|x-t|\le2\Delta t\). So \(|E|\le2\Delta t^2\) and \(|E|/\Delta t\le2\Delta t\). For \(\varepsilon=0.04\), any \(\Delta t<0.02\) works.

card.rule: Uniform continuity bounds the error sliver by epsilon times the step, whatever the position t.
card.limits: The proof uses the picture only to set up the error term; the details are what make it rigorous. It also leans on the accepted fact that a continuous function on a closed interval is uniformly continuous.

concepts.title: Two meanings of the derivative
concepts.question: What do f' and f'' tell you about how a function grows?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The derivative \(f'(x)\) has two interpretations: as a rate of change of \(f\) with respect to \(x\), and as the slope of the tangent line at \((x,f(x))\). The second derivative \(f''(x)\) measures how fast the derivative is changing.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The rate-of-change meaning explains how a function grows. If f' is positive, f increases. If f'' is positive, the slope is increasing, so the graph curves upward. Together, the two signs describe the shape of the graph.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\): \(f'(x)=3x^2-3\) and \(f''(x)=6x\). At \(x=1\), \(f'(1)=0\) and \(f''(1)=6>0\): the slope is zero and is increasing, so \(x=1\) is a local minimum.

card.rule: Use the sign of f' for the direction of change and the sign of f'' for how that direction is changing.
card.limits: When f' = 0 and f'' = 0 at a point, the signs alone do not decide. For x cubed at 0, the point is not an extreme; for x to the fourth at 0, it is a minimum.

concepts.title: A polynomial inequality by sign analysis
concepts.question: Why does \(p(x)-p''(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\) force \(p(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(p\) be a polynomial of even degree with positive leading coefficient, and suppose \(p(x)-p''(x)\ge0\) for all real \(x\). Then \(p(x)\ge0\) for all real \(x\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Such a polynomial tends to plus infinity at both ends, so it has a finite minimum value p(a) at some point a. Suppose p(a) is negative. At a relative minimum, p''(a) is at least 0. But the hypothesis gives p(a) at least p''(a), which is at least 0, a contradiction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(p(x)=x^2+2\): \(p-p''=x^2\ge0\). The minimum is at \(a=0\), where \(p(0)=2\) and \(p''(0)=2\). Indeed \(p\ge2>0\) everywhere.

card.rule: Argue by contradiction at the minimum point, where the second derivative cannot be negative.
card.limits: The hypotheses carry the weight. Without even degree and a positive leading coefficient there may be no minimum, and if p - p'' is negative somewhere the conclusion can fail, as for x squared minus 1.

concepts.title: Locating roots with a sketch of a cubic
concepts.question: How can a rough graph and a derivative locate the roots \(a<b<c\) of a cubic?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(a<b<c\) be real with \(a+b+c=6\) and \(ab+bc+ca=9\). Then \(0<a<1<b<3<c<4\). The method: study the cubic \(P(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x-k\) with \(k=abc\), whose zeros are \(a,b,c\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A cubic with three zeros is positive between the first two and negative between the last two, with a relative maximum between a and b and a relative minimum between b and c. The derivative locates those turning points, and the values P(0) and P(4) pin down the outer roots.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: \(P'(x)=3(x-1)(x-3)\), so the turning points are at 1 and 3, giving \(a\) below 1, \(b\) between 1 and 3, and \(c\) above 3. Since \(P(1)=4-k\) is positive and \(P(3)=-k\) is negative, \(k\) lies between 0 and 4. Then \(P(0)=-k\) is negative and \(P(4)=4-k\) is positive, so the first root is right of 0 and the last is left of 4.

card.rule: Sketch the cubic, use its derivative for the turning points, and test signs at chosen points.
card.limits: The turning points do not depend on the unknown k, but the signs at them do. Outside the stated sums, the roots may be complex, and the sketch with three real zeros no longer applies.

media.alt: Graph of a cubic curve rising to the right that crosses the x-axis at three points a, b and c from left to right. It is above the axis between a and b, with a hump, and below it between b and c, with a dip. Two further points on the axis: u, between a and b, below the hump, and v, between b and c, below the dip.

concepts.title: The tangent-line approximation
concepts.question: How well does the tangent line approximate a function near a point?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For small \(h\), \(f(a+h)\approx f(a)+h\,f'(a)\). This comes from the definition of the derivative as the limit of \(\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\) as \(h\to0\), the slope of secant lines that approach the tangent line.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: When h is small, the quotient is close to f'(a), so multiplying by h gives the change in f. The linear function ℓ(h) = f(a) + h f'(a) follows the tangent line. It is very useful in combination with other geometric information, such as convexity.

card.rule: Near a point, replace the function by f(a) plus h times f'(a).
card.limits: The approximation is good only when h is small. For a strongly curved graph, the error grows quickly with h, and f'' controls how fast.

concepts.title: Bernoulli's inequality by convexity
concepts.question: How does convexity prove \((1+x)^\alpha\ge1+\alpha x\) for real exponents \(\alpha\ge1\)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Bernoulli's inequality: \((1+x)^\alpha\ge1+\alpha x\) for \(x>-1\) and \(\alpha\ge1\), with equality when \(x=0\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Let \(f(u)=u^\alpha\). Then \(f(1)=1\), \(f'(1)=\alpha\) and \(f''(u)=\alpha(\alpha-1)u^{\alpha-2}\ge0\) for \(u>0\), so the graph curves upward. A graph that curves upward lies above its tangent line at \((1,1)\). Setting \(x=u-1\) gives the inequality.

card.rule: A convex function lies above its tangent line, so f(1 + x) is at least its linear approximation 1 + αx.
card.limits: The proof needs α at least 1, so that f'' is not negative. For an exponent between 0 and 1, the graph curves downward and the inequality reverses.

media.alt: Graph of the curve f of x, flat near the horizontal axis on the left and bending steeply upward on the right, through the marked point (1,1). A straight line touches the curve at that point; on both sides the curve stays on or above the line, pulling away to the right. Ticks labelled 1 on each axis.

concepts.title: Rolle's theorem
concepts.question: What does Rolle's theorem guarantee when a smooth function starts and ends at the same height?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Rolle's theorem: if \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(f(a)=f(b)\), then there is a point \(u\) in \((a,b)\) with \(f'(u)=0\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The book treats this as intuitively obvious and gives a picture-based argument. Between a and b the graph has a local maximum or minimum, and at such a point the tangent line is horizontal.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take \(f(x)=x^2-4x+3\) on \([1,3]\). Both endpoint values are 0. The derivative \(2x-4\) vanishes at \(u=2\), which lies inside the interval.

card.rule: Equal endpoint values on an interval force a horizontal tangent somewhere inside.
card.limits: Both hypotheses matter. A corner inside the interval, as for the absolute value function, can give equal endpoint values and still have no horizontal tangent.

One dotted horizontal line touches the peak and carries the label f prime of u equals zero. A second, lower dotted horizontal line joins a point on the rising part to a point on the falling part, at equal heights.

concepts.title: The mean value theorem
concepts.question: What does the mean value theorem say about the average slope of a differentiable function?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), there is a point \(u\) in \((a,b)\) with \(f'(u)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Tilt the picture for Rolle's theorem. Subtract from f the straight line through the two endpoints; the result has equal endpoint values, and its zero derivative gives the equality. So a global property, the average rate of change, equals a local one, a derivative.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=x^3\) on \([0,3]\) the secant slope is \(27/3=9\). Solving \(3u^2=9\) gives \(u=\sqrt3\approx1.73\), inside the interval.

card.rule: Somewhere inside the interval the instantaneous slope equals the average slope.
card.limits: Differentiability on the open interval is needed. For the absolute value function on [-1,2], the average slope is 1/3 but the derivative takes only the values -1 and 1.

A lower dotted line slants upward through a point on the rising part and a point on the falling part. A parallel dotted line touches the curve near its top. A label above says the derivative at u equals the difference quotient of f over b minus a.

concepts.title: A fixed point from bounded slope
concepts.question: Why must a differentiable function with derivative bounded by k less than 1 have a fixed point?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(f\) is differentiable on the real line and \(|f'(x)|\le k\) for all x, with a constant \(k<1\), then \(f(x)=x\) for some x.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Say f(0)=v is positive and suppose f(x) is never x for x at least 0. By the intermediate value theorem f(x) stays above x. The mean value theorem on [0,b] gives a derivative equal to \((f(b)-v)/b\), which exceeds \(1-v/b\). For large b this is near 1, contradicting the bound k.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=\cos(x)/2\) we have \(|f'|\le1/2\). The theorem gives a fixed point; it is near 0.45.

card.rule: A uniform bound below 1 on the slope traps the graph in a cone that must cross y = x.
card.limits: The constant k must be below 1 for all x together. A function whose slope is below 1 at each point, but approaches 1, can have no fixed point.

A thin curve bends steeply upward to the right; a thick wobbly curve starts at the same dot, rises slowly and flattens. Dotted straight lines from that dot, one labelled slope equals k, outline a cone, with a few dotted pieces elsewhere on the page.

concepts.title: How much rigor to demand
concepts.question: How does the book decide which calculus facts to prove and which to accept as obvious?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The book admits that some of the simplest, most obvious statements about differentiable functions rest on deep properties of the real numbers. It does not prove them all. It gives a hand-waving proof of one tool, Rolle's theorem, so that you can reason more rigorously about many problems.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A full real analysis course proves these facts from the construction of the reals. A problem solver needs the statements and their hypotheses first, and the picture-based argument supplies a reason to trust them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the fixed point argument, the intermediate value theorem and the mean value theorem are used as tools, and only the problem-specific steps are proved.

card.rule: Use named theorems as tools and check their hypotheses; do not try to reprove foundations.
card.limits: A picture is a reason to believe a statement and a guide to its proof, but not a proof for every case. Check hypotheses in each use.

concepts.title: Matching a function on a sequence
concepts.question: If a continuous function equals a known function at the points 1, 1/2, 1/3, ..., what is known at 0?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Problem (Putnam 1992): an infinitely differentiable \(f\) satisfies \(f(1/n)=\dfrac{n^2}{n^2+1}\) for \(n=1,2,3,\dots\). The tempting guess \(f(x)=\dfrac1{x^2+1}\) is only known to hold at the points \(1/n\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Let \(v=f-w\), where \(w(x)=1/(x^2+1)\). Then \(v(1/n)=0\) for every n. The points \(1/n\) approach 0 and v is continuous, so \(v(0)=\lim v(1/n)=0\). The sequence form of continuity does the work.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Since \(w(1/n)=\dfrac1{1/n^2+1}=\dfrac{n^2}{n^2+1}\), the function w agrees with f at every point \(1/n\), and so \(f(0)=w(0)=1\).

card.rule: Continuity transfers agreement on a sequence to agreement at its limit point.
card.limits: Agreement on a sequence gives agreement at the limit point only. It says nothing about other points, which is why the derivatives need more work.

media.alt: Cropped formula: f of one over n equals n squared over n squared plus one, followed by a comma.
Cropped formula fragment, not a diagram: two horizontal fraction bars with the numeral 1 under one of them. Most of the expression is missing, so little can be read.

concepts.title: Rolle's theorem used infinitely often
concepts.question: How can Rolle's theorem be applied infinitely many times to show every derivative of f and w agree at 0?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: With \(v=f-w\) vanishing at each \(1/n\), Rolle's theorem gives a zero of \(v'\) strictly between \(1/(n+1)\) and \(1/n\). These zeros approach 0, so \(v'(0)=0\). The same step applies to \(v'\), then \(v''\), and so on.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each derivative is continuous and vanishes on a sequence tending to 0, so it vanishes at 0, and Rolle's theorem supplies a new sequence of zeros for the next derivative. Hence all derivatives of v at 0 are 0, and f has the same derivatives at 0 as w.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(w=1/(1+x^2)=1-x^2+x^4-\cdots\), the derivatives at 0 are \(w^{(k)}(0)=0\) for odd k and \((-1)^{k/2}k!\) for even k. So \(f''(0)=-2\) and \(f^{(4)}(0)=24\).

card.rule: Repeat the zero-then-Rolle step to get every derivative at the limit point.
card.limits: The zeros of the derivative lie strictly between the old zeros, so they form a new sequence. This does not say v is zero everywhere; only its derivatives at 0 are found.

concepts.title: Logarithmic differentiation
concepts.question: How does taking logarithms make the derivative of a product easier?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=x(x+1)(x+2)\cdots(x+n)\), take logarithms: \(\log f=\log x+\log(x+1)+\cdots+\log(x+n)\). Then \(\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}=\dfrac1x+\dfrac1{x+1}+\cdots+\dfrac1{x+n}\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The logarithm turns a product into a sum, and the derivative of the logarithm of f is f'/f. Multiply the sum by f(x) to recover f'(x).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: At \(x=1\), \(f(1)=(n+1)!\), so \(f'(1)=(n+1)!\left(1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1{n+1}\right)\). For n=3 this gives \(24\cdot\frac{25}{12}=50\).

card.rule: Log first, differentiate the sum, then multiply back by f.
card.limits: The method works where f is not zero. Remember to multiply by f at the end; f'/f alone is not the derivative.

media.alt: Cropped formula tail: a plus sign, then a fraction with 1 above a bar, a large closing bracket and a full stop. It is only the end of a longer expression.

concepts.title: Spotting derivatives of expressions in f
concepts.question: Why build a bank of derivatives of functions of f, and what does f'/f lead to?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Useful items: \((f^2)'=2ff'\), \((\log f)'=f'/f\), and \((f^2+f'^2)'=2f'(f+f'')\). If a problem contains \(f'/f\), antidifferentiation gives \(\log f\), which sheds light on f.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Logarithmic differentiation is part of a larger idea: recognize an expression as the derivative of something familiar built from f, then integrate or compare to learn about f.

card.rule: See the expression as the derivative of a combination of f and its derivatives.
card.limits: The bank is only helpful if the expression in the problem matches a derivative. Try multiplying by f' or dividing by f to make it match.

concepts.title: A quantity that cannot increase
concepts.question: How does multiplying an equation by f' show that f is bounded?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Problem (Putnam 1997): \(f+f''=-xg(x)f'\) with \(g\ge0\). Multiply by \(f'\): \(ff'+f'f''=-xg(x)f'^2\). The left side is half the derivative of \(E=f^2+f'^2\), so \(E'=-2xg(x)f'^2\), which is at most 0 for \(x\ge0\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: For \(x\ge0\), E does not increase, so \(f(x)^2\le E(x)\le E(0)=f(0)^2+f'(0)^2\). Hence \(|f(x)|\le C=\sqrt{f(0)^2+f'(0)^2}\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If \(f(0)=3\) and \(f'(0)=4\), then for \(x\ge0\) we get \(|f(x)|\le\sqrt{9+16}=5\).

card.rule: A quantity with nonpositive derivative is bounded by its starting value.
card.limits: The bound is for x at least 0. For negative x, the sign of the right side flips, so the argument must be redone; the book leaves that case as an exercise.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: only a large square root sign with a long overbar; nothing is written under the bar.

concepts.title: Definite integrals as limits of sums
concepts.question: How can the limit of a sum be recognized as a definite integral?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(\Delta=\dfrac{b-a}{n}\) and \(S_n=\Delta\big(f(a)+f(a+\Delta)+\cdots+f(b-\Delta)\big)\). If f is integrable, then \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each term f(a + jΔ) times Δ is the area of a thin rectangle of width Δ. The n rectangles together approximate the area under the graph, and the approximation improves as n grows.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,1]\) with \(n=4\): \(\Delta=1/4\) and \(S_4=\frac14\left(0+\frac1{16}+\frac4{16}+\frac9{16}\right)=\frac7{32}\). The integral is \(1/3\).

card.rule: A limit of a sum with n terms and a step Δ is an integral.
card.limits: A sum of n terms that are not tied to a common step Δ times a function of the position is not directly an integral. First rewrite it.

concepts.title: Turning a sum into an integral
concepts.question: How do you find the integral hidden in the limit of a sum such as n/(k²+n²)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: To evaluate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n\dfrac n{k^2+n^2}\), extract a factor \(\Delta=1/n\): each term is \(\frac1n\cdot\dfrac1{(k/n)^2+1}\). So the sum is \(\Delta\sum f(k/n)\) with \(f(x)=\dfrac1{x^2+1}\) on \([0,1]\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The sum has n terms, and the points k/n fill [0, 1]. Once the factor 1/n is pulled out, what remains depends on k only through k/n, which is the pattern of a Riemann sum.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The limit is \(\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\arctan 1-\arctan 0=\frac\pi4\). With \(n=10^5\), the sum is 0.785396, close to 0.785398.

card.rule: Pull out 1/n, write the rest as a function of k/n, and read off f, a, b.
card.limits: Each term tends to 0, but this alone does not decide the limit of the sum, since the number of terms grows too. Check that the sum has the form Δ times f at evenly spaced points.

concepts.title: Bounding a sum by integrals
concepts.question: How can integrals bound a sum of values of an increasing function?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For increasing \(f\), the sum \(2\big(f(1)+f(3)+\cdots+f(2n-1)\big)\) is trapped between integrals of f whose ends are \(2n-1\) and \(2n+1\). For \(f=\log x\), use the antiderivative \(x\log x-x\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Each term f(2j - 1) times the width 2 is a rectangle under the graph on the next interval, or over it on the previous interval, because f increases. Adding the rectangles compares the sum with the area under the curve.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(1\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9=945\), the logarithm is 6.851. The integrals give bounds 5.89 and 8.19 for it, so the sandwich holds.

card.rule: Increasing functions turn sums of equally spaced values into integral bounds.
card.limits: The method needs f monotone. For a function that rises and falls, rectangles are not all above or all below the graph.

concepts.title: Symmetry in an integral
concepts.question: How does the substitution x → π/2 − x evaluate the integral of 1/(1 + tan^α x)?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(f(x)=\dfrac1{1+\tan^\alpha x}\) and \(g(x)=f(\pi/2-x)\). Since \(\tan(\pi/2-x)=1/\tan x\), \(g(x)=\dfrac{\tan^\alpha x}{1+\tan^\alpha x}\), so \(f(x)+g(x)=1\) for all x in the interval.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The substitution \(x\to\pi/2-x\) maps [0, π/2] onto itself, so \(\int f=\int g\). Their sum is \(\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\pi/2\), so each integral is \(\pi/4\). The exponent α is a red herring.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Numerical integration for \(\alpha=1,2,3\) and \(\sqrt2\) each gives 0.785398, which is \(\pi/4\). The graph of f has central symmetry about \((\pi/4,\,1/2)\).

card.rule: Pair the integrand with its mirror image; their sum is constant.
card.limits: The trick needs a transformation that maps the interval to itself and an identity such as f + g = 1. Without both, the integrals need not match.

concepts.title: Searching for natural transformations
concepts.question: What is the strategy of looking for a transformation that leaves an integral unchanged?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: The tan integral worked because x → π/2 − x leaves integration invariant and simplifies the integrand. The moral: look for natural transformations and the invariants they preserve. Symmetry takes many forms, including reflections, rotations, and the circle inversion of the book's geometry chapter.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A transformation is useful for integrals when it maps the interval of integration onto itself (or onto another interval of interest) and changes the integrand in a controlled way, such as f(x) + g(x) = 1.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The map \(x\to a+b-x\) sends [a, b] onto itself. For \(\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{x^2+(1-x)^2}dx\) it gives the mirror integrand, and the pair add to 1.

card.rule: Ask what transformation preserves the interval and how it changes the integrand.
card.limits: Not every integral has such a symmetry. If no natural transformation simplifies the integrand, the trick does not apply.

media.alt: A displayed integral from 2 to 4. The integrand is a fraction: the numerator is the square root of the natural log of 9 minus x, times dx; the denominator is that same square root plus the square root of the natural log of x plus 3.

concepts.title: A map of order three
concepts.question: How does the map τ(x) = 1/(1 − x), which has order three, combine three integrals into one?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-x}{x^3-3x+1}\) and \(\tau(x)=\dfrac1{1-x}\). Then \(f(\tau(x))=f(x)\) and \(\tau(\tau(\tau(x)))=x\). The substitution \(x\to\tau(x)\) turns one integral of \(f^2\) into the next.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The three given integrals have limits chosen so that τ carries the first to the second and the second to the third, and the third back to the first. Changing variables turns all three into integrals of f² times derivatives of τ and τ∘τ over the first range.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Starting at 1/2: τ(1/2) = 2, τ(2) = −1, τ(−1) = 1/2. Each of the three points has f = 2/3. After the changes of variable the integrand has a rational antiderivative, so the sum of the integrals is a rational number.

card.rule: A map that fixes the integrand and cycles the ranges lets you add the integrals into one.
card.limits: This is a very contrived problem: the limits are chosen to fit τ. The book gives only a sketch and leaves the algebra to the reader.

concepts.title: Series whose terms are functions
concepts.question: How is the sum of an infinite series of functions defined?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: For terms \(a_n(x)\), define the partial sum function \(S_n(x)=a_1(x)+\cdots+a_n(x)\) and \(S(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n(x)\) at each x where the limit exists. The limit is taken separately at each x.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: This matches the definition of a series of constants: fix x and ask whether the sequence of partial sums converges. The sum is therefore a new function of x.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(a_n(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{(1+x^2)^n}\), the partial sums are \(S_n(x)=1-\dfrac1{(1+x^2)^n}\) for \(x\ne0\), and \(S_n(0)=0\). So \(S(x)=1\) for \(x\ne0\) and \(S(0)=0\).

card.rule: Fix x, take the limit of the partial sums, and read off the new function.
card.limits: The limit may exist for some x and fail for others. The sum function is defined only where the limit exists.

concepts.title: Continuous terms, discontinuous sum
concepts.question: Why can an infinite sum of continuous functions fail to be continuous?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: In the series \(\sum x^2/(1+x^2)^n\) every term and every partial sum is continuous, yet \(S(0)=0\) while \(S(x)=1\) for \(x\ne0\), so S has a jump at 0.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Continuity and summing a series each involve a limit. Taking the limit in n and the limit as x approaches 0 in a different order gives different answers: first n gives 1, first x gives 0 for each fixed n.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: At \(x=0.1\), \(S_{10}\approx0.095\) but \(S_{1000}\approx0.99995\). Each \(S_n\) is continuous and gets close to 0 near \(x=0\) for small x, but larger n pushes the rise closer to 0.

card.rule: Infinite series of functions cannot be treated like finite sums.
card.limits: Finite sums of continuous functions are continuous. The failure is specific to infinite sums, and other interchanges, such as differentiating term by term, can fail in the same way.

concepts.title: Uniform convergence
concepts.question: What is uniform convergence of functions, and why does the series of x²/(1+x²)^n fail it?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A sequence \(f_n\) converges uniformly to f if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is one N, independent of x, with \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) for all \(n\ge N\) and all x in the domain.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: This has the same spirit as uniform continuity: the N response to an epsilon challenge does not depend on x. Pointwise convergence lets N depend on x.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Here \(|S_n(x)-S(x)|=(1+x^2)^{-n}\) for \(x\ne0\). For \(\varepsilon=1/2\), the error is exactly 1/2 at \(x^2=2^{1/n}-1\), a point that moves toward 0 as n grows. So no single N works.

card.rule: Uniform means one N works for every x.
card.limits: Convergence can be uniform on part of the domain, away from the trouble point, and fail on all of it. The domain must be stated.

concepts.title: What uniform convergence protects
concepts.question: Which pathologies does uniform convergence prevent, and so why does the book say Don't worry?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If \(f_n\to f\) uniformly and each \(f_n\) is continuous, then f is continuous. If \(f_n\to f\) uniformly, then \(\int f_n\to\int f\). Uniformly convergent power series can be differentiated and integrated term by term.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Uniformity lets the two limits be interchanged: the closeness of f_n to f holds with a single N at all points, so the properties of f_n carry over to f.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: On \([0,1/2]\), \(f_n(x)=x^n\to0\) uniformly, and \(\int_0^{1/2}x^n\,dx=\dfrac{(1/2)^{n+1}}{n+1}\). For n = 3 this is \(1/64\). These tend to \(\int 0=0\).

card.rule: Uniform convergence of the terms makes the usual limit operations safe.
card.limits: These results need uniform convergence. Pointwise convergence alone is not enough, as the example with a jump shows.

concepts.title: Radius of convergence
concepts.question: What are the center and radius of convergence of a power series, and where is convergence uniform?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: A power series has terms \(a_n(x-c)^n\). If it converges to f(x) for all x with \(|x-c|\lt R\), then c is the center and R the radius of convergence, and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) the convergence is uniform on \(|x-c|\le R-\varepsilon\).

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Inside the radius, shrink the disc a little and the error is controlled by a geometric decay that is the same for all x in the smaller disc.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The series \(1+x+x^2+\cdots\) converges to \(1/(1-x)\) for \(|x|\lt1\): center 0, radius 1. On \(|x|\le0.9\), the error after the term \(x^n\) is at most \(0.9^{n+1}/0.1\), which drops below 0.01 once n is 65.

card.rule: Uniform convergence holds on every closed disc strictly inside the radius.
card.limits: The convergence is generally not uniform on the whole open disc up to the radius. Behavior at the boundary depends on the series.
