concepts.title: Taylor polynomial with remainder by integrating inequalities
concepts.question: How does integrating a bound on the third derivative three times give a Taylor polynomial plus error?

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Start with -M3 ≤ f'''(t) ≤ M3 and integrate from a to x. By the fundamental theorem, the integral of f''' is f'' minus its value at a. Repeat three times; each step integrates an inequality, which is valid because u ≤ v implies the integral of u is at most the integral of v.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(f=\sin\) at \(a=0\) with all derivatives bounded by 1, the degree-3 polynomial at \(x=0.5\) is \(0.5-0.5^3/6=0.479167\). The actual value is 0.479426, an error of 0.000259, below the bound \(0.5^4/24=0.0026\).

card.rule: Integrate the derivative bound once per degree; each step builds the next term.
card.limits: The bound needs derivatives bounded on the whole interval from a to x. If the bounds grow as fast as k! times a constant to the k-th power, the remainder tends to 0 only for small distances.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: a short bar above a longer fraction bar, with the digit 2 below it. It looks like part of a fraction with denominator 2 whose numerator is cut off; nothing else can be read.
Cropped formula piece: a short bar above a longer fraction bar, with a small dot and a vertical mark below. It is an unreadable fragment of a fraction; no numbers or letters can be made out reliably.

concepts.title: Local data determine the whole function
concepts.question: Why can derivatives at one point give a series that converges everywhere?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If the derivative bounds \(M_k\) do not grow exponentially, the remainder \(M_{n+1}|x-a|^{n+1}/(n+1)!\) tends to 0 and the Taylor series converges to f. For \(\sin x\), all \(M_k\le1\), so the series converges for all real x.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The factorial in the denominator beats any fixed power of |x - a|. So for each x the remainder shrinks once n is large enough, whatever the starting point.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(x=10\), the terms \(10^k/k!\) grow up to about 2756 near k=10, but \(10^{40}/40!\approx1.2\times10^{-8}\). The series still converges.

card.rule: Complete local information at one point yields global information.
card.limits: The terms can grow before they shrink, so a few terms may be far from the value. The bound needs the derivatives to stay bounded by a reasonable amount.

concepts.title: Expanding opportunistically, and why the answer is unique
concepts.question: Why can any power series found by substitution or geometric series be trusted to be the Taylor series?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Expansions can be found opportunistically: \(\dfrac1{1+x^2}=1-x^2+x^4-\cdots\) from the geometric series, and \(e^{x^2}\) by putting \(t=x^2\) in the series of \(e^t\). The expansion is unique, so it equals the Taylor series.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: The Taylor polynomial \(P_2\) at a is the only quadratic with \(\dfrac{f(x)-P_2(x)}{(x-a)^2}\to0\). Any other quadratic leaves a nonzero limit. So any series matching f to this order must have the same coefficients.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For \(e^x\) at 0 and \(x=0.01\): with \(P_2=1+x+x^2/2\), the ratio is 0.00167; with the quadratic \(Q=1+x+x^2\), it is -0.498. In \(e^{x^2}=1+x^2+x^4/2+\cdots\), the fourth derivative at 0 is \(4!/2=12\).

card.rule: Find a series any way you can; uniqueness says it is the Taylor series.
card.limits: Uniqueness applies to a series that does represent f near the point. The shortcut also needs the substitution to stay in the range where the original series converges.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: the digit 1 on top of a fraction bar with the digit 2 below it, that is, the fraction one half, with nothing else in the crop.

Cropped formula piece: an integral from 0 to infinity of a bracketed expression that starts with x minus x cubed over a denominator, then terms x squared over 2 squared, x to the fourth over 2 squared times 4 squared, and x to the sixth over 4 squared.

concepts.title: Eulerian mathematics
concepts.question: What is Eulerian mathematics, and when is giving up rigor a good idea?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Eulerian mathematics is non-rigorous reasoning that may even be incorrect in some sense, yet leads to an interesting mathematical truth. It is named for Euler. The book says rigor is not evil, but too much attention to it can inhibit creativity early in an investigation and early in a person's education.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A fuzzy, inspired idea may later produce a rigorous proof, and a rigorous proof can sometimes hide the essence of an argument. Lack of rigor is not the same as nonsense, though there is a fine line between a brilliant non-rigorous argument and silliness.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Treating the difference operator on sequences as if it were a derivative is not correct, since sequences have no limits. It suggests a quadratic guess for a sequence problem, and the guess turns out to be right.

card.rule: Use non-rigorous ideas to find a candidate, then confirm the candidate properly.
card.limits: An Eulerian argument gives a hint, not a proof. The answer must still be checked, because the same method can give a wrong guess.

concepts.title: A calculus hunch for a discrete problem
concepts.question: How can calculus ideas guide the solution of a problem about integer sequences or integer parts?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: If every second difference of a sequence is 1, think of \(d^2A/dn^2=1\), which suggests a quadratic in n. For a product of positive numbers with sum S, maximize \(x^{S/x}\); logarithmic differentiation gives \(x=e\), so use parts near 2.718.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Neither step is valid as stated: sequences have no limits, and parts must be integers. But the hunch narrows the search to a quadratic, or to parts of size 2 and 3, and then ordinary checking finishes the problem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With second differences 1 and \(a_{19}=a_{94}=0\), guess \(a_n=\frac12(n-19)(n-94)\), so \(a_1=\frac12(-18)(-93)=837\). For the sum 10, the best product is \(3\cdot3\cdot2\cdot2=36\).

card.rule: Let calculus point to the form of the answer, then confirm with discrete reasoning.
card.limits: The calculus answer need not be an integer or fit the constraints. It points to a neighborhood; the discrete problem still needs a direct argument.

media.alt: A displayed definition: f of x is defined to equal the quantity S divided by x, raised to the power x, followed by a comma. Here S is a constant.

concepts.title: Euler's proof that there are infinitely many primes
concepts.question: How does factoring the harmonic series show that there are infinitely many primes?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(S_k=1+\frac1k+\frac1{k^2}+\cdots=\dfrac k{k-1}\). Expand the product \(S_2S_3S_5S_7\cdots\) over primes. By unique factorization, each \(1/n\) appears exactly once, so the product equals the harmonic series, which is infinite.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: A finite list of primes would give a finite product of finite numbers, which cannot equal an infinite series. So the list of primes cannot be finite. The book notes the argument can be made rigorous with partial sums and products.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The term \(1/360\) with \(360=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5\) arises only from \(1/2^3\), \(1/3^2\), \(1/5\). The product over \(2,3,5,7,11\) is \(77/16=4.8125\); the harmonic sum passes 4.8125 at n = 69.

card.rule: Unique factorization turns the harmonic series into a product over primes.
card.limits: The infinite sum and product are used without justification. The idea is Eulerian: it works because it can be rigorized with partial sums and products.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: a large summation sign with the condition d divides Q sub n written underneath it. The terms being summed are not part of this crop.
A displayed limit statement: as k tends to infinity, the fraction phi of n sub k over n sub k tends to 0, where phi is the totient function.
A displayed identity: one over zeta of s equals the sum over n from 1 to infinity of mu of n divided by n to the power s, ending with a full stop.
A displayed sum over r with 1 less than or equal to r less than or equal to n of mu of r times the square of the floor of n over r, ending with a full stop.

concepts.title: Euler's evaluation of the zeta function at 2
concepts.question: How did Euler use the zeros of sin √x / √x to sum 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + ...?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(f(x)=\dfrac{\sin\sqrt x}{\sqrt x}=1-\dfrac x{3!}+\dfrac{x^2}{5!}-\cdots\), with zeros \(\pi^2,4\pi^2,9\pi^2,\dots\). Pretend it factors as \(\prod\left(1-\dfrac x{n^2\pi^2}\right)\) and compare the coefficients of x.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: In the product, the coefficient of x is \(-\sum\dfrac1{n^2\pi^2}\). In the series it is \(-1/6\). Equating gives \(\sum 1/n^2=\pi^2/6\). Writing factors as \((1-x/r)\) keeps the constant term equal to 1, as needed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Check: \((1-\frac x2)(1-\frac x3)\) has x-coefficient \(-(\frac12+\frac13)=-\frac56\). Numerically \(\sum_{n<10^6}1/n^2=1.644933\) and \(\pi^2/6=1.644934\).

card.rule: Treat a function with known zeros like a polynomial; compare coefficients.
card.limits: The infinite factorization is assumed by analogy with polynomials. Complete rigor is much more complicated, but the result is correct.

Cropped formula piece: a large opening parenthesis followed by three fractions with numerator 1 and denominators cut off, joined by plus signs, with a further plus sign at the end. The denominators are not visible.
A displayed identity piece: the fraction sin x over x, followed by an infinite product over n from 1 to infinity of cosine of x over 2 to the n, then a comma. The equals sign is cut off.

concepts.section: Beauty, Simplicity, and Symmetry: The Quest for a Moving Curtain
concepts.title: Random coin bias and generating functions
concepts.question: Why is the chance of exactly k heads equal to 1/(n+1) when the coin's bias p is chosen uniformly at random?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Let \(U(n,k)=\displaystyle\int_0^1\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\,dp\). Then \(U(n,k)=\dfrac1{n+1}\) for every k from 0 to n. For the problem with 2000 flips and 1000 heads, the answer is 1/2001.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: Set \(f(x)=\sum_k U(n,k)x^k=\int_0^1\sum_k\binom nk(px)^k(1-p)^{n-k}dp=\int_0^1(1-p+px)^n\,dp\), using the binomial theorem. This equals \(\dfrac{x^{n+1}-1}{(n+1)(x-1)}=\dfrac{1+x+\cdots+x^n}{n+1}\), so all coefficients are equal.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Computing: \(U(2,1)=1/3\), \(U(5,2)=1/6\), \(U(7,0)=1/8\), \(U(10,10)=1/11\). For \(p=1/2\) the chance of 1000 heads in 2000 flips is 0.0178, but averaging over all p gives 0.0005.

card.rule: Average the binomial probability over p, and the generating function collapses.
card.limits: The sum and integral are interchanged, which is safe here because the sum is finite. The proof shows how the probabilities are uniform but not why.

media.alt: A displayed expression: the binomial coefficient n choose k, multiplied by p to the power k, times the quantity one minus p raised to the power n minus k, ending with a full stop.

A displayed formula: f of x equals the integral from 0 to 1, with respect to p, of a sum over k from 0 to n of n choose k times p to the k times x to the k times the quantity one minus p raised to the power n minus k.
Cropped formula piece: a large opening parenthesis containing x raised to the power n plus 1, above a fraction bar whose lower part is cut off. It is the start of a longer expression.
Cropped formula piece: a large opening parenthesis followed by x raised to the power n. Nothing else is shown; the rest of the expression is cut off.

concepts.section: Beauty, Simplicity, and Symmetry: The Quest for a Moving Curtain
concepts.title: Ranks explain the uniform answer
concepts.question: Why does a symmetry argument about ranks explain why every number of heads is equally likely?

blocks.label: Definition or statement
blocks.text: Choose n + 1 independent uniform numbers. Call the first one A, the dial setting. Each of the other n numbers stands for a toss: it counts as heads if it is below A, which has probability A. So the number of heads is the rank of A among the n + 1 numbers.

blocks.label: Why it is true
blocks.text: All n + 1 numbers are uniform and independent, so any of them is equally likely to be the smallest, the next, and so on. The rank of A is therefore uniform, giving each count probability 1/(n + 1). This is a moving-curtain argument: it shows why.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For four tosses there are five numbers, and A has each of five ranks with probability 1/5. Listing all 120 orderings of five distinct ranks, A has each rank in exactly 24.

card.rule: Uniform numbers have uniformly distributed ranks.
card.limits: The argument needs the numbers to be independent and drawn from the same uniform distribution. With different distributions, the ranks are not equally likely.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: How the nine chapters divide the work
concepts.question: Which chapters teach the method, which teach subject tools, and which chapter bridges the two?

paragraphs: Read as a whole, the book has three parts. Chapters 1 to 3 give the method: the three levels, strategies for investigating and arguing, and tactics that find order. Chapters 5 to 9 are organised by subject (algebra, combinatorics, number theory, geometry, calculus) and work mostly at the tactic and tool level, from the problem solver's point of view.

Chapter 4 is the bridge. Its three crossover tactics (graphs, complex numbers, generating functions) connect branches of mathematics and sit early so that you reach powerful ideas quickly. Some of it is advanced, and the author says it may be worth reading Chapters 5 to 7 first, or at least alongside it.

The two halves feed each other: progress in method helps your mathematics and the reverse. Read the start of each early section closely, skim as it gets harder, and come back later. The subject chapters you choose by interest and background.
card.example: A reader meets generating functions in Chapter 4 and finds the examples need more algebra than they have. Following the author's hint, they read the opening sections of Chapters 5 to 7 alongside, return to Chapter 4, and later reread the Chapter 2 sections they had skimmed.
card.rule: Take the method from Chapters 1 to 3, the subject tools from Chapters 5 to 9, cross between branches through Chapter 4, and keep moving back and forth among them.
card.limits: The roles are a reading aid, not walls: the geometry chapter's Section 8.4 is mostly about problem-solving strategies and tactics, and the author wants a second pass over every page.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Investigation feeds argument
concepts.question: How do the strategies of Chapter 2 hand a conjecture to the argument methods that prove it?

paragraphs: Chapter 2 treats every solution as two jobs. Investigation discovers what is going on; argument convinces others, or yourself, of the discovery. The startup strategies (get your hands dirty, find a penultimate step, wishful thinking, an easier problem) serve the first job. Direct deduction, contradiction and induction serve the second.

The link between them is a conjecture. In the author's words, your initial investigation may suggest a tentative method of argument. Experiments produce a statement worth proving, and its shape picks the style: an if-then claim, a claim that something cannot happen, or a claim indexed by the integers.

The four-consecutive-numbers problem shows the hand-off. A table of values showed that the product is one less than a perfect square. Once that was seen, the author says the problem turned into an exercise, and factoring finished it.
card.example: Try n = 1 to 4 for f(n) = n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3): the values 24, 120, 360, 840 are each one less than a square. Conjecture that f(n) is always one less than a square, prove it by factoring, and note that no two consecutive positive integers are both squares.
card.rule: Let experiments suggest what to prove, then choose the argument style that fits the claim: direct deduction, contradiction or induction.
card.limits: A problem can split into cases or sub-problems that need different methods, and how rigorous and clear an argument must be depends on its audience.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Chapter 3's tactics as ways to find order
concepts.question: How do symmetry, extremes, pigeonholes and invariants each find or impose order on a messy problem?

paragraphs: Chapter 3 begins from one observation: problems are often hard because they look chaotic, with parts missing or unconnected. Its tactics search for order. The most dramatic form is symmetry, found or imposed in a concrete way, for example by reflection.

Three tactics find order more abstractly, which the author calls pseudosymmetry. The extreme principle puts things in order and watches the largest and smallest. The pigeonhole principle notes that more guests than rooms forces some to share. Invariants fix attention on one aspect that does not change, such as parity.

The tactics also overlap. A symmetry is itself an invariance under some transformation. A monovariant, a quantity that changes in one direction only, often calls on the extreme principle. The author says invariants underlie many seemingly different tactics and tools.
card.example: In a knockout tournament the number of players left falls by one with each game. It starts at n and ends at 1, so exactly n - 1 games are played, whatever the pairings.
card.rule: Faced with a chaotic problem, ask which order is available: a symmetry, a ranking, too few boxes, or a quantity that stays fixed or moves one way.
card.limits: Our reading: the families are the author's way to group tactics, not a procedure that picks one for you. Each tactic still needs the right structure in the problem, and several may fit.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Crossovers: one problem, two branches
concepts.question: What is a crossover tactic, and how do graphs, complex numbers and generating functions each work as one?

paragraphs: A crossover connects two or more branches of mathematics, usually in a surprising way. The seed is in Chapter 2: reformulating a problem is a strategy, but carrying it out is tactical and often needs specialised knowledge. The lockers problem, where a combinatorics question became a number theory lemma, is an early case.

Chapter 4 develops three of the most productive crossovers. Graph theory turns objects and their relationships into dots and lines. Complex numbers are both algebraic and geometric, so you can translate between the two. Generating functions store a sequence as coefficients, so adding exponents becomes multiplying powers.

In each case the translation is where the work lies. The author introduces the lights puzzle by saying it is not a problem about lights; once the lights sit at roots of unity, a sum that no move changes settles it.
card.example: In the handshake problem the people are dots and the handshakes are lines. The number of hands a person shook becomes the degree of a dot, and the degrees add up to twice the number of lines.
card.rule: To cross over, restate the problem in the language of another branch, work with that branch's tools, then translate the result back.
card.limits: The author says Chapter 4 only scratches the surface of three rich topics, and parts of it are advanced. A crossover also needs real knowledge of the branch you cross into.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Symmetry from Chapter 3 to the last page
concepts.question: Where does symmetry recur across the book, and what does it do for the solver each time?

paragraphs: Symmetry returns throughout the book. Chapter 3 calls an object symmetric if some non-trivial action leaves it unchanged, and says this gives free information. Gaussian pairing uses it for sums: write 1 + 2 + ... + 100 forwards and backwards, and every column adds to the same total. Chapter 5 brings the same habit to algebra.

Chapter 8 asks why symmetry is so useful. Many situations, suitably rearranged, reveal structure that a chosen transformation leaves invariant. In the author's hexagon example, rearranging six triangles so the side lengths alternate turns a lopsided figure into a symmetric one and leaves routine trigonometry.

Chapter 9 uses symmetry to evaluate an integral. The last example asks for the chance of exactly 1000 heads in 2000 tosses when the coin's bias is itself random. Calculus and generating functions give 1/2001; the reason is that uniform numbers have uniform rankings. The book ends on the word symmetry.
card.example: A hexagon in a circle has three sides of length 2 in a row, then three of length 1. Each side is the base of an isosceles triangle with its apex at the centre. Reassemble the six triangles so the lengths alternate 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1: the circle is unchanged and the angles become equal.
card.rule: When a problem looks messy, look for a transformation that leaves part of it unchanged, or rearrange the problem so that one exists.
card.limits: Symmetry seldom finishes a problem on its own: the hexagon was reduced to routine trigonometry, and that computation still had to be done.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Counting as a proof tool in number theory
concepts.question: How can a counting argument settle a question about divisibility?

paragraphs: The author says algebra, combinatorics and number theory are intimately connected. Two Chapter 7 examples show counting proving facts about divisibility, because anything that counts selections or arrangements is a whole number.
First, a product of k consecutive integers equals k! times a binomial coefficient. Binomial coefficients count selections, so they are integers, and the product is a multiple of k!.

Second, for Fermat's little theorem take all words of length p over an alphabet of a letters; there are a^p. Shifting the last letter to the front sorts the words into families. A word that repeats one letter throughout is alone, and for prime p every other family has exactly p words. So p divides a^p - a.
card.example: 7 x 8 x 9 x 10 x 11 = 55440, and 55440 = 5! x C(11, 5) = 120 x 462. The product of five consecutive integers is a multiple of 5!, because C(11, 5) counts the ways to choose 5 items from 11.
card.rule: To show a number is an integer or a multiple of n, look for something it counts, or for a split of a counted set into equal-sized groups.
card.limits: Our reading: the grouping argument needs the groups to be equal in size. With a composite word length the shift families can be smaller, so the proof relies on the length being prime.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: From well-ordering to unique factorization
concepts.question: Which chain of results leads from the well-ordering principle to unique factorization, and where does the polynomial version branch off?

paragraphs: A mathematics chapter is a chain in which each result is proved from the one before. In Chapter 7, well-ordering (from Chapter 3) gives the division algorithm. With the extreme principle and contradiction, that shows the gcd is the smallest positive combination ax + by. This gives the lemma that a prime dividing a product divides a factor, and the lemma gives unique factorization.

Chapter 5 runs a parallel chain for polynomials. The division algorithm gives a quotient and a remainder of smaller degree than the divisor. Dividing P(x) by x - a and substituting x = a shows the remainder is P(a), the remainder theorem. A zero a therefore makes x - a a factor: the factor theorem.

The author says that unique factorization was a consequence of the division algorithm, which was a consequence of well-ordering and the fact that 1 is an integer. A result is only as secure as its first links, so knowing the chain tells you what a proof really needs.
card.example: Integers: 333 = 6 x 51 + 27. Polynomials: x^3 + x^2 + 7 = (x^2 + 3)(x + 1) + (-3x + 4). In both, the remainder is smaller than the divisor: smaller in size for the integers, smaller in degree for the polynomials.
card.rule: When a result is hard to see, trace it back through the earlier results it was built from, and rebuild it link by link.
card.limits: Each link needs its hypotheses. The book asks you to show by example that the division algorithm fails in the even integers, so a chain proved for one number system need not carry over to another.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Geometry's ladder from angle facts to Power of a Point
concepts.question: How do basic angle facts climb to inscribed angles, similar triangles and the Power of a Point?

paragraphs: Chapter 8 climbs a ladder. The angle sum of a triangle and the equal base angles of an isosceles triangle come first. With radii as the equal sides, they prove the inscribed angle theorem: an inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc. So inscribed angles on the same arc are equal.

Equal angles give similar triangles: if two triangles share an angle, one more equal pair is enough, because the angle sum forces the third. The Power of a Point follows. Two lines through P meet a circle; the triangles sharing the angle at P get a second equal pair from equal inscribed angles, and cross-multiplying the side ratios gives equal products.

Section 8.4 turns this experience into an eight-point checklist: draw carefully, add auxiliary objects sparingly, angle chase, seek right triangles, parallels and concyclic points, compare areas, exploit similar triangles, look for symmetry, and create phantom points. The author says it covers all three levels and is not complete.
card.example: Two chords cross at a point P inside a circle. One is cut into pieces of 3 and 8, so the power of P is 3 x 8 = 24. A second chord through P has pieces 4 and x, so 4x = 24 and x = 6.
card.rule: In geometry, trace a theorem back to the facts it uses and rebuild it in the same order when you meet a similar problem.
card.limits: Our reading: knowing why a theorem holds does not tell you which theorem a new problem needs. The checklist is the author's aid for that choice, and he calls it incomplete.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Calculus: from convergence to the moving curtain
concepts.question: How do convergence, continuity and uniform continuity support the picture-first proof of the fundamental theorem?

paragraphs: Chapter 9 stacks definitions. A sequence converges to L if, for any tolerance, its terms eventually stay within it. A function is continuous at a point if every sequence approaching the point is mapped to a sequence approaching the function value. Continuity gives the intermediate value theorem. Uniform continuity asks for one delta per epsilon across a whole domain.

The chain is put to work on the fundamental theorem of calculus. First comes a picture: let g(t) be the area under the graph up to t, a moving curtain. It grows fast where the graph is tall, so g'(t) = f(t). Defining g is the define-a-function tool of Chapter 5, and interpreting the integral dynamically is the crux move.

The picture is not yet a proof, because the curtain grows by f(t) times the time step plus a small error area E(t). Uniform continuity bounds E(t) by epsilon times the step, so E(t) over the step tends to 0. The author wants both: the picture explains why, and the definitions make it rigorous.
card.example: For x squared on [-3, 3]: |x1^2 - x2^2| = |x1 + x2| |x1 - x2|, which is at most 6 |x1 - x2|. So delta = epsilon / 6 works for every pair of points at once.
card.rule: To make a picture-first proof rigorous, find the error term and bound it with the definitions in the chain: convergence, continuity, uniform continuity.
card.limits: Uniform continuity belongs to a function on a set. The author accepts without proof that continuous functions on closed intervals have it, and notes that 1/x on the range from 0 to infinity does not.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: One method in action: primes as sums of two squares
concepts.question: How do strategies, tactics and tools from several chapters combine in one solution of a hard problem?

paragraphs: The end of Chapter 7 asks which primes p can be written as x squared plus y squared. The author calls the section a model of how many problem-solving techniques come together in the solution of a hard problem. Read it in layers, as Chapter 1 teaches you to read any solution.

Strategy: experiment with small primes and conjecture that the condition is remainder 1 on division by 4. Stay loose, bend the rules and make the problem easier by working modulo p, where a square root u of -1 makes x squared plus y squared factor. Tactics: a modulo 4 filter rules out remainder 3, and the pigeonhole principle on the multiples of u produces a small pair x, y.

Tools: Gaussian pairing arranges (p - 1)! into a perfect square, and a theorem from Chapter 3 then supplies an explicit square root of -1. The author postponed that step, assuming the root exists for the time being, and proved it last.
card.example: For p = 29, u = 17 works because 17 squared is 289 = 10 x 29 - 1. Then 2u = 34 reduces to 5 modulo 29, giving y = 2 and x = 5, and indeed 25 + 4 = 29.
card.rule: On a hard problem, expect to chain several earlier ideas: experiment to find the statement, relax a rule to gain a foothold, then bring a tactic or tool to each hurdle.
card.limits: The result covers primes only: the author says he is not producing a complete theory of x squared plus y squared equals n. He also warns that the narrative meanders, as real investigations do.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: To save pages, Zeitz sets the second edition's problems in smaller type. What does he say about their importance?
options: They are now secondary, so the smaller type reflects their lower rank
They are optional enrichment that readers can skip on a first pass
They remain the heart of the book, as in the first edition
They matter less than the new geometry chapter that took their space
optionExplain: Smaller type can suggest lower rank, but Zeitz says the reason is only length.
Skipping feels natural for small print, yet he asks the serious reader to attempt as many as possible.
Right: he says the size must not fool the reader, and the problems stay central.
The new chapter adds material, but he does not rank it above the problems.
questions.explain: Zeitz says the smaller size is only a way to control length. The card next shows what he asks of the reader.
questions.rule: Small print does not mean small importance.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: True or false: the second edition adds a new chapter on geometry titled "Geometry for Americans".
questions.explain: This is the first change the preface lists. The chapter is an introduction aimed at beginners.
questions.rule: New in the second edition: geometry, more calculus, more problems.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: Maya has little time with the new edition. Which plan matches the preface's advice for a serious reader?
options: Study the exposition closely and leave the problems for later, since they repeat it
Read every problem statement and try as many as she can, even if some stay unsolved
Work only the added easy problems, since the smaller print marks the rest as extras
Start the problems only after finishing the whole book, since exposition must come first
optionExplain: It is a common habit to treat problems as practice for later, but the author calls them the heart of the book.
Right: the minimum asked is reading every statement, plus attempts on as many as possible.
The easy problems are new, but nothing in the preface marks the others as extras.
Reading first sounds orderly, yet the preface asks for attempts alongside the reading, not after it.
questions.explain: The preface sets a floor (read every statement) and a goal (attempt as many as possible). It does not set an order or a limit to the easy ones.
questions.rule: Read every statement; attempt as many as possible.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A geometry expert reads the new chapter. Zeitz expects the expert to feel ____ with its slow pace and missing topics.
questions.explain: He says experts are bound to be dissatisfied, because the chapter is written for beginners and is only an introduction. His hope is that it gives novices confidence to investigate geometry boldly.
questions.rule: A chapter for beginners will not satisfy experts.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: Which summary of the second edition's changes does the preface contradict?
options: The geometry chapter is long, yet only an introduction to the subject
The calculus chapter was expanded and gained many new problems
Several chapters gained more problems, especially easy ones
Problems were cut back to keep the book's length under control
optionExplain: This is stated: the chapter is long but only an introduction.
This is stated: the calculus chapter was expanded with many new problems.
This is stated: more problems were added, especially easy ones.
Right: length was controlled by smaller type and two columns, and problems were added, not cut.
questions.explain: The author kept the length under control by changing the layout, not by removing problems.
questions.rule: Length was controlled by layout, not by cutting problems.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A reader works on a hard problem for an hour without solving it. What does the first-edition preface say about that hour?
options: It is wasted unless the reader then looks up the solution in the Hints appendix
It is wasted, because a problem the reader cannot solve was too hard for the audience of this book
It counts only if the reader afterwards solves a similar but easier problem
It is well spent, because honest thinking about a problem has value even when unsolved
optionExplain: Hints help, but the preface does not tie the value of the time to looking anything up.
A failed attempt feels like proof of a mismatch, yet the preface expects some problems to stay unsolved.
Chasing a success feels fair, but the value of the time does not depend on a later success.
Right: the first-edition preface says any time spent thinking honestly about a problem is well spent.
questions.explain: The first-edition preface says some problems are not meant to be solved and that honest thought about any problem is time well spent. This is why attempting matters more than finishing.
questions.teaches: The first-edition preface says not every problem is meant to be solved, and that any time spent thinking honestly about a problem is time well spent.
questions.rule: Honest attempts are never wasted time.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: Which question best fits what Zeitz means by a problem, as opposed to an exercise?
options: A very long calculation in which every step is known but tedious
A question whose route to an answer is not apparent and needs investigation
A hard question on the topic covered in last week's lecture
A question with one numerical answer that can be checked against the back of the book
optionExplain: Length feels like difficulty, but a known route makes it an exercise however long it is.
Right: a problem cannot be answered immediately and needs investigation first.
Hard questions on recent material are the typical exercise: hard, but the method is signalled.
Having a known answer says nothing about whether the route is apparent.
questions.explain: Zeitz separates the two by whether the way forward is apparent. The card next shows his definitions.
questions.rule: Problems puzzle; exercises do not.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: True or false: in Zeitz's usage, an exercise is a question that is easy.
questions.explain: Exercises may be hard or easy. What defines them is that the path to the solution is always apparent.
questions.rule: Hard work does not make a problem.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A teacher sets four tasks. Which one is a problem in Zeitz's sense?
options: Differentiate ten polynomials straight after the lecture on the power rule
Multiply two large matrices by hand, following the procedure shown in class
Decide whether a given odd arrangement of tiles can occur, with no method suggested
Solve three equations of the same type that were solved on the board earlier this morning
optionExplain: It is drill on a technique just covered, so the path is apparent.
It is long and technical, but every step is known, so it is an exercise.
Right: no method is signalled and the answer may be yes, no or unclear, so it needs investigation.
It repeats a worked type, so the path is apparent.
questions.explain: Only the third task leaves the way forward unclear. The others differ in length but not in clarity of route.
questions.rule: Look for the missing path, not the heavy work.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: Sort each task as an exercise or a problem in Zeitz's sense.

items.t: Compute a messy integral by the method taught this week
Row-reduce a large system exactly as shown in class
Evaluate a long sum with the identity learned yesterday
Find out whether a game has a winning strategy for the first player
Show that a puzzling quantity can never take a certain value, with no tool suggested
Investigate a pattern, guess a rule, then decide how to prove it

questions.explain: The three exercises have signalled methods, though some involve heavy work. The three problems leave the route open and need investigation.
questions.rule: Signalled route means exercise; open route means problem.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A student reasons that an integral which took pages and stalled twice must be a problem, not an exercise. What is wrong?
options: Hard technical work does not make a problem, as an exercise can be hard with a clear path
Nothing, because a long and difficult solution is what separates problems from exercises
Getting stuck shows the integral is unsolvable, and that is what defines a problem
Exercises are always short, so any long solution must belong to a problem rather than an exercise
optionExplain: Right: Zeitz says an exercise may involve hairy technical work yet never puzzle, because the path is apparent.
This confuses effort with puzzlement; Zeitz separates the two by whether the path is clear.
Problems are sometimes unsolvable, but being stuck does not show that, and unsolvability is not the definition.
Zeitz says exercises may be hard or easy, so length does not decide it.
questions.explain: Heavy work belongs to exercises as well. The test is whether the way forward was apparent at the start.
questions.rule: Effort is not the test; puzzlement is.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: According to Zeitz, why can an employer value a problem solver more than someone fast at routine technique?
options: Routine technique is rare among graduates, so few candidates can offer it to a firm at all
Problem solvers finish routine technical work faster than everyone else
Employers in industry hire only people with a record in math contests
Computers can invert a matrix, a routine task, but cannot solve a poorly defined problem
optionExplain: Rarity feels like value, but Zeitz says the opposite: a computer can supply the routine skill.
Speed is a plausible reason, but Zeitz gives a different one: what computers cannot do.
His own contest background is not offered as a hiring rule for industry.
Right: in industry, solving a poorly defined problem matters much more than inverting a matrix, which a computer can do.
questions.explain: Zeitz uses matrix inversion as his example of a routine task that machines handle. Open-ended, poorly defined problems are the part they do not.
questions.teaches: In industry, being able to solve a poorly defined problem is much more important to an employer than a routine task such as inverting a matrix, because a computer can do the latter but not the former.
questions.rule: Machines handle routine technique; people are needed for poorly defined problems.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: In Zeitz's gym and backpacking comparison, what do the gym-goer and the backpacker have in common?
options: Both have a great deal of fun along the way
Both end the trip lost, tired and sore
Both are protected from injury by gradual training
Both get stronger
optionExplain: Fun is exactly what he says separates them, since the gym-goer has not had much of it.
That describes the backpacker's experience, not the gym-goer's.
Injury and safety are not part of the comparison.
Right: the point is that both get stronger, so the difference lies elsewhere.
questions.explain: Strength is shared; the difference is in experience and in what each has to share. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Both get stronger; only one has an adventure.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: In the analogy, the average math student is like a visitor to a ____ who repeats low weights on machines.
questions.explain: The gym-goer does many repetitions with low weights on machines, like a student who does many exercises.
questions.rule: Gym is to exercises as backpacking is to problems.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A writing coach says drafting by formula is like paddling a pool, while real drafting is a river trip with rapids, wrong turns and a thrilling landing. What is the coach doing?
options: Making the reader want one experience over the other through a vivid contrast
Comparing the average word counts of two groups of working writers over a year
Defining each term of the craft carefully before building an argument on top of them
Ranking a list of drafting rules from the easiest to the hardest for a beginner
optionExplain: Right: it is the same device as the gym and backpacking contrast, an image that persuades.
Nothing in the passage reports numbers or groups.
A definition would state what drafting is; this describes how it feels.
No rules are listed; the coach offers two pictures.
questions.explain: The coach, like Zeitz, uses a contrast of two experiences to move the reader. It carries a claim, but gives no evidence for it.
questions.rule: Imagery can carry a claim without proving it.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: True or false: by the analogy, the gym-goer comes home with more to share with others than the backpacker does.
questions.explain: The backpacker returns energized and cannot stop talking about the trip. The gym-goer has little to share.
questions.rule: Adventure gives more to tell than repetition.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A classmate says the analogy shows with data that problem solvers learn faster than exercise doers. What is wrong with this reading?
options: The analogy says that gym-goers do not get any stronger from their repeated training
It is an image meant to persuade; the passage cites no data on learning speed
The analogy concerns travel safety rather than learning
It proves the claim, though only for readers who like hiking
optionExplain: The analogy says both get stronger, so this overstates it.
Right: the passage is a vivid illustration, and it offers no study or numbers.
The comparison is about two ways of building strength, not safety.
An analogy does not prove a claim, whoever the reader is.
questions.explain: The analogy illustrates what Zeitz thinks learning from problems is like. Taking it for evidence reads more into it than it holds.
questions.rule: An analogy illustrates; it does not prove.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A reader gets lost in several problems and ends up sore. According to Zeitz's stated goal for the book, what does this mean?
options: The book has failed, because the analogy promised steady progress without much effort
The reader has misused the book and should return to exercises before trying again
It is part of the planned trip, and the reader should end up toughened and happy
It shows the reader is not among the bright math students the book is written for
optionExplain: An easy ride is the gym, not the backpacking trip; Zeitz promises effort.
Falling back on exercises is the gym-goer's route, which the analogy contrasts with problems.
Right: Zeitz says reading the book and working on some of its 660 problems should feel like the trip, with getting lost and sore along the way.
He says problem solving is easy for any bright math student to learn, and being lost is expected.
questions.explain: Zeitz states that his goal is for working through the problems to feel like the backpacking trip. Getting lost and sore is an expected part of that, with a toughened and happy reader at the end.
questions.teaches: Zeitz says his goal is that reading the book and working on some of its 660 problems should be like the backpacking trip: the reader will get lost and sore, but end up toughened, happy and ready for more adventures.
questions.rule: Getting lost is part of the trip, not a sign of failure.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: What does Zeitz say produces the elite problem-solving culture he describes?
options: Formal graduate study leading to a career in research mathematics
Math clubs and contests that pass on folklore problems and ideas
Engineering apprenticeships in industry
Private tutoring in calculus at an early age
optionExplain: Research is a higher level of mathematics, but not what he names as the source.
Right: members were raised with math clubs and often took part in contests.
Industry is mentioned only as a place that values problem solvers.
Calculus is only the level of mathematics he hopes readers have.
questions.explain: The culture is passed on through clubs and contests. The card next shows how Zeitz places himself in it.
questions.rule: Clubs and contests carry the culture.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: True or false: Zeitz says the problem-solving culture is found only in the United States.
questions.explain: He says it is prevalent in parts of Eastern Europe and exists in small pockets in the United States.
questions.rule: The culture is strong in Eastern Europe, small in the US.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A fitness author opens with her Olympic past and calls herself a missionary for her sport. How should a reader take this?
options: Accept the advice, since a champion cannot be wrong about training
Reject the advice, since personal history is irrelevant to judging a practical book
Skip the opening and read only the numbered rules that follow
As a reason to listen and as persuasion, then judge the advice on its merits
optionExplain: Credentials feel decisive, but they show knowledge, not that every claim is right.
Background does tell the reader whether the author knows the field, so it is not irrelevant.
Skipping loses the author's stated aim, which tells the reader what the book wants to do.
Right: it earns attention and also works on the reader, so weigh both.
questions.explain: Zeitz uses his own background and a missionary image in the same way. The reader can value the experience while noticing that it is also meant to win trust.
questions.rule: Credentials earn attention, not agreement.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: Zeitz says problem solving is something that is easy for any ____ math student to learn.
questions.explain: He concludes from his teaching of students outside the problem-solving culture that any bright math student can learn it.
questions.rule: His claim is for bright math students, not for anyone.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A reviewer writes that Zeitz claims anyone can learn problem solving. What does this reading get wrong?
options: He says only contest winners can learn it, and only if they started young
He says it can be learned only in countries where the culture is already strong
It drops his limit to bright math students and his basis in teaching experience
He says it cannot be taught at all, and is only picked up through years of contests
optionExplain: He wants to reach students who are not contest veterans.
He says the culture is regional, but that his own students outside it can learn.
Right: his claim is about any bright math student, and it comes from his teaching experience.
His first principle is that problem solving can be taught and learned.
questions.explain: The reviewer widens the claim. Zeitz names bright math students and rests the claim on his experience as a teacher.
questions.rule: Report the claim at the strength the author gave it.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: Many fine books of good mathematics already exist. According to the preface, why did Zeitz write this one anyway?
options: Those books were too hard for contest teams, so he wrote an easier and shorter one
No text worked for his students, and mathematics itself is not enough on its own
His publisher asked for a competitor to a leading geometry book of that period
He wanted to replace the older geometry books with a more complete treatment
optionExplain: Difficulty is not the stated problem; the books lacked something else.
Right: he could not find a suitable text for his students at the University of San Francisco.
No publisher request is mentioned as the reason.
He says the first edition has no geometry chapter and recommends other geometry books.
questions.explain: He credits other books with good mathematics but says that is not enough for novices. His book adds psychology, strategy and a coaching tone.
questions.teaches: Zeitz says he wrote the book because he could not find any text suitable for his students at the University of San Francisco; there are many nice books with lots of good mathematics, but mathematics itself is not enough.
questions.rule: Good mathematics alone does not teach problem solving.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: Alongside mathematical knowledge, what does Zeitz say success in problem solving depends on crucially?
options: Raw speed in calculation, which lets a student finish far more work than the others do
Memorized solutions to old contest problems that recur in somewhat altered forms
Natural talent that neither practice nor teaching can change in any student
Psychological factors such as confidence, concentration and courage
optionExplain: Speed is a familiar mark of a strong student, but he does not name it.
Memory of old problems resembles folklore, but he does not reduce success to memorizing answers.
His first principle is that problem solving can be taught and learned.
Right: he calls attributes like confidence, concentration and courage vitally important.
questions.explain: Zeitz puts psychology among the main causes of success. The card next shows his full list.
questions.rule: Confidence, concentration and courage matter.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: True or false: Zeitz writes in the formal tone of a standard textbook.
questions.explain: He says the book is organized like a standard math textbook, but its tone is much less formal, like a friendly coach.
questions.rule: Textbook structure, coach's voice.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: A student who knows the needed algebra freezes at an unfamiliar question and quits after five minutes. Which of Zeitz's principles does this case point to?
options: Knowledge of folklore is as important as mastery of technical tools
Success depends crucially on psychological factors such as confidence
Technical tools alone decide whether a student succeeds at problem solving
Rigorous argument matters more than no-holds-barred investigation does
optionExplain: Folklore matters, but the student's trouble is not a gap in known problems.
Right: the student has the knowledge and lacks the nerve to keep investigating.
This is the reverse of his view, and the case shows tools were not enough.
He ranks investigation at least as high as rigor, so this is not his principle.
questions.explain: The needed algebra is known, so the failure lies in confidence and persistence. This is the kind of case Zeitz's psychological principle covers.
questions.rule: Knowing the tools does not ensure using them.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: Order the non-psychological ingredients from broadest to most narrowly defined, as Zeitz describes them.
items: Strategic principles
Tactical approaches
Technical tools
questions.explain: Zeitz describes strategic principles, then more focused tactical approaches, then narrowly defined technical tools.
questions.rule: Strategy, then tactics, then tools.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: Which summary of Zeitz's principles contradicts the preface?
options: Confidence, concentration and courage are vitally important
Problem solving can be taught and can be learned
Knowledge of folklore, such as the pigeonhole principle, is as important as technical tools
Rigorous argument matters, but investigation is only an optional extra
optionExplain: This is stated in his second principle.
This is his first principle.
This is his last principle, with the pigeonhole principle as an example.
Right: he says no-holds-barred investigation is at least as important as rigorous argument.
questions.explain: The preface ranks investigation at least level with rigor, so calling it an optional extra misstates the principle.
questions.rule: Investigation is at least as important as rigor.

questions.unitTitle: Preface to the Second and First Editions
questions.q: In the first edition's layout, a reader wants only the algebra chapter. What does the preface say about reading it?
options: Part II must be read in order, each chapter resting on the one before
Part II is the core of the book, and Part I is background reading
Part II chapters can be read independently of one another, and Part I is the core
Part II should be read only with the instructor's manual at hand
optionExplain: Chapters in sequence is the usual textbook pattern, but the preface says these are independent.
This reverses the preface: Part I, the methodology overview, is the core.
Right: Part II's four chapters (algebra, combinatorics, number theory, calculus) can be read independently, and Part I is the core.
The manual serves instructors; it is not a condition for reading.
questions.explain: Part I is an overview of problem-solving methodology and the core. Part II outlines four subjects from the problem solver's point of view, each readable on its own.
questions.teaches: Part I is an overview of problem-solving methodology and is the core of the book; Part II has four chapters, on algebra, combinatorics, number theory and calculus, that can be read independently of one another.
questions.rule: Part I is the core; Part II chapters stand alone.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Which best separates a mathematical problem from an exercise?
options: A problem has a longer written solution than an exercise
A problem asks for a proof, while an exercise asks for a number
A problem comes from a contest, while an exercise comes from a textbook
For a problem you must first work out which approach to use
optionExplain: Length is tempting, but a long calculation can still be routine.
The kind of answer does not decide it; either can be either.
The source does not decide it; the solver's knowledge of the method does.
Right: a problem demands thought before the approach is found.
questions.explain: The difficulty of the work seems the natural dividing line, but the author draws it at whether the approach is known. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Ask whether you already know how to proceed.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: True or false: In the author's sense, a question is an exercise only if the right answer is easy to reach.
questions.explain: An exercise is a question where you know how to proceed. You can still slip and get it wrong, so the label depends on knowing the method, not on guaranteed success.
questions.rule: An exercise is defined by a known method, not by an easy answer.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: A calculus student differentiates x³ + 5x with ease. A classmate who has not yet met derivatives gets the same task. Which fits?
options: An exercise for the student and a problem for the classmate
An exercise for both, since the task is identical
A problem for both, since any calculus task needs thought
A problem for the student, since she must carry out several steps
optionExplain: Right: the student knows what to do; the classmate must find an approach.
The task is identical, which tempts, but the label depends on what each solver knows.
Thought is needed by the classmate only; the student has a ready technique.
Several steps do not make a problem when each step is a known technique.
questions.explain: The same question can sit on either side of the line, because the author's test is whether the solver already knows the approach.
questions.rule: The label depends on the solver as well as the question.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Dev struggles with a long sum of fractions, then learns induction. For Dev, the label on a similar sum later changes from problem to ____.
questions.explain: Experience moves questions from problem to exercise: once a technique is known, the next question of that type no longer demands a search for an approach.
questions.rule: Learning a technique turns its questions into exercises.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Sam says multiplying 25 by 38 on paper is a problem, because he might slip. What is wrong with that claim?
options: Questions about arithmetic are exercises by definition, for every solver
A slip is possible, but he knows what to do, so it is an exercise
A problem must ask for a proof, and a product is only a number
Nothing is wrong, since any chance of error makes a question a problem
optionExplain: Subject does not decide it; an arithmetic puzzle could demand an approach.
Right: the author defines an exercise by a known method, even if care is needed.
Problems to find exist too; the kind of answer is not the test.
Slips are possible in exercises too; the test is the known method.
questions.explain: Care is needed for exercises, and slips can happen, but the author's test is whether you must first find the approach. Sam knows exactly what to do.
questions.rule: Possible slips do not turn an exercise into a problem.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Priya's first three attempts at a hard puzzle all fail. What does the author say about failed first attempts?
options: They show the puzzle is an exercise she is applying badly
They show she lacks talent, since a real problem yields to a sound first approach
They are common: the first approach often fails, and sometimes the first dozen do
They show she should stop, since a problem reveals its method quickly
optionExplain: If it were an exercise she would know the method, so failure to find one points to a problem.
It feels natural to blame ability, but the author says early failure is common.
Right: failure of early approaches is part of working on a problem.
The author says the harder the problem, the more time it needs.
questions.explain: Because a problem demands a search for the approach, early failures are expected. The harder the problem, the longer the search.
questions.rule: Expect early failures when working on a problem.
questions.teaches: For a real problem the first approach often fails, and sometimes the first dozen approaches fail.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: According to the author, what makes a problem good?
options: It has a short answer that a reader can check against the back of the book
It is mysterious at first yet interesting enough to spend effort on
It can be solved quickly by applying one standard technique carefully
It comes from a famous competition entered by many thousands of students
optionExplain: A checkable answer is pleasant, but the author does not make it the test.
Right: it needs both ingredients, the mystery and the interest.
That describes an exercise, not a problem.
Source is not the test; mystery and interest are.
questions.explain: A fair guess names some feature of the question. The card next gives the author's two ingredients.
questions.rule: A good problem is mysterious and interesting.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Which are reasons the author gives for why inexperienced solvers give up? Select all that apply.
options: They make some progress at first but cannot go further
They find the problem statement too long to read
They do not know how to begin
They are not allowed to use a calculator
They try a few things, nothing works, and they stop
They have been told the problem has no solution
optionExplain: Right: the second reason on the author's list.
Length of the statement is not on the author's list.
Right: the first reason on the author's list.
Tools are not among the reasons the author gives.
Right: the third reason on the author's list.
That is a different situation, and not one of the three reasons.
questions.explain: The author lists three ways beginners stall: no idea how to begin, early progress that stops, and a few failed tries followed by quitting.
questions.rule: Beginners stall at the start, in the middle, or after a few failed tries.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Lena reads a logic puzzle twice and sees no way in. Omar sketches a small case, tries a picture, then rereads. Which fits the author's account?
options: Omar must already know the answer, since only that explains his confidence
Both are experienced solvers, since each of them read the puzzle with great care
The puzzle is an exercise for Lena, since Omar was able to make a start on it
Lena cannot begin; Omar tries several approaches, as an experienced solver does
optionExplain: Confidence is not knowledge; trying approaches is how experienced solvers begin.
Careful reading is shared, but Lena has no way to begin, which the author ties to inexperience.
Lena's difficulty makes it a problem for her; Omar's start does not change that.
Right: it matches the author's contrast between beginner and experienced solver.
questions.explain: The author contrasts the solver who has no way to begin with the one who confidently tries several approaches. Omar's sketch, picture and reread are such approaches.
questions.rule: Experienced solvers start by trying several approaches.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: In the Census-Taker problem, suppose the mother had named the sum 21 instead of 13. Then the ages are 1, 2 and ____.
questions.explain: With product 36, only the triple 1, 2, 18 has sum 21, so that sum would have settled it. The real mother's hint works only because the sum 13 is shared by two triples.
questions.rule: A sum that would not settle the ages must be shared by two triples.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: A reader says the mother's remark about the sum adds nothing, since only the dog clue matters. What is the flaw?
options: The dog clue alone picks one triple out of all eight with product 36
The remark shows the sum is shared by two triples, which leaves two to choose from
The sum remark directly shows the oldest daughter is nine
The first statement already fixed the ages completely, so no later clue matters at all
optionExplain: The dog clue only says there is an oldest daughter; it cannot choose among eight triples.
Right: that remark cuts eight triples to two.
It shows only that two triples remain; the oldest is decided by the dog clue.
The product 36 leaves eight triples, which is why the census-taker asks for more.
questions.explain: The remark about the sum is a clue in disguise: it tells us that the sum belongs to more than one triple. Only then does the dog clue decide.
questions.rule: Read every statement in a puzzle as information.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Ravi, an experienced solver, tries five approaches; none solves the problem, but he learns which cases fail. How does the author view this?
options: It is typical: early approaches may fail to solve it but still bring progress and techniques
It shows he is not really experienced, since an expert solves every problem he tries
It is wasted effort, since only an approach that finishes the whole problem counts as real progress
It means he should wait for a better strategy before trying anything else
optionExplain: Right: this is the author's picture of how an experienced solver proceeds.
Experience is about how to begin and keep going, not about guaranteed success.
The author counts some progress as real progress even without a full solution.
The author has the experienced solver keep trying approaches, not wait.
questions.explain: An experienced solver's approaches may not solve the problem, but some progress is made, then more specific techniques come into play.
questions.rule: Experienced solvers make progress by trying approaches, not by guaranteed success.
questions.teaches: An experienced solver's confident approaches may not solve the problem, but some progress is made, specific techniques then come into play, and the problem is resolved at least some of the time.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Climbers take the south ridge, cross a snowfield early, and carry ice axes. Which of these choices is the broadest plan?
options: Starting early while the snow is still hard
Carrying ice axes for the snowfield
Scouting a river bank for a safe crossing
Taking the south ridge to reach the summit
optionExplain: It is a specific answer to one obstacle, not the overall plan.
It is a piece of equipment for a single obstacle.
It deals with one obstacle on the way, not the whole climb.
Right: it is the overall plan that the other choices serve.
questions.explain: A fair guess picks the choice that sets the route. The card next gives the names of the three levels.
questions.rule: Strategy is the broadest level.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Match each level of problem solving to its description.
pairs: Ideas for getting started and keeping going, mathematical or psychological
Methods that serve in many different settings
Narrow techniques aimed at one specific situation
questions.explain: The levels run from broad to narrow: strategy for starting and pursuing, tactics for methods with wide use, tools for tricks with a single use.
questions.rule: Strategy, then tactics, then tools: from broad to narrow.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: A cyclist plans a long trip. Which of her choices is at the tool level?
options: Following the coast road instead of the mountain road
Starting at dawn so that a steep climb is done in cool air
Tightening one loose bolt with a 10 mm spanner
Studying the week's weather before choosing any route
optionExplain: This sets the route, which is a strategic choice.
This meets a particular obstacle with a method that works in many places: a tactic.
Right: a narrow technique for one specific job is a tool.
This is a general plan for getting started, so it sits at the strategic level.
questions.explain: The spanner job is narrow and specific, like the climbers' ropes and axes. The route choice and the weather study are broader plans, and the early start answers one obstacle.
questions.rule: A tool is a narrow technique for a specific job.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: The party drops the south ridge for the east ridge. Which levels does the author's scheme suggest they must rethink?
options: Only the tools, since the summit they want has not changed
The strategy, and probably the tactics and tools for the new route's obstacles
Nothing, since tactics work in many settings and so cover any route that is chosen
Only the strategy, since tactics and tools are fixed once chosen
optionExplain: The summit is unchanged, but the route, which is the strategy, has changed.
Right: a new route brings new obstacles, and each obstacle needs its own tactics.
Tactics are general, but the author says different tactics are needed for each obstacle.
Tactics and tools serve a route's obstacles, so a new route can call for new ones.
questions.explain: Tactics and tools exist to carry out a strategy. When the route changes, the obstacles change, and the tactics and tools for them can change too.
questions.rule: Change the strategy and the lower levels may change with it.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Sort each statement: would it appear in a short summary of the climb, or only in a detailed log?

items.t: We chose to climb by the south ridge
We had to cross a dangerous river to reach the ridge
We tied the rope with one particular knot and clipped in twice
We held hands in the river so that each of us kept balance
We had to cross a difficult snowfield to reach the ridge
We carried two ice axes each and checked boot laces twice

questions.explain: A summary reports the strategy and sometimes the main tactical hurdles. Tool details are minor, though essential: the climb fails without them, but they are not what you would report.
questions.rule: Summaries state strategy and tactics; tool details stay in the log.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: A colleague uses the word tactic for what this book calls a tool. What does the author's own wording say about this?
options: Neither: the labels are not standard, so readers must check each writer's definitions
The colleague is wrong, because tactic has one standard meaning in all of mathematics
The author is wrong, because problem solving already has an agreed standard vocabulary
Both are wrong, because the only accepted word is heuristics
optionExplain: Right: the author says these are not standard definitions.
The author says the labels are his own, so there is no single standard meaning.
The author notes that problem solving has no standard vocabulary at all.
Heuristics was promoted by Polya and others, but it did not become the standard term.
questions.explain: The author uses strategy, tactics and tools as his own labels. He adds in a footnote that problem solving lacks a standard vocabulary, with no standard name even for its theory.
questions.rule: Check how a writer defines strategy, tactics and tools.
questions.teaches: Problem solving has no standard vocabulary: there is not even a standard name for its theory, although Polya and others tried to popularize the term heuristics.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: In the author's use of the term, every problem has exactly one crux move.
questions.explain: A guess either way is fair. The card next explains what a crux is and says something about how many a problem has.
questions.rule: A crux is the key obstacle, not a feature every problem must have.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: The key obstacle on a climbing route, a term the author borrows for solutions, is called the ____ move.
questions.explain: The term comes from climbing, where the crux is the one difficult section that decides whether the climb succeeds. The author uses it for mathematical problems.
questions.rule: The crux is the obstacle that unlocks the rest.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: A recipe is routine except one step: setting a custard without curdling. Once that works, the rest is easy. How does the author's term apply?
options: There is no crux here, since a recipe contains no real problems, only steps
Every step is a crux, since each one is needed for the finished dish
The crux is the last step, since finishing the dish counts for the most
The custard step is the crux move, and the other steps are exercises
optionExplain: A recipe can hold a hard step, so this is not a safe conclusion.
Being needed is not enough; a crux is the key difficulty.
The crux depends on difficulty, not on position.
Right: one hard step clears the way for routine work.
questions.explain: One difficult step that unlocks the rest is what the author means by a crux. The remaining steps are routine, so they are exercises for this cook.
questions.rule: One hard step that unlocks the rest is the crux.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: Once the cook has set custard a hundred times, the custard step is still the crux, because a crux depends only on the recipe.
questions.explain: The author notes that whether an obstacle is a mere exercise depends on the climber's ability and experience. For a practised cook the custard step is routine, so it need not be a crux for her.
questions.rule: A crux depends on the solver as well as the task.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: In a proof, one step is long but routine for its writer; another is a short idea that unlocks the rest. Which is the crux?
options: The long step, since it takes the most effort and the most space
Both, since a crux is any step that the proof needs in order to be complete and correct
The short idea, since a crux is about difficulty and unlocking, not length
Neither, since a crux appears only in contest problems and not in proofs
optionExplain: Effort and length are tempting, but a routine step is an exercise.
Needed steps are many; a crux is the key one.
Right: the idea that clears the way is the crux, however short.
The term applies to mathematical problems in general.
questions.explain: A crux is defined by what solving it makes possible. A long routine step is an exercise.
questions.rule: Judge a crux by what it unlocks, not by its length.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: A solution has two separate hard moves, and solving each opens a new stretch of easy work. How does the author's term apply?
options: Only the first counts, since a crux is the earliest hard move
Each can be a crux move, because a problem may have several
Only the second counts, since a crux is the final hard move
Neither counts, since a problem has at most one crux move
optionExplain: A crux is not defined by position.
Right: the author says some problems have several crux moves.
A crux is not defined by position.
The author allows several, as well as none.
questions.explain: Each hard move that unlocks easy work after it fits the definition. The author notes that some problems have several crux moves and many have none.
questions.rule: A problem can have several crux moves, or none.
questions.teaches: Some problems have several crux moves.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: A beginner cannot see how to solve a problem. What does the author advise first?
options: Step back and make a loose plan that improves the situation
Pick the most advanced technique known and apply it at once to the whole problem
Try random ideas until one works, however long that takes
Look up the final answer and check each step against it
optionExplain: Right: the author's first move is strategic thinking.
Power is tempting, but the author asks for a plan before techniques.
The author calls this not a terrible method, but advises beginners to be organized.
Checking against an answer is not an approach to solving.
questions.explain: A fair guess names a first move. The card next gives the author's advice for beginners.
questions.rule: Start with a plan, not with a technique.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: The author calls trying whatever comes to mind a terrible method that cannot work.
questions.explain: He calls it by no means a terrible method: with a fertile imagination, a good store of methods and enough time it can succeed. He still advises beginners to be more organized.
questions.rule: Random trying can work, but beginners do better with an organized approach.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Your home Wi-Fi drops every evening. Sort each step: a loose strategic plan, or a specific technique?

items.t: Decide first to find out when the drops happen
Update the router to a named firmware version
Plan to compare the drops across rooms before changing anything
Run a ping test and read the dropped-packet count
