Decide to find out whether one appliance lines up with the drops
Change the Wi-Fi channel to channel 11

questions.explain: A strategic step is a loose plan that leaves you better placed, with little technical content. Updating firmware, running a ping test and changing a channel are specific techniques.
questions.rule: A strategy improves the situation before techniques are chosen.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Two solvers try whatever comes to mind. One has a fertile imagination, many methods and ample time; the other is a beginner on a deadline. Whom does the author expect to do better?
options: The beginner, since fewer methods mean fewer wrong turns to take along the way
Both equally, since random trying treats all kinds of solver in the same way
Neither, since the author says that random trying cannot succeed for anyone
The first, who may succeed; the beginner should be organized
optionExplain: Fewer methods means fewer chances, not fewer wrong turns.
The author ties the method's success to imagination, methods and time.
The author says it is by no means a terrible method.
Right: the author's conditions for random trying fit the first solver.
questions.explain: Random trying draws on imagination, a store of methods and time. The beginner on a deadline lacks at least the time and the store of methods, which is why an organized approach is advised.
questions.rule: Random trying needs imagination, methods and time.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: A student says her strategy is to multiply out the whole expression. What does the author's idea of strategy say about this?
options: It is a strategy, since it is the first thing that she tries on the problem
It is a strategy, because every strategy has to involve a good deal of algebra
It is concrete computation at the tactic or tool level, not a loose plan
It is a strategy, since it is hard to carry out
optionExplain: Being first does not make a step strategic.
Strategy may have barely any mathematical content.
Right: a strategy is a plan, not the computation that carries it out.
Difficulty does not decide the level.
questions.explain: A strategy is a less focused plan that may barely mention mathematics. Multiplying out is concrete work at the tactic or tool level.
questions.rule: Strategy is the loose plan; computation belongs to the lower levels.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Marco has made some progress, then stalls. What can the author's idea of strategy still do for him?
options: Nothing, since strategy matters only before any work on the problem has been done
Replace tactics and tools, which are then no longer needed at all
Tell him exactly which tool he should use at the next step
Help him continue, since strategies serve pursuit as well as starting
optionExplain: The author says strategies help us get started and also continue.
Strategies are vague outlines and still need tactics and tools.
A strategy gives a loose direction, not a specific technique.
Right: the author says strategies help us get started and help us continue.
questions.explain: Strategic thinking is not only for the first move. When progress stops, returning to a loose plan can show a new direction, which tactics and tools then carry out.
questions.rule: Strategy helps you continue as well as begin.
questions.teaches: Strategies help us get started, and they also help us continue.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Multiply four consecutive natural numbers and add 1, for 1, 2, 3 and 4. What kind of number results each time?
options: A perfect square in all four cases
A prime number in each of the four cases
A multiple of 5 in each of the four cases
A perfect cube in each of the four cases
optionExplain: Right: 25, 121, 361 and 841 are all squares.
Primes are a common guess, but 25 is 5 times 5.
25 is, but 121 is not.
None of 25, 121, 361 or 841 is a cube.
questions.explain: Here a short computation settles it. The card next shows how this pattern becomes a proof.
questions.rule: Look for a pattern before searching for a proof.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Put the author's steps for the four-consecutive-numbers proof in order.
items: Orient: split the claim into hypothesis and conclusion
Try the penultimate step and find no easy test for non-squares
Experiment with small values and see each product is one less than a square
Conjecture that the product plus 1 is always a perfect square
Factor the expression and finish with the difference of two squares
questions.explain: The author orients first, tries the penultimate step (which fails), experiments with numbers, forms the conjecture, and only then uses a tactic and a tool to prove it.
questions.rule: Orient, experiment, conjecture, then prove.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Before proving a claim about sums of odd numbers, Jo adds 1, then 1+3, then 1+3+5, and studies the totals. At which level is this?
options: Tactic: a method that works across many branches of mathematics
Strategy: experimenting with small cases to find a pattern
Tool: a narrow trick that suits one particular situation
None: experiments are not part of solving a problem
optionExplain: The author files experimenting under strategy; factoring is the tactic in his example.
Right: the author calls this getting your hands dirty, a strategy.
Experiments are not tied to one situation; a tool is much narrower.
In the author's example, experiments produced the conjecture that cracked the problem.
questions.explain: Plugging in small cases needs little technique and aims at a pattern, which is what the author means by a strategy.
questions.rule: Experimenting with small cases is a strategy.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: The pattern says the product of four consecutive numbers plus 1 equals (n² + 3n + 1)². For n = 6 the product plus 1 is the square of ____.
questions.rule: Test a conjectured formula on a new value.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: A reader argues: f(n) lies below a square, so it cannot be a square. Which step is missing?
options: Nothing is missing: any number below a perfect square is not a perfect square
Showing that n itself is not a perfect square for any choice of n
Showing that no positive square lies exactly one below another
Showing that f(n) is even for every natural number n
optionExplain: Four lies below nine and is a square, so this fails.
This says nothing about the product.
Right: the gaps between positive squares are 3, 5, 7 and so on.
Evenness does not decide squareness.
questions.explain: Being below a square is not enough. The proof needs that f(n) is exactly one below a square, and that no positive square sits exactly one below another because squares spread apart.
questions.rule: Being one less than a square rules out being a square.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.section: The Three Levels of Problem Solving
questions.q: Expanded, \(f(n)+1\) is \(n^4+6n^3+11n^2+6n+1\). A solver tries \((n^2+an+1)^2\) and matches the \(n^3\) terms. Which \(a\) results?
options: \(a=6\), because the \(n^3\) coefficient in the expansion is 6
\(a=11\), because the \(n^2\) coefficient in the expansion is 11
\(a=1\), because the constant term in the expansion is 1
\(a=3\), since matching the \(n^3\) terms gives \(2a=6\)
optionExplain: The expansion doubles \(a\), so the coefficient is \(2a\), not \(a\).
The \(n^2\) coefficient is \(a^2+2\), not \(a\).
The constant term 1 comes from the last 1, not from \(a\).
Right: expanding \((n^2+an+1)^2\) gives \(2a\) as the \(n^3\) coefficient; \(n^2\) and \(n\) terms then agree.
questions.explain: In \((n^2+an+1)^2\) the coefficient of \(n^3\) is \(2a\), so \(a=3\). Then \(a^2+2=11\) and \(2a=6\) agree with the other terms, so the guess works.
questions.rule: Match coefficients of a guessed form with the expansion.
questions.teaches: Once the conjecture is known, the proof can also be done by substituting \(u=n^2+3n\), which gives \(u(u+2)+1=(u+1)^2\), or by undetermined coefficients, a useful tool.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Which family of problems may have no actual solution?
options: Recreational problems
Contest problems
Open-ended problems
Problems to find
optionExplain: Brain teasers have answers, though they may be hard to see.
Contest problems are written with complete solutions.
Right: the author says they are vaguely worded and may have no actual solution.
This is a kind of problem, not a family, and such problems have specific answers.
questions.explain: A fair guess draws on what each family sounds like. The card next describes all three.
questions.rule: Open-ended problems may have no complete solution.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Match each family of problems to its description.
pairs: Brain teasers needing little formal mathematics
Written for timed formal exams, often needing special tools or ingenuity
Vaguely worded, possibly with no solution, and partial results are common
questions.explain: Recreational problems are teasers with little formal mathematics, contest problems are for timed exams, and open-ended problems may not have a complete solution at all.
questions.rule: Recreational, contest, open-ended: teaser, exam, expedition.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: You are asked to find all the patterns you can in a multiplication table and prove those you can. Which family is this?
options: Open-ended: loosely posed, with no promised complete solution
Recreational: a brain teaser with one firm answer and little mathematics
Contest: a timed exam question that comes with a complete solution
A problem to find only, since it asks for patterns to be found
optionExplain: Right: this matches the Pascal's Triangle example in the author's description.
A brain teaser has a firm answer; this task does not.
There is no time limit or promised solution here.
That is a kind, not a family, and the task also asks for proofs.
questions.explain: The task is loosely worded, asks you to discover and prove what you can, and may leave you with partial results, which marks it as open-ended.
questions.rule: Loose wording and partial results mark an open-ended problem.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Sort each task: is it a problem to find or a problem to prove?

items.t: What is the smallest positive integer divisible by every number from 1 to 10?
Show that the sum of any two odd integers is even
In how many ways can 5 people be seated in a row?
Prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers
Find the length of the shortest path between two points that avoids a given circle
Show that among any six integers, two differ by a multiple of 5

questions.explain: Problems to find ask for a specific piece of information, such as a number or a length. Problems to prove require a general argument that holds for every case.
questions.rule: Find asks for a result; prove asks for a general argument.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: A student says the handshake puzzle asks for one number, so its solution needs no general argument. Where is the flaw?
options: Problems to find ask only for proofs, and not for specific numbers
A problem to find can still need a general argument; the line can blur
The author says the handshake puzzle is really a problem to prove
General arguments are used only in open-ended problems, not in contest ones
optionExplain: That reverses the kinds: find asks for specific information.
Right: the author says this of the handshake puzzle.
The author calls it a problem to find.
Arguments appear in every family.
questions.explain: The author labels the handshake puzzle a problem to find, but notes its solution may involve a very general argument, so the find and prove kinds can overlap.
questions.rule: A problem to find can still call for a general argument.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Ines is preparing for hard contests and wonders whether brain teasers are worth her time. What does the author say?
options: Not worth it: they need little formal mathematics, so they teach nothing transferable
Worth it only after she has mastered every contest tool in the book
Worth it only if the teasers come from a published collection
Worth it: their basic strategy helps later with harder problems
optionExplain: The author argues the opposite: because they rely on basic strategy, they transfer.
The author says no special knowledge is needed first.
The source is not the test; the author does recommend Gardner's collections but not as a condition.
Right: time spent on them helps later.
questions.explain: Because recreational problems rely on basic strategic principles, thinking about them builds habits that carry over to harder, more mathematical problems.
questions.rule: Practice on teasers carries over to harder problems.
questions.teaches: Time spent thinking about a recreational problem will help with more mathematically sophisticated problems later.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Why does the author say the AHSME and AIME feature problems to find?
options: Their questions are easy enough that no proof is needed in any of them
They are graded by machine, which suits specific answers
Their time limits leave no room to write out any argument at all
Their writers prefer arithmetic to argument when setting questions
optionExplain: Ease is not the reason the author gives.
Right: machine grading needs answers a machine can check.
The AIME gives three hours; the reason is grading, not time.
The author gives no such preference; the reason is grading.
questions.explain: A fair guess looks for a cause. The card next gives the author's reason.
questions.rule: Machine grading goes with problems to find.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Put these stages of the contest ladder in order, from first to last.
items: AHSME: a multiple-choice test taken by many high-school students
AIME: three hours and 15 questions, for the top 2000 or so AHSME scorers
USAMO: five essay questions, for the top 150 or so AIME participants
A training program for the top USAMO scorers, which picks the US team
IMO: nine hours and six essay questions over two days
questions.explain: Each stage takes the top scorers of the one before: AHSME, then AIME, then USAMO, then a training program that picks the team for the IMO.
questions.rule: Each contest stage selects from the one before.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: A new contest is graded entirely by machine. By the author's pattern, it mostly sets problems to ____.
questions.explain: The author says the AHSME and AIME feature problems to find because they are graded by machine, so a new machine-graded contest would do the same.
questions.rule: Machine grading goes with problems to find.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: A student fully solves two of the twelve Putnam questions. Given the author's remark about scores, how does this compare?
options: It is likely above the median, since the median score is often zero
It is likely below the median, since most entrants solve at least half
It is likely at the median, since half of entrants solve exactly two
It cannot be compared, since the author gives no information on scores
optionExplain: Right: the author says the median is often zero.
The author says the median score is often zero, so few solve many.
Nothing suggests two is typical.
The author gives the median: often zero.
questions.explain: If the median is often zero, solving even two questions fully would usually put a student above the middle.
questions.rule: On the Putnam, the median score is often zero.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: A friend says the USAMO is machine-graded like the AIME, since only AIME scorers qualify. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since exams that are used to qualify students share a format
The USAMO is a multiple-choice exam, like the AHSME and unlike the AIME
Qualifying says nothing about format; the USAMO is an essay exam of proofs
The USAMO is machine graded, but it sets problems to prove
optionExplain: Qualifying says nothing about format, so this assumption fails.
The USAMO is not multiple choice; it is an essay exam.
Right: an essay exam of proofs is not machine graded.
A machine cannot grade essay proofs; the author ties machine grading to problems to find.
questions.explain: Entry rules do not fix format. The USAMO is a three-and-a-half-hour essay exam featuring mostly problems to prove.
questions.rule: Format comes from the exam, not from who qualifies.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Hamid wants problems that readers mail solutions to, some of which stay unsolved for years. Which source does the author describe?
options: The AHSME, taken by hundreds of thousands of students each year in school
Problem departments in mathematical journals that print solutions
The IMO, an exam taken by national teams over two days
ARML, a contest between teams from different regions
optionExplain: It is a timed multiple-choice exam, not a place to mail solutions.
Right: readers propose problems or mail in solutions.
The IMO is a timed exam, not a mailed department.
ARML is a team contest, not a mailed department.
questions.explain: Journals such as the American Mathematical Monthly invite readers to propose problems or mail in solutions, and print the most interesting ones; some problems stay unsolved for years.
questions.rule: Journals offer problems with no time limit.
questions.teaches: Mathematical journals run problem departments where readers mail in solutions and the most interesting are published, and some problems stay unsolved for years.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: How does the author suggest a reader move through this book?
options: Strictly from chapter 1 to the end, never skipping a page
Only the chapters that match a favourite branch of mathematics
Non-linearly: skim harder parts at first, then return
The problems first, with the text read only if they fail
optionExplain: Cover-to-cover reading is the usual habit, but the author rejects it.
Interest guides chapters 5 to 9, but the book is also about method.
Right: the book is meant to be perused, not read start to finish.
The author wants the text read, and examples tried before their solutions.
questions.explain: A fair guess draws on how technical books are usually read. The card next gives the author's plan.
questions.rule: Peruse the book; do not read it in a straight line.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Match each part of the book to what it covers.
pairs: An overview of strategies and tactics
A bridge of crossover tactics linking branches of mathematics
Mathematical ideas by subject, at the tactic or tool level
questions.explain: The book has two parts with a bridge between them: general method first, specific mathematical subjects last, and three crossover tactics in the middle.
questions.rule: Method first, bridge in the middle, subjects last.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Dana is midway through a section of chapter 2 and finds it needs experience she lacks. What does the author advise?
options: Stop reading the book until her mathematical background is complete
Read the start closely, skim or skip ahead, then come back later
Reread the section until all of it makes sense before moving on
Skip the whole section from its first page, since it will be too hard
optionExplain: Waiting is tempting, but the author invites a first pass now.
Right: read the beginning carefully, skim as it gets harder, and reread later.
Persistence feels right, but the author allows skimming and a return visit.
The beginning of each section is simple and should be read carefully.
questions.explain: The sections run from simple to sophisticated, so the start is for careful reading and the harder end can be skimmed or skipped on a first pass.
questions.rule: Read the start of a section closely; skim as it hardens.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: A reader finishes chapters 5 to 9 and her mathematical knowledge has grown. What does the author suggest next?
options: Put the early chapters aside, since they are now too easy
Start the book over at chapter 5 with more care
Move on to a different book, since the main work is done
Return to earlier sections she skimmed and reread them
optionExplain: The author sees the early chapters as worth revisiting, not outgrown.
The author sends you back to the earlier chapters, not to chapter 5.
Nothing in the author's plan ends the book at this point.
Right: as mathematical knowledge grows, skimmed sections can be reread.
questions.explain: Mathematics learned in later chapters makes the harder ends of the early sections easier, so the author suggests going back.
questions.rule: Return to skimmed sections as your mathematics grows.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: True or false: The author puts chapter 4 early because its material is gentle.
questions.explain: Chapter 4 is pretty advanced. It comes early to give the reader a quick route to sophisticated ideas that apply very broadly.
questions.rule: Chapter 4 is early for reach, not for ease.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Ravi skims hard sections once and skips problems he cannot solve. How does this compare with the author's ideal?
options: It falls short: the ideal is every page read twice and every problem read
It matches: the author expects hard sections and unsolved problems to be dropped for good
It exceeds the ideal, since the author asks for only one pass
It is fine, but only if he has also skipped chapter 4
optionExplain: Right: that is the author's stated ideal.
The author wants to come back to skimmed material.
The author's ideal is two passes at least.
Chapter 4 is not special in this ideal.
questions.explain: The author's ideal goes beyond a single skim: he hopes every page is read at least twice, and every problem read even when not solved.
questions.rule: Ideally read every page twice and read every problem.
questions.teaches: Ideally you will read every page of the book at least twice, and read, if not solve, every single problem in it.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: You reach a worked example in a maths book. What should you do before reading its solution?
options: Try to solve it yourself, or at least ponder it briefly
Read the solution first so your own attempts are not wasted
Skip examples, since they matter less than the surrounding text
Copy the statement into your notes and read on at once
optionExplain: Right: the author asks for restraint before looking.
Efficiency is tempting, but attempts are where the learning happens.
The author wants examples worked actively.
Copying is passive; the author asks for pencil-and-paper work.
questions.explain: Many readers go straight to the solution. The card next gives the author's request.
questions.rule: Try the example before you read the solution.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: A filled-in square, named after the mathematician Paul ____, marks the end of a solution.
questions.explain: The author uses the Halmos symbol, a filled-in square, to show that a solution is complete.
questions.rule: A filled-in square ends a solution.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: Sam opens a textbook where the worked solution sits right below the statement. Which habit follows the author's advice?
options: Read statement and solution together to save time for more problems
Read the solution twice before trying anything, to avoid forming wrong habits
Cover the solution, try the example with pencil and paper, then compare
Try the example only if it looks easy, and otherwise skip it
optionExplain: Speed is tempting, but the author wants you to try first.
Careful reading is good, but the author asks you to try before looking.
Right: attempt first, even briefly, then read.
The author asks for an attempt, or at least pondering, on each example.
questions.explain: The advice is to attempt each example before reading the solution, and at the least to ponder it for a few moments.
questions.rule: Cover the solution and try first.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: True or false: If a beginner cannot solve a classic problem alone in a reasonable time, the author takes this as a sign she should stop reading the book.
questions.explain: The author says classics are usually too hard for the beginning reader to solve alone in a reasonable time, yet he includes them on purpose. Failing to solve one is expected.
questions.rule: Classics are meant to stretch beginners.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: According to the author, which is the most important reason the book includes classic problems?
options: They provide the best practice for contest speed
They illustrate important ideas of the book
They belong to the essential repertoire of every young mathematician
They are beautiful works of art to be pondered and enjoyed
optionExplain: Speed is not among the author's reasons.
This is one of the three reasons, but not the one he calls most important.
This is also one of the three reasons, not the most important.
Right: the author names beauty as the most important reason.
questions.explain: The author gives three reasons: classics illustrate important ideas, they are part of a young mathematician's essential repertoire, and, most important, they are beautiful.
questions.rule: Classics are included above all for their beauty.
questions.teaches: Classic problems are included for three reasons: they illustrate important ideas, they are part of a young mathematician's essential repertoire, and, most important, they are beautiful works of art.

questions.unitTitle: What This Book Is About and How to Read It
questions.q: A woodworking student only drills joints and does not study fine furniture by masters. What does the author's jazz analogy say is missing?
options: More drills, since craft matters far more than art in learning
A teacher who grades every joint she cuts and corrects each mistake
Instruction and inspiration from great examples, plus practice
Nothing: practising the basics is enough to learn the whole art
optionExplain: The author spends more pages on craft but does not say that craft alone suffices.
Grading is not what the analogy is about.
Right: the jazz student needs scales and also great recordings.
The analogy says practice alone is not enough.
questions.explain: In the analogy, a jazz student practises scales and improvises, but also listens to great recordings for instruction and inspiration. The woodworker needs the same.
questions.rule: Practise the craft and study great work.
questions.teaches: Learning jazz piano improvisation takes practising scales and your own improvisations, but also listening to great recordings for instruction and inspiration.

questions.q: A friend shows you a short, elegant proof of a puzzle result. What does the neat page most likely leave out?
options: The reason the result matters to mathematicians
The final answer, which is saved for the last line
The false starts and experiments that led to the idea
The definition of every word used in the problem
optionExplain: Importance is not what a proof page hides; the page may say nothing about it, but the tidy form hides something else.
The answer is on the page; the neat form removes the path to it.
Right: the polished page shows the argument and usually hides how the discovery was made.
Definitions are normally included for the reader; they are not what tidying removes.
questions.explain: A finished write-up is built for the reader, so the experiments and misconceptions behind it are dropped. The card next names the two parts of a solution.
questions.rule: A neat proof is the argument; the investigation stays hidden.

questions.q: The two parts of the solution to every problem are the investigation and the ____.
questions.explain: The investigation is where you discover what is going on; the argument is where you convince others (or yourself) of the discovery.
questions.rule: Investigate first, then argue.

questions.q: Ravi tabulates eight cases of a counting question, notices a doubling pattern, then writes three lines showing why it must hold. Which step is the argument?
options: Tabulating the first eight cases
Noticing the doubling pattern in the table
Wondering whether the pattern could be a coincidence
Writing the three lines that show why the pattern must hold
optionExplain: Tabulating is experiment: he is still finding out what is going on.
Spotting a pattern is discovery, so it belongs to the investigation.
Doubt drives the investigation; only a reasoned case settles it.
Right: this step convinces a reader that the pattern is not a coincidence.
questions.explain: The argument is the part written to convince. Everything before it, including the pattern-spotting, is investigation.
questions.rule: Argument is the part that convinces.

questions.q: Sort each activity into the part of the solution it belongs to.

items.t: Trying small numbers to see what happens
Guessing a formula from a table of values
Writing each step so a reader can check it follows
Stating the hypothesis and conclusion, then proving the result
Rereading the problem and restating it in new notation

questions.explain: Experiments, guesses and restating the problem find out what is going on; stating and proving in checkable steps is the argument.
questions.rule: Discover first; justify in checkable steps.

questions.q: A problem's early experiments suggest a pattern that smells like a proof by contradiction. According to the authors, what role does that hunch play?
options: It is a tentative choice of argument that can still change, even from case to case
It fixes the method, so the whole solution must be one style
It must be discarded, since a proof method cannot be chosen before the answer is known
It matters only for written proofs, not for working things out
optionExplain: Right: the investigation may suggest a tentative method, and a problem can divide into cases needing different methods.
The authors say a problem may divide into cases or sub-problems that each need a different method.
They say the opposite: initial investigation may suggest a tentative method of argument.
The method also steers the investigation; the authors note fluency in argument helps you steer and modify it.
questions.explain: Investigation and argument feed each other: a hunch about how to argue can guide what you try next, and it may change per case.
questions.rule: Let the investigation suggest a style of argument, then stay flexible.
questions.teaches: The initial investigation may suggest a tentative method of argument, and a problem may split into cases or sub-problems that each need a completely different method.

questions.q: A technician finds why a server crashes, then writes a clear note for the team. A colleague says the note is not important since the bug is already fixed. What do the authors' two parts imply?
options: The note is the real work, because the fix will fade from memory
The idea is complete once the technician is convinced of it
The fix is the discovery only; without the note nobody else can rely on it
Notes matter only in mathematics, where proofs are written down
optionExplain: The authors rate the investigation as the heart of the work; the argument supports it, it does not replace it.
The argument is aimed at convincing others, or at least checking your own discovery.
Right: an idea that cannot be communicated is of little use to others, even if it is brilliant.
The authors say many strategies work on many kinds of problems, not just mathematical ones.
questions.explain: The authors stress the process of investigation, but add that a brilliant idea is useless if it cannot be communicated to anyone else.
questions.rule: A discovery nobody else can check is not yet a solution.
questions.teaches: A brilliant idea is useless if it cannot be communicated to anyone else.

questions.q: A mouse is shut in a cage with bars at slightly different spacings. Which behaviour gives it the best chance of getting out?
options: Trying one bar after another, so that all sides get tested
Throwing itself at the bars on one favourite side with more force
Sitting still to save energy until the trap opens
Choosing the side that looks easiest and staying with it
optionExplain: Right: the openings differ a little, and testing different places is how the mouse finds the wider one.
Force on a single side repeats the same trial; if the gap is not there, it never will be.
Waiting does not search for the opening; the trap will not open itself.
A side that looks easy may be the narrowest; the opening cannot be known in advance.
questions.explain: Testing different places is what finds the opening. The card next gives the lesson in the authors words.
questions.rule: Vary the trials.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: The fundamental method of mice and men: try, try again, and ____ the trials so that you do not miss the few favourable possibilities.
questions.explain: Repeating a failed trial teaches nothing new; changing it explores another side of the problem.
questions.rule: Try again, but change the try.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Dev is stuck on an inequality. He has tried a substitution three times, each time with the same change of variable. What follows Polya's advice?
options: Try a different approach, such as plugging in small numbers or drawing a graph
Repeat the substitution carefully, since the error must be small
Stop for good, since three failures show it cannot be solved
Copy the answer from a friend to see where the substitution should go
optionExplain: Right: a new kind of trial explores another side of the problem.
A third identical trial is the mouse hitting the same bar; a different variable would at least vary it.
Three failed trials of one kind are no proof of impossibility, and the advice is to keep varying.
This skips the exploring; the lesson is to learn from your own failed trials.
questions.explain: The advice is not to try more, but to try differently. A new method, a graph or small cases are new trials.
questions.rule: Change the trial, not just the effort.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Sort each reaction to a failed attempt by whether it fits Polya's advice.

items.t: Re-attack the problem using a different diagram
Repeat the identical algebra in the same order, hoping to catch a slip
Try a smaller version of the problem to see what changes
Push harder along the line that has failed three times
Switch from algebra to experiments with small numbers

questions.explain: Fresh angles explore other sides of the problem; repeating the same failed push is what the mouse story warns against.
questions.rule: Varied trials fit; identical repeats do not.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: According to Polya, what advantage does a person have over the mouse when varying trials?
options: A person need not fail at all, because reasoning shows the opening
A person gets unlimited attempts, while the mouse tires out
A person can vary trials mentally and learn more from the failures
A person is physically stronger, so each trial pushes harder
optionExplain: He says we cannot know in advance where the opening is; failure is part of finding it.
Polya does not credit endless tries; he credits what can be done with them.
Right: no bodily crashing is needed, and each failure can teach more.
Strength is the mouse's way; the person's gain is mental, not bodily.
questions.explain: Polya says a man can throw himself at the obstacle mentally, vary his trials more, and learn more from the failure of his trials.
questions.rule: Failed trials are information, if you vary them.
questions.teaches: A person can vary trials mentally, without bodily effort, and can learn more from the failure of trials than a mouse can.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: A cook's sauce splits each time. She has changed the heat only. Which next step best follows the mouse's method?
options: Give up on sauces and serve plain pasta
Change a different factor, such as the order of adding the butter
Keep the heat setting and cook it for longer each time
Wait to see whether the sauce fixes itself
optionExplain: Giving up after one dimension of trials is too early; many sides remain.
Right: it explores another side of the problem, as the mouse moved from bar to bar.
Longer cooking at one setting repeats the same trial and may make things worse.
Waiting does not explore; the opening has to be found by varied trials.
questions.explain: The same method fits cooking: vary what you change, because the key difference may lie in a variable you have not touched.
questions.rule: Vary a different thing each time.
questions.teaches: Polya says we must try and try again until we recognise the slight difference between the various openings on which everything depends.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: A student has worked a hard problem for 20 minutes and is stuck. Which is the best view of what to do?
options: Stop at once; stuck means the problem is beyond reach
Copy the method of the last problem and try it unchanged
Vary the approach a few times; if nothing works, set it aside for later
Never stop; every problem yields to enough force
optionExplain: Early stopping gives up before the real work of varying attempts has been done.
This ignores that a different kind of attempt may be needed.
Right: giving up for now, after real varied effort, is part of problem solving.
Not stopping is not wise: sometimes a problem simply cannot be solved yet.
questions.explain: A sensible solver neither quits at once nor never quits. The card next gives the authors' view.
questions.rule: Stop late, and temporarily.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a good problem solver does not give up on a problem under any circumstances.
questions.explain: They say this moral is too simplistic: all good solvers occasionally admit defeat, and knowing when to give up is part of the art.
questions.rule: Knowing when to stop is part of the art.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Lena set a puzzle aside after an hour of varied attempts and plans to retry it next week. What kind of giving up is this?
options: A sensible, temporary retreat that keeps the problem alive
A failure, because she did not finish within the hour
A proof that the puzzle is impossible
A sign she lacks the talent for such puzzles
optionExplain: Right: she varied her attempts, then deliberately set it aside, at least temporarily.
Finishing is not required to count the effort as sound; the authors accept temporary retreat.
Stopping does not show impossibility; that would need an argument.
The authors blame lack of confidence and concentration, which can be built, not fixed talent.
questions.explain: A deliberate break after real effort is the kind of giving up the authors accept.
questions.rule: Giving up for now is allowed.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it shows the mental toughness the authors want or the early quitting they describe.

items.t: Believing the problem can be solved and working on
Stopping when the first frustration appears
Keeping the mind on one problem for a long stretch
Walking away because the first attempt failed
Doubting that you can solve it before you start

questions.explain: The authors name confidence and concentration as the attributes beginners lack; without them people reach their frustration limit early.
questions.rule: Confidence and concentration keep you working.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: The authors say you may fail to solve a problem and still gain something. According to them, how does it compare to the mouse's situation?
options: It is much worse, because the mouse could always try again
It is safe: unlike the mouse, you will not die if you do not solve it
It is equally dangerous, because a failed problem also costs a life
It is identical, which is why you must finish each problem
optionExplain: The mouse could not try forever either; the point is that you can keep trying other approaches.
Right: several failed attempts are fine, and failure carries no such danger.
The authors point out the opposite difference between the two cases.
They say solving every problem is not important.
questions.explain: The authors contrast the mouse with the solver: you will not die if you fail, so failure need not inhibit you.
questions.rule: Failure costs little, so keep trying other approaches.
questions.teaches: Unlike Polya's mouse, you will not die if you do not solve the problem, so failed attempts are fine as long as you keep trying other approaches.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: A chess player loses to the same opening five times. She leaves it for a month and then studies a new defence. Which words fit best?
options: She gave up temporarily after varied effort, then came back with a new approach
She quit, and a problem solver should not do that
She wasted the month, because only continuous effort can solve it
She proved the opening cannot be beaten
optionExplain: Right: stopping for now is acceptable when it is followed by a return.
She did not quit for good: she changed the approach and returned.
Rest and a fresh approach may serve better than constant effort.
Losses do not prove impossibility; that would need an argument.
questions.explain: The idea reaches beyond mathematics: a break can be part of working at a problem.
questions.rule: A pause with a plan to return is not quitting.
questions.teaches: It is hard to work on a problem if you do not believe you can solve it, and impossible to keep working past your frustration threshold.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: You want to be able to work for hours on a hard problem. Which training plan fits best?
options: Practise only problems you already solve easily, to keep your confidence high
Begin with easy problems, then raise the difficulty step by step
Start with the hardest problems you can find, to harden yourself fast
Wait until you feel confident and then try your first real problem
optionExplain: Staying at the easy level builds confidence but never stretches your stamina.
Right: successes build confidence, and a rising load stretches how long you can concentrate.
Hopeless problems break confidence; failures pile up with nothing to build on.
Confidence comes from working problems, so waiting does not produce it.
questions.explain: Confidence and stamina grow with practice. The card next explains the plan.
questions.rule: Raise the load gradually.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Easy problems, in the authors' sense, are ones you can solve after a ____ effort.
questions.explain: Easy means solvable with a modest effort, so that each success builds your confidence.
questions.rule: Easy means solvable with modest effort.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Omar can focus on a hard problem for 15 minutes before quitting. Which plan follows the authors' advice?
options: Keep adding problems a bit harder than the last, and let sessions grow longer
Do a long set of routine exercises, since they are quick to finish
Jump to Olympiad-level problems and refuse to stop until one is solved
Spend a month reading about confidence before starting any problem
optionExplain: Right: a gradually increasing load raises both confidence and the frustration threshold.
Routine exercises are not problems; they do not stretch you.
A jump this large risks repeated failure and burnout.
Confidence is built by working on problems, not by reading about it.
questions.explain: The load must rise gradually and must consist of real problems.
questions.rule: Gradual load, real problems.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Which of these habits work against building mental toughness? Select all that apply.
options: Only working problems that you can finish in a minute
Raising the difficulty a little each week
Dropping every problem the moment it feels frustrating
Taking problems that are interesting to you
optionExplain: Right to flag: nothing here stretches you, so the frustration threshold stays low.
This is the recommended habit, so it is not an error.
Right to flag: quitting at the first frustration keeps the threshold exactly where it is.
Interest helps: you do not mind working longer on interesting problems.
questions.explain: Staying with the trivial and quitting at once both stop the threshold from rising. A rising load and interesting problems help.
questions.rule: Stretch gradually; do not stay trivial or bolt.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, working through the chapter's psychological strategies promises an immediate improvement in solving problems.
questions.explain: They say they promise no such thing: improvement in solving comes with time, but first you have to learn to really work.
questions.rule: Learn to work first; skill comes later.
questions.teaches: The authors are not promising improvement in solving problems from the psychological strategies; that will come with time, but first you have to learn to really work.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: A learner only repeats drills whose method she already knows, and her confidence stays flat. What do the authors' ideas suggest is missing?
options: Real problems, where she must find the method herself, which give the brain a workout
More drills of the same kind, done faster
A higher frustration threshold gained by avoiding hard cases
Natural talent that she either has or lacks
optionExplain: Right: routine drills are exercises; problems are what exercise the brain and build confidence.
Speed on known drills does not stretch her, and the authors distinguish exercises from problems.
The threshold rises when the load rises, not by avoiding difficulty.
The authors say confidence and concentration can be built.
questions.explain: Exercises repeat a known method; problems need you to find one. The authors say working on problems, not exercises, builds confidence automatically.
questions.rule: Work on problems, not just exercises.
questions.teaches: As long as you work on problems rather than exercises, your brain gets a workout and your subconscious gets used to success, so confidence rises automatically.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: A puzzle asks you to do something that looks impossible at first glance. What is the best first move?
options: Ask the setter whether the puzzle is a trick
Prove at once that it cannot be done
Assume it can be done, and look for a way
Say it is impossible and move on, to save time
optionExplain: The setter's answer takes away the investigation, which is the point.
A proof of impossibility is a hard task; starting there is premature.
Right: optimism keeps you working; impossibility can be argued later.
A first-glance verdict skips the work of understanding the problem.
questions.explain: Looking impossible and being impossible differ. The card next shows an interview puzzle that tests this.
questions.rule: Begin optimistically.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a problem that looks impossible after a quick glance should be declared impossible, to save time.
questions.explain: They say not to admit defeat after a cursory glance: begin optimistically and assume the problem can be solved.
questions.rule: Do not admit defeat at a glance.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Nia has tried a tiling puzzle three ways without success. Which action follows the authors' advice?
options: Try to prove it impossible; if no proof comes, come back to it later
Declare it impossible, since three tries is plenty
Insist that it can be solved and never examine impossibility
Delete the puzzle from her notes so it stops bothering her
optionExplain: Right: after several failed attempts, test for impossibility, and if that also fails, leave the problem open.
Several failed attempts allow thinking about impossibility, but three tries do not prove it.
After several failed attempts, trying to prove impossibility is allowed.
The authors want you to go back to it later, not to erase it.
questions.explain: Optimism comes first; after several failures, trying to prove impossibility is allowed; if that fails, return later.
questions.rule: Several failures, then test impossibility, then return.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Sort each response to a seemingly impossible problem.

items.t: Assume it is solvable and start experimenting
Announce it cannot be done after a glance
After many failures, look for a proof of impossibility
Reject it as dishonest to even try, because it looks impossible
Park an unproved case and return to it later

questions.explain: Optimism first, a proof of impossibility only after several failures, and a return if nothing is proved.
questions.rule: Optimism, then proof of impossibility, then return.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: According to the authors, what is wrong with announcing at once that a problem is impossible?
options: It wastes the setter's time and so is impolite
It is dishonest, since you have not taken time to understand the problem
It is only a tactical blunder, since impossibility is likely anyway
Nothing; it is a good way to save time on hopeless questions
optionExplain: Politeness is not their concern.
Right: they call immediate declarations of impossibility dishonest.
They do not call it tactical, and they do not call it likely.
They say it feels good but it is far better to take one's time.
questions.explain: The authors say it might feel good to dispose of a problem quickly, but it is far better to take time to understand it, and quick declarations of impossibility are dishonest.
questions.rule: A snap verdict of impossibility is dishonest.
questions.teaches: The authors call immediate declarations of impossibility dishonest, since there is no time pressure and it is far better to take one's time to understand a problem.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: A company gives candidates a puzzle that looks impossible and watches how they react. What do the authors suggest the personnel department wanted to see?
options: How quickly someone would give up
How fast someone could prove impossibility
Whether someone could recite a known solution
How well someone knew the topology of diagrams
optionExplain: Right: the authors suspect the puzzle was crafted to test persistence and confidence.
The authors say the puzzle is solvable; no proof of impossibility was wanted.
It is a puzzle to be worked out; the authors do not suggest a known recital.
Topology explains why the solution works, but is not what the interviewers tested.
questions.explain: The authors note that the software company's personnel people were crafty and wanted to see how quickly someone would give up.
questions.rule: Employers can test confidence by posing seemingly impossible puzzles.
questions.teaches: The software company's personnel people were crafty: they wanted to see how quickly someone would give up on a puzzle that looks impossible.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: A problem has awkward large numbers and you cannot see how to start. What is a good first try?
options: Solve the same problem with small numbers, and see what happens
Work out the answer for the large numbers with a calculator, whatever the method
Give up, since large numbers make a problem unsolvable
Ask which formula the teacher would use and apply it blindly
optionExplain: Right: removing the ugly part gives a version you can explore.
Pushing numbers through hides any pattern and does not help you understand.
Large numbers are not a reason to stop; they are the difficulty to be removed.
A blind formula does not explore; the easy cousin does.
questions.explain: Making the difficulty disappear, even illegally, can reveal what matters. The card next states the strategy.
questions.rule: Reduce the difficulty first.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: If the given problem is too hard, solve an ____ one.
questions.explain: That is the make it easier strategy: temporarily avoid the hard part.
questions.rule: Solve an easier problem first.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: Which easier version best helps with a question about the sum of 1/(1x2) + 1/(2x3) + ... + 1/(99x100)?
options: Solve a different question about 99 and 100 only
Take the same sum but stop at 2, 3, 4 and so on, and look at the totals
Replace all the fractions by decimals and add on a calculator
Wait until you can recall the answer
optionExplain: It drops most of the sum and leaves nothing to compare.
Right: small cases with the same structure may show a pattern.
This keeps the difficulty and gives no insight.
Recall is not a strategy; the easier cousin is.
questions.explain: Shortening the sum keeps its structure and removes its size. The totals 1/2, 2/3, 3/4 point to a pattern.
questions.rule: Shrink the size, keep the structure.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: True or false: After solving an easier version of a problem, you may conclude the original problem is solved, without any link between them.
questions.explain: The original is solved only if the easier version is equivalent to it or can be changed back step by step.
questions.rule: Link the easy version back to the original.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: In the box puzzle the authors call something a tool but not a strategy. Which is it?
options: Mutating a diagram into a topologically equivalent one
Making the problem easier
Cultivating an optimistic attitude
Taking one's time to understand the problem
optionExplain: Right: it applies to a certain kind of problem, so it is a tool, not a strategy.
They call this a strategy.
They call this a psychological strategy.
This is a general attitude, not a tool tied to one type of problem.
questions.explain: A strategy is general; a tool is specific. The topological trick is specific to diagrams.
questions.rule: Strategies are general; tools are specific.
questions.teaches: Mutating a diagram into a topologically equivalent one is not a strategy but a tool, in the authors' language.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: A party planner cannot work out seating for 60 guests with many constraints. She plans for 6 guests first. If that fails to scale, what do the authors say is still gained?
options: She is forced to focus on the key difficulty, and may find an intermediate question
Nothing, since an easy version that is not equivalent is worthless
A guarantee that the 60-guest plan is then possible
Proof that the original is impossible
optionExplain: Right: at worst, you must face the key difficulty, which may yield a helpful question.
Even then it shows what the main difficulty is.
Nothing guarantees this; the box puzzle was a lucky case.
Failure of the easy version proves nothing about impossibility.
questions.explain: The authors say that, at worst, ignoring the difficulty forces you to focus on it and may suggest an intermediate question.
questions.rule: A failed easy version still shows the key difficulty.
questions.teaches: At worst, eliminating the hard part forces you to focus on the key difficulty and possibly to formulate an intermediate question whose answer helps with the problem.
questions.section: Mental Toughness: Learn from Polya's Mouse

questions.q: True or false: A monk walks up a mountain path from 8AM to noon, rests overnight, and walks down the same path from 8AM to noon the next day, at any speeds he likes. There must be a clock time at which he is at the same spot on both days.
questions.explain: It is true. The card next shows a surprisingly short reason.
questions.rule: Some problems have startlingly short solutions.

questions.q: Most mathematicians are ____, believing the totality of their subject already exists and is discovered rather than created.
questions.explain: To a Platonist, problem solving is the art of seeing the solution that is already there.
questions.rule: The Platonist solver discovers, not invents.

questions.q: A van drives from depot to town 6AM to 10AM on Monday, and back on the same road 6AM to 10AM on Tuesday. Which idea shows it passes some spot at the same clock time on both days?
options: Split the road into equal pieces and check the van on each piece
Imagine Monday's trip replayed on Tuesday by a second van, so the two vans meet
Compute its average speed on each day and compare the two
Assume the van drives at constant speed on both days
optionExplain: This sorts the road but does not show a shared spot and time.
Right: two vans on one road in opposite directions must meet, and the meeting point is the shared spot and time.
Average speeds say nothing about location at a given clock time.
The problem gives no such speeds; the result holds without it.
questions.explain: The second-van idea mirrors the second monk: replaying one trip on the other's day turns 'same spot' into 'meeting'.
questions.rule: Replay one journey alongside the other so they must meet.

questions.q: Which statements fit the authors' account of creativity here? Select all that apply.
options: Creativity is a receptiveness to ideas floating around in plain view
The second monk is a character in the problem statement
To the Platonist, the solution is already there to be seen
Only a gifted few can ever have such ideas
optionExplain: Right: that elusive receptiveness is what they call creativity.
Wrong: the second monk is invented by the solver; the problem mentions only one monk.
Right: for the Platonist, the solver finds a solution that already exists.
Wrong: the authors believe almost everyone can learn to become more creative.
questions.explain: Creativity is receptiveness, the second monk is the solver's invention, and the Platonist sees solutions as already present.
questions.rule: Creativity is receptiveness, and the helpful idea is often invented by the solver.

questions.q: What do the authors find extraordinary about the second-monk solution?
options: The insight seems to come from nowhere, yet instantly resolves the problem
It needs advanced calculus to be justified
It works only if the monk walks at constant speed
It was found by exhaustive checking of cases
optionExplain: Right: the unexpected, clever insight of inventing a second monk.
The solution uses only the idea that two paths meet.
Speeds are left free; the solution works for any speeds.
Nothing like that is involved; it is a one-idea solution.
questions.explain: The authors stress how pleasing and surprising the second-monk idea is.
questions.rule: A creative idea can come from nowhere and settle the problem at once.
questions.teaches: The extraordinary thing about the second-monk solution is the unexpected insight of inventing a second monk, an idea that seems to come from nowhere yet instantly resolves the problem.

questions.q: Two cyclists ride the same trail in opposite directions on different days. Which representation shows at a glance that they share a spot and time?
options: A plot of position against clock time, with both rides on the same axes, so the two curves must cross
A list of each rider's speed on every kilometre
A table of the riders' ages and bike models
A map of the trail without any times marked
optionExplain: Right: one rises across the day and the other falls, so their curves cross; this is the authors' more conventional solution.
A speed list hides when and where the riders are.
Irrelevant to location and time.
A map shows places but not when they were reached.
questions.explain: The authors later give a more conventional solution of the monk problem with a distance-time graph in which the two paths must cross.
questions.rule: A position-time graph makes the meeting visible.
questions.teaches: The monk problem also has a more conventional solution, a distance-time graph in which the two paths, one rising and one falling, must intersect.

questions.q: You read a brilliant solution to a puzzle. Which reaction will help you most next time?
options: Forget it, since you cannot re-use an idea from another problem
Memorise the exact steps and reproduce them on the same problem
Ask what the key idea was, and where you could use it
Admire it and conclude such ideas are for other people
optionExplain: Ideas travel between problems; that is how experience grows.
The same problem again does not train you to use the idea elsewhere.
Right: pulling out the idea and testing it elsewhere makes it yours.
Admiration without use leaves you where you started.
questions.explain: Treating a good idea as a tool you can use is the mindset the card next describes.
questions.rule: Make good ideas your own.

questions.q: Learn to shamelessly ____ new ideas and make them your own.
questions.explain: The authors say the ideas are not patented, so it is fine to master them and use them often.
questions.rule: Appropriate ideas freely.

questions.q: Eli solves a puzzle by a neat trick. According to the authors, what should he do with the solution afterwards?
options: Analyse it for its novel idea, and think where else it could apply
File it away as a closed case and move on to the next puzzle
Rewrite the solution in more elegant language, but change nothing else
Avoid using the trick, to keep his own thinking original
optionExplain: Right: every problem should be analysed for its novel-idea content.
A closed file discards the idea.
Polish helps readers but does not build your stock of ideas.
The authors encourage using such ideas, not avoiding them.
questions.explain: Each new problem should be analysed for its novel-idea content and the idea stretched to the limit.
questions.rule: Extract the idea, then re-use it.

questions.q: Sort each reaction to someone else's clever solution.

items.t: Nice idea, it is similar to ones I have had; let me put it to work
I could never have thought of that
What is the key idea here, and when else could it apply?
This is not mine, so I will not use it
I will try to stretch it by using it in a new kind of problem

questions.explain: The helpful reactions treat the idea as a tool to master and extend; the others close the door.
questions.rule: Use and stretch ideas; do not defer to them.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, some people do seem to be inherently more creative, yet almost everyone can learn to become more creative.
questions.explain: They say both: natural differences exist, but creativity can be grown, partly by cultivating a confident attitude.
questions.rule: Creativity can be learned.
questions.teaches: Some people do seem naturally more creative, but the authors believe almost everyone can learn to become more creative.

questions.q: A cook learns a sauce trick from a chef, then uses its technique in a soup and a dessert. What do the authors predict from practising this habit?
options: The cook will run out of ideas, since each technique can be used only once
The cook will increasingly come up with new ideas of her own
Nothing; borrowed techniques stay borrowed, however often you use them
The cook should now stop reading cookbooks to stay original
optionExplain: Ideas can be reused many times.
Right: the more you appropriate and manipulate ideas, the more you produce your own.
They say the opposite: familiarity breeds new ideas of your own.
The authors want you to keep looking out for new ideas.
questions.explain: Appropriating and manipulating ideas trains the mind to produce new ones.
questions.rule: Practice with borrowed ideas yields new ones.
questions.teaches: The more you get used to appropriating and manipulating ideas, the more you will be able to come up with new ideas of your own.

questions.q: On a dark night you want to see a faint cluster of stars. Which way of looking works best?
options: Glance slightly to one side of it, so its image falls at the edge of your vision
Stare directly at the spot where the cluster should be
Cover one eye and stare harder
Look at a bright lamp first, to wake the eye
optionExplain: Right: the edge of the retina is the most sensitive part, so faint objects show up there.
Direct gaze uses the centre, which is sharp in daylight but less sensitive in the dark.
Straining does not change which receptors respond best to faint light.
A bright lamp makes dark vision worse.
questions.explain: The eye's most sensitive receptors are at the edges. The card next applies this to problems.
questions.rule: In the dark, look to the side.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' analogy, gazing directly at one point is the best way to start a problem, because you begin in the dark.
questions.explain: In the dark, gazing straight at an object fails; the analogy says to relax and take ideas from the periphery.
questions.rule: Look wide, not hard.

questions.q: A grid of numbers shows no pattern along its rows. Which next step follows the authors' advice?
options: Conclude there is no pattern, since rows are how tables are read
Copy the table into a spreadsheet and sort each row
Scan the whole grid, including columns and diagonals, for familiar numbers
Compute row totals more precisely, in case a pattern is hidden
optionExplain: Who said patterns have to be in rows? This quits too early.
Sorting rows still treats the rows as the unit.
Right: a wide scan can show patterns that row-by-row reading misses.
This keeps your gaze on the one reading that has failed.
questions.explain: The table's patterns ran along diagonals, which only a wide look reveals.
questions.rule: Scan the whole before fixing on rows.

questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it keeps you loose or locks you into one view.

items.t: Trying an unusual reading of the problem for a minute
Using the one method I know until it works
Scanning the whole picture before fixing on a detail
Staring harder at the spot that has failed
Consciously bending a rule to see what happens

questions.explain: Staying with one method and staring harder are the gaze fixed on one point; the rest are the wide view the authors recommend.
questions.rule: Do not get locked into one method.

questions.q: In the authors' second experiment, a card with a letter is moved into the edge of your vision while you stare ahead. What do you notice first?
options: Nothing at all until the card reaches the centre
The movement of the card, long before you can read the letter
You can read the letter before you notice any movement
The colour of the card but not its motion
optionExplain: You do notice movement at the edge.
Right: peripheral vision is more sensitive to movement but less sharp for detail.
The edge of vision is poor at reading detail.
The experiment contrasts motion and detail, not colour.
questions.explain: The experiments show peripheral vision as both less acute and more sensitive than central vision.
questions.rule: Peripheral vision is less acute but more sensitive.
questions.teaches: Peripheral vision is less acute yet more sensitive than central vision: you notice a moving card at the edge long before you can read its letter.

questions.q: A programmer fixes an error message that points at line 40, but the fault persists. Which step best reflects peripheral vision?
options: Look at what runs before and around line 40, and at other parts of the system
Recheck line 40 for the fourth time, character by character
Rewrite line 40 in a more elegant style
Ignore the error message, since it cannot be trusted
optionExplain: Right: widening the view may reveal the actual cause.
This keeps gazing at the same spot.
Style does not address a fault that lies elsewhere.
The message is information; peripheral vision adds to it, not replaces it.
questions.explain: The advice carries beyond maths: be willing to look away from the obvious spot, and break or bend rules in the search.
questions.rule: Widen your look when the obvious spot fails.
questions.teaches: Try to consciously break or bend the rules.

questions.q: You must link nine points in a 3 by 3 grid with four connected straight lines. What is the main obstacle?
options: The lines must be perfectly straight, and drawing them is hard
You may be assuming the lines have to stay inside the square of points
Four lines are too few for nine points, whatever you do
The points are too close together to be joined
optionExplain: Straightness is part of the task, not what blocks you.
Right: the problem never says the lines may not leave the square.
The task is possible, so the count is not the obstacle.
Spacing is not the issue.
questions.explain: A boundary can exist only in your head. The card next generalises that.
questions.rule: Check which limits are really stated.

questions.q: Ask yourself: am I imposing ____ that I do not need to?
questions.explain: The authors suggest spending a minute asking whether you impose unneeded rules or can bend them.
questions.rule: Question your own restrictions.

questions.q: A 1.2 m rod must go in a bag whose box may have no side longer than 1 m. Which box can hold the rod laid along its longest diagonal?
options: A cube of side 0.6 m, with a diagonal of about 1.04 m
A flat box 1 m by 0.1 m by 0.1 m, with a diagonal of about 1.005 m
A cube of side 0.8 m, with a diagonal of about 1.39 m
A cube of side 0.5 m, with a diagonal of about 0.87 m
optionExplain: Its longest diagonal is about 1.04 m, still shorter than 1.2 m.
A long thin box does not reach 1.2 m.
Right: the diagonal of a cube of side s is s times the square root of 3, about 1.39 m here.
The longest diagonal of this cube is about 0.87 m, less than 1.2 m.
questions.explain: The longest diagonal of a box with sides a, b, c has length sqrt(a squared + b squared + c squared). Only the 0.8 m cube exceeds 1.2 m.
questions.rule: Go beyond the flat view: use the diagonal of a box.

questions.q: Sort each assumption in the nine-point puzzle by where it comes from.

items.t: Only four straight lines may be used
The lines must stay inside the square of points
The path must be one unbroken chain of lines
Each line must turn only at one of the nine points
Every one of the nine points must be touched

questions.explain: The count, straightness, continuity and coverage are stated; staying inside the square and turning only at the points are assumptions.
questions.rule: Separate the stated from the assumed.

questions.q: What do the authors say about solvers who obey every rule they see?
options: They solve fewer problems than mischievous ones, so break or bend a few rules
They solve more problems, because they make fewer mistakes
They are safest, but should avoid puzzle-style problems
They should stop bending rules only when working with others
optionExplain: Right: they advise bending rules, saying it harms no one and you will start solving new problems.
The authors say the reverse.
They give no such split.
No such exception is mentioned.
questions.explain: The authors recommend breaking or at least bending a few rules; it harms nobody, is fun, and leads to new solutions.
questions.rule: Obedience alone solves fewer problems.
questions.teaches: The authors say obedient solvers solve fewer problems than mischievous ones, and advise breaking or at least bending a few rules since it harms no one and leads to new solutions.

questions.q: A sofa will not turn into a narrow hall on a flat floor. What does the sword-in-a-box example suggest?
options: Check whether you are limiting yourself to the floor plane, and tilt it in three dimensions
Saw the sofa in half, since the hall rule cannot be bent
Push harder along the floor, as repetition may succeed
Assume the sofa will not fit and stop
optionExplain: Right: the sword was impossible in two dimensions and easy once it left that flat world.
This breaks the object, not a self-imposed limit.
This repeats a failed flat approach.
Giving up skips the question of self-made limits.
questions.explain: The sword puzzle was unsolvable in two dimensions, and the box diagonal solved it once the solver left the flat world.
questions.rule: Escape the dimension you were assuming.
questions.teaches: The sword problem is unsolvable if you limit yourself to two-dimensional space; liberated from that flat world, a long diagonal solves it.

questions.q: What comes next in O, T, T, F, F, S, S, E, ...?
options: T, since pairs of letters repeat
E, as the last letter repeated once
N
O, since the pattern repeats from the start
optionExplain: The letters do not run in a repeating pair pattern.
The sequence does not repeat the last term.
Right: the letters are the first letters of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, so nine comes next.
The pattern would have to repeat after eight terms, which nothing suggests.
questions.explain: If numbers are not the key, letters may be. The card next gives the principle.
questions.rule: Question the form.

questions.q: In the sequence 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221, each term ____ the previous term.
questions.explain: Each term is a description of its predecessor: 21 is one 2 and one 1, which is written 1211.
questions.rule: Each term describes the one before.

questions.q: In the sequence 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221, what is the next term?
optionExplain: Right: 111221 reads three 1s, two 2s, one 1, written 312211.
This misreads the groups of digits in 111221.
This only extends the pattern of digits and does not describe 111221.
It does not describe the digit groups of 111221.
questions.explain: Read 111221 aloud: three 1s, then two 2s, then one 1, giving 3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1.
questions.rule: Describe the previous term, group by group.

questions.q: In the same sequence, the term after 312211 is ____.
questions.explain: Group 312211 as 3, 1, 22, 11 and describe each group: one 3, one 1, two 2s, two 1s, which reads 13112221.
questions.rule: Group the digits, then describe each group.

questions.q: In the authors' table puzzle, rows gave no pattern. Which hidden sequences lay along diagonals? Select all that apply.
options: The multiples of three, in order
The prime numbers
The Fibonacci numbers
The perfect squares
optionExplain: Right: the first multiples of three, in order, were hidden in the table.
Right: another diagonal held the primes.
Right: what remained was the Fibonacci numbers.
Squares were not among the hidden sequences.
questions.explain: Scanning the table as a whole showed multiples of three, then primes, with the Fibonacci numbers left over, all along diagonals.
questions.rule: Patterns need not follow rows.
questions.teaches: In the table puzzle the multiples of three, the primes and the Fibonacci numbers lay along diagonals, so the pattern was not in the rows.

questions.q: What is the next letter in J, F, M, A, M, J, J, A, ...?
options: S
A, since the list repeats from its start
M, since the list repeats every five terms
J, since the list returns to January
optionExplain: Right: these are the first letters of the months, so September comes next.
The list does not restart after eight terms.
Nothing in the list repeats in fives.
The list has not yet finished the year.
questions.explain: Reciting the terms aloud helps: the authors say reading a sequence out loud can be enough of a restatement to inspire the solution.
questions.rule: Say the terms aloud to hear their form.
questions.teaches: For many people, reciting a sequence aloud, as one-two-one-one rather than one thousand two hundred eleven, is enough of a restatement to inspire the solution.

questions.q: In a motel puzzle, guests spent $27 and the porter kept $2, so $29 seems to be accounted for, not $30. What is the best view?
options: The $27 already contains the porter's $2, so adding them again is double counting
A dollar really has gone missing, and the puzzle shows the porter lied
The desk clerk must have kept an extra dollar
The guests paid $29, not $27
optionExplain: Right: the guests' $27 is the desk's $25 plus the porter's $2.
No money vanished; the puzzle's sum is built to mislead.
The desk received $25 and nothing else.
They paid $30 and received $3 back, so they spent $27.
questions.explain: The $27 is the total spent; the porter's $2 is part of it. The card next names the quantity that stays fixed.
questions.rule: Check what is already counted.

questions.q: In the motel puzzle, the quantity that really stays fixed is the amount the guests spent, which is $____.
questions.explain: The guests spent $27, which equals the $25 for the room plus the $2 the porter kept.
questions.rule: The guests' spending balances against desk plus porter.

questions.q: Three friends pay $40 each for a $100 bill. The waiter returns $3 to each and keeps the rest. Which statement balances correctly?
options: The $111 spent plus the $9 returned plus the $11 kept equals $131
The $100 bill plus the $9 returned equals $109
The $111 spent equals the $100 bill plus the waiter's $11
The $111 spent plus the waiter's $11 equals $120
optionExplain: Every dollar is counted twice in this sum.
It leaves out the waiter's $11 in the accounts.
Right: the total spent is the bill plus the waiter's share.
That adds $122, not $120, so it double counts the waiter's $11.
