questions.explain: The authors reject the determinant (hard for arbitrary n) and checking Ch for each basis vector (needs a basis).
questions.rule: Check whether a route is workable.
questions.teaches: The hunt for a penultimate step for invertibility failed because the determinant formula is very complicated for arbitrary n, and checking each basis vector requires finding a basis.

questions.q: A planner cannot prove that a schedule works for every team. What does the authors' example suggest she try?
options: Look for a single case where it fails, which may be easier to find
Stop, because a failed proof means the schedule fails
Assume it works
Hide the question from her team
optionExplain: Right: a single counterexample settles the opposite claim; there is no guarantee it exists, but it is worth investigating.
A failed proof is not a verdict.
That is not proof.
That is not a strategy.
questions.explain: The authors say they have no way of knowing whether the other path will work, but wishful thinking and make it easier demand that they investigate it.
questions.rule: Try the opposite target.
questions.teaches: The authors had no way of knowing whether searching for non-invertibility would work, but the strategic ideas of wishful thinking and make it easier demanded that they investigate that path.

questions.q: Which is the correct factorisation of 1 - x - x squared + x cubed?
options: (1 - x)(1 - x squared)
(1 - x)(1 + x squared)
(1 + x)(1 - x squared)
(1 - x) squared
optionExplain: Right: expanding gives 1 - x squared - x + x cubed.
Expanding gives 1 - x + x squared - x cubed, which is different.
Expanding gives 1 + x - x squared - x cubed.
Expanding gives 1 - 2x + x squared.
questions.explain: The pattern factors into two simple factors. The card next shows how this helps.
questions.rule: Look for a factoring pattern.

questions.q: Let q be p minus its second derivative. Then p minus its first derivative, minus its second, plus its third, equals q minus ____.
questions.explain: p - p'' is q and p' - p''' is the derivative of q, so the whole expression is q - q'.
questions.rule: The expression equals q - q'.

questions.q: Differentiate both sides of (f(x)) squared = (integral from 0 to x of [(f(t)) squared + (f'(t)) squared] dt) + 1990. What equation results?
options: 2 f(x) f'(x) = (f(x)) squared + (f'(x)) squared
f(x) squared = f(x) squared + f'(x) squared
2 f(x) f'(x) = 2 (f(x) squared + f'(x) squared)
2 f(x) f'(x) = integral of (f squared + f'(t) squared) + 1990
optionExplain: Right: the chain rule on the left, the fundamental theorem on the right, and the constant vanishes.
This forgets the chain rule's factor on the left.
The factor 2 does not appear on the right.
The integral disappears after differentiating.
questions.explain: The derivative of the integral is the integrand at x, and the derivative of 1990 is 0.
questions.rule: Differentiate to remove the integral.

questions.q: True or false: Differentiating both sides discards the constant 1990, so a solution of the differentiated equation must still be checked against the original equation.
questions.explain: Our reading: differentiating loses information such as the starting value, so the final answer must satisfy the original too.
questions.rule: Check solutions back in the original.

questions.q: After the substitution, the authors ask a simpler question about q. Which is it?
options: Is q a constant?
If q is a polynomial with q(x) - q'(x) at least 0 for all x, is q(x) at least 0 as well?
Is q equal to zero everywhere?
Is q' bigger than q for large x?
optionExplain: Nothing suggests it.
Right: it may or may not be true, but wishful thinking demands that it be investigated.
That is too strong.
That comes later, in the proof.
questions.explain: The authors note that the answer may not solve the original problem, but is worth investigating.
questions.rule: Pose the simpler question explicitly.
questions.teaches: After setting q = p - p'', the authors ask whether q at least 0 follows from q - q' at least 0 for all real x; it may not solve the original problem, but wishful thinking demands that it be investigated.

questions.q: A spreadsheet formula repeats the sub-expression (price - discount) four times. What simplification mirrors the authors' step?
options: Add four more copies of the sub-expression
Round all numbers
Name the repeated part once, such as net = price - discount, and rewrite the formula using it
Delete the formula and start again
optionExplain: That makes it longer.
That changes the problem.
Right: like q = p - p'', this makes the structure visible.
That abandons the structure.
questions.explain: Naming a repeated block collapses a long expression. The authors also call factoring an important algebraic tactic.
questions.rule: Name repeated sub-expressions.
questions.teaches: Factoring is an important algebraic tactic, and motivated by a factorisation pattern one can rewrite an expression in terms of a single simpler quantity.

questions.q: n squared + n + 41 gives the primes 43, 47, 53, 61, 71 for n = 1 to 5. What is justified?
options: Nothing beyond these five cases, which suggest a conjecture
That every value is prime
That the pattern fails soon
That only n up to 5 is allowed
optionExplain: Right: five cases do not prove a rule.
Five cases are not enough.
No evidence of failure yet.
The formula is defined for all n.
questions.explain: Patterns from small cases are conjectures only. The card next shows two famous failures.
questions.rule: A pattern is not a proof.

questions.q: n squared + n + 41, at n = 40, equals ____.
questions.explain: 40 squared + 40 + 41 = 1600 + 81 = 1681, which is 41 squared, so it is not prime.
questions.rule: The prime pattern breaks at n = 40.

questions.q: Joining n points on a circle by all chords gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 regions for n = 1 to 5. How many regions are there for n = 6?
optionExplain: Not the correct count.
Right: the count for six points is 31, so the doubling pattern is false.
The doubling guess is exactly what fails.
Not the correct count.
questions.explain: Our check: for points in general position the count is 1 + C(n,2) + C(n,4), which gives 31 for n = 6.
questions.rule: Verify the next case before trusting a pattern.

questions.q: Sort each reaction to a pattern that fits several cases.

items.t: Treat it as a conjecture and test more cases
Declare it a theorem after five cases
Try to find a reason why it should hold
Ignore the next case because it spoils the pattern
Look for a counterexample in a bigger case

questions.explain: Conjecture, test and explain are sound; declaring a theorem from a few cases or ignoring a counterexample are not.
questions.rule: Test, explain, and look for counterexamples.

questions.q: In these examples, what lesson do the authors draw about experimentation?
options: That the formulas given are exceptions with no relevance
That conjecture must always be correct if it is simple
That a relatively uninformed investigation can lead us astray
That experiment is worthless
optionExplain: They say there are many examples like these.
These simple patterns fail.
Right: they warn that experiment-and-conjecture is only part of an investigation.
They say it is easy to be seduced by it, not that it is worthless.
questions.explain: The authors say it is easy to be seduced by the ease of experimentation and conjecture, but sometimes a relatively uninformed investigation leads us astray.
questions.rule: Experiment is only part of investigation.
questions.teaches: It is easy to be seduced by the ease of experimentation and conjecture, but this is only part of mathematical investigation; a relatively uninformed investigation can lead us astray.

questions.q: A shop owner sees sales rise for five months and forecasts continued growth forever. Which comment fits the authors' warning?
options: The forecast is only a conjecture and needs a reason
Five months of growth settle the matter
Sales cannot be forecast at all
The shop owner should stop collecting data
optionExplain: Right: a pattern needs an explanation before it is trusted.
Five cases are not a proof.
Forecasting is not forbidden.
Data are useful as evidence.
questions.explain: The warning applies to any pattern: you need to know why it holds.
questions.rule: A trend is not a reason.
questions.teaches: The authors call the doubling conjecture for the circle regions practically inescapable after five cases, and add that there are many other examples like these.

questions.q: Which description of a good mathematical argument matches the authors' view?
options: It must be as short as possible, whoever reads it
It must use symbols rather than words
It must avoid glaring flaws and vagueness, with clarity judged by the intended audience
It must spell out every step in full, whoever reads it
optionExplain: Short is not the criterion.
The authors favour complete sentences.
Right: rigor and clarity depend on the audience.
Full detail for an expert reader is not always needed.
questions.explain: Who reads the argument matters. The card next states the authors' view.
questions.rule: Judge clarity by audience.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the ultimate clarity of an argument depends more on its intended audience than on anything else.
questions.explain: They say the ultimate clarity of your argument depends more on its intended audience than anything else.
questions.rule: Clarity depends on the audience.

questions.q: You explain a short proof to a friend who has taken no mathematics courses. Which approach fits the authors' view?
options: State the hypothesis and conclusion, and give each step in simple words
Say 'obvious' and move on, as for an expert
Skip the conclusion, since the proof will make it clear
Use as many symbols as possible so it looks rigorous
optionExplain: Right: a newcomer needs more explicit steps.
A newcomer needs more than that.
The conclusion must be stated.
Symbols without explanation reduce clarity.
questions.explain: More detail is needed when the audience knows less, but no gaps are allowed.
questions.rule: Match the detail to the reader.

questions.q: Sort each feature of an argument by whether it should be avoided for any audience.

items.t: A glaring logical gap in a step
A deliberately vague statement
Leaving a standard textbook fact unproved
Writing a routine calculation in full
Skipping a key step that the reader could not supply

questions.explain: Gaps and deliberate vagueness are never acceptable; how much routine detail to include depends on the reader.
questions.rule: No gaps for anyone; detail varies.

questions.q: Why do the authors say it is hard to decide whether an argument is logically correct?
options: Because arguments are rarely written down
Because the more complicated the argument, the harder it is to check
Because mathematicians disagree about the rules of logic
Because correctness depends on the reader's mood
optionExplain: Written arguments are the topic.
Right: complexity makes errors harder to spot.
They do not suggest this.
No such claim.
questions.explain: The authors say it is easier said than done to avoid glaring flaws, and the more complicated an argument, the harder to decide if it is correct.
questions.rule: Complexity hides flaws.
questions.teaches: The more complicated an argument is, the harder it is to decide whether it is logically correct, so avoiding glaring gaps is easier said than done.

questions.q: An engineer explains a fix to a customer and to a fellow engineer. Which parallel with the authors' view is right?
options: The explanation should differ in detail, though both must be free of gaps
Both explanations should be identical, for fairness
Only the engineer needs an explanation
Neither needs an explanation, once the fix works
optionExplain: Right: the same sound reasoning, presented for different readers.
The audiences differ in what they know.
The customer also deserves one.
Communication matters.
questions.explain: The authors say fluency in argument also helps steer and modify your investigations, so it matters beyond presentation.
questions.rule: Adapt the detail, keep the soundness.
questions.teaches: Fluency in mathematical argument will help you to steer and modify your investigations, so the authors want you to be comfortable with argument styles.

questions.q: Which of these claims is best proved by assuming it is false and reaching an absurdity?
options: There is no largest even number
The sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared
If n is even then n squared is even
4 is divisible by 2
optionExplain: Right: assuming there is one leads to a larger even number, an absurdity.
That statement is indexed by integers and suits induction.
A direct argument is enough.
A single calculation shows this.
questions.explain: Statements that something cannot happen often suit contradiction. The card next names the three styles.
questions.rule: Cannot happen suggests contradiction.

questions.q: Match each style of argument with the kind of claim it suits.
pairs: A statement for every integer from a start
questions.explain: Deduction proves if-then claims, contradiction proves impossibility, and induction proves statements indexed by integers.
questions.rule: Shape of the claim suggests the style.

questions.q: Which style best suits proving that n factorial is greater than 2 to the power n for every integer n at least 4?
options: Contradiction using irrational numbers
Mathematical induction
Direct deduction from a single case
No argument is needed, since it is obvious
optionExplain: Nothing here is irrational.
Right: the claim is indexed by integers from 4 upward.
A single case does not cover all n.
The authors call for argument, not intuition.
questions.explain: Claims indexed by integers fit induction.
questions.rule: Integer-indexed claims suit induction.

questions.q: Sort each claim by the style that suits it best.

items.t: There are no positive integer solutions of this equation
The sum of the angles of every n-gon is 180(n - 2)
The square root of 2 is not rational
The inequality holds for every integer n at least 4
There is no smallest positive real number

questions.explain: Impossibility claims suit contradiction; claims for every integer from a starting point suit induction.
questions.rule: Impossibility versus integer-indexed.

questions.q: How do the authors describe the structure of most arguments seen globally?
options: As an induction on the length of the argument
As a sequence of unrelated experiments
As deductive in shape, though local pieces may take many forms
As a chain of contradictions
optionExplain: Not their description.
Experiments belong to the investigation.
Right: overall, if P then Q, with other styles inside.
They do not say this.
questions.explain: The authors say viewed globally, most arguments have a simple deductive structure, but locally the pieces can take many forms.
questions.rule: Global deduction, local variety.
questions.teaches: Viewed globally, most arguments have a simple deductive structure, but locally the individual pieces of an argument can take many forms.

questions.q: A lawyer wants to show a contract could not have been signed on a Sunday, because an office was closed. Which style does this resemble?
options: Contradiction: assume it was signed and show that this conflicts with the office being closed
Induction on the number of signatures
An experiment with small cases
None, since styles apply to numbers only
optionExplain: Right: an impossibility argument.
There is no integer indexing here.
That is investigation, not argument.
Styles apply to reasoning in general.
questions.explain: Impossibility is the signature of contradiction. The authors add that contradiction is usually helpful for proving directly that something cannot happen.
questions.rule: Use contradiction for impossibility.
questions.teaches: A contradiction argument is usually helpful for proving that something cannot happen.

questions.q: A friend's proof is a string of equations with no words. What is the most helpful addition?
options: A longer title
Complete sentences linking the steps, and a clear statement of the hypothesis and conclusion
More equations, to be more rigorous
Removal of every equation
optionExplain: A title does not help the reader follow the logic.
Right: this is what the authors recommend.
More symbols do not add clarity.
Equations are fine when displayed and labelled.
questions.explain: The reader needs to see the logic, not only the symbols. The card next lists the conventions.
questions.rule: Sentences link the steps.

questions.q: The abbreviation QED stands for the Latin quod erat ____, meaning which was to be demonstrated.
questions.explain: QED, from the Latin, marks the end of an argument: which was to be demonstrated.
questions.rule: QED marks the end.

questions.q: Which of these is a complete sentence suitable for an argument?
options: Since n is odd, n = 2k + 1 for some integer k.
n odd, so 2k + 1
n = 2k + 1 k integer
odd => 2k + 1
optionExplain: Right: it has a subject, a verb and a reason.
A fragment without a verb.
No connecting verb or reason.
Symbols only; the logic is not stated.
questions.explain: Arguments should be complete sentences with nouns and verbs.
questions.rule: Write sentences, not fragments.

questions.q: Match each symbol with what the authors say it means.
pairs: The symbol for is an element of
The symbol for is a subset of
Every member lies in a larger set
The symbol for is equivalent to
questions.explain: The four verbs listed are element of, subset of, implies and is equivalent to.
questions.rule: Learn the four verbs.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the end-of-argument marks the authors list?
options: AWD, for and we are done
The Halmos symbol
EOF, for end of file
QED
optionExplain: It is listed.
The authors use this.
Right: not listed.
It is listed.
questions.explain: The authors list the Halmos symbol, QED, AWD (and we're done) and W5 (which was what we wanted).
questions.rule: Several marks exist for the same purpose.
questions.teaches: Besides the Halmos symbol and QED, the authors mention AWD for and we're done and W5 for which was what we wanted.

questions.q: A technical report states an important formula in the middle of a paragraph and refers to it three pages later as the formula above. How would the authors improve it?
options: Display the formula on its own line and label it, so later references can cite the label
Hide the formula in a footnote
Delete the later reference
Write the formula in words only
optionExplain: Right: complicated equations should be displayed and labelled if referred to later.
That makes it harder to find.
Referring back is useful.
The formula should be shown.
questions.explain: Display and labelling are practical aids for any technical writing.
questions.rule: Display and label what you will cite.
questions.teaches: Complicated equations should always be displayed on a single line, and labelled if they are referred to later.

questions.q: In writing a proof, what should the new name A := B + C mean?
options: A is defined to be the sum of the already defined B and C
B plus C is proved to equal A
A, B and C are all new names
A and B + C are only approximately equal
optionExplain: Right: the left side is the new name.
The sign defines; it does not prove.
B and C must already be defined.
A is defined exactly as B + C.
questions.explain: The colon marks the new name. The card next gives the other abbreviations.
questions.rule: New name on the left.

questions.q: ISTS stands for it is ____ to show.
questions.explain: ISTS means it is sufficient to show: proving the smaller statement would be enough.
questions.rule: ISTS names a sufficient target.

questions.q: You want to prove that n squared minus 1 is divisible by 8 for odd n. Which line is an honest use of ISTS?
options: ISTS that n is prime
ISTS that n squared minus 1 is divisible by 5
ISTS that (n - 1)(n + 1) is divisible by 8, since n squared minus 1 equals that product
ISTS that n squared minus 1 is positive
optionExplain: n need not be prime.
That is a different claim.
Right: the product is the same quantity.
Positivity does not give divisibility.
questions.explain: ISTS must name a statement whose truth guarantees the goal. Here it is the same quantity factored.
questions.rule: ISTS must really suffice.

questions.q: True or false: A solver writes A := 5 and later B := A + 3 and concludes B = 8. The use of the colon-equals sign is correct.
questions.explain: A is defined as 5, a known quantity, and then B as A + 3 using the already defined A, so B = 8.
questions.rule: Define new names from known ones.

questions.q: Which side of A := B + C is the new definition, according to the authors?
options: The left side, usually a simple variable
The right side, the expression B + C
Both sides equally
Neither side; it is a statement of fact
optionExplain: Right: the thing on the left is the new definition, and the colon is the point of an arrow.
The right side uses already defined variables.
Only one side is new.
It defines.
questions.explain: The authors suggest thinking of the colon as the point of an arrow: we always distinguish left from right.
questions.rule: The colon points at the new name.
questions.teaches: Think of the colon in := as the point of an arrow: the left side is the new definition, usually a simple variable, and the right side uses already defined variables.

questions.q: A spreadsheet user writes Total := Sales - Returns in a note before building the formula. What does this do for readers?
options: It proves Sales are greater than Returns
It declares what Total means, using quantities already known
It hides which cell is the total
It allows Sales to be changed later without effect
optionExplain: It defines, not proves.
Right: a definition-style note.
It does the opposite.
Defined names follow their definitions.
questions.explain: The convention comes from computer science, as the authors note.
questions.rule: State definitions before use.
questions.teaches: The colon-equals notation is borrowed from computer science and is slowly becoming more common in mathematics.

questions.q: To prove that a statement holds for all positive integers n, a student writes: without loss of generality, let n = 5, and checks it. What is the verdict?
options: Valid, since induction is not needed
Invalid: the case n = 5 does not represent all n
Valid, because 5 is typical
Valid if n = 5 is checked twice
optionExplain: Induction would be a proper method; this is not.
Right: it checks one case only.
A single typical case proves nothing about the others.
Repetition does not make it general.
questions.explain: WLOG requires that one case stands for all the others. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A single case is not general.

questions.q: True or false: WLOG stands for without loss of generality.
questions.explain: That is what the abbreviation means: you single out one case when the others are logically similar.
questions.rule: WLOG is a shorthand for a promise.

questions.q: Sort each use of WLOG by whether it is valid.

items.t: A statement is symmetric in a and b: WLOG a is at most b
The claim is about all n: WLOG n equals 5
The colours are interchangeable: WLOG the vertex is blue
Odd and even n behave differently: WLOG n is even
Replacing the polynomial by its negative gives the same problem: WLOG its leading coefficient is positive

questions.explain: Valid uses rely on a real symmetry or relabelling; invalid ones assume a special case that does not represent the rest.
questions.rule: Use WLOG only for true symmetries.

questions.q: A solver proves a statement for even n and writes: WLOG the odd case is the same. Why is this wrong?
options: Even and odd cases may behave differently, so the odd case needs its own argument
WLOG may only be used for even numbers
WLOG must be written in capitals
The even case was never proved
optionExplain: Right: the cases are not logically the same.
WLOG is not limited to even numbers.
Notation is not the issue.
The even case is fine.
questions.explain: The solver breaks the promise that the other case is the same.
questions.rule: Check the cases really match.

questions.q: In the authors' contradiction proof of the roots problem, a polynomial Q has no real roots. Why is WLOG valid when they assume Q is positive?
options: Because a polynomial with no real roots is always zero
Because the authors need a shortcut
Because a polynomial without real roots is always positive or always negative, and the negative case is handled by changing signs
Because every polynomial is positive
optionExplain: Not so.
Convenience is not a reason.
Right: the argument is the same for the opposite sign.
Many polynomials take negative values.
questions.explain: A continuous polynomial with no real roots cannot change sign, so only positive and negative remain, and they are mirror images.
questions.rule: WLOG works when cases mirror each other.
questions.teaches: The authors use WLOG in the roots proof to assume Q is positive for all real x, and in the network colouring proof to assume the ball A is white.

questions.q: In a game with two identical players, a rule applies to Player 1 and Player 2 alike. A planner analyses only Player 1 and says: WLOG. When is this fine?
options: When the players really are interchangeable in every way the argument uses
Never, because analysing both players is a rule
Only if Player 1 is stronger
Only if Player 2 agrees
optionExplain: Right: that is the symmetry that makes WLOG honest.
No such rule.
Strength is not the criterion.
Agreement does not make an argument valid.
questions.explain: WLOG relies on genuine symmetry.
questions.rule: Symmetry earns the shortcut.
questions.teaches: With WLOG, just make sure that you really can argue the specific and truly prove the general; the shortcut is only honest when the cases are logically similar.

questions.q: To prove that if n is even then n squared is divisible by 4, what is the natural first step?
options: Assume n is even and write n = 2k
Assume n squared is divisible by 4
Assume n is odd
Check n = 2 only
optionExplain: Right: start from the hypothesis and express it usefully.
That is the conclusion, not the hypothesis.
That is the opposite of the hypothesis.
One case is not a proof.
questions.explain: A direct proof starts with the hypothesis. The card next describes the form.
questions.rule: Start from P.

questions.q: A deductive argument takes the form: if P, then ____.
questions.explain: A direct proof shows that P implies Q.
questions.rule: If P then Q.

questions.q: Given n = 2k, which line completes the direct proof that n squared is divisible by 4?
options: Then n squared = 4k squared, which is a multiple of 4
Then n squared = 2k squared, which is even
Then n squared = 2 + k squared
Then n squared = k squared, which is a multiple of 4
optionExplain: Right: squaring 2k gives 4k squared.
That drops a factor of 2 and weakens the result.
That is not the square.
That loses the factor.
questions.explain: (2k) squared = 4k squared, and 4 times an integer is divisible by 4.
questions.rule: Square the expression carefully.

questions.q: Put the steps of the direct proof in a logical order.
items: State the hypothesis: n is even
Write n = 2k for some integer k
Compute n squared = (2k) squared = 4k squared
Note that 4k squared is a multiple of 4
Conclude that n squared is divisible by 4
questions.explain: A direct proof starts from the hypothesis and moves step by step to the conclusion.
questions.rule: Hypothesis to conclusion in order.

questions.q: According to the authors, what does deduction have to do with Sherlock Holmes?
options: Deduction was named after Holmes
Nothing: it means direct proof in this chapter
It is the method Holmes uses, in full detail
It is a rival of induction
optionExplain: No such claim.
Right: they say deduction has nothing to do with Holmes.
The authors say they do not mean that.
It is not a rival; it is a style.
questions.explain: The authors say Deduction here has nothing to do with Sherlock Holmes: it is also known as direct proof.
questions.rule: Deduction means direct proof here.
questions.teaches: The authors say deduction, in this chapter, has nothing to do with Sherlock Holmes: it is also known as direct proof, and is the simplest form of argument in terms of logic.

questions.q: A teacher says: if a student attends every class, then they will learn the material. A student attended every class. What does a direct argument conclude?
options: The student will fail the class
Nothing, because the conclusion is not stated
The student learned the material, if the stated rule holds
The student did not learn the material
optionExplain: That does not follow.
The conclusion is given.
Right: P holds, so Q follows, provided the implication is true.
That reverses the implication.
questions.explain: A direct argument only draws Q when P is given and the implication holds. It does not assert P is true in general.
questions.rule: If P and P implies Q, then Q.
questions.teaches: Once the penultimate step is isolated, the problem reduces to the simple deductive statement that the truth of that step implies the conclusion.

questions.q: All squares are rectangles. Which statement must also be true?
options: Some squares are not rectangles
Any shape that is not a rectangle is not a square
All rectangles are squares
No rectangle is a square
optionExplain: That contradicts the statement.
Right: it is the contrapositive.
That reverses the direction.
That contradicts the statement too.
questions.explain: One reversal keeps the truth and another does not. The card next names them.
questions.rule: Reverse and negate to stay true.

questions.q: Match each form with its name, for the statement: if P then Q.
pairs: If not Q then not P
If not P then not Q
questions.explain: The converse swaps the parts, the contrapositive swaps and negates them, and the inverse negates without swapping.
questions.rule: Swap, swap and negate, or negate.

questions.q: The statement is: if a number ends in 0 then it is divisible by 5. Which statement is equivalent to it?
options: If a number does not end in 0 then it is not divisible by 5
If a number ends in 5 then it ends in 0
If a number is not divisible by 5 then it does not end in 0
If a number is divisible by 5 then it ends in 0
optionExplain: That is the inverse, and 15 is a counterexample.
That is false.
Right: this is the contrapositive.
That is the converse, and 15 is a counterexample.
questions.explain: Only the contrapositive is equivalent. For example 15 shows the converse and the inverse fail.
questions.rule: Only the contrapositive is equivalent.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it must be true, given that if n is even then n squared is even.

items.t: If n squared is not even, then n is not even
If n squared is even, then n is even
If n is not even, then n squared is not even
If n is even, then n squared is even

questions.explain: Only the original and its contrapositive follow from the statement alone; the converse and the inverse need their own proofs.
questions.rule: Converse and inverse need separate proofs.

questions.q: True or false: To prove an implication, you may prove its contrapositive instead.
questions.explain: The contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original, so proving it proves the original. The authors note this equivalence.
questions.rule: A statement and its contrapositive are equivalent.
questions.teaches: The contrapositive of P implies Q is the statement not Q implies not P, and the two are logically equivalent, so proving one proves the other.

questions.q: A rule says: if a customer is a member, then they get a discount. A customer got no discount. What follows?
options: The customer is not a member
The rule is false
The customer might still be a member who got a discount elsewhere
Nothing can be said
optionExplain: Right: this is the contrapositive of the rule.
A customer without a discount does not break the rule.
If the rule holds, a member would have received the discount.
The contrapositive gives a conclusion.
questions.explain: No discount means the condition failed, which is the contrapositive at work. Whether a discount would imply membership is the converse, a separate question; when both directions hold, the two statements are equivalent.
questions.rule: Not Q implies not P.
questions.teaches: Some statements and their converses are both true; in that case the two are logically equivalent, which has to be proved in both directions.

questions.q: You have proved that if n is even then n squared is even. What have you shown about n is even versus n squared is even?
options: One direction of an equivalence; the converse is still needed
That they are equivalent
That n squared is even only when n is even
Nothing about the relationship
optionExplain: Right: the other direction remains.
Only one direction is proved.
That is the converse.
One direction is shown.
questions.explain: Equivalence is a two-way street. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Both directions.

questions.q: To prove that P and Q are equivalent, first prove one direction, and then its ____.
questions.explain: The authors say to prove one direction and then its converse.
questions.rule: Prove a direction, then its converse.

questions.q: To prove that n is divisible by 6 if and only if it is divisible by both 2 and 3, which pair of statements is enough?
options: If n is divisible by 2 and 3 then n is divisible by 6, and that is all
If n is divisible by 6 then it is divisible by 2 and 3, and the converse
If n is divisible by 6 then it is divisible by 2, plus if n is divisible by 6 then it is divisible by 3
n = 6 is divisible by 2 and 3
optionExplain: The other direction is missing.
Right: both directions are proved.
Both are in the same direction.
One example proves neither.
questions.explain: Divisible by 6 implies divisible by 2 and 3, and divisible by both implies divisible by 6.
questions.rule: State and prove both directions.

questions.q: True or false: A solver proves that if x = 3 then x squared = 9, and claims that x = 3 and x squared = 9 are equivalent.
questions.explain: The converse fails: x squared = 9 also holds for x = -3.
questions.rule: Check the converse.

questions.q: What does the authors' notation P if and only if Q, written with a double arrow, mean?
options: P and Q are logically equivalent: each implies the other
P implies Q only
P and Q cannot both be true
Q is the converse of P
optionExplain: Right: both directions hold.
That is a single arrow.
That is not the meaning.
The converse is a related statement, not the double arrow.
questions.explain: The authors write P implies Q and Q implies P as P is equivalent to Q.
questions.rule: Equivalent means implies both ways.
questions.teaches: When both P implies Q and Q implies P are true, the authors say P and Q are logically equivalent, and write P if and only if Q.

questions.q: A recipe claims: the sauce is thick if and only if it has been reduced. A cook reduces it and it is still thin. What follows?
options: The claim is true in one direction only
Nothing can be concluded
The claim is false, since reduction did not give thickness
The claim was proved by this check
optionExplain: A claim of equivalence needs both directions.
A counterexample is informative.
Right: one direction fails, so the equivalence fails.
A counterexample contradicts a claim.
questions.explain: An equivalence breaks if either direction fails.
questions.rule: One failing direction breaks equivalence.
questions.teaches: The authors note that p implies q is not logically equivalent to its converse, so equivalence cannot be claimed from one direction.

questions.q: For b = 1 to 5, b squared + b + 1 gives 3, 7, 13, 21 and 31, none a perfect square. What does this show?
options: Proof that it is sometimes a square
Evidence for a claim that still needs an argument
Proof that it is never a square
A reason to give up
optionExplain: None of these is a square.
Right: the pattern suggests no solutions, but a proof is needed.
Five cases are not a proof.
The evidence suggests a plan.
questions.explain: Experiments suggest the claim but do not prove it. The card next gives a method.
questions.rule: Evidence is not proof.

questions.q: In a proof by contradiction, you assume the statement is false and derive an ____ conclusion.
questions.explain: The false assumption leads to something impossible, so it cannot be true.
questions.rule: Assume false; reach absurdity.

questions.q: To prove that the equation b squared + b + 1 = a squared has no positive integer solutions by contradiction, what is the first step?
options: Assume that there is a positive integer solution
Assume that b is prime
Assume that the equation has no solution
Assume a equals b
optionExplain: Right: assume the opposite of the claim.
Primes are not involved.
That is the claim itself.
That is a special case, not the negation of the claim.
questions.explain: The negation of there are no solutions is there is at least one.
questions.rule: Negate the claim to start.

questions.q: Put the steps of the contradiction argument in order.
items: Suppose positive integers a and b satisfy b squared + b + 1 = a squared
Then b < a and (a - b)(a + b) = b + 1
Since a is at least b + 1, a - b is at least 1 and a + b is at least b + 2
So (a - b)(a + b) is at least b + 2, which is more than b + 1
This is impossible, so no such a and b exist
questions.explain: The argument assumes the opposite, factors, bounds the factors, and meets an impossibility.
questions.rule: Assume, derive, hit the impossible.

questions.q: Which useful tactic do the authors point out in this contradiction proof?
options: Induction on b
Working modulo b
Factoring, as in an earlier example of the chapter
Drawing a picture
optionExplain: No induction is used.
No congruences are used.
Right: a squared - b squared factors as (a - b)(a + b).
No picture is used.
questions.explain: The authors say that, as in an earlier example, they employ the useful tactic of factoring.
questions.rule: Factoring makes inequalities visible.
questions.teaches: The authors again use the useful tactic of factoring, as in an earlier example, to turn a squared - b squared into (a - b)(a + b).

questions.q: Prove that x squared + x = y squared has no positive integer solution. What assumption starts a proof by contradiction?
options: Suppose positive integers x and y satisfy the equation
Suppose x equals y
Suppose the equation has no solutions
Suppose x is prime
optionExplain: Right: assume the opposite of the claim, then show an absurdity, such as y being between x and x + 1.
That is a special case.
That is the claim.
Primes are unrelated here.
questions.explain: If x squared + x = y squared, then y lies strictly between x and x + 1, which is impossible for integers.
questions.rule: Assume what you want to refute.
questions.teaches: The authors say contradiction is usually helpful for proving directly that something cannot happen, as in the solutions of this equation.

questions.q: Suppose a over b is in lowest terms. Which pair of numbers is impossible for a and b?
optionExplain: They share no factor above 1.
Right: both are even, so the fraction can be reduced and is not in lowest terms.
These share no common factor.
They share no factor above 1.
questions.explain: Lowest terms means the pair has no common factor above 1. The card next uses this.
questions.rule: Lowest terms forbids two even numbers.

questions.q: In the proof, a squared = 2 b squared shows that a squared is ____.
questions.explain: A square equal to 2 times an integer is even.
questions.rule: 2 times an integer is even.

questions.q: From a = 2t and 2 b squared = a squared, what equation follows for b?
options: b squared = 2 t squared
b squared = t squared
b = 2t
b squared = 4 t squared
optionExplain: Right: 2 b squared = 4 t squared, so b squared = 2 t squared.
The factor 2 is lost.
That does not follow.
That omits dividing by 2.
questions.explain: Substituting gives 2 b squared = (2t) squared = 4 t squared, so b squared = 2 t squared, and b is even by the same reasoning.
questions.rule: Substitute and divide by 2.

questions.q: Sort each statement from the proof by whether it is supported.

items.t: a squared even implies a even, because an odd number has an odd square
b is even, since b squared = 2 t squared
a and b are both even, contradicting that the fraction is in lowest terms
a is even because a equals 2
The root of 2 is irrational because its decimals look random

questions.explain: The supported steps use parity and the minimal denominator; claiming a equals 2 or appealing to random-looking decimals is not an argument.
questions.rule: Use parity and minimality.

questions.q: What do the authors call choosing the fraction with the smallest denominator?
options: An application of the extreme principle
An application of induction
A trick that works only for the square root of 2
A proof that the root is rational
optionExplain: Right: of all possible quotients, pick the one with the smallest denominator.
No induction is used.
They present a general principle.
It leads to a contradiction, not to rationality.
questions.explain: The authors say, now we shall use the extreme principle: of all the possible ways of doing this, pick the quotient for which the denominator is smallest.
questions.rule: Pick the extreme member.
questions.teaches: Choosing, among all quotients equal to the root of 2, the one with the smallest denominator is an application of the extreme principle.

questions.q: Adapting the proof to the square root of 3, which step must change?
options: The final contradiction step
Nothing; the steps are identical
The step 'a squared is even implies a is even', which becomes about divisibility by 3
The assumption that b is as small as possible
optionExplain: It stays: a common factor contradicts lowest terms.
The parity step changes.
Right: a squared divisible by 3 forces a divisible by 3, and then b as well.
Minimality is still used.
questions.explain: The same shape works with divisibility by 3 in place of parity. The authors set this as an exercise and ask where the argument breaks for the square root of 49.
questions.rule: Replace parity by the right divisibility.
questions.teaches: The authors ask readers to prove the square root of 3 and of 6 irrational with the same argument, and to find where it breaks down for the square root of 49.

questions.q: You want to show a polynomial has at least one real root. What is the negation of that statement?
options: It has no real root
It has exactly one real root
It has two real roots
It has no integer roots
optionExplain: Right: the opposite of at least one is none.
That is only one way to have a root.
That still has roots.
Integer roots are a different matter.
questions.explain: The negation of at least one is none. The card next uses it.
questions.rule: Negate carefully.

questions.q: A good question to ask is: what happens if we ____ the conclusion?
questions.explain: The authors suggest asking what happens if you negate the conclusion and whether that gives something easy to work with.
questions.rule: Negate the conclusion.

questions.q: The negation of the polynomial having a real root is that it has none. What does that tell you about its sign, for a polynomial that is continuous?
options: It must be zero somewhere
It must stay on one side of zero, always positive or always negative
It must change sign at least once
Nothing can be said
optionExplain: That would be a root.
Right: with no root and continuity, it cannot cross zero.
A sign change forces a root.
A usable inequality follows.
questions.explain: A continuous function that never equals zero keeps one sign. That gives a usable inequality.
questions.rule: No root means one sign.

questions.q: True or false: If the negation of the conclusion looks harder to work with than the conclusion itself, contradiction is still the best choice.
questions.explain: Contradiction helps when the negation is easier to handle. If it is not, another style may be better.
questions.rule: Choose contradiction when the negation is easier.

questions.q: How do the authors describe the situation where contradiction helps, using their mountaineering analogy?
options: A summit that is easy to reach
A steep rock face with handholds on both sides
A conclusion like a vertical glass wall, while its negation has lots of footholds
A smooth slope with a clear path
optionExplain: Not their picture.
Not their picture.
Right: the negation is easier to climb.
That would favour a direct approach.
questions.explain: The authors say sometimes the conclusion seems like a vertical glass wall, but its negation has lots of footholds.
questions.rule: Climb the face that has footholds.
questions.teaches: Sometimes the conclusion seems like a vertical glass wall while its negation has lots of footholds, so the negation is easier to investigate.

questions.q: A building has 10 meeting rooms and only 9 meetings are scheduled at 2 pm. To show at least one room is empty, which contradiction assumption works?
options: Suppose every room is in use at 2 pm
Suppose no meeting is scheduled
Suppose exactly one room is empty
Suppose there are 11 rooms
optionExplain: Right: then there would be at least 10 meetings, but only 9 exist.
That is a different claim.
That is consistent with the facts.
That changes the problem.
questions.explain: The negation of at least one empty is none empty, which gives a count that conflicts with 9 meetings.
questions.rule: Negate to get a count.
questions.teaches: Contradiction can prove positive statements, such as at least one real root exists, as well as impossibility statements.

questions.q: Which pair of numbers leaves the same remainder when divided by 3?
options: 7 and 9
5 and 7
6 and 10
10 and 22
optionExplain: 7 leaves remainder 1 and 9 leaves 0.
5 leaves 2 and 7 leaves 1.
6 leaves 0 and 10 leaves 1.
Right: both leave remainder 1, and their difference 12 is a multiple of 3.
questions.explain: Same remainder is the idea behind congruence. The card next gives the notation.
questions.rule: Same remainder, same class.

questions.q: If a - b is a multiple of m, we write that a is congruent to b modulo ____.
questions.explain: Congruence modulo m means the difference is a multiple of m.
questions.rule: Difference a multiple of m.

questions.q: Which of these statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: 38 is congruent to 3 modulo 7
38 is congruent to 4 modulo 7
17 is congruent to 102 modulo 5
32 is congruent to 0 modulo 8
10 is congruent to 2 modulo 3
optionExplain: Wrong: 38 - 4 = 34, not a multiple of 7.
Right: 32 = 4 x 8.
Wrong: 10 - 2 = 8, not a multiple of 3.
questions.explain: Check each by subtracting and looking for a multiple of the modulus.
questions.rule: Difference a multiple of the modulus.

questions.q: 10 is congruent to 3 and 12 is congruent to 5, both modulo 7. What is the product 120 congruent to, modulo 7?
options: 1, since 3 x 5 = 15 is congruent to 1
15, since the product of the remainders is 15
0, since 120 is even
3, the first remainder
optionExplain: 15 is congruent to 1 modulo 7, and 120 leaves remainder 1, not 15.
Evenness is irrelevant.
Only the product of both matters.
questions.explain: Products respect congruence: 10 x 12 is congruent to 3 x 5 = 15, which is congruent to 1 modulo 7.
questions.rule: Multiply congruent residues.

questions.q: Who invented the congruence notation, according to the authors?
options: Euler
Gauss
Euclid
Fermat
optionExplain: Not named by the authors.
Right: they say the notation, invented by Gauss, is very convenient.
He lived long before this notation.
Not named by the authors.
questions.explain: The authors credit Gauss and call the notation very convenient, urging a minimal amount of basic survival number theory early.
questions.rule: Learn basic number theory early.
questions.teaches: The congruence notation was invented by Gauss, and the authors urge you to learn at least a minimal amount of basic survival number theory as soon as possible.

questions.q: A clock shows 9 now. What does it show after 100 hours, using congruence modulo 12?
options: 9 o'clock
4 o'clock
1 o'clock
5 o'clock
optionExplain: 100 is not a multiple of 12.
That ignores the starting time.
Right: 100 is congruent to 4 modulo 12, and 9 + 4 = 13 is congruent to 1.
100 leaves remainder 4 mod 12, so 9 + 4 = 13, which is 1 o'clock.
questions.explain: Clock arithmetic is congruence modulo 12.
questions.rule: Clocks are arithmetic modulo 12.
questions.teaches: If you divide a by b and get a remainder r, then a is congruent to r modulo b, and a is congruent to b modulo m exactly when a = b + mk for some integer k.

questions.q: Modulo 7, which number y satisfies 3y congruent to 1?
optionExplain: 3 x 4 = 12, which leaves remainder 5.
3 x 2 = 6, which leaves remainder 6.
3 x 6 = 18, which leaves remainder 4.
questions.explain: A multiplicative inverse y of x satisfies xy congruent to 1. The card next shows why one exists modulo a prime.
questions.rule: Inverse means product 1.

questions.q: If xy is congruent to 1 modulo p, then y is called the multiplicative ____ of x modulo p.
questions.explain: A multiplicative inverse undoes multiplication by x modulo p.
questions.rule: xy congruent to 1 modulo p.

questions.q: Modulo 13, which number is the inverse of 5?
optionExplain: 5 x 3 = 15, which leaves remainder 2.
5 x 10 = 50 leaves remainder 11.
5 x 2 = 10 leaves remainder 10.
questions.explain: Test multiples of 5 for remainder 1 modulo 13: 5 x 8 = 40 = 39 + 1.
questions.rule: Search the multiples for remainder 1.

questions.q: Put the steps of the proof that the multiples are all different in order.
items: Assume ux and vx are congruent modulo p for different u and v in 1 to p - 1
Then (u - v)x is a multiple of p
The factor x is not a multiple of p, and u - v is nonzero with absolute value less than p
A prime cannot divide the product of two numbers neither of which it divides
This contradiction shows the multiples are all different modulo p
questions.explain: The proof assumes two multiples agree, rewrites the difference, and uses primality to reach a contradiction.
questions.rule: Assume equal, factor, use primality.

questions.q: After showing the p - 1 multiples are different and nonzero modulo p, how do the authors conclude that one equals 1?
options: There are only p - 1 nonzero remainders, and the multiples fill them all, so exactly one is 1
They compute all of the multiples for a general p
They assume the multiple equal to 1 exists
They use induction on p
optionExplain: Right: p - 1 different nonzero values cover all p - 1 nonzero remainders.
No computation is needed.
That would be circular.
No induction is used.
questions.explain: The p - 1 multiples are distinct and nonzero, so each nonzero remainder appears exactly once, including 1.
questions.rule: Distinct and nonzero means all residues appear.
questions.teaches: Because the p - 1 multiples are different and nonzero modulo p, exactly one of them has to equal 1, which gives a unique inverse.

questions.q: Modulo 12, the numbers relatively prime to 12 are 1, 5, 7 and 11. What is the inverse of 5 modulo 12?
optionExplain: 5 x 11 = 55 leaves remainder 7.
Right: 5 x 5 = 25 = 2 x 12 + 1, so 5 is its own inverse.
5 x 7 = 35 leaves remainder 11.
questions.explain: The authors generalise to any modulus m for numbers sharing no factor with m: each has a unique inverse. For instance, 7 x 7 = 49 is also congruent to 1 modulo 12.
questions.rule: Coprime numbers have inverses.
questions.teaches: The result generalises: for any positive integer m, each number sharing no factor with m has a unique inverse modulo m, as in the example m = 12 with the numbers 1, 5, 7 and 11.

questions.q: Infinitely many dominoes stand in a row. What two facts guarantee that all of them fall?
options: The first one is pushed over, and each falling domino hits the next one
The first domino is heavy, and all the others are light
The last domino is pushed
Every domino is pushed at once
optionExplain: Right: a start plus a rule for passing the fall along.
Weight is not the point.
There is no last domino.
That is not an inductive chain.
questions.explain: The fall of each depends on the one before. The card next turns this into a proof method.
questions.rule: Start the chain and pass it on.

questions.q: In induction, the assumption that P(n) is true for some arbitrary n is called the inductive ____.
questions.explain: The inductive hypothesis is the assumption of P(n), from which P(n + 1) must be derived.
questions.rule: Assume P(n), prove P(n+1).

questions.q: To prove that 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2, the step assumes it for n. What do you add to both sides to reach n + 1?
options: n squared
n
optionExplain: The sum grows by one term, not by a square.
Right: then the right side is n(n + 1)/2 + (n + 1) = (n + 1)(n + 2)/2.
The next term is n + 1, not n.
That would double the sum.
questions.explain: Adding the next term n + 1 gives n(n + 1)/2 + (n + 1) = (n + 1)(n + 2)/2, which is the formula for n + 1.
questions.rule: Add the next term to both sides.

questions.q: True or false: A student claims that n squared + n + 1 is even for all n, proving only that if it is even for n then it is even for n + 1. The proof is complete.
questions.explain: The step is true, but there is no base case: for n = 1 the value is 3, which is odd. A step without a base case proves nothing.
questions.rule: A base case is required.

questions.q: Which examples do the authors give of assertions suited to induction?
options: The area of a circle, and the volume of a sphere
The roots of a quadratic, and the roots of a cubic
The interior angles of any n-gon add to 180(n - 2) degrees, and n! > 2^n for n at least 4
Every prime is odd, and every square is positive
optionExplain: These are not integer-indexed statements.
These are not integer-indexed statements.
Right: both are indexed by integers from a starting point.
Neither is indexed by integers in this way.
questions.explain: The authors say induction proves assertions indexed by integers, of the form P(n) for all n at least n0.
questions.rule: Induction suits integer-indexed claims.
questions.teaches: Induction is suited to assertions such as: the interior angles of any n-gon add to 180(n - 2) degrees, and n factorial exceeds 2 to the power n for all n at least 4.

questions.q: A student proves the angle sum of an (n+1)-gon by cutting off a triangle at the border and applying the n-gon result, but says nothing about whether such a triangle exists. What is the gap?
options: For a concave polygon it is not obvious that a border triangle can be cut off
The base case should be n = 2
The induction must be strong
The angle sum of a triangle is unknown
optionExplain: Right: the authors call the proof partial for this reason.
The base case is the triangle, n = 3.
Standard induction can work once the decomposition is justified.
It is a well-known fact, 180 degrees.
questions.explain: The authors call the argument partial because the decomposition is fine for convex polygons but not obvious for concave ones.
questions.rule: Justify the decomposition step.
questions.teaches: The polygon argument is only a partial solution because it is not obvious that a concave polygon can always be decomposed to extract a triangle on the border.

questions.q: Compare n factorial with 2 to the power n for n = 1 to 5: 1 and 2, 2 and 4, 6 and 8, 24 and 16, 120 and 32. From which n does factorial win?
optionExplain: Right: from 4 on, n factorial is larger in this table.
1 is less than 2.
6 is less than 8.
It wins already at n = 4.
questions.explain: The starting point of an induction is where the claim first holds. The card next proves it from there.
questions.rule: Find the starting point first.

questions.q: To get from n! to (n + 1)!, multiply both sides of the hypothesis by ____.
questions.explain: (n + 1)! = (n + 1) times n!, so multiply both sides by n + 1.
questions.rule: Multiply by n + 1.

questions.q: The step gives (n + 1)! > 2 to the power n times (n + 1). Why is this at least 2 to the power n times 2, when n is at least 4?
options: Because n + 1 equals 2
Because n + 1 is bigger than 2
Because 2 to the power n is positive
Because factorial is always bigger
optionExplain: n + 1 is at least 5.
Right: 2 to the power n times (n + 1) exceeds 2 to the power n times 2.
That does not compare n + 1 with 2.
That is the claim itself.
questions.explain: n + 1 is at least 5, so 2 to the power n times (n + 1) is greater than 2 to the power n times 2, which is 2 to the power (n + 1).
questions.rule: Compare the multipliers.

questions.q: Sort each step of a student's proof of n! > 2 to the power n by whether it is valid.

items.t: Base case: 4! = 24 is greater than 16
Multiply the hypothesis by n + 1, a positive number
Base case: 1! = 1 is greater than 2
Subtract n + 1 from both sides to reach the goal
n + 1 is greater than 2, so the product is greater than twice 2 to the power n

questions.explain: A correct base case, multiplication by a positive number, and a comparison of multipliers are valid; a false base case and an arbitrary subtraction are not.
questions.rule: Check each step.

questions.q: How do the authors choose the operation that moves from the hypothesis to the goal?
options: They compare the left side of the hypothesis with the left side of the goal and ask how to get from one to the other
They guess and check until something works
They apply the result for n = 1 repeatedly
They avoid the hypothesis
optionExplain: Right: they think strategically about how n! becomes (n + 1)!.
They reason about the sides of each statement.
That would not reach n + 1.
The hypothesis is the starting point of the step.
questions.explain: The authors look at the two left sides and observe that multiplying by n + 1 gets from one to the other.
questions.rule: Compare hypothesis and goal.
questions.teaches: The authors say to think strategically: compare the left side of the inductive hypothesis with the left side of the goal and ask how to get from one to the other.

questions.q: Prove 2 to the power n is greater than n squared for n at least 5. Which base case begins the induction?
options: n = 5, since 32 is greater than 25
n = 4, since 16 is greater than 16
n = 3, since 8 is greater than 9
n = 1, since 2 is greater than 1
optionExplain: Right: the claim is asserted only for n at least 5, and 32 > 25 checks it.
16 is not greater than 16.
8 is not greater than 9.
The claim is not asserted below 5, so the induction cannot start at 1.
questions.explain: Our reading: 32 > 25 at n = 5 starts the chain; a step multiplies the inequality by 2. The authors note multiplying both sides of an inequality by a positive number does not change its truth.
questions.rule: Start where the claim first holds.
questions.teaches: Multiplying both sides of an inequality by a positive number does not change its truth, which is the key move in the inductive step.

questions.q: Straight lines divide the plane into regions. To prove a two-colour claim about the regions by induction, what should n be?
options: The area of the plane
The number of lines
The number of regions
The number of colours
optionExplain: The plane is infinite.
Right: add one line at a time.
The number of regions is a result of the lines, not a free choice.
There are always two colours.
questions.explain: Experiments with one line, then two, suggest the index. The card next shows the step.
questions.rule: Index by what you add.

questions.q: In the two-colouring argument, the index n is the number of ____ drawn in the plane.
questions.explain: The statement P(n) says that any division of the plane by n lines can be coloured well.
questions.rule: Induct on the number of lines.

questions.q: A good colouring exists for n lines. You draw the (n + 1)st line. What do you do to get a good colouring for n + 1 lines?
options: Keep colours on one side of the new line and invert all colours on the other side
Invert all colours on both sides of the new line
Recolour only the regions touching the new line
Keep every colour as it was
optionExplain: Right: regions along the new line then have different colours.
That leaves regions along the line with the same relation as before, so some neighbours match.
That would damage other adjacencies.
Regions that the new line cuts would have two parts of one colour sharing a border.
questions.explain: Inverting on one side makes the two parts of each cut region differ, and leaves other adjacencies intact.
questions.rule: Flip colours on one side of the new line.

questions.q: True or false: A solver inverts all colours on both sides of the new line and says the new colouring is good. This is correct.
questions.explain: Inverting everywhere keeps every pair of old neighbours different but leaves the two halves of each cut region the same colour, so they would share a border with equal colours.
questions.rule: Flip on one side only.

questions.q: What do the authors say about the index in induction problems like this?
options: It is always obvious from the statement
It can never be changed after it is chosen
Sometimes what plays the role of the index is not obvious, and the crux can be a clever choice of it
It is always the first number mentioned
optionExplain: They say sometimes it is not obvious.
They say a clever choice can be the crux.
Right: that, or a neat way of travelling between P(n) and P(n + 1).
Not so.
questions.explain: The authors note that the statement of the problem may not involve integers directly.
questions.rule: The index may be hidden.
questions.teaches: Sometimes it is not obvious what plays the role of the index n; the crux move can be a clever choice of this variable and a neat method of travelling between P(n) and P(n + 1).

questions.q: Circles are drawn in the plane, dividing it into regions. To two-colour the regions by induction, what is a good step from n circles to n + 1?
options: Add the new circle and invert all the colours inside it
Remove the first circle
Colour the new circle red
Add the new circle and leave colours unchanged
optionExplain: Right: regions along the new circle then differ, as with lines and one side.
That does not add the new circle.
Regions are coloured, not curves.
Regions cut by the new circle would have two parts of one colour sharing a border.
questions.explain: Our reading: the same trick applies, with the inside of the new circle in place of one side of the new line.
questions.rule: Look for the same flip with a new curve.
questions.teaches: The authors say that the statement does not involve integers directly, but when you experiment you naturally start with one line, then two, so the natural thing to induct on is the number of lines.

questions.q: True or false: In some inductive arguments, proving P(n + 1) needs the truth of earlier cases such as P(n - 1) as well as P(n).
questions.explain: That happens whenever the next term of a sequence depends on two or more previous terms. The card next names the method.
questions.rule: Some steps need several earlier cases.

questions.q: Strong induction assumes P(n0), P(n0 + 1), ..., P(n) are all ____, and uses them to prove P(n + 1).
questions.explain: The stronger hypothesis assumes every earlier case.
questions.rule: Assume all earlier cases.

questions.q: With a_2 = 4, a_3 = 9 and the rule a(u+1) = 2 a(u) + 2 - a(u-1) at u = 3, what is a_4?
optionExplain: That is 2 a_3 only.
That is 2 a_3 + 2 without subtracting a_2.
Right: 2 x 9 + 2 - 4 = 16, which is 4 squared.
That adds 2 a_3 + 2 and forgets to subtract a_2.
questions.explain: The step uses both a_3 and a_2: a_4 = 18 + 2 - 4 = 16.
questions.rule: Use the two previous terms.

questions.q: True or false: A solver proves a_(u+1) = (u+1) squared using only the truth of a_u = u squared, and calls it standard induction. The proof is valid.
questions.explain: The rule for a(u+1) involves a(u-1) too, so the proof needs P(u-1) as well. It requires the stronger hypothesis.
questions.rule: Use every case the step needs.

questions.q: How do the authors picture strong induction with dominoes?
options: Dominoes with springs that grow stiffer, so each needs the force of all the fallen ones to its left
Dominoes arranged in two rows
Dominoes that fall in either direction
Dominoes that never fall without a push
optionExplain: Right: domino n needs the force of all falling neighbours, not just the nearest.
Not their picture.
Not their picture.
That is standard induction's picture with a base case.
questions.explain: The authors say: dominoes with springs that keep them from falling, with the springs getting stiffer as n increases.
questions.rule: Strong induction needs all earlier dominoes.
questions.teaches: The authors picture strong induction as dominoes with springs that grow stiffer as n increases, so domino n needs the force of all the falling neighbours to its left, not just the nearest.

questions.q: Show that every Fibonacci number F_n is at most 2 to the power n, where F_(n+1) = F_n + F_(n-1). Which hypothesis does the step need?
options: The claims for n and n - 1
Only the claim for n
The claim for n + 1
No hypothesis; it is direct
optionExplain: Right: F_(n+1) = F_n + F_(n-1) is at most 2^n + 2^(n-1), which is less than 2^(n+1).
F_(n+1) depends on two earlier terms.
That is the goal.
The terms depend on earlier terms.
questions.explain: The step needs two earlier cases, so it uses strong induction. The authors note that strong induction sometimes works when standard induction does not.
questions.rule: Match the hypothesis to the dependency.
questions.teaches: Sometimes strong induction will work when standard induction does not, because to prove P(n + 1) you may need to know something about earlier cases.

questions.q: The vertices of a triangulated polygon must be coloured so that vertices joined by an edge of a triangle differ. What is the fewest colours that will work for every triangulation?
options: Four
Three
Two
As many as there are vertices
optionExplain: Three suffice, as the card shows.
Right: a triangle needs three, and three always suffice.
A single triangle has three mutually adjacent vertices.
That is not necessary.
questions.explain: A triangle forces three colours. The card next shows that three are enough.
questions.rule: At least three, and three suffice.

questions.q: In a triangulation of a polygon, three ____ suffice to colour the vertices, whatever the triangulation.
questions.explain: The theorem says any triangulation can be 3-coloured with no two adjacent vertices alike.
questions.rule: Three colours suffice.

questions.q: A square is triangulated by one diagonal, giving two triangles. How many colours do its four vertices need?
options: Three
Two
Four
One
optionExplain: Right: the diagonal's two endpoints get two colours, and the other two vertices can both take the third.
The triangle on three vertices needs three colours.
Three are enough here.
Adjacent vertices must differ.
questions.explain: Colour the diagonal's ends red and white, and give the other two vertices blue.
questions.rule: Three colours work for a triangulated square.

questions.q: Put the steps of the strong-induction proof in order.
items: Choose any edge of the triangulated (n + 1)-gon and the triangle T on it
T splits the polygon into smaller triangulated polygons L and R
Colour L with three colours by the inductive hypothesis
Colour R by the hypothesis, then rename its colours so the shared vertices agree with T
Conclude that the whole (n + 1)-gon is three-coloured
questions.explain: The proof picks an edge, splits the polygon, colours each part, and renames colours to glue them.
questions.rule: Split, colour each, rename to match.

questions.q: Why do the authors need the stronger hypothesis here?
options: Because the polygon has no base case
Because three colours cannot be proved otherwise
Because it is not obvious that a boundary triangle exists, and an arbitrary edge splits the polygon into two pieces of varying sizes
Because standard induction never works for polygons
optionExplain: The base case is the triangle.
The theorem is not about proof power.
Right: the pieces can have any smaller sizes.
They say it might, with a boundary triangle.
questions.explain: The authors say it is easier to pick an arbitrary edge and assume P(k) for all k at most n than to find a boundary triangle.
questions.rule: An arbitrary split needs all smaller cases.
questions.teaches: It is not obvious that a triangulation has a boundary triangle, so the authors pick an arbitrary edge and assume the truth of P(k) for all k up to n.

questions.q: In gluing R to T, the shared vertices have y white and z red in T, while R's own colouring made y red and z blue. Which renaming of R's colours fixes it?
options: Red to white, blue to red, and white to blue
Red to blue, and blue to white
Swap white and blue only
Leave R unchanged
optionExplain: Right: y becomes white and z becomes red, as T requires.
That would give y blue.
That leaves y red.
The shared vertices would not agree.
questions.explain: The authors say if lucky the colourings coincide, otherwise just rename the colours. It may also turn out that one of L or R does not exist, which does not matter.
questions.rule: Rename colours to make vertices match.
questions.teaches: It may turn out that one of the pieces L or R does not exist, as happens for n = 4, but that does not matter for the argument.

questions.q: An inductive step fails, but you believe the statement is true. Which response is most helpful?
options: Assume the false step is true
Try proving a stronger statement, so that the hypothesis does more work
Abandon induction and never try it again
Check more small cases
optionExplain: That makes the proof invalid.
Right: a stronger hypothesis may carry the step.
Failure of one attempt is not a verdict on the method.
Small cases will not repair a failed step.
questions.explain: A stronger statement gives a stronger hypothesis. The card next shows an example.
questions.rule: Strengthen the claim.

questions.q: The authors replace the 3n by 3n + ____ to strengthen the hypothesis.
questions.explain: The stronger statement has 1 over the square root of 3n + 1 on its right side.
questions.rule: Replace 3n by 3n + 1.

questions.q: At n = 1 the strengthened statement says 1/2 is at most 1 over the square root of 4. How do the two sides compare?
options: They are equal, since the square root of 4 is 2
The left side is larger
The statement is false
The right side is undefined
optionExplain: Right: 1/2 equals 1/2, a sharp inequality.
1/2 is not larger than 1/2.
It is an equality, which satisfies at most.
The square root of 4 is 2.
questions.explain: At n = 1 the base case is an equality, about as sharp as an inequality can be.
questions.rule: A sharp base case supports the step.

questions.q: True or false: For n = 1, the step needed by the weaker statement is that (1/square root of 3) times (3/4) is at most 1/square root of 6, and this inequality is true.
questions.explain: It is false: about 0.433 is not at most about 0.408. So the weaker statement cannot be pushed from 1 to 2 by induction.
questions.rule: Test the step on small n.

questions.q: After squaring and cross-multiplying, what does the strengthened inequality reduce to, according to the authors?
options: 19n is at most 20n, which is true
20n is at most 19n
19 is at most 20 times n squared
n is at most 1
optionExplain: Right: after tedious multiplying, the step reduces to this true inequality.
The inequality runs the other way.
Not the stated reduction.
Not the stated reduction.
questions.explain: The authors note the step then reduces, after tedious multiplication, to 19n at most 20n, which certainly holds.
questions.rule: A stronger claim can leave room.
questions.teaches: With the strengthened hypothesis, squaring and cross-multiplying reduces the step to 19n at most 20n, which is true.

questions.q: To prove the sum of 1/k squared, for k from 1 to n, is less than 2, a solver proves instead that it is at most 2 - 1/n. Which idea does this follow?
options: Proving only the base case
Changing the problem to a different one
Strengthening the hypothesis so the step has enough power
Weakening the statement so the base case is easier
optionExplain: The step still needs proof.
The new claim implies the original.
Right: the stronger claim carries more into the next case.
It strengthens, since 2 - 1/n is less than 2.
questions.explain: Our reading: 2 - 1/n implies the original bound, and its step uses 1/(n+1) squared at most 1/n - 1/(n+1). The authors say to stay flexible in defining hypotheses and conclusions.
questions.rule: Prove something stronger.
questions.teaches: Behind the idea of strong induction is the notion that one should stay flexible in defining hypotheses and conclusions.

questions.q: You are halfway through a problem and out of ideas. Which statement matches the authors' advice?
options: Many strategies can be applied at different stages, so bring a few back to mind
Strategies are only for starting a problem, so you must start again
Strategies matter only for competition problems
Stuck means the problem should be dropped
optionExplain: Right: they are useful throughout an investigation.
Many strategies help at later stages too.
The authors present them as general.
They suggest more strategies first.
questions.explain: Powerful strategies should stay in the back of your mind. The card next names three of them.
questions.rule: Strategies are not only for starting.

questions.q: The three strategies of this part are: draw a picture, recast the problem, and change your point of ____.
questions.explain: The section covers drawing a picture, recasting the problem in other ways, and changing your point of view.
questions.rule: Picture, recast, change viewpoint.

questions.q: A solver has experimented with numbers and still sees no pattern. Which move uses a strategy that can help at this stage?
options: Wait for the solution to appear
Recast the numbers as points on a graph or in a picture
Repeat the same experiments more slowly
Erase everything and begin the orientation again
optionExplain: Strategies need to be applied.
Right: reformulating can show a pattern that numbers hide.
A new view is needed, not more of the same.
Orientation is for the start.
questions.explain: Recasting changes the form of the problem, which can help at any stage.
questions.rule: Reformulate when numbers stall.

questions.q: Sort each strategy by when it is mainly used.

items.t: Reading the problem carefully
Classifying it as find or prove
Drawing a picture
Changing your point of view
Recasting it in another field of mathematics

questions.explain: Reading and classifying belong to orientation; drawing, recasting and changing the viewpoint can be used throughout.
questions.rule: Orientation first; reformulation any time.

questions.q: How do the authors describe drawing a picture, recasting a problem and changing the point of view?
options: As manifestations of the fundamental peripheral vision strategy
As rules of logic
As three unrelated tricks
As things to avoid in rigorous work
optionExplain: Right: each opens the mind to other ways of seeing the problem.
They are strategies, not logic.
They connect them.
They recommend them.
questions.explain: The authors say converting to pictures is just one aspect of the peripheral vision strategy, and changing the point of view is another manifestation.
questions.rule: All reformulations stem from peripheral vision.
questions.teaches: Drawing a picture, recasting the problem in other ways, and changing your point of view are all manifestations of the fundamental peripheral vision strategy.

questions.q: A novelist stuck in the middle of a draft rewrites a scene from a minor character's side, and sketches the plot as a timeline. Which part of the authors' list is this?
options: The startup strategies
Argument by contradiction
Changing the point of view and drawing a picture, used at a later stage
Orientation
optionExplain: Those are also for starting.
No proof is involved.
Right: both are strategies usable at different stages.
Orientation is at the start.
questions.explain: The authors say many strategies can be applied at different stages of a problem, not just the beginning.
questions.rule: Reformulation works beyond mathematics.
questions.teaches: The authors say they discuss only a few powerful ideas here and will discuss more advanced strategies in later chapters.

questions.q: Train A runs from city X to city Y between 8:00 and 12:00; Train B runs on the same track from Y to X between 9:00 and 11:00. Must they pass each other?
options: Yes, at some time between 9:00 and 11:00 they must be at the same place
No, because they leave at different times
Only if they travel at the same speed
Only if the track is double
optionExplain: Right: A is still on the way when B sets off, and B reaches X before A reaches Y, so they cross.
Different departure times do not prevent a meeting.
Speed does not decide this.
The same track is stated.
questions.explain: A graph makes the answer visible. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Draw position against time.

questions.q: To draw a journey as a graph, plot position against ____.
questions.explain: Position-time graphs show where an object is at each moment.
questions.rule: Plot position against time.

questions.q: Train A goes at constant speed from X to Y between 8:00 and 12:00; B goes at constant speed from Y to X between 9:00 and 11:00. When do they meet?
optionExplain: B has reached X by then, and A is three-quarters along.
At 10:30 A is five-eighths along and B is one quarter from X; not equal positions.
Right: A is half-way (position 1/2) and B has covered half of its trip, so both are at 1/2.
A is one-eighth of the way along at 9:30, while B has just left Y.
questions.explain: Put X at 0 and Y at 1. A's position at 10:00 is 2/4 = 1/2. B has been going for 1 hour at speed 1/2 per hour, so it is at 1 - 1/2 = 1/2.
questions.rule: The crossing point of the two lines is the meeting.

questions.q: Which statements about the monk's two position-time paths are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The first day's path starts at the bottom and ends at the top
The second day's path starts at the top and ends at the bottom
The two paths cross only if the monk walks at the same speed both days
Where the paths cross, the monk is at the same spot at the same clock time on both days
optionExplain: Right: he climbs on the first day.
Right: he descends on the second day.
Wrong: the crossing does not depend on speeds.
Right: this is exactly what is wanted.
questions.explain: One path goes from the bottom corner to the top, the other from top to bottom, over the same times, so they must cross; speeds do not matter.
questions.rule: Crossing means same place and same time.

questions.q: How much freedom does the graph argument allow in the monk's speed?
options: He may race, stand still, or even walk backward, since the paths must still cross
He must walk at a constant speed
He must never stop
He must be faster going down
optionExplain: Right: the authors list those possibilities as allowed.
The argument does not need constant speed.
Stopping is allowed.
No such requirement.
questions.explain: The authors note that nothing is specified about the speed: he could race at 1000 miles per hour, sit still, or travel backward.
questions.rule: Speed does not matter, only start and end.
