questions.teaches: Nothing is specified about the monk's speed: he could race at 1000 miles per hour for a few minutes, sit still for hours, or even travel backward, and the paths must still cross.

questions.q: Maya runs a trail from the car park to the lookout on Saturday between 7 and 9, and back on Sunday between 7 and 9, at varying speeds. Which feature of a graph shows a spot passed at the same clock time both days?
options: The area under the paths
The point where the two paths cross
The highest point of either path
The steepest part of either path
optionExplain: Area does not show a shared spot.
Right: there, position and time coincide for both days.
That is the farthest point, not a shared point.
Steepness is speed.
questions.explain: On the shared axes, a rising and a falling path between the same times must cross, and the crossing is the common spot and time.
questions.rule: Look for the crossing point.
questions.teaches: The authors say it is obvious from the graph that no matter how the two paths are drawn they must intersect somewhere.

questions.q: To count pairs (s, t) in the unit square with 3s + 7t and 5s + t both integers, which point is useful to draw?
options: The point (3, 7) and the point (5, 1)
The point (3s + 7t, 5s + t), whose coordinates must be integers
The point (s, t) in the plane
The point (s + t, s - t)
optionExplain: These are coefficients, not the unknown pair.
Right: integer coordinates mean a lattice point.
The authors say this does not help much.
Nothing is gained by this.
questions.explain: The useful point is the pair of expressions that must be integers. The card next uses it.
questions.rule: Draw the point whose coordinates must be integers.

questions.q: A point whose coordinates are both integers is called a ____ point.
questions.explain: Lattice points are the points with integer coordinates.
questions.rule: Integer coordinates mean a lattice point.

questions.q: Count pairs (s, t) with 0 < s, t < 1 for which 2s + t and s + 3t are both integers. How many are there?
optionExplain: Right: the parallelogram with corners (0,0), (2,1), (1,3), (3,4) has area 5 and 4 interior lattice points.
That counts a boundary point such as (s, t) = (0, 0) or corners; the strict inequalities remove it.
The strict inequalities allow fewer.
There is one more interior lattice point.
questions.explain: Our check by counting lattice points inside the parallelogram spanned by (2,1) and (1,3): the interior points correspond one-to-one to the pairs, and there are 4 of them.
questions.rule: Count the lattice points inside the parallelogram.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say plotting (s, t) as a point in the plane is the most helpful viewpoint for the problem with 3s + 7t and 5s + t.
questions.explain: They say one may be tempted to view (s, t) as a point, but that does not help much. Viewing (3s + 7t, 5s + t) as a point does.
questions.rule: Pick the useful point, not the obvious one.

questions.q: What do the authors say the problem generalises to, using a theorem about lattice polygons?
options: Fermat's little theorem
Euler's formula
Pick's Theorem, which relates area to boundary and interior lattice points
Pythagoras' theorem
optionExplain: Not mentioned.
Not mentioned.
Right: they say the problem can be generalised nicely using Pick's Theorem.
Not mentioned.
questions.explain: The authors point to Pick's Theorem, which links the area of a lattice polygon to its numbers of boundary and interior lattice points.
questions.rule: Lattice problems connect to Pick's Theorem.
questions.teaches: The lattice-point problem can be generalised nicely using Pick's Theorem, which relates the area of a lattice polygon to the number of its boundary and interior lattice points.

questions.q: Which picture helps to count the integer pairs (x, y) with x squared + y squared at most 9?
options: A disc of radius 3 centred at the origin, counting the lattice points inside and on it
A line through the origin
A rectangle with sides 3 and 9
A single point at (3, 3)
optionExplain: Right: there are 29 such points.
A line is not the region.
That is not the region.
A point is not a region.
questions.explain: Read (x, y) as a lattice point and the inequality as a disc. The authors report that Gauss computed the analogous count for radius 300, which is 282,697.
questions.rule: Inequalities in two variables describe regions.
questions.teaches: Variables treated as coordinates turn conditions into regions of the plane, and counting solutions becomes counting lattice points inside the region.

questions.q: An 8 by 8 chessboard has two diagonally opposite corners removed. Can 31 dominoes, each covering two adjacent squares, tile what remains?
options: No
Yes, since 62 squares make 31 dominoes
Only if the dominoes are placed in rows
Yes, with a clever arrangement exists
optionExplain: Right: a colour count shows it is impossible.
Counting squares is not enough.
Placement style does not change the colour count.
No arrangement can work.
questions.explain: Count colours, not squares. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Count colours.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: Every domino on a coloured board covers exactly one square of each ____.
questions.explain: Adjacent squares on a chessboard have different colours, so a domino covers one of each.
questions.rule: A domino covers one black and one white square.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: A 6 by 6 board has two diagonally opposite corners removed. Can the rest be tiled by 17 dominoes?
options: Yes, if the remaining squares are connected
Only with one vertical domino
No, because the board then has 16 squares of one colour and 18 of the other
Yes, because 34 squares make 17 dominoes
optionExplain: Connectedness is not enough.
Orientation does not matter.
Right: the removed corners have the same colour.
That ignores colours.
questions.explain: A 6 by 6 board has 18 squares of each colour; removing two of the same colour leaves 16 and 18, so 17 dominoes cannot cover them.
questions.rule: Unequal colour counts forbid a tiling.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: True or false: When two removed squares have different colours, so the remaining colour counts are equal, the colour argument proves a domino tiling exists.
questions.explain: The argument shows only that unequal counts forbid a tiling. Equal counts are necessary but not shown to be sufficient.
questions.rule: The count proves impossibility, not possibility.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: How do the authors describe the problem before the colouring idea?
options: It seems geometric or combinatorial, with many cases and subcases
It seems impossible to state
It seems purely algebraic
It seems to need calculus
optionExplain: Right: the colouring turns it into a question about counting colours.
It is easy to state.
It seems geometric.
It needs no calculus.
questions.explain: The authors say at first it seems a geometric combinatorial problem with many cases, but it is really a question about counting colours.
questions.rule: A reformulation can remove the cases.
questions.teaches: At first the chessboard problem seems geometric or combinatorial with many cases and subcases, but it is really just a question about counting colours.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: A theatre row has 7 seats marked A and 5 seats marked B, alternating. Couples must sit in adjacent seats. Can every seat be filled by couples?
options: Yes, if the couples are seated left to right
No, because each couple takes one A seat and one B seat, and the counts differ
Yes, because 12 seats make 6 couples
Only with a gap in the middle
optionExplain: Order does not fix the counts.
Right: 7 A-seats and 5 B-seats cannot both be used up.
Each couple takes one A seat and one B seat.
Gaps do not repair the imbalance.
questions.explain: This is the colouring argument in a new setting. The authors note the idea of using colouring to reformulate a problem is quite old.
questions.rule: Pair items by type and count the types.
questions.teaches: The idea of introducing colouring to reformulate a problem is quite old, as the authors note before applying it to the gallery problem.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: True or false: In a polygonal gallery with 5 sides, one guard standing at a suitable place can see every point of every wall.
questions.explain: That is the case for 3, 4 and 5 sides, although for the non-convex 5-sided case it takes a few pictures to be convinced. The card next gives the general result.
questions.rule: Small galleries need one guard.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: The minimum number of guards g(n) for an n-sided gallery equals the floor of n divided by ____.
questions.explain: The solution shows g(n) = floor of n over 3.
questions.rule: g(n) = floor(n/3).
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: A triangulated 12-sided gallery has its vertices three-coloured with 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green. Where should guards be placed, and how many?
options: On the 3 green vertices, using 3 guards
On the 5 red vertices, using 5 guards
On one vertex of each colour, using 3 guards
On all 12 vertices
optionExplain: Right: the least-used colour gives the fewest guards.
That uses more guards than necessary.
Guards of mixed colours do not cover every triangle by design.
That is wasteful.
questions.explain: Each triangle has a green vertex, so 3 green guards cover every triangle.
questions.rule: Use the least-used colour.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: Which statements are part of the correct argument? Select all that apply.
options: Each triangle of the triangulation has exactly one vertex of each colour
A guard at a vertex sees the whole triangle that contains it
The smallest colour class can have more than n/3 vertices
Guards on one colour class cover all triangles
optionExplain: Right: the three vertices of a triangle are adjacent, so they differ.
Right: a triangle is convex.
Wrong: if all three classes had more than n/3 vertices, the total would exceed n.
Right: every triangle contains a vertex of that colour.
questions.explain: The argument uses properties of triangles and the pigeonhole count on colour classes.
questions.rule: Each triangle has all three colours.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: How did the elegant colouring solution of the gallery problem arise historically, according to the authors?
options: Fisk found it first, in 1973
It was found by computer search in 1978
Klee posed it in 1973, Chvatal solved it with a complicated proof, and Fisk found the colouring proof in 1978
Chvatal found the colouring proof immediately in 1973
optionExplain: Klee posed it in 1973.
Not stated.
Right: it took several years for the colouring idea to be applied.
His proof was rather complicated.
questions.explain: The authors say it took several years before anyone applied colouring to the problem.
questions.rule: Good reformulations can take time to be found.
questions.teaches: The Gallery Problem was proposed by Victor Klee in 1973 and solved shortly after by Vaclav Chvatal with a rather complicated proof; S. Fisk found the elegant colouring argument in 1978.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: Having shown that floor(n/3) guards suffice, what must still be shown to prove that g(n) equals floor(n/3)?
options: An example gallery with n sides that really needs floor(n/3) guards
Nothing; the upper bound alone gives equality
A proof that more guards than floor(n/3) never help
A proof by contradiction on n
optionExplain: Right: the authors build one by making floor(n/3) spikes, adapting the 9-sided example.
A bound is not an equality.
More guards cannot reduce the requirement.
No such proof is needed.
questions.explain: The authors adapt the nine-sided construction: if floor(n/3) = r, make r spikes.
questions.rule: Prove both the upper and lower bound.
questions.teaches: To show g(n) is exactly floor(n/3), the authors adapt the construction of the 9-sided gallery: if floor(n/3) = r, make r spikes, each needing its own guard.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: An equation contains the square root of 1 - x squared. Which substitution turns that root into a simple expression?
options: x = 1/t
x = e to the t
x = cos t, so that the root equals sin t
x = t squared
optionExplain: That gives another radical.
It makes the root harder.
Right: sin squared plus cos squared equals 1.
That does not simplify the root.
questions.explain: The identity cos squared + sin squared = 1 removes the radical. The card next applies it.
questions.rule: Use sin squared + cos squared = 1.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: With x = cos t, the square root of 1 - x squared equals ____ t (for t between 0 and pi).
questions.explain: Because sin squared t = 1 - cos squared t and sin t is non-negative on that range.
questions.rule: sqrt(1 - cos squared t) = sin t.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: Check x = 24/25 in 5(sqrt(1 - x) + sqrt(1 + x)). What is the value of the left side?
optionExplain: That ignores the radicals.
The radicals sum to 8/5, so the result is 8.
That is the coefficient only.
questions.explain: 1 - 24/25 = 1/25, whose root is 1/5; 1 + 24/25 = 49/25, whose root is 7/5; the sum 8/5 times 5 is 8, matching the right side 6 x 24/25 + 8 x 7/25 = 8.
questions.rule: Check candidate solutions by substitution.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: True or false: The authors say x = sin t is equally good here, since root(1 plus or minus sin t) has equally simple half-angle formulas.
questions.explain: They chose cosine because the square roots of 1 plus or minus cos t are half-angle expressions, but the roots of 1 plus or minus sin t are not.
questions.rule: Choose the substitution that matches the formulas.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: Which tool lets the authors combine a cos t + b sin t into a single sine?
options: Writing it as the square root of (a squared + b squared) times sin(alpha + t)
The law of cosines
Differentiating the sum
Squaring both sides only
optionExplain: Right: for an angle alpha whose sine and cosine are a and b over that root.
Not their tool.
Not their tool.
Not their tool.
questions.explain: The authors rewrite a cos t + b sin t as sqrt(a squared + b squared) times sin(alpha + t).
questions.rule: A cosine plus a sine is one sine.
questions.teaches: A sum a cos t + b sin t can be written as the square root of (a squared + b squared) times sin(alpha + t), for a suitable angle alpha.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: What is the largest value of 3 cos t + 4 sin t over all angles t?
optionExplain: The coefficients are larger than 1.
Right: the root of 9 + 16 is 5, and a single sine reaches 1.
That adds the coefficients, which cannot be reached at once.
That multiplies the coefficients.
questions.explain: By the tool, 3 cos t + 4 sin t = 5 sin(alpha + t), so its maximum is 5. The authors say a quantity of this shape often hides a trigonometric problem.
questions.rule: Reduce sums of sine and cosine to one sine.
questions.teaches: Recasting to trigonometry is a tactic that demands specialised knowledge, and the authors say the problem looks like 3-4-5 triangles in disguise.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: Two equal planets of radius R do not touch. The total area of surface points seen by no other planet is claimed to equal the area of one planet. What is that area?
options: 4 pi R squared
2 pi R squared
pi R squared
8 pi R squared
optionExplain: Right: the surface area of a sphere is 4 pi R squared.
That is the area of a hemisphere.
That is the area of a disc.
That is two spheres.
questions.explain: The area is 4 pi R squared per planet. The card next explains why the total is always one planet's worth.
questions.rule: The total equals one planet's surface.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: If a location is private on one planet, it is ____ on all the other planets.
questions.explain: From the private point's planet, all other planets lie on the far side, so their matching points are visible.
questions.rule: Private on one means public on the rest.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: Location x is private on planet 3. Which statement must be true?
options: x is not private on any other planet
x is private on planet 1 as well
x is private on every planet
Nothing can be said about the other planets
optionExplain: Right: it is public on every other planet.
That contradicts the key observation.
It is private on at most one.
The key fact applies to all others.
questions.explain: Private on one planet means public on all others.
questions.rule: At most one planet has x private.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: True or false: With three planets, the total private area is three times the area of one planet.
questions.explain: The authors report that the total private area is equal to that of a single planet, for any number of planets.
questions.rule: The total is one planet's area, whatever n is.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: How do the authors make it possible to talk about the same location on different planets?
options: By requiring the planets to be in a line
By giving planets different radii
By measuring distances between the centres
By assuming a universal coordinate system, such as longitude and latitude
optionExplain: No such requirement is given.
All radii are equal.
They use a coordinate system, not distances.
Right: the north pole of each planet is then the point nearest the ceiling.
questions.explain: The authors let a universal coordinate system refer to the same location on any planet.
questions.rule: Use a shared coordinate system.
questions.teaches: The authors assume a universal coordinate system, such as longitude and latitude, so that the same location can be named on every planet; for planets floating in a room, the north pole is the point nearest the ceiling.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: After showing that a location private on one planet is public on the others, what remains to prove that the total private area equals one planet's area?
options: That planets have different radii
That the planets can touch
That any given location is private on some planet
That every planet has a private point
optionExplain: They have equal radii.
They do not touch.
Right: with at most one and at least one, each location is private on exactly one planet.
That is not the stated remaining step.
questions.explain: The authors say the penultimate step is to prove that any location must be private on some planet, leaving it as an exercise. A footnote notes exceptional points form a set of measure zero.
questions.rule: At most one plus at least one gives exactly one.
questions.teaches: A footnote says there may be exceptional points that do not obey the rule, but they form a set of measure zero and do not affect the result.
questions.section: Pictures Don't Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways!

questions.q: A hat floats in a river, and a swimmer moves away from it and then returns at the same speed through the water. In the water's frame, how long does the return take compared with the trip away?
options: The same time
Twice as long
Half as long
It depends on the current
optionExplain: Right: she covers the same distance at the same speed.
Her speed through the water is unchanged.
Her speed through the water is unchanged.
In the water's frame the current is zero.
questions.explain: From the water's frame the current disappears. The card next uses this.
questions.rule: Move to the water's frame.

questions.q: From the hat's point of view, the swimmer swims away for one hour and then returns in ____ hour(s).
questions.explain: She moves at the same speed relative to the hat before and after turning, so the return takes the same time.
questions.rule: Away and back take equal times.

questions.q: A rower passes a bridge, loses a hat there, rows upstream for 30 minutes, turns and rows downstream at the same speed through the water, and catches the hat 2 km below the bridge. What is the current's speed?
options: 4 km per hour
2 km per hour
1 km per hour
0.5 km per hour
optionExplain: That would be 2 km in 30 minutes.
Right: the trip took 1 hour in the hat's frame, and the hat drifted 2 km.
That would be 2 km in 2 hours.
That would be 2 km in 4 hours.
questions.explain: In the hat's frame the rower is away for 30 minutes and back in 30 minutes, so 1 hour in total. The hat drifted 2 km in that hour.
questions.rule: Total time in the water's frame.

questions.q: True or false: In the hat problem, the answer to the current's speed depends on how fast the swimmer swims through the water.
questions.explain: The swimmer's speed through the water cancels in the hat's frame; only the hat's drift and the elapsed time matter.
questions.rule: The swimmer's speed does not enter.

questions.q: What do the authors point to as another example of the power of a natural point of view?
options: The Four Bugs problem, which combines a clever point of view with symmetry
The monk problem
The locker problem
The Gallery Problem
optionExplain: Right: it appears later in the next chapter.
That is a different example.
That is a different example.
That is a different example.
questions.explain: The authors refer ahead to the Four Bugs problem, which combines a clever point of view with the fundamental tactic of symmetry.
questions.rule: A clever viewpoint pairs well with symmetry.
questions.teaches: The Four Bugs problem in the next chapter combines a clever point of view with the fundamental tactic of symmetry, as another example of the power of a natural viewpoint.

questions.q: Pat's train usually arrives at 6:00, when Sal meets it. One day Pat arrives at 5:00, walks along Sal's route, is met, and they get home 20 minutes earlier than usual. For how long did Pat walk?
options: 40 minutes
60 minutes
50 minutes
20 minutes
optionExplain: That doubles the saving.
That ignores that Sal met Pat before 6:00.
Right: Sal saved 20 minutes of round trip, so he turned 10 minutes before 6:00, at 5:50.
That is the time saved, not the walking time.
questions.explain: The natural viewpoint is Sal's trip. He skipped the stretch between the meeting point and the station, 10 minutes each way, so he met Pat at 5:50 and Pat walked from 5:00 to 5:50. Spending a few minutes looking for the natural viewpoint pays off.
questions.rule: Follow the person whose trip tells you the answer.
questions.teaches: Spending a few minutes searching for the natural point of view can pay big dividends.

questions.q: A problem is full of parts that look unrelated and you do not know where to start. Which first reflex is most useful?
options: Work out every possible case by brute force before thinking about structure
Wait for a flash of inspiration before you write anything down at all
Ask whether some order or pattern is hiding that you could find or impose
Rewrite the whole problem in more formal notation and then stop there
optionExplain: Brute force is rarely feasible and shows no structure; it is the reflex of someone who has not looked for order.
Waiting feels patient, but nothing in the problem changes while you wait.
Right: many fundamental tactics are a search for order, which can quickly simplify a chaotic-looking problem.
Formal notation can help, but alone it changes the look of the problem, not its structure.
questions.explain: Looking for order is the thread of the chapter's first tactics. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Treat a tactic as a learned, non-obvious method that searches for order in a messy problem.

questions.q: According to the author, ____ alone rarely solves problems; we need the more focused power of tactics.
questions.explain: Strategies such as drawing a picture give direction, but a tactic supplies a concrete method that simplifies the problem.
questions.rule: Strategy gives direction; tactics do the focused work.

questions.q: A student refuses a climbing tip because pushing away from the rock feels wrong. Which lesson from the author's analogy fits learning tactics?
options: A technique that feels unnatural is probably a poor one and should be dropped early, since good methods feel easy from the start
A useful tactic can feel unnatural, so learn it on purpose and practise it until it is a habit
Only common-sense moves deserve a place in problem solving or in teaching it, because anything else cannot be learned by practice
Tactics replace strategy, so strategy no longer needs any study at all
optionExplain: Feeling is not evidence; the climber's stance really is more secure once he overcomes the instinct.
Right: the author says some tactics are peculiar at first, yet mastering them brings a dramatic improvement.
Chapter 2 was mostly common sense; the author says tactics here are less natural, so this contradicts the book.
The author says strategy alone is not enough, not that it is unnecessary.
questions.explain: The climbing tip is non-obvious but sound, and the same is true of the chapter's tactics.
questions.rule: Do not judge a tactic by how natural it feels; judge it by whether it simplifies problems.

questions.q: Sort each method: is it a Chapter 2 strategy or a Chapter 3 tactic?

items.t: Draw a picture
Keep trying with wishful thinking
Aim for a penultimate step
Pigeonhole principle
Extreme principle
Invariants

questions.explain: The first three are general strategies the author uses throughout; the last three are named tactics in this chapter.
questions.rule: Strategies point the way; tactics are specific moves.

questions.q: True or false: according to the author, the chapter's tactics are as natural to most people as the strategies of Chapter 2.
questions.explain: The author says most strategic ideas were plain common sense, while the tactics are less natural because few people would think of them.
questions.rule: Treat a tactic as a learned, non-obvious method that searches for order in a messy problem.

questions.q: A solver lists the largest and smallest item in a puzzle before calculating. Which family does the author place this tactic in?
options: Pseudosymmetry: an abstract way of finding order, like pigeonhole and invariants
Geometric symmetry, because the method needs a reflection to work properly
Strategy, because it needs no special knowledge and applies everywhere, and it gives a way to find order in any problem
Brute force, because the solver checks the extreme cases one by one, which also finds order by examining every case in turn
optionExplain: Right: the extreme principle, the pigeonhole principle and invariants are the three methods the author calls pseudosymmetry.
Reflection is a concrete kind of symmetry; the extreme principle finds order without any reflection.
It is a named tactic, and the author says such tactics are less natural than strategies.
It does not check every case; it focuses on two special elements.
questions.explain: Symmetry finds order concretely, for example by reflection. Three further tactics find order in more abstract, almost metaphorical ways.
questions.teaches: The author calls the extreme principle, the pigeonhole principle and invariants three methods of 'pseudosymmetry': they find or use order more abstractly than reflection does.
questions.rule: Treat a tactic as a learned, non-obvious method that searches for order in a messy problem.

questions.q: The endless pattern ... 2, 5, 2, 5, 2, 5 ... runs in both directions. Which action leaves it looking exactly as before?
options: Shift everything one place along the list
Delete the first term and keep the rest
Replace every 2 by a 5 and leave the 5s alone
Shift everything two places along the list
optionExplain: A one-place shift puts a 5 where a 2 stood, so the pattern changes.
Deleting a term breaks the alternation at that point.
That makes every term 5, a different pattern.
Right: after a shift of two places each 2 lands on a 2 and each 5 on a 5.
questions.explain: Any action that leaves a pattern unchanged is a symmetry. The card next gives the definition.
questions.rule: An object is symmetric when some non-trivial action, whatever its kind, leaves it unchanged; that action is a symmetry.

questions.q: An object is symmetric if a non-trivial action leaves it ____; such actions are its symmetries.
questions.explain: The definition asks only that the object look the same afterwards; the kind of action is left open.
questions.rule: Symmetric means: some non-trivial action leaves the object unchanged.

questions.q: How many non-trivial rotations about its centre, with angles strictly between 0 and 360 degrees, leave a square unchanged?
options: One: only the 180-degree turn
Two: 90 and 180 degrees
Three: 90, 180 and 270 degrees
Four: 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees
optionExplain: A 180-degree turn works, but so do the quarter turns.
The 270-degree turn also works, so two undercounts.
Right: each of these turns maps the square onto itself, and 360 is a full turn back to start.
A 360-degree turn is the trivial action of doing nothing, and the angle is excluded by the range.
questions.explain: A quarter turn, a half turn and a three-quarter turn all fix the square; 360 degrees is the trivial action.
questions.rule: Count only non-trivial actions.

questions.q: Does the action leave the object unchanged? Sort each case.

items.t: Rotate a circle by 37 degrees about its centre
Reflect a square in one of its diagonals
Shift ... 3, 1, 4, 3, 1, 4 ... three places to the right
Rotate a square by 45 degrees about its centre
Shift ... 3, 1, 4, 3, 1, 4 ... one place to the right
Reflect a 3-4-5 right triangle in its shorter leg

questions.explain: A circle, a diagonal-reflected square and a three-place shift of the repeating list all map onto themselves. The other three cases change the object.
questions.rule: Test the action: after it, is the object exactly as before?

questions.q: True or false: if 'action' meant only rotations and reflections, the list ... 3, 1, 4, 3, 1, 4 ... would stop being symmetric.
questions.explain: Our reading: the list is unchanged only by shifts, which are neither rotations nor reflections. The author keeps 'action' vague so that such cases still count.
questions.rule: An object is symmetric when some non-trivial action, whatever its kind, leaves it unchanged; that action is a symmetry.

questions.q: A strip of wallpaper repeats one flower every 20 cm along its length. Which action leaves the endless strip unchanged?
options: Slide it 20 cm along its length
Slide it 10 cm along its length
Rotate it a quarter turn in its plane
Slide it 20 cm across its width
optionExplain: Right: the pattern repeats every 20 cm, so this slide leaves it looking the same.
A 10-cm slide lines a flower up with blank space, so the pattern changes.
A quarter turn would put the strip's length across the wall and change how it looks.
A slide across the width moves the flowers sideways relative to the strip's edges.
questions.explain: Symmetries need not be turns or mirrors: sliding qualifies. The author even avoids the formal language of transformations in this definition.
questions.teaches: The author gives only an informal definition and says in a note that he avoids the language of transformations and automorphisms that a mathematically precise definition would need.
questions.rule: An object is symmetric when some non-trivial action, whatever its kind, leaves it unchanged; that action is a symmetry.

questions.q: A tile pattern looks identical after any 90-degree turn about its centre. What must you study to know the whole pattern?
options: Every one of the four parts, studied one at a time
Only the outer edge of the tile, since that frames the rest
Two opposite corners of the tile and nothing else at all
One quarter of it, and then the centre
optionExplain: That is the work symmetry lets you skip.
The edge alone does not show the interior, and the copies do not depend on the edge.
Two corners do not cover a quarter of the pattern, and the centre is missing.
Right: the other three quarters are copies of the first, and the centre of rotation is a special point.
questions.explain: Symmetry hands you information for free. The card next says how.
questions.rule: A symmetry means you need only study part of the object, plus the point or line it leaves fixed.

questions.q: Symmetry gives you ____ information: in a figure with 90-degree rotation symmetry you need only look at one quarter.
questions.explain: The other quarters are copies of the first, so they cost no extra effort to understand.
questions.rule: Symmetry is free information.

questions.q: A flower bed is a regular hexagon, unchanged by every 60-degree turn about its centre. How much must you study to know it?
options: One third of it, plus its centre
One sixth of it, plus its centre
One half of it, with the centre skipped
All six parts, to check they match
optionExplain: One third would suit a 120-degree symmetry, not a 60-degree one.
Right: six turns of 60 degrees fill the full circle, so one sixth shows the whole and the centre is special.
Half would be more than needed, and the centre is the point worth special study.
Checking all six repeats exactly what the symmetry already guarantees.
questions.explain: Divide a full turn, 360 degrees, by the angle of the symmetry to get how many copies there are.
questions.rule: The number of copies is a full turn divided by the turn angle.

questions.q: A figure is unchanged by reflection in line m. A solver studies both halves and never looks at m. What did she overlook?
options: The line m, which the reflection leaves in place and which deserves study
That a reflection symmetry gives no information about the figure at all, so studying either half is a waste of effort
That only the larger of the two halves should ever be studied, because the smaller half repeats nothing of the first
That she should have rotated the figure instead of reflecting it
optionExplain: Right: the author says the special centre of a symmetry is worthy of close investigation.
A symmetry does give free information; that is its point.
The two halves are mirror images, so neither is privileged.
Nothing in the problem calls for a rotation; the reflection was the symmetry.
questions.explain: Look at one half, but also at what stays put: the mirror line.
questions.rule: Study one part and the special point or line.

questions.q: True or false: for a figure unchanged by quarter turns, the direction of a labelled arrow is the same in every quarter.
questions.explain: Our reading: the symmetry transfers only what the turn preserves. The arrow's direction changes with each turn, so it differs between quarters.
questions.rule: Rely on symmetry only for what the action preserves.

questions.q: A pond is a perfect circle and you must plan a path. Which statement about the pond's symmetry would the author's idea support?
options: Only the shore matters, since the middle carries no information about it
Each direction needs a separate calculation, since turns change things
Symmetry says nothing here, since a circle has too few corners to use
Its centre is the special point, and every direction from it looks alike
optionExplain: The centre is exactly the point a rotation leaves in place.
A rotation of the circle leaves it unchanged, so one direction represents all.
The number of corners is irrelevant; the circle has infinitely many symmetries.
Right: the circle is unchanged by every rotation, so the fixed centre is the distinguished point.
questions.explain: A circle has infinitely many rotation symmetries about its centre, so the centre is the one distinguished point.
questions.teaches: The author notes that a circle has infinitely many symmetries, such as rotation through any angle, so the only distinguished point is its centre.
questions.rule: A symmetry means you need only study part of the object, plus the point or line it leaves fixed.

questions.q: You notice a figure is almost, but not quite, symmetric about a line. What does the author suggest?
options: Drop symmetry altogether, because it only works when it is exact
Proceed as if it were symmetric
Wait until you can prove the symmetry exactly before using it at all
Redraw the figure until its lines match up exactly on both sides
optionExplain: Near-symmetry can still point to the right idea; discarding it throws that away.
Right: the author advises exploring the near-symmetry, because it will probably teach you something.
Waiting wastes the hint, and you may never be able to prove symmetry that is not there.
Redrawing hides the way the problem actually differs from the symmetric one.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's reason.
questions.rule: Hunt for symmetry everywhere, and let an almost-symmetry guide you.

questions.q: An informal second meaning of symmetry, which the author calls vague but useful, is ____.
questions.explain: The author says to look for harmony and beauty, and that making a problem more harmonious often puts you on the right track.
questions.rule: Harmony is an informal form of symmetry.

questions.q: Two equations in x and y are the same except for a small extra term in one. What does the card's advice suggest?
options: Ignore the pair, since only an exact swap of x and y is a useful symmetry
Remove the extra term from the problem for good and solve what remains, then trust the answer for the original problem as well
Ask what you would do if the extra term were absent, then use what you learn
Solve each equation in isolation, with no comparison between the two of them
optionExplain: The author says not to worry if something is almost symmetrical.
Deleting the term changes the problem; the symmetric version is only a guide.
Right: proceeding as if the pair were symmetric can reveal a method, which you then adjust for the extra term.
Treating them separately throws away the resemblance that could show the way.
questions.explain: Use the near-symmetry as a guide and then correct for the difference.
questions.rule: A near-symmetry is a guide, not a replacement for the problem.

questions.q: True or false: the author says a result found by pretending a near-symmetric problem is symmetric is a proof.
questions.explain: Our reading: the author recommends this as a way to learn something useful, not as a proof; the findings must be checked against the actual problem.
questions.rule: Hunt for symmetry everywhere, and let an almost-symmetry guide you.

questions.q: Which items fit the author's advice on finding symmetry, and which go against it?

items.t: Look for symmetry in an algebra problem, not only in a picture
Continue with the symmetric version of a nearly symmetric problem
Treat an improvement in harmony as a good sign
Abandon symmetry the moment one detail breaks it
Restrict the search to figures with mirrors or turns
Wait for a precise definition of beauty before using it

questions.explain: The author asks you to look in unlikely places, not to worry about near-misses, and to use harmony as a guide even undefined.
questions.rule: Search widely, and accept near-misses as guides.

questions.q: A rota for 12 staff treats every day the same except Fridays, which have one extra task. How might the author's advice help you plan?
options: Plan only the Fridays carefully and ignore the rest of the week
Discard the pattern entirely because Fridays break its regularity
Wait until Fridays look like every other day before planning anything
Plan the symmetric rota first, then adjust it for Fridays
optionExplain: That ignores the structure that makes most days easy.
The near-symmetry is useful; breaking it in one place is no reason to drop it.
Fridays will never match, so waiting wastes the free structure.
Right: proceeding as if the rota were symmetric gives a plan that you then correct for the exception.
questions.explain: Rule-breaking, in the author's sense, means working as if an almost-true rule were true, then repairing.
questions.teaches: The author ties this advice to two Chapter 2 strategies: peripheral vision (look in unlikely places) and rule-breaking (do not worry if something is almost, but not quite, symmetrical).
questions.rule: Hunt for symmetry everywhere, and let an almost-symmetry guide you.

questions.q: A geometry problem shows a lopsided figure with no obvious pattern. Which opening move follows the author's habit?
options: Measure every length and angle in the figure before thinking further
Decide that a lopsided figure cannot offer any useful order
Check whether a rotation or reflection could make the figure orderly
Convert the whole problem into coordinates before looking at the shape
optionExplain: Measuring collects data but does not look for structure.
Lopsided figures are where imposing a symmetry can help most.
Right: the author says to check whether rotations or reflections will impose order on the problem.
Coordinates may be a later tool; the author's first advice is to look for order.
questions.explain: The card next gives three questions to ask.
questions.rule: Ask of a figure: is symmetry present, can it be imposed, and how can it be used?

questions.q: The three questions: is symmetry present, if not can it be ____, and how can it then be exploited?
questions.explain: Symmetry can be missing from the original picture and still be imposed, for example by reflecting part of it.
questions.rule: If symmetry is absent, try to impose it.

questions.q: A river and two houses on the same bank form a picture with no symmetry. Which move follows the three questions?
options: Impose a symmetry by reflecting one house in the river, then use it
Conclude that without symmetry present nothing more can be done, and move on to a different kind of method
Search only for a rotation, since reflections rarely help, and give up if none is found in the figure
Replace the river by a single point and solve from there
optionExplain: Right: question two asks whether symmetry can be imposed, and a reflection in the river does it.
Question two exists for the case when symmetry is not present.
The author names reflections as one of the two simplest symmetries to check.
Replacing the river throws away the line that suggests the mirror.
questions.explain: When the answer to question one is no, go on to question two.
questions.rule: No symmetry present is a reason to try imposing one.

questions.q: Which first checks fit the author's three questions, and which do not?

items.t: Look for a rotation that leaves the figure unchanged
Look for a reflection that leaves the figure unchanged
Try to add a reflection that creates a missing symmetry
Measure every angle before looking at anything else
Convert every point to coordinates before looking at the shape
Wait to see whether the answer shows itself

questions.explain: The three questions ask whether symmetry is there, whether it can be created, and how to use it. Measuring, converting and waiting do not look for order.
questions.rule: Look for, then create, then use symmetry.

questions.q: True or false: if a figure turns out to have no symmetry, the author's questions are finished and you should look elsewhere.
questions.explain: Question two asks whether symmetry can be imposed, so absence of symmetry leads to the next question, not to giving up.
questions.rule: Absent symmetry may still be imposed.

questions.q: Which action leaves a 3 by 5 rectangle, which is not a square, looking unchanged?
options: Reflection in a diagonal of the rectangle
Reflection in the line joining the midpoints of two opposite sides
A quarter turn about its centre
A turn of 45 degrees about its centre
optionExplain: A diagonal reflection works for a square, not for a rectangle with unequal sides.
Right: that reflection maps the rectangle onto itself.
A quarter turn would swap the 3 and the 5.
A 45-degree turn moves the corners to places where there are none.
questions.explain: A rectangle that is not a square has fewer symmetries than a square.
questions.teaches: The line joining the midpoints of two opposite sides is also a mirror line for a square, alongside its diagonals and its quarter-turn rotations.
questions.rule: Ask of a figure: is symmetry present, can it be imposed, and how can it be used?

questions.q: A square is inscribed in a circle that is itself inscribed in a larger square. How do the two areas compare?
options: The larger square has twice the area of the smaller
The larger square has four times the area of the smaller
The larger square has one and a half times the area
The larger square has the square root of 2 times the area
optionExplain: Right: turning the small square by 45 degrees shows it is half the large one.
Four would hold if the sides had a ratio of 2, but the ratio of sides is the square root of 2.
One and a half has nothing in the figure to support it.
The square root of 2 is the ratio of the sides, not of the areas.
questions.explain: The card next shows how to see it without algebra.
questions.rule: Turn the inner figure until its corners meet the points where the circle touches the outer figure.

questions.q: To solve the nested-squares problem the author turns the small square by ____ degrees.
questions.explain: After a 45-degree turn its corners line up with the points where the circle touches the large square.
questions.rule: A 45-degree turn lines the corners up with the tangency points.

questions.q: An equilateral triangle sits inside a circle inside a larger equilateral triangle. Turned to meet the tangency points, how do the areas compare?
options: The large triangle has twice the area of the small one
The large triangle has three times the area of the small one
The large triangle has four times the area of the small one
The two triangles have the same area as each other
optionExplain: Twice is the answer for squares, not triangles.
Three counts only the corner triangles and leaves out the middle one.
Right: the tangency points are midpoints of the large triangle's sides, so the small triangle is one of four equal pieces.
The circle sits strictly inside the large triangle, so the areas differ.
questions.explain: The same turn works because the circle touches each side at its midpoint.
questions.rule: Choose the turn that brings corners to tangency points.

questions.q: A solver turns the inner square by 20 degrees, sees nothing special and concludes symmetry cannot help. What went wrong?
options: She should not have turned the figure, since turning changes areas, so no turn can ever help
She picked a turn without letting the inscribing hypothesis choose the angle
She should have turned the circle in place of the square, since the square is already in its best position
She should have used a smaller angle, so the area stayed fixed
optionExplain: A turn does not change a shape's area, so turning is allowed.
Right: the author says the hypothesis that the shapes are inscribed tells you which turn to try.
A circle looks the same in every position, so turning it shows nothing new.
The area stays fixed for every angle, so a smaller angle changes nothing.
questions.explain: Let the hypotheses decide which symmetry to use.
questions.rule: The hypotheses choose the turn.

questions.q: True or false: if the circle does not touch the larger square, turning the inner square by 45 degrees still gives the area ratio.
questions.explain: The tangency of circle and large square is what fixes where to turn; without it the outer square can have any size.
questions.rule: Check each hypothesis you rely on.

questions.q: A square tile holds a circle touching all four sides, with a square of area 18 cm squared inscribed in it. Tile area?
options: 72 cm squared
27 cm squared
54 cm squared
36 cm squared
optionExplain: 72 doubles it twice, as if the sides doubled.
27 is one and a half times the small square.
54 is three times the small square.
Right: the tile is a square twice the area of the inscribed square.
questions.explain: Tile area is twice the inscribed square's area.
questions.teaches: The author notes the problem can be solved algebraically, by calling the small square's side x and using the Pythagorean theorem, but that the symmetry route is nicer.
questions.rule: Turn the inner figure until its corners meet the points where the circle touches the outer figure.

questions.q: Your cabin is 2 miles north of a stream; Grandma's is 12 west and 1 further north. Shortest walk via the stream?
options: 13 miles
12 miles
14.4 miles
15 miles
optionExplain: Right: reflecting Grandma's across the stream makes the shortest route a straight line of 13 miles.
12 is only the east-west distance; the route also goes north and south.
About 14.4 is the walk that heads to the stream point nearest you and then to Grandma's.
15 comes from adding the legs 5 and 12 and more; no straight route is that long.
questions.explain: The card next shows the trick that gives the answer.
questions.rule: To go via a line, reflect the destination across the line and travel straight to the reflection.

questions.q: To find the shortest route that touches a stream, reflect one of the two points ____ the stream.
questions.explain: The reflection turns the bent route into a straight one without changing its length.
questions.rule: Reflect one point across the line the path must touch.

questions.q: You are 3 miles north of a river. A friend is 5 miles north of it, 6 miles east. Shortest walk via the river?
options: 8 miles
10 miles
6.3 miles
11 miles
optionExplain: 8 is only one leg of that right triangle.
Right: reflect the friend to 5 miles south of the river; the right triangle has legs 6 and 8, so the length is 10.
About 6.3 is the direct walk, which skips the river.
11 adds 3, 5 and 6 as if the route had three straight legs.
questions.explain: The legs are the east-west gap and the sum of the two distances to the river.
questions.rule: Legs: the gap along the line, and the sum of the distances to it.

questions.q: Put the steps of the stream method in order.
items: Draw a picture of the cabins and the stream
Reflect one cabin across the stream
Join the other cabin to the reflection with a straight line
Fold the segment back at the stream to get the real route
questions.explain: The straight line to the reflection has the same length as the real route, which touches the stream where the line crosses it.
questions.rule: Draw, reflect, join, fold back.

questions.q: True or false: if Grandma's cabin stood on the stream bank, the shortest route is the straight segment to it.
questions.explain: Our reading: a point on the line is its own reflection, so the straight segment already touches the stream at its end.
questions.rule: To go via a line, reflect the destination across the line and travel straight to the reflection.

questions.q: Towers X and Y stand on opposite sides of a wall, and a cable must touch the wall. What does reflection add?
options: It halves the length of the cable by folding the route, which is why the reflection helps the cost
It is needed, since a bent route is always shorter, so the reflection must be used again
It turns the problem into one that calculus must solve
Nothing: the straight line from X to Y already crosses the wall
optionExplain: Reflection preserves lengths and never halves them.
A bent route is never shorter than the straight segment.
The reflection is meant to avoid calculus, not to force it.
Right: when the points lie on opposite sides, the shortest route is already straight and touches the wall.
questions.explain: The reflection trick is for two points on the same side of the line.
questions.teaches: The author says the stream problem could be done with calculus, but you would have to differentiate a sum of two square roots, which is very ugly.
questions.rule: To go via a line, reflect the destination across the line and travel straight to the reflection.

questions.q: A figure is unchanged by reflection in a line k. Which part of the plane does the reflection leave exactly in place?
options: The two halves, each in its own place
One end of the figure, whichever it is
The points on the line k itself
No part, since a reflection moves everything
optionExplain: The two halves are swapped with each other.
An end point is moved unless it happens to lie on the line.
Right: points on the mirror line map to themselves.
Points on the line are exactly the ones that do not move.
questions.explain: The card next explains why these fixed things matter.
questions.rule: Ask what the symmetry leaves unchanged, and study that.

questions.q: For a rotation symmetry the fixed object is the ____ of rotation.
questions.explain: The centre is the one point that a turn leaves in place.
questions.rule: A rotation fixes its centre; a reflection fixes its axis.

questions.q: A pattern is unchanged by 120-degree turns about a point O. According to the advice, which point should you focus on?
options: Any corner of the pattern, since every corner looks alike, so the choice of corner decides the answer
The point farthest from O, since it shows the most
The point O, which every one of the turns leaves in place
The midpoint of two corners, since it is easy to find, and the other points can then be ignored
optionExplain: Corners are moved by the turns, so each gives only a copy.
The farthest point is moved by the turns as well.
Right: the centre of the symmetry is the distinguished, fixed point.
A midpoint of two corners is moved by a turn in general.
questions.explain: The fixed point is the anchor of a rotational symmetry.
questions.rule: Anchor on the centre of the symmetry.

questions.q: Match each symmetry action with what it leaves fixed.
questions.explain: The mirror line and the rotation centre stay put. Our reading: a shift moves every entry, and the trivial action fixes everything, which is why it is excluded as trivial.
questions.rule: What stays fixed depends on the action.

questions.q: True or false: in the stream problem, the stream is the axis of the reflection, so it stays fixed while the two cabins swap sides.
questions.explain: Each cabin has a mirror image across the stream, while points of the stream do not move.
questions.rule: Ask what the symmetry leaves unchanged, and study that.

questions.q: A merry-go-round is turning, and a child studies how it looks after each quarter turn. Which part is the natural anchor?
options: The horse nearest the child, since it is closest
The central pole, which no quarter turn moves
The outer rim, since it is the longest part
The ticket booth, since it stands beside the ride
optionExplain: Each horse moves to the next horse's place.
Right: the pole sits at the centre of the turns and stays fixed.
The rim is carried round by the turns.
The booth is not part of the symmetric object.
questions.explain: Look at what each turn leaves in place.
questions.teaches: In the four-bugs problem, the author focuses on the centre of the square, which never moves, as the only distinguished point of the situation.
questions.rule: Ask what the symmetry leaves unchanged, and study that.

questions.q: Four bugs sit at the corners of a unit square and each chases its counterclockwise neighbour at speed 1. How long before they meet?
options: 1 minute
2 minutes
About 1.4 minutes
Half a minute
optionExplain: Right: by symmetry each bug closes in on the centre at the same rate, and the time works out to the side length divided by the speed.
Two minutes would be the time to walk two sides at speed 1, longer than the bugs need.
1.4 is the length of a diagonal, which no bug follows.
Half a minute would put the bugs at a half-side from start, which does not reach the centre.
questions.explain: The card next shows the reasoning.
questions.rule: In a symmetric chase, track the distance from the fixed centre to one chaser, using its radial speed.

questions.q: In the four-bugs problem each bug's inward speed is its speed times the cosine of ____ degrees.
questions.explain: The bug heads at 45 degrees to the line from the centre, so cos 45 gives the inward part of its velocity.
questions.rule: Inward speed = speed times cosine of the angle to the radial line.

questions.q: Four bugs start at the corners of a square of side 6 and chase their neighbours at speed 3. How long until they meet?
options: 1 minute
6 minutes
3 minutes
2 minutes
optionExplain: 1 minute is the unit-square answer at speed 1, not this case.
6 treats the side length as a time, as if the speed were 1.
3 repeats the speed instead of dividing a length by a speed.
Right: the centre is 3 times the square root of 2 away, and the inward speed is 3 times cos 45, so the time is 2.
questions.explain: For a square the time is the side length divided by the speed.
questions.rule: Time = side over speed, for a square.

questions.q: True or false: the answer depends on which bug you follow, since the four bugs take different paths.
questions.explain: By symmetry all four bugs behave identically, so it does not matter which one you pick.
questions.rule: In a symmetric chase, track the distance from the fixed centre to one chaser, using its radial speed.

questions.q: A solver says: each bug moves at speed 1 toward the centre, so the time is the distance to the centre. What is wrong?
options: The centre of the square moves as the bugs advance, so the closing speed changes with time
The bugs stop forming a square after the first moment, which is why the distances cannot be compared
The bugs travel at more than the stated speed
Each bug heads at 45 degrees to the radial line, so only part of its speed shrinks that line
optionExplain: The centre of the square does not move.
The bugs keep the shape of a square as they shrink.
The speed is given as 1.
Right: the inward component of the velocity is less than the full speed.
questions.explain: Only the component along the line you track counts.
questions.rule: Use the component of velocity along the tracked line.

questions.q: Three bugs start at the corners of a unit equilateral triangle and chase at speed 1, 30 degrees off the radial line. Time to meet?
options: 2/3 of a minute
1 minute
1/2 of a minute
3/2 of a minute
optionExplain: Right: the centre is 1 over the square root of 3 away, the inward speed is cos 30, and the ratio is 2/3.
One minute is the square's answer, which has a different angle.
One half ignores the angle.
Three halves inverts the ratio.
questions.explain: The method adapts once the angle between heading and radial line is known.
questions.teaches: A natural frame of reference, here a radial one that rotates with the square, can make an otherwise intractable problem easy; the author says to forget that the radial line is rotating.
questions.rule: In a symmetric chase, track the distance from the fixed centre to one chaser, using its radial speed.

questions.q: What is the integral of cos squared x from x = 0 to x = pi/2?
options: pi/2
pi/4
optionExplain: pi/2 would be the area under the constant 1 itself.
Right: it is half of the area pi/2 under the constant 1.
1/2 forgets the length of the interval.
1 is not the area under this curve on that interval.
questions.explain: The card next gives an argument that needs no antiderivative.
questions.rule: Draw the graphs, find a mirror line that swaps two integrands, and use their sum.

questions.q: On 0 to pi/2 the graphs of sine and cosine are mirror images in the vertical line x = ____.
questions.explain: Reflecting in x = pi/4 swaps sin x with cos x.
questions.rule: Sine and cosine swap under reflection in x = pi/4.

questions.q: Using the same idea, what is the integral of sin squared x from 0 to pi?
options: pi
pi/2
pi/4
optionExplain: pi is the integral of the constant 1, the sum of the two.
1/2 forgets the length of the interval.
Right: sin squared and cos squared have equal integrals on this interval and sum to 1, so each is half of pi.
pi/4 belongs to the interval from 0 to pi/2.
questions.explain: Split the area under the constant 1 equally between the partners.
questions.rule: Equal areas with a constant sum: halve the total.

questions.q: True or false: by the same pairing, the integral of cos cubed x from 0 to pi/2 equals pi/4.
questions.explain: Our reading: sin cubed plus cos cubed is not constant, so the pairing gives no half. The true value is 2/3, not pi/4.
questions.rule: Draw the graphs, find a mirror line that swaps two integrands, and use their sum.

questions.q: A student claims the integral of cos squared on 0 to pi/2 equals that of cos, by mirror symmetry. What is wrong?
options: The mirror does not exist on this interval, so the pairing of the two integrals fails
The integral of cos on that interval is not defined, so neither integral can be compared
The student should have used 0 to pi instead
The mirror swaps cos squared with sin squared, not with cos
optionExplain: The reflection in x = pi/4 exists on 0 to pi/2.
That integral is defined; it equals 1.
The interval given is the one the mirror works on.
Right: a reflection pairs each function with its own mirror image.
questions.explain: A symmetry pairs like with like.
questions.rule: Pair the integrand with its own mirror image.

questions.q: On [0, 6], f and g mirror each other in x = 3 and f + g = 4. Find the area under f.
optionExplain: 24 is the combined area of f and g.
Right: the two areas are equal and sum to 4 times 6 = 24, so each is 12.
8 divides 24 by 3 instead of 2.
6 is the interval's length, not an area.
questions.explain: Equal mirror areas with a constant sum split the total in half.
questions.teaches: The author calls the cosine integral a simple calculus problem that has a more conventional solution, and says the picture-plus-symmetry method also applies in many harder situations.
questions.rule: Draw the graphs, find a mirror line that swaps two integrands, and use their sum.

questions.q: True or false: a broken path from A to B to C is at least as long as the straight segment AC.
questions.explain: The straight line is the shortest path between two points, so a detour cannot be shorter.
questions.rule: Look for a way to compare a sum of several lengths with a single length, using reflections to chain them.

questions.q: A tactic for geometric inequalities is to compare the sum of several lengths with a ____ length.
questions.explain: A chain of segments is at least as long as the one segment joining its ends.
questions.rule: Compare a sum with a single length.

questions.q: Points P, Q and R satisfy PQ = 3 and QR = 4. What does the straight-line fact say about PR?
options: PR is at least 7
PR is exactly 7
PR is at most 7
PR is at most 1
optionExplain: That reverses the inequality.
PR equals 7 only if Q lies on the segment PR.
Right: PR is no longer than the path through Q, which has length 3 + 4.
1 is the smallest possible value of PR, not its largest.
questions.explain: The direct distance is at most the length of the detour.
questions.rule: Direct distance is at most the length of any detour.

questions.q: A 3 by 4 rectangle has its corners on a circle. What is the product of its two diagonals?
optionExplain: Right: with AB = CD = 3 and AD = BC = 4 the left side is 9 + 16 = 25, and the diagonals are both 5.
12 is the rectangle's area.
24 doubles the area instead of using the theorem.
49 squares the sum 3 + 4.
questions.explain: Ptolemy turns a sum of products of lengths into one product.
questions.rule: Cyclic quadrilateral: the two product-sums equal the diagonal product.
questions.teaches: Ptolemy's theorem, which the author uses to merge two lengths into one: in a cyclic quadrilateral the products of opposite sides sum to the product of the diagonals.

questions.q: True or false: lengths that do not meet end to end can be added and compared with a single segment using the straight-line fact.
questions.explain: The comparison needs one connected path from a start to an end; join the pieces end to end first.
questions.rule: Make the lengths into a connected chain.

questions.q: A cable runs from tower X to a wall, then to tower Y on the same side. Which gives a lower bound?
options: Reflect Y in the wall and use the straight segment from X to the reflection
Add the heights of the two towers together
Take the average of the two towers' distances to the wall
Treat the wall as if it were not there at all
optionExplain: Right: any route touching the wall is at least as long as the straight segment to the reflection.
Heights do not bound a horizontal route.
An average distance is not a bound on a route.
The wall is part of the requirement.
questions.explain: This is the stream trick used as an inequality.
questions.teaches: In the hexagon problem the author reflects about the symmetry line BE; the reflected points make two quadrilaterals cyclic, so that Ptolemy's theorem applies.
questions.rule: Look for a way to compare a sum of several lengths with a single length, using reflections to chain them.

questions.q: Which list reads the same when its order is reversed, and so has a symmetry?
optionExplain: This list grows steadily, so reversing it gives a different list.
Reversing gives 8, 4, 6, 4, 2, which differs from the original.
Right: reversing 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 gives the same list.
Reversing gives 1, 4, 6, 3, 1, so the middle entries do not match.
questions.explain: A list that is unchanged by reversal pairs each entry with a mirror entry. The card next says why that matters.
questions.rule: Whenever things can be paired up, test whether the pairing exposes a symmetry that simplifies the problem.

questions.q: According to the author, in nearly any situation where you can imagine ____ things up, you can think about symmetry.
questions.explain: Pairing is the common thread of symmetry in algebra and number problems.
questions.rule: Pairing is a way to see symmetry.

questions.q: The row 1, 8, 28, 56, 70 of Pascal's triangle continues in the mirror pattern. What are the next four entries?
optionExplain: These are numbers from another row of the triangle, not the mirror of this one.
Right: the row reads the same in reverse, so it continues 56, 28, 8, 1.
Repeating 70 adds an entry that the mirror pattern does not have.
These grow, but a symmetric row must shrink back to 1.
questions.explain: Use the mirror to extend the list.
questions.rule: A symmetric list repeats itself in reverse.

questions.q: True or false: the author says that thinking about symmetry always pays off whenever you can pair things up.
questions.explain: The author says symmetry almost always pays off. The word almost leaves room for cases where no pairing helps.
questions.rule: Whenever things can be paired up, test whether the pairing exposes a symmetry that simplifies the problem.

questions.q: Which situations offer a pairing to test, and which show no obvious pairing?

items.t: The entries of one row of Pascal's triangle
The numbers 1 to 100 in order, to be added
The divisors of a given integer
A list of unrelated phone numbers
A set of random digits from a lottery draw
The letters of a word with no repeated pattern

questions.explain: Ordered numbers and divisors can be matched from the two ends. Unrelated lists have no natural partner for each item. Our reading: the last three have nothing to pair.
questions.rule: Look for a natural partner for each item.

questions.q: A seating plan has 12 people at a round table, each facing the person opposite. Which observation uses the author's idea?
options: Each person is unique, so the pairs give no information, and seating plans cannot be simplified at all
Six is too many pairs to be useful in a plan, since a plan should use only a few of them
Only the host's seat needs to be planned at all
Opposite seats form six pairs, so one pair's arrangement tells you about the others
optionExplain: Pairs with a shared structure carry information about each other.
The number of pairs does not decide whether a pairing helps.
Ignoring the other seats ignores the structure.
Right: matching each seat with its opposite is a pairing that exposes a symmetry.
questions.explain: Pairing applies outside algebra, wherever objects can be matched.
questions.teaches: The author's example of a symmetric sequence is a row of Pascal's triangle such as 1, 6, 15, 20, 20, 15, 6, 1.
questions.rule: Whenever things can be paired up, test whether the pairing exposes a symmetry that simplifies the problem.

optionExplain: 5000 comes from 50 pairs of 100, off by one in each pair.
5100 comes from 51 pairs of 100, which counts too many pairs.
10100 is 100 times 101, which counts every pair twice.
Right: 50 pairs, each adding to 101, give 5050.
questions.explain: The card next shows how pairing gets the answer fast.
questions.rule: Pair the ends of a run of numbers inward; equal pair sums make the total a product.

questions.q: Pairing 1 with 100, 2 with 99 and 3 with 98 gives pairs that each add to ____.
questions.explain: Each time the first number goes up by 1 the second goes down by 1, so the sum stays at 101.
questions.rule: Pairs from the two ends have equal sums.

questions.q: Add 3 + 7 + 11 + ... + 39, in which each term is 4 more than the one before. What is the total?
optionExplain: 195 results from miscounting the terms.
225 is not a multiple of the pair sum.
Right: there are 10 terms and 5 pairs each adding to 42, so the total is 210.
420 is the sum of ten pair sums, so it counts every pair twice.
questions.explain: Count the terms, form pairs and multiply.
questions.rule: Total = number of pairs times the pair sum.

questions.q: A student pairs 1 to 99 as (1, 99), (2, 98), ... and says there are 50 pairs of 100. What is wrong?
options: There are 99 terms, so 49 pairs and the middle 50 is left unpaired
The pairs should add to 101 instead of 100, so the total must be recomputed with that sum
Pairing cannot be used for odd numbers of terms, so another method has to replace it here
The last pair should be written as (50, 50) twice
optionExplain: Right: 49 pairs of 100 plus the middle 50 give 4950.
Pairs from 1 to 99 add to 100; 101 belongs to the sum to 100.
Pairing works if you count the unpaired middle term separately.
50 is a single term, so it cannot be used twice.
questions.explain: For an odd count, one term is left over.
questions.rule: With an odd number of terms the middle one is unpaired.

questions.q: True or false: the sum 2 + 4 + 6 + ... + 100 pairs into 25 pairs that each add to 102.
questions.explain: There are 50 terms, so 25 pairs, and the first and last add to 102; the total is 2550.
questions.rule: Check the count and the pair sum for each new list.

questions.q: A stack of logs has 30 logs in the bottom row, 29 in the next, down to 1 in the top row. How many logs?
optionExplain: 435 is the sum to 29, missing the bottom row.
Right: 15 pairs each adding to 31, total 465.
900 is 30 times 30, which treats every row as full.
930 is 30 times 31, which counts every pair twice.
questions.explain: The same pairing works when the numbers run downward.
questions.teaches: The author says many Gauss anecdotes are attributable only to Gauss himself, so no one knows how true they are, and the sum story is a simple variant of several.
questions.rule: Pair the ends of a run of numbers inward; equal pair sums make the total a product.

questions.q: A student writes 1 + 2 + ... + 99 forward and backward, one line under the other. What does each column add to?
optionExplain: 99 would be the largest term, not the sum of a column.
98 is one less than the last term of the sum.
198 is twice the column total.
Right: the first column adds 1 and 99, and every other column adds to the same 100.
questions.explain: Each column of the two lines has the same total. The card next uses this.
questions.rule: Add the sum to its own reversal; twice the sum is the column count times the common column sum.

questions.q: When S is written forward and backward and the lines are added, the result is ____ times S.
questions.explain: Each line is S, so the two lines together make 2S.
questions.rule: The added lines make 2S.

questions.q: Find 7 + 12 + 17 + ... + 502 (100 terms, each 5 more than the last). What is the total?
optionExplain: 50900 is 2S, which forgets to halve.
25200 uses 504 as the column sum in place of 509.
Right: 2S = 100 times 509, so S = 25450.
5090 divides by 10, as if there were ten terms.
questions.explain: The column total is the first plus the last term.
questions.rule: S = (number of terms) times (first + last) over 2.

questions.q: Which statements describe plain pairing, and which describe the forward-and-backward method?

items.t: An odd number of terms leaves a middle term over
You must decide how to treat an unpaired term
You pair the first term with the last
You add the sum to its own reversal
The same steps work for an odd or an even number of terms
You halve 2S at the end

questions.explain: Plain pairing must handle a leftover middle term. The forward-and-backward method adds whole columns, so the count's parity does not matter.
questions.rule: Forward and backward needs no middle-term fix.

questions.q: True or false: for 1 + 2 + ... + 99, the forward-and-backward method gives 2S = 99 times 100.
questions.explain: There are 99 columns, each adding to 100, so 2S = 9900 and S = 4950, the same as plain pairing with the middle term counted.
questions.rule: Add the sum to its own reversal; twice the sum is the column count times the common column sum.

questions.q: A theatre has 21 rows: 8 seats in front, each row 3 more than the last. How many seats?
optionExplain: Right: the back row has 68 seats, so 2S = 21 times 76 and S = 798.
1596 is 2S, which forgets to halve.
756 takes the back row to have 64 seats, a slip in counting the steps.
819 uses an average row of 39 seats, but the average of 8 and 68 is 38.
questions.explain: Find the last term, then use the column total.
questions.teaches: The author says the advantage of the forward-and-backward method is that it does not matter whether the number of terms is even or odd, which plain pairing must treat separately.
questions.rule: Add the sum to its own reversal; twice the sum is the column count times the common column sum.

questions.q: Which of 28, 36, 40 and 48 has an odd number of divisors?
optionExplain: 28 has six divisors, an even number.
Right: 36 has nine divisors, and it is a perfect square.
40 has eight divisors, an even number.
48 has ten divisors, an even number.
questions.explain: The odd one out has a special form. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Pair d with n over d; the number of divisors is odd exactly when n is a perfect square.

questions.q: A divisor of n pairs with itself only when n is a perfect ____.
questions.explain: If d is its own mate then d times d equals n, so n is a perfect square.
questions.rule: A self-paired divisor means a square.

questions.q: Which of 220, 225, 230 and 240 has an odd number of divisors?
optionExplain: 220 is not a perfect square, so its divisors all pair up.
230 is not a perfect square, so its divisors all pair up.
240 is not a perfect square, so its divisors all pair up.
Right: 225 is 15 squared, so 15 pairs with itself and the count is odd.
questions.explain: Test whether the number is a perfect square.
questions.rule: Odd number of divisors if and only if a perfect square.

questions.q: A student says 1 and n are always paired with themselves, so every number has an odd count of divisors. What is wrong?
options: 1 and n are not divisors of n, so they cannot belong to any pair
1 pairs with n, not with itself, unless n is 1
Divisors cannot be paired at all, which is why every number has an odd count
Only prime numbers pair 1 with n, and other numbers pair 1 with a different divisor
optionExplain: Both 1 and n divide n.
Right: 1 pairs with n, which is a different number for n greater than 1.
The mate of d is n over d, which is a divisor.
Every number pairs 1 with n, whether prime or not.
questions.explain: Only the square root can be its own mate.
questions.rule: The self-paired divisor is the square root.

questions.q: True or false: a number that is not a perfect square can still have exactly one self-paired divisor.
questions.explain: A self-paired divisor d satisfies d times d equals n, which makes n a perfect square. Without that there is none.
questions.rule: Pair d with n over d; the number of divisors is odd exactly when n is a perfect square.

questions.q: Pairing each divisor d of 28 with 28 over d, what is the product of all six divisors of 28?
optionExplain: 784 is 28 squared, which counts two pairs only.
168 is 28 times 6, which treats the product as a sum of pairs.
Right: there are three pairs, each with product 28, so the total is 28 cubed = 21952.
28 is the product of one pair.
questions.explain: Pair products are all equal, as pair sums were in the Gaussian sum.
questions.teaches: The author says to look for any kind of symmetry, not only in sums, and investigate whether a clever pairing of items simplifies things; here pairing works for a product.
questions.rule: Pair d with n over d; the number of divisors is odd exactly when n is a perfect square.

questions.q: What remainder does 10! (1 times 2 times ... times 10) leave on division by 11?
optionExplain: Right: the answer is 10, which is congruent to -1 modulo 11.
1 is the product of each inverse pair, not of the whole product.
0 would need a factor that is a multiple of 11, and none is.
5 has no connection to the product.
questions.explain: The card next shows a way to get the remainder without multiplying.
questions.rule: Pair each factor with its inverse mod p; only 1 and p - 1 stand alone, so (p - 1)! is congruent to -1.

questions.q: Modulo a prime p, the only factors of (p - 1)! that are their own mates are 1 and ____.
questions.explain: Squares of 1 and p - 1 are congruent to 1, and no other factor squares to 1 when p is prime.
questions.rule: Self-mates: 1 and p - 1 only.

questions.q: Using inverse pairs modulo 7, what remainder does 6! leave on division by 7?
optionExplain: Right: the pairs are (2, 4) and (3, 5), leaving 1 and 6, so the product is congruent to 6, that is -1.
1 would result if 6 were not one of the unpaired factors.
0 would need a multiple of 7 among the factors.
3 comes from nothing in the pairing.
questions.explain: Pair the factors, keep 1 and 6.
questions.rule: The product of the pairs is 1; multiply by p - 1.

questions.q: A student pairs 2 with 6 modulo 13, because 2 times 6 = 12. What is wrong?
options: Mates must multiply to 0 modulo 13, so that their product vanishes
2 has no mate at all, because 13 is a prime number
6 is its own mate modulo 13, so it cannot pair with 2
Mates must multiply to 1 modulo 13; 2 and 7 do, as 14 leaves 1
optionExplain: A product congruent to 0 would need a multiple of 13.
