Every nonzero residue has a mate when 13 is prime.
6 times 6 = 36 is congruent to 10, not 1.
Right: the mate of 2 is 7, because 14 is congruent to 1 modulo 13.
questions.explain: A mate is an inverse: the product must leave remainder 1.
questions.rule: Mates multiply to 1, not to p - 1.

questions.q: True or false: the pairing argument works unchanged modulo 8, because every nonzero residue modulo 8 has an inverse.
questions.explain: Our reading: 2, 4 and 6 have no inverse modulo 8, since their multiples are all even. Primality is what guarantees inverses.
questions.rule: Pair each factor with its inverse mod p; only 1 and p - 1 stand alone, so (p - 1)! is congruent to -1.

questions.q: Modulo 11, which numbers x from 1 to 10 satisfy x times x congruent to 1?
options: 1 and 5
1 and 9
1 and 10
2 and 6
optionExplain: 5 times 5 = 25 is congruent to 3.
9 times 9 = 81 is congruent to 4.
Right: 1 times 1 = 1 and 10 times 10 = 100, which is 1 more than 99.
2 and 6 are mates of each other, but neither squares to 1.
questions.explain: Only the self-mates square to 1.
questions.teaches: If x squared is congruent to 1 then (x - 1)(x + 1) is a multiple of p, and since p is prime one of the two factors is, so x is congruent to 1 or -1.
questions.rule: Pair each factor with its inverse mod p; only 1 and p - 1 stand alone, so (p - 1)! is congruent to -1.

questions.q: For x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 = 0, which substitution leads to a quadratic equation?
options: u = x squared, with no division
u = x + 1/x, after dividing by x squared
u = x + 1, since the equation has a term in x
u = x - 1/x, after dividing by x squared
optionExplain: x squared alone leaves the odd powers in the equation.
Right: the coefficients are symmetric, so the terms regroup into x + 1/x and x squared + 1/x squared.
x + 1 does not make the powers pair up.
x - 1/x gives x squared - 2 + 1/x squared, a sign that does not fit the sum.
questions.explain: The card next shows the steps.
questions.rule: Divide a symmetric-coefficient equation by the middle power of x and substitute u = x + 1/x.

questions.q: After dividing by x squared the author substitutes u = x + ____.
questions.explain: The sum x + 1/x is the symmetric quantity to which the pairs of terms reduce.
questions.rule: Substitute u = x + 1/x.

questions.q: Divide x^4 + 2x^3 - x^2 + 2x + 1 = 0 by x^2 and set u = x + 1/x. Which quadratic results?
optionExplain: Right: x^2 + 1/x^2 = u^2 - 2, so the equation becomes u^2 - 2 + 2u - 1 = 0.
This forgets the -2 from x^2 + 1/x^2 = u^2 - 2.
This adds 2 where it should subtract, giving a wrong constant.
This changes the sign of the middle coefficient.
questions.explain: Keep track of the identity x squared + 1/x squared = u squared - 2.

questions.q: True or false: the same substitution works on x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x^2 + x + 1 = 0.
questions.explain: The coefficients 1, 2, 3, 1, 1 do not read the same backwards, so dividing by x squared does not give terms that pair as x + 1/x.
questions.rule: Divide a symmetric-coefficient equation by the middle power of x and substitute u = x + 1/x.

questions.q: A solver substitutes u = x + 1/x into x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 = 0 before dividing. What is wrong?
options: The substitution needs a negative sign, which changes the quadratic that results
The equation has no symmetry to use, so a different method is the only option
The terms are not yet expressed in x + 1/x, so the substitution has nothing to replace
The division is only valid for even degrees, which is why the odd degree case fails
optionExplain: The sign is correct; the order of steps is not.
The coefficients are symmetric, which is why the method works.
Right: dividing by x squared raises the symmetry so that terms pair up.
The division is valid for any nonzero x here.
questions.explain: Divide first to make the powers symmetric.
questions.rule: Divide by the middle power first.

questions.q: Divide x^4 - 3x^3 + 4x^2 - 3x + 1 = 0 by x^2 and set u = x + 1/x. Which quadratic results?
optionExplain: This forgets the -2 from x^2 + 1/x^2.
The constant 4 - 2 is positive, not negative.
The middle term has the sign of -3 in the equation.
questions.explain: The same pattern works for a different set of coefficients.
questions.teaches: The author says the substitution works because u is unchanged when some roots are swapped; this idea is the germ of Galois theory.
questions.rule: Divide a symmetric-coefficient equation by the middle power of x and substitute u = x + 1/x.

questions.q: To prove (a + b)(b + c)(c + a) is at least 8abc for positive numbers, which first move is most promising?
options: Multiply out all three factors into six terms, then compare the terms one by one
Test several numbers and find the pattern, then state it as the proof for all cases
Divide both sides by abc and expand the result, then compare the terms one by one
Bound each factor, such as a + b, from below and multiply the bounds
optionExplain: Expanding is the move the author calls rarely wise.
Tests suggest the truth but never prove it for all positive values.
Dividing leaves factors that are still expanded.
Right: a + b is at least 2 times the square root of ab, and the other factors are permutations.
questions.explain: The card next shows the way.
questions.rule: Do not expand a symmetric product; prove one factor's bound and permute the variables.

questions.q: The two-variable AM-GM inequality says a + b is at least 2 times the square root of ____.
questions.explain: The arithmetic mean of two positive numbers is at least their geometric mean.
questions.rule: a + b is at least 2 times the square root of ab.

questions.q: Which argument proves (a^2 + b^2)(b^2 + c^2)(c^2 + a^2) is at least 8 a^2 b^2 c^2 for positive numbers?
options: Show a^2 + b^2 is at least 2ab, permute cyclically, and multiply the three bounds
Expand the product and compare the terms with 8 a^2 b^2 c^2
Replace a, b and c by 1 and check the result
Show each factor is at least 8 and multiply
optionExplain: Right: the three bounds multiply to 8 a^2 b^2 c^2.
Expansion is long and hides the structure.
One substitution cannot prove the claim for all positive numbers.
The factors are not all at least 8, so the bound is false.
questions.explain: The factors are cyclic permutations of the first.
questions.rule: Bound one factor and permute.

questions.q: A solver multiplies out (a + b)(b + c)(c + a) and then cannot compare the result with 8abc. What does the author's method avoid?
options: Using positive numbers, which are not needed here, since the inequality holds for any signs
Permuting the variables, which is not allowed in a cyclic expression, since it changes the claim
Expanding, which hides the symmetry that the factored form shows
Using any inequality at all in a proof, since an identity is required
optionExplain: Positive numbers are needed for the bound.
Permuting is the main move.
Right: the factored form makes the cyclic pattern visible.
Inequalities are used by the author.
questions.explain: Keep the structure visible by factoring.
questions.rule: Do not expand a symmetric product.

questions.q: True or false: for a = 1, b = 2 and c = 3, (a + b)(b + c)(c + a) equals 8abc.
questions.explain: The left side is 3 times 5 times 4 = 60 and the right side is 48, so the inequality is strict here.
questions.rule: Do not expand a symmetric product; prove one factor's bound and permute the variables.

questions.q: A box has sides a, b and c, all positive. Which statement follows from the author's inequality?
options: The volume is at least eight times the product of the pair sums
The sum of the sides is at most eight
Every pair of sides adds to at least 8
The product of the three side-pair sums is at least eight times the box's volume
optionExplain: This reverses the inequality.
Nothing bounds the sum by 8.
The sides can be small, so pair sums are not at least 8.
Right: (a + b)(b + c)(c + a) is at least 8abc, and abc is the volume.
questions.explain: Read the inequality in words.
questions.teaches: The inequality becomes an equality only when a = b = c.
questions.rule: Do not expand a symmetric product; prove one factor's bound and permute the variables.

questions.q: True or false: moving a to b, b to c and c to a turns the term a^2 b into b^2 c.
questions.explain: Each variable moves one place along, so a^2 b becomes b^2 c; the cyclic sum adds a^2 b, b^2 c and c^2 a.
questions.rule: Write symmetric expressions as cyclic sums, and keep factoring guesses symmetric.

questions.q: The cyclic sum of x^3 over the variables x, y, z is x^3 + y^3 + ____.
questions.explain: Moving each variable one place along turns x^3 into y^3 and then z^3.
questions.rule: A cyclic sum adds all the cyclic shifts.

questions.q: For (a, b, c) = (1, 2, 3), what is the cyclic sum a^2 b + b^2 c + c^2 a?
optionExplain: 25 uses a b^2 + b c^2 + c a^2, a different cyclic sum.
Right: 1 times 2 plus 4 times 3 plus 9 times 1 = 2 + 12 + 9.
36 comes from squaring a + b + c = 6.
14 is the sum of the squares.
questions.explain: Evaluate each shifted term and add.
questions.rule: Shift the variables, then add.

questions.q: True or false: guessing the factor a + b + c of a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc keeps the leftover terms symmetric.
questions.explain: A symmetric guess keeps the remaining error terms symmetric, while a guess such as a - b singles out two variables.
questions.rule: Keep every factoring guess symmetric.

questions.q: Which is the other factor of a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc, besides a + b + c?
options: a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - ab - bc - ca
a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + ab + bc + ca
optionExplain: Right: it is symmetric, and at a = b = c = 1 it is 0, as the cubic is. At (1, 2, 3): 6 times (14 - 11) = 18, matching the cubic.
At a = b = c = 1 this gives 6, but the cubic is 0 there, so a zero is needed.
At a = b = c = 1 this gives -3, not 0.
At a = b = c = 1 this gives 9, but the cubic is 0 there.
questions.explain: Plug in a = b = c = 1: the cubic is 0, so the second factor must vanish there.
questions.rule: Test a guessed factor at a simple point.
questions.teaches: The symmetric guess a + b + c leads to the factorisation a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc = (a + b + c)(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - ab - bc - ca).
questions.hint: At a = b = c = 1 the cubic equals 0, so the other factor must too.

questions.q: If a + b + c = 0, what is a^3 + b^3 + c^3 in terms of abc?
options: abc
-3abc
3abc
optionExplain: 0 would need abc to be 0 as well, but abc is -30.
abc leaves out the factor of 3.
-3abc has the wrong sign.
Right: the factor a + b + c is 0, so a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc = 0.
questions.explain: A zero factor makes the whole product zero.
questions.teaches: The author says the cyclic-sum notation saves time and, once you get used to it, reduces the chance of an error.
questions.rule: Write symmetric expressions as cyclic sums, and keep factoring guesses symmetric.

questions.q: A problem involves 30 points with many relationships. Which points are most likely constrained in interesting ways?
options: The points that sit nearest the middle of the figure, because they are the most balanced
The extreme ones, such as the largest triangle or the closest pair
The points listed first in the problem statement, because they set up the rest of the problem
Every point is as constrained as any other
optionExplain: Central points have neighbours on all sides and so are the least constrained.
Right: nothing lies beyond an extreme element, so its position is limited by the others.
The order of a list is an accident of how the problem is written.
Points in a problem do differ in how restricted they are.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's principle.
questions.rule: Put the elements in order and study the largest and smallest.

questions.q: The author calls the act of assuming that the elements are arranged in order ____.
questions.explain: Monotonizing means assuming, when possible, that the elements are in order, and it gives free information.
questions.rule: Monotonize: assume the elements are in order.

questions.q: Each number in a finite set is the average of two others in the set. Which number is best to study first?
options: The one nearest the middle value, since it balances the rest of the numbers in the list
The first one written down, since it starts the list and so fixes the others
The largest, since an average of two others cannot exceed it
Any of them, since every number plays the same role
optionExplain: The middle number is the least constrained by the average condition.
The order of writing is an accident of the problem's wording.
Right: the largest equals an average of two numbers that cannot be larger, so both must equal it.
The numbers do not play the same role: the extremes are constrained most.
questions.explain: Ask which element the condition can limit.
questions.rule: Study the element the condition constrains most.

questions.q: Which of these is an application of the extreme principle, and which is not?

items.t: Consider the triangle of smallest area
Look at the person with the most handshakes
Examine the longest path in the figure
Pick a random point and test it
Check three small cases and guess a pattern
Draw the figure larger so it is easier to read

questions.explain: The first three single out the smallest, the largest or the longest. The others are different tactics: random choice, experiments and drawing.
questions.rule: Single out the largest or smallest.

questions.q: True or false: every set of real numbers has a largest and a smallest element, so the principle can always be applied.
questions.explain: Only finite sets of real numbers must have both. The author's example of the infinite set 1, 2, 1/2, 4, 1/4, ... has neither.
questions.rule: Put the elements in order and study the largest and smallest.

questions.q: In a round-robin tournament every player's score is different. A coach studies the highest and lowest scores first. Which idea of the card is this?
options: Symmetry, since the scores are paired and the pairs can be compared
Monotonizing the scores and focusing on the extremes, which are the most constrained
Invariants, since the scores stay unchanged while the games are played
Pigeonhole, since scores must collide when there are more players than scores
optionExplain: The scores are not paired or reflected here.
Right: ordering the scores and looking at the top and bottom is the extreme principle.
The scores here differ and may change from game to game.
All scores are different, so there is no collision to use.
questions.explain: The extreme principle applies in any ranked setting.
questions.teaches: The author notes the principle seems almost trite, yet works wonders, and his first example of it is the Affirmative Action problem of Chapter 2.
questions.rule: Put the elements in order and study the largest and smallest.

questions.q: You want to show something is impossible for a finite set of points. Which style of proof does the extreme principle suggest?
options: Check every possible arrangement one by one until a counterexample is found or none remain
Draw a large figure and measure it carefully enough to be sure of the result
Assume it is possible, take the extreme example, and find a more extreme one
Prove it only for the smallest case
optionExplain: Checking all cases is infeasible when the number is unspecified.
Measuring a figure cannot prove a general statement.
Right: a more extreme example contradicts the choice of the extreme one.
A single case does not prove the general claim.
questions.explain: The card next shows the standard pattern.
questions.rule: Suppose the claim fails, take the extreme example, and derive a more extreme one.

questions.q: The extreme principle is often used in a proof by ____: assume the claim is false and look at the extreme example.
questions.explain: The more extreme example that you construct contradicts the choice of the extreme one.
questions.rule: Extreme principle often goes with contradiction.

questions.q: Every midpoint of two points of a finite set lies in the set. Which extreme shows the set is one point?
options: The closest pair of points, whose midpoint would be closer still
The pair of points farthest apart, whose midpoint would be even closer to the others
The point nearest the centre of the plane, whose neighbours can then be compared with it
The point with the largest coordinates
optionExplain: Right: the midpoint of the closest pair is in the set and lies closer to each point, contradicting the choice.
The midpoint of the farthest pair is not a farther pair, so no contradiction arises.
A centre point does not use the midpoint property.
Coordinates depend on the axes and do not link to the property.
questions.explain: Look for the extreme that the property makes smaller.
questions.rule: Choose the extreme the property can undercut.

questions.q: In the points problem a solver minimises area over all triples, including collinear ones of area zero. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, since a triangle of area zero is the smallest of all, so a collinear triple settles the question
The points must instead be all of one colour
The smallest triangle must have a right angle, which is why a collinear triple cannot occur
A collinear triple is not a triangle, so the smallest area must be taken over true triangles
optionExplain: A zero area makes the 'smaller triangle' step impossible.
The problem uses both colours; the argument does not change them.
No right angle is needed.
Right: the argument needs genuine triangles, which exist when the points do not all lie on a line.
questions.explain: Our reading: the proof assumes a real triangle exists.
questions.rule: Choose the extreme among genuine objects.

questions.q: True or false: in the black and white points proof, the new triangle made from the other-colour point has smaller area than the one chosen.
questions.explain: The point of the other colour lies between two same-colour vertices, so it lies on a side of the chosen triangle, and a triangle with it as a vertex has smaller area.
questions.rule: Suppose the claim fails, take the extreme example, and derive a more extreme one.

questions.q: In a finite town, every resident has a neighbour who earns strictly more. Which resident exposes a contradiction?
options: The lowest earner, whose neighbours all earn more already
A resident chosen at random from the electoral roll
The top earner
The resident with the largest number of neighbours
optionExplain: The lowest earner satisfies the claim, so no contradiction arises there.
A random resident satisfies the claim as likely as not.
Right: the claim fails for the person who earns the most.
The number of neighbours does not decide who earns the most.
questions.explain: Choose the extreme that the claim cannot cover.
questions.teaches: The author says the point-colouring problem seems at first to need many complicated diagrams showing that you can always draw a new point; the extreme principle makes it quick.
questions.rule: Suppose the claim fails, take the extreme example, and derive a more extreme one.

questions.q: Which of these sets is certain to have a smallest element?
options: Any non-empty set of positive integers
Any non-empty set of positive fractions
Any infinite set of real numbers
Any set that has no largest element
optionExplain: Right: non-empty sets of positive integers always have a least element.
Fractions such as 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, ... get ever smaller.
The integers all together have no smallest member.
Having no largest element says nothing about a smallest.
questions.explain: The card next gives the principle.
questions.rule: Make sure an extreme exists: finite sets always have one, and so do non-empty sets of positive integers.

questions.q: The principle that every non-empty set of positive integers has a least element is called the ____ Principle.
questions.explain: Well-ordering is what lets you pick a least counterexample among positive integers.
questions.rule: Non-empty sets of positive integers have a least element.

questions.q: Which set has both a smallest and a largest element?
options: All positive real numbers less than 1
All the positive multiples of 3
All fractions strictly between 0 and 1
The set of all multiples of 3 between 10 and 100
optionExplain: The numbers get arbitrarily close to 0 and there is no largest below 1.
There is a smallest multiple, 3, but there is no largest.
The fractions between 0 and 1 get arbitrarily close to both ends.
Right: it is a finite set of reals, so it has a minimum (12) and a maximum (99).
questions.explain: Finite sets have both extremes.
questions.rule: Finite sets of reals have a minimum and a maximum.

questions.q: A solver says the positive real numbers have a least element because every one of them is positive. What is wrong?
options: Positive reals have a least element but no largest, so the principle applies only at the small end
Positive reals get arbitrarily small, so no least positive real exists
Positive numbers are not covered by well-ordering at all
The least element is 0, which is a positive number, so the principle applies and the argument works
optionExplain: The positive reals have neither a least nor a greatest element.
Right: halving any positive real gives a smaller positive real.
The principle covers positive integers, not positive reals.
Zero is not positive.
questions.explain: Well-ordering is a property of positive integers.
questions.rule: Well-ordering applies to positive integers, not positive reals.

questions.q: True or false: in the infinite set 1, 2, 1/2, 4, 1/4, 8, 1/8, ... there is a smallest element.
questions.explain: The entries 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ... keep decreasing without reaching a smallest, and the entries 2, 4, 8, ... have no largest.
questions.rule: Make sure an extreme exists: finite sets always have one, and so do non-empty sets of positive integers.

questions.q: A scientist records the waiting times of a finite list of 40 buses. She wants the shortest wait. Does the shortest wait exist?
options: No, because waiting times are real numbers and real numbers have no smallest value
Only if the times are whole minutes, since only then is there a smallest value
Only if the list is infinite
Yes, because a finite list of numbers has a smallest value
optionExplain: Being real is no obstacle for a finite set.
Whole numbers are not needed for finite sets.
An infinite list would raise the problem, not remove it.
Right: a finite set of reals always has a minimum.
questions.explain: Finite lists have extremes whatever the type of number.
questions.teaches: The author warns that Well-Ordering is not always true for infinite sets, so extremal arguments there can work but must be used with care.
questions.rule: Make sure an extreme exists: finite sets always have one, and so do non-empty sets of positive integers.

questions.q: Joining the side midpoints of a triangle makes a smaller triangle. What fraction of the area is it?
options: One half
One quarter
One third
One eighth
optionExplain: A half would not fit the four-piece division.
Right: the four congruent pieces each have a quarter of the area, and the middle one is the medial triangle.
A third has no basis in the figure.
An eighth is too small to fit the division into four equal triangles.
questions.explain: The card next uses this fact.
questions.rule: Take the largest triangle ABC and build the triangle LMN that has ABC as its medial triangle.

questions.q: To show the points all lie inside a triangle of area less than 4, the author starts from the triangle of ____ area among them.
questions.explain: Maximality is what rules out any point outside the larger triangle.
questions.rule: Start from the largest triangle.

questions.q: The largest triangle ABC formed by a finite point set has area 5. What area does the enclosing triangle LMN have?
options: A triangle of area 10
A triangle of area 15
A triangle of area 20
A triangle of area 25
optionExplain: Twice the area is a figure that does not contain the points.
Three times is not the ratio of a triangle to its medial triangle.
Right: LMN has four times the area of ABC, so 20.
Five times is not the ratio either.
questions.explain: Multiply the largest triangle's area by 4.
questions.rule: The enclosing triangle has four times the area.

questions.q: A solver takes the triangle ABC of smallest area and builds LMN around it. What goes wrong?
options: A point outside LMN need not form a bigger triangle than the smallest one, so there is no contradiction
The medial triangle construction works only for right triangles, so the argument fails for other shapes
The area of LMN would be a quarter of ABC, so the contradiction is that the areas are unequal
The points could not form any triangle
optionExplain: Right: the contradiction needs maximality, which the smallest triangle does not provide.
The construction works for any triangle.
LMN has four times the area, not a quarter.
The points form triangles in this problem.
questions.explain: The extreme chosen must be the one the contradiction needs.
questions.rule: Choose the extreme that leads to the contradiction.

questions.q: True or false: because every triangle has area less than 1, the enclosing triangle LMN has area strictly less than 4.
questions.explain: The largest triangle is one of the triangles and so has area less than 1, and LMN has four times its area.
questions.rule: Take the largest triangle ABC and build the triangle LMN that has ABC as its medial triangle.

questions.q: The largest triangle among finitely many trees has area 40 square metres. What area does the enclosing fence triangle have?
options: 160 square metres
80 square metres
120 square metres
40 square metres
optionExplain: Right: four times the largest triangle's area.
Double the area does not fit the construction.
Triple the area does not fit the construction.
40 is the area of the largest triangle itself, which cannot enclose the others.
questions.explain: The construction multiplies the largest triangle's area by four.
questions.teaches: The author says the tactic here is the extreme principle, while the crux move is the clever geometric construction of the triangle whose medial triangle is ABC.
questions.rule: Take the largest triangle ABC and build the triangle LMN that has ABC as its medial triangle.

questions.q: Ten couples, a host and hostess: the 21 others all give different handshake counts, none with a partner. How many did the hostess shake?
optionExplain: 0 would put the hostess among the extreme people, whose partner shook 20.
Right: she shook 10 hands.
20 is possible only for the partner of the person with 0.
21 is more hands than there were other people.
questions.explain: The card next shows how to see it.
questions.rule: Make the problem small, then pair the person with the most handshakes with the one with none, and repeat.

questions.q: In the small case the person who shook the most hands is partnered with the person who shook ____ hands.
questions.explain: The person with the most shook everyone except their partner, so only their partner can have shaken none.
questions.rule: The extremes are partners.

questions.q: Host, hostess and 3 couples: the 7 others give different handshake counts. Who partners the person with 5?
options: The person who shook 0 hands
The person who shook 2 hands
The person who shook 6 hands
The person who shook 1 hand
optionExplain: The person who shook 0 hands is the partner of the person who shook 6.
Shaking 2 hands pairs with shaking 4, leaving the hostess with 3.
The person who shook 6 hands is partnered with the person who shook 0.
Right: after the 0 and 6 people are paired, the 5 and 1 persons play the same extreme roles.
questions.explain: Strip the first pair and repeat the argument.
questions.rule: Pair 0 with the maximum, then 1 with the next maximum, and so on.

questions.q: A solver says the host's own handshake number is unknown, so the problem cannot be solved. What does the solver miss?
options: The host's number is the same as the hostess's, which pins down every other pair at once
The host shook hands with everyone
The other 2n + 1 people have all-different numbers from 0 to 2n, which pins down the pairs
The puzzle can be solved only by checking all cases, one handshake pattern at a time
optionExplain: The host's number is not given and not needed.
That would contradict the host's partner having a different number.
Right: different answers force the numbers 0 to 2n, and the extremes then fix the pairs.
The extremes argument avoids checking all cases.
questions.explain: The data you need are the distinct numbers of the others.
questions.rule: Use the forced set of numbers, not the unknown one.

questions.q: True or false: if two invited people gave the same handshake number, the extreme argument would still force the hostess's count.
questions.explain: Our reading: the argument needs the numbers 0 to 2n to appear exactly once each. Repeats break the step that forces the extremes.
questions.rule: Make the problem small, then pair the person with the most handshakes with the one with none, and repeat.

questions.q: A host and hostess invite 5 couples and hear 11 different handshake counts from the others. Which counts occur?
options: Each of 1, 2, 3, ..., 11 exactly once
Each of 0, 1, 2, ..., 11 with one missing at random
Each of 0, 1, 2, ..., 10 exactly once
Any 11 different numbers, since the counts are unrestricted
optionExplain: 11 is impossible, since a person has at most 10 others to shake hands with.
11 is impossible, so the list cannot include it.
Right: nobody shakes their own or their partner's hand, so 10 is the largest possible count, and 11 different counts must be exactly 0 to 10.
The counts are capped at 10 and cannot be below 0, so only 11 values fit.
questions.explain: Count the largest possible number first.
questions.teaches: Because nobody shakes hands with themselves or their partner, the largest possible count is 2n at a party of n couples plus host and hostess, which forces the different answers to be exactly 0 to 2n.
questions.rule: Make the problem small, then pair the person with the most handshakes with the one with none, and repeat.

questions.q: You can show that removing two extreme items always leaves a smaller problem of the same kind. Which proof style does this suggest?
options: Induction on the size of the problem
Proof by exhaustion of every case
Proof by a single numerical example
Proof by symmetry of the whole figure
optionExplain: Right: a smaller problem of the same kind is the structure induction needs.
Exhaustion cannot cover an unlimited number of cases.
An example does not prove the general claim.
Nothing in the description is symmetric.
questions.explain: The card next gives the formal argument.
questions.rule: Remove the extreme pair, show a smaller case of the same kind remains, and conclude by induction.

questions.q: After the two extreme people are removed from the party, every other person's handshake count drops by exactly ____.
questions.explain: Everyone shook hands with the person who shook the most, and with nobody from the person who shook none.
questions.rule: Removing the extremes lowers every count by one.

questions.q: Four couples, host and hostess. X shook 8 hands; X and X's partner leave. Without their handshakes, what is the largest remaining count?
optionExplain: 7 was the largest count before the removal.
Right: the remaining counts were 1 to 7, and each falls by one to 0 to 6.
8 was the count of the removed person.
5 would mean two counts had dropped.
questions.explain: Subtract one from everybody's count.
questions.rule: Counts drop by one, leaving a party with one fewer couple.

questions.q: Put the steps of the induction in order.
items: Check the base case with one couple
Assume the claim holds for n couples
In a party with n + 1 couples, find the person who shook the most hands and their partner
Remove those two and apply the hypothesis to the smaller party
Add back the hostess's handshake with the removed person
questions.explain: The base case starts the induction; the extremes are removed to reach the smaller party where the hypothesis holds; the removed person's handshake is added back.
questions.rule: Base case, hypothesis, remove extremes, apply, restore.

questions.q: A solver concludes that the hostess shook only n hands in the party with n + 1 couples. What did she forget?
options: The base case for one couple is what the induction step must have used
That the host shook hands with nobody, which pins down the removed person
That partners shook hands with each other
The hostess also shook hands with the removed extreme person
optionExplain: The base case is not the missing step.
The host's count is unknown and unneeded.
No one shakes hands with a partner.
Right: she shook X's hand, which the reduced party no longer counts, so she shook n + 1.
questions.explain: Count what the removal hid.
questions.rule: Add back the hand that the removal hid.

questions.q: A claim about n couples is proved by removing an extreme pair, leaving n - 1 couples under the same conditions. Which tactic fits?
options: A symmetry argument finished by reflection in the plane of the guests
A pigeonhole argument finished by a count of the handshakes made
An extreme-principle argument finished by induction
A coordinate argument finished by algebra on the numbers of handshakes
optionExplain: No reflection is involved in stripping off a pair.
No collision of pigeons is involved.
Right: the extremes give the reduction and induction finishes it.
No coordinates are used.
questions.explain: The extremes decide what to remove.
questions.teaches: The author notes that problems often involve the extreme principle plus a particular argument style, such as contradiction or induction, and a common tactic is to use the extremes to strip a problem down to a smaller version.
questions.rule: Remove the extreme pair, show a smaller case of the same kind remains, and conclude by induction.

questions.q: The numbers 10 and 15 are erased and replaced by their GCD and LCM. What numbers appear?
options: 5 and 30
25 and 6
10 and 15
1 and 150
optionExplain: Right: GCD(10, 15) = 5 and LCM(10, 15) = 30.
25 and 6 mix up the sum, difference or other combinations.
10 and 15 are the original numbers, not the replacements.
1 and 150 would be the GCD and the product.
questions.explain: The card next studies what repeated replacement does.
questions.rule: Track the least element; the smallest one that ever occurs divides the rest, so it can be set aside.

questions.q: In the erase-and-replace process the least element never ____.
questions.explain: The GCD of two distinct numbers that do not divide each other is smaller than the smaller one.
questions.rule: The least element never rises.

questions.q: The numbers 12, 18 and 20 are repeatedly replaced as described until nothing changes. Which list results?
optionExplain: 6 is a chain, but the least element must be the GCD of the originals, which is 2.
4 does not divide 90, and it is not the GCD of the originals.
The greatest element must be the LCM of the originals, which is 180, not 360.
Right: it is a divisor chain, 2 divides 12 and 12 divides 180, with least 2 (the GCD) and greatest 180 (the LCM).
questions.explain: The final list is a divisor chain.
questions.rule: The final list is a chain of divisors.

questions.q: A solver says the process may go on forever, because GCDs get smaller and LCMs get larger without limit. What is wrong?
options: GCDs never get smaller, so nothing changes and the process never has to stop
The values stay between the GCD of the originals and their LCM, so only finitely many lists exist
LCMs always equal the product, so they stop and the process halts at once
The numbers erased are always equal, so the list cannot change from step to step
optionExplain: A GCD of two non-dividing numbers is smaller than both.
Right: the least element is at least the GCD of all originals, the greatest at most the LCM, which allows finitely many lists.
LCMs equal the product only for numbers with no common factor.
The process erases two distinct numbers.
questions.explain: Bounded values give finitely many states.
questions.rule: Bounds give finitely many possible lists.

questions.q: True or false: once the smallest-ever least element is reached, it divides every other number in the list.
questions.explain: If it did not divide some number x, replacing it and x would create a smaller GCD, contradicting its minimality.
questions.rule: Track the least element; the smallest one that ever occurs divides the rest, so it can be set aside.

questions.q: Numbers 4, 6 and 9 are replaced by GCD and LCM until nothing changes. Which are the least and greatest entries?
options: 2 and 18
1 and 36
1 and 54
3 and 36
optionExplain: 2 is the GCD of 4 and 6 but not of 9.
Right: the least is the GCD of 4, 6 and 9, which is 1, and the greatest is their LCM, 36.
54 is the product of 6 and 9, not the LCM of all three.
3 is the GCD of 6 and 9 but not of 4.
questions.explain: Use the GCD and LCM of all the original numbers.
questions.teaches: After experiments the author conjectures that the list ends as a divisor chain whose least element is the GCD and whose greatest element is the LCM of all the original numbers.
questions.rule: Track the least element; the smallest one that ever occurs divides the rest, so it can be set aside.

questions.q: Which of these functions has a smallest value over all real numbers x?
options: 1/x for x greater than 0
e^x
optionExplain: 1/x gets closer to 0 but never reaches it.
x^3 goes to minus infinity.
e^x gets closer to 0 but never reaches it.
Right: x^2 + 1 is at least 1, and it equals 1 at x = 0.
questions.explain: The card next explains why this matters for proofs.
questions.rule: On an infinite domain, prove that the extreme exists, for example by checking the behaviour at the ends.

questions.q: A polynomial that is never negative must have ____ degree, because otherwise it would go negative at one end.
questions.explain: An odd-degree polynomial heads to minus infinity at one end, so it takes negative values.
questions.rule: Never-negative polynomial: even degree, positive leading coefficient.

questions.q: Which polynomial is certain to attain a smallest value over the real numbers?
options: x^4 + x
x^3 - x
optionExplain: Right: its degree is even and its leading coefficient is positive, so it tends to plus infinity at both ends.
An odd-degree polynomial heads to minus infinity at one end.
A negative leading coefficient with even degree is unbounded below.
Degree 5 is odd, so the polynomial heads to minus infinity at one end.
questions.explain: Even degree and a positive leading coefficient give a minimum.
questions.rule: Check the ends of the domain.

questions.q: A solver says 1/x on the positive reals has a minimum point because it is bounded below by 0. What is wrong?
options: The function does have a minimum, at the point x = 1, since the values never go below 1 near it
The function is not bounded below, since it blows up near 0, so there is no value to compare it with
Being bounded below does not mean the lower bound is ever reached
A function must be defined at 0 to have a minimum, and this one is not
optionExplain: At x = 1 the function equals 1, and larger x give smaller values.
The function is bounded below by 0, so it does not drop without limit.
Right: 1/x gets as close to 0 as you like but never equals it.
The domain here is the positive reals, and a minimum can occur at any point of it.
questions.explain: An infimum need not be a minimum.
questions.rule: A lower bound is not a minimum.

questions.q: True or false: the argument also needs g to have a minimum, and it does because g has the same leading term as f.
questions.explain: The terms f', f'', ... have lower degree than f, so they do not change the leading term, and g tends to plus infinity at both ends.
questions.rule: On an infinite domain, prove that the extreme exists, for example by checking the behaviour at the ends.

questions.q: Let f(x) = x^2 and let g be the sum of f and its first two derivatives. Which identity ties g' to f and g?
options: g' = g - f
g' = g + f
g' = f'
optionExplain: Right: g = x^2 + 2x + 2, so g' = 2x + 2, which equals g - f.
g + f = 2x^2 + 2x + 2, which is not 2x + 2.
f' = 2x, which is missing the constant 2.
2f' = 4x, which is not 2x + 2.
questions.explain: The derivative drops the first term and keeps the rest, which is g minus f.
questions.teaches: Because f has degree n, its (n + 1)th derivative is zero, so g' = g - f in general; at a minimum point x0 of g, g'(x0) = 0 would force g(x0) = f(x0), which is not negative.
questions.rule: On an infinite domain, prove that the extreme exists, for example by checking the behaviour at the ends.

questions.q: You cannot prove a hard inequality directly. Which move does the author suggest?
options: Prove a weaker statement and stop there
Try proving a stronger statement
Check one example and call it proved
Remove the hypotheses you cannot use
optionExplain: A weaker claim does not give the result asked.
Right: the author notes that sometimes stronger statements are easier to prove.
One example does not prove a general claim.
Hypotheses cannot be dropped without changing the problem.
questions.explain: The card next shows an example.
questions.rule: Guess a stronger, pairable statement, order the terms, and prove it by contradiction.

questions.q: Sometimes ____ statements are easier to prove than the one the problem asks.
questions.explain: A stronger statement gives a more specific target and can pair the terms neatly.
questions.rule: A stronger statement can be easier to prove.

questions.q: To show six ordered terms sum to at least 3 times 101, which pairing gives three sums to check?
options: a1 with a2, a3 with a4, a5 with a6
a1 with a3, a2 with a4, a5 with a6
a1 with a4, a2 with a3, a5 with a6
a1 with a6, a2 with a5, a3 with a4
optionExplain: These pairs put the small terms together, so their sums are small.
This pairing does not pair opposite ends.
This pairing leaves the largest terms together.
Right: this is the Gaussian pairing from the ends inward, so each pair sum can be compared with 101.
questions.explain: Pair the smallest with the largest.
questions.rule: Pair opposite ends of the ordered list.

questions.q: To prove three pair sums are at least n + 1, a solver assumes all three fail. What assumption is enough?
options: Assume exactly two fail, since three is too many
Assume none fail, since that is the claim
Assume at least one fails
Assume the terms are not in order
optionExplain: Two failures is not the negation of the claim.
Assuming none fail assumes the conclusion.
Right: if the claim fails, at least one pair sum is at most n, and that is enough to start.
Ordering the terms is allowed and helpful.
questions.explain: The negation of 'all pairs are big' is 'some pair is small'.
questions.rule: Negate 'all' as 'at least one'.

questions.q: True or false: if the smallest and largest terms sum to at most n, closure forces a term larger than the largest.
questions.explain: The sum of two positive terms exceeds the larger one, so a term equal to it would exceed the largest term, which is impossible.
questions.rule: Guess a stronger, pairable statement, order the terms, and prove it by contradiction.

questions.q: A coach proves each best-and-worst pair of scores averages at least 50. Does that prove the team average is at least 50?
options: No: pairs of scores say nothing about the whole average
Yes, when the scores pair up: the stronger pairwise claim implies the bound
No: the average claim is the stronger of the two
Yes, but only if every score on the team is the same
optionExplain: Pairs that cover all the scores determine the total.
Right: if every pair of opposite-end scores averages at least 50, the whole average does too.
The pairwise claim is the stronger one.
Equal scores are not needed.
questions.explain: A stronger claim implies the weaker.
questions.teaches: The author notes that the pairing proves something slightly stronger than needed: the terms might not pair nicely and yet the total could still be large enough, but there is no harm in trying the stronger statement.
questions.rule: Guess a stronger, pairable statement, order the terms, and prove it by contradiction.

questions.q: Thirteen people are in a room. Which statement must be true?
options: At least two of them were born on the same date in the calendar year
Every calendar month has a birthday in this room or more people share one
At least two of them were born in the same calendar month
Exactly one calendar month is shared by two people and the other months are not shared
optionExplain: There are 365 or more dates, which is more than 13, so dates need not repeat.
Some months could have nobody born in them.
Right: 13 people and only 12 months force a shared month.
Several months might be shared, or three people might share one month.
questions.explain: A repeat is forced because the number of people exceeds the number of months. The card next names the idea.
questions.rule: More pigeons than holes means some hole has at least two pigeons.

questions.q: If you have more pigeons than ____, at least one hole must contain at least two pigeons.
questions.explain: That the pigeons outnumber the holes is what forces a repeat.
questions.rule: More pigeons than holes forces a shared hole.

questions.q: A drawer holds socks in 4 colours. How few socks taken in the dark guarantee a matching pair?
optionExplain: Right: four socks could be four colours, but a fifth must repeat one.
Four socks could each be a different colour, with no pair.
Three socks may all differ, so a pair is not certain.
Eight is more than needed: five already guarantees a pair.
questions.explain: The colours are the holes and the socks are the pigeons.
questions.rule: Holes: colours; pigeons: socks taken.

questions.q: With 9 pigeons in 8 holes, a student says hole 3 must hold two pigeons. What is wrong?
options: The principle requires equal numbers of holes and pigeons
The principle says all holes hold two pigeons
The principle fails when the numbers are small
The principle shows some hole has two, but not which one
optionExplain: It needs more pigeons than holes, not equal numbers.
It says only that some hole holds at least two.
It holds for any numbers with more pigeons than holes.
Right: the principle gives existence of a crowded hole, not its identity.
questions.explain: It says that some hole holds two or more, and nothing about which.
questions.rule: The principle proves existence, not location.

questions.q: True or false: with 8 pigeons and 8 holes, the principle forces some hole to contain two pigeons.
questions.explain: Each of the 8 holes can hold exactly one pigeon, so no repeat is forced. The principle needs more pigeons than holes.
questions.rule: More pigeons than holes means some hole has at least two pigeons.

questions.q: A library has 367 members. Every member has a birthday, and a year has at most 366 dates. What does the principle say about birthdays?
options: Every date is a birthday of someone
Exactly two members share a birthday
No two members share a birthday
Two members share a birthday
optionExplain: Some dates may have no member at all.
Three or more could share, so exactly two is not forced.
The principle forces a repeat, so this is false.
Right: 367 members and 366 dates force a shared date.
questions.explain: People are the pigeons and dates are the holes.
questions.teaches: The principle is also called the Dirichlet principle, and the author notes it played a crucial role in at least a third of the problems of the 1994 Putnam exam.
questions.rule: More pigeons than holes means some hole has at least two pigeons.

questions.q: In most pigeonhole problems, which job is usually the hardest?
options: Counting that the pigeons outnumber the holes and writing the result down
Noticing that the problem has numbers in it that can be counted
Working out what the pigeons and the holes should be
Writing out the final sentence of the proof
optionExplain: Counting is easy once the pigeons and holes are chosen.
Numbers appear in many problems and are no signal.
Right: the author calls this frequently the crux move.
The write-up is routine compared with the choice of holes.
questions.explain: The card next lists the three parts.
questions.rule: Spot the pigeonhole, choose the pigeons and holes, and expect a finishing step.

questions.q: Put the three parts of a pigeonhole solution in the author's order.
items: Recognise that the problem might need the pigeonhole principle
Figure out what the pigeons and the holes must be
Do the remaining work after applying the principle
questions.explain: First notice that pigeonhole may help, then choose pigeons and holes, then finish what the principle leaves undone.
questions.rule: Recognise, choose pigeons and holes, finish.

questions.q: To show that among 30 people two have the same number of letters in their first name, what must you choose?
options: Pigeons: the 30 people; holes: the possible name lengths
Pigeons: the letters; holes: the people
Pigeons: the names; holes: the alphabet's 26 letters
Pigeons: the possible lengths; holes: the people
optionExplain: Right: if there are fewer possible lengths than 30, some two people share a length.
This reverses the roles and counts the wrong things.
Names are not placed in single letters here.
This puts the larger number in the holes, so no collision is forced.
questions.explain: Put the objects you must show collide in the roles of pigeons.
questions.rule: Pigeons are what you place; holes are the categories.

questions.q: A solver finds that the pigeonhole principle gives two integers with the same remainder, and stops. What is missing?
options: The principle gives no shared remainder at all, so another argument is needed to finish
The final step, showing that the difference of those two integers is a multiple of n
The remainders must all be different, which is why the difference is divisible by n
The two integers must be equal
optionExplain: The shared remainder is exactly what the principle gives.
Right: the principle gives the shared remainder; the multiple of n still needs to be shown.
Different remainders would contradict the principle.
Two different integers can share a remainder.
questions.explain: Plan the step after the principle.
questions.rule: Pigeonhole often supplies a penultimate step.

questions.q: True or false: according to the author, the pigeonhole principle usually completes a solution by itself, with no further work.
questions.explain: The author says there is often more work to do: the principle sometimes yields only the penultimate step or an intermediate result.
questions.rule: Spot the pigeonhole, choose the pigeons and holes, and expect a finishing step.

questions.q: Eight words are written using only 7 different first letters. Which choice of pigeons and holes proves two share a first letter?
options: That the letters are the pigeons and the words are the holes in the given list
That the dictionary is the pigeon and each word is a hole in the list
That the words are the pigeons and the 7 allowed first letters are the holes
That the word lengths are the pigeons and the vowels are the holes in the list
optionExplain: This reverses the roles.
A dictionary is a single object, not a collection of pigeons.
Right: 8 words into 7 first letters forces a repeat.
Word length and vowels do not set the holes.
questions.explain: Decide the roles before counting.
questions.teaches: The author says quick and beautiful solutions are characteristic of pigeonhole problems.
questions.rule: Spot the pigeonhole, choose the pigeons and holes, and expect a finishing step.

questions.q: Every point of the plane is coloured red or blue. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: Some two points exactly one mile apart have the same colour
Some two points of the same colour are two miles apart
Every point has a point one mile away of the other colour
Half of all points are red
optionExplain: Right: an equilateral triangle of side one mile has three vertices and only two colours.
Two miles apart is not guaranteed by a three-point configuration.
A colouring may avoid giving a point a differently coloured neighbour at exactly that distance.
Colourings can be wildly unbalanced.
questions.explain: The card next gives the pigeonhole argument.
questions.rule: Choose points that are all the required distance from each other, with more points than colours.

questions.q: The vertices of an equilateral triangle of side one mile are three points, but only ____ colours are available.
questions.explain: Three vertices and two colours make a pigeonhole situation.
questions.rule: More points than colours forces a repeat.

questions.q: Every point of the plane is red or blue. Which configuration guarantees two same-coloured points exactly 5 cm apart?
options: The four vertices of a square of side 5 cm
Two points chosen 5 cm apart
A circle of radius 5 cm
The three vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 5 cm
optionExplain: The two same-coloured vertices of a square could be the opposite ones, far apart.
Two points could have different colours.
A circle holds infinitely many points, and the same-coloured ones need not be 5 cm apart.
Right: any two vertices are 5 cm apart, and three points have two colours.
questions.explain: Every pair of chosen points must be exactly the required distance apart.
questions.rule: Every pair in the configuration must be at the required distance.

questions.q: A solver uses the vertices of a unit square to show two same-coloured points one apart. What is wrong?
options: Four vertices are too few to force any repeat of two colours, so a larger figure is required
Two same-coloured vertices might be opposite corners, not one unit apart
A square cannot be drawn inside a coloured plane, so another figure has to be used
Opposite corners of a square must always share a colour, so the pair found is at distance one
optionExplain: Four vertices and two colours do force a repeat; the trouble is where it falls.
Right: red, blue, red, blue around the square puts the same colours at opposite corners.
A square can be drawn anywhere in the plane.
A colouring may give opposite corners different colours.
questions.explain: Every pair must be at the right distance.
questions.rule: A repeat only helps if all pairs are at the right distance.

questions.q: True or false: with three colours, the three vertices of the same equilateral triangle are enough to force two same-coloured points a mile apart.
questions.explain: Our reading: three vertices could each have a different colour. With three colours you need more cleverness, and the book leaves it as an exercise.
questions.rule: Choose points that are all the required distance from each other, with more points than colours.

questions.q: Every point of a plane is painted one of two colours. A surveyor wants two same-coloured points exactly 40 m apart. What can she do?
options: Mark any 40 m line and check its ends
Mark an equilateral triangle of side 40 m; two of its corners match in colour
Mark a circle of radius 40 m and pick two points
Choose any two corners of a square of side 40 m
optionExplain: The two ends of one line can differ in colour.
Right: the same pigeonhole argument works for any distance.
Points on the circle need not be 40 m from one another.
Two corners of a square may be the diagonal.
questions.explain: The distance of one mile in the book is only a scale.
questions.teaches: The author first solves the problem with a circle of radius one mile around a point: if any circle point has the colour of the centre, done; if all are blue, two circle points are one mile apart.
questions.rule: Choose points that are all the required distance from each other, with more points than colours.

questions.q: Five points lie in a unit square. Which is the smallest of these bounds guaranteed on some pair's distance?
options: The square root of 2, about 1.41
The square root of 2 over 2, about 0.71
optionExplain: 1/2 is not guaranteed: the four corners and the centre of the square keep every pair at least 0.71 apart.
The square root of 2 is the diagonal of the whole square and is a weak bound.
1/4 is smaller than any bound the cut can prove.
Right: cutting into four quarters gives a diagonal of the square root of 2 over 2.
questions.explain: The card next shows how the bound arises.
questions.rule: Cut the region into one fewer piece than there are points, and bound the distance inside a piece.

questions.q: To place five points, the author partitions the unit square into ____ smaller squares.
questions.explain: Four holes for five pigeons force a shared square.
questions.rule: One fewer piece than points.

questions.q: Five points are placed in an equilateral triangle of side 2. Cutting it into four equilateral triangles of side 1, what do you conclude?
options: Two of the points are exactly 1 apart
Two of the points are at least 1 apart
Two of the points are at most 1 apart
All of the points are at most 1 apart
optionExplain: The principle gives at most, not exactly.
The bound is an upper bound; a lower bound is not forced.
Right: two points share a small triangle, whose longest distance is its side, 1.
Only two of the points are forced to share a piece.
questions.explain: Two in a piece are no farther apart than the piece's longest distance.
questions.rule: Within a piece, distance is at most its diameter.

questions.q: A solver puts four points at the corners, the fifth at the centre, and checks only that case. What is wrong?
options: It checks one arrangement only, while the claim covers every placement of five points
It gives the wrong distance from the centre to a corner, so the bound on the distances fails
A fifth point cannot be placed in the middle, so the claim cannot be tested at all
The corners are not part of the unit square, so the points cannot be placed there
optionExplain: Right: a single arrangement does not prove the statement for all placements.
The centre is the square root of 2 over 2 from each corner, as stated.
The middle is a valid position.
The corners belong to the closed square.
questions.explain: A proof must cover all placements.
questions.rule: Check all placements, not one.

questions.q: True or false: for four points in the unit square, the same cutting forces two within the square root of 2 over 2.
questions.explain: Four points can occupy the four corners, each a full unit from its neighbours, so no pair need be close.
questions.rule: Cut the region into one fewer piece than there are points, and bound the distance inside a piece.

questions.q: Seventeen sensors lie in a 4 by 4 field. Cut it into sixteen 1 by 1 squares. What does the principle give?
options: Two sensors are at most 1 apart
Two sensors are at least 1 apart
Two sensors are at most the square root of 2 apart
No two sensors are within 4 of each other
optionExplain: Within a unit square the longest distance is the diagonal, not the side.
The principle gives an upper bound, not a lower one.
Right: two sensors share a 1 by 1 square, whose diagonal is the square root of 2.
Sensors in one square are within the square root of 2.
questions.explain: The diagonal of the piece is the bound.
questions.teaches: The book's statement covers points placed anywhere inside or on the boundary of the square, so boundary points count as well.
questions.rule: Cut the region into one fewer piece than there are points, and bound the distance inside a piece.

questions.q: Among any 13 integers, which statement must be true?
options: Two of them differ by a multiple of 12
Two of them differ by exactly 12, which the principle cannot show
Two of them add up to a multiple of 12, which the principle cannot show
One of them is a multiple of 12, which the principle cannot show
optionExplain: Right: 13 integers and 12 possible remainders force two with the same remainder.
Same remainder gives a difference that is a multiple of 12, not exactly 12.
Nothing forces sums to be multiples of 12.
All 13 could avoid multiples of 12.
questions.explain: The card next gives the idea.
questions.rule: Among n + 1 integers, two share a remainder mod n, so their difference is a multiple of n.

questions.q: Two integers have a difference that is a multiple of n exactly when they have the same ____ on division by n.
questions.explain: Writing a = qn + r and b = pn + r gives a - b = (q - p)n.
questions.rule: Same remainder means the difference is a multiple of n.

questions.q: Among any 8 integers, what is the largest n for which two must differ by a multiple of n?
optionExplain: Mod 8 would need 9 integers, since there are 8 remainders.
Right: 8 integers into 7 remainders forces a shared remainder mod 7.
Mod 9 would need 10 integers.
Mod 6 is guaranteed as well, but 7 is larger.
questions.explain: n + 1 integers guarantee a divisor n.
questions.rule: n + 1 integers guarantee a difference divisible by n.

questions.q: A solver says 7 integers must have two differing by a multiple of 7. What is wrong?
options: A repeated remainder would not make the difference divisible by 7
Seven integers have no remainders to compare at all
There are 8 remainders mod 7, so a repeat is forced
The integers 0 to 6 have 7 different remainders, so none needs to share
optionExplain: A shared remainder does make the difference a multiple of 7; the issue is whether one is forced.
Every integer has a remainder; the trouble is that 7 integers can use all 7 remainders.
There are exactly 7 remainders mod 7, not 8.
Right: n integers can use all n remainders once each.
questions.explain: You need more integers than remainders.
questions.rule: Pigeons must outnumber holes.

questions.q: True or false: among any 13 integers, two have a difference that is a multiple of 12.
questions.explain: There are 12 remainders mod 12 and 13 integers, so two share a remainder.
questions.rule: Among n + 1 integers, two share a remainder mod n, so their difference is a multiple of n.

questions.q: On a clock face with 12 hour marks, 13 people each choose a mark. What must be true?
options: Every mark is chosen by someone
Two people chose marks 6 apart
No mark is chosen twice
Two people chose the same mark
optionExplain: Some marks can go unchosen.
Opposite marks are not forced.
A repeat is forced.
Right: 13 choices among 12 marks force a repeat.
questions.explain: The same count is the remainder argument in disguise.
questions.teaches: The author says this simple problem is a building-block that will be used in many other problems later.
questions.rule: Among n + 1 integers, two share a remainder mod n, so their difference is a multiple of n.

questions.q: A set has 10 elements. How many subsets does it have, counting the empty set and the whole set?
optionExplain: 100 is 10 squared, not the count of subsets.
Right: each element is in or out, giving 2 to the power 10.
512 is the count for 9 elements.
2048 is the count for 11 elements.
questions.explain: The card next compares this count with the number of possible sums.
questions.rule: Subsets are the pigeons and sums are the holes; more subsets than sums forces a repeat.

questions.q: In the subset-sums problem the pigeons are the ____ of the numbers.
questions.explain: The subsets are what we place into holes labelled by their sums.
questions.rule: Pigeons: subsets. Holes: sums.

questions.q: Seven different numbers are chosen from 1 to 20. Why do two different non-empty subsets of them have the same sum?
options: There are 127 non-empty subsets but at most 119 possible sums
There are 127 non-empty subsets and 140 possible sums
There are 14 non-empty subsets and 20 possible sums
There are 7 subsets, one for each number, and 20 sums
optionExplain: Right: 127 subsets exceed the 119 values from 1 up to 14 + 15 + ... + 20.
140 is 7 times 20, which would need all seven numbers to equal 20; distinct numbers give at most 119.
Fewer subsets than sums gives no collision.
Fewer subsets than sums gives no collision.
questions.explain: Count the subsets, count the largest possible sum, compare.
questions.rule: More subsets than possible sums forces equal sums.

questions.q: Two subsets A and B have equal sums, but disjoint ones are wanted. A solver calls the argument hopeless. What is wrong?
options: Equal sums cannot be repaired
She should remove only elements from A
Removing the common elements leaves disjoint sets whose sums are still equal
She should add elements to A and B
optionExplain: The repair step works.
Removing only from A changes only A's sum.
Right: removing the same elements from both keeps the sums equal.
Adding elements risks breaking the equality.
questions.explain: Repair rather than abandon a partial solution.
questions.rule: Remove common elements from both sets.

questions.q: True or false: after the common elements are removed, one of the two sets could be empty.
questions.explain: If one set were empty after the removal, the other would have a positive sum equal to zero, which is impossible. The sets are different, so neither is contained in the other.
questions.rule: Subsets are the pigeons and sums are the holes; more subsets than sums forces a repeat.

questions.q: Two distinct subsets A and B of positive numbers have equal sums, and A is contained in B. What does this tell you?
options: This cannot happen
B must be empty, since the sums cancel
A must be empty, with sum zero
It happens whenever two sums are equal
optionExplain: Right: the extra positive elements of B would make its sum larger.
Sums do not cancel; both sums are positive when the sets are non-empty.
A empty would have sum zero while B has a positive sum, so they could not be equal.
Equal sums of different positive subsets do not force one to lie inside the other.
questions.explain: Overlap repairs use that all numbers are positive.
questions.teaches: Dividing into cases is a way to handle the overlap: either A and B are disjoint, or you remove the common elements. The author calls abandoning a partial solution bad problem-solving form.
questions.rule: Subsets are the pigeons and sums are the holes; more subsets than sums forces a repeat.

questions.q: A hundred people have birthdays spread over 12 months. What is the largest number you can be sure some month contains at least?
optionExplain: 8 rounds down; 12 months with at most 8 people each hold only 96, not 100.
Right: 100 divided by 12 is about 8.3, and rounding up gives 9.
10 is not forced: 4 months with 9 and 8 months with 8 add to 100.
12 would need a month to hold a person for each month.
questions.explain: The card next gives the general rule.
questions.rule: At least one hole has \(\lceil p/h \rceil\) or more pigeons; always round up.

questions.q: The ceiling of 3.2, written \(\lceil 3.2 \rceil\), is ____.
questions.explain: The ceiling is the smallest integer that is at least the number.
questions.rule: The ceiling rounds up to the next integer.

questions.q: A school has 250 students in 8 classes. The biggest class must have at least how many students?
optionExplain: 31 comes from rounding down; eight classes of 31 hold only 248.
30 is far below; eight classes of 30 hold only 240.
33 is not forced: classes of 32 and 31 can add to 250.
Right: 250 over 8 is 31.25, and rounding up gives 32.
questions.explain: Divide the pigeons by the holes, then round up.
questions.rule: Divide, then round up.

questions.q: A solver rounds 41 over 10 down to 4 as the best guarantee for some row. What is wrong?
options: The fullest row has exactly 4 rooks, so 4 is the exact value
The ceiling of 4.1 is 4, since 4 is the nearest integer
Rounding up gives 5
The board has too many rows for the rule to be applied
optionExplain: The fullest row can hold more than 4; the rule gives a lower bound only.
The ceiling of 4.1 is the next integer up, 5.
Right: with at most 4 in each of 10 rows only 40 rooks fit, so some row holds 5.
The number of rows is the number of holes, which is what the rule uses.
questions.explain: Round up, not down.
questions.rule: The guarantee is the ceiling.

questions.q: True or false: with 91 passengers on 10 buses, some bus must carry at least 10.
questions.explain: 91 divided by 10 is 9.1, and rounding up gives 10; with 90 passengers the guarantee was only 9.
questions.rule: One extra pigeon can raise the guarantee by one.

questions.q: There are 25 students and 24 desks. What does the intermediate principle say about the fullest desk?
options: At least 2 students share some desk
Exactly 1 student shares each desk
At least 25 students share some desk
No desk need be shared
optionExplain: Right: \(\lceil 25/24 \rceil = 2\), which is the basic principle.
Some desk holds at least two, so not each desk has one.
25 would put every student at one desk, which is not forced.
More students than desks forces a shared desk.
questions.explain: The basic principle is the special case where p is larger than h.
questions.teaches: The basic pigeonhole principle is a corollary of this statement: when p > h the quantity \(\lceil p/h \rceil\) is at least 2.
questions.rule: At least one hole has \(\lceil p/h \rceil\) or more pigeons; always round up.

questions.q: Which claim can the pigeonhole principle prove?
options: 36 coins in 12 boxes: some box holds at least 4
37 coins in 12 boxes: some box holds at least 4
35 coins in 12 boxes: some box holds at least 4
24 coins in 12 boxes: some box holds at least 3
optionExplain: 36 coins can sit 3 to a box, so 4 is not forced.
Right: 37 is 3 times 12 plus 1, and the ceiling of 37 over 12 is 4.
35 coins can sit 3 to a box with room to spare, so 4 is not forced.
24 coins can sit 2 to a box, so 3 is not forced.
questions.explain: The card next describes the numerical hint.
questions.rule: A count that is one past a multiple of the number of holes is a sign to try pigeonhole.

questions.q: In the rooks problem, 41 is one more than 4 times ____.
questions.explain: The 10 is the number of rows, the holes.
questions.rule: Look for one more than a multiple of the number of holes.

questions.q: A hall has 15 rows and 46 people. What is the largest size some row is guaranteed to reach?
options: At least 3 people
At least 5 people
At least 6 people
At least 4 people
optionExplain: 3 is guaranteed, but 4 is the larger guarantee.
5 is not forced: rows of 3 and 4 can hold 46.
6 is not forced: no row needs more than 4 to hold 46.
Right: 46 is 3 times 15 plus 1, so the ceiling of 46 over 15 is 4.
questions.explain: Compute the ceiling.
questions.rule: The ceiling gives the target.

questions.q: A solver says that 41 over 10 rounding up to 5 proves five non-attacking rooks exist. What is wrong?
options: The ceiling of 41 over 10 is not 5
Rooks in one row never attack each other
The match is only a hint; five rooks in one row would attack each other
Five rooks cannot fit on a board
optionExplain: The ceiling is 5.
Rooks in the same row attack each other.
Right: the author says the match suggests probing, but a row with five rooks is not a set of non-attacking rooks.
Rooks fit easily on a 10 by 10 board.
questions.explain: A numerical match is not a proof.
questions.rule: A hint needs a proof behind it.

questions.q: True or false: with 40 rooks on a 10 by 10 board, the numbers still force some row to have 5 rooks.
questions.explain: Forty rooks can sit four to a row, so no row need have five.
questions.rule: A count that is one past a multiple of the number of holes is a sign to try pigeonhole.

questions.q: A bakery boxes 61 buns in 20 trays and wants to say some tray has at least 4. Does the hint apply?
options: No: 61 is not a multiple of 20
Yes, but only if 61 is even
No: pigeonhole needs equal numbers
Yes: 61 is 3 times 20 plus 1, so the ceiling of 61 over 20 is 4
optionExplain: One past a multiple is exactly the hint.
Parity is irrelevant.
Pigeonhole needs more pigeons than holes, not equal numbers.
Right: some tray has at least 4.
questions.explain: Check whether the count is one past a multiple.
questions.teaches: The author says the numerical match is not a solution, but it suggests that we probe carefully for one using the pigeonhole principle.
questions.rule: A count that is one past a multiple of the number of holes is a sign to try pigeonhole.

questions.q: A 10 by 10 board holds 41 rooks. One row holds at least 5 and is removed. At least how many rooks remain?
optionExplain: 36 subtracts only 5, which assumes the row held no more than 5.
Right: the removed row could hold up to 10 rooks, so at least 31 remain.
41 ignores the removal entirely.
5 is the least the removed row holds, not what remains.
questions.explain: The card next carries on.
questions.rule: Pigeonhole, remove the crowded row, pigeonhole again, until you have a row of each size.

questions.q: After removing the first row, the author applies the principle to 31 rooks in ____ rows.
questions.explain: One of the 10 rows has gone, leaving 9.
questions.rule: Each removal leaves one fewer row.

questions.q: Twenty-six rooks stand on an 8 by 8 board. By the author's method, how many non-attacking rooks are guaranteed?
optionExplain: Right: the ceilings give rows with at least 4, 3, 2 and 1 rooks: 26 over 8, then 18 over 7, then 10 over 6, then 2 over 5.
Three rows would stop one step early; the fourth step still gives 1.
A fifth row would need at least 5 left after removing at most 8 more rooks, and there are not enough.
More than 4 is not guaranteed by these counts.
questions.explain: Remove at most 8 rooks each time.
questions.rule: Subtract the worst case each time.

questions.q: A solver subtracts 5 for the removed row and applies pigeonhole to 36 rooks in 9 rows. What is wrong?
options: There are 10 rows left, not 9
The principle cannot be used twice
The removed row may hold up to 10 rooks, so only 31 are certain to remain
The 5 rooks should be added back
optionExplain: One row was removed, leaving 9.
The author applies the principle repeatedly.
Right: using too few rooks removed overstates what is left.
Adding them back undoes the removal.
questions.explain: Subtract the largest possible removal.
questions.rule: Subtract the maximum, not the minimum.

questions.q: True or false: with 40 rooks on 10 by 10, the chain gives rows with at least 4, 4, 3, 2 and 1 rooks.
questions.explain: Our reading: 40 over 10 gives 4, then 30 over 9 gives 4, then 20 over 8 gives 3, then 10 over 7 gives 2, then 0 over 6 gives 0, so a fifth row is not guaranteed.
questions.rule: Pigeonhole, remove the crowded row, pigeonhole again, until you have a row of each size.

questions.q: A librarian uses pigeonhole once and finds the result too weak for her goal. What does the author advise?
options: Use it once to gain a foothold, then use it again and keep extracting information
Abandon the principle and try brute force
Use it only once and trust the result
Apply it to the same rooms again
optionExplain: Right: the author says not to give up when one use is not enough.
Giving up on the principle throws away progress already made.
One use may not give enough information.
Applying it to the same rooms gives the same fact.
questions.explain: Wishful thinking in the author's sense is not giving up.
questions.teaches: The author says to first try for a neat solution with one pigeonhole argument; if that fails, use it once for a foothold and then again, extracting information each time. He later notes that a very simple one-step solution to the rook problem also exists.
questions.rule: Pigeonhole, remove the crowded row, pigeonhole again, until you have a row of each size.

questions.q: Two non-attacking rooks are chosen. The next row has at least 3 rooks. Can one of them attack neither?
options: No, because every rook in the row attacks one of them
Yes, because only 2 columns are taken and the row has 3 rooks
Only if the row is the first row
Only if the two chosen rooks are in adjacent columns
optionExplain: A rook attacks only if it shares a row or column, and the row differs.
Right: at most 2 of the 3 rooks are in taken columns, so one rook is free.
The order of the rows matters, but the row's position is not the issue.
Adjacent columns do not matter.
questions.explain: The card next explains the counting.
questions.rule: Choose rooks from the rows in order of increasing rook count, picking one in a column not yet used.

questions.q: A row with k rooks has a rook in a column not already used, provided at most ____ columns are already used.
questions.explain: If k - 1 columns are taken, at most k - 1 of the row's k rooks are blocked, leaving one free.
questions.rule: A row with k rooks can lose at most k - 1 to used columns.

questions.q: Put the rows in the order in which you should pick their rooks.
items: The row with at least 1 rook
The row with at least 2 rooks
The row with at least 3 rooks
The row with at least 4 rooks
The row with at least 5 rooks
questions.explain: Start with the sparsest row, which needs no free column. Each later row has one more rook than there are used columns.
questions.rule: Sparsest row first.

questions.q: A solver starts with the 5-rook row, then the 1-rook row, whose rook shares a column. What went wrong?
options: The rows should have been chosen at random
The rook in the crowded row should have been chosen last
Rooks in different rows can never share a column
The sparsest row should have been used first, while no columns were taken
optionExplain: Random order has no guarantee of free columns.
That does not describe the error; the order of rows is what failed.
Rooks in different rows can share a column and attack that way.
Right: the author takes the rows in increasing order so each row can escape the used columns.
questions.explain: Order the rows by how few rooks they hold.
questions.rule: Process the sparsest row first.

questions.q: True or false: choosing from the row with at least 3 rooks, at most 2 of its rooks lie in used columns.
questions.explain: Two rooks have been chosen, so only 2 columns are taken. The row has at least 3 rooks, so at least one is free.
questions.rule: Choose rooks from the rows in order of increasing rook count, picking one in a column not yet used.

questions.q: Guests must share no row or seat number. Rows hold at least 1, 2, 3 and 4 guests. In what order should you pick?
options: From the row with at least 4 guests down to the row with at least 1
In any order, since the rows are all different
From the row with at least 1 guest up to the row with at least 4
From the row with at least 2 guests, then at least 1
optionExplain: The sparse rows would be left with no free number.
Order matters because of the free-column count.
Right: each later row has more guests than there are used seat numbers.
Starting with the 2-guest row leaves the 1-guest row exposed later.
questions.explain: The counting argument needs the rows in increasing order.
questions.teaches: The five rows delivered by repeated pigeonhole contain at least 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 rooks, which is exactly the count that the greedy choice needs.
questions.rule: Choose rooks from the rows in order of increasing rook count, picking one in a column not yet used.

questions.q: Running totals P1, ..., P5 are built from a1, ..., a5. What is P5 - P2?
options: a1 + a2
a5 - a2
optionExplain: Right: P5 contains a1 to a5, P2 contains a1 and a2, and the difference is the rest.
That would be P5 minus P1, since P1 holds only a1.
That is the sum already removed, P2.
The difference of two totals is a sum of terms, not a difference of two terms.
questions.explain: The card next explains why this is useful.
