questions.rule: Let the running totals be the pigeons; the difference of two is a sum of consecutive given terms.

questions.q: The difference of two running totals is a sum of ____ terms of the original list.
questions.explain: P(j) - P(i) is the sum of the terms from position i + 1 to position j.
questions.rule: A difference of running totals is a block sum.

questions.q: For 6, 6, 9, 3, 9, with running totals 6, 12, 21, 24, 33, which block of consecutive terms sums to a multiple of 5?
options: 6 + 6, from the first and second terms
3 + 9, from the fourth and fifth terms
6 + 9, from the second and third terms
9 + 3, from the third and fourth terms
optionExplain: 6 + 6 = 12 is not a multiple of 5.
3 + 9 = 12 is not a multiple of 5.
Right: the totals 6 and 21 both leave remainder 1 mod 5, and their difference is 6 + 9 = 15.
9 + 3 = 12 is not a multiple of 5.
questions.explain: Find two totals with the same remainder.
questions.rule: Equal remainders of totals mean a block sum divisible by n.

questions.q: A solver takes the n original numbers as pigeons and says two share a remainder because there are n of them. What is wrong?
options: There are more remainders than numbers
n numbers can have n different remainders, so nothing is forced
Differences of the numbers are never useful
Remainders mod n cannot be 0
optionExplain: There are exactly n remainders, not more.
Right: n pigeons in n holes need not share, so the plain principle gives nothing.
Differences were useful in the earlier remainder problem.
A remainder of 0 is a valid hole.
questions.explain: Count pigeons against holes before relying on them.
questions.rule: n pigeons in n holes force nothing.

questions.q: True or false: if two running totals have the same remainder mod n, the sum of the terms between them is a multiple of n.
questions.explain: The difference of the totals is that sum, and equal remainders make the difference divisible by n.
questions.rule: Let the running totals be the pigeons; the difference of two is a sum of consecutive given terms.

questions.q: A cashier takes 12 payments, in whole pounds. She wants some run of consecutive payments totalling a multiple of 12 pounds. What are the pigeons?
options: The individual payments
The pounds in each payment, one by one
The days of the month
The running totals after each payment
optionExplain: Individual payments give differences that are not run sums.
Single pounds are not what the totals count.
Days of the month have no part in the sums.
Right: a difference of two running totals is a run of payments.
questions.explain: Choose pigeons whose differences give what you want.
questions.teaches: The author says the pigeons may be sums themselves: choose them so that their differences are still sums, which keeps the final claim in the needed form.
questions.rule: Let the running totals be the pigeons; the difference of two is a sum of consecutive given terms.

questions.q: You have n running totals and n possible remainders. A total with remainder 0 would finish the proof. What do you do?
options: Add one more number to get n + 1 totals
Give up on pigeonhole, since n totals are too few
Treat the remainder-0 case separately and use the other n - 1 remainders for the rest
Assume that no total has remainder 0 and ignore the other case
optionExplain: You cannot add numbers that the problem does not give.
n pigeons can still be forced to repeat once a hole is removed.
Right: either a total leaves remainder 0 and you are done, or there are only n - 1 holes for n pigeons.
Ignoring a case leaves a gap in the proof.
questions.explain: The card next gives the argument.
questions.rule: Remove a hole by splitting off the case that finishes by itself, and apply pigeonhole to the rest.

questions.q: If none of the n totals has remainder 0, the n totals fall into only ____ holes.
questions.explain: The remainder 0 is excluded, leaving the n - 1 non-zero remainders.
questions.rule: Excluding one remainder leaves n - 1 holes.

questions.q: Among 9 integers with running totals P1, ..., P9, none leaves remainder 0 mod 9. How many holes can the totals fall into?
optionExplain: 9 includes the excluded remainder 0.
Right: only remainders 1 to 8 remain.
10 is more than the number of remainders.
7 removes one remainder too many.
questions.explain: Count the non-zero remainders.
questions.rule: Non-zero remainders mod n: n - 1 of them.

questions.q: A solver says the first case, a total with remainder 0, shows nothing about the original numbers. What is wrong?
options: A total with remainder 0 cannot exist
A total is never a sum of the original numbers
Only the last total can have remainder 0
A total with remainder 0 is itself a sum of several of the original numbers divisible by n
optionExplain: Totals can leave any remainder, including 0.
A total is a sum of the first k original numbers.
Any of the totals can have remainder 0.
Right: the total Pk is a1 + ... + ak, a sum of several of the integers.
questions.explain: Check what a single total represents.
questions.rule: A total is a sum of the first k numbers.

questions.q: True or false: if every one of the n totals has a non-zero remainder, two of them must share a remainder.
questions.explain: The n totals fall into n - 1 holes, so the pigeonhole principle forces a repeat.
questions.rule: Remove a hole by splitting off the case that finishes by itself, and apply pigeonhole to the rest.

questions.q: A shop logs 10 sale amounts. To find a run of sales totalling a multiple of 10, which move mirrors the author's case split?
options: Check whether any total is itself a multiple of 10, otherwise use 9 holes for 10 totals
Add an extra counter so there are 11 totals
Check only the first total
Count only totals that are multiples of 10
optionExplain: Right: either a total is a multiple of 10 or the totals fall into 9 holes.
The data is not yours to change.
One total cannot decide the case.
Counting only multiples loses the pigeonhole step.
questions.explain: Split off the finishing case first.
questions.teaches: The author notes that sometimes, as in the subset-sums problem, you can reduce the number of pigeonholes needed by dividing into cases.
questions.rule: Remove a hole by splitting off the case that finishes by itself, and apply pigeonhole to the rest.

questions.q: From the numbers 1 to 10, you pick 6. What must be true of the chosen numbers?
options: One of them is a prime number
One of them is a multiple of 3
Two of them are such that one divides the other
One of them is greater than 8
optionExplain: The six numbers 1, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 contain no prime.
The six numbers 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 contain no multiple of 3.
Right: with n = 5, any 6 numbers from 1 to 10 contain a divisor pair.
The six numbers 1 to 6 contain nothing greater than 8.
questions.explain: The card next gives the holes.
questions.rule: Put numbers with the same odd part in the same hole; n holes force a divisor pair among n + 1 numbers.

questions.q: Each number from 1 to 2n can be written as 2 to the power r times an ____ number.
questions.explain: Remove all factors of 2 and an odd number remains.
questions.rule: Every number is a power of 2 times an odd number.

questions.q: For n = 8 (numbers 1 to 16), which pigeonhole contains 12?
optionExplain: 2 and 4 have odd part 1.
24 is beyond 16.
The hole with odd part 3 also holds 3.
Right: 12 = 4 times 3, so it joins the numbers with odd part 3.
questions.explain: Divide out the 2s to find the odd part.
questions.rule: Hole = all numbers with the same odd part.

questions.q: A solver makes holes from numbers with the same last digit. Why does that fail to prove the divisor claim?
options: Two numbers with the same last digit need not divide one another
There are too many last digits to use
Last digits are always 0
It forces the numbers to be equal
optionExplain: Right: 3 and 13 share a last digit, yet neither divides the other.
There are only ten last digits, fewer than needed holes in general.
Last digits range from 0 to 9.
Different numbers can share a last digit.
questions.explain: A hole must force the divisibility property.
questions.rule: Choose holes that force the property you want.

questions.q: True or false: choosing the n numbers n + 1 to 2n avoids any pair in which one divides the other.
questions.explain: A multiple of any of them is at least 2(n + 1) > 2n, so no number in the range divides another in it. This shows n + 1 numbers are needed.
questions.rule: Put numbers with the same odd part in the same hole; n holes force a divisor pair among n + 1 numbers.

questions.q: A tournament numbers its 200 players 1 to 200, and 101 players are chosen for a team. What can the organiser say?
options: Two team members have consecutive numbers
Two team members have numbers where one divides the other
No team member's number divides another's
The team contains the number 200
optionExplain: Consecutive numbers are not forced.
Right: n = 100, and any 101 numbers from 1 to 200 contain a divisor pair.
That contradicts the result.
Nothing forces 200 in the team.
questions.explain: Apply the odd-part holes.
questions.teaches: The author describes the difficulty here as lying in the pigeonholes, not in the pigeons.
questions.rule: Put numbers with the same odd part in the same hole; n holes force a divisor pair among n + 1 numbers.

questions.q: Which set has the property that, for any two members, one divides the other?
optionExplain: 2 and 3 do not divide one another.
Right: each member divides the next.
4 and 6 do not divide one another.
10 and 15 do not divide one another.
questions.explain: The card next builds such sets.
questions.rule: State the property a hole must give, find seeds in a small case, then generalise the partition.

questions.q: A set in which any two members divide one another has a smallest member, which the author calls a ____.
questions.explain: The seed is the smallest element; other members are built from it.
questions.rule: Each hole grows from a seed.

questions.q: For n = 4 (numbers 1 to 8), which partition into 4 chains is right?
optionExplain: 2 and 3 do not divide one another.
5 and 7 do not divide one another.
Right: the seeds are the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, and doubling covers the rest.
3 and 4 do not divide one another.
questions.explain: Take the odd numbers as seeds and double.
questions.rule: Odd seeds, doubled repeatedly, partition 1 to 2n.

questions.q: For n = 5 a solver takes the seeds 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 because they are even. Why does that fail?
options: The number 1 is not covered, and 1 must be the smallest member of its own set
Even seeds produce more than five sets, which is too many
Even seeds cannot be multiplied up to cover larger numbers
Even seeds divide each other, which breaks the property
optionExplain: Right: 1 divides every number, so it must be the smallest member of its own set, and it is not an even seed.
Five seeds give five sets, as needed.
Multiplying seeds is how the sets grow, so even seeds can be multiplied.
Having members that divide each other is the property wanted, not a defect.
questions.explain: Every number must belong to some set.
questions.rule: Make sure every number is covered, starting with 1.

questions.q: True or false: for n = 5 the odd seeds 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 cover every number from 1 to 10 once doubled repeatedly.
questions.explain: The partition is {1, 2, 4, 8}, {3, 6}, {5, 10}, {7}, {9}, which covers 1 to 10.
questions.rule: State the property a hole must give, find seeds in a small case, then generalise the partition.

questions.q: A coach wants groups of players, numbered 1 to 12, so that in any group one number divides another. Which seeds should she use?
options: The six even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12
Only the two numbers 1 and 2
The five primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11
The six odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11
optionExplain: Without the seed 1 the number 1 is left out.
Two seeds cannot cover the numbers 1 to 12.
Primes would leave 1 and 9 uncovered.
Right: odd seeds, multiplied up by 2, cover 1 to 12 in six chains.
questions.explain: Odd seeds reach every number.
questions.teaches: The author says the only 'natural' collection of seeds is the odd numbers, since the even seeds fail to include the number 1.
questions.rule: State the property a hole must give, find seeds in a small case, then generalise the partition.

questions.q: An integer 2 by 2 matrix has an inverse with integer entries. Which values can its determinant take?
options: Any integer
0 or 1 only
1 or -1 only
Any positive integer
optionExplain: Other integers would have inverse determinants that are fractions.
0 would make the matrix not invertible.
Right: det X and det of its inverse are integers whose product is 1.
-1 is possible as well.
questions.explain: The card next uses this.
questions.rule: Define a function of the parameter, show it has few possible values, and pigeonhole to a constant.

questions.q: Five values that are each 1 or -1 must include at least ____ copies of one value.
questions.explain: Five pigeons in two holes put at least three in one hole.
questions.rule: Five values in two classes: at least three alike.

questions.q: A quadratic polynomial takes the value 7 at three different inputs. What can you say about it?
options: It has three roots
It is the constant polynomial 7
It has a minimum value of 7
Nothing, since quadratics can take any value any number of times
optionExplain: Three equal values do not mean roots; 7 is not 0.
Right: a non-constant quadratic takes any value at most twice.
A minimum at 7 would be reached once or twice only.
A non-constant quadratic takes each value at most twice.
questions.explain: Equal values at three inputs force a constant polynomial.
questions.rule: A quadratic with three equal values is constant.

questions.q: A solver gets two equal values among f(0) to f(4) and says that is enough to make the quadratic constant. What is wrong?
options: Equal values never help
A quadratic needs five equal values
Equal values imply the quadratic has a root
Two equal values are not enough; three are needed for a quadratic
optionExplain: Equal values help once there are three.
Three equal values suffice.
Equal values say nothing about roots.
Right: a quadratic can take a value twice without being constant.
questions.explain: Count the repeats you need.
questions.rule: Three equal values force a quadratic to be constant.

questions.q: True or false: if only f(0) to f(3) are known to be 1 or -1, four values, three equal values are still guaranteed.
questions.explain: Four values can split two and two between 1 and -1, so no value is forced to occur three times.
questions.rule: Define a function of the parameter, show it has few possible values, and pigeonhole to a constant.

questions.q: A cubic's values at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 are each 1 or -1. How many inputs must share a value?
options: At least 3 of the 5 inputs
At least 4 of the 5 inputs
At least 5 of the 5 inputs
At least 2 of the 5 inputs
optionExplain: Right: \(\lceil 5/2 \rceil = 3\).
4 is not forced: values 1, 1, 1, -1, -1 split 3 and 2.
5 is not forced.
2 is true but weaker than the ceiling gives.
questions.explain: Apply the ceiling rule to the two classes.
questions.teaches: The define-a-function tool belongs to a larger strategy, generalising the scope of a problem before attacking it; the author also notes that a quadratic polynomial cannot take the same value at three different inputs unless it is constant.
questions.rule: Define a function of the parameter, show it has few possible values, and pigeonhole to a constant.

questions.q: A region in the plane has area 1.36. At least how many lattice points can you make it cover by sliding it, without turning?
optionExplain: 1 is less than the area allows.
Right: the area exceeds 1, so the region can be slid onto 2 lattice points.
3 would need area greater than 2.
A region this size can always be slid onto lattice points.
questions.explain: The card next shows the stacking argument.
questions.rule: Region of area greater than n: stack its lattice pieces; a point under n + 1 pieces gives a translation covering n + 1 lattice points.

questions.q: If the region's area is greater than the whole number n, it can be slid to cover at least ____ lattice points.
questions.explain: The area argument gives a point under at least n + 1 pieces.
questions.rule: Area greater than n gives n + 1 lattice points.

questions.q: A region of area 3.2 can always be slid to cover at least how many lattice points?
optionExplain: Right: 3.2 is greater than 3, so n + 1 = 4.
3 would only need area greater than 2.
5 would need area greater than 4.
2 would need area greater than 1.
questions.explain: n is the largest whole number below the area.
questions.rule: n = whole number less than the area.

questions.q: Put the steps of the lattice-point argument in order.
items: Cut the region along the lattice lines into pieces
Stack all the pieces on one unit square
Find a point lying under at least n + 1 pieces
Rebuild the region and slide it onto lattice points
questions.explain: The cut gives pieces, stacking turns the problem into one about one square, the pigeonhole step finds the crowded point, and the translation uses it.
questions.rule: Cut, stack, find the crowded point, slide.

questions.q: A solver says a region of area exactly 1 must cover 2 lattice points after sliding. What is wrong?
options: The area must be an integer above 2
Sliding changes the area
The area must exceed 1; a half-open unit square covers one lattice point in every position
Lattice points cannot lie on a region
optionExplain: The condition is greater than n, not greater than n + 1.
Sliding keeps the area unchanged.
Right: with area exactly n the guarantee of n + 1 can fail.
Lattice points can lie in or on a region.
questions.explain: Our reading: the argument uses strict inequality.
questions.rule: The area must be strictly greater than n.

questions.q: A bed of area 5.5 square metres is placed on a 1-metre grid. At least how many grid crossings can it cover?
optionExplain: 5 would need only area greater than 4.
7 would need area greater than 6.
11 doubles the count with no basis.
Right: 5.5 is greater than 5, so n + 1 = 6.
questions.explain: Grid crossings are lattice points.
questions.teaches: The argument applies the pigeonhole principle to an infinite set, the points of the unit square, by using area in place of counting.
questions.rule: Region of area greater than n: stack its lattice pieces; a point under n + 1 pieces gives a translation covering n + 1 lattice points.

questions.q: A cube has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces. What is v - e + f?
optionExplain: 0 would come from an arithmetic slip, such as 8 + 6 - 12 - 2.
1 does not match the cube's counts.
26 adds all three counts rather than combining them with signs.
Right: 8 - 12 + 6 = 2, the value Euler's formula gives for any polyhedron without holes.
questions.explain: The card next shows that the same value turns up for every such solid.
questions.rule: v - e + f = 2 for a polyhedron without holes.

questions.q: A quantity that stays the same while other properties of a problem change is called an ____.
questions.explain: An invariant is an aspect of the problem, often a number, that does not change as the problem evolves.
questions.rule: An invariant is a quantity that does not change.

questions.q: A polyhedron without holes has 8 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces does it have?
optionExplain: Right: v - e + f = 2 gives f = 2 - 8 + 12 = 6.
2 is the value of v - e + f, not of f.
4 comes from 12 - 8, forgetting the 2.
18 comes from adding 8 and 12 and subtracting 2.
questions.explain: Use the invariant to fill in the missing number.
questions.rule: v - e + f = 2 for a polyhedron without holes.

questions.q: A solver applies v - e + f = 2 to a picture-frame solid with a hole through it. What does the book say?
options: The formula holds for every solid, holes or not
The formula is stated for polyhedra without holes, so it cannot be assumed here
The formula holds only for cubes
The formula holds only when v equals f
optionExplain: The book's condition excludes this solid.
Right: the book states Euler's formula for a polyhedron without holes.
It is not limited to cubes.
Nothing in the statement requires v to equal f.
questions.explain: Check the condition under which an invariant holds.
questions.rule: An invariant holds only under its stated conditions.

questions.q: True or false: in the motel room paradox, g - p - d stops being zero if the porter pockets a larger amount.
questions.explain: The quantity g - p - d is always zero, because what the guests spent splits into the porter's share and the desk's. The apparent paradox comes from adding p to g.
questions.rule: Find a quantity that stays the same while other things change, and reason from it.

questions.q: Lines through a point P meet a circle at X and Y; PX times PY is the same for every line. What kind of quantity is that?
options: An extreme value, the largest product over all lines
A pigeonhole count of lines through P
An invariant, known as the power of the point P
A monovariant that grows as the line turns
optionExplain: It is the same for every line, so no line gives a largest product.
No counting of objects into boxes is involved.
Right: it does not depend on which line is drawn.
A monovariant changes in one direction; this quantity does not change.
questions.explain: A value that ignores the choice of line is an invariant.
questions.teaches: The author's second example is the Power of a Point theorem, known as POP: the product PX times PY does not depend on the line drawn through P, and is called the power of the point P with respect to the circle.
questions.rule: Find a quantity that stays the same while other things change, and reason from it.

questions.q: A square is turned about its centre. Through which angles does it look unchanged?
options: 0 and 180 degrees only
0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees
0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees
Every angle
optionExplain: The 90-degree turns also work.
Right: these four turns carry the square onto itself.
A 45-degree turn moves the corners to places where there are none.
A circle is unchanged by every angle; a square is not.
questions.explain: The card next links this to invariants.
questions.rule: A symmetry is an invariance under a set of transformations.

questions.q: The author says that symmetry is logically contained within the concept of ____.
questions.explain: A symmetric object is invariant under the transformations that preserve it.
questions.rule: Symmetry is invariance.

questions.q: The quantity x + 1/x is unchanged when x is replaced by which value?
options: x squared
-x
optionExplain: Right: replacing x by 1/x gives 1/x + x, the same quantity.
Replacing x by x squared gives x squared + 1/x squared, which is different.
Replacing x by -x changes the sign of the quantity.
Replacing x by x + 1 changes the quantity.
questions.explain: Check which replacement leaves the quantity alone.
questions.rule: x + 1/x is unchanged when x is replaced by 1/x.

questions.q: Which of these stay unchanged under the stated action?

items.t: A square under a 180-degree turn about its centre
A circle under any turn about its centre
x + 1/x under replacing x by 1/x
A square under a 45-degree turn about its centre
x - 1/x under replacing x by 1/x
x + 1/x under replacing x by 2x

questions.explain: The first three are unchanged. A 45-degree turn moves a square's corners, swapping x and 1/x reverses the sign of x - 1/x, and doubling x changes the sum.
questions.rule: Test each action on the object.

questions.q: True or false: the product of x and 1/x is also unchanged when x is replaced by 1/x.
questions.explain: The product equals 1 for every nonzero x, so swapping the two factors leaves it as it was.
questions.rule: A symmetry is an invariance under a set of transformations.

questions.q: The author's footnote says the invariance of u under swapping some roots is the germ of which later theory?
options: Euler's formula for polyhedra, which counts faces
Pigeonhole theory, which counts boxes
Galois theory, which decides which polynomials can be solved with radicals
Extremal theory, which finds the largest element
optionExplain: Euler's formula concerns solids, not roots.
Pigeonhole arguments count objects, not roots.
Right: the footnote calls it the germ of Galois theory.
The extreme principle looks at largest and smallest elements.
questions.explain: The footnote names a nineteenth-century achievement.
questions.teaches: The author's footnote calls this idea the germ of Galois theory, one of the greatest achievements of nineteenth-century mathematics, which among other things gives a systematic way of deciding which polynomials can be solved with radicals and which cannot.
questions.rule: A symmetry is an invariance under a set of transformations.

questions.q: For n = 136 the digit sum is 1 + 3 + 6 = 10. What is 136 - 10?
options: 126, which is not a multiple of 9
130, which is a multiple of 9
10, which is a multiple of 9
126, which is 9 times 14
optionExplain: 126 is a multiple of 9.
130 is not a multiple of 9, and 136 - 10 is 126.
10 is not a multiple of 9.
Right: 126 = 9 times 14.
questions.explain: The card next states the general fact.
questions.rule: n - s(n) is divisible by 9 for every positive integer n.

questions.q: For every positive integer n, n minus the sum of its digits is divisible by ____.
questions.explain: The remainder of n - s(n) on division by 9 is always zero.
questions.rule: n - s(n) is a multiple of 9.

questions.q: For n = 2025, what is n minus its digit sum?
options: 2016, which is not a multiple of 9
2020, which is a multiple of 9
2025, because the digit sum is zero
2016, which is 9 times 224
optionExplain: 2016 is a multiple of 9.
2020 comes from subtracting 5, not the digit sum.
The digit sum is 2 + 0 + 2 + 5 = 9, not zero.
Right: the digit sum is 9, and 2025 - 9 = 2016 = 9 times 224.
questions.explain: Compute s(n), subtract, then divide by 9.
questions.rule: n - s(n) is a multiple of 9.

questions.q: A solver tests the claim that n - s(n) is divisible by 11 only on n = 1, getting 0. What is the flaw?
options: Zero is not divisible by 11
One passing case proves nothing, and n = 20 gives 18, which is not a multiple of 11
n = 1 is not a positive integer
The digit sum of 1 cannot be computed
optionExplain: Zero is divisible by every positive integer.
Right: a claim for every n needs more than one passing case, and 20 - 2 = 18 refutes it.
1 is a positive integer.
The digit sum of 1 is 1.
questions.explain: Test a conjectured invariant on more than one case.
questions.rule: A single passing case does not establish an invariant.

questions.q: True or false: n - s(n) equals 9 for each of n = 10, 11, 12 and 13.
questions.explain: The values are 10 - 1, 11 - 2, 12 - 3 and 13 - 4, and each equals 9.
questions.rule: n - s(n) is divisible by 9 for every positive integer n.

questions.q: A player takes a number, subtracts its digit sum, then repeats this on each new result. Every result is a multiple of what?
options: 10, because digits are written in base ten
7, because the digit sum is subtracted seven times
9, because each result has the form n - s(n)
2, because digits are added in pairs
optionExplain: The fact concerns 9, not the base 10.
Nothing makes seven subtractions relevant.
Right: n - s(n) is divisible by 9 whatever n is.
Nothing makes the results even.
questions.explain: Apply the invariant at every stage.
questions.teaches: The author describes this as a non-numeric invariant, and notes it can be recast numerically by saying the remainder of n - s(n) on division by 9 is the invariant quantity zero.
questions.rule: n - s(n) is divisible by 9 for every positive integer n.

questions.q: A counter starts at 0. Each step adds 1 or subtracts 2. After 4 steps, which value is impossible?
optionExplain: Right: after 4 steps the value is 4 - 3k for k subtractions, and 0 is not of that form.
1 is reachable with one subtraction.
-2 is reachable with two subtractions.
-5 is reachable with three subtractions.
questions.explain: Look at what the possible values have in common.
questions.rule: Pick one reachable total, then rule out any target with a different remainder.

questions.q: Adding 1 and subtracting 2 change a total by amounts that differ by ____.
questions.explain: The difference between +1 and -2 is 3, so the possible totals at one time differ by multiples of 3.
questions.rule: Changes +1 and -2 differ by 3.

questions.q: A counter starts at 0. Each step adds 2 or subtracts 1. After 10 steps, which value is impossible?
optionExplain: 20 occurs when every step adds 2.
-10 occurs when every step subtracts 1.
Right: after 10 steps the value is 3k - 10 for k additions, and 12 is not of that form.
11 occurs with seven additions and three subtractions.
questions.explain: Find one reachable value, then compare remainders mod 3.
questions.rule: All totals at a fixed time share a remainder.

questions.q: A solver finds a target has the same remainder mod 3 as every reachable total, and concludes it is reachable. What is the flaw?
options: A shared remainder rules targets out, but does not show this one is reachable
The remainder mod 3 can only be 0
Targets cannot be compared by remainders
Reachable totals never share a remainder
optionExplain: Right: the invariant is a necessary condition only.
The shared remainder can be 0, 1 or 2.
Comparing remainders is exactly how targets are ruled out.
In this problem they do share one.
questions.explain: Decide whether the invariant proves or only excludes.
questions.rule: An invariant excludes targets; it does not construct them.

questions.q: True or false: if each step adds 1 or subtracts 3, all totals at a fixed time still share a remainder mod 3.
questions.explain: Adding 1 and subtracting 3 differ by 4, not by a multiple of 3. Subtracting 3 leaves the remainder alone while adding 1 changes it, so different remainders occur.
questions.rule: Pick one reachable total, then rule out any target with a different remainder.

questions.q: A frog starts at 0, and each jump goes 5 right or 2 left. After exactly 8 jumps, which position is impossible?
optionExplain: 40 occurs when every jump goes right.
Right: the position is 40 - 7k for k left jumps, and 20 is not of that form.
12 occurs with four left jumps.
5 occurs with five left jumps.
questions.explain: The two jump lengths differ by 7.
questions.teaches: In the author's solution, one convenient scenario fixes the remainder: if one person enters every minute, the population after 3 to the power 1999 minutes is exactly 3 to the power 1999.
questions.rule: Pick one reachable total, then rule out any target with a different remainder.

questions.q: Is the sum 3 + 5 + 8 + 11 + 14 odd or even?
options: Even, because two terms are even
Even, because the list has five terms
Odd, because the last term is 14
Odd, because three of the terms are odd
optionExplain: The number of even terms does not decide the parity.
The number of terms alone does not decide the parity.
The last term alone does not decide the parity.
Right: the sum is odd exactly when the number of odd terms is odd, and 3, 5 and 11 are odd. The sum is 41.
questions.explain: Count the odd terms.
questions.rule: Ask of every integer problem whether even or odd restricts what can happen.

questions.q: A product of integers is odd exactly when the set contains no ____ element.
questions.explain: A single even factor makes the whole product even.
questions.rule: A product is odd only if every factor is odd.

questions.q: A sum of 17 integers contains exactly 9 odd integers. What is the parity of the sum?
options: Even, because the count of terms is odd
Even, because 8 of the terms are even
Odd, because the number of odd terms is odd
It cannot be known without the values
optionExplain: The total count of terms does not decide parity.
Even terms do not change the parity of a sum.
Right: 9 is odd, so the sum is odd.
Only the number of odd terms matters, and it is known.
questions.explain: Count only the odd terms.
questions.rule: A sum is odd exactly when it has an odd number of odd terms.

questions.q: A solver treats 0 as odd in 0 + 2 + 5 and calls the sum even. What is the flaw?
options: Two is odd, so the sum is even by count
Zero is even, so only one odd term remains and the sum, 7, is odd
A sum of three terms is always odd
Parity cannot be applied to a sum with zero
optionExplain: Two is even, not odd.
Right: the author notes that zero is even.
The number of terms does not decide parity.
Zero is an ordinary even integer in parity arguments.
questions.explain: Check how the facts classify zero.
questions.rule: Zero is even.

questions.q: True or false: a product with one even factor can still be odd if all its other factors are odd.
questions.explain: Any product with an even factor is even, so it is odd only when no factor is even.
questions.rule: Ask of every integer problem whether even or odd restricts what can happen.

questions.q: A bag holds 25 coins worth 1 or 2 cents each, totalling 40 cents. What can be said of the number of 1-cent coins?
options: It is odd, because 25 is odd
It is even, because 40 is divisible by 5
Nothing, as 1-cent coins can take any parity
It is even
optionExplain: The total count is 25, but the amount from 1-cent coins matches 40's parity.
Divisibility by 5 does not decide parity.
The total of 40 restricts the parity.
Right: the total is the 1-cent count plus an even amount, so the count has the parity of 40. It is 10.
questions.explain: Write the total as the 1-cent count plus an even amount.
questions.teaches: The author calls parity the simplest divisibility invariant, and says the facts about sums and products of parities should have been known since childhood.
questions.rule: Ask of every integer problem whether even or odd restricts what can happen.

questions.q: Each handshake involves two people. If everyone adds up their own handshakes, the grand total of all these counts is what?
options: Even, because each handshake is counted twice
Odd when the group has an odd size
Equal to the number of handshakes
Twice the number of people
optionExplain: Right: each handshake adds one to two people's counts.
The size of the group does not decide the parity of the total.
The total is twice the number of handshakes, not equal to it.
The total depends on the handshakes, not the number of people.
questions.explain: Count how many times each handshake appears in the total.
questions.rule: Two parties per event makes the total count even, so an even number of parties have odd counts.

questions.q: Each game involves exactly two players, so the sum of the players' game counts counts every game ____.
questions.explain: A game adds one to each of its two players' counts.
questions.rule: Each event is counted once per party.

questions.q: Could each of 15 people at a party shake hands with exactly 3 others?
options: Yes, because 3 is odd and 15 is odd
No, because the counts would sum to 45, which is odd
Yes, because 15 is divisible by 3
No, because 3 does not divide 45
optionExplain: Odd sizes do not make the arrangement possible.
Right: the sum of the counts must be even, and 15 times 3 is 45.
Divisibility of 15 by 3 does not matter.
3 divides 45, and that is not the reason.
questions.explain: Add up the counts and check the parity.
questions.rule: The sum of the counts is even.

questions.q: A solver proves the tennis claim only for a round-robin tournament. What is the flaw?
options: The problem fixes no structure, so the argument must hold for every tournament
Round robins have too many games to count
Round robins cannot have an odd number of players
Round robins always produce a single winner
optionExplain: Right: the author notes that assuming a particular structure was a common failure.
The count of games does not matter.
Round robins can have an odd number of players.
A single winner has nothing to do with the claim.
questions.explain: Check which assumptions the problem actually gives.
questions.rule: Use only what the problem fixes.

questions.q: True or false: if some games involved three players, the sum of game counts would still have to be even.
questions.explain: A three-player game would be counted three times, so the sum could be odd and the argument would fail.
questions.rule: Two parties per event makes the total count even, so an even number of parties have odd counts.

questions.q: A network has 31 computers, and each cable links exactly two of them. Can exactly 5 computers have an odd number of cables?
options: Yes, because 31 is odd and 5 is odd
Yes, because 5 is a factor of 31
No, because 31 is not divisible by 5
No, because the number with odd counts must be even
optionExplain: The odd size does not allow an odd number of odd counts.
5 does not divide 31, and divisibility is not the point.
Divisibility is not the reason.
Right: the cable counts sum to twice the number of cables, which is even.
questions.explain: Add up the cable counts across all computers.
questions.teaches: The author observes that the sum of the game counts is even not only at the end of the tournament but at any time.
questions.rule: Two parties per event makes the total count even, so an even number of parties have odd counts.

questions.q: For n = 3 and the arrangement (a1, a2, a3) = (2, 3, 1), what is (a1 - 1)(a2 - 2)(a3 - 3)?
optionExplain: 1 would be the product of the first two factors only.
2 has the wrong sign: the third factor is 1 - 3 = -2.
Right: the factors are 1, 1 and -2.
-6 does not match the factors 1, 1 and -2.
questions.explain: Compute each factor first.
questions.rule: Make the factors sum to zero; an odd count of odd integers cannot sum to an even number.

questions.q: For every arrangement of 1 to n, the sum (a1 - 1) + (a2 - 2) + ... + (an - n) equals ____.
questions.explain: The a's are a rearrangement of 1 to n, so their sum equals the sum of 1 to n.
questions.rule: The sum of the factors is zero.

questions.q: Five integers sum to 0, and four of them are odd. What can be said of the fifth?
options: It is odd, because the total is even
It is zero, because the sum is zero
It is even
It cannot be known without the values
optionExplain: An odd fifth term would make the sum odd.
The fifth need not be zero; it can be 2 or -4.
Right: four odd numbers sum to an even number, and the total is even, so the fifth is even.
The parity is forced.
questions.explain: Combine the parities of the terms.
questions.rule: An odd count of odd integers cannot sum to an even number.

questions.q: A solver says the argument shows the product is even for every n, since the sum is zero. What does n = 2 show?
options: The arrangement 1, 2 gives 1, so the sum is not zero
The product 0 is odd for n = 2
No arrangement exists for n = 2
The arrangement 2, 1 gives 1 times -1 = -1, so the argument needs n odd
optionExplain: The arrangement 1, 2 gives factors 0 and 0, so the product is 0 and the sum is 0.
Zero is even.
Two arrangements exist.
Right: with two terms, two odd factors sum to an even number, so no contradiction arises.
questions.explain: Test the claim on the smallest even n.
questions.rule: The argument uses that n is odd.

questions.q: True or false: for n = 4, every arrangement of 1, 2, 3, 4 gives an even product.
questions.explain: Some arrangements give an odd product; for example 2, 1, 4, 3 gives factors 1, -1, 1, -1 with product 1.
questions.rule: Make the factors sum to zero; an odd count of odd integers cannot sum to an even number.

questions.q: The numbers b1, ..., b9 are a rearrangement of 10, 11, ..., 18. Why is (b1 - 10)(b2 - 11)...(b9 - 18) even?
options: The factors are consecutive integers, so one is even
The nine factors sum to 0, and nine odd integers would sum to an odd number
Nine is divisible by three, so a factor is even
The b's are larger than the numbers subtracted
optionExplain: The factors need not be consecutive integers.
Right: the same argument applies with 9 factors.
Divisibility of 9 by 3 plays no role.
Size comparisons do not decide parity.
questions.explain: Add the factors and use parity.
questions.teaches: The author calls the second solution especially clever and advises being on the lookout for easy invariants: rearrange the problem to get simple numbers such as zero or one.
questions.rule: Make the factors sum to zero; an odd count of odd integers cannot sum to an even number.

questions.q: A line L passes through the interior of the segment PQ. What does this say about P and Q?
options: They lie on opposite sides of L
They lie on the same side of L
They both lie on L
One of them lies on L
optionExplain: Right: crossing the interior means the endpoints are on opposite sides.
If both were on the same side, the segment would not cross L.
Endpoints on L would not give an interior crossing.
An endpoint on L would not give an interior crossing.
questions.explain: Think about where the endpoints must be.
questions.rule: Follow the left-right state around the loop; an odd loop forces the start and end onto the same side.

questions.q: If a line passes through the interior of a segment, its endpoints lie on ____ sides of the line.
questions.explain: That is what crossing the segment means.
questions.rule: A crossing flips the side.

questions.q: A closed chain has 7 points P1 to P7. A line crosses P1P2, ..., P6P7, with P1 on the left. Where is P7?
options: On the right, opposite to P1
On the left, the same side as P1
On the line itself
Its side cannot be determined
optionExplain: The sides alternate, so after an even number of flips it is back on the left.
Right: six crossings flip the side an even number of times.
The chain is crossed in the interior, so no point lies on the line.
The sides are fixed by the alternation.
questions.explain: Flip the side once per segment.
questions.rule: Each crossing flips the side.

questions.q: A solver finds a line works for 4 points and concludes it works for 1997 points. What is the flaw?
options: Parity matters: the line works only for an even number of points, and 1997 is odd
Large numbers of points cannot be crossed by one line
Four points is too few to form a closed chain
The line must pass through every point as well
optionExplain: Right: small experiments cannot be extended without understanding the parity pattern.
The size does not matter; the parity does.
Four points form a closed chain.
The line only needs to cross the segments.
questions.explain: Look for what changes between 4 points and 1997.
questions.rule: Small cases reveal a pattern; the proof explains it.

questions.q: True or false: for a closed chain of 1998 points, the side-alternation argument produces a contradiction.
questions.explain: With an even number of points, P1998 is on the right, opposite to P1, so the last segment can be crossed.
questions.rule: Follow the left-right state around the loop; an odd loop forces the start and end onto the same side.

questions.q: A closed polygon has 11 sides. Can one straight line pass through the interior of every side?
options: Yes, because 11 is prime
Yes, because a straight line always cuts a polygon
No, because 11 is odd
No, because 11 sides cannot close
optionExplain: Primality is irrelevant.
A line can miss a polygon entirely.
Right: the argument for an odd closed chain applies.
A polygon with 11 sides closes normally.
questions.explain: Count the number of sides and use parity.
questions.teaches: The author says a few experiments with much smaller numbers of points convince you that the line can be drawn if and only if the number of points is even.
questions.rule: Follow the left-right state around the loop; an odd loop forces the start and end onto the same side.

questions.q: 12 and 27 have equal exponent parities for the primes 2 and 3. Is 12 times 27 a perfect square?
options: No, because 12 and 27 are not squares
No, because 3 is odd in both
Yes, because both are divisible by 3
Yes, because 12 times 27 = 324 = 18 squared
optionExplain: A product of non-squares can still be a square.
The exponent of 3 is odd in both, which makes it even in the product.
Divisibility by 3 alone does not make a product a square.
Right: matching parities give a perfect-square product.
questions.explain: Multiply the two numbers and check.
questions.rule: Same parity pattern means the product is a perfect square; patterns are the pigeonholes.

questions.q: With the 9 primes up to 23, the number of possible exponent-parity patterns is 2 to the power 9, which equals ____.
questions.explain: Each of the 9 exponents has two parities, chosen independently.
questions.rule: There are 2^9 = 512 patterns.

questions.q: Nine positive integers have only 2, 3 and 5 as prime factors, giving 8 parity patterns. What follows?
options: All nine have different patterns
Their product of all nine is a perfect square
Three of the integers share a pattern
Two of the integers share a pattern, so their product is a perfect square
optionExplain: Nine integers cannot all have different patterns among eight.
The product of all nine need not be a square.
Only two sharing is forced.
Right: 9 integers in 8 patterns forces a repeat.
questions.explain: Count the pigeons against the holes.
questions.rule: More integers than patterns forces a repeated pattern.

questions.q: A solver says there are 9 times 2 = 18 parity patterns for 9 primes. What is the flaw?
options: There are only 9 patterns, one per prime
Zero is not allowed as an exponent
Each exponent's parity is chosen independently, so the count is 2 to the ninth
The count should be 9 factorial
optionExplain: Each prime has two choices, so there are more than 9 patterns.
Zero is allowed and counts as even.
Right: 2 times 2 and so on, nine times, gives 512.
The patterns are not arranged in orders.
questions.explain: Count the choices for each prime independently.
questions.rule: Independent choices multiply.

questions.q: True or false: with exactly 512 integers, two must share a parity pattern.
questions.explain: 512 integers could take each of the 512 patterns once, so no repeat is forced; 513 integers are needed.
questions.rule: Same parity pattern means the product is a perfect square; patterns are the pigeonholes.

questions.q: After pairing numbers into squares c_i, why can the square roots of the c_i be treated as new pigeons?
options: They are all equal to each other
They are integers with the same allowed primes, so each again has one of 512 patterns
They are larger than the original numbers
They are all odd integers
optionExplain: The square roots are not equal to each other.
Right: the second pigeonhole step then pairs two square roots with the same pattern.
Their size does not give a pattern.
The roots need not be odd.
questions.explain: Check what primes the square roots can contain.
questions.teaches: The author uses the pigeonhole principle twice: from 1,985 integers 1,472 form 736 pairs with square products, then among the 736 square roots two share a pattern, giving a fourth power.
questions.rule: Same parity pattern means the product is a perfect square; patterns are the pigeonholes.

questions.q: A rectangle has its lower-left corner at a lattice point and measures 3 by 2.5. How many of its corners are lattice points?
optionExplain: Right: the corners (0, 0) and (3, 0) are lattice points; the corners at height 2.5 are not.
One would count only the anchored corner.
Three would need another integer coordinate pair.
Four would need both sides to be integers.
questions.explain: List the four corners and their coordinates.
questions.rule: Count lattice-point corners two ways: by tile (even total) and by corner multiplicity (w + 2g + 4b).

questions.q: A rectangle anchored at a lattice point has an integral side exactly when its number of lattice corners is ____.
questions.explain: It has two lattice corners if one side is integral and four if both are; otherwise only one.
questions.rule: Goodness equals an even lattice-corner count.

questions.q: A tiling has S = 24, with g = 9 corners counted twice and b = 1 counted four times. What is w?
optionExplain: 4 would come from forgetting the 4 times b.
6 would come from forgetting 2 times g.
14 would come from subtracting g and b without weights.
questions.explain: Use S = w + 2g + 4b.
questions.rule: S = w + 2g + 4b.

questions.q: A solver says S counts only the corners of the big rectangle. What is the flaw?
options: S counts the corners of the largest tile only
S counts each lattice corner exactly four times
S counts only corners that lie outside the rectangle
S counts every lattice corner once per tile, so interior corners are counted twice or four times
optionExplain: S sums over all tiles.
Corners are counted once, twice or four times, not always four.
The corners lie on or inside the rectangle.
Right: only the corners of the big rectangle are counted once.
questions.explain: Decide how many tiles share each corner point.
questions.rule: Interior corner points are counted more than once.

questions.q: True or false: the evenness of S depends on every small rectangle having an integral side.
questions.explain: A tile without an integral side could have exactly one or three lattice corners, which would make S odd.
questions.rule: Count lattice-point corners two ways: by tile (even total) and by corner multiplicity (w + 2g + 4b).

questions.q: A floor measuring 7.5 by 4.2 is covered by rectangular tiles, each with at least one whole-number side. Is this possible?
options: No, because the floor would need a whole-number side
Yes, if the tiles are laid in rows
Yes, because each tile has a whole-number side
Only if the floor were square
optionExplain: Right: the tiling theorem says the floor must have an integral side.
Laying in rows does not change the theorem.
Each tile's side does not carry over to the floor without the theorem.
Squareness is not required.
questions.explain: Apply the result to the floor's sides.
questions.teaches: The author names two crux moves: anchoring the lower-left corner at a lattice point, which gives free information, and deducing the parity rule for goodness; the rest is counting in two ways, a tactic treated in Chapter 6.
questions.rule: Count lattice-point corners two ways: by tile (even total) and by corner multiplicity (w + 2g + 4b).

questions.q: What is the remainder when 10 cubed, which is 1000, is divided by 9?
optionExplain: 0 would mean 9 divides 1000, which it does not.
3 does not match 1000 = 9 times 111 + 1.
Right: 1000 = 9 times 111 + 1.
10 is larger than 9, so it cannot be a remainder.
questions.explain: Divide 1000 by 9 and look at what is left.
questions.rule: Replace each number by its remainder modulo a well-chosen m, and track that.

questions.q: Since 10 is congruent to 1 modulo 9, 10 to the k is congruent to ____ modulo 9 for every nonnegative integer k.
questions.explain: Each power of 1 is 1, so every power of 10 leaves remainder 1.
questions.rule: 10 to the k leaves remainder 1 modulo 9.

questions.q: What remainder does 7384 leave on division by 9?
optionExplain: Right: the digit sum is 22, and 22 leaves remainder 4.
2 is a digit of 22, not its remainder.
7 is a digit of 7384, not the remainder.
22 is the digit sum, not a remainder modulo 9.
questions.explain: Use the digit sum, then reduce again.
questions.rule: A number and its digit sum agree modulo 9.

questions.q: A solver says 10 to the k is congruent to 1 modulo 11 too, so digit sums give remainders mod 11. What is wrong?
options: Modulo 11, 10 is congruent to 0
Modulo 11, all powers of 10 are 10
Modulo 11, 10 is congruent to -1, so powers of 10 alternate between 1 and -1
Digit sums are defined only for 9
optionExplain: 10 leaves remainder 10 on division by 11, not 0.
Powers of 10 do not all leave remainder 10.
Right: 10 is congruent to -1 modulo 11, so the powers alternate in sign.
Digit sums exist for any modulus; they do not work for 11.
questions.explain: Compute 10 and 100 modulo 11.
questions.rule: The shortcut needs the base to be congruent to 1.

questions.q: True or false: a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder on division by 3.
questions.explain: 10 is congruent to 1 modulo 3 as well, so every power of 10 leaves remainder 1 and the same argument applies.
questions.rule: Replace each number by its remainder modulo a well-chosen m, and track that.

questions.q: A number is written in base 8. Its octal digit sum is found. Modulo which number do the number and its octal digit sum agree?
options: 9, because 8 is congruent to -1 modulo 9
8, because the base is 8
6, because 8 is congruent to 2 modulo 6
7, because 8 is congruent to 1 modulo 7
optionExplain: 8 is congruent to -1 modulo 9, which alternates signs.
The base itself leaves remainder 0 modulo 8.
8 is congruent to 2 modulo 6, which gives no constant weight.
Right: 100 in decimal is 144 in octal, with digit sum 9, and both leave remainder 2 modulo 7.
questions.explain: Look for a modulus in which the base is congruent to 1.
questions.teaches: The author notes that congruence notation is not required, but it is a convenient shorthand that helps systematise thinking, and the important thing is to be aware that an invariant may be a quantity modulo m for a properly chosen m.
questions.rule: Replace each number by its remainder modulo a well-chosen m, and track that.

questions.q: A chamber holds (10, 11, 111) particles of types X, Y, Z. An X and a Y collide and both become Z. New population?
optionExplain: Z gains two particles, not one.
Right: X and Y each lose one, and Z gains two.
Y loses a particle in this collision rather than gaining two.
X and Y lose particles; they do not gain them.
questions.explain: Two particles disappear and two new ones appear.
questions.rule: Track the gaps between populations modulo 3; a gap that is not 0 modulo 3 can never close.

questions.q: In the chamber, each collision changes the gap between two populations by 0 or by a multiple of ____.
questions.explain: A collision shifts counts by 1 and 2, so gaps change by 0 or 3.
questions.rule: Gaps are invariant modulo 3.

questions.q: The starting populations are (7, 9, 14) under the same collision rules. Can the particles all become one type?
options: Yes, because 14 is the largest population
Yes, because the total is divisible by 3
No, because no gap between two populations is a multiple of 3
No, because 7 is odd
optionExplain: The size of 14 does not decide it.
The total of 30 does not decide it; the gaps do.
Right: the gaps are 2, 5 and 7, none of which is divisible by 3, and two populations must reach zero together.
Oddness plays no role.
questions.explain: Check the three gaps modulo 3.
questions.rule: A gap not divisible by 3 can never reach zero.

questions.q: Populations start at (7, 10, 14). A solver sees the X-Y gap, 3, divisible by 3, and says one type is reachable. Flaw?
options: The gap of 3 proves it cannot happen
The invariant does not rule it out, but that is not a proof that it can happen
Gaps modulo 3 are never useful
The solver should have used the Y-Z gap only
optionExplain: A gap of 3 is consistent with a zero gap.
Right: an invariant excludes outcomes; reaching one needs a construction.
Gaps modulo 3 are the invariant used here.
No single gap decides the question.
questions.explain: Decide whether the invariant proves or only excludes.
questions.rule: An invariant is a necessary condition only.

questions.q: True or false: if the X-Y gap started at 2, X and Y could not both reach zero.
questions.explain: The gap stays congruent to 2 modulo 3, while both being zero would give a gap of 0.
questions.rule: Track the gaps between populations modulo 3; a gap that is not 0 modulo 3 can never close.

questions.q: Red, green, blue tokens number (4, 6, 9). Two of different colours become two of the third. Which pair might reach zero together?
options: Red and green, whose gap is 2
Red and blue, whose gap is 5
No pair, because totals are fixed
Green and blue, whose gap of 3 is a multiple of 3
optionExplain: A gap of 2 is not congruent to 0 modulo 3.
A gap of 5 is congruent to 2 modulo 3.
One pair is not ruled out.
Right: the gap between green and blue is 3, congruent to 0.
questions.explain: Compute each gap modulo 3.
questions.teaches: The author first experiments: the X-Y gap stays at 1, while the Y-Z gap goes 100, 103, 106, back to 103, which looks chaotic until modular arithmetic suggests that the gaps are invariant modulo 3.
questions.rule: Track the gaps between populations modulo 3; a gap that is not 0 modulo 3 can never close.

questions.q: 66 times 62 equals 4092. Does the area alone rule out tiling this rectangle with 12 by 1 strips?
options: No, because 4092 = 12 times 341
Yes, because 66 and 62 are not multiples of 12
Yes, because 4092 is even
No, because strips have area 1
optionExplain: Right: the area is divisible by 12, so the area test passes.
The sides not being multiples of 12 does not change the area.
Evenness is not the relevant test.
Each strip has area 12.
questions.explain: Divide the area by the area of one strip.
questions.rule: Colour so every tile is balanced, then show the region is not.

questions.q: A colouring is called homogeneous if each colour occurs the same ____ of times.
questions.explain: In a homogeneous colouring all colours appear equally often.
questions.rule: Homogeneous means equal counts of each colour.

questions.q: A 14 by 21 rectangle is cut using multiples of 6 along each side. What size of piece is left over?
options: 2 by 3
2 by 21
14 by 3
optionExplain: 12 by 18 is the largest homogeneous piece.
Right: 14 = 12 + 2 and 21 = 18 + 3, leaving a 2 by 3 piece.
2 by 21 has a side divisible by 3 but contains a homogeneous portion.
14 by 3 is not a corner remainder.
questions.explain: Subtract the largest multiple of 6 from each side.
questions.rule: Cut off pieces with a side divisible by the strip length.

questions.q: A solver says any rectangle with area divisible by 12 can be tiled by 12 by 1 strips. What does the book's example show?
options: Every rectangle with area divisible by 12 can be tiled
Area never matters in tiling problems
66 by 62 has area divisible by 12 but cannot be tiled
Only square rectangles can be tiled
optionExplain: The example contradicts the claim.
Area is a necessary condition, so it does matter.
Right: divisibility of the area is necessary but not sufficient.
Squares are not required.
questions.explain: Find a case where the area test passes and tiling fails.
questions.rule: Divisible area is necessary, not sufficient.

questions.q: True or false: a 24 by 17 rectangle can be tiled by 12 by 1 strips.
questions.explain: The side 24 is a multiple of 12, so each row of length 24 holds two strips and 17 such rows fill the rectangle.
questions.rule: Colour so every tile is balanced, then show the region is not.

questions.q: Can a 10 by 15 board, with area 150, be tiled by 6 by 1 strips?
options: Yes, because 150 is divisible by 6
Yes, because 15 is divisible by 5
No, because 10 is even
No, because the leftover 4 by 3 corner is not coloured homogeneously
optionExplain: Divisible area is necessary but not sufficient.
Divisibility by 5 does not matter.
Evenness of 10 does not matter.
Right: with 6 colours the 4 by 3 piece has colour counts 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1.
questions.explain: Use a 6-colour diagonal pattern.
questions.teaches: The author finds the conjecture by experimenting with smaller configurations m by n where neither m nor n is a multiple of 12 yet the product mn is.
questions.rule: Colour so every tile is balanced, then show the region is not.

questions.q: Each step adds 1 or subtracts 2. Modulo which number are these two changes equal?
optionExplain: Right: 1 and -2 differ by 3.
Modulo 2 they differ: 1 is odd and -2 is even.
They differ by 3, not by 4.
They differ by 3, not by 5.
questions.explain: Find the difference of the two changes.
questions.rule: Pick m so that the allowed changes agree modulo m.

questions.q: Modular arithmetic reduces the infinite set of integers to the finite set of possible ____ modulo m.
questions.explain: Each integer is replaced by its remainder on division by m.
questions.rule: Reduce integers to remainders.

questions.q: Match each problem to the modulus or colour count that serves it.
pairs: Relating a number to its digit sum
questions.explain: Digit sums use 9, the room puzzle 3, the strips 12 colours, and pairs the crude modulus 2.
questions.rule: Match the modulus to the problem's step sizes.

questions.q: A solver uses parity for the room puzzle, with steps +1 or -2, and finds no obstruction. What is wrong?
options: The puzzle has no invariant at all
Parity does not separate the steps well; modulo 3 makes the changes agree
Parity can never be an invariant
The room must contain an even number of people
optionExplain: The invariant exists modulo 3.
Right: the changes are equal modulo 3, which is the modulus that fits.
Parity is an invariant in many problems.
Nothing forces the room to be even.
questions.explain: Look at whether a different modulus fits better.
questions.rule: A modulus must fit the step sizes.

questions.q: True or false: if each step adds 1 or subtracts 4, all totals at a fixed time share a remainder modulo 5.
questions.explain: The two changes differ by 5, so any two possible totals differ by a multiple of 5.
questions.rule: Pick m so that the allowed changes agree modulo m.

questions.q: Each step adds 3 or subtracts 4. Which modulus makes all totals at a fixed time share a remainder?
optionExplain: Modulo 1 everything agrees, so it says nothing.
Modulo 3 the steps are 0 and 2, which differ.
Right: 3 and -4 differ by 7.
Modulo 12 the steps are 3 and 8, which differ.
questions.explain: Find the difference between the two steps.
questions.teaches: The author says that colouring is related to parity and modular arithmetic, except that we are not constrained by the algebraic properties of integers.
questions.rule: Pick m so that the allowed changes agree modulo m.

questions.q: In a knockout tournament, each game removes the loser. With 8 players, how many games are played until one remains?
optionExplain: Right: each game removes one player, so 7 games remove 7 players.
3 counts rounds, not games.
4 counts the games in the first round only.
8 counts players, not games.
questions.explain: Count how many players must be removed.
questions.rule: Track a quantity that moves in one direction only, and use where it starts and ends.

questions.q: A quantity that may change at each step, but only ever in one direction, is called a ____.
questions.explain: A monovariant is monotone: it never reverses direction.
questions.rule: A monovariant changes in only one direction.

questions.q: 100 contestants play an elimination tournament. How many games are played?
options: 100, because each player plays once
50, because players are paired off
98, because the last two players do not play
99, because each game removes exactly one player
optionExplain: Players can play several games.
Pairing off gives 50 games in one round only.
The last two do play the final game.
Right: the number of players left drops by one per game, from 100 to 1.
questions.explain: Find how the number of remaining players changes per game.
questions.rule: n contestants require n - 1 games.

questions.q: A solver says an elimination tournament with n players needs n - 1 games only if n is a power of 2. What is wrong?
options: Players who lose may continue to play
Games with byes remove two players
n - 1 counts rounds, not games
Each game removes one player whatever the structure, so byes do not change the count
optionExplain: In elimination, a loser is out.
A bye removes nobody and is not a game.
n - 1 counts games.
Right: the monovariant is the number of players left, which falls by one per game.
questions.explain: Check what happens to the player count at every game.
questions.rule: The count falls by one per game, whatever the pairing.

questions.q: True or false: with 20 players, the number of games is the same whether or not some players get a bye in some round.
questions.explain: A bye is not a game, and every game still removes exactly one player, so there are 19 games.
questions.rule: Track a quantity that moves in one direction only, and use where it starts and ends.

questions.q: A 4 by 6 chocolate bar is broken along grid lines into 24 squares. Each break splits one piece in two. How many breaks?
options: 24, because there are 24 squares
23, because the number of pieces rises by one per break
10, the number of grid lines
12, because each break halves a piece
optionExplain: That would be one break per square, but the first square needs none.
Right: the pieces count goes from 1 to 24 in steps of one.
The count of grid lines does not determine the breaks.
Breaks need not halve a piece.
questions.explain: Find the quantity that moves one way by exactly one each time.
questions.teaches: The author says monovariants, also called semi-invariants, are often used to show that certain final configurations must occur and to determine how long the system runs, and that many arguments combine them with the well-ordering principle.
questions.rule: Track a quantity that moves in one direction only, and use where it starts and ends.

questions.q: Cards 3, 1, 2 have 3 on top. The rule reverses the first 3 cards. What is the new order?
optionExplain: That would reverse only part of the deck.
That moves 3 to the middle rather than reversing.
Right: reversing all three cards turns 3, 1, 2 into 2, 1, 3.
That sorts the deck, which is not what reversal does.
questions.explain: Reverse the first k cards where k is the top card.
questions.rule: Reverse the first k cards, where k is the top card.

questions.q: The extreme principle picks the largest label that ever appears in the first ____ of the deck.
questions.explain: That largest first-place value is called L1.
questions.rule: Take the largest first-place value that ever occurs.

questions.q: Start with the deck 2, 3, 1 and apply the rule until 1 is on top. How many moves are made?
options: Two moves, ending at 1, 2, 3
One move, ending at 3, 2, 1
Three moves, ending at 1, 3, 2
No moves, since 1 is in the deck
optionExplain: Right: 2, 3, 1 becomes 3, 2, 1, which becomes 1, 2, 3.
After one move the top card is 3, not 1.
The order 1, 3, 2 does not arise.
The top card is 2, so a move is needed.
questions.explain: Apply the rule at each step.
questions.rule: Reverse the first k cards.

questions.q: A solver says the first-place number rises from 2 to 6 at times, so the argument fails. What is the fix?
options: The first card does decrease, so the solver miscounted
Only the last card matters in the argument
A finite deck does not give a largest value
The first card is not monotone; the successive maxima L1, L2, ... strictly decrease
optionExplain: The first-place value can rise.
The first card, not the last, is tracked.
A finite set of values has a largest.
Right: the monotone quantity is the sequence of maxima of first-place values.
questions.explain: Find which quantity is actually monotone.
questions.rule: The maxima L1 > L2 > ... decrease.

questions.q: True or false: after the largest first-place value L1 has appeared, it can appear in first place again.
questions.explain: The card L1 sits in the L1-th place and later reversals involve fewer than L1 cards, so it cannot move back to the top.
questions.rule: The successive largest first-place values form a strictly decreasing sequence, ending at 1.

questions.q: Four cards start as 3, 4, 2, 1. The top card k reverses the first k cards. How many moves put 1 on top?
optionExplain: After two moves the top card is 4.
The process stops as soon as 1 is on top.
The process halts after 3 moves.
questions.explain: Simulate the rule step by step.
questions.teaches: In the author's six-card example the successive largest first-place values are L1 = 6 at step 3, L2 = 5 at step 6 and L3 = 4 at step 8.
questions.rule: The successive largest first-place values form a strictly decreasing sequence, ending at 1.

questions.q: A process moves among 5 possible states without revisiting any. At most how many moves can it make?
optionExplain: 3 moves visit only 4 states.
5 moves would visit 6 states.
Right: visiting all 5 states takes 4 moves, and a fifth move would repeat.
10 is not bounded by the number of states in this way.
questions.explain: Count states visited against moves made.
questions.rule: Finite states mean repeat or halt; rule out the repeat to show halting.

questions.q: If there are only finitely many states, either a state repeats or the evolution will eventually ____.
questions.explain: A process that does not repeat must reach a state with no further move.
questions.rule: Finite states: repeat or halt.

questions.q: A deterministic machine has 10 possible states and runs for 11 steps from its start state. What must be true?
options: The machine has halted
Some state has occurred twice
Every state has occurred once
No state has occurred twice
optionExplain: A machine that runs 11 steps has not necessarily halted.
Right: 12 states have been visited, counting the start, but there are only 10.
Not every state need be visited.
The principle forces a repeat.
questions.explain: Count the states visited against the available states.
questions.rule: More visits than states forces a repeat.

questions.q: A solver says: there are finitely many states, so the process must halt. What is the flaw?
options: Finite state sets never halt
Halting needs infinitely many states
The process must repeat at the first step
It may repeat states forever; halting needs repeats to be ruled out
optionExplain: Processes with finitely many states can halt.
Infinitely many states are not needed.
A repeat can occur later.
Right: the principle gives repeat or halt, not halt.
questions.explain: Check which of the two alternatives has been shown.
questions.rule: Finite states give repeat or halt.

questions.q: True or false: with infinitely many possible states, the process must still repeat or halt.
questions.explain: The principle needs finitely many states; with infinitely many, the run can go on without repeating.
questions.rule: Finite states mean repeat or halt; rule out the repeat to show halting.

questions.q: A whole-number score starts at 40, and every move lowers it by at least 1 but not below 0. At most how many moves occur?
options: Unlimited
optionExplain: A score from 40 to 0 allows 40 moves of size 1.
Right: each move lowers the score by at least 1 and it cannot go below 0.
41 would take the score below 0.
A bounded integer score limits the moves.
questions.explain: Bound the number of moves by the range of the score.
questions.teaches: In the author's formal solution, f_i denotes the value of the first card after i steps, and the aim is to show that f_m = 1 for some m, after which f_n = 1 for all n at least m.
questions.rule: Finite states mean repeat or halt; rule out the repeat to show halting.

questions.q: Let s = (-1 + sqrt 5)/2, which satisfies s squared + s - 1 = 0. What is 1 - s equal to?
options: s
2s
s squared
optionExplain: 1 - s is about 0.382, while s is about 0.618.
2s is about 1.236.
Right: from s squared + s = 1 we get 1 - s = s squared.
1/s is about 1.618.
questions.explain: Rearrange s squared + s - 1 = 0.
questions.rule: Rearrange s squared + s - 1 = 0 to relate 1 - s to s squared.

questions.q: In Conway's checker problem a checker at distance d from the target has weight s to the power ____.
questions.explain: The weights decrease geometrically with distance.
questions.rule: Weight is s to the power of the distance.

questions.q: A jump toward C removes weights s^d and s^(d-1) and adds s^(d-2). What is the net change?
options: Zero, because 1 - s - s squared equals 0
Positive, because the checker gets closer
Negative, because two checkers are removed
s^(d-2), the added weight
optionExplain: Right: the change is s^(d-2) times (1 - s - s squared), which is 0.
The sum is designed to be unchanged on such jumps.
Removing two checkers is balanced by the added weight.
The added weight is cancelled by the removed ones.
questions.explain: Factor out s^(d-2).
questions.rule: Jumps toward C leave the sum unchanged.

questions.q: A solver finds a jump away from C changes the sum by s^d(-1 - s + s squared) and calls it positive. Flaw?
options: s^d is negative
-1 - s + s squared equals -2s, which is negative
-1 - s + s squared equals 0
Jumps away from C remove no checkers
optionExplain: s^d is positive for every d.
Right: since s squared = 1 - s, the factor is -2s.
The factor is 0 for jumps toward C, not away.
Jumps always remove the jumped checker.
questions.explain: Use s squared = 1 - s in the factor.
questions.rule: Jumps away from C decrease the sum.

questions.q: True or false: with the target on row 4, the starting sum is 1/s, so the argument cannot rule it out.
questions.explain: 1/s is about 1.618, greater than 1, so a checker on C with the others would not exceed the starting sum and the contradiction fails.
questions.rule: Weight positions by s^distance; the sum starts at 1, never increases, but occupying C would force it above 1.

questions.q: Why would a checker standing on C make the Conway sum greater than 1?
options: It alone weighs more than 1
Checkers on C weigh nothing
The other checkers have weight 0
It alone weighs 1, and the other checkers add a positive amount
optionExplain: A checker at distance 0 has weight s^0 = 1.
Weight s^0 is 1, not 0.
Other checkers have positive weights.
Right: the sum is at least 1 plus a positive amount, but never exceeds 1.
questions.explain: Add the weights at distance 0 and elsewhere.
questions.teaches: The author notes a further case: a jump that leaves the distance to C unchanged, such as from (1, 4) to (-1, 4), also decreases the Conway sum.
questions.rule: Weight positions by s^distance; the sum starts at 1, never increases, but occupying C would force it above 1.

questions.q: A score starts at 20 and falls by at least 1 each move, staying at or above 0. At most how many moves occur?
options: Unlimited
optionExplain: 10 would need each move to lower the score by 2.
19 undercounts: 20 moves of size 1 fit.
Right: each move lowers it by at least 1 and it cannot go below 0.
A bounded score limits the moves.
questions.explain: Divide the available range by the smallest step.
questions.rule: A bounded quantity moving in steps of at least 1 shows halting; a never-increasing quantity shows a larger value is unreachable.

questions.q: Another term for a monovariant is a ____-invariant.
questions.explain: The author uses semi-invariant as a second name for monovariant.
questions.rule: A monovariant is also called a semi-invariant.

questions.q: Which of these quantities is a monovariant in its process?

items.t: Players remaining in a knockout tournament
The Conway sum of the checkers
Number of pieces of a chocolate bar after each break
The top card in the card-reversal problem
The room population when each minute adds 1 or subtracts 2
The remainder of the room total mod 3 after each minute

questions.explain: Players remaining only fall, the Conway sum never rises, and the piece count only rises. The top card goes up and down, and the room total goes up or down.
questions.rule: A monovariant moves one way.

questions.q: A solver says a score that falls by smaller and smaller amounts proves the process halts. What is wrong?
options: Shrinking decreases need not reach a final value; steps of at least 1 are needed
Scores that fall can never be bounded
A score that falls cannot halt anything
Halting needs the score to rise
optionExplain: Right: the steps must be bounded below for a bounded score to run out.
A score can be bounded below by 0.
Falling scores are the standard tool.
Rising scores bounded above also work, but this is not the flaw.
questions.explain: Check what keeps the number of moves finite.
questions.rule: Steps of at least 1, bounded range.

questions.q: True or false: a quantity that does not increase can show that a position needing a larger value is unreachable.
questions.explain: If the quantity starts at v and never rises, any position requiring a value above v cannot be reached.
questions.rule: A bounded quantity moving in steps of at least 1 shows halting; a never-increasing quantity shows a larger value is unreachable.

questions.q: A row of lamps; each move turns off one lit lamp and may toggle any lamps to its right. Must the process end?
options: Yes, because the row read as a binary number strictly decreases
No, because toggling can turn lamps on
Yes, because the number of lamps is even
No, because the lamps to the right are arbitrary
optionExplain: Right: the leftmost bit changed goes from 1 to 0 and only lower bits change, so the value drops.
Lamps to the right carry less weight than the lamp turned off.
Evenness of the lamp count plays no role.
Only less significant bits change, so the value still drops.
questions.explain: Assign each lamp a binary place value.
questions.teaches: According to the author, monovariants are used in the analysis of evolving systems, to show that certain final configurations must occur and to determine the duration of the system, often together with the well-ordering principle.
questions.rule: A bounded quantity moving in steps of at least 1 shows halting; a never-increasing quantity shows a larger value is unreachable.

questions.q: Six friends have texted each other in some pairs. What picture shows which pairs have texted?
options: A dot for each friend, with a line between two dots when those friends have texted
A dot for each friend, with a smaller dot inside it for every text sent
A single dot, with a loop for every friend who has texted anyone
A dot for each pair of friends, with no lines drawn between dots
optionExplain: Right: Dots for objects and lines for related pairs is exactly a graph.
A dot inside a dot is not a line joining a pair, so it cannot show who texted whom.
Loops join a vertex to itself, so they cannot record pairs of different people.
Dots for pairs with no lines record nothing about which pairs are related.
questions.explain: Dots for the objects and a line for each related pair is the picture of a graph. The card next sets out the exact words.
questions.rule: Objects are dots; related pairs are lines.

questions.q: True or false: in this book, a graph may contain a loop, an edge joining a vertex to itself.
questions.explain: By convention a graph has no loops and no repeated edges. A structure that has either is called a multigraph.
questions.rule: No loops and no repeated edges in a graph.

questions.q: The edges between four vertices are P-Q, Q-R, Q-R and R-S. Which description is correct?
options: A multigraph, because Q and R are joined by two edges
A graph, because every edge joins two different vertices
A multigraph, because the vertex R has more than one neighbor
A graph, because no edge runs from a vertex to itself
optionExplain: Right: A repeated edge between the same pair is what makes it a multigraph.
Having no loops is only half the convention: repeated edges are also excluded from a graph.
Having several neighbors is allowed in a graph; it is the doubled Q-R edge that breaks the convention.
The absence of loops does not help: the doubled Q-R edge already rules out a graph.
questions.explain: Q-R appears twice, and a graph may join a pair at most once. So the object is a multigraph.
questions.rule: Check both loops and repeated edges before calling it a graph.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A dot standing for one object
A line joining two related vertices
Two vertices joined by an edge
