An edge from a vertex to itself
Dots and lines where loops or repeated edges are allowed
questions.explain: These five words are the whole vocabulary of the section. Loop and multigraph are the two ways to leave the convention.
questions.rule: Know the five words exactly.

questions.q: A graph has 4 vertices. Because there are no loops or repeated edges, what is the most edges it can have?
optionExplain: 4 is the number of vertices; edges are counted by pairs of vertices, not by vertices.
8 doubles the vertex count; it does not count distinct pairs.
Right: Each edge joins a different pair, and 4 vertices make \(\binom42 = 6\) pairs, each used at most once.
16 counts ordered choices, including a vertex joined to itself, which a graph forbids.
questions.explain: Pairs of different vertices are the only places an edge can go, and each is used once: 4 vertices give 6 pairs. In a multigraph there would be no upper limit.
questions.rule: A graph on \(n\) vertices has at most \(\binom n2\) edges.

questions.q: Two islands are joined by three separate bridges, and each bridge matters to the question. Which model fits?
options: A graph, with one edge standing for all three bridges
A multigraph, with three edges between the two island vertices
A graph, with one loop at each island for the bridges
A graph, with the three bridges as vertices
optionExplain: One edge cannot count three bridges, so information the question needs is lost.
Right: Separate bridges between the same pair of islands are repeated edges.
Loops join an island to itself, not one island to another.
Making bridges the vertices changes the question to bridges meeting bridges.
questions.explain: When parallel connections matter, a graph cannot hold them. The book allows multigraphs for questions about travelling along every edge once (Eulerian paths) and notes this is virtually the only place in the text where they are relevant.
questions.rule: Use a multigraph only when parallel edges matter.
questions.teaches: The book lets multigraphs in for Eulerian-path questions, which it says is virtually the only place in the text where they are relevant.

questions.q: A school wants to see which of its clubs share at least one member. What could the dots and lines be?
options: Dots are students, with a line between students in different clubs
Dots are rooms, with a line between rooms that are next to each other
Dots are clubs, with a line between every pair of clubs
Dots are clubs, with a line between two clubs that share a member
optionExplain: This relates students, and it records different clubs rather than shared membership.
Rooms and adjacency have nothing to do with membership.
Joining every pair forgets which clubs actually share a member.
Right: The objects are clubs and the relation is sharing a member.
questions.explain: The objects asked about become dots, and the relation asked about becomes lines. The card next states this as a method.
questions.rule: Dots for objects, lines for the asked-about relation.

questions.q: When a problem is recast as a graph, the related pairs of objects become ____.
questions.explain: Objects become vertices and related pairs become edges.
questions.rule: Related pairs become edges.

questions.q: Seven people each shake hands exactly once with every other person. Recast as a graph, how many edges are there?
optionExplain: 14 is twice the number of people; it is not the number of pairs.
Right: There is one edge per pair of people: \(\binom72 = 21\).
42 counts each handshake twice, once from each person.
49 counts each person with each person, including themselves.
questions.explain: One edge for each pair of people gives \(\binom72 = 7 \cdot 6/2 = 21\). Counting 42 would count every handshake from both ends.
questions.rule: One edge per related pair, so each pair is counted once.

questions.q: Sort each item: does it become a vertex or an edge when the situation is recast as a graph?

items.t: A city on a rail map
A rail line joining two adjacent cities
A guest at a party
A friendship between two guests
An email account
A message from one account to another

questions.explain: Things being related are vertices; the relation between two of them is an edge.
questions.rule: Objects are vertices; relations are edges.

questions.q: A puzzle splits people into two groups so that nobody has more related people in their own group than in the other. What does this ask of the graph?
options: Delete every edge between two people who belong to different groups
Join every two people who are in the same group by a new edge
Remove all the vertices of the smaller group and keep only the rest
Colour each vertex one of two colours so every vertex has at least as many neighbors of the other colour as of its own
optionExplain: Deleting edges changes the relations instead of splitting the vertices.
Joining same-group people invents relations that were not given.
Removing vertices throws people away instead of placing everyone.
Right: Groups are colours, and the condition is about neighbors of each colour.
questions.explain: A split into two groups is a two-colouring of vertices, and the condition counts neighbors of each colour. The book restates its Affirmative Action problem in exactly this way.
questions.rule: A split into groups is a colouring of the vertices.
questions.teaches: The book restates the Affirmative Action problem as colouring the vertices of any graph black and white so each vertex has at least as many neighbors of the other colour as of its own.

questions.q: Eight committees must meet at different hours if they share a member. Which graph records the clashes?
options: Dots are hours of the day, with a line between hours that are next to each other in time
Dots are members, with a line between members of the same committee
Dots are committees, with a line between two committees that share a member
Dots are committees, with a line between committees of equal size
optionExplain: Hours are what we assign, not the objects that clash.
This relates members, which can hide which committees clash.
Right: Clashing committees are the related pairs.
Equal size does not make two committees clash.
questions.explain: The clash relation is the one to draw. The book notes that the handshake problem (people) and the Gallery problem solution (networks of pipes) both become graph questions in this way.
questions.rule: Draw the relation that creates the conflict.
questions.teaches: The book recasts both the Handshake problem (people) and the solution of the Gallery problem (networks of pipes) as graph questions.

questions.q: Five mathematicians sleep twice each during a lecture, and every pair of them overlaps. To prove three sleep together, what could the dots be?
options: The ten separate naps, with a line between two naps that overlap
The five mathematicians, with a line between two who ever slept
The moments of the lecture, with a line between consecutive moments
The five mathematicians, with a loop for every nap they took
optionExplain: Right: The overlap itself is between naps, so naps are the objects.
With one dot per person, two naps of the same person are merged and the overlap data is lost.
Moments in time carry no information about who was asleep.
Loops describe a person with themselves, not two people overlapping.
questions.explain: The relation of interest is overlapping in time, and that holds between naps. The card next builds the graph.
questions.rule: Pick the objects that can overlap.

questions.q: In the graph of the five mathematicians' naps there are ____ vertices.
questions.explain: Five mathematicians with two naps each give 10 nap intervals, one vertex per nap.
questions.rule: One vertex for each nap.

questions.q: Seven mathematicians each sleep exactly twice, and every pair overlaps at some time. At least how many edges does the nap graph have?
optionExplain: Right: Each of the \(\binom72 = 21\) pairs of mathematicians gives its own overlapping pair of naps.
14 is the number of naps, which counts vertices, not edges.
42 counts every pair of mathematicians twice.
49 pairs every mathematician with every mathematician, including themselves.
questions.explain: Different pairs of mathematicians give different pairs of naps, so there are at least \(\binom72 = 21\) edges, on 14 vertices.
questions.rule: One overlapping pair of naps for each pair of mathematicians.

questions.q: Put the steps of the argument for the five mathematicians in order.
items: Make each nap a vertex and join naps that overlap
Count at least ten edges, one for each pair of mathematicians, on ten vertices
Conclude that the graph contains a cycle
Stack the intervals of the cycle in time and look for a gap
Show that an interval straddling the gap gives three overlapping naps
questions.explain: The graph is built first, a cycle is found from the counts, and the cycle then forces the triple overlap by the stacking argument.
questions.rule: Graph, count, cycle, stack.

questions.q: A student says: naps X and Y overlap and Y and Z overlap, so X, Y and Z overlap at one moment. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because overlapping is transitive
X and Z might miss each other; the loop of overlaps has to close first
Y cannot overlap two different naps
Three naps of different mathematicians can never overlap
optionExplain: Overlap is not transitive: X may end before Z starts while Y spans both.
Right: A chain X-Y-Z is not a cycle.
A long nap can overlap many shorter ones.
That is the statement to be proved, so it cannot be an objection.
questions.explain: A path of overlaps leaves the two ends free to miss each other. Only a closed loop of overlaps forces three naps to share a moment.
questions.rule: A chain is not enough; the loop must close.

questions.q: A loop of overlapping naps has seven naps, not four. What happens to the stacking argument?
options: It fails, because the book proves it only for four naps and no more
It needs a separate gap argument for every length
It works only when the number of naps is even
It works the same way for a cycle of any finite length
optionExplain: The example uses four naps, but the reasoning is not special to four.
The same gap-straddling idea is reused for any length.
Nothing in the argument depends on parity.
Right: The book says the argument works for cycles of any finite length.
questions.explain: The four-nap case is only an illustration. The book notes that a little experimenting shows the argument works with a cycle of any finite length, so finding some cycle is enough.
questions.rule: Any cycle of overlapping naps does the job.
questions.teaches: The book says a little experimenting shows the stacking argument works for a cycle of any finite length, so the problem reduces to showing the graph contains some cycle.

questions.q: Each guest at a party reports how many hands they shook, and the reports are added. How many times does each handshake enter the total?
options: Once, because a handshake is one event
Three times, counting the hand as well
Twice, once for each of the two people involved
It depends on who shook hands first
optionExplain: Counting events once misses that both people report it.
The hand is not a third participant.
Right: Every handshake is reported by both people.
Order does not matter: both people report it.
questions.explain: Both people report every handshake. The card next calls this the handshake lemma.
questions.rule: Each edge is seen from both ends.

questions.q: In any graph, the sum of the degrees of all vertices equals twice the number of ____.
questions.explain: Every edge contributes one to the degree of each of its two ends, so it is counted twice.
questions.rule: Degree sum = twice the edges.

questions.q: A graph has 9 vertices and every vertex has degree 4. How many edges does it have?
optionExplain: 36 is the degree sum; the number of edges is half of it.
13 adds the vertex count and the degree, which does not follow from the lemma.
Right: The degrees add to \(9 \cdot 4 = 36\), which is twice the number of edges, so there are 18.
9 is the number of vertices, not the number of edges.
questions.explain: The degree sum is 36, so edges \(= 36/2 = 18\).
questions.rule: Edges = degree sum divided by 2.

questions.q: True or false: a graph can have 7 vertices that all have degree 3.
questions.explain: Seven vertices of degree 3 give degree sum 21. The lemma says the sum is twice the number of edges, so it must be even; no such graph exists.
questions.rule: An odd degree sum rules a graph out.

questions.q: A student adds the degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 of a graph and says it has 12 edges. What is wrong?
options: The degrees should have been multiplied, not added
A graph with degree 3 vertices must have 3 edges
The graph is disconnected, so the lemma fails
Each edge was counted at both ends, so the number of edges is 6
optionExplain: Adding is the right operation for the lemma.
Degree 3 means three edges at that vertex, not three in the graph.
The lemma does not need connectedness.
Right: The sum counts each edge twice.
questions.explain: The sum 12 is twice the number of edges, so the graph has 6 edges.
questions.rule: Halve the degree sum to count edges.

questions.q: Two islands share no bridge. Town road-degrees are 3, 2, 2, 1 on one island and 2, 2, 2 on the other. How many roads?
optionExplain: 14 is the degree sum.
Right: The degrees add to 8 + 6 = 14, which is twice the number of roads.
4 counts only the first island.
3 counts only the second island.
questions.explain: The lemma does not need the network to be connected: both islands together are one graph with degree sum 14, so 7 roads. The book observes that the lemma does not require connectivity.
questions.rule: The lemma holds for disconnected graphs too.
questions.teaches: The book observes that the handshake lemma does not require connectivity.

questions.q: Five vertices have edges 1-2, 2-3, 3-4 and 4-5. Which statement is correct?
options: Some pair of vertices has no path of edges between them
The edges form a closed loop
Vertex 3 is a neighbor of every other vertex
You can walk from any vertex to any other along edges
optionExplain: Following the edges reaches every vertex from any start.
A loop would need an edge from 5 back to 1.
Vertex 3 neighbors only 2 and 4.
Right: The vertices form a line, so all are reachable.
questions.explain: A line of vertices lets you reach everything. The card next names this connected.
questions.rule: Connected means a path between every pair.

questions.q: A connected graph that contains no cycles is called a ____.
questions.explain: A tree is connected and cycle-free.
questions.rule: Tree = connected + no cycles.

questions.q: A graph has edges 1-2, 2-3, 3-1 and 4-5. How many connected components does it have?
optionExplain: One component would need a path between 1 and 4.
Right: The triangle on 1, 2, 3 is one component and the edge 4-5 is the other.
Three would count the triangle's edges apart.
Five counts every vertex alone.
questions.explain: Vertices 1, 2, 3 reach each other, and 4, 5 reach each other, but nothing links the two groups.
questions.rule: Components are the pieces that are internally connected.

questions.q: Sort each graph: is it a tree or not?

items.t: Five vertices in a line, joined one after another
A triangle
One centre joined to four other vertices
Two separate single edges
A square with one diagonal added
Three vertices in a line

questions.explain: Trees are connected and have no cycle. The triangle and the square with a diagonal have cycles; the two separate edges are not connected.
questions.rule: Tree = connected and no cycle.

questions.q: A graph is two separate paths of three vertices each. A student says it has no cycles, so it is a tree. What is wrong?
options: It is not connected, and a tree has to be connected
It has a cycle that is hard to see
Trees need at least five vertices
A path of three vertices is not a tree
optionExplain: Right: No cycles is only half the definition.
Two paths contain no cycle at all.
Size is not part of the definition.
A path of three vertices is connected and cycle-free, so it is a tree.
questions.explain: The student checked no cycles but skipped connectedness. Two separate pieces mean a path is missing between some pairs.
questions.rule: Check connectedness as well as the absence of cycles.

questions.q: A network of 8 computers has no cycles but splits into 3 separate connected pieces. What is the best name for it?
options: A tree, because it has no cycles
A cycle with three parts
A forest: a collection of trees, one per component
A multigraph with three loops
optionExplain: It is not connected, so it is not a tree.
There are no cycles at all.
Right: A cycle-free graph in several pieces is a forest.
Multigraphs need loops or repeated edges, which are not present.
questions.explain: The book calls a non-connected graph without cycles a forest, and each of its connected components is a tree.
questions.rule: A forest is a cycle-free graph whose components are trees.
questions.teaches: A non-connected graph containing no cycles is called a forest, and each of its connected components is a tree.

questions.q: A connected network of cables has no closed loops of cable. What must it contain?
options: A computer attached to every other computer
At least two endpoints, each attached to a single cable
Exactly one endpoint with a single cable
At least one closed ring of cables
optionExplain: A star-shaped network has no such computer.
Right: Loop-free networks have dead ends.
A line has two ends, not one.
That would contradict having no closed loops.
questions.explain: A network with no loops must stop somewhere, and at least two places. The card next proves it.
questions.rule: Loop-free connected networks have dead ends.

questions.q: True or false: a tree with two or more vertices has exactly two leaves.
questions.explain: A tree has at least two leaves, but it can have more. A star with four outer vertices has four leaves.
questions.rule: At least two leaves, not exactly two.

questions.q: A tree has six vertices: one centre joined to each of the other five. How many leaves does it have?
optionExplain: One leaf contradicts the theorem.
Two is the minimum, but this tree has more.
The centre has degree 5, so it is not a leaf.
Right: The five outer vertices each have degree 1, and the centre has degree 5.
questions.explain: Only the centre has degree greater than 1, so the five others are leaves.
questions.rule: A leaf is a degree-1 vertex.

questions.q: Put the steps of the proof that a tree has a leaf at each end of a longest path in order.
items: Take a longest path \(x_1 x_2 \ldots x_n\) in the tree
Suppose \(x_1\) has a neighbor \(y\) other than \(x_2\)
Note \(y\) cannot lie on the path, or a cycle would form
Then \(y\) \(x_1 x_2 \ldots x_n\) is a longer path, which contradicts the choice
So \(x_1\) has degree 1, and the same holds for \(x_n\)
questions.explain: The proof picks a longest path, assumes an end can be extended, and shows that contradicts maximality.
questions.rule: Longest path, extend, contradict.

questions.q: A proof says: \(x_1\) has another neighbor \(y\), so add \(y\) to the path and get a longer path, a contradiction. What is missing?
options: A proof that the tree is connected to the vertex \(y\) by some path
A reason why \(y\) is not already on the path, which uses the absence of cycles
A check that the vertex \(y\) has degree exactly 1
A second longest path to compare it with, of equal length
optionExplain: Having a neighbor \(y\) already gives an edge to it.
Right: The new path is only longer if \(y\) is new.
\(y\) may have any degree.
No second path is needed.
questions.explain: If \(y\) were already on the path, the edge from \(x_1\) to \(y\) would close a cycle. Since a tree has no cycles, \(y\) is new and the longer path is a genuine contradiction.
questions.rule: State why the new vertex is not already on the path.

questions.q: Six stations form a ring, each linked to the next, and the last back to the first. Does the leaf theorem say it has a leaf?
options: No: the ring is not a tree, and every station has degree 2
Yes, every connected graph has two leaves
Yes, the longest path ends at two leaves
No, because it has too few stations
optionExplain: Right: A ring is not a tree.
A cycle shows connected graphs need not have leaves.
The ends of a path in a ring are joined by an edge, so they have degree 2.
Size is not the obstacle.
questions.explain: The theorem is about trees, and a ring contains a cycle. The proof picks a longest path and shows its end cannot be extended, an argument the book names as using the extreme principle and contradiction.
questions.rule: The no-cycle hypothesis is essential.
questions.teaches: The proof applies the extreme principle (choose a longest path) together with argument by contradiction.

questions.q: Ten offices must be cabled so every office can reach every other, with no closed loop of cable. How many cables are needed?
optionExplain: 8 leaves some office cut off.
10 would close a loop.
Right: A loop-free connected network on 10 offices has 9 links.
11 would make several loops.
questions.explain: Each new office joins by one cable, giving 9 for 10 offices. The card next proves this for every tree.
questions.rule: Connect \(n\) points without loops using \(n - 1\) links.

questions.q: A tree with 12 vertices has ____ edges.
questions.explain: A tree on \(v\) vertices has \(v - 1\) edges, so 12 vertices give 11.
questions.rule: Edges \(=\) vertices \(- 1\).

questions.q: A tree has 20 edges. How many vertices does it have?
optionExplain: 19 subtracts one instead of adding one.
20 treats edges and vertices as equal.
Right: Since edges \(=\) vertices \(- 1\), vertices \(=\) edges \(+ 1 = 21\).
40 doubles the edge count, as in the handshake lemma.
questions.explain: A tree has one more vertex than edges, so 20 edges means 21 vertices.
questions.rule: Vertices = edges + 1 for a tree.

questions.q: In the induction step a student removes a vertex of degree 3 from the tree and claims what is left is a tree. What is wrong?
options: Removing a vertex that is not a leaf can disconnect the tree
Removing any vertex always removes exactly one edge
A tree on \(v + 1\) vertices has no vertex of degree 3
The base case is \(v = 1\) and not \(v = 2\)
optionExplain: Right: Only a leaf can be removed safely.
Removing a vertex removes every edge at it, which is three here.
Trees can have vertices of any degree.
The book starts at \(v = 2\), but that is not the flaw here.
questions.explain: A vertex of degree 3 joins three parts of the tree; removing it leaves three separate pieces. A leaf joins nothing else, so its removal keeps the rest connected.
questions.rule: Remove a leaf, not an arbitrary vertex.

questions.q: Put the steps of the proof that a tree on \(v\) vertices has \(v - 1\) edges in order.
items: Check the base case: two vertices joined by one edge
Assume every tree on \(v\) vertices has \(v - 1\) edges
Take a tree on \(v + 1\) vertices and remove a leaf with its edge
Observe that the rest is a tree on v vertices
Add the leaf back to get \((v - 1) + 1 = v\) edges
questions.explain: An induction proof: base case, hypothesis, a reduction to the smaller case, and the step back up.
questions.rule: Base case, hypothesis, remove a leaf, add it back.

questions.q: A tree has 14 vertices. A gardener cuts off a leaf with its edge, then cuts a leaf off what remains. How many edges are left?
optionExplain: 13 is the original edge count.
12 is the vertex count after two cuts.
10 subtracts one cut too many.
Right: After two cuts there is a tree on 12 vertices, with 11 edges.
questions.explain: Cutting a leaf leaves a tree, so after two cuts the tree has 12 vertices and \(12 - 1 = 11\) edges. This repeatable step is why the induction works.
questions.rule: A tree minus a leaf is a smaller tree.
questions.teaches: Plucking a leaf cannot disconnect a tree or create a cycle, so what remains is again a tree; that is what lets the induction go from \(v + 1\) to \(v\).

questions.q: A graph has 12 vertices and 12 edges. What must be true?
options: It contains a cycle
It is a tree
It is connected
It has no cycle unless it is connected
optionExplain: Right: Twelve edges on twelve vertices is more than a tree has.
A tree on 12 vertices has only 11 edges.
Extra edges do not force connection.
The cycle appears whether or not it is connected.
questions.explain: A cycle-free graph has fewer edges than vertices, so 12 and 12 cannot be cycle-free. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: As many edges as vertices forces a cycle.

questions.q: If a graph has \(e\) edges and \(v\) vertices and \(e \ge v\), then the graph must contain a ____.
questions.explain: That is the criterion: at least as many edges as vertices forces a cycle.
questions.rule: \(e \ge v\) forces a cycle.

questions.q: Which of these graphs must contain a cycle? Select all that apply.
options: 9 vertices and 8 edges
9 vertices and 10 edges
100 vertices and 99 edges
9 vertices and 9 edges
optionExplain: 8 edges on 9 vertices is exactly a tree's count, so the criterion is silent and a tree is possible.
Right: Edges exceed vertices.
99 edges on 100 vertices is below the vertex count, so a tree is possible.
Right: Edges equal vertices.
questions.explain: The criterion applies when \(e \ge v\). When \(e \le v - 1\), a cycle may or may not exist.
questions.rule: Only \(e \ge v\) guarantees a cycle.

questions.q: A graph has 8 vertices in two separate connected pieces, and 8 edges in all. Must it contain a cycle?
options: No, because each piece may be a tree
Yes, because \(e \ge v\) holds whether or not the graph is connected
No, because the criterion needs a connected graph
Yes, but only if each piece has 4 vertices
optionExplain: Two trees on 8 vertices have 6 edges, not 8.
Right: Connectedness is not a hypothesis.
The statement holds for any graph.
The sizes of the pieces do not matter.
questions.explain: With 8 vertices in two pieces, a cycle-free graph would have \(8 - 2 = 6\) edges. Eight edges exceed that, so a cycle exists.
questions.rule: The criterion does not need connectivity.

questions.q: A graph has 6 vertices and 4 edges. A student says: 4 < 6, so there is no cycle. What is wrong?
options: Cycles need at least as many vertices as edges
A graph with 6 vertices must have 6 edges
The test works one way only; fewer edges than vertices does not rule out a cycle
The student should have compared with \(2 \cdot 6\)
optionExplain: A cycle on 3 vertices has 3 vertices and 3 edges.
Graphs may have any number of edges.
Right: \(e \ge v\) is sufficient, not necessary.
Doubling the vertices has no role here.
questions.explain: A triangle with a separate edge and one more vertex has 6 vertices, 4 edges and a cycle. The criterion only says that \(e \ge v\) forces a cycle.
questions.rule: Few edges do not prove there is no cycle.

questions.q: A cycle-free network has 20 vertices and 14 edges. Into how many separate connected pieces does it fall?
optionExplain: Right: A cycle-free graph has \(e = v - k\), so \(k = 20 - 14 = 6\).
5 subtracts one too few.
7 adds one.
14 repeats the edge count.
questions.explain: Each piece is a tree, with one fewer edge than vertices. Missing edges count the pieces: \(20 - 14 = 6\). In general a collection of \(k\) trees with \(v\) vertices has $\(e = v - k\)$ edges.
questions.rule: Cycle-free: edges \(=\) vertices \(-\) number of pieces.
questions.teaches: In a forest with k connected components, v vertices and e edges, \(e = v - k\).

questions.q: Six scientists each take two shifts, and every two scientists have shifts that overlap. How might you show three are on shift together?
options: Check every possible arrangement of the twelve shifts by hand
Treat shifts as vertices, count overlaps against shifts to force a cycle, then use the cycle
Assume all the overlaps happen at the same moment
Compare the average shift length with the total time
optionExplain: Brute force is too large and the overlap structure is not used.
Right: A graph and counting argument finishes the job.
That assumption is the claim to be proved and is not given.
Average length says nothing about overlap.
questions.explain: The same chain as the five-mathematician problem applies. The card shows it step by step.
questions.rule: Recast, count, find a cycle, use it.

questions.q: Ten vertices and at least ten edges force a ____ in the nap graph.
questions.explain: At least as many edges as vertices forces a cycle.
questions.rule: \(e \ge v\) forces a cycle.

questions.q: Six scientists have two shifts each and every pair overlaps. What does the shift graph have at least?
options: 12 edges on 15 vertices
6 edges on 12 vertices
15 edges on 12 vertices
30 edges on 12 vertices
optionExplain: The two numbers are swapped.
6 counts scientists, not pairs.
Right: Edges: one per pair of scientists, \(\binom62 = 15\). Vertices: \(6 \cdot 2 = 12\).
30 counts ordered pairs.
questions.explain: There are 15 pairs and 12 shifts, so \(e = 15 \ge v = 12\).
questions.rule: Edges come from pairs of people, vertices from shifts.

questions.q: Suppose each of the five mathematicians slept exactly three times instead of twice. The nap graph has at least 10 edges. What follows?
options: The argument still forces a cycle, since 10 edges are enough
The conclusion is now false
The graph must be a tree
The edge count 10 is below the 15 vertices, so this argument no longer forces a cycle
optionExplain: Ten is less than fifteen, so the criterion does not apply.
The argument gives no conclusion, which is not the same as the claim being false.
At least 10 edges does not mean exactly 14.
Right: Fifteen vertices need at least fifteen edges for the criterion.
questions.explain: Our reading: the argument stalls because 10 < 15, but the book does not claim the result fails. Changing the number of naps changes whether the criterion fits.
questions.rule: Check \(e \ge v\) before using the criterion.

questions.q: True or false: since 10 edges on 10 vertices force a cycle, all five mathematicians must be asleep at one moment.
questions.explain: The cycle argument gives three overlapping naps, not five. It proves that some three mathematicians sleep together at some moment.
questions.rule: A cycle forces three naps to overlap, not all of them.

questions.q: Eight engineers each work exactly two shifts, and every pair of engineers has overlapping shifts. Does the same method show three shifts overlap?
options: Yes: at least 28 edges on 16 vertices force a cycle, and a cycle gives a triple overlap
No, because there are more edges than vertices, so a cycle is unlikely
No, because the method needs exactly five people to work
Yes, because 16 is a power of two, which always works
optionExplain: Having more edges than vertices is what makes the method work.
The method works for any number of people with two shifts each.
Powers of two have no role.
questions.explain: Eight engineers give \(\binom82 = 28\) pairs and 16 shifts. Once the graph question is isolated, the original story drops out. The book calls this reducing the problem to a pure graph theory question.
questions.rule: Reduce to the pure graph question and answer that.
questions.teaches: After recasting, the book reduces the problem to a pure graph theory question that can be answered without the original story.

questions.q: You trace a drawing without lifting your pencil or retracing a line. At a junction where you neither start nor stop, how many lines meet?
options: An odd number of them, at least three
Exactly three
Exactly one
An even number
optionExplain: An odd number would leave a line unused.
Three lines would leave one unused.
One line is a dead end, where you would have to stop.
Right: Each pass through the junction uses a pair of lines.
questions.explain: Every pass through uses one line in and one line out. The card next explains what this means for odd junctions.
questions.rule: Passing through a vertex uses two edges.

questions.q: A path that uses every edge of a graph exactly once is called an ____ path.
questions.explain: That is the definition of an Eulerian path.
questions.rule: Eulerian = every edge once.

questions.q: A connected graph has degrees 4, 2, 3, 2, 3. If it has an Eulerian path, where must it start and end?
options: At the vertex of degree 4
At the two vertices of degree 3
At any two vertices
It cannot have such a path at all, whatever the degrees
optionExplain: Degree 4 is even, so no end is forced there.
Right: The odd-degree vertices must be the ends.
The ends are forced, not free.
Two odd vertices are allowed.
questions.explain: The vertices of degree 3 are the only odd ones, so the path begins at one and ends at the other.
questions.rule: Odd vertices are the ends.

questions.q: True or false: a connected graph with four vertices of odd degree can have an Eulerian path.
questions.explain: Only the start and the end of an open path can have odd degree, and a closed path has no odd vertices. Four odd vertices are too many.
questions.rule: More than two odd vertices means no Eulerian path.

questions.q: A student finds exactly one vertex of odd degree and says the path starts there and ends at a vertex of even degree. What is wrong?
options: The end of an open path must also have odd degree, so one odd vertex alone does not work
A path may not start at an odd vertex, so all must be even
The path must start and end at the same vertex, as a circuit does
Even-degree vertices can never be visited by an open path
optionExplain: Right: An open path has two odd ends.
Odd vertices are exactly where it must start or end.
That describes a closed path, which has no odd vertices.
Even vertices are the ones passed through freely.
questions.explain: An open path uses one unpaired edge at its start and one at its end, so both ends have odd degree. By the handshake lemma, a graph cannot have exactly one odd vertex anyway.
questions.rule: An open Eulerian path has two odd ends.

questions.q: A street sweeper must clear every street once and finish at the depot where it started. What must be true of the junction degrees?
options: The depot alone has odd degree and all other junctions even
Exactly two junctions have odd degree
Every junction has degree 2
Every junction, including the depot, has even degree
optionExplain: A closed route starting and ending at the depot uses edges there in pairs.
Two odd junctions give an open path.
Degree 2 is allowed but not required.
Right: A closed path has no start or end vertex.
questions.explain: A closed route has no unpaired edge at any vertex, including the depot, so all degrees are even.
questions.rule: Closed Eulerian path: no odd vertices.
questions.teaches: If the path is closed, with no start or end, every vertex has even degree.

questions.q: Four connected networks have these vertex-degree lists. Which one can be traced in one stroke using every line once?
optionExplain: Right: Two odd vertices is the allowed pattern.
Four odd vertices are too many.
Four odd vertices again.
Six odd vertices are too many.
questions.explain: Only the list with two odd-degree vertices fits. The card next states Euler's rule.
questions.rule: Two odd vertices: start at one and finish at the other.

questions.q: A connected graph has an Eulerian path exactly when it has zero or ____ odd-degree vertices.
questions.explain: With zero or two odd-degree vertices, and connected, an Eulerian path exists.
questions.rule: Zero or two odd vertices.

questions.q: A connected graph has degrees 4, 4, 2, 2, 2, 2. What kind of Eulerian path does it have?
options: An open one from a degree 4 vertex to the other
A closed one, since no vertex has odd degree
An open one between two degree 2 vertices
None, since it has no odd vertices
optionExplain: Even vertices are not forced to be ends.
Right: Zero odd vertices gives a closed path.
Degree 2 is even; it forces nothing.
Zero odd vertices is allowed by the theorem.
questions.explain: With zero odd vertices the path is closed: you can start anywhere and come back.
questions.rule: Zero odd vertices: closed path.

questions.q: True or false: adding an edge between the two odd-degree vertices of a connected graph gives it a closed Eulerian path.
questions.explain: Each of the two odd degrees goes up by one and becomes even, so no odd vertex remains and the path is closed. The theorem covers multigraphs, which matters if the two vertices were already joined.
questions.rule: Joining the two odd vertices closes the path.

questions.q: Two separate triangles have all degrees 2. A student says Euler's rule gives an Eulerian path. What is wrong?
options: Degree 2 is odd, so the criterion fails
The rule needs exactly two odd vertices, and a triangle has none
Triangles have no Eulerian path of any kind
The graph is not connected, and the rule needs a connected graph
optionExplain: Two is even.
Zero odd vertices is also allowed.
A single triangle has a closed Eulerian path.
Right: Connectedness is a hypothesis.
questions.explain: Without a connection no path can pass from one triangle to the other, so no single path uses all six edges.
questions.rule: Check connectedness before counting odd vertices.

questions.q: A town has four junctions of odd degree and wants a street sweeper route over every street once. At least how many new streets must be added?
optionExplain: One street fixes two odd junctions at most.
Right: Each new street changes the parity of two junctions; four odd junctions need two streets.
Four would be one per junction, but each street covers two.
Three leaves one junction odd.
questions.explain: Pair the four odd junctions and join each pair: two streets, giving zero odd junctions.
questions.rule: Each new street fixes at most two odd vertices.
questions.teaches: The book says Eulerian paths have a complete theory, with a necessary and sufficient condition.

questions.q: Starting at s, you travel along unused roads until you are stuck at f, but some roads are still unused. What would repair the route?
options: Add a closed side trip of unused roads at a point where they meet your route
Start again at f and travel backwards along the route
Delete the unused roads from the map
Walk the same route a second time
optionExplain: Right: A side trip can use the leftover roads.
Starting again from f does not use the leftover roads.
Deleting them means the route no longer covers every road.
Repeating the route breaks the use-each-road-once rule.
questions.explain: A closed side trip from a shared point uses the leftover roads without breaking the rule. The card next gives the recipe.
questions.rule: Leftover edges can be spliced in as closed trips.

questions.q: In the recipe, after removing the traveled edges, every vertex of the leftover subgraph has ____ degree.
questions.explain: The traveled path uses an even number of edges at every vertex other than s and f, so evenness remains in the leftover subgraph.
questions.rule: Leftover degrees are even.

questions.q: Edges: s-a, a-b, b-c, c-f, b-d, d-e, e-b. The walk s, a, b, c, f is stuck. At which vertex should the unused triangle be spliced in?
options: b
a
c
d
optionExplain: Right: b is the only vertex that lies on both the walk and the triangle.
a is on the walk but not on the triangle.
c is on the walk but not on the triangle.
d is on the triangle but not on the walk.
questions.explain: The triangle b-d-e touches the walk only at b, so the closed trip b, d, e, b is inserted there: s, a, b, d, e, b, c, f.
questions.rule: Splice at a vertex shared by the walk and the leftover edges.

questions.q: Put the steps of the construction in order.
items: Start at s and travel along unused edges until stuck
Remove the traveled edges and find a vertex u where the leftover edges meet the path
Travel the leftover subgraph from u until back at u
Splice that closed trip into the path at u
Repeat while any edge is unused
questions.explain: The path is built first, then repaired by inserting closed trips.
questions.rule: Walk, remove, loop, splice, repeat.

questions.q: A student says the side trip from u in the leftover subgraph might end at some other vertex. Why is that mistaken?
options: The leftover graph has exactly two odd vertices, so it can end elsewhere
All leftover degrees are even, so the trip can only get stuck back at u
The side trip is not allowed to end before all edges are used
The leftover edges are all one single edge, so no trip exists
optionExplain: Both odd vertices were s and f, which the first walk handled.
Right: Even degrees mean you can always leave.
The trip ends when stuck.
Several edges can remain.
questions.explain: At an even-degree vertex other than the starting vertex, every entry leaves an unused edge to leave by. Only the starting vertex can run out.
questions.rule: With all degrees even, you can only get stuck where you began.

questions.q: After splicing in one closed trip, some edges are still unused. What does the book's method do next?
options: Declare that no Eulerian path exists and stop the search
Restart from s and try a different first edge, discarding the trip
Remove the traveled edges again and travel what is left, repeating as often as needed
Add a new edge to join the leftover pieces together
optionExplain: The theorem says a path exists, so failure is not a conclusion.
A restart would repeat the same issue.
Right: The step repeats.
New edges would change the graph.
questions.explain: The trip from u may return to u before using all leftover edges, so the remove-and-travel step may repeat several times. The graph is finite, so it ends.
questions.rule: Repeat the splice step until no edge is left.
questions.teaches: The remove-the-traveled-edges-and-travel-the-subgraph step may need to be repeated several times, because the side trip can end at its starting point before using all leftover edges.

questions.q: A salesperson must visit every town exactly once. In the road graph, which route is wanted?
options: A path that uses each edge of the graph exactly once
The shortest path between two towns
A path that visits each vertex exactly once
A path with no neighbors
optionExplain: That describes an Eulerian path.
Shortest paths between two towns need not visit every town.
Right: Towns are vertices, and each must be visited once.
Every town on a route has neighbors.
questions.explain: Visiting every vertex once is the Hamiltonian idea. The card defines it.
questions.rule: Hamiltonian: visit each vertex once.

questions.q: True or false: a Hamiltonian path uses every edge of the graph exactly once.
questions.explain: A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once; using every edge exactly once is an Eulerian path.
questions.rule: Vertices once = Hamiltonian; edges once = Eulerian.

questions.q: Six guests will sit around a round table so that each guest's two neighbors are friends. What should be found in the friendship graph?
options: An Eulerian path
A Hamiltonian cycle
A tree with six vertices
A vertex of degree 6
optionExplain: Eulerian paths concern edges, not people.
Right: A closed route through all guests gives a seating order.
A tree has no closed ring.
A guest cannot be a friend of themselves.
questions.explain: Going round the table is a closed route through every vertex exactly once, a Hamiltonian cycle.
questions.rule: Seating around a table is a Hamiltonian cycle.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A closed path visiting every vertex exactly once
Roles of edges and vertices swapped
questions.explain: The two kinds of path are duals: one covers all edges, the other all vertices.
questions.rule: Swap edges and vertices to move from Euler to Hamilton.

questions.q: A graph has one centre joined to three outer vertices and no other edges. Does it have a Hamiltonian path?
options: Yes: start at the centre, then visit the three outer vertices in turn
Yes, because the graph is connected, which is enough
No, because it has an odd number of vertices in total
No: after two outer vertices the path cannot reach the third without revisiting the centre
optionExplain: Moving from one outer vertex to another needs the centre again.
Connected graphs need not have Hamiltonian paths.
Four vertices is even, and parity is not the issue.
Right: Outer vertices touch only the centre.
questions.explain: A path through an outer vertex must enter and leave via the centre, so at most two outer vertices can be visited, and only as the two ends.
questions.rule: Connected is not enough for a Hamiltonian path.

questions.q: A planner asks for a degree-counting test that settles whether any graph has a Hamiltonian cycle, like the odd-vertex test for Eulerian paths. What does the book say?
options: No necessary and sufficient condition is known at present
Count vertices of odd degree: zero or two works
Count edges: at least twice the vertices works
The test is the same as for Eulerian paths
optionExplain: Right: Hamiltonian paths lack a complete theory.
That test is for Eulerian paths only.
No such edge-count test is claimed.
The two kinds of path do not share a test.
questions.explain: The book says Eulerian paths have a complete theory, while very little is known about Hamiltonian paths and exact conditions are unknown, which is unfortunate since many practical problems need them.
questions.rule: No exact test is known for Hamiltonian paths.
questions.teaches: The book says very little is known about Hamiltonian paths: necessary and sufficient conditions for them are unknown.

questions.q: A party has 8 guests, and each guest knows at least 4 others. Can everyone be seated round a table with acquaintances on both sides?
options: No, because 8 is too many guests
Only if one guest knows everybody
Yes, a theorem guarantees such a seating
Only if the guests all know exactly 4 others
optionExplain: Size alone does not prevent it.
A guest knowing everyone is not required.
Right: Degree at least half the guests suffices.
Knowing at least 4 is enough.
questions.explain: With every degree at least \(v/2 = 4\), a Hamiltonian cycle exists. The card next states the theorem.
questions.rule: Degree at least \(v/2\) gives a seating order.

questions.q: If every vertex of a graph with v vertices has degree at least ____, the graph has a Hamiltonian cycle.
questions.explain: The condition is that every degree is at least half the number of vertices.
questions.rule: Degree at least \(v/2\).

questions.q: A graph has 40 vertices and its smallest degree is 19. Does this theorem guarantee a Hamiltonian cycle?
options: Yes, because 19 is close to 20
Yes, because 19 is more than 10
No, because no Hamiltonian cycle exists
No: the theorem needs every degree to be at least 20
optionExplain: Close is not enough for the hypothesis.
The threshold is half the vertices, not a quarter.
The theorem is silent; a cycle may still exist.
Right: Half of 40 is 20.
questions.explain: The hypothesis fails at degree 19, so the theorem says nothing. A Hamiltonian cycle may or may not exist.
questions.rule: Check the threshold \(v/2\) exactly.

questions.q: A 50-vertex ring has degrees 2, far below 25. A student says it therefore has no Hamiltonian cycle. What is wrong?
options: The ring has fewer than 50 vertices
The theorem gives a sufficient condition, not a necessary one
Degree 2 is not allowed in a graph
A Hamiltonian cycle needs degree at least 25
optionExplain: The ring has exactly 50.
Right: The theorem only goes one way.
Degree 2 is common.
That reverses the theorem.
questions.explain: Going around the ring once visits every vertex once, so a Hamiltonian cycle exists despite small degrees. The theorem tells you when a cycle must exist, not when it cannot.
questions.rule: A failed hypothesis proves nothing.

questions.q: Which statements agree with the theorem? Select all that apply.
options: A multigraph on 10 vertices with every degree at least 5: the theorem applies
10 vertices, every degree at least 5: a Hamiltonian cycle exists
10 vertices, every degree 4: no Hamiltonian cycle exists
10 vertices, every degree 4: the theorem does not decide, so a cycle may still exist
optionExplain: The theorem is stated for graphs, not multigraphs.
Right: Degree 5 equals \(v/2\).
Failing the hypothesis does not prove there is no cycle.
Right: Below \(v/2\) the hypothesis is not met.
questions.explain: Meeting the hypothesis gives a Hamiltonian cycle; missing it gives no information; and the statement is for graphs, not multigraphs.
questions.rule: Meeting the bound proves a cycle; missing it proves nothing.

questions.q: A graph has 12 vertices, every degree at least 6. Why can it not split into two separate pieces?
options: Each piece must have exactly 6 vertices, so the 12 split evenly
Two pieces would need 12 edges running between them, which is impossible
A piece holding a vertex also holds its 6 neighbors, so it has at least 7 vertices, and two pieces would need 14
Separate pieces always contain at least one vertex of degree 1
optionExplain: Pieces could have different sizes; the point is the minimum.
There are no edges between separate pieces.
Right: Counting vertices in each piece.
That is not forced.
questions.explain: The degree hypothesis forces connectivity: every piece has at least 7 vertices, but 12 is less than 14. The book's hint for proving the theorem is that the hypothesis forces G to be connected.
questions.rule: High minimum degree forces connectedness.
questions.teaches: The book hints that the first step in proving the theorem is to show the degree hypothesis forces G to be connected.

questions.q: Two climbers must stand at equal height at every moment while walking. What should one state of the system record?
options: Only the one height that both of them currently share
Where both climbers stand, a pair of positions at the same height
How far along the route each of them has walked so far
The combined height of the two climbers added together
optionExplain: The height alone does not tell the positions.
Right: A state needs both locations.
Distance walked misses where they are.
A total loses which climber is where.
questions.explain: The state is the pair of positions, with the equal-height requirement. The card builds a graph from these pairs.
questions.rule: State = pair of positions at equal height.

questions.q: Each vertex of the new graph records the positions of the two men as an ordered ____ of locations.
questions.explain: A configuration is an ordered pair (x, y) of locations at the same elevation.
questions.rule: A vertex is an ordered pair (x, y).

questions.q: A range has one peak P and feet L and R at the start elevation. The men start at (L, R) and both climb one step. Where are they?
options: (L, R)
(R, L)
(P, L)
(P, P)
optionExplain: That is the start, before any step.
That is the swapped configuration, reached after descending.
Mixing P with L puts them at different heights.
Right: Both climb to the peak at the same time.
questions.explain: Climbing keeps them at equal height, and the next interesting level is the peak, so both reach P.
questions.rule: Each step moves both men to equal-height positions.

questions.q: Put the steps of the recasting in order.
items: Label the interesting locations of the range
Take as vertices all ordered pairs of locations at the same elevation
Join two vertices when the men can move between them in one step
Look for a path from the start pair to the swapped pair
questions.explain: The method is: choose the states, join the legal moves, then ask a path question.
questions.rule: States, moves, path.

questions.q: A student takes as vertices all pairs (x, y) of interesting locations, regardless of height. What is wrong?
options: The men must stay at the same elevation, so only equal-height pairs are legal configurations
Pairs must contain two different locations, never the same spot twice
A graph cannot have that many vertices, because pairs grow too fast
The pairs should be unordered, so that (x, y) and (y, x) coincide
optionExplain: Right: Equal height is part of the rules.
Both men may stand at the same location.
Large graphs are fine.
Order tells which man is where.
questions.explain: Pairs at different heights cannot occur while the men stay level, so they are not configurations.
questions.rule: Only legal configurations are vertices.

questions.q: If the two men can both be at the same spot at the same time, starting from the two ends, can they also swap places?
options: No: once they meet, the walk is over and nothing more can happen
Only if the range has a single peak, so the two sides match
Yes: the rest of the walk mirrors what they did, with roles exchanged and the order reversed
Only if they happen to meet exactly at the top of a peak
optionExplain: Meeting does not stop them walking on.
The number of peaks is irrelevant.
Right: The graph is symmetrical.
The meeting point can be anywhere.
questions.explain: The book notes that a path from the start to a configuration (j, j) already does the trick, since the graph is symmetrical.
questions.rule: Reaching a meeting pair is enough.
questions.teaches: The book says a path from the start to a configuration where both men are at the same spot suffices, because the graph is symmetrical.

questions.q: One man stands on a peak and the other in a trough, both at the same height. Can the pair take a joint step that keeps them level?
options: Yes, both can step upward together and stay level
Yes, both can step downward together and stay level
Yes, provided they both agree to walk backward along the path
No: the peak man can only go down and the trough man only up
optionExplain: The peak man cannot go up.
The trough man cannot go down.
Backward is another direction along the range, still down from a peak.
Right: From a peak every direction is down.
questions.explain: Their only moves change the heights in opposite directions. The card next lists the degrees of the other pair types.
questions.rule: A peak and a trough cannot move together.

questions.q: A vertex of the form (peak, peak) in the configuration graph has degree ____.
questions.explain: Each man can step down either side, so there are \(2 \cdot 2 = 4\) joint moves.
questions.rule: (peak, peak) has degree 4.

questions.q: A component of the configuration graph has vertices of degrees 1, 2, 2, 4, 2 and x. By the handshake lemma and the degree facts, what is x?
optionExplain: 2 would make the degree sum 13, which is odd.
3 is odd but never occurs among these vertices.
Right: The sum must be even, so x is odd; the only odd degree allowed is 1.
0 would make the sum odd.
questions.explain: The others add to 11, so x is odd. The only odd degree in this graph is 1, which fits the second end vertex.
questions.rule: Parity forces the other odd vertex.

questions.q: A student says a (peak, slope) vertex has degree 4, since the peak man has 2 moves and the slope man has 2. What is wrong?
options: The peak man has only 1 move, so the degree must be 3
The slope man's upward move cannot match the peak man's downward moves, so the count is 2
The slope man has 3 moves, so the degree must be 5
The men may end at different heights, so the count is not fixed
optionExplain: A peak man has 2 downward moves.
Right: Multiplying counts ignores the level requirement.
A slope man has 1 up and 1 down.
Different heights are not allowed.
questions.explain: The men must move to equal heights. The peak man can only go down, so the slope man must also go down, giving \(2 \cdot 1 = 2\).
questions.rule: Count only moves that keep the men level.

questions.q: True or false: if the range were allowed to drop below the starting elevation, the start vertex would still have degree exactly 1.
questions.explain: Our reading: a man at an end could face a lower neighbor while the other man's neighbor is higher, and then there would be no level joint move; the book's degree facts are for ranges that never drop below the start.
questions.rule: The facts depend on the range staying at or above the start.

questions.q: In a new range, the pair (P, T), a peak and a trough at the same height, is a vertex of the graph. Can the men ever be in it, starting at the ends?
options: No: it is isolated, so no path reaches it
Yes, after climbing
Yes, if they walk backward
Only if P and T are close together on the graph
optionExplain: Right: Isolated vertices cannot be reached.
Climbing cannot reach an isolated vertex.
Backward steps are already edges.
Distance does not matter.
questions.explain: The graph contains all legal configurations, including unreachable ones such as isolated (peak, trough) pairs. The book notes that such vertices mean the whole graph is not connected, which is why the argument looks only at the start's component.
questions.rule: Isolated vertices are never reached.
questions.teaches: The graph includes vertices like (g, q) that are isolated, so it is not all connected; the argument works inside the connected component of the start vertex.

questions.q: Part of a network has exactly one vertex with an odd number of links, and all others have an even number. Is this possible?
options: Yes, if it is connected
No: the number of link ends in a network is even
Yes, if the odd vertex has one link
Yes, but only for a tree
optionExplain: Connectedness changes nothing.
Right: Link ends come in pairs.
A degree of one is odd, and the sum would still be odd.
Trees also obey the lemma.
questions.explain: Each link has two ends, so the sum of degrees is even and odd vertices come in pairs. The card applies this to Tibet.
questions.rule: Odd-degree vertices come in pairs.

questions.q: The proof applies the ____ lemma to the component of the graph that contains the start vertex.
questions.explain: The degree sum in that component is twice its number of edges, hence even.
questions.rule: Use the handshake lemma on the start's component.

questions.q: A graph has exactly two vertices of odd degree, P and Q. What is forced?
options: P and Q are neighbors
P and Q lie in the same connected component
P and Q lie in different components of the graph
Both have degree 1
optionExplain: They may be far apart.
Right: A component cannot contain exactly one odd vertex.
Each component would then contain exactly one odd vertex.
Their degrees can be 3 or larger.
questions.explain: If P's component contained no other odd vertex, it would have exactly one, which is impossible. So Q is also there.
questions.rule: Exactly two odd vertices are in the same component.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Tibet proof in order.
items: Label the interesting locations and form the graph of equal-height pairs
Check the degree of each kind of pair
Note that only the start pair and swapped pair have odd degree
Apply the handshake lemma to the start pair's component
Conclude the swapped pair is in that component, so a path exists
questions.explain: The proof first builds the graph, counts degrees, and then uses parity.
questions.rule: Build, count degrees, apply parity.

questions.q: A student claims the swapped pair is reachable because the whole configuration graph is connected. What is wrong?
options: The graph has no vertices of degree 1
The handshake lemma does not apply to connected graphs
Only one configuration exists
The graph is not connected; it has isolated vertices such as (peak, trough) pairs
optionExplain: It has two vertices of degree 1.
The lemma holds for every graph.
Many pairs exist.
Right: The argument needs only the component of the start.
questions.explain: Isolated vertices show the graph is not connected. The proof does not need the whole graph to be connected, only that parity forces the swapped pair into the start's component.
questions.rule: Argue within the start's component.

questions.q: In a puzzle's state graph, only two states have an odd number of legal moves: the initial state and the target. Can the target be reached?
options: Yes: the initial state's component must contain the other odd state, the target
No, because the initial state has odd degree and so is stuck
Only if the puzzle has an even number of states overall
Only if the whole graph is a tree with no cycles
optionExplain: Right: Parity forces the target into the same component.
Odd degree is no obstacle.
State counts do not matter.
Trees are not required.
questions.explain: The same parity argument applies. The book's moral: just about anything can be analyzed with graphs, but one needs the insight to build the graph and the crux move of defining vertices and edges cleverly.
questions.rule: Parity pairs up odd vertices.
questions.teaches: The book's moral: the hard part is the insight of building a graph and defining its vertices and edges in a clever way; a very simple parity analysis then solves the problem.

questions.q: On the plane with a real axis across and an imaginary axis up, which point stands for \(3 - 2i\)?
optionExplain: This swaps the two coordinates.
Right: The real part is the horizontal coordinate and the imaginary part the vertical one.
This changes the sign of the imaginary part.
This negates the real part and flips the imaginary part.
questions.explain: Real part across, imaginary part up. The card next names these parts.
questions.rule: Real part is across, imaginary part is up.

questions.q: For \(z = 5 - 7i\), the imaginary part \(\mathrm{Im}\,z\) equals ____.
questions.explain: Im z is the real coefficient of i, here \(-7\).
questions.rule: Im z is the real number b.

questions.q: Which complex number is the vector from the origin to the point \((-3, 4)\)?
optionExplain: This reverses both signs.
Right: The point \((a, b)\) corresponds to \(a + bi\).
This swaps the coordinates.
This flips the sign of the vertical coordinate.
questions.explain: The horizontal coordinate is the real part and the vertical coordinate is the imaginary part, so \((-3, 4)\) is \(-3 + 4i\).

questions.q: Sort each item: is it the real part or the imaginary part?

items.t: The 3 in \(3 + 4i\)
The 4 in \(3 + 4i\)
The 5 in \(5 - 2i\)
The horizontal coordinate of the point
The vertical coordinate of the point

questions.explain: The real part is the horizontal coordinate, the imaginary part is the vertical coordinate, and both are real numbers.
questions.rule: Re is horizontal; Im is vertical.

questions.q: A student says \(\mathrm{Im}(3 + 4i) = 4i\). What is wrong?
options: The imaginary part is 3
The imaginary part is \(-4\)
The imaginary part is the real number 4, without the \(i\)
The imaginary part is \(3 + 4\)
optionExplain: 3 is the real part.
The sign is positive.
Right: Im z is b, a real number.
Parts are not added.
questions.explain: In \(a + bi\) the imaginary part is \(b\). The \(i\) marks the direction, but is not part of the number \(b\).
questions.rule: Drop the \(i\) when naming Im z.

questions.q: A ship sails 3 km east and 4 km north, a displacement \(3 + 4i\). A second ship leaves a different harbour and does the same. Is its displacement the same complex number?
options: No: it starts at a different point, so the number changes
No: only the first ship's displacement is a vector
Yes, but only if both harbours are on the real axis
Yes: a vector is fixed by its magnitude and direction, wherever it starts
optionExplain: The starting point changes where the ship ends, not the displacement.
Both displacements are vectors.
The start can be anywhere.
Right: Displacement does not depend on the starting point.
questions.explain: The book stresses that a vector can start anywhere; what defines it uniquely is its magnitude and direction. The origin is only the usual place to draw it.
questions.rule: A vector can start anywhere.
questions.teaches: A vector can start anywhere, not only at the origin; what defines it uniquely is its magnitude and direction.

questions.q: An arrow runs from the origin straight up to the point \((0, 5)\). What angle does it make with the positive horizontal axis, counterclockwise?
options: A quarter turn, \(\pi/2\)
No turn, \(0\)
A half turn, \(\pi\)
Three quarters of a turn, \(3\pi/2\)
optionExplain: Right: Straight up is a quarter turn from the horizontal.
That is the direction of the positive horizontal axis.
That points to the left.
That points straight down.
questions.explain: A quarter turn counterclockwise points up. The card next calls this angle the argument.
questions.rule: Angles go counterclockwise from the real axis.

questions.q: The magnitude of \(3 + 4i\) is ____.
questions.rule: |z| is the square root of \(a^2 + b^2\).

questions.q: Which is the polar form of \(-3\)?
options: \(3\,\mathrm{Cis}\,0\)
\(3\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/2)\)
\(9\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\pi\)
\(3\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\pi\)
optionExplain: This is the point \(+3\).
This is the point \(3i\).
The magnitude is 3, not 9.
Right: The point \(-3\) is 3 units from the origin, pointing left.
questions.explain: Length 3 and angle \(\pi\) (pointing left) give \(3\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\pi = 3(-1 + 0i) = -3\).
questions.rule: Length first, then the direction.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Its angle counterclockwise from the real axis
Length times Cis of the angle
questions.explain: A complex number can be given by its two coordinates or by its length and angle.
questions.rule: Polar form = length and angle.

questions.q: A student computes \(\arg(-1 - i)\) as \(\arctan(1) = \pi/4\). What is wrong?
options: The point lies in the third quadrant, so the angle is \(5\pi/4\)
The magnitude should be used instead of the angle here
The angle should be \(-\pi/4\)
The point has no argument, since it lies on no axis
optionExplain: Right: The tangent alone cannot tell which quadrant.
Magnitude is not an angle.
That would be the fourth quadrant.
Every nonzero number has an argument.
questions.explain: Both \(1 + i\) and \(-1 - i\) have the ratio \(b/a = 1\), but they point in opposite directions. Locate the quadrant first.
questions.rule: Check the quadrant before choosing the angle.

questions.q: A text refers to the absolute value of a complex number \(z\). Which quantity is meant?
options: Its angle \(\arg z\)
Its length \(|z|\), the same as its magnitude
Its real part \(\mathrm{Re}\,z\)
Its conjugate
optionExplain: The angle is the argument.
Right: Magnitude, modulus and absolute value are three names for one quantity.
The real part is only one coordinate.
The conjugate is another complex number.
questions.explain: The book uses magnitude, modulus and absolute value as synonyms, and also the informal word length.
questions.rule: Magnitude = modulus = absolute value.
questions.teaches: Magnitude is also called modulus or absolute value, and informally length; the argument is informally called the angle.

questions.q: The point \((3, 4)\) is reflected in the horizontal axis. Where does it land?
optionExplain: That reflects in the vertical axis.
That reflects through the origin.
Right: Reflecting in the horizontal axis keeps the horizontal coordinate and flips the vertical one.
That reflects in the diagonal.
questions.explain: Only the vertical coordinate changes sign. The card next calls this the conjugate.
questions.rule: Conjugation flips the sign of the imaginary part.

questions.q: True or false: the conjugate \(\bar z\) is the reflection of \(z\) in the imaginary axis.
questions.explain: The conjugate reflects in the real axis: \(a + bi\) becomes \(a - bi\).
questions.rule: Conjugate = reflection in the real axis.

options: \(4 + 9\) with a leftover \(i\)
optionExplain: Right: This is \(z\bar z = a^2 + b^2 = 4 + 9 = 13\).
The cross terms cancel, so no \(i\) remains.
The \(i\) terms cancel exactly.
Subtracting the squares forgets that \(i^2 = -1\).
questions.rule: \(z\bar z\) adds the squares.

questions.q: If \(z\) is a real number, then \(\bar z\) equals ____.
questions.explain: A real number lies on the real axis, so reflecting it in the real axis changes nothing.
questions.rule: Real numbers are their own conjugates.

questions.q: A student writes \(z + \bar z = 2\,\mathrm{Im}\,z\). What is wrong?
options: The sum is 0
The sum is \(2a\), so it equals twice the real part
The sum is \(2bi\)
The sum equals \(|z|^2\)
optionExplain: That would be the difference.
Right: The imaginary parts cancel and the real parts double.
That is the difference \(z - \bar z\).
That is the product, not the sum.
questions.explain: \((a + bi) + (a - bi) = 2a\), so \(\mathrm{Re}\,z = (z + \bar z)/2\).
questions.rule: Adding conjugates keeps the real part.

questions.q: For \(z = 5 - 2i\), what is \((z - \bar z)/(2i)\)?
optionExplain: The sign of the imaginary part is negative.
This leaves the \(i\) in place.
Right: \(z - \bar z = -4i\), and dividing by \(2i\) gives \(-2\).
5 is the real part.
questions.explain: The difference \(z - \bar z = 2bi\), so \((z - \bar z)/(2i) = b = \mathrm{Im}\,z\). The book lists both \(\mathrm{Re}\,z = (z + \bar z)/2\) and \(\mathrm{Im}\,z = (z - \bar z)/(2i)\).
questions.rule: \(\mathrm{Im}\,z = (z - \bar z)/(2i)\).
questions.teaches: The book lists \(\mathrm{Im}\,z = (z - \bar z)/(2i)\), next to \(\mathrm{Re}\,z = (z + \bar z)/2\).

questions.q: Two arrows start at the origin. Where does their sum point?
options: To the midpoint of the segment joining the two tips
Along the longer of the two arrows only
Perpendicular to both of the arrows in the plane
Along the diagonal of the parallelogram the two arrows span
optionExplain: The midpoint of the tips is half the sum.
The shorter arrow also contributes.
Nothing makes the sum perpendicular.
Right: Vector addition is the parallelogram rule.
questions.explain: The sum is the diagonal from the common start. The card next states this as a rule.
questions.rule: Sum of arrows is the parallelogram diagonal.

questions.q: The real part of \((3 + 2i) + (1 - 5i)\) is ____.
questions.explain: Real parts add: \(3 + 1 = 4\).
questions.rule: Add real and imaginary parts separately.

questions.q: What is the distance between the points \(1 + 2i\) and \(4 + 6i\)?
optionExplain: 7 adds the horizontal and vertical differences.
25 forgets the square root.
Right: The distance is \(|z - w| = |3 + 4i| = 5\).
3 is only the horizontal difference.
questions.explain: The difference is \(3 + 4i\), whose magnitude is \(\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\).
questions.rule: Distance = \(|z - w|\).

questions.q: True or false: \(z - w\) is the vector that starts at \(z\) and ends at \(w\).
questions.explain: \(z - w\) runs from \(w\) to \(z\), since adding it to \(w\) gives \(z\).
questions.rule: z - w points from w to z.

questions.q: What is the midpoint of the segment joining \(2 + 6i\) and \(8 - 2i\)?
optionExplain: This is the sum, not the half-sum.
This is half of the difference.
This is the difference.
Right: The midpoint is \((z + w)/2 = (10 + 4i)/2\).
questions.explain: Add the two numbers and halve: \((10 + 4i)/2 = 5 + 2i\).
questions.rule: Midpoint = half the sum.

questions.q: Three ropes pull a buoy with forces \(z_1, z_2, z_3\) that sum to zero. Drawn end to end, what shape do the arrows form?
options: A straight line
A closed triangle
An open path of three arrows
A parallelogram
optionExplain: A line would need the arrows to be parallel and cancel.
Right: Forces that balance bring the path back to its start.
An open path has a nonzero sum.
A parallelogram needs four sides.
questions.explain: If \(z_1 + z_2 + z_3 = 0\), placing the vectors tip to tail returns to the start. The book states this for any number of vectors summing to zero: they form a closed polygon.
questions.rule: Vectors that sum to zero close up.
questions.teaches: If complex numbers \(z_1, \dots, z_n\) sum to zero, drawn as vectors placed end to end they form a closed polygon.

questions.q: Two complex numbers each have length 2. What is the length of their product?
optionExplain: This keeps one length and ignores the other.
This cubes or doubles the product.
Right: Lengths multiply: \(2 \cdot 2 = 4\).
This divides instead of multiplying.
questions.explain: Lengths multiply. The card next states the full rule including angles.
questions.rule: Multiply lengths, add angles.

questions.q: When two complex numbers are multiplied, their angles are ____.
questions.explain: The angle of the product is the sum of the angles.
questions.rule: Angles add under multiplication.

questions.q: What is \((2\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/6))(3\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/3))\)?
options: \(5\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/2)\)
\(6\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/2)\)
optionExplain: This adds the lengths.
Right: Lengths multiply, giving 6, and angles add, giving \(\pi/6 + \pi/3 = \pi/2\).
This multiplies the angles.
This adds the lengths and multiplies the angles.
questions.explain: \(2 \cdot 3 = 6\) and \(\pi/6 + \pi/3 = \pi/2\), so the product is \(6\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/2) = 6i\).
questions.rule: Product: multiply lengths, add angles.

questions.q: A student writes \((3\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/4))(2\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/4)) = 6\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/16)\). What is wrong?
options: The angles should be added, giving \(\pi/2\)
The lengths should be added together, giving 5
The angle should be 0
The product has no angle
optionExplain: Right: Angles add; they are not multiplied.
Lengths multiply.
Nothing makes the angle vanish.
Every nonzero number has an angle.
questions.explain: The correct product is \(6\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/4 + \pi/4) = 6\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/2)\).
questions.rule: Do not multiply the angles.

questions.q: True or false: if \(z\) and \(w\) both lie on the unit circle, then \(zw\) also lies on the unit circle.
questions.explain: Both have length 1, so the product has length \(1 \cdot 1 = 1\), and only the angle changes.
questions.rule: Unit circle numbers stay on the unit circle when multiplied.

optionExplain: This forgets the angle \(5\pi/2\).
This raises 2, not \(\sqrt2\), to the tenth power.
Right: The length is \((\sqrt2)^{10} = 32\) and the angle is \(10\pi/4 = 5\pi/2\), a quarter turn after two full turns.
This takes the angle in the wrong direction.
questions.explain: Repeated use of the rule: length \((\sqrt2)^{10} = 32\) and angle \(10 \cdot \pi/4 = 5\pi/2\), which is \(\pi/2\) after whole turns. The book lists this result as a practice identity.
questions.rule: Use lengths and angles for big powers.
questions.teaches: The book lists \((1 + i)^{10} = 32i\) and \((1 - i\sqrt3)^5 = 16(1 + i\sqrt3)\) among its practice identities.

questions.q: The arrow from the origin to \(2\) is turned a quarter turn counterclockwise. Which number does it point to?
optionExplain: That is a half turn.
Right: A quarter turn counterclockwise from the positive real axis points straight up.
That is a quarter turn clockwise.
That is an eighth of a turn and a longer arrow.
questions.explain: Up is \(2i\). The card next shows this is multiplication by \(i\).
questions.rule: A quarter turn counterclockwise is multiplication by \(i\).

questions.q: Multiplication by \(i\) rotates a vector by ____ radians counterclockwise.
questions.explain: A quarter turn is \(\pi/2\) radians (90 degrees).
questions.rule: Times \(i\) is a quarter turn.

questions.q: What is \(i(3 + i)\)?
optionExplain: This leaves the number unchanged.
This turns the arrow clockwise instead of counterclockwise.
This treats \(i^2\) as \(+1\).
Right: \(i \cdot 3 = 3i\) and \(i \cdot i = -1\).
questions.explain: \(3i + i^2 = -1 + 3i\). The vector \((3, 1)\) becomes \((-1, 3)\), a quarter turn counterclockwise.
questions.rule: Times \(i\) sends \((a, b)\) to \((-b, a)\).

questions.q: Match each multiplier to what it does to a vector.
pairs: Stretch to three times the length, same direction
Shrink to a fifth of the length, same direction
questions.explain: Each multiplier acts through its length (stretch) and its angle (rotation).
questions.rule: Length stretches, angle rotates.

questions.q: A student says multiplying by \(3 + 4i\) rotates a vector by \(4/3\) radians. What is wrong?
options: The vector is stretched by a factor of 7 and is not rotated at all
The rotation is clockwise, and it is by 5 radians
The rotation is the angle \(\arctan(4/3) \approx 0.93\) radians; \(4/3\) is only its tangent
Multiplying by \(3 + 4i\) only stretches
optionExplain: The stretch factor is 5, not 7.
5 is the length and the rotation is counterclockwise.
Right: The angle of \(3 + 4i\) is the argument, not the ratio.
It both rotates and stretches.
questions.explain: The multiplier \(3 + 4i = 5\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\theta\) with \(\theta = \arctan(4/3)\). It rotates by \(\theta\) and stretches by 5.
questions.rule: Rotation angle is the argument.

questions.q: A graphics program must rotate every point \(60^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin and double its distance from the origin. Which number do you multiply by?
options: \(\sqrt3 + i\)
\(\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\)
optionExplain: Right: Rotating by \(\pi/3\) and doubling is \(2\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/3) = 2(\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i)\).
This rotates by \(45^\circ\).
This rotates by \(30^\circ\).
This rotates correctly but forgets to double.
questions.explain: One number does both jobs: \(2\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/3) = 1 + i\sqrt3\). Every complex number is at once a point, a vector and a transformation.
questions.rule: Rotate-and-stretch is one multiplication.
questions.teaches: Every complex number is simultaneously a point, a vector, and a geometric transformation (a rotation followed by a stretch).

questions.q: A complex number of length 6 is divided by one of length 2. What is the length of the quotient?
optionExplain: This multiplies the lengths.
This subtracts the lengths.
This adds the lengths.
Right: Division undoes multiplication, so lengths divide.
questions.explain: The quotient has length \(6/2 = 3\). The card next adds the rule for angles.
questions.rule: Lengths divide.

questions.q: When complex numbers are divided, their angles are ____.
questions.explain: Division undoes multiplication: multiplying adds angles, so dividing subtracts them.
questions.rule: Angles subtract in division.

questions.q: What is \((12\,\mathrm{Cis}\,\pi)/(3\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/4))\)?
options: \(4\,\mathrm{Cis}(5\pi/4)\)
\(9\,\mathrm{Cis}(3\pi/4)\)
\(4\,\mathrm{Cis}(3\pi/4)\)
optionExplain: This adds the angles.
This subtracts the lengths.
This multiplies the lengths and adds the angles.
Right: Lengths divide (\(12/3 = 4\)) and angles subtract (\(\pi - \pi/4 = 3\pi/4\)).
questions.rule: Divide lengths, subtract angles.

questions.q: A student computes \((8\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/2))/(2\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/6))\) as \(4\,\mathrm{Cis}(2\pi/3)\). What is wrong?
options: The angles should be subtracted, giving \(\pi/3\)
The lengths should be subtracted from each other, giving 6
The quotient should have length 16
The angle should be \(\pi/12\)
optionExplain: Right: Dividing subtracts angles.
Lengths divide.
Dividing does not multiply the lengths.
The student did not divide the angles.
questions.explain: \(\pi/2 - \pi/6 = \pi/3\), so the quotient is \(4\,\mathrm{Cis}(\pi/3)\).
questions.rule: Subtract, do not add.

questions.q: True or false: dividing a complex number by a number of length 1 leaves its length unchanged.
questions.explain: The quotient has length \(r/1 = r\); only the angle changes, by a clockwise rotation.
questions.rule: Dividing by a unit number only rotates.

options: \(\tfrac13 - \tfrac14 i\)
optionExplain: This keeps the angle instead of reversing it.
Right: The reciprocal has length \(1/5\) and the opposite angle, so it is \(\bar z/|z|^2\).
This has length 1, not \(1/5\).
This takes reciprocals of the parts, which is not valid.
questions.explain: By the division rule, \(1/z\) has length \(1/|z|\) and angle \(-\arg z\): the conjugate direction stretched by \(1/|z|^2\). So \(1/(a + bi) = (a - bi)/(a^2 + b^2)\), which the book asks you to see without computation.
