It depends on k
optionExplain: This is the reverse.
They are not equal.
Right: k^2 < k(k + 1), so the fraction is larger.
The comparison holds for all k.
questions.explain: The telescoping series is smaller, which is the wrong way for an upper bound. The card next fixes it.
questions.rule: Bound the terms by a telescoping series after shifting the index so that the inequality points the right way.

questions.q: True or false: For \(s\ge2\) and \(k\ge1\), \(\frac1{k^s}\le\frac1{k^2}\).
questions.explain: A bigger exponent makes the denominator at least as large.
questions.rule: Larger s, smaller terms.

questions.q: Using \(\frac1{k^2}\le\frac1{k(k-1)}\) for \(k\ge2\), what upper bound follows for \(\zeta(2)\)? Answer: ____
questions.explain: Add the first term 1 to the telescoped total 1.
questions.rule: Bound the tail, add the head.

questions.q: Compare \(\zeta(3)\) and \(\zeta(2)\).
options: zeta(3) > zeta(2)
zeta(3) < zeta(2)
They are equal
Not comparable
optionExplain: The reverse.
Right: every term of zeta(3) is smaller.
The terms differ.
Termwise comparison works.
questions.explain: 1/k^3 <= 1/k^2 for all k.
questions.rule: Larger exponent, smaller zeta.

questions.q: A student reasons \(\frac1{k^2}<\frac1{k(k+1)}\), so \(\zeta(2)<1\). What is wrong?
options: The series starts at 2
The sum 1 is wrong
Nothing
The inequality is reversed
optionExplain: The inequality is the issue.
The telescoped sum is 1.
The argument fails.
Right: 1/k^2 is larger than 1/(k(k + 1)).
questions.explain: k^2 is smaller than k(k + 1), so its reciprocal is larger.
questions.rule: Check the direction.

questions.q: To show \(\sum\frac1{k^2+1}\) converges, which comparison works?
options: No comparison
1/(k^2 + 1) < 1/k^2 and the shifted telescoping bound
optionExplain: The inequality is false.
Larger than a divergent series is not the case.
The comparison works.
Right: smaller than a series we showed convergent.
questions.explain: Use the shown bound for 1/k^2.
questions.rule: Compare to a convergent series.
questions.teaches: When convergence is the question, the first few terms, even the first few trillion, do not matter, so you may shift the index of summation to suit you.

questions.q: What is the leading coefficient of \(5x^3-2x+7\)?
optionExplain: Right: it multiplies the highest power x^3.
3 is the degree, not a coefficient.
7 is the constant term.
-2 multiplies a lower power.
questions.explain: The leading coefficient belongs to the highest power. The card next names these parts.
questions.rule: Degree is the largest exponent with a non-zero coefficient, and monic means that coefficient is 1.

questions.q: A polynomial whose leading coefficient is 1 is called ____.
questions.explain: Monic polynomials are the standard case in this chapter.
questions.rule: Monic: leading coefficient 1.

questions.q: Sort each polynomial: is it monic?

items.t: x

questions.explain: Check the coefficient of the highest power only.
questions.rule: Look at the top term.

questions.q: What is the smallest of Z, Q, R, C such that \(3x^2+\tfrac12x\) is in that set's polynomials?
options: Z
Q
R
C
optionExplain: Z needs integer coefficients; 1/2 is not.
Right: coefficients 3 and 1/2 are rational.
R works but is not smallest.
C works but is not smallest.
questions.explain: Q is the smallest set containing both coefficients.
questions.rule: Pick the coefficient set that contains them all.

questions.q: A student says \(3x^4+0x^5+2\) has degree 5 because it contains \(x^5\). What is wrong?
options: The coefficient of x^5 is zero, so the degree is 4
The degree is the number of terms
The degree is the constant term
Nothing
optionExplain: Right: degree counts only non-zero coefficients.
That would be 2.
That would be 2.
The degree is 4.
questions.explain: A term with zero coefficient is absent.
questions.rule: Degree ignores zero coefficients.

questions.q: Over the integers modulo 5, written \(\mathbb{Z}_5[x]\), what is \(7x^2+10x+3\) after reducing coefficients?
optionExplain: 7 is 2 modulo 5.
Right: 7 is 2 and 10 is 0 modulo 5.
10 is 0 modulo 5.
7 is not 1.
questions.explain: Reduce each coefficient modulo 5.
questions.rule: Reduce coefficients in Z_n.
questions.teaches: Occasionally the coefficients are taken from Z_n, the integers modulo n.

questions.q: What is the coefficient of x in \((1+2x)(3+x)\)?
optionExplain: 5 adds 2 and 3.
6 is only the product 2 times 3.
Right: 1 times 1 plus 2 times 3.
3 is the constant term.
questions.explain: Two products contribute to x. The card next states the pattern.
questions.rule: The coefficient of x^j in a product is the sum of a_s b_t over all s and t adding to j.

questions.q: True or false: \(c_j\) is the sum of all products \(a_sb_t\) with \(s+t=j\).
questions.explain: Each pair of exponents adding to j contributes.
questions.rule: Exponents add.

questions.q: What is the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+x+x^2)^2\)? Answer: ____
questions.explain: Three pairs of exponents add to 2.
questions.rule: Count the pairs with s + t = 2.

questions.q: What is the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((1+x+x^2)^2\)?
optionExplain: 3 is the coefficient of x^2.
1 is the coefficient of x^4.
4 is too large.
Right: a1 b2 + a2 b1 = 2.
questions.explain: Only the pairs (1, 2) and (2, 1) are available.
questions.rule: Out-of-range exponents contribute 0.

questions.q: A student claims \(c_j=a_jb_j\). Which example refutes this?
options: (1+x)^2 has degree 1
Nothing refutes it
optionExplain: Right: two pairs, (0,1) and (1,0), contribute to x.
c_0 is 1.
The degree is 2.
The claim fails.
questions.explain: The index adds, it does not match.
questions.rule: s + t = j, not s = t = j.

questions.q: Two dice are rolled. The numbers of ways to roll each total are the coefficients of the square of x + x^2 + ... + x^6. In how many ways can a total of 7 occur?
optionExplain: 7 is the total, not the count.
5 forgets one pair.
12 counts all ordered pairs.
questions.explain: The coefficient of x^7 sums over s + t = 7 with both between 1 and 6.
questions.rule: Coefficients count ways.
questions.teaches: The indices s and t run over non-negative integers with s + t = j, so c_j has at most j + 1 products.

questions.q: Dividing \(x^2+3x+5\) by \(x+1\) gives quotient \(x+2\). What is the remainder?
options: 2x
optionExplain: 5 is the original constant.
2x is not constant.
0 would mean x + 1 divides it.
questions.explain: Multiply back and subtract. The card next states the general form.
questions.rule: Dividing f by g leaves a remainder of smaller degree than g; g divides f exactly when the remainder is zero.

questions.q: True or false: In the division algorithm the remainder has smaller degree than the divisor.
questions.explain: Degree measures size, so the process stops when degree drops.
questions.rule: Remainder degree < divisor degree.

questions.q: What is the remainder when \(x^3+x^2+7\) is divided by \(x^2+3\)?
optionExplain: The signs are reversed.
This is the quotient.
The remainder has an x-term.
questions.explain: Subtract (x^2 + 3)(x + 1) from the dividend.
questions.rule: Multiply back to check.

questions.q: Using the remainder of \(n^3+50\) on division by \(n+2\), what is the largest positive n with \(n+2\) dividing \(n^3+50\)? Answer: ____
questions.explain: The remainder is 42, so n + 2 must be a divisor of 42.
questions.rule: Divisibility reduces to dividing the constant remainder.

questions.q: A student divides \(x^2+3x+5\) by \(x+1\), subtracts \(x(x+1)\), and reports the remainder \(2x+5\). What is wrong?
options: The remainder should be x^2
The divisor must be x - 1
The remainder has degree 1, not less than the divisor's degree, so division is unfinished
Nothing
optionExplain: The remainder is smaller.
The divisor is x + 1.
Right: subtract 2(x + 1) to reach remainder 3.
The division is incomplete.
questions.explain: Keep dividing until the degree is below the divisor's degree.
questions.rule: Finish the division.

questions.q: In integer division, the remainder is smaller than the divisor. What plays that role for polynomials?
options: Its leading coefficient is smaller
Its constant term is zero
Its degree is smaller than the divisor's degree
It has fewer terms than the quotient
optionExplain: Coefficients are unconstrained.
Remainders need not vanish at 0.
Right: degree is the size measure.
The count of terms is unrelated.
questions.explain: Size for polynomials means degree.
questions.rule: Degree measures size.
questions.teaches: The same division algorithm holds for polynomials with coefficients in Z, Q, R, C and Z_n, and the book notes it is as important for polynomials as for integers.

questions.q: Adding 9 to both sides of \(x^2+6x=5\) gives which equation?
optionExplain: 6 is the coefficient, not the shift.
The right side also gains 9.
The sign is wrong.
questions.explain: Half of 6 is 3, so the square is (x + 3)^2. The card next shows the method.
questions.rule: To solve a quadratic, complete the square; the formula is only a record of that method.

questions.q: True or false: Abel proved that, in general, there is no elementary formula for the zeros of polynomials of degree 5 or higher.
questions.explain: This is the book's footnote.
questions.rule: No general formula past degree 4.

questions.q: Completing the square in \(x^2+4x-1=0\) gives \((x+2)^2=\)____.
questions.explain: Add 4 to both sides: x^2 + 4x + 4 = 5.
questions.rule: Add (b/2)^2 to both sides.

questions.q: For \(x^2+2bx+c=0\), what are the solutions?
options: x = b +/- sqrt(b^2 - c)
x = -b +/- sqrt(b^2 - c)
x = -b +/- sqrt(b^2 + c)
x = -2b +/- sqrt(c)
optionExplain: The sign of b is wrong.
Right: (x + b)^2 = b^2 - c.
c is subtracted when it moves across.
The shift is b, not 2b.
questions.explain: Complete the square with b squared.
questions.rule: Shift by half the x coefficient.

questions.q: A student writes \(x^2+6x=5\Rightarrow(x+3)^2=5\). What step was skipped?
options: Dividing by 6
Taking a square root
Nothing
Adding 9 to the right side as well
optionExplain: No division is needed.
The root comes next.
The equation changed.
Right: adding 9 on the left must be balanced.
questions.explain: Whatever you add to one side must be added to the other.
questions.rule: Keep equations balanced.

optionExplain: The shift is +5 because the middle term is -10.
The shift is half of 10.
questions.rule: Complete the square with the coefficient's sign.
questions.teaches: Formulas for the zeros of any cubic or quartic polynomial were discovered in the 16th century.

questions.q: What is the remainder when \(x^2-3x+4\) is divided by \(x-1\)?
optionExplain: Right: 1 - 3 + 4.
4 is the constant term.
-1 forgets part of the sum.
0 would mean x - 1 is a factor.
questions.explain: You do not need to divide: just evaluate. The card next explains.
questions.rule: To find a remainder on division by x - a, just evaluate the polynomial at a.

questions.q: True or false: The remainder of \(P(x)\) divided by \(x-a\) is \(P(a)\).
questions.explain: This is the remainder theorem.
questions.rule: Remainder = value at a.

questions.q: What is the remainder when \(x^{100}+2x+3\) is divided by \(x+1\)? Answer: ____
questions.explain: Put x = -1.
questions.rule: Use a = -1 for x + 1.

questions.q: What is the remainder when \(x^3+2x^2-5\) is divided by \(x+2\)?
optionExplain: 11 is P(2), the wrong sign of a.
-8 is the cube only.
3 is wrong.
questions.explain: The divisor x + 2 means a = -2.
questions.rule: Mind the sign of a.

questions.q: A student says the remainder of \(x^3-2x+3\) on division by \(x+2\) is \(P(2)=7\). What is wrong?
options: The remainder is always 0
The divisor is x - 2
The divisor x + 2 means a = -2, so the remainder is P(-2) = -1
Nothing
optionExplain: Remainders need not vanish.
The divisor is x + 2.
Right: x + 2 = x - (-2).
The sign is wrong.
questions.explain: Rewrite x + 2 as x - (-2).
questions.rule: a is the root of the divisor.

questions.q: What is the remainder when \(x^{100}\) is divided by \(x^2-1\)?
options: x
optionExplain: The remainder would need P(1) = 1 and P(-1) = 1.
x^2 - 1 does not divide x^100.
x + 1 gives -1 + 1 = 0 at x = -1.
Right: write the remainder as ax + b; x = 1 and x = -1 both give 1 = a + b and 1 = -a + b, so a = 0, b = 1.
questions.explain: A remainder of degree less than 2 is ax + b; substitute x = 1 and x = -1.
questions.rule: Substitute convenient values.
questions.teaches: The substitute-convenient-values tool applies to any identity true for all x, and has many applications.

questions.q: The polynomial \(x^3-7x+6\) equals 0 at \(x=2\). Which must be a factor?
optionExplain: x + 2 would correspond to a zero at -2.
6 is the constant term.
Right: a zero at 2 gives the factor x - 2.
The factor is linear.
questions.explain: Zeros and linear factors correspond. The card next states this.
questions.rule: A zero a gives the factor x - a, and a known factor x - a means P(a) = 0.

questions.q: True or false: If \(P(a)=0\), then \(x-a\) is a factor of \(P(x)\).
questions.explain: This is the factor theorem.
questions.rule: Zero gives factor.

questions.q: The polynomial \(x^3-2x^2-5x+6\) has the zero 3; its other zeros are 1 and ____.
questions.explain: Dividing by x - 3 leaves x^2 + x - 2 = (x + 2)(x - 1).
questions.rule: Divide out a known factor.

questions.q: A polynomial of degree 4 has the zeros 1, 2 and 3. How many further linear factors does the factor theorem leave?
options: Two
One
None
Four
optionExplain: Two would be a degree-5 polynomial.
Right: the quotient by (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3) has degree 1.
The degree is 4, not 3.
Four is the whole degree.
questions.explain: Each known zero takes away one degree.
questions.rule: Degree minus known zeros.

questions.q: A student says \(P(5)=0\), so \(x+5\) is a factor. What is wrong?
options: The factor is x^2 - 5
P has no factors
The factor is x - 5
Nothing
optionExplain: The factor is linear.
P has at least this factor.
Right: a zero at 5 gives x - 5.
The sign is wrong.
questions.explain: x - a vanishes at a.
questions.rule: Factor sign opposes zero sign.

questions.q: View \(x^n-y^n\) as a polynomial in x. Which zero shows that \(x-y\) is a factor for every n?
options: x = y
x = -y
optionExplain: Right: y^n - y^n = 0.
At x = 0 the value is -y^n.
x = -y gives (-y)^n - y^n, usually non-zero.
x = 1 gives 1 - y^n.
questions.explain: Substitute x = y.
questions.rule: A zero in x gives a factor in x.
questions.teaches: This is why x - y divides x^n - y^n for every n, which explains the long factorisation formula for the difference of nth powers.

questions.q: How many zeros does \((x-1)(x+3)^2(x-5)^3\) have, counting each as often as it repeats?
optionExplain: 3 counts distinct zeros.
Right: 1 + 2 + 3.
5 miscounts.
8 is too many.
questions.explain: Multiplicity counts repeats. The card next states the general theorem.
questions.rule: A polynomial of degree n has n complex zeros if you count each as often as its multiplicity.

questions.q: True or false: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra guarantees that every polynomial in C[x] of degree at least 1 has a complex zero.
questions.explain: This is the statement of the theorem.
questions.rule: At least one complex zero.

questions.q: How many distinct zeros does \((x-1)(x-2i)(x+2i)(x-7)^3(x+6)^2\) have? Answer: ____
questions.explain: List each zero once.
questions.rule: Distinct = ignore multiplicity.

questions.q: How many complex zeros, counted with multiplicity, does \(x^4+x+1\) have?
options: It depends on the coefficients
optionExplain: Right: the degree is 4.
1 is only the guaranteed minimum.
2 is not the degree.
The count is fixed by the degree.
questions.explain: A degree-n polynomial has n zeros with multiplicity.
questions.rule: Degree = number of zeros.

questions.q: A student says \(x^2+1\) has no zeros, so the Fundamental Theorem is false. What is wrong?
options: The theorem is about odd degrees only
x^2 + 1 is not a polynomial
Nothing
The theorem allows complex zeros: i and -i
optionExplain: The theorem is for all degrees.
It is a polynomial.
The student ignored C.
Right: the zeros i and -i exist in C.
questions.explain: The guarantee is in C[x].
questions.rule: Zeros may be complex.

questions.q: Write \(3x^2-12\) in the factored form of the theorem.
optionExplain: The leading coefficient 3 is missing.
The zeros are +/-2.
The zeros are distinct.
Right: leading coefficient 3, zeros 2 and -2.
questions.explain: The factored form includes the leading coefficient a_n.
questions.rule: Do not forget a_n.
questions.teaches: The count of exactly n zeros uses the fact that a polynomial of degree n has at most n distinct zeros, which the book leaves as an exercise.

questions.q: A monic cubic has zeros 0, 1 and 2. Which polynomial is it?
optionExplain: Right: one factor per zero.
These factors have the opposite zeros.
This has degree 2.
This has no zero at 0.
questions.explain: Each zero gives a factor, and monic fixes the constant. The card next uses this idea.
questions.rule: If you cannot see zeros, build a new polynomial that has them, then fix the constant with a convenient value.

questions.q: True or false: If \(P(k)=\frac{k}{k+1}\), then \((x+1)P(x)-x\) vanishes at \(x=0,1,\dots,n\).
questions.explain: At x = k it equals (k + 1) P(k) - k = 0.
questions.rule: Clear the denominator to create zeros.

questions.q: A polynomial P of degree at most 1 satisfies P(k) = k/(k+1) for k = 0 and 1. What is P(2)? Answer: ____
questions.explain: The formula gives (n + 1 + (-1)^(n+1))/(n + 2) with n = 1.
questions.rule: Use the polynomial, not the pattern.

questions.q: For \(n=2\), what is \(P(3)\)?
optionExplain: 3/4 is the pattern's value at 3.
3/5 is wrong.
1 is for n = 1 and n = 3.
questions.rule: The pattern fails at n + 1 in general.

questions.q: To find C in \((x+1)P(x)-x=Cx(x-1)\cdots(x-n)\), a student substitutes \(x=0\). Why does that fail?
options: The left side is undefined
C is 0
Nothing
Both sides are 0, so no information about C results
optionExplain: The left side is defined.
C is non-zero.
The value is useless.
Right: x = 0, 1, ..., n all make the right side zero.
questions.explain: Choose a value where the right side is non-zero, namely x = -1.
questions.rule: Avoid the known zeros.

questions.q: A polynomial P of degree at most 2 has P(1) = 1, P(2) = 4 and P(3) = 9. What is P(4)?
optionExplain: 14 is wrong.
18 is wrong.
Right: Q(x) = P(x) - x^2 has three zeros but degree at most 2, so Q = 0 and P = x^2.
12 is wrong.
questions.explain: Define a new polynomial with obvious zeros.
questions.rule: Subtract a guess to expose zeros.
questions.teaches: The value x = -1 was convenient because it kills the troublesome term (x + 1) P(x) on the left.

optionExplain: 5 forgets the sign.
6 is the product, a_0.
-6 is wrong.
questions.explain: Expand and read off the x coefficient. The card next generalises.
questions.rule: Coefficients are plus or minus the sums of products of zeros taken k at a time, alternating in sign.

questions.q: True or false: For a monic quadratic with zeros r and s, the constant term is rs and the x coefficient is -(r + s).
questions.explain: This is the pattern for degree 2.
questions.rule: Sum with minus sign, product with plus.

questions.q: The product of the zeros of \(x^3+2x^2-5x-7\) is which value? Answer: ____
questions.explain: For a cubic, a_0 = -qrs.
questions.rule: a_0 = (-1)^n times the product.

questions.q: A monic quartic has zeros 1, 2, 3, 4. What is its \(x^2\) coefficient?
optionExplain: The sign of an even-degree-difference term is plus.
10 is the sum of zeros.
24 is the product.
questions.explain: Sum all six products of two zeros.
questions.rule: a_2 = + sum of pair products.

questions.q: A student says for \(x^3+a_2x^2+a_1x+a_0\), \(a_2=q+r+s\). What is missing?
options: A factor 2
A product instead of a sum
Nothing
A minus sign: a_2 = -(q + r + s)
optionExplain: No factor 2.
It is a sum.
The sign is wrong.
Right: the x^2 coefficient is minus the sum.
questions.explain: The sign is (-1) to the power k.
questions.rule: Signs alternate.

questions.q: How many monomials appear, before collecting like terms, when (x - r1)(x - r2)(x - r3)(x - r4)(x - r5) is multiplied out?
optionExplain: Right: each factor offers 2 choices, 2^5 = 32.
25 is 5 squared.
10 is 5 choose 2.
5 is the number of factors.
questions.explain: Each of the 5 factors contributes either x or minus its zero.
questions.rule: 2 choices per factor.
questions.teaches: For four factors there are 16 monomials, and exactly 6 of them use two x's and two constants.

questions.q: A quartic has zeros a, b, c, d with abcd = -1984 and ab = -32. What is cd?
optionExplain: Right: -1984 divided by -32.
The signs cancel.
32 is wrong.
-32 is ab.
questions.explain: Divide the total product by the known pair. The card next builds on this.
questions.rule: Name the quantity you need, find the step before it, and use sums and products of pairs instead of single zeros.

questions.q: True or false: \(ac+ad+bc+bd=(a+b)(c+d)\).
questions.explain: Factor a from the first two terms and b from the last two.
questions.rule: Group cross terms.

questions.q: Solve \(u+v=18\) and \(62u-32v=-200\). What is u? Answer: ____
questions.explain: Substitute v = 18 - u.
questions.rule: Solve the 2 by 2 system.

questions.q: With \(ab=-32\) and \(cd=62\), which expression gives k, the sum of all six pair products?
optionExplain: This is the product of the pairs.
This is the sum of the zeros.
Right: ab + cd = 30, and the four cross terms factor.
The cross terms are added.
questions.explain: k = ab + cd + (a + b)(c + d).
questions.rule: Pair products split into three groups.

questions.q: A student solves for each of a, b, c, d individually before finding k. Which advice does this ignore?
options: Use a calculator
Avoid the factor theorem
Compute what the target needs (u and v), not the values of the zeros
Never use equations
optionExplain: Calculators are not the point.
The factor theorem is not forbidden.
Right: the target k only needs u = a + b and v = c + d.
Equations are allowed.
questions.explain: Aim at the penultimate step.
questions.rule: Compute what you need.

questions.q: A quartic \(x^4-10x^3+kx^2-50x+24\) has two zeros with product 4. What is k?
optionExplain: 30 forgets the cross term.
Right: cd = 6, 4v + 6u = 50 and u + v = 10 give u = v = 5, so k = 4 + 6 + 25.
24 is the product of all zeros.
50 is the coefficient of x.
questions.explain: Use ab = 4, cd = 6, u + v = 10 and 4v + 6u = 50.
questions.rule: Same method, new numbers.
questions.teaches: An easier solution of the original problem exists by showing that the quartic factors into two quadratics, one having constant term -32.

questions.q: Which of these could be a rational zero (lowest terms) of \(3x^2+5x-2\)?
optionExplain: Right: numerator 2 divides -2, denominator 3 divides 3.
3 does not divide -2.
5 does not divide -2.
5 does not divide 3.
questions.explain: Numerators come from the constant term, denominators from the leading coefficient.
questions.rule: List the candidates a/b with a dividing the constant term and b dividing the leading coefficient, then test them.

questions.q: True or false: In lowest terms, the numerator of a rational zero divides the constant term and the denominator divides the leading coefficient.
questions.explain: This is the theorem.
questions.rule: Numerator: constant term; denominator: leading coefficient.

questions.q: How many candidate rational zeros does \(2x^3+x^2-7x-6\) have? Answer: ____
questions.explain: Divisors of 6 over divisors of 2, with both signs, after removing duplicates.
questions.rule: List candidates systematically.

questions.q: What does the theorem say about the zeros of \(x^2-3\)?
options: Zeros must be integers
The only rational candidates are +/-1, +/-3, and none works, so sqrt(3) is irrational
It has no zeros
It has rational zeros
optionExplain: The theorem does not say that.
The zeros are +/-sqrt(3).
None of the candidates is a zero.
questions.explain: Test each candidate.
questions.rule: Use it to prove irrationality.

questions.q: A student says \(1/2\) might be a zero of \(x^2+3x+5\). What is wrong?
options: The numerator 1 must be 5
The denominator 2 would have to divide the leading coefficient 1
Fractions cannot be zeros
Nothing
optionExplain: The numerator must divide 5, and 1 does.
Right: b must divide 1.
Fractions can be zeros.
The candidate is not allowed.
questions.explain: Check both divisibility conditions.
questions.rule: Check b against the leading coefficient.

questions.q: What do the candidates \(\pm1,\pm2\) show for \(x^3-2\)?
options: The cube root of 2 is irrational, since none of them is a zero
The cube root of 2 equals 1
The cube root of 2 is an integer
Nothing
optionExplain: P(1) is not 0.
P(2) is not 0.
They show irrationality.
questions.explain: A real zero is the cube root of 2; test the candidates.
questions.rule: Test candidates to show no rational zero.
questions.teaches: In practice the theorem is used not just to find zeros but also to prove that zeros are irrational.

questions.q: A monic polynomial with integer coefficients has the zero 2.5. Is that possible?
options: Yes, any rational can be a zero
Yes, but only if the degree is 2
No, a rational zero would be an integer
No, zeros must be even
optionExplain: Only for non-monic polynomials.
Degree does not change this.
Right: 5/2 would need a denominator dividing 1.
Parity is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Monic fixes the denominator. The card next states the consequence.
questions.rule: Show the number is not an integer and that it solves a monic integer polynomial.

questions.q: True or false: A non-integer zero of a monic integer polynomial must be irrational.
questions.explain: A rational zero would have denominator 1.
questions.rule: Monic + non-integer = irrational.

questions.q: The number \(\sqrt2+\sqrt3\approx3.146\) solves the monic equation \(x^4-10x^2+1=0\) and is not an integer, so it is ____ (rational or irrational).
questions.explain: A rational zero of a monic integer polynomial must be an integer.
questions.rule: Monic + non-integer = irrational.

questions.q: The polynomial \(2x-1\) has the zero 1/2. Why does this not contradict the theorem?
options: 1/2 is irrational
It is not monic
The degree is 1
It has integer coefficients
optionExplain: 1/2 is rational.
Right: the leading coefficient is 2, so denominator 2 is allowed.
Degree is irrelevant.
The theorem needs monic.
questions.explain: Drop monic and rational non-integers appear.
questions.rule: Monic is essential.

questions.q: A student says: 1/2 is not an integer, so it is irrational. What is missing?
options: The number must be negative
The number must be even
It would need to be a zero of a monic integer polynomial
Nothing
optionExplain: Sign is irrelevant.
Parity is irrelevant.
Right: 1/2 is a non-integer but rational.
The reasoning is incomplete.
questions.explain: Non-integer is not enough by itself.
questions.rule: Both parts are needed.

questions.q: Which number is guaranteed irrational because it solves the monic integer equation \(x^2-x-1=0\) and lies between 1 and 2?
optionExplain: 1.5 is rational and does not satisfy it.
7/4 is rational.
1 does not satisfy the equation.
Right: it is non-integer and a zero of a monic polynomial.
questions.explain: Check that the number is a zero and between consecutive integers.
questions.rule: Monic polynomial plus bounds.
questions.teaches: In the book's example the sum of square roots is first shown not to be an integer, then shown by induction to be a zero of a monic polynomial.

questions.q: Since \(2\le5\), which is true?
options: -6 and -15 cannot be compared
optionExplain: Right: multiplying 2 <= 5 by -3 reverses the direction.
This keeps the direction.
The numbers differ.
Both are numbers on a line.
questions.explain: Multiplying by a negative number reverses the order. The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: Adding keeps the direction; multiplying by a negative reverses it; reciprocals reverse it when the signs match.

questions.q: True or false: If \(x\ge y\) and \(a\ge b\), then \(x+a\ge y+b\).
questions.explain: Both sides of the sum increase by non-negative amounts.
questions.rule: Addition preserves order.

questions.q: If \(x\ge2\), then multiplying by -3 gives \(-3x\le\)____.
questions.explain: Multiplying by a negative number reverses the order, and -3 times 2 is -6.
questions.rule: Negative multiplier: flip.

questions.q: Here \(x=-2<y=3\). How do \(\frac1x\) and \(\frac1y\) compare?
options: They are equal
Cannot be compared
optionExplain: The reversal rule needs the same sign.
They differ.
Right: -1/2 < 1/3; the signs differ, so no reversal.
They can be compared.
questions.explain: Check the signs before reversing.
questions.rule: Reciprocals reverse only for the same sign.

questions.q: A student multiplies \(x\ge y\) by \(-2\) and writes \(-2x\ge-2y\). What is wrong?
options: The inequality should become equality
The student must add 2
Nothing
The inequality must reverse: -2x <= -2y
optionExplain: There is no equality.
Adding is unrelated.
The direction is wrong.
Right: negative multiplier.
questions.explain: A negative factor flips the order.
questions.rule: Watch the sign.

questions.q: Solve \(|x-3|=5\) for x.
options: x = 8 or x = -2
x = 8 only
x = 2 or x = -8
optionExplain: Right: the points at distance 5 from 3.
The point 3 - 5 = -2 also works.
The signs are reversed.
5 is the distance, not x.
questions.explain: Read |x - a| as the distance from x to a.
questions.rule: Absolute value is distance.
questions.teaches: The set of x with |x - a| = b consists of the points on the real number line at distance b from a.

questions.q: Which of these grows fastest as x becomes very large?
options: log base 2 of x
optionExplain: x^10 is eventually overtaken by 2^x.
Logarithms are the slowest.
x^2 is far slower than x^10.
Right: exponentials eventually beat every power.
questions.explain: Exponentials win in the end. The card next states the hierarchy.
questions.rule: For large enough x, logarithms are beaten by powers and powers are beaten by exponentials.

questions.q: Exponential functions eventually dominate every ____ function.
questions.explain: For b > 1, b^x outgrows any power of x.
questions.rule: Exponentials beat powers.

questions.q: At \(x=100\), which is larger?
options: They are equal
Cannot tell
optionExplain: The numbers differ greatly.
They can be computed.
questions.explain: Compare the sizes.
questions.rule: Exponential eventually wins.

questions.q: At \(x=10\), which is larger, \(2^x\) or \(x^{10}\)?
options: They are equal
Cannot tell
optionExplain: Right: 10^10 versus 1024.
Not yet at x = 10.
They differ.
They can be computed.
questions.explain: Eventually does not mean immediately.
questions.rule: Check where the crossing occurs.

questions.q: True or false: The expression \(0.001x^2\) stays below \(100000x+20000000\) for every x, since 0.001 is tiny.
questions.explain: A quadratic eventually dominates any linear function; here it exceeds the right side for x above 10^9. Constants only move the crossing point.
questions.rule: Eventual means for large enough x.

questions.q: For very large x, which is bigger: \(x^{0.1}\) or \(\log_2x\)?
options: log_2 x
They stay equal
Neither
optionExplain: The logarithm is overtaken.
Right: any positive power eventually beats a logarithm.
They do not stay equal.
One of them wins.
questions.explain: The hierarchy puts powers above logarithms.
questions.rule: A tiny power beats a logarithm.
questions.teaches: Any power x^a with a > 0 eventually dominates log_b x for every b > 1, however small a is.

questions.q: Which is larger, \(\sqrt{19}+\sqrt{99}\) or \(\sqrt{20}+\sqrt{98}\)?
options: The first
They are equal
Cannot tell
The second
optionExplain: The first is about 14.31.
They differ in the third decimal.
The comparison can be decided.
Right: about 14.37 versus 14.31.
questions.explain: Both are close to 14.3. The card next shows how to decide exactly.
questions.rule: Keep each step equivalent, watch for direction reversals, and square only positive quantities.

questions.q: True or false: Squaring both sides of an inequality between positive numbers preserves its direction.
questions.explain: For positive numbers, squaring is increasing.
questions.rule: Square positives only.

questions.q: To compare \(\sqrt7+\sqrt{15}\) with \(\sqrt8+\sqrt{14}\), after squaring you compare \(\sqrt{105}\) with \(\sqrt{\)____\(}\).
questions.explain: The squares are 22 + 2 sqrt105 and 22 + 2 sqrt(8 x 14) = 22 + 2 sqrt112, so the first is smaller.
questions.rule: Square, then compare the cross terms.

questions.q: For positive a and b, an unproved comparison between a and b has both sides replaced by their reciprocals. What happens to the direction?
options: The direction is kept
It becomes equality
The inequality is undefined
The direction reverses
optionExplain: This holds for positives only if you flip.
Equality does not follow.
It remains defined.
Right: the larger positive number has the smaller reciprocal.
questions.explain: Reciprocal is decreasing on positives.
questions.rule: Reciprocal flips.

questions.q: A student compares \(-3\) and \(2\) by squaring: \(9>4\), so \(-3>2\). What is wrong?
options: Squaring is never allowed
Squaring is not order-preserving when a side is negative
9 is not larger than 4
Nothing
optionExplain: Squaring positives is fine.
Right: the step is not reversible.
9 is larger than 4.
The conclusion is false.
questions.explain: Squaring loses the sign.
questions.rule: Only square non-negative sides.

questions.q: Compare \(\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{17}\) with \(\sqrt{12}+\sqrt{16}\).
options: The first is smaller
The first is larger
They are equal
Cannot tell
optionExplain: Right: squares 28 + 2 sqrt187 and 28 + 2 sqrt192.
The cross term is smaller.
Not equal.
Decidable.
questions.explain: Square both sides.
questions.rule: Same method, new numbers.
questions.teaches: The book writes a question mark over the inequality sign while it is unproved, and turns it upside down when a step reverses the direction.

options: They are equal
Cannot tell
optionExplain: The first is farther from 1.
They differ by a small gap.
Decidable.
Right: both are just below 1, and the second is closer.
questions.explain: Compare how far each is from 1. The card next does it with a function.
questions.rule: Turn a comparison of two numbers into a comparison of one function at two inputs, then show the function is monotone.

questions.q: True or false: The function \(f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}\) is increasing for positive x.
questions.explain: It equals 1/(1 + 1/x), and 1/x decreases.
questions.rule: x/(x+1) increases.

questions.q: Which is larger, \(\frac78\) or \(\frac89\)? Answer: ____
questions.explain: Use f(x) = x/(x + 1).
questions.rule: Consecutive such fractions increase.

options: They are equal
Cannot tell
optionExplain: Right: (x + 1)/x = 1 + 1/x decreases.
This is smaller.
They differ.
Monotone again.
questions.explain: The reciprocal function reverses the order.
questions.rule: Check which way the function goes.

questions.q: A student says \(\frac{1998}{1999}>\frac{1999}{2000}\) because its denominator is smaller. What is wrong?
options: The denominators are equal
A smaller denominator makes the fraction smaller
The numerators also differ, so one feature cannot decide
Nothing
optionExplain: The denominators differ.
A smaller denominator makes it larger, but the numerator is smaller too.
Right: both numerator and denominator change.
The conclusion is false.
questions.explain: Compare the whole fractions.
questions.rule: Do not use one feature alone.

questions.q: For positive n, which is larger, \(\frac{n}{n+1}\) or \(\frac{n+1}{n+2}\)?
options: n/(n+1) for every positive n
(n+1)/(n+2) for every positive n
It depends on n
They are equal
optionExplain: This reverses the order.
Right: f is increasing, so f(n + 1) > f(n).
The function is monotone for all positive n.
They differ by 1/((n+1)(n+2)).
questions.explain: Apply the monotone function at n and n + 1.
questions.rule: One argument covers every n.
questions.teaches: The book gets monotonicity from the principle that if the denominator increases the fraction decreases, and notes the uglier form is easier to analyse.

questions.q: Two positive numbers add up to 10. What is the largest their product can be?
optionExplain: 4 times 6 is 24.
3 times 7 is 21.
Right: 5 times 5.
2 times 8 is 16, and 20 is not attainable here.
questions.explain: The product is largest when the numbers are equal. The card next states this.
questions.rule: Arithmetic mean at least geometric mean for positives, with equality only when the numbers are equal.

questions.q: True or false: The arithmetic mean of two positive numbers is at least their geometric mean, with equality only when the numbers are equal.
questions.explain: This is AM-GM for n = 2.
questions.rule: AM >= GM.

questions.q: Two positive numbers have product 36. What is the smallest possible sum? Answer: ____
questions.explain: x + y >= 2 sqrt(xy) = 12.
questions.rule: Sum >= 2 sqrt(product).

questions.q: For which positive pairs does \(\frac{x+y}{2}=\sqrt{xy}\)?
options: Exactly the pairs with x = y
Exactly the pairs with y = 2x
All pairs
No pairs
optionExplain: Right: (x - y)^2 = 0.
y = 2x gives strict inequality.
Only equal pairs.
Equal pairs work.
questions.explain: Equality needs (x - y)^2 = 0.
questions.rule: Equality iff equal.

questions.q: A student applies AM-GM to \(x=-4,\ y=-9\), writing \(\frac{x+y}{2}=-6.5\ge6=\sqrt{36}\). What is wrong?
options: AM-GM needs positive numbers; here the mean is negative
The geometric mean is 6.5
The geometric mean is 36
Nothing
optionExplain: Right: -6.5 is less than 6.
sqrt(36) is 6.
sqrt(36) is 6.
The claim is false.
questions.explain: The hypothesis of positivity matters.
questions.rule: Check positivity.

questions.q: A farmer has 36 m of fence for a rectangle. What is the largest possible area?
options: 72 square metres
81 square metres
90 square metres
324 square metres
optionExplain: 72 corresponds to sides 8 and 9.
Right: sides 9 and 9 (sum 18).
90 is not attainable.
324 is 18 squared.
questions.explain: The sides sum to 18, so the product is at most 81.
questions.rule: Fixed perimeter: square is best.
questions.teaches: With S, P and D the sum, product and difference of x and y, the proof gives S^2 - 4P = D^2.

questions.q: Which pair summing to 20 has the largest product?
options: 8 and 12
5 and 15
1 and 19
10 and 10
optionExplain: Right: 100.
questions.explain: The nearer the numbers, the larger the product. The card next states the principle.
questions.rule: For a fixed sum, the closer the two numbers, the larger their product.

questions.q: True or false: With a fixed sum, a pair of positive numbers further apart has a smaller product.
questions.explain: P = (S^2 - D^2)/4 shrinks as D grows.
questions.rule: Closer means bigger product.

questions.q: Two positive numbers sum to 30 and differ by 4. What is their product? Answer: ____
With the sum fixed at 30, the distance grows from 4 to 6. What happens to the product?
options: It increases
It stays the same
It decreases, from 221 to 216
It becomes negative
optionExplain: Larger distance gives a smaller product.
D changes the product.
The numbers stay positive.
questions.rule: Distance up, product down.

questions.q: A student says the product grows when the numbers move apart, because the bigger number gets bigger. What is overlooked?
options: The bigger number shrinks
The sum changes
Nothing
The smaller number shrinks by the same amount, and the net effect lowers the product
optionExplain: The bigger one grows.
The sum is fixed.
The conclusion is wrong.
Right: moving a apart keeps the sum but lowers the product.
questions.explain: Keep track of both numbers.
questions.rule: Both numbers move.

questions.q: Which is larger, 1998 x 2000 or 1999 x 1999?
options: They are equal
Cannot tell
optionExplain: This pair is further apart.
Right: same sum 3998, smaller distance.
They differ by 1.
Decidable.
questions.explain: Both pairs have sum 3998.
questions.rule: Same sum: choose the closer pair.
questions.teaches: Given a fixed amount of fencing, the rectangle of maximum area is a square, and this follows from the principle without calculus.

questions.q: Three positive numbers have sum 12. What is the largest their product can be?
optionExplain: Right: 4 x 4 x 4.
3 x 4 x 4 uses sum 11.
3 x 4 x 5 is 60.
36 is not maximal.
questions.explain: Equal numbers give the best product. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Among positive numbers with a fixed sum, the product is maximal exactly when all are equal.

questions.q: True or false: In the n-variable AM-GM inequality, equality holds if and only if all the numbers are equal.
questions.explain: This is part of the statement.
questions.rule: Equality iff all equal.

questions.q: Four positive numbers have product 81. What is the smallest possible sum?
optionExplain: 4 is the count.
81 is the product.
Right: G = 3, so sum >= 4 x 3.
9 is G squared.
questions.explain: Sum >= n times the geometric mean.
questions.rule: A >= G.

questions.q: Put the steps of the moving-points proof in order.
items: Pick a point L below the mean A and a point R above it
Move the nearer point onto A and shift the other to keep the pair's balance
The sum is unchanged, the product has risen, and one more point equals A
Repeat; after finitely many steps all points equal A
questions.explain: Each move keeps the sum and raises the product, and the process terminates.
questions.rule: Move, compare, repeat.

questions.q: A student says: numbers 1, 5, 9 have mean 5, so their geometric mean is 5. What is wrong?
options: The geometric mean is 15
The geometric mean is 9
Nothing
The geometric mean is the cube root of 45, below 5, since the numbers are not equal
optionExplain: 15 is the sum.
9 is the largest.
The claim is false.
Right: G < A unless all numbers are equal.
questions.explain: The means coincide only for equal numbers.
questions.rule: G <= A.

questions.q: Positive \(a,b,c\) have product 27. What is the smallest possible value of \(a+b+c\)?
optionExplain: 3 is the geometric mean.
Right: a = b = c = 3.
27 is the product.
6 is not attainable.
questions.explain: Sum >= 3 times the cube root of 27.
questions.rule: Fixed product: sum is at least n G.
questions.teaches: The argument is called algorithmic because it gives a concrete step-by-step procedure that ends after finitely many steps, and it recasts an inequality as an optimisation problem.

questions.q: For positive x, what is the smallest possible value of \(x+\frac1x\)?
optionExplain: x + 1/x is 2 at x = 1.
It is always positive for positive x.
Right: at x = 1.
4 is not the minimum.
questions.explain: At x = 1 the sum is 2. The card next shows it is the minimum.
questions.rule: Pair each ratio with its reciprocal, apply AM-GM to each pair, and count the terms.

questions.q: True or false: For \(x>0\), \(x+\frac1x\ge2\), with equality only at \(x=1\).
questions.explain: This is AM-GM for x and 1/x.

questions.q: What is the smallest value of \(3x+\frac3x\) for \(x>0\)? Answer: ____
questions.explain: Factor out 3.
questions.rule: Scale the minimum.

questions.q: For positive a, b, c, what is the smallest value of \((a+b+c)\left(\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c\right)\)?
optionExplain: Right: n squared with n = 3.
3 is n.
6 is wrong.
27 is not the bound.
questions.explain: Use the n squared bound.
questions.rule: Bound is n squared.

questions.q: A student says \(x+\frac1x\ge2\) for all real \(x\). Which value refutes this?
options: x = 1, giving 2
x = 2, giving 2.5
x = -1, giving -2
x = 0.5, giving 2.5
optionExplain: At x = 1 the claim holds.
At x = 2 the claim holds.
Right: AM-GM needs positive x.
At x = 0.5 the claim holds.
questions.explain: Check a negative value.
questions.rule: Positivity matters.

questions.q: For \(x>0\), what is the smallest value of \(\frac{(x+1)^2}{x}\)?
optionExplain: 2 is the minimum of x + 1/x only.
1 is wrong.
8 is not minimal.
questions.explain: Expand: x + 2 + 1/x.
questions.rule: Expand, then use x + 1/x >= 2.
questions.teaches: Equality holds in the n-variable product of sums when all a_i are equal, and the n squared terms split into n ones and (n^2 - n)/2 reciprocal pairs.

questions.q: What does \(\frac{2}{\sqrt n+\sqrt{n-1}}\) equal after rationalising?
options: 2(sqrt n + sqrt(n-1))
sqrt n - sqrt(n-1)
2(sqrt n - sqrt(n-1))
2/(sqrt n - sqrt(n-1))
optionExplain: This is the denominator itself.
The factor 2 stays.
Right: multiply top and bottom by sqrt n - sqrt(n-1); the denominator becomes 1.
This is the reciprocal.
questions.explain: The denominator becomes n - (n - 1) = 1. The card next uses this.
questions.rule: Bound each term above and below by differences, sum them, and refine the first few terms if the bound is too crude.

questions.q: True or false: Massage means loosening up an expression so that it becomes easier to deal with.
questions.explain: It includes adding zero and multiplying by one.
questions.rule: Massage to simplify.

questions.q: What is \(\sum_{n=1}^{100}2(\sqrt n-\sqrt{n-1})\)? Answer: ____
questions.explain: Only the last term 2 sqrt 100 survives.
questions.rule: Telescope: last minus first.

questions.q: Which interval contains \(\sum_{n=1}^{99}\frac1{\sqrt n}\), using the lower bound \(2(\sqrt{100}-1)\) and the upper bound \(2\sqrt{99}\)?
options: Between 20 and 22
Between 10 and 15
Between 0 and 10
Between 18 and 20
optionExplain: The upper bound is below 20.
The lower bound is 18.
The lower bound is 18.
Right: 18 < sum < 19.9.
questions.explain: Evaluate the two bounds.
questions.rule: Bounds give an interval.

questions.q: The bound \(\frac1{\sqrt1}<2(\sqrt1-\sqrt0)=2\) overestimates the first term by exactly 1. What does the book do?
options: It ignores the problem
It uses a larger bound
It starts the sum at n = 2 and treats the first term 1 separately
It discards the term
optionExplain: The estimate is refined.
A larger bound makes it worse.
Right: the first term is added exactly.
The term is kept as 1.
questions.explain: Crude bounds for small n can be corrected by hand.
questions.rule: Treat early terms exactly.

questions.q: What is the integer part of \(\sum_{n=1}^{100}\frac1{\sqrt n}\)?
optionExplain: 17 is too small.
19 is the upper bound only.
20 is too large.
Right: between 18.27 and 19, actual 18.59.
questions.explain: Add the exact first term 1 to the telescoping bounds for n = 2 to 100.
questions.rule: Bracket the sum, then read the integer part.
questions.teaches: The first term is replaced by its exact value because the bracketing trick is a silly overestimate there, which sharpens the bounds enough to decide the integer part.

options: 125 is larger than 121
121 is larger than 125
They are equal
Cannot tell
optionExplain: Right: 5 times 25 is 125 and 11 squared is 121.
The product is larger.
They differ by 4.
Decidable.
questions.explain: The product of sums of squares exceeds the square of the sum of products here.
questions.rule: The product of the two sums of squares is at least the square of the sum of products, with equality for proportional sequences.

questions.q: True or false: Equality in the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality holds if and only if the ratios a_i/b_i are all equal.
questions.explain: This is the equality condition.
questions.rule: Equality iff proportional.

questions.q: For \(a=(1,2,3)\) and \(b=(4,5,6)\), what is \((\sum a_i^2)(\sum b_i^2)-(\sum a_ib_i)^2\)? Answer: ____
questions.rule: The gap is a sum of squares.

questions.q: For \(a=(1,2,3)\), which choice of b gives equality?
optionExplain: Right: proportional to a.
Not proportional.
Not proportional.
Not proportional.
questions.explain: Equality needs a_i/b_i all equal.
questions.rule: Proportional means equality.

questions.q: A student writes \((x+y+z)^2\ge3(x^2+y^2+z^2)\) as the case \(a=b=c=1\). What is wrong?
options: Nothing
The inequality is reversed: (x + y + z)^2 <= 3(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)
It needs a = 2
It needs z = 0
optionExplain: The direction is wrong.
Right: the square of the sum is at most n times the sum of squares.
a = b = c = 1 is correct.
z need not vanish.
questions.explain: Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the square of the sum above.
questions.rule: Square of the sum <= n times sum of squares.

questions.q: Real x, y, z satisfy \(x+y+z=6\). What is the smallest possible \(x^2+y^2+z^2\)?
optionExplain: 6 is the sum.
18 is not the minimum.
36 is the square of the sum.
questions.rule: Fixed sum bounds the sum of squares below.
questions.teaches: For positive numbers the inequality takes the form (a + b + c)(x + y + z) >= (sqrt(ax) + sqrt(by) + sqrt(cz))^2, a way to bound the product of two unrelated sums from below.

questions.q: By Cauchy-Schwarz for positive numbers, \((a+b)(x+y)\ge\) which expression?
options: (a x + b y)
(ax + by)^2
a b x y
(sqrt(ax) + sqrt(by))^2
optionExplain: This is missing the square.
This squares the wrong quantity.
This multiplies everything.
Right: substitute square roots into the two-sequence form.
questions.explain: Replace a by sqrt a and so on in the basic inequality.
questions.rule: Choose the second sequence so the right side collapses to something you can bound with AM-GM.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's solution of the 1995 IMO problem, AM-GM shows x + y + z is at least 3 when xyz = 1.
questions.explain: This is the final step.
questions.rule: Finish with AM-GM.

questions.q: With \(a=1,b=4,x=9,y=1\), what lower bound does \((a+b)(x+y)\ge(\sqrt{ax}+\sqrt{by})^2\) give? Answer: ____
questions.explain: sqrt(1 x 9) = 3 and sqrt(4 x 1) = 2.
questions.rule: Use the square-root form.

questions.q: With \(u=\sqrt{y+z},\,v=\sqrt{z+x},\,w=\sqrt{x+y}\), what does \(u^2+v^2+w^2\) equal?
options: x + y + z
xyz
optionExplain: Each variable appears twice, not once.
Right: each variable appears twice.
Three would count too many.
The product is not the sum.
questions.explain: Add y + z, z + x and x + y.
questions.rule: Count how often each variable appears.

questions.q: A student concludes \(S\ge(x+y+z)^2\) from the Cauchy-Schwarz step. What is missing?
options: The factor 2(x + y + z): the inequality is 2S >= x + y + z
The student must square again
S should equal 3
Nothing
optionExplain: Right: S times 2(x + y + z) is at least (x + y + z)^2.
No further squaring.
S is at least 3/2.
The statement is incomplete.
questions.explain: Divide both sides by 2(x + y + z).
questions.rule: Track the factors.

questions.q: Positive x and y satisfy \(x+y=1\). What is the smallest value of \(\frac1x+\frac1y\)?
optionExplain: 2 is not attainable.
1 is too small.
8 is not the minimum.
questions.explain: Use the positive form with a = b = 1.
questions.rule: Pair a sum with a sum of reciprocals.
questions.teaches: Titu Andreescu's example: for a polynomial P with positive coefficients, if P(1/x) >= 1/P(x) holds at x = 1 it holds for every x > 0, proved with Cauchy-Schwarz on suitable square-root sequences.

questions.q: For \(a=(1,2)\) and \(x=(3,5)\), compare the average of the products with the product of the averages.
options: 6 is larger than 6.5
They are equal
Cannot tell
6.5 is larger than 6
optionExplain: The product of averages is smaller.
They differ by 0.5.
Decidable.
questions.explain: Compute both. The card next gives the general statement.
questions.rule: Two sequences ordered the same way have an average of products at least the product of their averages.

questions.q: True or false: Chebyshev's inequality needs both sequences to be monotonic in the same direction.
questions.explain: Opposite orders reverse the inequality.
questions.rule: Same direction.

questions.q: For \(a=x=(1,2,3)\), what is the average of the products minus the product of the averages? Answer: ____
questions.rule: Compute both sides.

questions.q: For \(a=(1,2,3)\) and \(x=(3,2,1)\) (opposite orders), how do the two averages compare?
options: Average of products is larger
Average of products is smaller (10/3 < 4)
They are equal
Cannot tell
optionExplain: That is the same-order case.
They differ.
Decidable.
questions.explain: The inequality reverses.
questions.rule: Opposite order reverses.

questions.q: A student applies Chebyshev to \(a=(1,3)\) and \(x=(5,2)\), claiming the average of products is at least the product of averages. What check refutes it?
options: 5.5 is less than 7
5.5 is larger than 7
Both equal 7
The sequences are equal
optionExplain: Right: the orders are opposite.
7 is the product of averages.
They differ.
The sequences differ.
questions.explain: Check that both sequences rise.
questions.rule: Check the ordering.

questions.q: For \(a=(1,2,3)\) and \(x=(2,2,5)\), what is \(3(ax+by+cz)-(a+b+c)(x+y+z)\) (with the sequences read in order)?
optionExplain: 0 would mean proportional constant sequences.
6 is only one pair.
63 is the first term.
questions.explain: The difference is the sum of (a_i - a_j)(x_i - x_j) over pairs.
questions.rule: Pair differences.
questions.teaches: The argument used for Chebyshev, writing a difference as a sum of products of ordered differences, can be adapted to many other situations.

questions.q: A diner offers 3 soups and 4 salads. How many different meals consist of one soup and one salad?
optionExplain: This counts a meal of one dish, a soup or a salad, not a meal with both.
Raising 3 to the power 4 has no meaning here; no choice is repeated.
Each of the 3 soups can be paired with each of the 4 salads, so multiply.
Factorial of 4 arranges four things in a row; no arranging is asked.
questions.explain: Choosing a soup and a salad are two choices that are both made, so the counts multiply. The card next sets out all four operations.
questions.rule: Before computing, decide whether the pieces are alternatives (add), successive choices (multiply), unwanted cases (subtract) or a uniform overcount (divide).

questions.q: Match each counting situation to the operation it calls for.
pairs: A prize is a book or a game, not both
A trip has a choice of train, then a choice of seat
Every outcome was counted six times
Count everything, then remove outcomes you do not want
questions.explain: Alternatives add, successive choices multiply, a uniform overcount divides, and unwanted cases are subtracted from the total.
questions.rule: Name the structure first, then pick the operation.

questions.q: A trip uses one of 5 buses or 2 trams (not both), then 1 of 3 tours. How many journeys are there?
optionExplain: The ways to travel add (5 + 2 = 7) because they are alternatives; the tour is a further choice, so multiply: 7 x 3.
This multiplies buses by trams by tours, as if a journey used both a bus and a tram.
This adds all three counts, treating the tour as an alternative to travelling.
This multiplies buses by trams and then adds the tours, mixing up the steps.
questions.explain: A journey is a mode of travel followed by a tour. The modes are alternatives (add) and the tour is an extra step (multiply): (5 + 2) x 3 = 21.
questions.rule: Add alternatives inside a step, multiply across steps.

questions.q: Sort each situation by the operation that combines its counts.

items.t: A student takes French or Spanish this term, not both
A password is one letter followed by one digit
A snack is a fruit or a biscuit, not both
A gift set contains one scarf and one hat

questions.explain: Words like or (with no overlap) signal addition; words like and, then, followed by signal successive choices and multiplication.
questions.rule: Or means add, and-then means multiply, when nothing overlaps.

questions.q: A student counts passwords of one letter (26 options) followed by one digit (10 options) as 26 + 10 = 36. What is the flaw?
options: Letters and digits overlap, so 10 must be subtracted
The answer must be divided by 2 because two symbols are used
36 is right because there are 36 symbols available
A password uses both choices, so the counts multiply to 260
optionExplain: Letters and digits are different kinds of symbol; nothing overlaps.
Nothing was counted twice, so nothing is divided out.
The 36 symbols would be the count of one-symbol passwords, not of two-symbol passwords.
Every letter pairs with every digit, so there are 26 x 10 = 260 passwords.
questions.explain: A password needs a letter and a digit, so the choices are made in turn and multiply.
questions.rule: If a single outcome contains both choices, multiply.

questions.q: A competition asks for 10,000 ten-digit multiples of 7 that are reorderings of each other. What sort of problem is this, per the book?
options: Number theory, solved by divisibility tests for 7
Careful counting of the correct objects, though it resembles number theory
Geometry, solved by arranging digits as shapes
A problem that only a computer search can settle
optionExplain: The surface looks like number theory, but the book says the solution is not about divisibility tests.
The book says it looks like number theory but is a matter of counting the right things.
Digits here are symbols to be reordered; no shapes are involved.
The book solves it by hand once the basic counting skills are developed.
questions.explain: The point is that a question about divisibility can reduce to counting reorderings.
questions.rule: Look for the counting structure beneath the surface.
questions.teaches: A problem that looks like number theory can be a counting problem: the Czech and Slovak 1995 question about 10,000 reordered ten-digit multiples of 7 is solved later in the chapter by counting.

questions.q: A school has 6 morning clubs and 5 afternoon clubs. A pupil joins exactly one club, and no club meets twice. How many choices?
optionExplain: Multiplying treats joining a morning club and an afternoon club as one combined choice.
The clubs are alternatives with no overlap, so the counts add.
The pupil joins one club, but several clubs are available to choose from.
This counts only the morning clubs and ignores the afternoon ones.
questions.explain: With nothing shared, 6 + 5 = 11. The card next states this as the simple-addition rule.
questions.rule: Counts of collections that share no element add.

questions.q: True or false: If A and B are disjoint finite sets, then \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|\).
questions.explain: Disjoint sets share no element, so each element of the union is counted once in the sum.
questions.rule: Disjoint sets add.

questions.q: A phone accepts a four-digit or a six-digit passcode (digits 0-9), one of the two. How many passcodes exist?
optionExplain: This multiplies 10^4 by 10^6, as if every passcode were a four-digit code followed by a six-digit one.
This counts only the six-digit codes and leaves out the four-digit ones.
This counts the four-digit codes twice and loses the six-digit ones.
A four-digit code has 10^4 = 10,000 options and a six-digit code 10^6 = 1,000,000; the two lists are alternatives, so add.
questions.explain: Each length is built by multiplying digit choices, and then the two lengths are added: 10^4 + 10^6 = 1,010,000.
questions.rule: Build each case by multiplying, then add the cases.

questions.q: A pupil adds 14 chess players and 11 choir members to get 25 students in either, though 6 do both. What is wrong?
options: The 6 students in both groups are counted twice, so the true number is 19
Nothing is wrong; 25 is the number of students
The 6 should be added on top, giving 31
The two numbers should be multiplied, giving 154
optionExplain: Adding counts each of the 6 students in both groups twice; taking the 6 off once gives 14 + 11 - 6 = 19.
The groups overlap, so the sum includes some students twice.
Adding the shared students again counts them a third time.
Students who do chess or choir are a union of two groups, not pairs of students.
questions.explain: Overlap breaks the simple-addition rule. The true count of students in the union is 19.
questions.rule: Check disjointness before adding.

questions.q: Collection A has 8 outcomes and B has 5. If A or B together have 11 distinct outcomes, how many outcomes lie in both? ____
questions.explain: The sum 8 + 5 = 13 is 2 more than 11, so 2 outcomes were counted twice.
questions.rule: The excess of the sum over the union equals the overlap.

questions.q: A depot sorts parcels into three classes that share no parcel: 12 letters, 6 small boxes and 5 large boxes. How many parcels are there?
optionExplain: This multiplies the class sizes, as if a parcel were one item from each class.
This adds only two of the three classes.
Adding extends to any number of mutually exclusive classes, so 12 + 6 + 5.
This adds only the small and large boxes and leaves out the letters.
questions.explain: The rule is not limited to two sets: any number of mutually exclusive classes add.
questions.rule: Mutually exclusive classes add, however many there are.
questions.teaches: Simple addition extends to any number of mutually exclusive classes: the book's example is classes of 12, 6 and 5 items that total 12 + 6 + 5.

questions.q: A pizzeria has 4 crusts and 5 sauces. How many different bases consist of one crust and one sauce?
optionExplain: Adding counts a single pick, a crust or a sauce, not both.
This raises 4 to the power 5, which counts something else entirely (five-step choices from 4 options).
This is 5 factorial, an arrangement count that does not apply here.
Each crust pairs with each of the 5 sauces, giving 4 x 5.
questions.explain: A base needs both a crust and a sauce, so multiply. The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: A joint choice from two lists multiplies their sizes, whether or not the lists share items.

questions.q: True or false: To count meals of one soup and one salad by multiplying, the soup list and the salad list must share no item.
questions.explain: The product rule holds for any two finite sets, disjoint or not: each soup still pairs with each salad.
questions.rule: The size of A x B is |A| times |B|, overlap or not.

questions.q: A PIN has 4 digits, each from 0 to 9, and digits may repeat. How many PINs exist?
optionExplain: This adds the options of the four positions, treating each as an alternative.
Each of the 4 positions has 10 options, independent of the others: 10 x 10 x 10 x 10.
This is P(10, 4), the count if no digit could repeat.
This removes PINs starting with 0, but a PIN may start with 0.
questions.explain: With repeats allowed, each position is an independent choice from 10 digits: 10^4 = 10,000.
questions.rule: Repeats allowed gives n options at each of k steps: n^k.

questions.q: A has 3 elements and B = A. A pupil says A and B form 3 + 3 = 6 pairs. What is wrong?
options: The pairs are counted by multiplying, which needs no disjointness: 3 x 3 = 9
Overlap between A and B means the answer is 3 x 3 - 3 = 6
The sets are the same, so only 1 pair is possible
The answer is 3 + 3 = 6 because two sets are involved
optionExplain: A x B is a set of ordered pairs (x, y). Even when B is A, every x can pair with every y, giving 9 pairs.
Overlap matters for unions, not for ordered pairs; the pair (a, a) is just one of 9.
Different pairs such as (a, b) and (b, a) are different outcomes.
Two sets give two stages of choice, and stages multiply.
questions.explain: Overlap affects the union but not the number of ordered pairs.
questions.rule: Overlap is irrelevant to |A x B|.

questions.q: A five-course dinner has 7 options per course (16,807 dinners). If each course gets one more option, the number of dinners becomes ____.
questions.explain: With 8 options for each of 5 courses there are 8^5 = 32,768 dinners.
questions.rule: Every added option multiplies through all later choices.

questions.q: A licence plate is 2 letters (26 options each) followed by 3 digits (10 options each). How many plates exist?
optionExplain: This adds 26 + 26 + 10, treating the letter and digit positions as alternatives.
This uses 26 options at all five positions.
The five positions are filled in turn: 26 x 26 x 10 x 10 x 10.
This is 26 + 26 + 26 + 26 + 26, adding instead of multiplying.
questions.explain: The positions have different numbers of options, which multiply: 26^2 x 10^3 = 676,000.
questions.rule: Multiply the option counts of each position.
questions.teaches: When a joint event has several sub-events with different numbers of choices, the number of ways it occurs is the product of those numbers.

questions.q: In how many different orders can 4 friends stand in a line for a photo?
optionExplain: This is 4 x 4, as if each place could take any friend again.
This adds 4 + 3 + 2 + 1, but the places are filled in turn, so the counts multiply.
Four choices for the first place, three for the next, two, then one.
This is 2^3 or 4 x 2, with no basis in the choices.
questions.explain: Each friend is used once, so 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24. The card next names this n factorial.
questions.rule: n different objects can be ordered in n! ways.

questions.q: The value of 6! is ____.
questions.rule: n! is the product of the integers from n down to 1.

questions.q: Eight different books are arranged on a shelf. How many arrangements exist?
optionExplain: This is 8! = 8 x 7 x 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1.
This is 7!, one factor short.
This is 2^8, which counts yes/no answers about the books, not orders.
This is 8^2; the first book has 8 places, but the next has 7, not 8.
questions.explain: Eight different objects arranged in a row give 8! = 40,320.
questions.rule: Use n! for orderings of n different objects.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a seventh different book to a shelf of 6 different books multiplies the number of arrangements by 7.
questions.explain: 7! = 7 x 6!, so the count grows by a factor of 7.
questions.rule: Adding one object multiplies the count by n + 1.

questions.q: A student orders the five letters of HARDY by computing 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. What is the flaw?
options: The sum is right, since 15 words can be written
The student should have divided by 5, giving 3
The total should be 5^5 = 3,125
The five places are filled one after another, so the choice counts multiply to 120
optionExplain: Fifteen is far below the true count; for example, the first letter alone gives 24 words each.
Nothing was overcounted, so no division is needed.
That would allow a letter to repeat; HARDY has five different letters.
The choices are successive, not alternatives, so 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120.
questions.explain: Placing letters is a succession of choices, so multiply.
questions.rule: Successive choices multiply, not add.

questions.q: Given 6! = 720, how many ways can 7 different guests be seated in a row?
optionExplain: This is 6 x 720, using one factor too few.
This is 720 + 7, adding the new guest instead of multiplying.
This is 2 x 720, doubling instead of multiplying by 7.
questions.explain: The book advises learning (at least passively) the values of n! for n up to 10, along with common sequences, so that steps like this are quick.
questions.rule: Know the small factorials.
questions.teaches: Knowing 6! = 720 makes 7! quick: 7! = 7 times 6!.

questions.q: A club of 12 different members elects a president and then a secretary, who must be different people. How many outcomes?
optionExplain: This allows the same person to hold both posts.
12 choices for president, then 11 for secretary: 12 x 11.
This is the number of unordered pairs; president and secretary are different roles.
This is 12 + 12, adding instead of multiplying.
questions.explain: Order matters because the roles differ, so 12 x 11 = 132. The card next names this P(12, 2).
questions.rule: P(n, r) is the product of r consecutive integers counting down from n.

questions.q: The value of P(7, 2) is ____.
questions.explain: P(7, 2) = 7 x 6 = 42, a product of 2 factors.
questions.rule: P(n, r) has r factors.

questions.q: Gold, silver and bronze medals go to three different runners from a field of 10. How many outcomes are there?
optionExplain: This is 10^3, which allows one runner to win several medals.
This is C(10, 3), which ignores who got which medal.
This is 10 x 3, which does not follow from the steps.
questions.explain: Medals differ in rank, so order matters: P(10, 3) = 720.
questions.rule: Ranked prizes use P(n, r).

questions.q: A pupil computes P(9, 3) as 9 x 8 x 7 x 6 = 3,024. What went wrong?
options: The product has four factors but should have exactly three: 9 x 8 x 7 = 504
The pupil should have divided by 3! to get 504
Nothing; P(9, 3) is 3,024
The pupil should have used 9 x 9 x 9 = 729
optionExplain: For r = 3 the last factor is n - r + 1 = 7, not 6.
The division by 3! turns P into a combination; it does not repair the extra factor in a permutation.
Only three places are filled, so only three factors appear.
That would allow a letter to repeat.
questions.explain: Only r factors appear in P(n, r).
questions.rule: Stop after r factors.

questions.q: True or false: If the letters of CHERNOBYL could repeat, the number of three-letter words would be 9^3 = 729.
questions.explain: With repeats allowed each of the 3 places has 9 options, so 9 x 9 x 9 = 729.
questions.rule: Repeats allowed gives n^r.

questions.q: A programmer computes P(n, r) with a loop that multiplies n(n - 1)...(n - r), one factor too many. Programmers call this error:
options: Overflow, because the product grows too large
A race condition between two loops
OBOB, the off-by-one bug
A rounding error from division
optionExplain: Overflow is about size limits; here the loop bound is wrong by one.
Nothing runs in parallel; the loop bound is just off.
The correct last factor is n - r + 1, so ending at n - r adds a factor; programmers call this the off-by-one bug.
The product has no division, so no rounding enters.
questions.explain: The slip is one factor too many, called OBOB.
questions.rule: Check the last factor against n - r + 1.
questions.teaches: The slip of ending the product at n - r instead of n - r + 1 is a frequent source of minor errors, known to computer programmers as OBOB, the off-by-one bug.

questions.q: How many different words can be made by rearranging all five letters of LEVEL (two L's and two E's)?
optionExplain: This treats the two L's and the two E's as different letters.
This corrects for the L's only and forgets the E's.
This is 5 x 4, the product of two factors, not a correction for repeats.
The 120 orders of five labelled letters count each word 2 x 2 = 4 times.
questions.explain: Dividing 5! by 2! twice gives 30. The card next states the general formula.
questions.rule: Divide n! by the factorial of the size of each group of identical objects.

questions.q: True or false: Swapping the two S's in GAUSS gives a different arrangement of the letters.
questions.explain: The two S's are indistinguishable, so the swapped word is the same word. That is why 5! overcounts.
questions.rule: Identical objects swapped give the same arrangement.

questions.q: How many different arrangements are there of the ten letters of BOOKKEEPER (B, O twice, K twice, E three times, P, R)?
optionExplain: This is 10!, which treats all letters as different.
This divides only by 2!, correcting for just one repeated letter.
This divides by 2! x 2! x 2!, using 2 for the three E's instead of 3!.
questions.explain: Divide 10! by the factorial of each repeated letter's count.
questions.rule: Use the factorial of each group size.

questions.q: Put in order the reasoning that counts the permutations of PARADOXICAL, which has three A's.
items: Pretend the three A's carry labels A1, A2, A3 so all letters differ
Count all 11! orders of the labelled letters
Notice each real word is counted 3! times, from relabelling the A's
Divide 11! by 3!
questions.explain: The count with labels is too large by the uniform factor 3!, which is why division fixes it.
questions.rule: Label, count, find the uniform overcount, divide.

questions.q: A word has 4 letters, all different. The formula with four groups of size 1 gives ____.
questions.explain: Each group has size 1, so 1! = 1 and the formula gives 4! = 24.
questions.rule: If nothing repeats, the formula reduces to n!.

questions.q: A strip has 12 tiles: 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green, tiles of one colour being identical. How many colour patterns exist?
optionExplain: This is 12!, which treats every tile as different.
This divides by 5! x 4! x 3! x 3!, with an extra factor.
This is 5 x 4 x 3, the product of the group sizes.
questions.explain: The same reasoning as for letters applies to tiles. The book names this the Mississippi formula, after the word MISSISSIPPI with 4 I's, 4 S's and 2 P's: 11!/(4! 4! 2!) = 34,650 arrangements.
questions.rule: Same formula for any indistinguishable kinds.
questions.teaches: The book calls this the Mississippi formula, after its amusing example MISSISSIPPI, whose letters (1 M, 4 I's, 4 S's, 2 P's) can be arranged in 11!/(4! 4! 2!) = 34,650 ways.

questions.q: Ten people each shake hands once with every other person. Counting ordered pairs of people gives 90. How many handshakes are there?
optionExplain: This counts a handshake once for each person, so every handshake is counted twice.
This counts each person shaking hands with everyone, including themselves.
Each handshake appears as two ordered pairs, so halve 90.
This adds 10 + 9, but the pairs are formed by choices that multiply.
questions.explain: Every handshake is counted exactly twice among ordered pairs, so divide by 2. The card next states this as a general rule.
questions.rule: Multiply the choices of a joint event; divide only when every wanted outcome is counted equally often.

questions.q: True or false: Dividing by the overcounting factor gives the true count when every wanted outcome is counted the same number of times.
questions.explain: If each wanted outcome is counted k times, the counted total is k times the true total, so division by k restores it.
questions.rule: Uniform overcounting divides out.

questions.q: Six different friends sit on a bench; a seating and its reverse count as one. How many distinct seatings are there?
optionExplain: This counts a seating and its reverse as different.
This is 5!, which fixes one friend's place and does not model the reversal.
6! = 720 seatings, and each is paired with exactly one reverse, so 720 / 2.
This is 720 / 4, dividing by too large a factor.
questions.explain: Every seating has a different reverse, because the six friends are different, so each is counted exactly twice.
questions.rule: Find the factor by asking how many listed outcomes represent one real outcome.

questions.q: A pupil lists 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 three-letter words from A to E, then halves it to count sets. What is wrong?
options: Each set appears in 3! = 6 orders, so the divisor should be 6, giving 10 sets
Nothing; the set count is 30
The divisor should be 3, one for each letter
The product should not be divided at all
optionExplain: Three letters can be arranged in 6 ways, so each set was counted 6 times, not 2.
Halving corrects only a double count, as with pairs.
Three letters can be ordered in 3! = 6 ways, not 3.
Sets ignore order, but the list has every order, so division is needed.
questions.explain: The divisor is the number of orderings of each wanted outcome.
questions.rule: The divisor equals the number of repeats per wanted outcome.

questions.q: Six friends on a bench (reversal counts as the same) give 360 seatings. With a seventh friend there are ____ seatings.
questions.explain: 7! = 5,040, and halving gives 2,520.
questions.rule: Divide the n! orderings by the 2 reversals.

questions.q: Club sign-ups total 45; pupils joined one, two or three clubs. Why can one divisor not give the number of pupils?
options: A pupil counted twice must be divided by 2, three times by 3, but dividing by 2.5 works
Sign-ups cannot be counted, because pupils change clubs
Dividing always works, so the pupils number 45 / 3 = 15
Pupils are counted different numbers of times, so the overcount is not uniform
optionExplain: An average divisor does not repair a total whose repeats differ.
Sign-ups can be counted; the issue is how often each pupil appears.
Dividing by 3 is correct only if every pupil joined three clubs.
The sign-up total counts one-club pupils once and the others two or three times, so no one divisor fits.
questions.explain: Uniform overcounting divides out; non-uniform overcounting does not.
questions.rule: Check that every outcome is repeated equally often.
questions.teaches: When overcounting is not uniform, dividing cannot repair it; the book introduces inclusion-exclusion for situations where sets overlap and overcounting is not uniform.

questions.q: How many different 5-bit strings contain exactly two 1s (and so three 0s)?
optionExplain: This counts all 5-bit strings, whatever their number of 1s.
Choose which 2 of the 5 positions hold a 1: 5!/(2! 3!).
This is 5 x 4, which counts the two positions in order.
This is 5^2; the two positions hold different places, not repeats.
questions.explain: Ten strings have exactly two 1s. The card next names this number 5 choose 2.
questions.rule: The number of n-bit strings with r zeros is the binomial coefficient n choose r.

questions.q: The number of 6-bit strings with exactly two 0s is ____.
questions.rule: n choose r counts n-bit strings with r zeros.

questions.q: A control panel has 8 lamps, and exactly 3 must be on. How many different on/off patterns satisfy this?
optionExplain: This is 8 x 7 x 6, which counts the three on-lamps in order.
This is 2^8, all patterns whatever the number on.
This is 8 x 3, which follows from no counting step.
questions.explain: Each pattern is an 8-bit string with exactly three 1s, so the count is the binomial coefficient 8 choose 3.
questions.rule: Lamps on or off are bits.

questions.q: True or false: The number of 7-bit strings with three zeros equals the number with four zeros.
questions.explain: Both equal 7!/(3! 4!) = 35, since the formula is unchanged when r and n - r swap.
questions.rule: Swapping the roles of 0 and 1 leaves the count unchanged.

questions.q: A pupil counts 7-bit strings with three zeros as 7!/3! = 840. What was left out?
options: A multiplication by 4!, giving 20,160
Nothing: 840 is right because ones are different
A division by 7, giving 120
A division by 4! for the four identical ones, giving 35
optionExplain: Multiplying would count more than the total possible strings.
The four 1s are identical, so swapping them changes nothing.
The factor 7 has no role among identical symbols.
Both kinds of identical symbols need a factorial in the denominator.
questions.explain: Every kind of identical symbol contributes its factorial.
questions.rule: Divide by r! and (n - r)!.

questions.q: A code presses exactly 4 of 10 keypad buttons, and only which buttons matter. How many codes exist?
optionExplain: Choosing which 4 of the 10 positions are pressed is the same as writing a 10-bit string with four 1s.
This counts the order in which the buttons are pressed.
This counts four-digit codes, not sets of pressed buttons.
This is 10 x 4, which does not follow from any choice step.
questions.explain: A bit string with r zeros is fixed by choosing which r of its n positions hold zeros.
questions.rule: Strings with r zeros correspond to choices of r positions.
questions.teaches: A bit string with r zeros is fixed by choosing which r of the n positions hold zeros, so counting such strings is the same as counting those position choices.

questions.q: A teacher forms a 3-person committee (no roles) from a class of 30. How many different committees are possible?
optionExplain: This counts ordered picks, as if members had different roles.
This is 30 x 3, which matches no choice step.
30 x 29 x 28 ordered picks, divided by the 6 orders of each committee.
This is 30^3, allowing the same person to be chosen several times.
