questions.explain: Order is irrelevant, so each committee is counted 3! times among ordered picks. The card next shows the formula.
questions.rule: Choosing r of n without order gives P(n, r) divided by r!.

questions.q: The number of ways to choose a committee of no people from 10 people is ____.
questions.explain: There is exactly one such committee, the empty one, which matches the formula with 0! = 1.

questions.q: A coach chooses a starting team of 4 from 10 players, with no positions assigned. How many teams are possible?
optionExplain: This counts each team once for every order of its four players.
This is 10^4, which allows a player to be chosen again.
This is 10 x 4, which follows from no choice step.
P(10, 4) = 5,040 ordered picks, divided by 4! = 24.
questions.explain: Divide the ordered count by 4! to remove the order.
questions.rule: C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r!.

questions.q: Sort each task by whether order matters in the count.

items.t: Choose a president, vice-president and secretary from a class
Pick three toppings for a pizza
Award gold, silver and bronze medals
Choose a 4-person delegation with no roles

questions.explain: When roles differ, swapping people gives a different outcome, so P(n, r) counts it. Roles-free selections count C(n, r).
questions.rule: Roles mean permutation; no roles means combination.

questions.q: A pupil says the number of 3-topping pizzas from 8 toppings is 8 x 7 x 6 = 336. What is wrong?
options: The 336 should be multiplied by 3! to give 2,016
Order of toppings does not matter, so 336 should be divided by 3! to give 56
Pizzas depend on order, so 336 is right
The answer should be 8 + 7 + 6 = 21
optionExplain: Multiplying makes the overcount worse.
A pizza with the same three toppings in a different order is the same pizza, so each is counted 6 times.
A sausage-mushroom-garlic pizza is the same as a mushroom-garlic-sausage pizza.
The toppings are chosen in turn, so counts multiply.
questions.explain: The ordered count includes each set 3! times.
questions.rule: Divide by r! when order is irrelevant.

questions.q: True or false: Giving the 3 members of a 30-person committee distinct roles raises the outcomes to P(30, 3) = 24,360.
questions.explain: With roles, each of the 4,060 committees can be assigned in 6 ways, giving 4,060 x 6.
questions.rule: Roles multiply C(n, r) back up by r!.

questions.q: Compute C(12, 3), choosing 3 of 12 objects, by cancelling rather than expanding all the factorials.
optionExplain: This is 12 x 11 x 10, with no division by 3!.
This divides by 3 instead of 3!.
This is 12 x 3, which follows from no step.
questions.explain: A binomial coefficient is easy to compute as r descending factors over r!, for example C(11, 4) = (11 x 10 x 9 x 8) / (1 x 2 x 3 x 4) = 330, easier than 11!/(4! 7!).
questions.rule: Write r descending factors over r!.
questions.teaches: A computational shortcut: C(n, r) equals r descending factors from n divided by r!, which is much easier than expanding n!/(r!(n - r)!); the book's example is C(11, 4) = 330.

questions.q: Which story is counted by 8 + 3?
options: Picking one student and one teacher to form a pair
Arranging 8 students and 3 teachers in a row
Picking one person from a group of 8 students or from a group of 3 teachers
Choosing 3 of 8 students for a team
optionExplain: A pair of one student and one teacher is counted by 8 x 3.
A row of 11 distinct people is counted by 11!.
The two groups are alternatives that share no person, so the counts add.
A team of 3 from 8 is counted by C(8, 3).
questions.explain: A sum tells a story of alternatives. The card next explains how each operation becomes a story.
questions.rule: Translate an expression into a story about a collection; two stories about the same collection prove the two expressions equal.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, algebra shows how an identity is true, but a combinatorial argument shows why it is true.
questions.explain: The algebra checks the symbols, whereas the story explains the identity by counting one collection two ways.
questions.rule: Prefer the story that shows why.

questions.q: Match each expression to the story it tells.
pairs: One item from each of two shelves holding 5 and 4 items
One item from either of two shelves holding 5 and 4 items
A team of four chosen from ten people, order irrelevant
Five courses with three choices each
questions.explain: Product: both choices. Sum: either choice. Binomial coefficient: unordered selection. Power: the same choice repeated.
questions.rule: Learn the meaning of each operation.

questions.q: Which expression counts teams of 5 chosen from 13 people, with one team member designated captain?
optionExplain: This counts teams only and leaves out the captain.
This puts all five members in order, which gives each team more outcomes than a captain choice does.
Choose the team in C(13, 5) ways, then name the captain in 5 ways.
The captain would be chosen from all 13 people, but must lie on the team.
questions.explain: Team then captain is a product. Equivalently, 13 x C(12, 4) picks the captain first; both equal 6,435.
questions.rule: Two orders of choosing can describe the same count.

questions.q: A pupil says C(7, 2) + C(6, 2) = C(13, 2), choosing two people from a group of 7 or of 6. What is wrong?
options: The story counts a different collection: pairs mixing people from both groups are missed
Nothing; the story proves the identity
The sum should be a product, giving 21 x 15
The groups overlap, so something must be subtracted
optionExplain: C(13, 2) = 78 includes pairs with one person from each group, but C(7, 2) + C(6, 2) = 36 does not.
A story proves an identity only if both sides count the same collection, and here they differ.
Pairs are formed within a group, so the two counts are alternatives, not joint choices.
The groups can be disjoint; the missing pairs are those that cross the groups.
questions.explain: A story is evidence only if it covers exactly the collection counted on both sides.
questions.rule: Check that both sides count the same collection.

questions.q: Which statement explains why n x C(n - 1, 2) = 3 x C(n, 3)?
options: Both sides count 3-person committees without a leader
The left side counts pairs and the right side counts triples, which happen to agree
The identity holds only for n = 6, where both sides equal 60
Both sides count 3-person committees with one designated leader
optionExplain: Each side has a factor (n or 3) that selects a leader.
They are two descriptions of the same collection, so they do not just happen to agree.
It holds for every n at least 3; n = 6 is just one instance.
Left: choose the leader, then 2 others from the rest. Right: choose 3 people, then name one of them leader.
questions.explain: Both sides count the same collection by choosing the leader at different times.
questions.rule: Same collection, two orders of choosing.
questions.teaches: The book advises recasting counting problems as combinatorial stories and looking for hidden symmetries, to counteract the inherent dryness of counting.

questions.q: Which of these equals the number of ways to choose 2 of 9 people for a team?
options: The number of ways to choose 4 of the 9 people
The number of ways to choose 7 of the 9 people to leave off the team
The number of ways to choose 2 of 7 people
The number of ways to choose 3 of the 9 people
optionExplain: Four is neither 2 nor 9 - 2.
The 2 chosen are fixed once the 7 left-off people are fixed.
Seven people is a different pool, so the count differs.
Three is not the partner of 2 for n = 9.
questions.explain: Choosing the team and choosing who is left out are two views of one decision. The card next names this the symmetry identity.
questions.rule: Choosing r objects to take is the same as choosing n - r objects to leave.

questions.explain: The partner of 18 among 20 is 20 - 18 = 2, and C(20, 2) = 190.
questions.rule: C(n, r) = C(n, n - r).

questions.q: Without a long computation, find C(100, 98).
optionExplain: This is 100 x 99 and forgets to divide by 2!.
By symmetry it equals C(100, 2) = 100 x 99 / 2.
This is the lower index, not a count.
questions.explain: Replace 98 by its partner 2 and compute the small coefficient.
questions.rule: Use the smaller partner to compute.

questions.q: A pupil says C(10, 4) = C(10, 5) because 4 and 5 are neighbours. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; neighbouring r give equal coefficients
The partner of 4 is 4 - 1 = 3
The identity applies only when r is odd
optionExplain: The values differ: 210 versus 252.
The partner is found by subtracting from n, not from r.
The parity of r plays no part; the partner is always n - r.
Symmetry pairs r with n - r, which is 6 here.
questions.explain: Pair r with n - r, not with a neighbour.
questions.rule: The partner of r is n - r.

questions.q: For n = 10, match each r to its partner under the symmetry identity.
questions.explain: The partner of r is 10 - r. When r = n / 2 the partner is r itself, so the middle coefficient has no different partner.
questions.rule: The partner of r is n - r.

questions.q: The formula n!/(r!(n - r)!) at r = n involves 0!. For C(n, n) = 1 to match it, what must 0! equal?
options: n
Undefined, so C(n, n) is undefined
optionExplain: C(n, n) = n!/(n! x 0!) = 1/0!, which equals 1 only if 0! = 1.
Then the formula would divide by zero.
Then C(n, n) would be 1/n, not 1.
The convention 0! = 1 makes the formula agree with the count.
questions.explain: The convention 0! = 1 makes the factorial formula match the count 1 for choosing nobody or everybody.
questions.rule: Define 0! = 1.
questions.teaches: The book defines 0! to equal 1 so that the factorial formula matches the counts for choosing no objects, as in C(10, 0) = 1.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: A committee of 4 is chosen from 7 people, including Ana. How many committees include Ana?
optionExplain: This counts all committees of 4 from 7, with or without Ana.
This counts committees without Ana: 4 from the other 6.
Ana is in, so choose the 3 others from the remaining 6: C(6, 3).
This is only the number of other people.
questions.explain: Fixing one person splits the committees in two. The card next turns this into an identity.
questions.rule: Split on whether one fixed person is in the committee: C(n + 1, r + 1) = C(n, r) + C(n, r + 1).

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.explain: With n = 10 and r = 4 the summation identity gives C(11, 5).

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: Without computing C(13, 6) directly, find it from C(12, 5) = 792 and C(12, 6) = 924.
optionExplain: This is C(13, 5), one lower in r.
This doubles 924, using the same term twice.
This doubles 792, using the same term twice.
questions.explain: The summation identity builds the next coefficient from two known ones.
questions.rule: Add the two neighbours.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: Put the steps of the committee argument for C(18, 11) = C(17, 10) + C(17, 11) in order.
items: Consider all 11-member committees from 18 people and fix one person, Erika
Split them into two classes: those with Erika and those without
Count those with Erika by choosing 10 more from the remaining 17
Count those without Erika by choosing 11 from the remaining 17
Add the two counts, because every committee is in exactly one class
questions.explain: The argument is a partition into two exclusive classes, followed by addition.
questions.rule: Fix a person, split, count each case, add.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: In the Erika argument, a pupil counts committees without Erika as C(18, 11) since there are still 18 people. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; excluding one person does not change the pool
Erika is removed from the pool, so the 11 members come from the other 17
The count should be C(18, 10) because Erika's seat stays empty
The committees without Erika are C(17, 10)
optionExplain: The pool shrinks by one person.
Without Erika the pool has 17 people, giving C(17, 11).
There is no empty seat; the committee still has 11 members.
That is the count with Erika, who takes one seat.
questions.explain: Excluding Erika shrinks the pool; including her shrinks the vacancies.
questions.rule: With: n choose r. Without: n choose r + 1.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: A pupil says the Erika proof with concrete numbers 17 and 10 says nothing about general n and r. How does the book answer?
options: The same argument works when 17 and 10 are replaced by n and r; concrete numbers are easier to follow
The identity is only claimed for n = 17 and r = 10
Concrete numbers prove more than general symbols
The identity is first verified by computer for small cases
optionExplain: Nothing in the argument uses the particular values.
The book states it for all integers n and r with n at least r at least 0.
Symbols prove no less; the numbers are only for readability.
The book gives the committee argument, not a computer check.
questions.explain: The book proves the identity with n = 17 and r = 10 (assuming without loss of generality) because the argument carries over unchanged to n and r.
questions.rule: Concrete numbers illustrate a general argument.
questions.teaches: The book argues the summation identity with the concrete numbers n = 17 and r = 10, noting that the argument works for n and r but is easier to follow with concrete numbers.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: Row 4 of Pascal's triangle is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, and each inner entry sums the two above. Which is row 5?
optionExplain: The middle sums are 6 + 4 = 10, not 11.
The second entry is 4 + 1 = 5, not 4.
The ends are 1; the inner entries are 4 + 1, 6 + 4, 4 + 6 and 1 + 4.
This keeps the old middle entries instead of adding neighbours.
questions.explain: Each inner entry adds the pair above it. The card next shows what these entries count.
questions.rule: Entry (row n, column r) of Pascal's triangle is C(n, r), with rows and columns numbered from zero.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: The entry in row 6, column 2 of Pascal's triangle is C(6, 2) = ____.
questions.rule: Entry (n, r) is C(n, r).

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: What is the entry in row 7, column 3 of Pascal's triangle (counting from zero)?
optionExplain: This is C(7, 2), the entry in column 2.
This is C(8, 3), the entry one row down.
This is C(8, 4), the middle entry one row down.
questions.explain: Read off row 7, column 3, or compute C(7, 3) = 35.
questions.rule: Rows and columns start at zero.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: True or false: Row 8 of Pascal's triangle, counting rows from zero, contains 9 entries.
questions.explain: Row n has the entries for r = 0, 1, ..., n, which is n + 1 of them.
questions.rule: Row n has n + 1 entries.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: The row 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1 has 7 entries, so a pupil calls its 20 entry C(7, 3). What is wrong?
options: Rows are numbered from zero, so this is row 6 and the entry is C(6, 3)
Nothing; the row number is the number of entries
The entry is C(6, 4) since columns start at one
The entry is C(5, 3), the row above
optionExplain: The row of 7 entries is row 6, and 20 = C(6, 3).
The row number is one less than the number of entries.
Columns also start at zero, and C(6, 4) is a different entry.
Row 5 has only six entries and none of them is 20.
questions.explain: Zero-based numbering gives row n = number of entries - 1.
questions.rule: Row number = entries - 1.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: The coefficients of (x + y)^5 are 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1. Which row of Pascal's triangle, counting from zero, are they?
options: Row 6
Row 4
Row 10
Row 5
optionExplain: Row 6 has seven entries.
Ten is an entry of the row, not its number.
They are C(5, 0), ..., C(5, 5), the entries of row 5.
questions.explain: The book observes that the coefficients in the expansion of (x + y)^n are exactly the elements of Pascal's triangle.
questions.rule: Row n of the triangle gives the coefficients of (x + y)^n.
questions.teaches: The coefficients in the expansions of (x + y)^n for n = 0, 1, 2, ... are exactly the rows of Pascal's triangle, which the book says is no coincidence.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: When (x + y)^2 is multiplied out and like terms are combined, what is the middle term?
options: xy
2xy
optionExplain: This counts the cross-product only once.
The terms xy and yx arise separately and combine.
The exponents in each term add up to 2, not 4.
The cross terms add; they do not cancel.
questions.explain: Multiplying (x + y)(x + y) gives x^2 + xy + yx + y^2. The card next generalizes this.
questions.rule: The coefficient of x^(n-r) y^r in (x + y)^n is C(n, r), and the exponents in each term add up to n.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: True or false: In every term of the expansion of (x + y)^n, the exponent of x plus the exponent of y equals n.
questions.explain: Each term is built by choosing x or y from each of the n factors, so the exponents sum to n.
questions.rule: Exponents in each term sum to n.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: What is the coefficient of \(x^2y^3\) in the expansion of \((x+y)^5\)?
optionExplain: This is C(5, 1) or C(5, 4), a different term.
This is P(5, 2), which counts ordered choices.
This is C(4, 2), a coefficient from (x + y)^4.
questions.explain: The coefficient of x^(n-r) y^r is C(n, r). Here n = 5 and r = 3.
questions.rule: Read the coefficient from row n, column r.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: After combining like terms, the expansion of \((x+y)^7\) has ____ terms.
questions.explain: The exponent of y runs through 0, 1, ..., 7, which gives 8 different terms.
questions.rule: (x + y)^n has n + 1 terms.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: A pupil writes (x + y)^3 = x^3 + y^3. What is missing?
options: Nothing is missing, because a power distributes over a sum term by term
A single factor of 3 in front of both terms, so the right side is 3x^3 + 3y^3
A single extra term x^2 y^2, with coefficient 1, completing the symmetric pattern
The middle terms 3x^2 y and 3xy^2, with coefficients from row 3: 1, 3, 3, 1
optionExplain: Powers do not distribute: (x + y)^3 has cross terms.
Only the middle terms carry the coefficient 3.
The exponents must add to 3, so x^2 y^2 cannot occur.
Each term needs its binomial coefficient, and the cross terms do not vanish.
questions.explain: Cross terms are the whole point of the binomial coefficients.
questions.rule: Powers of a sum are not sums of powers.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: Putting x = 1 and y = 1 in the binomial theorem, what do the coefficients of (x + y)^n add up to?
options: n!
optionExplain: The left side is (1 + 1)^n = 2^n and the right side is the sum of the coefficients.
The left side is 2^n, which grows far faster.
Zero would come from x = 1, y = -1 for n at least 1.
Nothing in the expansion produces factorials.
questions.explain: Substituting convenient values is a standard way to prove identities from the binomial theorem; x = 1, y = -1 gives alternating coefficients that add to 0.
questions.rule: Substitute convenient values into the theorem.
questions.teaches: Substituting convenient values into the binomial theorem proves identities: x = y = 1 shows C(n, 0) + C(n, 1) + ... + C(n, n) = 2^n, and x = 1, y = -1 shows the alternating sum is 0.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: Multiplying (x + y)(x + y)(x + y) without combining like terms gives how many terms?
optionExplain: This is 3 x 2, adding the choices instead of multiplying.
This is the count of terms in the expansion of (x + y)^3 after combining.
Each of the 3 factors contributes x or y: 2 x 2 x 2.
This is the number of factors, not the number of terms.
questions.explain: Each factor gives two choices, so there are 2^3 = 8 terms before combining. The card next counts the like terms among them.
questions.rule: The coefficient of x^(n-r) y^r counts the words of n letters with r y's, which is C(n, r).

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: Multiplying out \((x+y)^7\) without combining like terms gives 2^7 = ____ terms.
questions.explain: Each of the 7 factors offers x or y.
questions.rule: n factors give 2^n unsimplified terms.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: What is the coefficient of \(x^5y^3\) in the expansion of \((x+y)^8\)?
optionExplain: This is P(8, 3) and counts the three positions in order.
This is 8!, which treats all factors as different.
This is C(8, 2), the coefficient of a different term.
The words with 5 X's and 3 Y's number 8!/(5! 3!).
questions.explain: The y's are placed in 3 of the 8 factors, which can be done in C(8, 3) = 56 ways.
questions.rule: Count words, not terms.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: Put the steps of the combinatorial proof that the coefficient of x^3 y^4 in (x+y)^7 is C(7, 3) in order.
items: Multiply out seven factors, choosing x or y from each, giving 2^7 unsimplified terms
Write each term as a word of seven letters, such as XXYXYYY
Select the words containing exactly 3 X's and 4 Y's
Count those words as rearrangements of XXXYYYY, giving 7!/(3! 4!) = C(7, 3)
questions.explain: The proof turns coefficients into words and then counts words with the repeated-letters formula.
questions.rule: Words first, then count the like ones.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: A pupil says the coefficient of \(x^2y^2\) in \((x+y)^4\) is 4!/2! = 12. Where is the error?
options: The coefficient should be 4! = 24, because all four factors are different when words are listed
The words with two X's and two Y's number 4!/(2! 2!) = 6; both repeated letters need dividing out
The coefficient should be 2 x 2 = 4, the product of the two exponents in the term
Nothing is wrong, since dividing by 2! already removes the repeated letters
optionExplain: That treats all four factors as different.
Both identical letters need a factorial in the denominator.
The coefficient counts words, not products of exponents.
12 divides out only the X's.
questions.explain: Row 4 of Pascal's triangle gives 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, with 6 in the middle.
questions.rule: Divide out every group of identical letters.

questions.section: Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem
questions.q: The same argument for \((x+y+z)^4\): what is the coefficient of \(x^2yz\)?
optionExplain: Words with two X's, one Y and one Z: 4!/(2! 1! 1!).
This is 4!, which treats the two X's as different.
This is C(4, 2), which fixes the places of the X's but not the Y and Z.
This is the number of factors only.
questions.explain: The same history-of-choices argument extends to three variables: coefficients are repeated-letters counts. The book asks readers to find the general multinomial theorem this way.
questions.rule: Coefficients are counts of words.
questions.teaches: The same argument extends to sums of three or more variables: the book asks the reader to find a multinomial theorem, and the coefficients are repeated-letters counts.

questions.q: A counting problem has a parameter n and no obvious method. What is a sensible first move?
options: State a formula and test it on n = 1000
Apply the largest binomial coefficient available
Count the answer by hand for n = 1, 2, 3 and look for a pattern
Wait for the general proof to appear
optionExplain: Testing large n before small cases wastes effort and hides the pattern.
No method has been chosen yet, so nothing justifies a coefficient.
Small cases are cheap to count and often reveal the pattern.
A proof usually follows a conjecture, which comes from examples.
questions.explain: Experimentation with small numbers is often a crucial first step. The card next adds conjecture and proof.
questions.rule: Experiment with small numbers, conjecture a formula, then prove it, and use small cases to test any counting method.

questions.q: Put the three steps of the standard attack on a counting problem in order.
items: Experiment with small numbers
Make a conjecture from the pattern
Prove the conjecture by induction
questions.explain: Experiment suggests, conjecture states, induction proves.
questions.rule: Experiment, conjecture, prove.

questions.q: Handshake counts for 2, 3, 4 and 5 people are 1, 3, 6 and 10. Following the pattern, how many handshakes among 6 people?
optionExplain: This continues with an increment of 4 instead of 5.
This continues by doubling 10.
The increments 2, 3, 4 grow by one each time, so the next is 10 + 5; also 6 x 5 / 2.
This is 6 x 2, matching no pattern in the data.
questions.explain: The data suggest n(n - 1)/2, a conjecture that still needs a proof.
questions.rule: Conjecture from data, then prove.

questions.q: A pupil checks a counting formula on n = 1, 2 and 3, finds it correct, and calls it proved. What is the flaw?
options: Checking a few cases supports a conjecture but does not prove it for every n
The pupil should have checked n = 4 as well, which would prove it
Small numbers are not allowed in counting
The formula should be tested on negative n
optionExplain: A proof, such as induction, must cover all n.
Any finite number of checks leaves later cases untested.
Small numbers are the book's recommended way to experiment.
Counting formulas are for positive integers n here.
questions.explain: Evidence from small cases is the experiment step; the proof is a separate step.
questions.rule: Check small cases to guess, then prove.

questions.q: Match each situation to the move that suits it.
pairs: Unsure whether a counting method double counts
Count a small case directly and compare
A pattern holds for n = 1 to 5
Conjecture it and prove it by induction
A sum is dry and algebraic
Recast it as a combinatorial story
questions.explain: Each move belongs to a stage: checking, proving, recasting, or seeing symmetry.
questions.rule: Match the move to the stage.

questions.q: Which action is an example of recasting a counting problem, as opposed to experiment or proof?
options: Computing the answers for n = 1, 2, 3
Proving the pattern by induction
Memorizing the values of n! up to 10
Rewriting an algebraic identity as a story about choosing teams
optionExplain: This is experimentation.
This is proof.
This is background knowledge, not a change of viewpoint.
Recasting changes how the problem is viewed.
questions.explain: Recasting means visualizing the problem creatively, devising combinatorial arguments and looking for hidden symmetries.
questions.rule: Recast to counter the dryness of counting.
questions.teaches: The book calls the strategy of recasting especially fruitful in counting: visualize problems creatively, devise combinatorial arguments, and look for hidden symmetries, to counteract the inherent dryness of counting.

questions.q: Which way of dividing a school's pupils into groups lets you count them by adding group sizes?
options: By clubs joined, since each club has its own members
By year group, since each pupil belongs to exactly one year
By pupils who own a bicycle
By pupils who walk, who take a bus, or who do either
optionExplain: A pupil in two clubs would be counted twice.
Disjoint, exhaustive groups add up to the whole.
Pupils without a bicycle are left out.
These groups overlap, since some pupils do both.
questions.explain: A valid split has no overlap and leaves nobody out. The card next names this a partition.
questions.rule: Split what you count into disjoint, exhaustive, easy-to-count pieces and add their sizes.

questions.q: True or false: In a partition of S, the pieces may overlap provided their union is all of S.
questions.explain: A partition needs pairwise disjoint pieces; overlapping pieces would be counted twice when summing.
questions.rule: Partition pieces are disjoint and cover S.

questions.q: Sets A1, A2, A3 partition S, with 12, 7 and 5 elements. Then |S| = ____.
questions.explain: The pieces are disjoint, so the sizes add: 12 + 7 + 5.
questions.rule: |S| is the sum of the sizes of the pieces.

questions.q: A pupil counts integers 1 to 20 divisible by 2 or 3 as 10 + 6 = 16, adding both multiple counts. What is the flaw?
options: The pieces should be multiplied, giving 60
The pieces overlap in the multiples of 6, so adding counts those numbers twice
The pieces are fine; 16 is the correct count
Multiples of 2 and 3 should be divided by 2 first
optionExplain: Multiplying would count pairs (a multiple of 2, a multiple of 3), which is not what is asked.
Multiples of 6 (6, 12, 18) are in both pieces, and the true count is 13.
The overlap makes 16 too large.
The overlap is not uniform, so no divisor fixes it.
questions.explain: The pieces are not disjoint, so they do not form a partition.
questions.rule: Check disjointness before adding.

questions.q: Which of these are partitions of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}? Select all that apply.
optionExplain: Right: the pieces are disjoint and cover the set.
The two pieces share 3, so they overlap.
The pieces leave out 5 and 6, so they do not cover the set.
Right: the odd and even numbers are disjoint and cover the set.
questions.explain: A partition must be disjoint and exhaustive.
questions.rule: Disjoint and exhaustive.

questions.q: Length-3 words over a, b, c split by number of a's into classes of 8, 12, 6 and 1. How many words in total?
optionExplain: This omits the single word with three a's.
This multiplies the class sizes.
This is 3 x 3, which ignores the third letter.
The classes are disjoint and exhaustive, so 8 + 12 + 6 + 1.
questions.explain: The total is 27, which agrees with the product rule 3 x 3 x 3. Partitioning deliberately focuses attention on addition: it breaks a complex count into smaller, simpler pieces.
questions.rule: Break up, then add.
questions.teaches: Partitioning is a tactic that deliberately focuses on addition, breaking a complex problem into several smaller and simpler pieces; it contrasts with encoding, which counts in one step.

questions.q: In a hall, each person sits on one chair and each chair holds one person. What does this tell you?
options: The number of people equals the number of chairs
There are more chairs than people
There are more people than chairs
Nothing, because the numbers are unknown
optionExplain: Pairing with no leftovers on either side means equal sizes.
Every chair is occupied, so no chair is spare.
Everyone has a seat, so nobody is standing.
Equal pairing alone tells you the two counts are equal, even if unknown.
questions.explain: A perfect pairing means the two sets have the same size. The card next calls it a bijection.
questions.rule: If each object matches exactly one code word and each code word matches exactly one object, count the code words.

questions.q: True or false: With each object given its own code word and some code words left over, objects and code words are equally many.
questions.explain: Unused words make the code words more numerous than the objects, so the pairing is not a bijection.
questions.rule: Every word must be used and every object must have its own.

questions.q: Four light switches are each on or off, and each pattern is encoded as a 4-letter string over {on, off}. How many patterns exist?
optionExplain: This is 2^3, one letter fewer.
This is the number of switches, not patterns.
There are 2 choices per letter and 4 letters: 2^4.
This is 4!, which counts orders of the switches.
questions.explain: The coding is a bijection between patterns and strings, so count strings.
questions.rule: Count the code words.

questions.q: A pupil encodes a 3-person team from 10 people as an ordered list of names and counts 720 teams. What is the flaw?
options: Nothing is wrong; ordered lists of three names are exactly the teams, so 720 teams exist
The encoding leaves some names unused, so the list count is too small for the number of teams
Names should be added instead of multiplied, giving 10 + 9 + 8 = 27 lists
Different orders of the same three names encode the same team, so the encoding is not one-to-one
optionExplain: Each team is counted several times.
Every team is coded; the problem is repeats.
The three names are chosen in turn, so counts multiply.
Each team appears 3! = 6 times, so the true number of teams is 720 / 6 = 120.
questions.explain: An encoding must give each object exactly one word.
questions.rule: One object, one word.

questions.q: Put the steps of an encoding argument in order.
items: Choose a simple code whose words are easy to count
Show each object gives exactly one word
Show each word comes from exactly one object
Count the words, and report that number as the count of objects
questions.explain: The first three steps establish the bijection; the last uses it.
questions.rule: Define, check both directions, count.

questions.q: To count the possible subsets of a 6-person club, which coding is better?
options: Writing the members' names in the order they joined
One yes/no letter per member, the same rule for every member
Writing the number of members in the subset
Using a separate code for each subset size
optionExplain: Different orders and lengths make the words hard to count.
A uniform code is easy to describe and works the same way in all cases.
Many different subsets share the same number.
The codes differ from case to case, which makes counting hard.
questions.explain: What we want is a uniform coding method, simple to describe and the same for every case.
questions.rule: Prefer a uniform code.
questions.teaches: A good encoding is uniform: simple to describe and working in essentially the same way for all cases, so that the code words are easy to count.

questions.q: How many subsets of {a, b, c, d} have exactly two elements?
optionExplain: Choose 2 of the 4 elements: C(4, 2).
This counts the 2^3 subsets of a three-element set.
This counts ordered pairs, P(4, 2).
This counts subsets of size 1 or 3.
questions.explain: Subsets of a given size are combinations. The card next adds them over all sizes.
questions.rule: Partition the subsets of an n-set by size k: the class with k elements has C(n, k) members.

questions.q: A 4-element set has ____ subset(s) with no elements.
questions.explain: Only the empty set has no elements.

questions.q: A pizza place offers 5 toppings; any subset, even none, is a pizza. Adding C(5, k) for k = 0 to 5 gives how many pizzas?
optionExplain: This leaves out the plain pizza with no toppings.
This is 5^2, not a sum of the classes.
This is 5!, which counts orders.
questions.explain: Each size class is counted by a binomial coefficient and the classes add.
questions.rule: Sum C(n, k) over k.

questions.q: A pupil lists the subsets of {a, b, c} as the 7 sets with at least one element. Which sets were missed?
options: The set {a, b, c} itself, which is not a subset of itself
Nothing: 7 is the right count
The empty set, so the subsets number 8
The sets of size 4
optionExplain: A set is a subset of itself.
The size-0 class contributes 1 subset.
The empty set (size 0) is a subset, as is the whole set; the class G_0 has one member.
A 3-element set has no subsets of size 4.
questions.explain: Count the empty set in G_0 and the full set in G_n.
questions.rule: Include the empty set and the set itself.

questions.q: For a 6-element set, match each size k to the number of subsets of that size.
questions.explain: The counts C(6, 0), C(6, 1), C(6, 2) and C(6, 3) are 1, 6, 15 and 20.
questions.rule: Class k has C(n, k) members.

questions.q: Which classes of subsets of a set S contain the empty set and S itself?
options: G_0 and G_n
G_1 only
Neither, since both are excluded from sub(S)
G_0 for both
optionExplain: The empty set has no elements and S has all n.
G_1 holds the one-element subsets.
Both are subsets and belong to sub(S).
S has n elements, so it is not in G_0 unless n = 0.
questions.explain: The book counts the empty set and the set itself among the subsets.
questions.rule: Include both extremes.
questions.teaches: The empty set and the whole set are both subsets: the empty set is counted in the class with 0 elements and the whole set in the class with n elements.

questions.q: Subsets of {a, b, c} are coded by whether a, b, c are in them (y or n). Which subset does the code yyn mean?
options: {a, b, c}
The empty set
{a, b}
optionExplain: This reads y as out and n as in.
The code yyy would mean the whole set.
The empty set is nnn.
y for a, y for b, n for c.
questions.explain: Each letter answers one question about one element. The card next counts all such strings.
questions.rule: A set with n elements has 2^n subsets, one for each yes/no string of length n.

questions.q: A set with 6 elements has ____ subsets.
questions.rule: n elements give 2^n subsets.

questions.q: A pizza has up to 8 optional toppings and any subset may go on it, including none. How many pizzas are possible?
optionExplain: This leaves out the plain pizza.
Two choices (on or off) for each of 8 toppings.
This is 2^6, two toppings fewer.
This is 8!, which counts orders.
questions.explain: The yes/no code gives 2^8 strings, one per pizza.
questions.rule: Count the strings.

questions.q: True or false: Adding one new element to a set doubles the number of its subsets.
questions.explain: A new element adds one more yes/no letter, and a letter with two choices doubles the number of strings.
questions.rule: Each element doubles the count.

questions.q: A pupil wants subsets of {a, b, c, d} that contain a, and counts 2^4 = 16 strings. What is the flaw?
options: Nothing; every subset is counted
The letter for a is fixed at y, so only the other three letters are free: 2^3 = 8
The count should be 4 x 2 = 8, multiplying by the elements
The count should be 2^5 = 32 to include a
optionExplain: Subsets without a are included in 16 but are not wanted.
Forcing one answer removes one free choice.
The count follows from letters, not from the number of elements times 2.
There are only four elements, so five letters have no meaning.
questions.explain: Count only the strings consistent with the condition.
questions.rule: Fixed letters are not free choices.

questions.q: Counting subsets of a set with n elements by size (a partition) and by yes/no strings (an encoding) gives two answers. What follows?
options: 2^n = n choose 2
The two counts differ because strings can repeat
optionExplain: Subsets are not orders, so no factorial arises.
This holds for no general n.
The strings are in one-to-one correspondence with subsets, so no repeat arises.
Both count the same collection, sub(S).
questions.explain: Two ways of counting one collection must agree: the book combines them into the identity.
questions.rule: Same collection, two counts, one identity.
questions.teaches: Combining the partition count with the encoding count gives the combinatorial identity C(n, 0) + C(n, 1) + ... + C(n, n) = 2^n.

questions.q: For n = 3, what is 1 x C(3, 1) + 2 x C(3, 2) + 3 x C(3, 3)?
optionExplain: This is 2^3, the plain sum without the weights.
This is 3 x 2^3, one factor of 2 too many.
This is 3 x 3, with no basis in the terms.
questions.explain: The weighted sum is 12 = 3 x 2^2. The card next shows why it is n times 2^(n-1).
questions.rule: Rewrite r C(n, r) as n C(n - 1, r - 1), then sum a whole row to get n times 2^(n-1).
The sum is n x 2^(n - 1).

questions.q: Which expression equals 6 x C(12, 6) by the rewriting r C(n, r) = n C(n - 1, r - 1)?
optionExplain: The lower index should be r - 1 = 5, not 4.
The outer factor should be n = 12, not r.
With n = 12 and r = 6 the identity gives 12 x C(11, 5) = 5,544.
The upper index should be n - 1 = 11.
questions.explain: Pull the weight into the factorial: r C(n, r) = n C(n - 1, r - 1).
questions.rule: r C(n, r) = n C(n - 1, r - 1).

questions.q: Put the steps of the algebraic proof of the sum identity in order.
items: Write r C(n, r) as n!/((r - 1)!(n - r)!)
Recognize that expression as n C(n - 1, r - 1)
Pull the factor n out of the sum, leaving a sum of C(n - 1, r - 1)
Recognize that remaining sum as a whole row total, 2^(n - 1)
questions.explain: Each step removes the weight and then recognizes a known sum.
questions.rule: Cancel the weight, then recognize the row.

questions.q: Sums 12 (n = 3) and 32 (n = 4) lead a pupil to guess n x 2^n. What does n = 3 show?
options: The guess is fine because 24 is a multiple of 12
The guess fails only for odd n
Nothing: small cases do not test a formula
n x 2^n would give 24, not 12, so the guess fails; n x 2^(n - 1) fits
optionExplain: A formula must match the value, not merely be a multiple.
It fails for n = 4 as well: 4 x 16 = 64, not 32.
Small cases are how a guess is tested.
Testing a guess against a small case catches the error.
questions.explain: The correct power is 2^(n - 1), as the proof shows.
questions.rule: Test conjectures on small cases.

questions.q: Why does the book want to turn the left side into n times a simpler sum?
options: Because factors of n always simplify binomial sums
The right side n x 2^(n - 1) suggests n times a sum that equals 2^(n - 1)
Because the left side is false unless rewritten
Because C(n - 1, r - 1) is easier to type
optionExplain: The aim is guided by this particular right side, not by a general law.
Working backwards from the target shows which sum to aim for.
The identity is true; the rewriting just reveals why.
Ease of typing plays no part in the reasoning.
questions.explain: The method is wishful thinking combined with the penultimate step: start with a complicated sum and try to make it look like a simpler one you know.
questions.rule: Aim for a sum you already know.
questions.teaches: The book motivates the rewriting by wishful thinking and the penultimate step: since the right side is n times 2^(n - 1), try to turn the left side into n times a simpler sum that equals 2^(n - 1).

questions.q: How many ways can a team of any size (at least one member) be chosen from 4 people, with one member named leader?
optionExplain: Pick the leader (4 ways), then each of the other 3 people is in or out: 4 x 2^3.
This is 2^4 and ignores the choice of a leader.
This is 4!, which counts orderings.
This is 4 x 2^4, which lets the leader also be in or out.
questions.explain: The card next explains the count. Choosing the leader first leaves 2^3 free choices.
questions.rule: Count teams with a leader by size (a sum) and by leader-then-yes/no (a product); the two counts agree.

questions.q: True or false: To encode a team with a leader, choose the leader first, then mark each other person in or out.
questions.explain: That gives n choices for the leader and 2 choices for each remaining person: n x 2^(n - 1).
questions.rule: Leader first (n ways), then n - 1 yes/no choices.

questions.q: A club of 10 members elects a nonempty committee of any size and names its chair. How many outcomes are there?
optionExplain: This is 10 x 2^10, treating the chair as also choosing in or out.
This is 2^10, the number of committees without a chair.
10 chairs, then each of the other 9 members is in or out: 10 x 2^9.
This is 2^9, which forgets to choose the chair.
questions.explain: Choose the chair first; the other members are free.

questions.q: A pupil counts teams with a leader from n people as 2^n choices of team times n choices of leader. What is the flaw?
options: Nothing; the product is n x 2^n
The product should be divided by n because teams repeat
The leader must be on the team, so choosing the leader from all n people overcounts
The leader and team should be added, not multiplied
optionExplain: This counts a leader who may be outside the team, and the empty team.
Dividing by n would remove the leader choice, which is wanted.
A leader chosen outside the team is not allowed; choosing the leader first and then the others avoids this.
They are joint choices, so they multiply once correctly defined.
questions.explain: Pick the leader first so the others cannot conflict.
questions.rule: Choose the leader first.

questions.q: With 5 people there are 80 teams with a leader. With 6 people the number is ____.
questions.rule: Add a person and the count becomes n x 2^(n - 1).

questions.q: Why does the book give a combinatorial proof of this identity after an algebraic one?
options: The algebraic proof is elegant but in a sense ignores the combinatorial meaning that the identity has
The algebraic proof is wrong for large n, so a combinatorial proof is needed to repair it
Combinatorial proofs are shorter than algebraic ones, which is why the book prefers them
The algebraic proof does not use the binomial theorem, so a second proof is needed to include it
optionExplain: The story shows what each side counts.
The algebraic proof is valid; it just does not explain the meaning.
The reason given is meaning, not length.
The reason concerns meaning, not which theorem is used.
questions.explain: A story explains why, while algebra only verifies.
questions.rule: Prefer the proof that shows meaning.
questions.teaches: The book follows its algebraic proof of the identity with a combinatorial one, because the algebraic proof, though elegant and instructive, in a sense ignores the combinatorial meaning that the identity has.

questions.q: How many different words can be made by rearranging all six letters of BOOBOO (2 B's and 4 O's)?
optionExplain: This treats all six letters as different.
This chooses the B slots and the O slots independently.
This is 6 x 5, which counts the two B slots in order.
Choose which 2 of the 6 slots hold a B.
questions.explain: Fifteen words. The card next shows why the O slots add no further choice.
questions.rule: Count only the choices that are free; once earlier choices fix something, do not count it again.

questions.q: True or false: Once the two slots holding B in BOOBOO are chosen, the four O slots are determined.
questions.explain: The remaining slots must hold the remaining letters, so no second choice exists.
questions.rule: Forced slots add no choice.

questions.q: A row of 8 flags contains 3 identical red and 5 identical blue ones. The number of different colour patterns is ____.
questions.explain: Choose the 3 slots for red; the other 5 slots are blue. C(8, 3) = 56.
questions.rule: Choose one kind; the other is forced.

questions.q: A pupil counts patterns with 3 red and 5 blue flags as C(8, 3) x C(8, 5) = 3,136. What is the flaw?
options: The pupil should have added the two coefficients, since red and blue placements are alternatives
After the red slots are chosen, the blue slots are fixed, so the second factor is not a free choice
The pupil should have divided 3,136 by 3! 5!, to remove the order of identical flags
Nothing is wrong, since the red and blue slots are separate choices that can be multiplied
optionExplain: The two choices are not alternatives; the second is not a choice at all.
The correct count is C(8, 3) = 56.
Dividing does not repair a double-counted choice.
The red and blue patterns cannot be chosen separately.
questions.explain: Ask what freedom of choice remains after each step.
questions.rule: Ask what is already decided.

questions.q: True or false: The number of arrangements of 2 B's and 4 O's equals the number with 4 B's and 2 O's.
questions.explain: Both are C(6, 2) = C(6, 4) = 15; choosing the B slots or the O slots is the same encoding.
questions.rule: Either kind may be the one you choose.

questions.q: A row of 6 tiles has 2 red, 2 green and 2 blue tiles of identical shape. How many colour patterns are there?
optionExplain: This chooses the green slots from all 6, ignoring the red ones already placed.
Choose red slots (C(6, 2) = 15), then green slots from the remaining 4 (C(4, 2) = 6); the blue slots are forced.
This is 6!, which treats all tiles as different.
This is 15 x 2, which does not follow from the steps.
questions.explain: Each step chooses from what remains, and the last colour is forced; this equals 6!/(2! 2! 2!).
questions.rule: Choose from what remains.
questions.teaches: Proper encoding demands careful information management: like storing data in a computer, an encoding should not waste 'memory' on redundant information that earlier choices have already fixed.

questions.q: From 4 boys and 6 girls, one boy and two girls are chosen to receive toys, with order ignored. How many groups of children?
optionExplain: This is C(10, 3), which ignores the requirement of one boy and two girls.
This is 4 x 6, one girl only.
This includes the ways to give out different toys.
questions.explain: Sixty groups of children. The card next adds the distribution of the toys.
questions.rule: Count the unordered selection first, then multiply by the number of ways to distribute different items among the chosen ones.

questions.q: Three different toys can be given to three chosen children in ____ ways.
questions.rule: Distinct items among chosen children: k!.

questions.q: From 5 boys and 3 girls, two boys and one girl each receive one of three different prizes. How many outcomes are there?
optionExplain: C(5, 2) x C(3, 1) = 30 groups, times 3! = 6.
This counts groups but leaves out who gets which prize.
This multiplies by 3 instead of 3!.
This multiplies by 12, an arbitrary factor.
questions.explain: Choose the children, then distribute the prizes.
questions.rule: Groups times arrangements.

questions.q: True or false: Three different toys go to 1 boy and 2 girls from 4 boys and 6 girls; the 60 groups are the outcomes.
questions.explain: The 60 counts groups of children only; each group can receive the toys in 3! ways, giving 360.
questions.rule: Restore order for different items.

questions.q: If the three toys were identical, the number of outcomes would be ____.
questions.explain: Identical toys add no choice, so only the groups of children count.
questions.rule: Identical items need no arrangement factor.

questions.q: Which expression gives the 360 by including order from the start, without the 3! at the end?
options: 4 x 3 x 6 x 5 x 4
optionExplain: The girls are chosen without order, so the toys cannot be matched to them.
This is the number of groups without any toys given out.
Pick the boy (4), give him one of the 3 toys (3), then pick the two girls in order (P(6, 2) = 30) and hand them the other toys in that order.
This puts three girls into the count instead of two.
questions.explain: Both routes count the same 360 outcomes; including order at once multiplies P(6, 2) = 30 by 4 x 3.
questions.rule: Restore order exactly once.
questions.teaches: Order can be included from the start: pick the boy (4 ways), pick his toy (3 ways), then pick the two girls in order (P(6, 2) = 30), giving 4 x 3 x 30 = 360, the same total as the unordered route.

questions.q: A problem asks for outcomes in which at least two of the three prize winners are boys. Which approach is safest?
options: Multiply the counts for boys and girls, then divide by 2
Count the outcomes with one boy and subtract from 1
Count only the outcomes with three boys
Count outcomes with exactly two boys and with exactly three boys, then add
optionExplain: No single divisor is justified by the wording.
Subtracting from 1 does not give a count of outcomes.
This leaves out the outcomes with exactly two boys.
Exact cases are disjoint and easy to count.
questions.explain: The phrase at least calls for a split into exact cases. The card next works one example.
questions.rule: When a count says at least, split into exact cases (or count the complement) instead of using a quick product.

questions.q: True or false: The phrase 'at least' is a hint to consider partitioning into exact cases or counting the complement.
questions.explain: Both tactics replace an open-ended condition with cases that can be counted exactly.
questions.rule: At least: split or complement.

questions.q: From 4 boys and 6 girls, three different toys go to exactly two boys and one girl. How many outcomes are there?
optionExplain: This multiplies the groups by 4 instead of 6.
C(4, 2) x C(6, 1) = 36 groups, times 3! = 6.
This counts groups only.
This is C(10, 3) x 3, an arbitrary factor.
questions.explain: Choose the children, then distribute the different toys.
questions.rule: Exact case: choose, then distribute.

questions.q: A quick method gives 4 x 3 x 8 x 3 = 288 for the toys problem, which is too large. Where does it overcount?
options: When a boy gets the leftover toy, the same outcome is reached in several ways; when a girl does, only once
It counts every outcome exactly twice, so halving the 288 would give the true count of 144
It forgets to multiply by 3! at the end, so the quick count is too small, not too large
It counts too few girls, because girls are only chosen for the leftover toy at the end
optionExplain: The leftover toy can be any of the three, so a boy-boy-boy outcome is counted three times.
The repeats differ between outcomes, so no common factor exists.
The multiplication by 3 for the leftover toy is exactly what causes the repeat.
Girls are counted once, correctly.
questions.explain: Non-uniform overcounting needs a case split.
questions.rule: Different repeats cannot be divided out.

questions.q: The partition into exactly two boys (216) and exactly three boys (24) gives a total of ____.
questions.explain: 216 + 24 = 240, smaller than the quick count 288.
questions.rule: Add the disjoint cases.

questions.q: From the same 10 children, three different toys go to three children with at least one boy. Which count is easiest?
options: Split into one, two and three boys and multiply the counts
Choose a boy (4 ways), give him a toy (3 ways), then fill the other two toys from the 9 others: 4 x 3 x 9 x 8 = 864
All outcomes P(10, 3) = 720 minus the outcomes with no boys, P(6, 3) = 120, giving 600
Count only outcomes with exactly one boy: 4 x 3 x 6 x 5 = 360
optionExplain: The cases are disjoint, so they add, not multiply.
An outcome with two boys is reached once for each boy, so it is counted more than once.
The complement (no boys) is a single easy case.
This leaves out outcomes with two or three boys.
questions.explain: The book notes you should also consider the tactic of counting the complement, which turns this at-least condition into one subtraction.
questions.rule: At least one: subtract none from all.
questions.teaches: The book adds a footnote that when a problem says at least, you should also consider counting the complement, a tactic developed in the next section.

questions.q: In Pascal's triangle, the diagonal run 1, 3, 6, 10 sums to 20. Which entry equals that sum?
options: The entry directly above the first term
The first entry of the next row, which is 1
The entry one row below the last term and one column to its right
The sum of the whole next row
optionExplain: The first term lies on the border and has no entry above it.
That entry is 1 and cannot match 20.
The sum matches the entry one row lower and one column over from the last term.
The next row's sum is a power of 2, not 20.
questions.explain: The 20 sits at row 6, column 3. The card next calls this the hockey stick identity.
questions.rule: A diagonal run starting at the border sums to the entry just beyond its end, one row down and one column over.

questions.explain: The run is C(3, 3) + C(4, 3) + C(5, 3) + C(6, 3) and equals C(7, 4) = 35.
questions.rule: Run sum = the next diagonal entry.

optionExplain: The hockey stick gives C(10, 4) = 210.
This is C(10, 3), the entry in the same column.
This is C(10, 5), the middle of row 10.
This is C(11, 3), one row too far down.
questions.explain: The run ends at row 9, column 3, so the sum is at row 10, column 4.
questions.rule: Sum equals C(n + 1, r + 1).

questions.q: A pupil says 1 + 3 + 6 + 10 equals C(6, 2) = 15, the entry in the same column. What went wrong?
options: The sum is C(5, 2) = 10, the last term itself
The run should have started at 3
Nothing: C(6, 2) = 15 is right
The sum lies one column over, C(6, 3) = 20, not C(6, 2) = 15
optionExplain: The sum is larger than its largest term.
The run correctly starts at the border.
The run adds to 20, not 15.
The entry is C(n + 1, r + 1), in the next column.
questions.explain: Move one row down and one column over.
questions.rule: Next row, next column.

questions.q: True or false: Extending the run to 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 makes the sum 35, the entry C(7, 3).
questions.explain: The run ends at C(6, 2), so the sum is C(7, 3) = 35.
questions.rule: Add a term, step the result down the diagonal.

questions.q: Which of these sums is covered by the hockey stick identity?
options: The run 3 + 6 + 10 + 15 starting inside the triangle
The column 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5, starting at the border and equal to the entry 15
The whole row 1 + 5 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1
The pair 5 + 10 taken from the middle of row 5
optionExplain: A run starting inside the triangle is outside the identity.
A parallel stick of any length that starts at the border qualifies.
A row is not a diagonal run.
Two entries of a row are not a diagonal run from the border.
questions.explain: The book says the identity works for any parallel hockey stick of any length or location that begins at the border of the triangle.
questions.rule: Border start, any length.
questions.teaches: The identity holds for any parallel hockey stick of any length or location, provided it begins at the border of the triangle.

questions.q: Three-letter subsets of {a, b, c, d, e, f} are listed in alphabetical order. How many start with b?
optionExplain: This counts the subsets that start with a, with five letters left.
After b, two more letters are chosen from the four letters c, d, e, f: C(4, 2).
This counts the letters left, not the pairs chosen from them.
This is C(6, 2), ignoring that the other letters come after b.
questions.explain: Six subsets start with b. The card next adds the classes for every starting letter.
questions.rule: Sort the (r + 1)-subsets by smallest element; each class is a binomial coefficient and the classes add up to the whole.

questions.q: True or false: Sorting the 3-element subsets of {a, b, c, d, e, f} by their first letter produces classes that do not overlap.
questions.explain: A subset written in alphabetical order has exactly one first letter, so it lies in exactly one class.
questions.rule: Smallest element gives disjoint classes.

questions.q: How many 4-element subsets of {1, 2, ..., 7} have 3 as their smallest element?
optionExplain: This is C(7, 4), the number of all 4-element subsets.
This is C(6, 3), allowing smaller elements to be chosen.
This is C(5, 3), counting 3 itself as available.
The other three come from {4, 5, 6, 7}: C(4, 3).
questions.explain: After 3 is fixed as the smallest, the rest come from the larger numbers.
questions.rule: The pool is the elements larger than the smallest.

questions.q: Put the steps of the classification proof in order.
items: Take all (r + 1)-element subsets of {1, ..., n + 1} and write each in increasing order
Let j be the smallest element of a subset and sort subsets into classes by j
Count class j by choosing r elements from the n + 1 - j larger numbers
Add the class sizes over j and set the total equal to C(n + 1, r + 1)
questions.explain: Classification by smallest element is a partition, so the class counts add.
questions.rule: Classify, count each class, add.

questions.q: A pupil counts the 3-subsets of {a, ..., f} starting with c as C(4, 2) = 6, as four letters remain. What is wrong?
options: Only d, e, f remain after c, so the count is C(3, 2) = 3
Nothing; any four of the other letters may be used
The count is C(2, 2) = 1
The count is C(5, 2) = 10
optionExplain: Letters before c are not allowed, since c must be the smallest.
Letters a and b would make c no longer the first letter.
That is the class that starts with d.
That is the class that starts with a.
questions.explain: The pool for class j is the letters after it.
questions.rule: Count only larger elements.

questions.q: Count the 2-element subsets of {1, 2, ..., 7} by their smallest element. What is the total?
optionExplain: This is 7 x 6, the number of ordered pairs.
This adds 7 + 6 + ... + 1, starting one class too high.
The classes have 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 members, which add to 21 = C(7, 2).
This is C(7, 3), the wrong coefficient.
questions.explain: Ordering the elements gives free information: this is another example of monotonizing, imposing a useful order on objects even though order is irrelevant to the count.
questions.rule: Impose an order to make classes.
questions.teaches: Writing unordered subsets in a standard (alphabetical) order is a simple way to obtain free information, another example of the book's monotonizing tactic.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: Using unit steps right (R) and up (U) along grid lines, how many different paths lead from (0, 0) to (3, 2)?
optionExplain: This is 3 x 2, the area of the rectangle.
This is the length of the path, not the number of paths.
This is 5 x 4 and counts the U steps in order.
Each path has 3 R's and 2 U's in some order: 5!/(3! 2!).
questions.explain: Ten paths. The card next gives the general count.
questions.rule: Shortest grid paths to (a, b) are strings of a R's and b U's, so there are C(a + b, a) of them.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A shortest path from (0, 0) to (10, 10) along grid lines has total length ____.
questions.explain: It needs 10 steps right and 10 steps up.
questions.rule: Length a + b.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: How many shortest grid paths join (0, 0) to (6, 4)?
optionExplain: This is 6 x 4, the area of the rectangle.
Strings with 6 R's and 4 U's: C(10, 4).
This is P(10, 4), which counts the U steps in order.
This is 2^10, all strings with either letter.
questions.explain: Choose which 4 of the 10 steps go up.
questions.rule: C(a + b, b).

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A pupil says there are 4 x 3 = 12 shortest paths from (0, 0) to (4, 3). What is wrong?
options: Paths are arrangements of 4 R's and 3 U's, so the count is C(7, 3) = 35
Nothing; paths multiply the two coordinates
The count is 4 + 3 = 7, the length of a path
The count is 7! = 5,040
optionExplain: The product of the sides counts something else.
The coordinates are step counts, and the order of steps varies.
That is the length, not the number of paths.
That treats all steps as different.
questions.explain: Paths are words with repeated letters.
questions.rule: Count arrangements of steps.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: True or false: There are as many shortest paths from (0, 0) to (7, 3) as from (0, 0) to (3, 7).
questions.explain: Both are C(10, 3) = C(10, 7) = 120; swapping the roles of R and U does not change the count.
questions.rule: Swap the letters; the count stays.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: Which statement is true about the paths from (0, 0) to (10, 10) of length 20?
options: They correspond to 20-bit strings with any number of zeros
There are 20 paths, one per step
They correspond to 20-letter strings with ten U's and ten R's, a repeated-letters problem
They are counted by 10 x 10
optionExplain: Only strings with exactly ten of each letter correspond to paths ending at (10, 10).
The number is the binomial coefficient, far larger.
The path coding turns the geometry into arrangements of letters.
The product counts grid squares, not paths.
questions.explain: The book calls this a Mississippi problem: arrangements of repeated letters.
questions.rule: Paths are repeated-letter words.
questions.teaches: The book describes the lattice-path count as a Mississippi problem, an arrangement of repeated letters.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: How many ordered pairs (a, b) of non-negative integers satisfy a + b = 7?
optionExplain: This misses the pair (7, 0) or (0, 7).
This counts each pair in both orders, but (a, b) is already ordered.
The pairs run from (0, 7) to (7, 0).
This is 7 x 7, allowing a and b to range freely.
questions.explain: Eight pairs, one for each value of a from 0 to 7. The card next uses this inside a triple.
questions.rule: Partition the solutions by one variable, count each class by the two-variable rule, and add.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: The number of ordered pairs of non-negative integers with a + b = 33 is ____.
questions.explain: The value of a runs from 0 to 33.
questions.rule: a + b = n has n + 1 solutions.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: Partitioning by c, how many non-negative triples (a, b, c) satisfy a + b + c = 4?
optionExplain: The classes c = 0, ..., 4 have 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 members.
This adds 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 and misses the class c = 0, which has 5 members.
This is 5 x 4, the product of two class sizes.
This counts one class only.
questions.rule: Sizes (n + 1) down to 1.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A pupil partitions a + b + c = 50 by c from 1 to 50 and gets 1,275. What is wrong?
options: The classes overlap, so the sum is too large
The sum should be a product, 50 x 51
Nothing; 1,275 is correct
The class c = 0 is missing, and it has 51 triples; the total is 1,326
optionExplain: The classes are disjoint; one class is missing.
The classes are alternatives, so they add.
Zero is allowed, which adds a class of 51 triples.
Non-negative integers include 0, so c runs from 0 to 50.
questions.explain: Check the endpoints of the range.
questions.rule: Include c = 0.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: True or false: The equation a + b + c = 10 has 66 solutions in non-negative integers.
questions.explain: The classes by c have 11, 10, ..., 1 members, and 11 x 12 / 2 = 66.
questions.rule: Add the sizes n + 1 down to 1.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: According to the book, which solution of the triples problem is ultimately more productive: the partition or the encoding?
options: The partition, because it uses only addition
The encoding, though partitioning solves it too
Neither, since the problem needs induction
They are equally productive for any number of variables
optionExplain: Addition is its feature, but the book prefers the encoding.
The book says the problem can be done by partitioning as well as encoding, but the encoding solution is more productive.
Both methods solve it without induction.
The book says the encoding is more productive.
questions.explain: Encoding generalizes to more variables, where the partition would need nested sums.
questions.rule: Partition solves it; encoding scales.
questions.teaches: Although partitioning solves the problem, the book says the encoding solution is ultimately more productive.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A triple of non-negative integers summing to 11 is written with dots and two plus signs. How many symbols does the string have?
optionExplain: This forgets the plus signs.
11 dots plus 2 plus signs.
This counts one plus sign only.
This adds three plus signs.
questions.explain: Thirteen symbols. The card next counts the strings.
questions.rule: Triples summing to n correspond to placing 2 plus signs among n + 2 positions: C(n + 2, 2).

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: True or false: In the dot-and-plus encoding, a triple with b = 0 is written with two plus signs next to each other.
questions.explain: A zero means no dots between the signs.
questions.rule: Zero means no dots.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: How many non-negative integer triples (a, b, c) satisfy a + b + c = 11?
optionExplain: This is C(12, 2), a string one symbol too short.
This is C(13, 3), choosing three symbols.
This is the length of the string.
questions.explain: Choose which 2 of 13 positions hold plus signs.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: For a + b + c = 5 a pupil uses 5 dots and 3 plus signs, getting C(8, 3) = 56. What is wrong?
options: Three variables need only two separators, so the count is C(7, 2) = 21
Nothing; each variable needs its own plus sign
The count should be C(8, 5) = 56 with no change
The count should be 5 + 3 = 8
optionExplain: Two plus signs split the dots into three groups.
Three groups need two dividers, not three.
That is the same number; it repeats the flaw.
The length of the string is not the number of strings.
questions.explain: k groups are separated by k - 1 signs.
questions.rule: k variables, k - 1 separators.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: For a + b + c + d = 10, the string needs three plus signs and has ____ symbols.
questions.explain: 10 dots plus 3 plus signs.
questions.rule: n + (k - 1) symbols.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A teacher hands out 8 identical stickers to 3 pupils, and some pupils may get none. How many distributions are there?
optionExplain: This is 8 x 3, the product of the counts.
This is 3^8 and treats the stickers as different.
Each distribution is a string of 8 dots and 2 plus signs: C(10, 2).
This is C(7, 2), one dot short.
questions.explain: The book solves the problem for a smaller number first, replacing 50 by 11, to see the dot picture, and then puts 50 back.
questions.rule: Try a smaller number first.
questions.teaches: The book first replaces 50 by the smaller number 11 to see the encoding, recalling how addition was drawn with dots in early school, and then substitutes 50 back.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: In how many ways can 6 identical balls be placed in 3 labeled urns, empty urns allowed?
optionExplain: This is 3^6, which treats the balls as different.
This is 6 x 3 and matches no counting step.
This is C(6, 3), ignoring the dividers.
Arrange 6 balls and 2 dividers: C(8, 2).
questions.explain: Twenty-eight ways. The card next gives the general formula.
questions.rule: b identical balls in u labeled urns can be placed in C(b + u - 1, b) ways.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: The number of ways to place 5 identical balls into 2 labeled urns is ____.
questions.explain: C(6, 1) = 6: the left urn holds 0 to 5 balls.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A baker's box holds 4 pastries chosen from 5 kinds, repeats allowed and order ignored. How many boxes are possible?
optionExplain: This is 5^4, which orders the pastries.
This is 4 balls into 5 urns: C(8, 4).
This is 5 x 4, which counts two ordered picks.
This is C(9, 4), one urn too many.
questions.explain: Kinds are urns and pastries are balls.
questions.rule: Kinds are urns; items are balls.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A pupil says 10 identical balls into 3 labeled urns can be done in 3^10 = 59,049 ways. What is wrong?
options: 3^10 treats the balls as different; identical balls give C(12, 2) = 66
Nothing; each ball chooses one of three urns
The count should be 10 x 3 = 30
The count should be C(10, 3) = 120
optionExplain: Sending ball 1 to urn A and ball 2 to urn B is the same as the reverse when the balls look alike.
That counts balls as distinct, which they are not.
The product matches no counting step.
That chooses three balls, not placements.
questions.explain: Identical balls: positions of dividers matter, not the identities of balls.
questions.rule: Identical balls: use the dot-divider count.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: True or false: Placing 4 identical balls into 2 labeled urns can be done in 5 ways.
questions.explain: The left urn holds 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 balls: C(5, 1) = 5.
questions.rule: Check small cases.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A multiset of 10 digits chosen from 0-9 (repeats allowed, order irrelevant) is counted by which model?
options: 10 labeled balls placed in 2 urns
10! orderings of ten digits
10 balls placed in 10 urns labeled 0 to 9
10 choose 5 subsets of digits
optionExplain: This model has the wrong numbers of balls and urns.
Order is irrelevant here.
Each digit chosen adds a ball to the urn with that digit's label.
Repeats would not be possible.
questions.explain: The number of multisets is C(19, 10) = 92,378, and each multiset is the content of a number's digits regardless of order.
questions.rule: Digits are urns; picks are balls.
questions.teaches: Choosing 10 digits with repetition allowed is the same as putting 10 balls into 10 urns labeled 0 to 9, which gives C(19, 10) = 92,378.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: 100 people are split among 8 teams. At least how many people must be in the largest team?
optionExplain: With 12 in every team only 96 people are placed.
This is the number of teams.
Twelve per team would hold only 96, so some team has 13 or more.
One team could hold all 100, but the question asks what is forced.
questions.explain: At least 13 people must share a team. The card next uses the same idea on digit reorderings.
questions.rule: To force many objects into one class, count the classes (the penultimate step) and apply the pigeonhole principle.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: True or false: In the sorority argument, the crux is how many sororities there are, not how large each sorority is.
questions.explain: Few classes force the many multiples of 7 to crowd into some class.
questions.rule: Count classes, not members.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: How many sororities are there among 4-digit strings (digits 0-9, repeats allowed, order irrelevant)?
optionExplain: This is 4 balls into 10 urns: C(13, 4).
This counts all 4-digit strings, not classes.
This is P(10, 4), which counts ordered digits without repeats.
This is C(10, 4), which forbids repeated digits.
questions.explain: Classes are multisets of digits.
questions.rule: Classes = multisets.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: With 1,428,571,428 multiples of 7 spread over 92,378 sororities, some sorority holds at least ____ of them.
questions.explain: The quotient is about 15,464.6, and the pigeonhole principle forces at least the next whole number.
questions.rule: Pigeonhole: round the quotient up.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A pupil says the largest sorority has 10! = 3,628,800 members, so it holds 10,000 multiples of 7. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; any class of that size must hold at least that many multiples of 7
10! is too small to hold 10,000 multiples of 7, so a larger class would be needed
The pupil should multiply 10! by 7, since only one member in seven is a multiple
Size alone does not show that the members are divisible by 7; the argument must come from the number of classes
optionExplain: Nothing forces a class to have many multiples of 7.
10! is larger than 10,000; the issue is divisibility.
Multiplication by 7 has no role in the argument.
The book warns that big sororities might contain few multiples of 7.
questions.explain: The crux is the count of sororities plus the pigeonhole principle.
questions.rule: Do not rely on class size.

questions.section: Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings
questions.q: A library holds 5,000 books, each in one of 40 categories. At least how many books must share a category?
optionExplain: This is the number of categories.
Pigeonhole: 5,000 / 40 = 125.
All books could share one category, but the question asks what is forced.
With 124 books per category only 4,960 are placed.
questions.explain: Working toward the number of classes is the penultimate step the book recommends: compute or at least estimate the number of sororities.
questions.rule: Compute the number of classes first.
questions.teaches: To apply the pigeonhole principle, the penultimate step is to compute, or at least estimate, the number of classes; in the sorority argument this is the number of sororities.

questions.q: Two sets of sizes 6 and 4 share 2 elements. How many elements are in their union?
optionExplain: This adds the sizes and so counts the shared elements twice.
Adding gives 10, but the 2 shared elements were counted twice.
This multiplies the sizes, which counts pairs, not elements.
This is the size of the overlap alone.
questions.explain: The union has 8 elements. The card next explains why overlap breaks the simple sum.
questions.rule: If sets overlap, the sum of their sizes counts shared elements more than once, by differing amounts.

questions.q: True or false: If sets overlap, the sum of their sizes counts an element in two sets twice and an element in one set once.
questions.explain: The sum counts an element once for each set containing it, so its weight is the number of sets it lies in.
questions.rule: Weight = number of sets containing the element.

questions.q: Sets A, B, C have sizes 5, 4, 3. An element in all three is counted ____ times by |A| + |B| + |C|.
questions.explain: It appears in each of the three sizes once.
questions.rule: Weight = number of sets containing the element.

questions.q: Two clubs have 20 and 15 members, 8 in both. A pupil halves 35 to count different members. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; every member of either club is counted exactly twice by the sum 35
The sum should be divided by 8, the size of the overlap, to remove the double count
The sum should be doubled to allow for membership of both clubs, giving 70 members
The shared members are counted twice but the others once, so a single divisor cannot fix it
optionExplain: Members in one club only are counted once.
The size of the overlap is not a divisor of the total.
Doubling makes the overcount larger.
The true number is 27, and 35 / 2 = 17.5 is not even a whole number.
questions.explain: The repeats are not uniform.
questions.rule: Uneven repeats are not divided out.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether its overcounting is uniform.

items.t: Ordered pairs of 10 people counted for each handshake
Sign-ups for clubs when pupils join one, two or three clubs
All orders of 3 chosen toppings counted for each pizza
Multiples of 2 plus multiples of 3 among 1 to 12

questions.explain: Uniform overcounting has one repeat factor for every outcome; overlap in sets gives factors that vary.
questions.rule: Same factor for everything: divide. Otherwise: inclusion-exclusion.

questions.q: Why does the book call the partitioning tactic a pretty utopian assumption?
options: It assumes the thing to count breaks into pairwise disjoint pieces, which real problems often do not
It assumes every set to be counted has an even number of elements, so halves are whole
It assumes all the pieces have equal size, so that the count is a multiple of one piece
It requires induction to prove, which real problems rarely allow for the pieces
optionExplain: Real problems often give overlapping sets.
Partitioning does not need even sizes.
