Pieces may have any sizes.
Partitioning needs no induction; its limit is overlap.
questions.explain: Reality is often messier, and the book turns to situations where sets overlap and overcounting is not uniform.
questions.rule: Disjointness is an assumption, not a given.
questions.teaches: The book calls the partitioning tactic a pretty utopian assumption, because it needs the thing to count to break into pairwise disjoint subsets, while reality is often messier.

questions.q: How many 4-bit strings contain at least one 1?
optionExplain: This counts every string, including the one with no 1.
This counts strings with exactly one 1.
All 16 strings except the single string 0000.
This is 2^3 and counts strings starting with 1 only.
questions.explain: Fifteen strings. The card next names this the complement.
questions.rule: To count 'at least one', count everything and subtract the case of none.

questions.q: True or false: In an n-bit string, the complement of containing at least one zero is containing no zeros at all.
questions.explain: Every string has either at least one zero or none, and these cases are exclusive.
questions.rule: Complement of at least one = none.

questions.q: How many 5-digit PINs (digits 0-9, repeats allowed) contain at least one 7?
optionExplain: This is 5 x 10^4 and counts a PIN with two 7's more than once.
This counts the PINs with no 7.
This subtracts only 10,000 and has no basis in the cases.
All 10^5 = 100,000 PINs minus the 9^5 = 59,049 with no 7.
questions.explain: Count all PINs, then take away those with no 7.
questions.rule: All minus none.

questions.q: A pupil counts 5-digit PINs with at least one 7 as 5 x 10^4 = 50,000, placing one 7 first. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; 50,000 is the count of PINs having a 7 in some place
A PIN with two 7's is counted once for each 7, so the count is too large
The PINs should be divided by 5, because each PIN was counted five times
The count should be 5 + 10^4 = 10,005, since placing a 7 is an alternative
optionExplain: The PIN 77000 is counted twice.
The overlap between choices makes the overcount uneven; the complement avoids it.
The repeats are uneven, so a single divisor fails.
The choices multiply, but the count is not valid anyway.
questions.explain: Use the complement to avoid overlaps.
questions.rule: At least one: complement.

questions.q: The number of 10-bit strings with at least one zero is ____.
questions.explain: There are 2^10 = 1,024 strings and one has no zeros.

questions.q: How many 5-card hands from a standard 52-card deck contain at least one heart?
optionExplain: All C(52, 5) = 2,598,960 hands minus the C(39, 5) = 575,757 hands with no heart.
This counts every hand.
This counts only the hands with no heart.
This is 13 x C(51, 4): pick a heart, then any four other cards; a hand with two hearts is counted twice.
questions.explain: The words at least alert you to the possibility of counting complements.
questions.rule: Watch for the words at least.
questions.teaches: Whenever a problem says at least, be alert to the possibility of counting the complement: compare the number of hands containing a suit with the number containing none of it.

questions.q: 4 children each order one of 5 flavors. How many orders have at least two children with the same flavor?
optionExplain: This counts only the orders with all flavors different.
This counts every order.
All 5^4 = 625 orders minus the P(5, 4) = 120 with all flavors different.
This subtracts 240, double the all-different count.
questions.explain: The complement of at least two the same is all different. The card next works the 31-flavor case.
questions.rule: Orders with some repeated flavor = all orders minus orders with all flavors different.

questions.q: True or false: The complement of having at least two children with the same flavor is having all children with different flavors.
questions.explain: Either two children match or every child differs.
questions.rule: Complement of a repeat = all distinct.

questions.q: 3 children each pick one of 5 flavors. The number of orders with at least two the same is ____.
questions.explain: 125 total minus P(5, 3) = 60 with all different.
questions.rule: Total minus all-different.

questions.q: A pupil says the number of orders with at least two the same flavor is P(31, 10). What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; P(31, 10) is the wanted count of orders with a repeated flavor
The wanted count should be 31^10 only, since every order has a repeated flavor
P(31, 10) counts the orders with all flavors different, which is the complement
The wanted count should be C(31, 10), the number of ways to choose ten flavors
optionExplain: P(31, 10) counts orders with no repeats.
That counts every order, repeats or not.
The wanted number is 31^10 minus P(31, 10).
That ignores which child asked for which flavor.
questions.explain: The product of falling factors counts the all-different case.
questions.rule: P(n, r) is the no-repeat case.

questions.q: Now there are only 9 flavors and 10 children. How many orders have all flavors different?
options: None, so every order has a repeated flavor
9!, one for each way to arrange the flavors
9^10, all orders
optionExplain: Ten children cannot all differ among nine flavors.
Only nine flavors exist for ten children.
That counts every order, not the all-different ones.
That chooses which child is left out and nothing else.
questions.explain: P(9, 10) = 0, so every order has a repeat (the pigeonhole principle again).
questions.rule: No room for all-different means all orders repeat.

questions.q: Three pupils who cannot be told apart each choose one of 5 flavors; an order lists cones per flavor. How many orders?
optionExplain: This is 5^3 and treats the pupils as distinguishable.
This is P(5, 3), requiring all flavors different.
This is 5 x 3 and matches no counting step.
This is 3 balls into 5 urns: C(7, 3).
questions.explain: The book assumes the children are distinguishable; if they are not, an order is just the number of cones of each flavor.
questions.rule: Check what the outcomes record.
questions.teaches: The book makes the humanistic assumption that the children are distinguishable; if only the number of cones per flavor matters, the orders are counted by the balls in urns formula instead.

questions.q: In a class, 25 pupils take French, 20 take German and 8 take both. How many take at least one of the two?
optionExplain: This counts the 8 pupils taking both languages twice.
Add 45 and take away the 8 counted twice.
This adds the overlap on top, 45 + 8.
This is 20 - 8, the pupils taking German only.
questions.explain: Thirty-seven. The card next states the principle.
questions.rule: Add the two sizes, then subtract the overlap once.
|A| + |B| - |A and B|.

questions.q: How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 4 or by 6?
optionExplain: This adds 25 + 16 and counts multiples of 12 twice.
25 are divisible by 4, 16 by 6, and 8 by both (the multiples of 12): 25 + 16 - 8.
This counts only the multiples of both 4 and 6.
This subtracts 4 where it should subtract 8.
questions.explain: Numbers divisible by both 4 and 6 are the multiples of 12.
questions.rule: Count the overlap with the least common multiple.

questions.q: True or false: If A and B are disjoint, the principle of inclusion-exclusion for two sets reduces to the simple addition rule.
questions.explain: For disjoint sets the intersection is empty and |A and B| = 0.
questions.rule: Disjoint: no correction.

questions.q: 14 pupils play chess, 11 sing and 6 do both; a pupil adds 14 + 11 + 6 = 31. What is wrong?
options: The 6 should be subtracted twice, giving 13
Nothing; the overlap is an extra group
The sum should be halved, giving 15.5
The 6 who do both should be subtracted once, giving 19, not added
optionExplain: Subtracting twice removes them from the union altogether.
The overlap is part of both sets already.
Halving is not meaningful for non-uniform overcounting.
Adding the overlap counts those pupils a third time.
questions.explain: The shared 6 are counted twice by the sizes, so subtract them once.
questions.rule: Subtract the overlap once.

questions.q: Why can counting the complement alone not settle how many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 4 or 6?
options: The complement, divisible by neither, is equally hard to count; PIE handles the overlap directly
The complement has more elements than the set itself, so subtraction would give a negative number
The complement cannot be defined for divisibility, because divisibility is not a property of a set
Complements only work for bit strings, where there is a natural universe of 2^n strings
optionExplain: The complement is no simpler than the original.
Its size is 67, not larger than the set in a way that matters; the issue is difficulty.
It is well defined: numbers divisible by neither.
They work for any set inside a universe.
questions.explain: Sometimes counting the complement fails, because the complement is as complicated as the original set.
questions.rule: PIE handles overlaps systematically.
questions.teaches: Counting the complement sometimes fails because the complement is as complicated as the original set; PIE is a systematic way to handle such situations.

questions.q: For three overlapping sets A, B and C, what is the sign pattern of the terms in the formula for |A union B union C|?
options: Plus for all terms
Minus for the single sets and plus for the overlaps
Plus for single sets, minus for pairwise overlaps, plus for the triple overlap
Plus for single sets and pairs, minus for the triple
optionExplain: Overlaps are counted too often and must be subtracted.
Single sets are added; their sum is the first approximation.
The signs alternate with the number of sets intersected.
The pairs correct an overcount, so they are subtracted.
questions.explain: The signs alternate. The card next gives the full formulas.
questions.rule: Alternate: add sizes of single sets, subtract two-fold intersections, add three-fold, and so on.

questions.q: In the formula for the union of four sets, the term |A and B and C and D| has sign: plus or ____ ?
questions.explain: For n = 4 (even) the last term is negative.
questions.rule: Sign of the last term: minus for even n, plus for odd n.

questions.q: Multiples of 2, 3, 5 in 1 to 30 number 15, 10, 6; pairs 5, 3, 2; all three 1. How big is the union?
optionExplain: This omits adding back the triple overlap.
This sums the three sizes only.
This adds the triple overlap but subtracts only part of the pairs.
questions.explain: Apply the alternating pattern: sizes, minus pairs, plus triple.
questions.rule: + singles - pairs + triple.

questions.q: True or false: The formula for the union of 5 sets has 10 pairwise-intersection terms.
questions.explain: Choosing which 2 of 5 sets intersect gives C(5, 2) = 10 terms.
questions.rule: C(n, 2) pairwise terms.

questions.q: A pupil computes the union of three sets as |A| + |B| + |C| - (pairwise overlaps) and stops. What is missing?
options: The triple overlap must be subtracted again
The triple overlap must be added back, since it was subtracted too often
Nothing; three sets need only two stages
The singles must be subtracted
optionExplain: That would remove the element altogether.
An element in all three sets is counted 3 times, subtracted 3 times, and needs one count restored.
The element in all three sets would have net count 0.
The singles are added at the start.
questions.explain: The signs alternate to the last stage.
questions.rule: Go through all the stages.

questions.q: How many terms, in all, does the inclusion-exclusion formula for four sets have?
optionExplain: It has 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 terms.
This is 4!, which counts orders.
This is 2^4 and includes the empty intersection.
This counts the singles and pairs only.
questions.explain: Each non-empty selection of sets gives one term, and there are 2^4 - 1 = 15 non-empty selections.
questions.rule: One term per non-empty selection of sets.
questions.teaches: The formula for four sets, as the book lists it, has 4 single sizes, 6 pairwise intersections, 4 triple intersections and 1 quadruple intersection: 15 terms in all.

questions.q: A point lies in all three of the sets A, B and C. How many times does |A| + |B| + |C| count it?
optionExplain: That would be the count after correction.
The point lies in more than two sets.
Each size includes the point once.
The point is inside every set, so it is counted.
questions.explain: Three times. The card next follows the point through the correction steps.
questions.rule: Add, subtract pairs, then add back triples, until every point has weight exactly one.

questions.q: A point lying in all three sets has weight 3 after adding, and after subtracting the three pairwise overlaps its weight is ____.
questions.explain: Each of the three pairs subtracts 1: 3 - 3 = 0.
questions.rule: Track each point's weight.

questions.q: A point lies in exactly two of three sets. After adding the sizes and then subtracting the pairwise overlaps, what is its weight?
optionExplain: That is the weight of a point in all three sets at this stage.
That is its weight before the pairs are subtracted.
It starts at 2, and it lies in exactly one pair: 2 - 1.
It is not in all three sets.
questions.explain: Such a point needs no further correction.
questions.rule: Weight 1 means correct.

questions.q: Put the correction steps for three sets in order.
items: Add the three set sizes
Subtract the three pairwise intersections
Add back the triple intersection
questions.explain: After the first step overlaps are overcounted; after the second, the triple region is undercounted; the third restores it.
questions.rule: Add, subtract, add back.

questions.q: A pupil says subtracting the pairwise overlaps once removes the triple region correctly. What is wrong?
options: A triple point lies in three pairs, so it is subtracted three times and ends at weight 0
Nothing; each triple point is in one pair
The triple region is subtracted twice and ends at weight 1
The triple region should be subtracted again
optionExplain: The triple region is subtracted three times and must be added back.
A point in all three sets lies in three pairs.
It is subtracted three times.
That would give weight -1.
questions.explain: Count how many pairs a point belongs to.
questions.rule: Triple points belong to three pairs.

questions.q: With four sets, what does the picture suggest about the sign of the four-fold overlap term?
options: It is plus, since four is an even number and even numbers of sets take a plus sign
It is zero, since four disks cannot overlap in a common region of the picture
It is the same as the pair terms, minus, since both involve an even number of sets
It continues the alternation: sizes plus, pairs minus, triples plus, four-fold minus
optionExplain: The sign alternates with the number of sets, and for four sets it is minus.
Four sets can overlap.
The sign depends on the number of sets in the intersection.
The book says it makes sense that in the general case we alternate between adding and subtracting.
questions.explain: The thickness argument is attractive but hard to generalize rigorously, so the book gives a rigorous proof next.
questions.rule: Alternate with the number of sets.
questions.teaches: The book finds the thickness argument attractive but hard to generalize rigorously to n sets, so it makes sense to alternate adding and subtracting and then proves the pattern with counting notation.

questions.q: If |A and B| = 5, |A and C| = 3 and |B and C| = 2, what is S_2, the sum of pairwise sizes?
optionExplain: This multiplies the three sizes.
This counts each pair in both orders, 2 x 10.
This is the size of one pair only.
questions.explain: S_2 is 10. The card next defines S_k for any k.
questions.rule: S_k adds the sizes of all k-fold intersections, each once; the union is S_1 - S_2 + S_3 - ...

questions.q: For five sets, the sum S_3 has ____ terms.
questions.explain: Choosing 3 of the 5 sets gives C(5, 3) = 10 terms.
questions.rule: S_k has C(n, k) terms.

questions.q: With S_1 = 31, S_2 = 10 and S_3 = 1 for three sets, what is the size of their union?
optionExplain: This is 31 + 10 + 1, adding all three.
This is 31 - 10, missing the S_3 term.
This is 31 - 10 - 1, subtracting S_3.
questions.explain: Signs alternate: plus, minus, plus.

questions.q: A pupil defines S_2 as the sum of |A_i and A_j| over all i, j, allowing i = j and order to matter. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; more terms make a more accurate sum
The sum would miss pairs
It would only change the sign
Intersections would be counted several times, and A_i with itself is not a pair
optionExplain: Extra terms change the value and break the formula.
It would include every pair, but too often.
The values change, not just the sign.
The increasing-index condition i < j makes each pair appear once.
questions.explain: Use increasing indices.
questions.rule: i < j lists each pair once.

questions.q: True or false: In the PIE formula for six sets, the last term S_6 has a minus sign.
questions.explain: The sign of S_k is (-1)^(k - 1), and for k = 6 that is -1.
questions.rule: Sign (-1)^(k - 1): odd k plus, even k minus.

questions.q: For four sets, how many different 3-fold intersections appear in S_3?
optionExplain: Choosing which 3 of the 4 sets gives C(4, 3) = 4.
This counts ordered choices, P(4, 3) / 2.
This is 4!, which counts orders of all four sets.
This is the single four-fold intersection.
questions.explain: The strictly increasing condition lists each combination exactly once.
questions.rule: C(n, k) terms in S_k.
questions.teaches: The condition on the indices gives exactly C(n, k) possible combinations of different sets in S_k, with no repeats.

questions.q: An element lies in exactly 4 of the sets. How many times does S_2 count it?
optionExplain: This counts the single sets, as S_1 does.
This counts ordered pairs.
Each pair of the 4 sets containing it gives one term: C(4, 2).
This is the size of a pair.
questions.explain: Six times. The card next uses this count for every k.
questions.rule: Each element of the union is counted C(r, 1) - C(r, 2) + ... = 1 times, because the alternating sum of a row of Pascal's triangle is 0.

questions.q: An element lying in exactly 5 sets is counted ____ times by S_3.
questions.explain: Choose 3 of the 5 sets: C(5, 3) = 10.
questions.rule: S_k counts x C(r, k) times.

questions.q: An element lies in exactly 4 sets. What is its net count in S_1 - S_2 + S_3 - S_4?
optionExplain: This is the row sum with the leading 1 included.
This adds the coefficients without alternating.
This subtracts the last coefficient only.
questions.explain: The alternating row sum minus the leading 1 leaves 1.

questions.q: Put the steps of the proof of PIE in order.
items: Take an element x of the union that lies in exactly r of the sets
Observe that S_k counts x exactly C(r, k) times
Write the right side's count of x as C(r, 1) - C(r, 2) + ... + (-1)^(r-1) C(r, r)
Use the alternating row sum (1 - 1)^r = 0 to conclude the count is 1
questions.explain: The proof reduces PIE to the identity that the alternating sum of a row of binomial coefficients is 0.
questions.rule: Reduce to one element.

questions.q: A pupil says S_k counts a given element C(n, k) times, where n is the total number of sets. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; every k-fold intersection contains x
Only the r sets that contain x matter, so S_k counts it C(r, k) times
S_k counts it r times for every k
S_k counts it k times
optionExplain: Intersections including sets that do not contain x are missing x.
An intersection that includes a set not containing x does not contain x.
The count depends on k.
The count is a binomial coefficient in r and k.
questions.explain: Count only the sets that contain x.
questions.rule: Use r, not n.

questions.q: To check whether a counting identity is true, what new idea does the book suggest, beyond algebra?
options: Examine how each side of the equation counts a representative element
Test it on a computer for large n
Prove it by induction on the number of sets
Choose the side with more terms and simplify
optionExplain: This is how the proof of PIE works.
The book describes a counting argument, not computer testing.
Induction is one proof, but the footnote idea is different.
The number of terms does not decide an identity.
questions.explain: The proof shows that one element is counted once on each side.
questions.rule: Count one element on both sides.
questions.teaches: A new counting idea from the proof: to see whether a combinatorial identity is true, examine how each side of the equation counts a representative element.

questions.q: In a group of 100, 30 own a bike, 20 own a scooter and 5 own both. How many own neither?
optionExplain: This subtracts 30 and 20 and forgets the 5 counted twice.
This is 30 + 20 - 5, the number owning at least one.
This subtracts only the larger owner count and 5.
questions.explain: Fifty-five. The card next states the general formula.
questions.rule: None of the sets = N - S_1 + S_2 - S_3 + ..., alternating down to the last S_k.

questions.q: In N - S_1 + S_2 - S_3 + ..., the sign in front of S_3 is plus or ____ ?
questions.explain: The signs alternate starting with minus for S_1, so S_3 comes with a minus.

questions.q: How many integers from 1 to 60 are divisible by none of 2, 3, 5? (Multiples: 30, 20, 12; pairs 10, 6, 4; triple 2.)
optionExplain: This ignores the sets.
This is 60 - 62 + 20, missing the S_3 term.
This is 60 - 62 + 20 - 4 and mixes up S_3.
questions.explain: Alternate signs through S_3.

questions.q: For three sets a pupil computes the number in none as N - S_1 + S_2 and stops. What is missing?
options: The term - S_3: the triple overlaps must be subtracted as well
Nothing is missing; two correction stages are enough to handle every overlap
The term + S_3, since the third stage adds back what the second removed
A division by 3, since three sets give each missing item a repeat factor of three
optionExplain: Without it elements in all three sets are mis-weighted.
The triple overlaps matter for three sets.
The sign of S_3 is minus.
No division arises.
questions.explain: Go through all k stages.
questions.rule: Do every stage.

questions.q: True or false: In the formula for four sets, the term S_4 comes with a plus sign.
questions.explain: The pattern N - S_1 + S_2 - S_3 + S_4 gives S_4 a plus.
questions.rule: Even index: plus.

questions.q: For k sets, the last term of complement PIE is plus or minus depending on k. Which is right?
options: Plus if k is odd and minus if k is even
Always plus
Always minus
Plus if k is even and minus if k is odd
optionExplain: This is the pattern for the union, not for the complement count.
The signs alternate.
The signs alternate.
The sign of S_k is (-1)^k in N - S_1 + S_2 - ...
questions.explain: In the complement form the sign of S_i is (-1)^i, so the last sign follows the parity of k.
questions.rule: Sign (-1)^k.
questions.teaches: In the complement form N - S_1 + S_2 - ... the last term S_k is plus or minus depending on whether k is even or odd.

questions.q: How many 5-card hands from a 52-card deck contain no diamond?
optionExplain: This counts all 5-card hands, diamonds allowed.
Choose all 5 cards from the 39 cards that are not diamonds: C(39, 5).
This counts hands made only of diamonds: C(13, 5).
This counts hands drawn from 26 cards: C(26, 5).
questions.explain: The hands with no diamonds draw from 39 cards. The card next uses such counts for all four suits.
questions.rule: When a condition says every category must appear, count the hands where some category is absent and use complement PIE.

questions.q: True or false: In the five-card hand problem, no hand can lack all four suits, so the four-fold intersection has size 0.
questions.explain: Omitting every suit would leave no cards to draw from, so no hand lacks all four suits.
questions.rule: Impossible intersections contribute 0.

questions.q: With S_1 = 2,303,028, S_2 = 394,680, S_3 = 5,148 and S_4 = 0, hands lacking at least one suit number ____.
questions.explain: S_1 - S_2 + S_3 - S_4 = 2,303,028 - 394,680 + 5,148 - 0 = 1,913,496, the size of the union of the missing-suit sets.
questions.rule: Union of the missing-suit sets.

questions.q: A pupil counts hands with all four suits as C(52, 5) - 4 x C(39, 5) = 295,932. What is missing?
options: Nothing is missing; subtracting the four one-suit-missing sets is enough to find the answer
The pairs, triples and quadruple of missing suits: hands lacking two suits were subtracted twice
A division by 4, since four suits are involved and each hand was counted four times
An addition of 4 x C(39, 5), which restores the hands that were subtracted once
optionExplain: Hands missing two suits are subtracted twice by this.
The later terms correct the overcount from the first stage.
Division does not correct non-uniform overlap.
That would cancel the first subtraction.
questions.explain: A hand missing two suits lies in two of the four sets.
questions.rule: Continue through all stages.

questions.q: Apply the same formula to 3-card hands to count those with all four suits. What value must it give, and does it?
options: 1, because one arrangement uses all suits
A negative number, showing the method fails
Undefined, since C(13, 3) is too small
optionExplain: Three cards cannot show four suits.
The terms cancel exactly to 0.
C(13, 3) = 286 is a legitimate count.
Three cards cannot cover four suits, and the formula agrees.
questions.explain: Checking a formula on a case with a known answer is a strong test.
questions.rule: Test on a case you know.

questions.q: How many 5-letter strings over {A, B, C} use all three letters?
optionExplain: 3^5 - 3 x 2^5 + 3 x 1 - 0: remove strings missing at least one letter.
This counts all strings, whatever letters they use.
This leaves out the +3 term for strings missing two letters.
This is 3 x 2^5 - 6, with no basis in the stages.
questions.explain: The sets are strings missing a given letter. The intersection of all three sets is empty, because a string cannot omit every letter, so the last term is 0.
questions.rule: Intersections of all sets can be empty.
questions.teaches: When the intersection of all the sets is impossible, as when a hand omits all four suits, the last term of the formula is 0.

questions.q: Two couples sit in a row of 4 seats. In how many seatings is nobody next to their partner?
optionExplain: This counts every seating.
This is the number of seatings with some couple together.
Complement PIE: 24 - (24 - 8).
This is 4! / 2, with no basis in the cases.
questions.explain: Eight seatings. The card next works the four-couple case.
questions.rule: For k chosen couples seated together there are 2^k (8 - k)! seatings; use complement PIE across the couples.

questions.q: Treating couple i as a single block that can be in 2 orders, |A_i| = 2 x 7! = ____.
questions.explain: Two orders times 7! arrangements of the 7 symbols: 2 x 5,040.
questions.rule: Glue a couple into one symbol.

questions.q: For four couples in a row, how many seatings have couples 1 and 2 both sitting together?
optionExplain: This allows only one order for one of the couples.
This is the count for one couple, 2 x 7!.
This is 6! and ignores the orders within blocks.
Two blocks with 2 orders each and 6 symbols to arrange: 2 x 2 x 6!.
questions.explain: Glue both couples: four orders in total, then permute 6 symbols.

questions.q: A pupil says |A_i| = 7!, gluing couple i into one symbol and permuting 7 symbols. What is missing?
options: A factor of 8, one for each seat that the glued couple might occupy in the row
A factor of 2 for the two orders (boy-girl or girl-boy) within the glued couple
A division by 2 for the repeated couple, since both orders look the same in a row
Nothing is missing; 7! counts every seating in which the couple sits side by side
optionExplain: The glued couple occupies two seats; seats are not multiplied.
The glued symbol can appear in two orientations.
Nothing is overcounted by gluing.
Orientation of the pair doubles the count.
questions.explain: A block of two different people has two orders.
questions.rule: Include the orientation factor.

questions.q: True or false: For four couples, the number of seatings in which at least one couple sits together is 26,496.
questions.rule: Union = total - none.

questions.q: Six children in a row include three pairs of twins. In how many orders is no child next to their twin?
optionExplain: This is the number of orders with some pair of twins adjacent.
This counts all orders.
This is 6 x 4 x 3 x 2 and does not follow from the stages.
questions.explain: The book calls the gluing device freezing several symbols together to define a single new symbol.
questions.rule: Freeze, count, alternate signs.
questions.teaches: Gluing several symbols into one new symbol is a tool the book describes as temporarily freezing them together; for k frozen couples the count is 2^k (n - k)! where n is the number of seats.

questions.q: A function is 1 on the even numbers from 1 to 10 and 0 elsewhere. What are its values at 4 and 7?
options: 0 at x = 4 and 1 at x = 7
1 at both
1 at x = 4 and 0 at x = 7
4 at x = 4 and 7 at x = 7
optionExplain: This reverses the rule: 1 means membership.
7 is not an even number.
4 is even and in A; 7 is odd and not in A.
The function takes only the values 0 and 1.
questions.explain: The function takes the value 1 on members and 0 on non-members. The card next calls it the indicator function.
questions.rule: An indicator function writes membership as 1 or 0; products give intersections, 1 minus gives complements, and sums count.

questions.q: True or false: The product of the indicator functions of A and B equals the indicator function of the intersection of A and B.
questions.explain: The product is 1 only when both indicators are 1, that is, when x is in both sets.
questions.rule: 1_A 1_B = 1_(A and B).

questions.q: For U = {1, ..., 30} and A the even numbers, the sum of the indicator of A over U is ____.
questions.explain: Each member of A contributes 1, so the sum is |A| = 15.
questions.rule: Sum of indicator = size.

questions.q: A pupil says 1_A(x) + 1_B(x) is the indicator of the union of A and B. What breaks this?
options: Nothing; sums of indicators give indicators of unions
The sum is 0 on the intersection
For an element in both sets the sum is 2, not 1
The sum fails for elements in neither set
optionExplain: The value 2 on the intersection shows it does not.
Both indicators equal 1 there.
The sum is not an indicator, since it takes the value 2 on the intersection.
For such elements both indicators are 0 and the sum is correct.
questions.explain: Use the product for intersections and the complement for unions.
questions.rule: Sum of indicators double counts.

questions.q: True or false: For an element x that belongs to A, the value of 1 - 1_A(x) is 0.
questions.explain: 1 - 1 = 0, and 0 is the indicator of the complement at x.
questions.rule: 1 - 1_A is the indicator of the complement.

questions.q: On U = {1, ..., 12}, what is the sum of 1_A(x) 1_B(x), with A the multiples of 2 and B of 3?
optionExplain: The product is 1 exactly at the multiples of 6, namely 6 and 12.
This is |A|, the number of multiples of 2.
This is |A| + |B|, the sum of the sizes.
This is 6 x 4, the product of the sizes.
questions.explain: The product (1 - 1_A)(1 - 1_B) is the indicator of the elements in neither set, which is how the next proof counts the complement.
questions.rule: Products of indicators encode 'in all of these'.
questions.teaches: A product of factors of the form 1 - 1_A is the indicator of the elements belonging to none of the sets, which the next idea uses to prove complement PIE.

questions.q: What is the expansion of (1 - a)(1 - b)(1 - c)?
options: 1 - (a + b + c) - (ab + ac + bc) - abc
1 + (a + b + c) + (ab + ac + bc) + abc
1 - a - b - c + abc
1 - (a + b + c) + (ab + ac + bc) - abc
optionExplain: The pair products come with a plus sign, since two negatives multiply.
Single terms come with minus signs.
This leaves out the pair products.
Each term chooses 1 or the negative variable from each factor.
questions.explain: Signs alternate with the number of variables in a term. The card next uses this for indicators.
questions.rule: Multiply out the product of (1 - indicator) factors and sum over the universe to get complement PIE.

questions.q: For an element x in the set A_1 only, the value g(x) = (1 - 1_(A_1)(x))(1 - 1_(A_2)(x))... equals ____.
questions.explain: The first factor is 1 - 1 = 0, so the whole product is 0.
questions.rule: g(x) = 1 only for x in none of the sets.

questions.q: True or false: Summing g(x) over all x in U gives the number of elements in none of the sets.
questions.explain: g is the indicator of the complement of the union, and the sum of an indicator is the size of its set.
questions.rule: N_0 = sum of g.

questions.q: Put the steps of the indicator-function proof in order.
items: Define g(x) as the product of the factors (1 - 1_(A_i)(x))
Observe that g(x) is 1 exactly when x lies in none of the sets, so N_0 is the sum of g
Multiply out the product into an alternating sum of indicator products
Sum each group over U to get N - S_1 + S_2 - S_3 + S_4
questions.explain: The proof turns a counting statement into an algebraic expansion.
questions.rule: Define, expand, sum.

questions.q: A pupil says the sum over U of 1_(A_1)(x) 1_(A_2)(x) equals |A_1| x |A_2|. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; a sum of products factors into the product of the two separate sums
The product of indicators is the indicator of the intersection, so the sum is |A_1 and A_2|
The sum is |A_1| + |A_2|, since the indicator of each set is counted once in the sum
The sum is 0, because an element cannot be in two sets at once in this universe
optionExplain: The sum counts elements in both sets, not pairs of elements.
The product is 1 only where both indicators are 1.
Sums of sizes would come from adding indicators.
The sum is the size of the overlap, which may be positive.
questions.explain: Sum the product, not the factors separately.
questions.rule: Sum of 1_A 1_B = |A and B|.

questions.q: The proof for four sets generalizes to n sets. What algebraic fact does the argument rely on?
options: The binomial theorem for (1 + x)^n, applied to a product of n identical factors
The expansion of (1 - a)(1 - b)(1 - c)... is an alternating sum 1 - (a + b + ...) + (ab + ...) - ...
Induction on the size of the universe, adding one element at a time to the set U
The summation identity of Pascal's triangle, used to split off one of the n sets
optionExplain: The product has different factors, not a power.
The same alternating pattern holds for any number of factors.
Induction on n is not used here.
That identity belongs to the other proof of PIE.
questions.explain: The argument uses only the algebraic expansion of the product, so it holds for every n.
questions.rule: One algebraic fact covers every n.
questions.teaches: The indicator proof generalizes to any number of sets because it uses only the algebraic fact that the expansion of (1 - a)(1 - b)(1 - c)... is an alternating sum of products.

questions.q: Let a(1) = 1 and a(n + 1) = a(n) + n. What is a(5)?
optionExplain: This adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 and misses the starting term.
This is a(6), one step too far.
This is 5 x 3, which follows from no step.
questions.explain: Eleven. The card next explains why the rule and the starting term fix all values.
questions.rule: A recurrence plus its boundary values determines every term; compute them in order.

questions.q: True or false: A recurrence relation together with its boundary values determines every term of the sequence.
questions.explain: Each term is computed from earlier ones, starting at the boundary values.
questions.rule: Rule plus start fixes the sequence.

questions.explain: The terms are 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
questions.rule: Compute in order.

questions.q: A pupil says the rule a(n + 1) = a(n) + a(n - 1) by itself fixes a(10). What is missing?
options: Two boundary values, since without starting terms the rule determines nothing
Nothing is missing; the rule alone is enough to fix every term, including a(10)
A closed-form formula for a(n), since a rule cannot give a value without one
The value of a(11), because each term is computed from the term after it
optionExplain: Different starting terms give different sequences from the same rule.
Without starting values the first computation cannot begin.
A formula is not needed to compute terms.
Later terms depend on earlier ones, not the reverse.
questions.explain: Always give the recurrence and its boundary values together.
questions.rule: Rule plus starting values.

questions.q: The rule a(n + 1) = a(n) + a(n - 1) with a(1) = 1 and a(2) = 2 gives a(5) = ____.
questions.explain: The terms are 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.
questions.rule: Changing the start changes the sequence.

questions.q: A pupil finds a recurrence with boundary values for a counting problem and says it is solved. In what sense is that so?
options: It gives a closed-form formula for every n, so each term can be written down directly
It is solved only for the first two values, which are the boundary values given
In a computational sense: any term can be computed step by step, though no formula is given
It is not solved at all, since a recurrence is a rule and does not count anything
optionExplain: A recurrence does not by itself give a closed form.
The rule computes all values.
The book calls such a problem solved at least in a computational sense.
The recurrence counts the objects through a partition into cases.
questions.explain: A recurrence plus boundary values solves a problem computationally; a closed form is a further question.
questions.rule: Computationally solved, not necessarily closed form.
questions.teaches: A recurrence with boundary values 'solves' a counting problem in a computational sense, since as many values as desired can be calculated, but it does not by itself give a closed-form formula.

questions.q: In how many ways can a 3 x 2 rectangle (3 columns, 2 rows) be tiled with 1 x 2 dominos?
optionExplain: This counts the tilings of a 2 x 2 rectangle.
This adds a tiling that does not exist.
This is 3!, which counts orders of three dominos.
One tiling has three vertical dominos; two have a vertical domino and a pair of horizontal ones.
questions.explain: Three tilings. The card next counts larger rectangles by partition.
questions.rule: Partition by the right end: t(n + 1) = t(n) + t(n - 1), which is the Fibonacci recurrence with starting values 1 and 2.

questions.q: Given t(7) = 21 and t(6) = 13, what is t(8), the number of tilings of an 8 x 2 rectangle?
optionExplain: This is 21 + 7, using the index instead of the value.
This doubles 21.
This is 21 + 8, using the index.
questions.explain: Each value is the sum of the two before it.
questions.rule: Add the two previous values.

questions.q: Put the steps of the recurrence argument in order.
items: Partition the tilings of the (n + 1) x 2 rectangle by what lies at the right end
Class V: one vertical domino at the right end, leaving a tiling of an n x 2 rectangle
Class H: two horizontal dominos at the right end, leaving a tiling of an (n - 1) x 2 rectangle
Add the class sizes: t(n + 1) = t(n) + t(n - 1)
questions.explain: A partition into two exclusive classes gives a sum of two earlier values.
questions.rule: Partition, count, add.

questions.q: A pupil says t(n + 1) = t(n) + t(n), since the right end is either a vertical or a horizontal domino. What is wrong?
options: Horizontal dominos come in pairs, so that class leaves an (n - 1) x 2 rectangle, not an n x 2 one
Nothing is wrong; both the vertical class and the horizontal class leave n columns to tile
The classes overlap, so the sum t(n) + t(n) should be halved to remove the shared tilings
A vertical domino at the end leaves n - 1 columns, and a horizontal pair leaves n columns
optionExplain: Two horizontal dominos fill the last two columns.
A horizontal pair uses two columns.
The classes are disjoint.
It leaves n columns after covering one.
questions.explain: Count the columns left after each end.
questions.rule: V leaves n columns; H leaves n - 1.

questions.q: You climb stairs one or two steps at a time: 1 way up one stair, 2 ways up two. How many ways up six?
optionExplain: This is 2 x 6, with no basis in the cases.
This is the count for five stairs.
Partition by the last step: ways(n + 1) = ways(n) + ways(n - 1), giving 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.
This is the count for seven stairs.
questions.explain: The tilings numbers are the Fibonacci numbers shifted by one: t(n) = F(n + 1), where F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1 and F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2). The recurrence is the same and only the boundary values differ.
questions.rule: Same recurrence, shifted boundary values.
questions.teaches: The tiling numbers satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence with different boundary values, so t(n) = F(n + 1) where F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1 and F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2).

questions.q: The numbers alpha and beta have sum 1 and product -1. Which quadratic equation has them as its roots?
optionExplain: This has sum -1 and product -1.
This has sum 1 and product 1.
A quadratic with roots of sum s and product p is x^2 - sx + p.
This has sum 0 and product -1.
questions.explain: The roots of x^2 - x - 1 = 0 are the golden ratio and its conjugate. The card next uses this.
questions.rule: A formula that satisfies the recurrence and the boundary values is the sequence.

questions.q: True or false: Any sequence of the form A alpha^n + B beta^n satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence, whatever the constants A and B.
questions.explain: Each of alpha^n and beta^n satisfies the recurrence, and sums of multiples of solutions are solutions.
questions.rule: Combinations of solutions are solutions.

questions.q: The numbers alpha satisfies alpha^2 = alpha + 1. What follows for alpha^(n+1)?
options: alpha^(n+1) = alpha^n + alpha^(n-1)
alpha^(n+1) = alpha^n x alpha^(n-1)
alpha^(n+1) = 2 alpha^n
alpha^(n+1) = alpha^(n-1) + 1
optionExplain: Multiply both sides of alpha^2 = alpha + 1 by alpha^(n - 1).
The equation adds the powers rather than multiplying them.
The equation does not say alpha equals 2.
Multiplying by alpha^(n - 1) turns the 1 into alpha^(n - 1) and the alpha into alpha^n.
questions.explain: Multiplying the quadratic relation by a power of alpha gives the recurrence for powers.
questions.rule: Powers of a root satisfy the recurrence.

questions.q: A pupil checks the formula only at n = 0 and n = 1, and calls it verified. What is missing?
options: A check at n = 2 would be enough, since three values pin down the formula completely
Nothing is missing; two values determine a formula for the whole sequence
A proof that the formula is rational, since all Fibonacci numbers are rational
A check that the formula satisfies the recurrence, since two values fix only the start
optionExplain: One more value still does not cover all n.
Many sequences share two values.
The formula involves the square root of 5 and is not rational.
Boundary values alone fix two terms, not the rest.
questions.explain: A verification needs both the recurrence and the boundary values.
questions.rule: Recurrence plus boundary values.

questions.q: Put the steps of the verification in order.
items: Define alpha and beta and note that alpha + beta = 1 and alpha beta = -1
Conclude both are roots of x^2 - x - 1, so alpha^n and beta^n satisfy the recurrence
Conclude that A alpha^n + B beta^n satisfies the recurrence for any A and B
Choose A and B to match the boundary values F_0 = 0 and F_1 = 1
questions.explain: The recurrence supplies a family of sequences, and the boundary values select one.
questions.rule: Recurrence, family, boundary values.

questions.q: A counting problem has a recurrence with boundary values but no known closed form. What is the book's attitude?
options: The problem is unsolved until a closed formula is found for every value of n
Knowing the recurrence is almost as good, since as many values as wanted can be computed
The recurrence is worthless without a closed form, since values cannot be computed from it
The recurrence must be replaced by induction before it can be used to count
optionExplain: The book says the recurrence is almost as good as a formula.
The book notes a closed form is sometimes impossible or extremely difficult to get.
The recurrence still computes every value.
Induction is not required to use a recurrence.
questions.explain: Closed forms are nice but not necessary.
questions.rule: A recurrence is almost as good as a formula.
questions.teaches: Knowing the recurrence formula is almost as good as a closed form, and sometimes it is impossible or extremely difficult to get a closed-form solution to a recurrence.

questions.q: In how many ways can a convex quadrilateral be cut into triangles by a diagonal?
optionExplain: This counts one diagonal only.
Either diagonal works.
This counts the four sides.
This counts all pairs of vertices, including sides.
questions.explain: Two ways. The card next counts larger polygons by a recurrence.
questions.rule: Triangulations of an n-gon: add, over the position of the third vertex, the product of the counts for the two sub-polygons.

questions.q: A hexagon has t(6) = t(5) + t(4) + t(4) + t(5), where t(4) = 2 and t(5) = 5. So t(6) = ____.
questions.rule: Add products over positions of the third vertex.

questions.q: Using t(2) = 1, t(3) = 1, t(4) = 2, t(5) = 5 and t(6) = 14, how many triangulations does a convex heptagon have?
optionExplain: This drops the middle class t(4) t(4) = 4 and totals 14 + 5 + 5 + 14.
This is the sum 14 + 5, using only the first two classes.
This doubles the correct total.
questions.explain: The middle class multiplies the counts of two quadrilaterals: 2 x 2.
questions.rule: Multiply for the two sub-polygons, add over positions.

questions.q: In an octagon, one class leaves a quadrilateral and a pentagon. A pupil counts it as 2 + 5 = 7. What is wrong?
options: The two polygons are triangulated independently, so their counts multiply: 2 x 5 = 10
Nothing is wrong; polygons of different sizes have counts that add, giving 2 + 5 = 7
The counts should be divided, giving 5 / 2, because the pentagon contains the quadrilateral
Only the pentagon's count matters, giving 5, because the quadrilateral adds no choices
optionExplain: Every triangulation of one polygon combines with every triangulation of the other.
Choices in separate regions are made together, so they multiply.
Nothing is overcounted in this class.
The quadrilateral also has two triangulations that combine with each of the pentagon's.
questions.explain: Independent regions multiply; different classes add.
questions.rule: Multiply within a class, add across classes.

questions.q: True or false: With t(2) = 1, the heptagon class with the third vertex next to the base contributes t(2) x t(6) = 14.
questions.explain: One side of the base triangle is a degenerate 2-gon contributing 1, and the other is a hexagon contributing t(6) = 14.
questions.rule: A degenerate side contributes a factor of 1.

questions.q: In how many ways can a product abcd be fully bracketed with two factors per multiplication? (2 factors: 1 way; 3 factors: 2.)
optionExplain: This is 3!, which counts orders of the factors, not brackets.
This counts the places for the last multiplication only.
Splitting at the last multiplication gives 1 x 2 + 1 x 1 + 2 x 1 = 5.
This is 2 x 2 and ignores the sub-counts.
questions.explain: The book notes that this sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, ... turns up in surprisingly many situations; the numbers are called the Catalan numbers.
questions.rule: Split at the last operation.
questions.teaches: The sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, ... of triangulation counts is known as the Catalan numbers, and such a recurrence turns up in surprisingly many situations.

questions.q: The sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14 counts triangulations of polygons with 2 to 6 sides. What is the next term?
optionExplain: This doubles 14.
This adds the last two terms, 14 + 5.
This is C(8, 4), the central binomial coefficient, not a Catalan number.
The recurrence gives t(7) = 14 + 5 + 4 + 5 + 14 = 42.
questions.explain: The next term is 42. The card next gives a formula for every term.
questions.rule: C_n = C(2n, n) / (n + 1), and a generating function turns the recurrence into a quadratic equation.

questions.q: Using \(C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}\), the value of \(C_3\) is ____.
questions.rule: Divide the central binomial coefficient by n + 1.

questions.q: What is \(C_6=\frac17\binom{12}{6}\)?
optionExplain: This is the central binomial coefficient without division.
This is 924 / 14, dividing by 2 (n + 1).
This is 924 / 6, dividing by n.
questions.explain: The divisor is n + 1 = 7.
questions.rule: Divide by n + 1.

questions.q: A pupil claims \(C_n=\binom{2n}{n}/n\). Which check shows this fails?
options: For n = 2 it gives 6 / 2 = 3, but C_2 = 2
For n = 1 it gives 1, which is correct, so the formula holds
It fails because the answer is not an integer
It cannot fail, since both are central binomial quotients
optionExplain: The correct divisor is n + 1 = 3, which gives 2.
One correct value does not prove a formula; n = 2 fails.
3 is an integer; it is the wrong integer.
The divisor matters.
questions.explain: Test a candidate formula on small values.
questions.rule: Check small cases.

questions.q: True or false: A convex octagon (8 sides) has 132 triangulations.
questions.explain: The triangulation count for n sides is C_(n - 2), and C_6 = 132.

questions.q: What feature of the Catalan recurrence suggests using generating functions?
options: The recurrence involves factorials, which generating functions are designed to handle
The recurrence has only two terms, which makes it suitable for generating functions
A sum of products over indices adding to a constant, like multiplying polynomials
The values are all integers, which generating functions need in order to work
optionExplain: The recurrence has no factorials.
It sums many products.
Squaring the generating function produces exactly such sums.
Integer values do not suggest generating functions.
questions.explain: The book remarks that the sum should remind you of multiplying polynomials, which should remind you of generating functions.
questions.rule: Convolution sums suggest generating functions.
questions.teaches: The sum over indices u + v = n + 1 resembles the rule for multiplying polynomials, which in turn suggests generating functions; the book uses this to find the closed form.

questions.q: Which of 1, 49, 51 and 53 is a prime number?
optionExplain: 1 has only the divisor 1, which feels like the definition, but by convention 1 is neither prime nor composite.
49 is odd and has no small obvious factor, but 49 = 7 · 7.
51 is odd and not a multiple of 5 or 7, but 51 = 3 · 17.
Right: its only divisors are 1 and 53.
questions.explain: 53 is not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7, and 8 · 8 = 64 > 53, so no larger divisor is possible. The card next gives the definition.
questions.rule: Test small divisors before calling a number prime.

questions.q: The statement \(b \mid a\) means that \(a = \) ____ \(\cdot\, m\) for some integer \(m\).
questions.explain: By definition \(b \mid a\) means \(a = bm\), a whole-number multiple of \(b\).
questions.rule: \(b \mid a\) means \(a = bm\).

questions.q: Which of these divisibility statements is false?
optionExplain: True: 54 = 6 · 9; it only seems false because the quotient is unfamiliar.
True: 121 = 11 · 11, a number divides its own square.
Right: 84 = 8 · 10 + 4, so 84 is not a whole-number multiple of 8.
questions.explain: Only 84 / 8 = 10.5 fails to be an integer, so 8 does not divide 84; the other three quotients are 9, 11 and 7.
questions.rule: Check whether the quotient is a whole number.

questions.q: Sort each number: is it composite, or not composite?
questions.explain: 91 = 7 · 13, 111 = 3 · 37 and 143 = 11 · 13 have a divisor besides 1 and themselves. 97 and 53 are prime, and 1 is neither prime nor composite.
questions.rule: Composite means a factor other than 1 and itself; 1 is excluded.

questions.q: A student lists the primes below 10 as 1, 2, 3, 5, 7. What does the book's convention say to change?
options: Remove 1: it is neither prime nor composite
Remove 2, because even numbers are divisible by 2
Add 9, because it is odd
Move 1 to the composites, since 1 = 1 · 1
optionExplain: Right: the book adopts this convention, so the list starts at 2.
2 is divisible only by 1 and 2, so it is prime.
9 = 3 · 3, so it is composite.
The convention puts 1 in neither group.
questions.explain: The only error is 1. Every other listed number has no divisors besides 1 and itself, and 4, 6, 8, 9 are correctly missing.
questions.rule: The primes begin 2, 3, 5, 7, 11.

questions.q: Treat divisibility as: the quotient a over b is a whole number. For which pair does b divide a?
optionExplain: Reversed roles: 7 over 91 is not an integer.
91 over 9 is about 10.1, not an integer.
91 over 14 is 6.5, not an integer.
Right: 91 over 7 is 13, an integer.
questions.explain: The relation has a direction: it asks whether a is exactly b times a whole number. 7 divides 91, but 91 does not divide 7.
questions.rule: The order of a and b matters in divisibility.
questions.teaches: The book also reads b divides a as a over b being an integer, the same relation as a = bm.

questions.q: Multiply the primes 2, 3, 5 and 7, then add 1. Which of 2, 3, 5 and 7 divides the result?
options: None of them
2 only, because the product is even
All of them, because each is a factor of the product
7 only, because it is the largest factor
optionExplain: Right: each divides the product, so each leaves remainder 1 on 211.
The product is even but adding 1 makes the result odd.
Each divides the product, not the product plus 1.
Being the largest factor gives no divisibility.
questions.explain: The product 210 is a multiple of each, so 211 leaves remainder 1 on division by each. The card next shows how Euclid uses this.
questions.rule: Product plus one is divisible by none of the factors.

questions.q: True or false: Euclid's proof starts by assuming that there are only finitely many primes.
questions.explain: A proof by contradiction assumes the opposite of the claim, here that the primes form a finite list, and reaches an impossibility.
questions.rule: Euclid assumes finitely many primes and derives a contradiction.

questions.q: For the list 3, 5, 7 the number is Q = 3 · 5 · 7 + 1 = 106. What does the argument tell us about the prime divisors of 106?
options: They must be among 3, 5 and 7
They are primes outside 3, 5, 7: here 2 and 53
There are none, because 106 is even
Only 53 counts, because Q must be prime
optionExplain: None of them divides 106, since each leaves remainder 1.
Right: 106 = 2 · 53 and neither is on the list.
An even number such as 106 has the prime divisor 2, and 106 = 2 · 53.
Q need not be prime, and 106 is composite.
questions.explain: Q leaves remainder 1 on division by 3, 5 and 7, so its prime divisors lie outside the list. Note that the list does not have to be the first few primes.
questions.rule: A prime divisor of Q is always off the list; the list may be any finite list.

questions.q: For the list 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, the number Q = 30031 is composite. Its smaller prime divisor is ____.
questions.explain: 30031 = 59 · 509. Neither prime is on the list, as Q leaves remainder 1 on division by each listed prime.
questions.rule: Whatever prime divides Q, it is not on the list.

questions.q: A student writes: 'Since 2·3·5·7 + 1 = 211 is prime, Euclid shows product plus one is prime for every list.' What is the flaw?
options: 211 is not prime, since it exceeds every listed prime
One example proves nothing; 2·3·5·7·11·13 + 1 = 30031 is composite
Euclid only works for lists of three primes
Euclid's argument needs Q to be composite every time
optionExplain: 211 is prime; being larger than the list does not make it composite.
Right: the proof only needs a prime divisor, not a prime Q.
The list can have any finite length.
The argument handles both cases, prime and composite.
questions.explain: A single prime Q is a coincidence. The proof splits into the case Q prime and the case Q composite, and the composite case really occurs.
questions.rule: Euclid needs a prime divisor of Q, not a prime Q.

questions.q: A friend changes the proof by adding 2 instead of 1: Q = 2·3·5 + 2 = 32. Why does this fail to produce a new prime?
options: 32 is larger than 5, so it must be composite and useless
2·3·5 + 2 is odd, which breaks the argument
Adding any number other than 1 makes the product prime
32 = 2^5 is divisible by the listed prime 2, so no new prime appears
optionExplain: Size is irrelevant; what matters is the divisibility by listed primes.
32 is even.
Offsets do not make a product prime.
Right: 2 divides both the product and 2, hence it divides the sum.
questions.explain: Remainder 1 is what keeps every listed prime away from Q. With +2 the prime 2 divides both terms, so a listed prime divides Q.
questions.rule: The +1 is essential: it leaves remainder 1 for every listed prime.
questions.teaches: Euclid's Q works because dividing Q by any listed prime leaves remainder exactly 1, so no listed prime divides Q.

questions.q: Can every whole number greater than 1 be broken into primes by repeated splitting?
options: No: some composite numbers cannot be split into smaller factors
Yes: split any composite factor again until all factors are prime
Only for even numbers, since 2 is the smallest prime
Only if the number is below a million
optionExplain: By definition, a composite has a factor other than 1 and itself, so it can be split.
Right: each split uses smaller numbers, so the process must end.
Odd numbers such as 91 = 7 · 13 split too.
Nothing limits the size of the number.
questions.explain: Each split produces strictly smaller numbers above 1, so the splitting cannot go on forever. The card next gives the argument.
questions.rule: Keep splitting composites; primes end the process.

questions.q: Factoring \(360\) completely gives \(2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot\) ____.
questions.rule: Repeat the splitting until every factor is prime.

questions.q: Which is the complete prime factorization of 504?
options: \(2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 21\)
\(4 \cdot 9 \cdot 14\)
optionExplain: Right: 8 · 9 · 7 = 504 and every factor is prime.
The product is 504, but 14 = 2 · 7 is not prime, so the splitting is incomplete.
Product 504 again, but 21 = 3 · 7 is still composite.
Product 504, but no factor is prime.
questions.explain: All four options multiply to 504, so being correct needs every factor to be prime. Only the first satisfies that.
questions.rule: A complete factorization has only prime factors.

questions.q: Put the steps of the strong induction argument in order.
items: Assume every number from 2 up to n - 1 factors into primes
Take n: if it is prime, it is its own factorization
If n is composite, write n = a · b with a and b both between 1 and n
Join the factorizations of a and b into one for n
questions.explain: Strong induction assumes the claim for all smaller numbers, handles the prime case, then splits a composite into two smaller factors whose factorizations are joined.
questions.rule: Assume for smaller numbers, then split n into two smaller factors.

questions.q: A student says 12 = 3 · 4, and 4 is not prime, so 12 has no prime factorization. What went wrong?
options: 3 · 4 is not a correct factorization of 12
12 is prime, so no factorization is needed
He stopped early: 4 = 2 · 2, so 12 = 3 · 2 · 2
Factorizations may only use the prime 2
optionExplain: 3 · 4 = 12 is correct.
12 = 3 · 4 is composite.
Right: a composite factor can be split again.
Any prime may be used.
questions.explain: A composite factor is not an obstacle; it is just a number smaller than 12 that factors in turn. The process stops only when every factor is prime.
questions.rule: Split composite factors until none remain.

questions.q: Euclid says the composite Q has at least one prime divisor p. Which fact justifies that step?
options: Q is greater than every listed prime
Q is odd, so it is divisible by an odd prime
Q leaves remainder 1 on division by each listed prime
Q factors into primes, and any one of those primes divides Q
optionExplain: Size does not make a prime divisor appear.
Q might be even, and 'odd' is not the reason.
That shows p is not listed, not that p exists.
Right: every integer above 1 is a product of primes.
questions.explain: The existence of p comes from factorization into primes: if Q is a product of primes, any of them divides Q.
questions.rule: Prime factorization supplies the prime divisor Euclid needs.
questions.teaches: The book calls this a 'tiny gap' in Euclid's proof: that Q has a prime factor needs proof, and this idea fills it.

questions.q: Two students factor 360 completely into primes and write different-looking lists. What must be true of the lists?
options: They contain the same primes the same number of times, in some order
They must be identical in order, as only one list exists
At least one of the lists must contain a mistake
They can use different primes if the product is 360
optionExplain: Right: factoring completely into primes gives the same result.
Order can differ; 2·2·2·3·3·5 and 5·3·3·2·2·2 are the same factorization.
Both can be right, differing only in order.
Different prime lists with the same product cannot exist.
questions.explain: Complete prime factorizations of one number agree except for order. The card next names this the FTA.
questions.rule: Different orders, same primes with same counts.

questions.q: In \(2^3 \cdot 3^2\), the numbers 3 and 2 written as powers are called ____.
questions.explain: Exponents count how many times each prime occurs in the PPF.
questions.rule: A PPF lists each prime with its exponent.

questions.q: What is the PPF of 3600?
optionExplain: That product is 1800, half of 3600.
That product is 10800.
That product is 720.
questions.rule: Collect equal primes into powers.

questions.q: Two lists of primes both multiply to 2310. What does the FTA tell you?
options: They can differ, as 2310 is large enough for several factorizations
They share only the prime 2
They contain the same primes in some order (2, 3, 5, 7, 11)
They must have the same number of primes but may choose different ones
optionExplain: Size does not allow a second factorization.
They share all five primes.
Right: 2310 has exactly one PPF.
Different primes would give a different product.
questions.explain: 2310 = 2 · 3 · 5 · 7 · 11, and by uniqueness any factorization into primes reproduces exactly these five primes.
questions.rule: A product determines its prime factors.

questions.q: True or false: The lists 4 · 9 and 2 · 18 are two different factorizations of 36, so the FTA fails for 36.
questions.explain: Neither list is a complete prime factorization, since 4, 9 and 18 are composite. Fully split, both give 2 · 2 · 3 · 3.
questions.rule: Only complete prime factorizations are unique.

questions.q: A toy number system has a number with two different complete factorizations into elements that cannot be factored further. What follows?
options: The FTA fails there: unique factorization is not a property of every number system
The FTA is false for the ordinary integers too
The toy system has no prime-like elements
Complete factorization cannot exist in the toy system
optionExplain: Right: uniqueness is a special feature of the integers.
The FTA is proven for the integers; one other system does not affect it.
It has them; they just do not give uniqueness.
Existence and uniqueness are separate; only uniqueness failed.
questions.explain: The book later builds a set of even integers where this happens. The integers have extra properties, derived in the chapter, that make the FTA true.
questions.rule: Unique factorization is a property of the integers, not of all number systems.
questions.teaches: The book says some number systems have unique factorization and others do not; the integers have special properties that make it true.

questions.q: Integers x and y satisfy 5x = 3y. Which statement about x must hold?
options: x is a multiple of 5
x is a multiple of 15
x is a multiple of 3
x is even
optionExplain: x = 3, y = 5 satisfies 5x = 3y, and 3 is not a multiple of 5.
x = 3 works and is not a multiple of 15.
Right: 5x is a multiple of 3 and 3 cannot come from 5.
x = 3 works and is odd.
questions.explain: Try small values: x = 3, y = 5. The statement is true, but proving it for all x needs a fact about primes. The card next explains which.
questions.rule: Different primes cannot swap roles.

questions.q: True or false: Proving that 5x = 3y implies 3 divides x uses unique factorization.
questions.explain: The argument says the 3 in the PPF of 5x cannot come from 5, which relies on there being only one PPF.
questions.rule: The 'obvious' step uses unique factorization.

questions.q: Integers satisfy 7a = 4b. Which pair of conclusions follows?
options: \(4 \mid a\) and \(7 \mid b\)
\(7 \mid a\) and \(4 \mid b\)
\(28 \mid a\) and \(28 \mid b\)
\(4 \mid b\) only
optionExplain: Right: 4 and 7 share no prime, so each factor must come from the other variable.
The primes swap: 7a has the 7 already, the 4 must be in a.
a = 4, b = 7 works and 28 does not divide 4.
4 divides 7a so it divides a, but 4 need not divide b: a = 4, b = 7 works.
questions.explain: Since 7a = 4b, 4 divides 7a. 4 and 7 have no common prime, so 4 divides a; similarly 7 divides b. Check a = 4, b = 7.
questions.rule: A factor on one side must be matched by the other variable if it shares no prime with the coefficient.

questions.q: In the even integers E, x = 30 and y = 6 satisfy 2x = 10y. Inside E, 10 divides x only if 30 / 10 = ____ lies in E.
questions.explain: 30 / 10 = 3 is odd, so it is not in E: 10 does not divide x there, although 2x = 10y holds.
questions.rule: Divisibility in E needs the quotient to lie in E.

questions.q: A proof argues: 5x = 3y, so 3 divides 5x; 3 does not divide 5, so 3 divides x. Which fact justifies the last step?
options: 3 is smaller than 5
x and y are both positive
Unique prime factorization: the 3 in 5x cannot be supplied by 5
3 · 5 = 15 is divisible by both
optionExplain: Size does not decide divisibility.
Positivity is not used in the argument.
Right: uniqueness fixes where the 3 sits.
15 plays no role; the claim is about x.
questions.explain: The step is correct but needs justification. It uses that 5x has only one set of prime factors, none of which can come from 5 alone.
questions.rule: Name the property the 'obvious' step uses.

questions.q: In the even integers E, 2 and 10 are both E-primes and 2x = 10y. Must 10 then divide x?
options: Yes: 2 and 10 are different primes, so the FTA applies
No: x = 30, y = 6 gives 60 = 60, yet 30 is not 10 times an even number
Yes, because x and y are even
No, because 2x = 10y has no solutions in E
optionExplain: E does not have unique factorization, so the argument does not work.
Right: the divisibility pattern fails in E.
x = 30, y = 6 are both even and 10 does not divide x in E.
It has solutions such as x = 30, y = 6.
questions.explain: In E, 2x = 10y holds for x = 30, y = 6, but 30 is not a multiple of 10 inside E. So divisibility facts that depend on the FTA can fail there.
questions.rule: Without unique factorization the 'obvious' divisibility step fails.
questions.teaches: In E, 2 and 10 are both E-primes and 2x = 10y holds for x = 30, y = 6, yet 10 does not divide x in E.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: What is the largest whole number that divides both 66 and 150?
optionExplain: 2 divides both, but it is not the largest common divisor.
3 divides both, but 6 is larger.
66 divides itself but 150 / 66 is not an integer.
questions.explain: List the divisors of 66 (1, 2, 3, 6, 11, 22, 33, 66) and check which divide 150; the largest is 6. The card next names this the GCD.
questions.rule: The GCD is the largest common divisor.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Match each notation with its meaning.
pairs: a and b are relatively prime
questions.explain: Round brackets give the gcd, square brackets the lcm, and a gcd of 1 means no shared divisor other than 1.
questions.rule: Round brackets for gcd, square brackets for lcm.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: What are the GCD and the LCM of 84 and 90?
options: GCD 6 and LCM 7560
GCD 3 and LCM 2520
GCD 6 and LCM 1260
GCD 1260 and LCM 6
optionExplain: 7560 is the product 84 · 90, a common multiple but not the least one.
3 divides both but 6 is larger; 2520 is a multiple of the lcm, not the least.
Right: 84 = 2²·3·7 and 90 = 2·3²·5 share 2·3, and 1260 is the smallest common multiple.
The roles are swapped: the lcm is never smaller than the gcd.
questions.explain: Dividing 84 and 90 by 6 gives 14 and 15, which share nothing, so the gcd is 6. The lcm is 84 · 15 = 1260.
questions.rule: The gcd divides both numbers; the lcm is a multiple of both.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Which pair of numbers is relatively prime?
options: 35 and 48
21 and 91
50 and 75
22 and 33
optionExplain: Right: 35 = 5 · 7 and 48 = 2⁴ · 3 share no prime.
Both are multiples of 7.
Both are multiples of 25.
Both are multiples of 11.
questions.explain: Relatively prime means no shared divisor above 1. Each wrong pair shares a visible factor (7, 25 or 11), while 35 and 48 share none.
questions.rule: Check for any shared prime factor.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: True or false: If two numbers are relatively prime, both of them must be prime.
questions.explain: 35 and 48 are relatively prime and both are composite; the book's own example is 4096 and 999.
questions.rule: Relatively prime describes a pair, not each number.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Three lights blink every 4, 6 and 10 seconds and start together. After how many seconds do they next blink together?
optionExplain: 120 is a common multiple, but not the least one.
30 is a multiple of 6 and 10 but not of 4.
2 is the gcd, not a common multiple.
Right: 60 is the least number that is a multiple of 4, 6 and 10.
questions.explain: Blinking together means a common multiple; the first time is the least, 60. The same definition extends beyond two numbers.
questions.rule: For simultaneous repeating events use the lcm.
questions.teaches: GCD and LCM also make sense for more than two integers: the book notes (70, 100, 225) = 5 and the LCM of 1 through 9 is 2520.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: For 12 and 18, multiply their GCD by their LCM. How does the result compare with 12 · 18 = 216?
options: It is smaller: 72
It is larger: 432
It is unrelated to 216
It is equal to 216
optionExplain: That would be the product of 12 and 6, not of the gcd and lcm.
Taking 36 · 12 mixes the lcm with one of the numbers.
A clean relation holds for all positive integers.
Right: gcd 6 times lcm 36 is 216.
questions.explain: gcd 6 and lcm 36 multiply to 216, exactly 12 · 18. The card next shows why this is no coincidence.
questions.rule: GCD times LCM equals the product.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: True or false: The GCD takes the smaller exponent of each prime and the LCM takes the larger.
questions.explain: The gcd is the most both numbers share (min exponent); the lcm must contain each number (max exponent).
questions.rule: Min exponents for the gcd, max exponents for the lcm.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: What is the GCD of \(2^4\cdot3\cdot5^2\) and \(2^2\cdot3^3\cdot7\)?
optionExplain: 2⁴ · 3 takes the larger power of 2 and the smaller power of 3, mixing the rules.
Right: 2² · 3 uses the smaller exponents: min(4,2) = 2 and min(1,3) = 1.
3 is shared but 2² is shared too, so the gcd is larger.
That is the LCM, which takes the larger exponent of every prime.
questions.explain: The prime 5 appears only in the first number and 7 only in the second, so they drop out. 2² · 3 = 12.
questions.rule: Use the smaller exponent, and a prime absent from one number gives exponent 0.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Two positive integers have GCD 7 and LCM 210, so their product is ____.
questions.rule: Product of gcd and lcm equals product of the numbers.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: A student finds the GCD of 24 = 2³·3 and 36 = 2²·3² as 2³·3² = 72 by taking larger exponents. What is wrong?
options: The exponents should be added, giving 2⁵·3³
72 is the LCM; the GCD takes the smaller exponents and equals 12
The student should use only the prime 2
Nothing is wrong, since 72 divides both numbers
optionExplain: Adding exponents gives the product 24 · 36 = 864.
Right: the max rule gives the lcm.
Both primes 2 and 3 are shared, so both count.
72 does not divide 24, so it cannot be a common divisor.
questions.explain: 72 cannot divide 24. The two rules are swapped: the gcd is 2² · 3 = 12 and the lcm is 2³ · 3² = 72.
questions.rule: Do not swap min and max.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Two gears with 24 and 36 teeth mesh with marked teeth aligned. After how many turns of the 24-tooth gear are the marks aligned again?
options: 36 turns, since the gears have 36 teeth on the larger one
12 turns, because the gcd is 12
864 turns, since 24 · 36 = 864
3 turns, since the lcm is 24 · 36 / 12 = 72 teeth
optionExplain: 36 teeth passing is 1.5 turns, not a whole alignment.
The gcd counts shared factors; alignment needs a common multiple.
864 teeth is a common multiple but not the least one.
Right: 72 teeth is 3 turns of the 24-tooth gear.
questions.explain: Marks realign after the first common multiple of the tooth counts, the lcm 72; that is 72 / 24 = 3 turns. The book notes the lcm formula can be proved without PPFs.
questions.rule: LCM = product divided by GCD.
questions.teaches: The identity (a, b)[a, b] = ab can be proved without prime factorizations, using only the definitions of gcd and lcm.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: A number g divides both 84 and 126. Which of these must g also divide?
options: 42, which equals 5 · 84 - 3 · 126
optionExplain: Right: g divides each term of the combination.
100 is not tied to 84 and 126; g = 21 does not divide it.
85 is only one more than 84, a coincidence of size.
40 is not built from 84 and 126; g = 21 does not divide it.
questions.explain: Whatever g divides 84 and 126 divides any combination of them. 5 · 84 - 3 · 126 = 42. The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: Common divisors divide every combination.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: A quantity \(ax + by\) with integer \(x\) and \(y\) is called a linear ____ of \(a\) and \(b\).
questions.explain: The book calls ax + by a linear combination of a and b.
questions.rule: ax + by is a linear combination of a and b.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Which argument shows that 15 and 16 are relatively prime?
options: A common divisor divides 16 - 15 = 1, so it equals 1
15 is odd and 16 is even, so they share no divisor
Their sum 31 is prime
Both are less than 20
optionExplain: Right: 16 - 15 is a combination of 15 and 16.
Parity only rules out the divisor 2; 3 or 5 might be shared.
A prime sum does not show the numbers themselves share nothing.
Size does not prevent shared divisors.
questions.explain: A common divisor of 15 and 16 divides the combination 16 - 15 = 1, which leaves only the divisor 1. The same argument works for any two consecutive integers.
questions.rule: Show a combination equals 1.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Does the equation 6x + 15y = 1 have integer solutions?
options: Yes: take x = 3 and y = -1
Yes: any equation of this form has solutions
No: 3 divides 6 and 15, hence every combination, but 3 does not divide 1
No: 6 and 15 are both composite
optionExplain: Solutions need the right-hand side to be a multiple of gcd(6, 15) = 3.
Right: the combination is always a multiple of 3.
Compositeness is not the cause; the shared factor 3 is.
questions.explain: Every value of 6x + 15y is a multiple of 3, so 1 is never reached. This is the contrapositive of the rule: a combination equal to 1 forces gcd 1.
questions.rule: A shared divisor g blocks any combination from being smaller than g.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: True or false: The rule that g divides ax + by holds only when x and y are positive.
questions.explain: The book allows x and y to be any integers, including negatives; that is how 16 - 15 = 1 is a combination of 15 and 16.
questions.rule: Coefficients can be any integers.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Two consecutive odd numbers are 2n - 1 and 2n + 1. A common divisor d of them must divide which number?
options: Their product, 4n² - 1
Their sum, 4n
n itself
Their difference, 2
optionExplain: d divides the product, but that is a weaker statement and does not pin d down.
The sum is also a combination, but it does not help to show d is small.
Nothing links d to n.
Right: the difference is a combination with coefficients 1 and -1.
questions.explain: d divides (2n + 1) - (2n - 1) = 2. Both numbers are odd, so d is odd and divides 2, so d = 1 and consecutive odd numbers are relatively prime.
questions.rule: A difference is a combination with a negative coefficient.
questions.teaches: The coefficients x and y may be any integers, so sums and differences of a and b are both linear combinations.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Divide 333 by 51, leaving a remainder smaller than 51. What are the quotient and remainder?
options: quotient 7, remainder -24
quotient 6, remainder 27
quotient 5, remainder 78
quotient 6, remainder 33
optionExplain: 7 · 51 = 357 overshoots, giving a negative remainder.
5 · 51 = 255 and 78 is larger than 51, so one more 51 fits.
questions.explain: The largest multiple of 51 not above 333 is 6 · 51 = 306, leaving 27. The card next states this in general.
questions.rule: Pick the largest multiple that fits, then take what is left.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: In \(b = qa + r\) the remainder satisfies \(0 \le r <\) ____.
questions.explain: The remainder is strictly smaller than the divisor a.
questions.rule: The remainder is at least 0 and less than the divisor.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: Divide 1000 by 37. What are the quotient and remainder?
options: quotient 26, remainder 38
quotient 27, remainder 1
quotient 28, remainder -36
quotient 27, remainder 0
optionExplain: The remainder 38 is not smaller than 37, so another 37 fits.
28 · 37 = 1036 overshoots, so the remainder would be negative.
27 · 37 = 999, not 1000, so 37 does not divide 1000.
questions.explain: The multiples 37 · 27 = 999 is the largest not exceeding 1000, so the remainder is 1.
questions.rule: The remainder is what is left after the largest multiple that fits.

questions.section: GCD, LCM, and the Division Algorithm
questions.q: If a divides b in the division algorithm, what is the remainder r?
options: a
optionExplain: That is the largest remainder possible, not what happens for exact divisibility.
