questions.explain: Impossibility arguments find an obstruction (a gcd or a modulus). Existence and completeness arguments build or describe solutions.
questions.rule: Impossibility and existence are different questions.

questions.q: A student finds (3, 4, 5) for x² + y² = z² and stops. Which question remains unanswered?
options: Can we find all solutions?
Do solutions exist?
Are there no solutions?
Is it in simple form?
optionExplain: Right: one solution does not show the set is complete.
(3, 4, 5) already shows existence.
A found solution rules that out.
(3, 4, 5) is already primitive.
questions.explain: The equation has many more solutions, such as (6, 8, 10) and (5, 12, 13). Finding every one and proving the list complete is question 4.
questions.rule: One solution is not all solutions.

questions.q: A student shows 91x + 35y = 7 has integer solutions because gcd(91, 35) = 7 divides 7, without finding x or y. Which question did this answer?
options: Is it in simple form?
Are there no solutions?
Can we find all solutions?
Do solutions exist?
optionExplain: The gcd was used to prove existence, not to divide anything out.
The result was the opposite: solutions exist.
No solutions were listed.
Right: existence can be proved without exhibiting a solution.
questions.explain: The book notes that sometimes you cannot solve the equation but can still show that at least one solution exists. That is question 2.
questions.rule: Existence can be shown without a formula.
questions.teaches: Sometimes an equation cannot be solved explicitly, yet one can still show that at least one solution exists.

questions.q: How many ordered pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfy xy = 12?
optionExplain: That counts each unordered pair once; (x, y) and (y, x) are different ordered pairs.
Right: (1,12), (2,6), (3,4) and their reverses.
That counts every divisor but also counts pairs twice for each choice of x.
Only two divisors would not cover all the factor pairs.
questions.explain: Each divisor x of 12 determines y = 12/x, and 12 has six divisors. The card next uses this to solve harder equations.
questions.rule: A product equal to a constant has finitely many integer solutions.

questions.q: True or false: True or false: (x − 4)(y − 4) expands to xy − 4x − 4y + 16.
questions.explain: (−4)(−4) = 16, so the constant term is 16.
questions.rule: Expand to check the factorization.

questions.q: How many ordered pairs of positive integers satisfy xy − 3x − 3y = 0?
optionExplain: That counts the six integer factor pairs of 9 including negatives, but the negative ones give x or y not positive.
That finds only (6, 6) and misses the swap (4, 12) and (12, 4).
9 is the constant, not the number of solutions.
questions.explain: Adding 9 to both sides gives (x − 3)(y − 3) = 9. The positive factor pairs 1·9, 3·3, 9·1 give the three pairs; negative factor pairs give a non-positive x or y.
questions.rule: Complete the product, then list the factor pairs.

questions.q: To make xy − 5x − 5y factor as (x − 5)(y − 5), add ____ to both sides.
questions.rule: Add the product of the two constants.

questions.q: From (x − 4)(y − 4) = 8 a student takes x − 4 = 2, y − 4 = 4 and reports one triangle, 6-8-10. What is missing?
options: The pair x − 4 = 3 and y − 4 = 3
The other factor pairs of 8, such as 1 · 8, which give the 5-12-13 triangle
Nothing: 8 has only one factorization
A check that 6-8-10 is a right triangle
optionExplain: Right: all factor pairs must be tried.
8 = 1 · 8 = 2 · 4 and their reverses.
It is one; the issue is incompleteness.
questions.rule: List every factor pair.

questions.q: How many ordered pairs of positive integers satisfy 1/x + 1/y = 1/4?
optionExplain: That counts only unordered pairs (5,20), (6,12), (8,8).
16 has 5 positive divisors, not 6.
(8, 8) is only one of several solutions.
Right: multiplying out gives (x − 4)(y − 4) = 16, with pairs (5,20), (6,12), (8,8), (12,6), (20,5).
questions.explain: Clear the fractions first: 4y + 4x = xy, so xy − 4x − 4y = 0, and adding 16 gives (x − 4)(y − 4) = 16. This follows the book's advice to eliminate the obvious difficulties first.
questions.rule: Clear fractions and radicals, then factor.
questions.teaches: Basic algebraic strategy says to eliminate the most obvious difficulties, such as fractions and radicals, before looking for the factorization.

questions.q: What remainders can a perfect square leave when divided by 4?
options: 1 or 3
0 or 1
0 or 2
optionExplain: Squares avoid 2 and 3: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 leave 0, 1, 0, 1, 0.
Even squares give remainder 0.
Right: even numbers square to multiples of 4, odd numbers to one more than a multiple of 4.
Odd squares give remainder 1, not 2.
questions.explain: (2k)² = 4k² and (2k + 1)² = 4(k² + k) + 1. The card next uses this to rule out equations.
questions.rule: Squares are 0 or 1 modulo 4.

questions.q: Modulo 4, the sum x² + y² can be 0, 1 or ____.
questions.explain: Adding two residues from {0, 1} gives 0, 1 or 2.
questions.rule: x² + y² mod 4 is 0, 1 or 2.

questions.q: Which equation x² + y² = n has no integer solutions?
optionExplain: Right: 7 ≡ 3 (mod 4), a residue x² + y² never takes.
questions.explain: Only 7 is congruent to 3 modulo 4. The others have solutions: 1² + 2², 2² + 2², 1² + 3².
questions.rule: n ≡ 3 (mod 4) has no representation as a sum of two squares.

questions.q: If x and y are both odd, what does x² + y² leave on division by 4?
optionExplain: That needs both even or one odd and one even in a special way; here each square is 1.
Two squares of 1 add to 2, not 1.
Right: 1 + 1 = 2.
Squares never add to 3.
questions.explain: Each odd square is 1 modulo 4, so the sum is 2. A value of 2 is possible for x² + y², so this does not rule out the case on its own.
questions.rule: Odd squares are 1 modulo 4.

questions.q: True or false: Because 21 ≡ 1 (mod 4), a value squares can give, the equation x² + y² = 21 must have a solution.
questions.explain: A filter can exclude but not prove existence. 21 = 3 · 7 is not a sum of two squares (21 − 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 is never a square), though this needs another argument.
questions.rule: A possible residue does not guarantee a solution.

questions.q: Does x² − y² = 2002 have integer solutions?
options: Yes: 2002 = 1001 · 2 factors as (x − y)(x + y) with x − y = 2, x + y = 1001
Yes, because 2002 is even
Cannot be decided without trying all values
No: x² − y² leaves 0, 1 or 3 modulo 4, and 2002 leaves 2
optionExplain: Then x = 501.5, not an integer.
Parity alone does not decide; here the residue mod 4 matters.
A single congruence settles it.
Right: the filter excludes it.
questions.explain: Squares are 0 or 1 modulo 4, so x² − y² is 0, 1 or −1 ≡ 3, never 2. Since 2002 ≡ 2, there are no solutions.
questions.rule: Try the filter modulo 4 for equations involving squares.
questions.teaches: The same filtering tactic can show that no solutions exist or that all solutions must satisfy a certain form, such as both variables being even.

questions.q: Which of these Pythagorean triples is primitive, meaning its entries share no common factor?
optionExplain: Right: gcd 1.
All three are multiples of 4: it is 4 · (3, 4, 5).
All three are multiples of 3: it is 3 · (5, 12, 13).
All three are multiples of 3: it is 3 · (3, 4, 5).
questions.explain: Check the gcd of each triple: only (20, 21, 29) has gcd 1. The card next explains why we can restrict to such triples.
questions.rule: Divide out the common factor.

questions.q: A solution of x² + y² = z² is primitive when x, y and z have no common factor other than ____.
questions.explain: Primitive means gcd(x, y, z) = 1.
questions.rule: Primitive: no common factor except 1.

questions.q: Divide the solution (45, 108, 117) of x² + y² = z² by the gcd of its entries. What primitive solution results?
optionExplain: That divides by 3 only; a factor 3 remains.
Right: the gcd is 9.
That is the unreduced solution.
questions.rule: Divide by the gcd.

questions.q: If x and y are both odd, what does x² + y² leave modulo 4, and what does that show?
options: 0, so z must be even and nothing is excluded
1, so z is odd and the case is possible
2, which no square can leave, so x and y are not both odd
3, so no solution exists for any x and y
optionExplain: Two odd squares add to 2 modulo 4, not 0.
Right: z² would be 2 modulo 4, but squares are 0 or 1.
The sum is 2, and the conclusion concerns odd x, y only.
questions.explain: Each odd square is 1 modulo 4, so the sum is 2, but z² must be 0 or 1 modulo 4. So at least one leg is even; both even is excluded by primitivity.
questions.rule: Squares are 0 or 1 modulo 4.

questions.q: True or false: In a Pythagorean triple, a common divisor d of x and y divides z because z = x + y.
questions.explain: z is not x + y. The correct reason: d² divides x² + y² = z², so d divides z.
questions.rule: Use squares, not sums.

questions.q: In x² + y² = z², a number d divides both x and z. What follows about y?
options: d divides y, since d² divides z² − x² = y²
d does not divide y
Nothing, since only d | x and d | y are covered
d divides y only if d is prime
optionExplain: Right: the same argument works for any two of the three.
d² divides y², so d divides y.
The argument is symmetric in all pairs.
No primality is needed: d² | y² gives d | y.
questions.explain: Since y² = z² − x² is divisible by d², d divides y. The pairwise divisor argument is symmetric, so primitive solutions are pairwise relatively prime.
questions.rule: A common divisor of any two divides the third.
questions.teaches: Similar arguments show that if d is a common divisor of any two of the variables, then d also divides the third, so a primitive solution is relatively prime in pairs.

questions.q: Using the pattern (2rs, r² − s², r² + s²) with r = 3 and s = 2, which triple appears?
optionExplain: 2rs = 12, not 6: both factors 3 and 2 are used.
r² + s² = 13, not 5.
r² + s² is 13, not 14; (5, 12, 13) is the right triple.
questions.explain: Check: 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169 = 13². The card next explains where the pattern comes from.
questions.rule: r and s generate triples.

questions.q: In the parametrization, \(z = r^2 + \)____.
questions.explain: The hypotenuse is r² + s²; the legs are 2rs and r² − s².
questions.rule: z = r² + s².

questions.q: Which primitive Pythagorean triple comes from r = 5 and s = 2?
optionExplain: The hypotenuse must be the largest entry r² + s² = 29.
z = 29, not 25: use r² + s²; 25 = r².
questions.explain: 20² + 21² = 400 + 441 = 841 = 29². Since 5 and 2 are relatively prime of opposite parity, the triple is primitive.
questions.rule: Plug r and s into the three formulas.

questions.q: True or false: If r and s are both odd, then (2rs, r² − s², r² + s²) is still a primitive triple.
questions.explain: With both odd, r² − s² and r² + s² are even, so all three entries are even. For r = 3, s = 1 you get (6, 8, 10).
questions.rule: r and s must have opposite parity.

questions.q: A student argues: z² − y² = x² = 36 = 3 · 12, so z − y = 3 and z + y = 12 must both be squares. What is wrong?
options: 36 is not a perfect square
z − y must equal z + y
Factors of a square are squares only if they are relatively prime; 3 and 12 share a factor
Squares can never be written as a product of two numbers
optionExplain: They differ by 2y.
Right: 6² = 3 · 12 neither is a square.
Squares have many factorizations.
questions.explain: A product of coprime positive numbers being a square forces each to be a square. Here 3 and 12 are not coprime (gcd 3), and neither is a square. In the actual argument, the factors z ± y have gcd 2, so dividing by 2 restores coprimality.
questions.rule: Check coprimality before concluding each factor is a square.

questions.q: Which primitive Pythagorean triple has hypotenuse 25?
optionExplain: All entries are multiples of 5, so it is not primitive.
Right: r = 4, s = 3: 2rs = 24, r² − s² = 7, r² + s² = 25.
A leg of 0 is not allowed.
The hypotenuse is 25, not 26.
questions.explain: We need r² + s² = 25 with r, s coprime and of opposite parity: (r, s) = (4, 3). That gives (24, 7, 25); the triple (15, 20, 25) is 5 · (3, 4, 5).
questions.rule: Solve r² + s² = z for the hypotenuse.
questions.teaches: The gcd g of z + y and z − y divides their sum and difference, 2z and 2y, so with y and z relatively prime g = 2.

questions.q: For m = 2, take x = y = 2 in (x² + y²)^m = (xy)^n. Which n makes the equation hold?
optionExplain: (xy)² = 16, not 64.
xy = 4, not 64.
questions.explain: The left side is 8² = 64 and the right side is 4ⁿ, so n = 3. The card next shows the general pattern.
questions.rule: Try small cases first.

questions.q: True or false: The extreme principle is used to avoid an infinite chain of arguments showing the variables can be halved forever.
questions.explain: Instead of repeating the parity argument endlessly, take the greatest power of 2 dividing x and y.
questions.rule: Use the greatest exact power, not an endless descent.

questions.q: For m = 4 the unique solution has x = y = 4, and n = ____.
questions.rule: n = m + 1 and x = y = 2^(m/2).

questions.q: For m = 3, which statement fits the book's result?
options: n = 4 and x = y = 2 work
There is exactly one solution, with x = y = 2^(3/2)
There are infinitely many solutions
There are no solutions, because m is odd
optionExplain: 2^(3/2) is not an integer.
The book shows at most one solution, and none for odd m.
Right: solutions exist only for even m.
questions.explain: The solution requires x = y = 2^(m/2) and n = m + 1. For odd m, 2^(m/2) is not an integer, so there are no solutions.
questions.rule: Odd m gives no solution.

questions.q: Suppose 2^u exactly divides x, 2^v exactly divides y with u < v, and n > m. Why is 2um = n(u + v) impossible?
options: Both sides are odd
u and v must be equal because they are exponents
The right side exceeds n·2u, which already exceeds the left side 2um
m and n have no common factor
optionExplain: Neither side is stated to be odd; the argument is about their size.
The case u < v is exactly what is being excluded.
Right: n(u + v) > 2nu > 2mu since n > m and v > u.
Relative primality is used later, not in this inequality.
questions.explain: If u < v then u + v > 2u, so n(u + v) > 2nu ≥ 2mu when n > m (and u ≥ 0). So the left side, 2um, can never equal the right.
questions.rule: Compare sizes of the exponents.

questions.q: What is the highest power of 2 dividing 12² + 20²? (12 = 4 · 3 and 20 = 4 · 5, with 3 and 5 odd.)
optionExplain: The factor 16 = 2⁴ is there, but 9 + 25 = 34 contributes one more 2.
544 / 64 is not an integer.
The common factor 4 only gives 2²; the squares give 16.
questions.explain: Pull out 4² = 2⁴: 12² + 20² = 2⁴(3² + 5²) = 2⁴ · 34. Since 3² + 5² ≡ 2 (mod 4), it contains exactly one factor 2, so 2⁵ ‖ 544.
questions.rule: The sum of two odd squares has exactly one factor of 2.
questions.teaches: If 2^r exactly divides both x and y, then 2^(2r+1) exactly divides x² + y², because the sum of two odd squares is 2 modulo 4.

questions.section: Can a Polynomial Always Output Primes?
questions.q: Euler's polynomial x² + x + 41 is prime for x = 0, 1, …, 39. What does it give at x = 41?
options: 1763 = 41 · 43, which is composite
A prime, since it worked for 40 values
1681 = 41², a prime power
41, which is prime
optionExplain: A pattern of 40 values does not continue forever.
That is the value at x = 40.
The value is much larger than 41.
questions.explain: At x = 41 all three terms are multiples of 41, so the result is divisible by 41. The card next shows a general version of this trick.
questions.rule: Plug in the constant term, or a prime value, to force a factor.

questions.section: Can a Polynomial Always Output Primes?
questions.q: True or false: A polynomial that gives primes for many consecutive inputs must give primes for every input.
questions.explain: Euler's x² + x + 41 gives primes for x = 0 to 39, yet f(41) = 41 · 43 is composite.
questions.rule: Many primes in a row is not all primes.

questions.section: Can a Polynomial Always Output Primes?
questions.q: Let f(x) = x² + x + 1, so f(2) = 7. Using f(u + f(u)) is a multiple of f(u), which value must be a multiple of 7?
optionExplain: 3 = 2 + 1, not 2 + 7; 13 is not a multiple of 7.
Right: 9 = 2 + 7.
5 = 2 + 3; 31 is not a multiple of 7.
6 = 2 + 4; 43 is not a multiple of 7.
questions.rule: Move by f(u) to get another multiple of f(u).

questions.section: Can a Polynomial Always Output Primes?
questions.q: For f(x) = x³ + x + 1, the inputs 1, 4, 7, 10 all give multiples of 3. The next such input is ____.
questions.explain: f(13) = 2211 = 3 · 737, since adding 3 to an input keeps f a multiple of 3.
questions.rule: Add the prime to the input.

questions.section: Can a Polynomial Always Output Primes?
questions.q: The proof shows p divides f(u + p) and concludes f(u + p) is composite. What case has been overlooked?
options: f(u + p) might equal p itself, which is prime; then try u + 2p, u + 3p, …
f(u + p) might equal 1
p might not be prime
The polynomial may have non-integer coefficients
optionExplain: Right: a polynomial equals p at only finitely many inputs.
Then it would not be a multiple of p, which is excluded.
The argument never uses that p is prime.
Integer coefficients are assumed.
questions.explain: A multiple of p is composite unless it is ±p. A non-constant polynomial takes the values ±p only finitely often, so moving by multiples of p eventually gives a composite value.
questions.rule: Handle the equal-to-p case.

questions.section: Can a Polynomial Always Output Primes?
questions.q: Let g(x) = 2x² + 3x + 5, so g(1) = 10, which is not prime. Which input gives a multiple of 10?
options: x = 10, because 10 divides 10
x = 2, since 2 divides 10
x = 11, because g(11) = 280
None, since 10 is not prime
optionExplain: g(10) = 235, not a multiple of 10.
g(2) = 19, which is not a multiple of 10.
Right: the bonus result says f(a + f(a)) is a multiple of f(a), with no primality needed.
The congruence argument never used primality.
questions.rule: f(a + f(a)) is a multiple of f(a) for every integer a.
questions.teaches: The proof never uses that p is prime, giving a bonus result: for any integer polynomial f and integer a, f(a + f(a)) is a multiple of f(a).

questions.section: If You Can Count It, It's an Integer
questions.q: Which number must divide the product of any four consecutive positive integers?
optionExplain: Right: four consecutive integers contain a multiple of 4 and a multiple of 3, and also two even numbers.
1 · 2 · 3 · 4 = 24 is not a multiple of 16.
1 · 2 · 3 · 4 = 24 is not a multiple of 30.
1 · 2 · 3 · 4 = 24 is not a multiple of 48.
questions.explain: The product of four consecutive integers is a multiple of 4! = 24, and 24 is the least possible product. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Test the smallest case.

questions.section: If You Can Count It, It's an Integer
questions.explain: The binomial coefficient is C(m + k − 1, k).
questions.rule: Product of k consecutive integers = k! · C(m + k − 1, k).

questions.section: If You Can Count It, It's an Integer
questions.q: What integer is 7 · 8 · 9 · 10 · 11 divided by 5!?
optionExplain: That is the product itself, before dividing.
C(11, 4) = 330 is a different binomial coefficient.
That is half of 462 and has no meaning here.
questions.explain: The product is 55440 and 5! = 120, so the quotient is 462, which equals the binomial coefficient C(11, 5).
questions.rule: Divide by k! to get a binomial coefficient.

questions.section: If You Can Count It, It's an Integer
questions.q: True or false: The product 4 · 5 of two consecutive integers is a multiple of 3! = 6.
questions.explain: 4 · 5 = 20, which leaves remainder 2 on division by 6. The theorem gives divisibility by 2! for two consecutive integers, not 3!.
questions.rule: Use k!, with k the number of factors.

questions.section: If You Can Count It, It's an Integer
questions.q: A student writes 4 · 5 · 6 / 3! = C(m + k, k) with m = 4, k = 3, giving C(7, 3) = 35. What is wrong?
options: 3! should be replaced by 4!
The answer should be C(6, 4) = 15
Nothing: C(7, 3) = 35 is correct
The coefficient is C(m + k − 1, k) = C(6, 3) = 20
optionExplain: k = 3 factors correspond to 3!, not 4!.
questions.explain: m(m + 1)(m + 2) with m = 4 equals 120. Dividing by 3! = 6 gives 20 = C(6, 3), where the top is m + k − 1 = 6.
questions.rule: The top of the binomial is m + k − 1.

questions.section: If You Can Count It, It's an Integer
questions.q: A librarian multiplies four consecutive shelf numbers, 12, 13, 14, 15, and claims the product must be a multiple of 24. How can this be justified quickly?
options: Each shelf number is a multiple of 24
It equals 24 times the number of ways to choose 4 items from 15, an integer
12 is a multiple of 24
The sum of the numbers is a multiple of 24
optionExplain: 12, 13, 14, 15 are not multiples of 24.
12 is smaller than 24.
The sum is 54, not a multiple of 24.
questions.explain: 12 · 13 · 14 · 15 = 4! · C(15, 4) = 24 · 1365 = 32760. A counting argument replaces a divisibility case analysis.
questions.rule: Recognize a binomial coefficient.
questions.teaches: The book's moral: keep your point of view flexible, because anything involving integers is fair game for combinatorial reasoning.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: Moving the last letter of fermats to the front gives which word?
options: sfermat
stamref
ermatsf
fermats
optionExplain: Right: the final s becomes the first letter.
That reverses the letters instead of shifting.
That moves the first letter to the end, the opposite shift.
A shift of one position changes the word, because its letters are not all equal.
questions.explain: A shift cycles the letters: the last letter moves to the front. The card next uses repeated shifts to group words.
questions.rule: Shift = move the last letter to the front.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: Shifting the word abcde once gives ____.
questions.explain: The last letter e moves to the front.
questions.rule: A shift moves the last letter to the front.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: Words of length 5 over {0, 1} are shifted. How many words are in the sorority of 00101?
optionExplain: Only boring words (all letters equal) form a sorority of size 1.
The word does not repeat after two shifts.
32 is the total number of words, not the size of one sorority.
questions.explain: Five shifts return to 00101, and no earlier shift does, so the sorority has five members.
questions.rule: List the shifts until the word returns.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: True or false: With a 3-letter alphabet and words of length 5, exactly 3 words satisfy s(u) = u.
questions.explain: A word fixed by the shift has all letters equal, and there is one such word for each of the 3 letters.
questions.rule: Fixed words are the boring words, a in number.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: A student notes s²(abab) = abab with length 4 and says abab must be a boring word. Why does the book's argument not apply?
options: abab is a boring word because it repeats ab
s² is not defined for a word of length 4
The word abab has no sisters
The claim s^r(u) = u with 0 < r < p forces a boring word only when the length p is prime
optionExplain: A boring word has all letters equal; abab has a and b.
Shifts can be repeated for any length.
It has the sister baba.
Right: 4 is not prime.
questions.explain: The claim that a short return time forces equal letters rests on the length being prime. For p = 4, abab returns after two shifts without being boring.
questions.rule: The prime length is essential.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: Over the alphabet {x, y}, words of length 3 are grouped into sororities by the shift. How many sororities are there?
optionExplain: Right: xxx and yyy alone, and two sororities of size 3: {xxy, yxx, xyx} and {xyy, yxy, yyx}.
That counts only the two boring words.
Eight words split as 1 + 1 + 3 + 3 gives four groups, not three.
That treats every word as alone.
questions.explain: Every word is its own sister, so every word belongs to some sorority and the sororities partition the 8 words. 2 + 3 + 3 = 8 with two singletons.
questions.rule: Sororities partition the set of words.
questions.teaches: Since any word is its own sister, every word lies in exactly one sorority, so the sororities partition all a^p words.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: Words of length 5 are made from 2 letters. Remove the 2 words with all letters equal. How many groups of 5 can the remaining words form?
optionExplain: That counts all words, not groups.
30 is the number of words left, not the number of groups of 5.
5 is the group size, not the number of groups.
questions.explain: There are 2⁵ = 32 words, 30 remain, and groups of 5 give 6. The card next shows why groups have size 5.
questions.rule: Divide the non-boring words by p.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: True or false: For prime p, a non-boring word has exactly p members in its sorority, including itself.
questions.explain: The p shifts of such a word are all different, and the shifts then cycle.
questions.rule: Non-boring sororities have exactly p members.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: With an alphabet of 3 letters and words of length 5, the non-boring words form ____ sororities.
questions.explain: 3⁵ − 3 = 240 non-boring words, in groups of 5: 240 / 5 = 48.
questions.rule: Number of sororities = (a^p − a)/p.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: What does the sorority count predict about 26⁷ − 26?
options: It is a multiple of 26 but not of 7
It leaves remainder 1 on division by 7
It is a multiple of 7
It is prime
optionExplain: The groups have size 7, not 26.
It equals a multiple of 7 exactly.
Right: 26⁷ − 26 non-boring words split into groups of 7.
It is a large even number, so it cannot be prime.
questions.explain: Groups of 7 partition the non-boring words, so 7 divides 26⁷ − 26. This is Fermat's theorem for a = 26 and p = 7.
questions.rule: The group size gives the divisor.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: A student tries p = 6, a = 2 and finds 2⁶ − 2 = 62, not a multiple of 6. Why is this no contradiction of the combinatorial proof?
options: The student should have used a = 3
62 is a multiple of 6 after all
Fermat's theorem fails for the prime 2
6 is not prime, so sororities need not have size 6; the word 010101 returns after 2 shifts
optionExplain: The issue is the length 6, not the letter count: with a prime length the proof works for any a.
62 / 6 is not an integer.
The length 6 is not prime; the prime 2 is a different matter.
Right: the proof needs p prime.
questions.explain: For a composite length, a non-boring word can return to itself after fewer than p shifts, so sororities of other sizes occur and the count a^p − a need not be divisible by p.
questions.rule: The proof needs a prime length.

questions.section: A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat's Little Theorem
questions.q: A system uses 5-symbol codes over an alphabet of 4 symbols; rotating a code gives an equivalent code. How many groups of 5 equivalent codes arise from the codes that are not all one symbol?
optionExplain: That is the total number of codes.
That is the number of non-uniform codes, not groups of 5.
That is 4⁴, which has no role here.
questions.explain: There are 4⁵ = 1024 codes, 4 uniform, and 1020 others. Rotation groups them in fives: 204 groups. This divisibility is exactly the statement that 5 divides 4⁵ − 4.
questions.rule: Fermat's theorem as: p divides a^p − a.
questions.teaches: Equivalently, Fermat's little theorem says that a^p − a is a multiple of p, which is what the grouping into sororities of size p shows.

questions.q: Which of 7, 11, 13 and 19 can be written as the sum of two squares?
optionExplain: Right: 13 = 2² + 3².
7 ≡ 3 (mod 4), and squares add to 0, 1 or 2 modulo 4.
11 ≡ 3 (mod 4), so no pair of squares works.
19 ≡ 3 (mod 4), so no pair of squares works.
questions.explain: Only 13 is congruent to 1 modulo 4; 7, 11, 19 are congruent to 3 and cannot be sums of two squares. The card next states this pattern.
questions.rule: Primes with remainder 3 modulo 4 fail.

questions.q: A prime \(p \equiv\) ____ \(\pmod 4\) cannot be a sum of two squares.
questions.explain: x² + y² leaves 0, 1 or 2 modulo 4, never 3.
questions.rule: p ≡ 3 (mod 4) has no representation.

questions.q: Which of 23, 31, 41 and 47 is a sum of two squares?
optionExplain: Right: 41 = 4² + 5².
questions.explain: Only 41 leaves remainder 1 modulo 4; the other three leave 3. Indeed 41 = 16 + 25.
questions.rule: Check the remainder modulo 4.

questions.q: The prime 53 leaves remainder 1 modulo 4. What does the pattern suggest?
options: 53 is a sum of two squares, namely 2² + 7²
53 is not a sum of two squares, since it is large
53 is a sum of two squares only if it is also 1 modulo 3
53 has no pattern, because experiments prove nothing
optionExplain: Right: the pattern from the experiments.
Size is not the criterion.
The pattern concerns modulo 4 only.
They suggest the pattern, which is proved later.
questions.explain: All primes tested with remainder 1 modulo 4 are sums of two squares, and 53 = 4 + 49 fits. The proof comes later in the section.
questions.rule: Test the conjecture on a new prime.

questions.q: True or false: The prime 2 is not a sum of two squares because 2 ≡ 2 (mod 4).
questions.explain: 2 = 1² + 1². The modulo-4 obstruction rules out remainder 3, not remainder 2.
questions.rule: The obstruction is for remainder 3.

questions.q: A student checks five primes with remainder 1 modulo 4, finds each is a sum of two squares, and declares the statement proved. According to the book, what is the status?
options: The experiments suggest the truth but do not prove it
It is proved, since five cases is enough
It is false, since five cases cannot be checked
It is proved if the primes are large enough
optionExplain: Right: a proof is still needed.
Finitely many cases never prove an infinite statement.
Checking cases is a legitimate way to form a conjecture.
Size does not change the logic.
questions.explain: Numerical experiments only suggest the truth. The book then constructs the proof using a square root of −1 modulo p and the pigeonhole principle.
questions.rule: Experiments suggest; proofs settle.
questions.teaches: The book stresses that numerical experiments only suggest the truth; a proof is still needed.

questions.q: Which of 4, 5, 6 and 7 satisfies x² ≡ −1 (mod 13)?
questions.explain: A square root of −1 modulo 13 is a number whose square is one less than a multiple of 13: 25 + 1 = 26. The card next uses it to factor x² + y².
questions.rule: Look for squares one less than a multiple of p.

questions.q: Since 5² ≡ −1 (mod 13), the number 5² + 1² = 26 is a multiple of ____.
questions.explain: 26 = 2 · 13, so 5² + 1² is a multiple of 13.
questions.rule: u² ≡ −1 makes x² + y² a multiple of p for suitable pairs.

questions.q: For p = 41 and u = 9, take y = k and x = 9k reduced to between −20 and 20. For which k among 1, 2, 3 and 4 does x² + y² equal 41?
optionExplain: x = 9 gives 81 + 1 = 82 = 2 · 41, a multiple of 41 but not 41.
questions.explain: Each k gives a multiple of 41; only k = 4 gives a small enough pair: (−5)² + 4² = 41.
questions.rule: Try k, reduce x mod p, look for x² + y² = p.

questions.q: For p = 101, u = 10 satisfies 10² ≡ −1 (mod 101). Does the pair y = 1, x = u immediately give x² + y² = 101?
options: No: it gives 2 · 101 = 202
Yes: 10² + 1² = 101, because u is below √101
No: x must be larger than √p
Cannot be decided without a square root table
optionExplain: Right: both entries are below √p, so the sum is less than 2p.
The method wants small values, not large ones.
u = 10 is already given.
questions.explain: When u < √p (here 10 < √101 ≈ 10.05), the pair (u, 1) has x² + y² < 2p, so it must equal p.
questions.rule: If u < √p, the pair (u, 1) works at once.

questions.q: True or false: For p = 13 and u = 5, the pair y = 1, x = 5 gives x² + y² = 13.
questions.explain: 5² + 1² = 26 = 2 · 13: a multiple of 13, not 13 itself. The pair must be reduced further, for example y = 3, x = 15 ≡ 2.
questions.rule: A multiple of p need not equal p.

questions.q: For p = 13, u = 5: the first pair (y, x) = (1, 5) gives 26. Taking y = 3 and x = 5 · 3 = 15, which pair after reducing x modulo 13 gives 13?
options: (x, y) = (3, 2)... which swaps roles
optionExplain: 234 = 18 · 13 is a multiple of 13 but not 13.
34 is not a multiple of 13.
3² + 2² = 13 works but is not the pair obtained from y = 3.
Right: x can be replaced by a congruent value.
questions.explain: Since 15 ≡ 2 (mod 13), x can be replaced by 2 without changing x² modulo 13, and 2² + 3² = 13. Reduction makes the numbers small enough.
questions.rule: Reduce x modulo p to make the pair small.
questions.teaches: After multiplying, x may be reduced modulo p, so a solution like y = 3, x = 15 becomes y = 3, x = 2, which is small enough to equal p.

questions.q: For p = 29 and u = 17, what is 2u = 34 equal to modulo 29?
optionExplain: A residue modulo 29 must lie between 0 and 28.
That is 29 minus 17, not 2u reduced.
questions.explain: 34 = 29 + 5, so 2 · 17 ≡ 5 (mod 29), a small value below √29 ≈ 5.39. The card next explains why some multiple is always small.
questions.rule: Reduce multiples of u modulo p.

questions.q: For \(p = 29\), \(t = \lfloor\sqrt{29}\rfloor =\) ____.
questions.explain: √29 ≈ 5.39, so its integer part is 5.

questions.q: For p = 53, u = 23 (so u² ≡ −1) and t = 7: for which k among 1, 2, 3 and 4 does ku reduce to an absolute value below √53 ≈ 7.28?
optionExplain: 23 is above √53.
4 · 23 = 92 ≡ 39 ≡ −14, absolute value above √53.
questions.explain: Reducing to the range −26 to 26: 23, −7, 16, −14. Only −7 is small enough, so (x, y) = (−7, 2) and 49 + 4 = 53.
questions.rule: Reduce into (−p/2, p/2) and look for a small value.

questions.q: True or false: If one of the reduced multiples lands to the left of the first mark √p, the pair (x, y) is immediately small enough.
questions.explain: A value below √p together with k ≤ t < √p gives x² + y² < 2p, so it equals p.
questions.rule: A value below √p finishes the search.

questions.q: Two multiples mu and nu fall in the same gap between marks. Why does the proof use k = |m − n| rather than m + n?
options: m + n is always odd, so it cannot be used
The sum would give a negative remainder
m − n is always 1
(m − n)u is a difference of nearby values, so it is small, while m + n could exceed t
optionExplain: Parity of m + n plays no role.
The remainder's sign does not matter; the size does.
m and n are any distinct integers from 1 to t.
Right: difference of two values in one gap is below √p.
questions.explain: Two values in the same gap differ by less than √p, and |m − n| ≤ t − 1 keeps y = k below √p. A sum m + n could be larger than t.
questions.rule: Take the difference of two points in one gap.

questions.q: For p = 73, u = 27 (27² = 729 ≡ −1 mod 73). Find x, y with x² + y² = 73, using the pigeonhole idea (t = 8).
optionExplain: 27² + 1 = 730 = 10 · 73, a multiple of 73 but not 73.
Right: k = 3 gives a value below √73 ≈ 8.54.
questions.explain: Multiples of 27 modulo 73 are 27, 54, 8, …; k = 3 gives 8, below √73. So (8, 3): 64 + 9 = 73. The marks √p, 2√p, … are irrational, so no multiple lands exactly on one.
questions.rule: Look for a multiple that reduces below √p.
questions.teaches: The long ticks sit at irrational positions (multiples of √p, which is irrational because p is prime), so no reduced value ever lands exactly on one.

questions.q: Wilson's theorem says that for a prime p, (p − 1)! is congruent to what modulo p?
options: p
optionExplain: Right: (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p), for example 4! = 24 ≡ −1 (mod 5).
4! = 24 leaves 4 on division by 5, not 1.
No prime p divides (p − 1)!, since all its factors are smaller than p.
p is congruent to 0, which contradicts that p does not divide (p − 1)!.
questions.explain: For p = 5, 4! = 24 = 5 · 5 − 1, so 4! ≡ −1. The card next uses this to find a square root of −1.
questions.rule: Wilson: (p − 1)! ≡ −1.

questions.q: For a prime \(p \equiv 1 \pmod 4\), \(\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!^{\,2} \equiv\) ____ \(\pmod p\).
questions.explain: The factorial is an explicit square root of −1.

questions.q: For p = 17, compute u = 8! modulo 17 (8! = 40320). Which value is u?
optionExplain: 8 is the argument of the factorial, not its residue; 8² = 64 ≡ 13.
questions.rule: Compute the factorial and reduce.

questions.q: For p = 7 (which is 3 modulo 4), what is (3!)² modulo 7?
optionExplain: That works only for p ≡ 1 (mod 4); here (p − 1)/2 = 3 is odd.
No factor of 3! is a multiple of 7.
questions.explain: Pairing gives (p − 1)! ≡ (−1)³ (3!)² = −(3!)². With (p − 1)! ≡ −1 this means (3!)² ≡ 1: no square root of −1 arises.
questions.rule: The sign (−1)^((p−1)/2) matters.

questions.q: True or false: For p = 11 the pairing argument shows ((p − 1)/2)!² ≡ −1 (mod 11).
questions.explain: (p − 1)/2 = 5 is odd, so the sign is −1 and (5!)² ≡ +1: indeed 5! = 120 ≡ −1 and its square is 1.
questions.rule: The argument needs p ≡ 1 (mod 4).

questions.q: For p = 5, compute u = ((5 − 1)/2)!. Is u a square root of −1 modulo 5?
options: u = 2! = 2, and 2² = 4 ≡ −1, so yes
u = 1! = 1, and 1² = 1, so no
No square root of −1 exists modulo 5
optionExplain: Right: the formula gives an explicit square root.
The formula uses ((p − 1)/2)!, not (p − 1)!.
The argument is 2, not 1.
questions.explain: (p − 1)/2 = 2, so u = 2! = 2 and 2² = 4 = 5 − 1. The formula finds a square root of −1 without trial and error.
questions.rule: Use ((p − 1)/2)! as the root.
questions.teaches: Not only does a square root of −1 exist when p ≡ 1 (mod 4), the book shows it can be computed explicitly, in contrast to the earlier trial-and-error value u = 17 for p = 29.

questions.q: A problem says: take a triangle, join the midpoints of two sides, and show the segment is parallel to the third side. What does the show part ask?
options: To measure the segment on one carefully drawn triangle and report
To compute one number for the segment from given lengths
To prove a property that holds however the triangle is drawn
To construct the figure with compass and ruler as the final answer
optionExplain: A measurement gives one case; the problem asks for a proof.
No lengths are given, so no single number can be requested.
Right: the claim is about every triangle, not about one drawing.
Drawing the figure is the first stage, not what is asked to be shown.
questions.explain: The second part of a geometry problem names a property that must hold for every legal drawing. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Draw the described diagram carefully first, then look for the property that stays the same however the diagram is drawn.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's typical geometry problem the diagram is handed over as a ready picture, so drawing it takes no effort.
questions.explain: The diagram is usually specified with words, and drawing it correctly is often a real challenge that frustrates beginners who do not investigate enough.
questions.rule: Draw the described diagram carefully first, then look for the property that stays the same however the diagram is drawn.

questions.q: Sort each sentence of a problem by whether it describes the diagram or states what to prove.

items.t: Let ABC be a triangle
Let D and E be the midpoints of BC and AC
Show that DE is half as long as AB
Prove that the three medians meet in one point
Draw a circle and choose a point P outside it
Show that the product PX times PY does not depend on the line

questions.explain: Sentences that place objects build the diagram; the sentence naming a property that must always hold is the rigidity statement.
questions.rule: Draw the described diagram carefully first, then look for the property that stays the same however the diagram is drawn.

questions.q: A student draws one circle and two lines through P, measures both products as 12, and writes: proved. What is missing?
options: More decimal places in the measurement of each product
A proof covering every circle, point and line, since one drawing covers a single case
A larger sheet of paper so the figure can be drawn bigger
Nothing is missing, because two products agreed
optionExplain: Better precision still leaves the claim checked in only one drawing.
Right: the claim is about all legal drawings, so one measurement is evidence, not proof.
Scale does not change the fact that only one case was tested.
Two lines in one drawing never settle a statement about all drawings.
questions.explain: A rigidity statement is proved for all drawings; a measurement only supports a guess.
questions.rule: Draw the described diagram carefully first, then look for the property that stays the same however the diagram is drawn.

questions.q: You suspect that the three angle bisectors of any triangle meet in one point. What is the best way to test this before trying a proof?
options: Draw one equilateral triangle by hand and see that the bisectors meet
Compute the three bisector lengths in one numeric example
Assume it is true and start the proof straight away
Build the figure in a dynamic geometry program and drag the vertices to see whether the bisectors keep meeting
optionExplain: The most symmetric triangle is the case where almost any guess comes true.
Lengths are not what the claim is about, and one example is still one case.
Testing a guess on many drawings is cheap and can reveal a false claim early.
Right: an accurate, modifiable picture lets you test the property across many triangles.
questions.explain: Accurate, flexible pictures make it easy to test a guess on many triangles.
questions.rule: Draw the described diagram carefully first, then look for the property that stays the same however the diagram is drawn.
questions.teaches: The book recommends supplementing pencil and compass with a program such as Geometer's Sketchpad, Geometer or Geogebra, because flexible accurate pictures that are easy to modify greatly help investigation.

questions.q: From a point P outside a circle, one line meets the circle at distances 4 and 9 from P. A second line meets it first at distance 3. How far is its second point?
optionExplain: Right: 4 times 9 is 36, and 36 divided by 3 is 12.
This halves the product instead of dividing it by the near distance.
This adds: 4 plus 9 is 13, and 13 minus 3 is 10; the quantity that stays fixed is a product.
Copying the far distance of the first line assumes both lines meet the circle in the same places.
questions.explain: The product of the two distances is the same for both lines, so 3 times the far distance equals 36. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: For a fixed point and circle, PX times PY is the same for every line through P that cuts the circle.

questions.q: The product PX times PY for a line through P is called the ____ of P with respect to the circle.
questions.explain: The power of the point P is the name for the product of its distances to the two points where the line cuts the circle.
questions.rule: For a fixed point and circle, PX times PY is the same for every line through P that cuts the circle.

questions.q: From P outside a circle, a line meets it at distances 5 and 16 from P. A second line meets it first at distance 8. How far is its second point?
optionExplain: This subtracts 8 from the sum 21, which treats the sum as the invariant.
Right: the product 5 times 16 is 80, and 80 divided by 8 is 10.
Repeating the near distance assumes the line meets the circle symmetrically.
This divides 20 by 8 and uses a chord piece instead of the distance to the far point.
questions.explain: Multiply the two distances on the first line, then divide by the near distance on the second.
questions.rule: For a fixed point and circle, PX times PY is the same for every line through P that cuts the circle.

questions.q: True or false: P lies inside a circle. One chord through P splits into pieces 6 and 4; another chord through P splits into pieces 3 and 8. These data fit the theorem.
questions.explain: Inside the circle the pieces of each chord multiply to the same number: 6 times 4 and 3 times 8 are both 24.
questions.rule: For a fixed point and circle, PX times PY is the same for every line through P that cuts the circle.

questions.q: P is outside a circle. A line cuts it at X and Y with PX = 4 and XY = 5. A student computes the power as 4 times 5 = 20. What is wrong?
options: The factor 5 should be squared, giving 100
Nothing; the chord length XY is the second factor
The power should add the two factors, giving 9
The second factor must be PY = 9, the distance from P to the far point, so the power is 36
optionExplain: Squaring the chord length has no part in the definition.
The factor is the full distance from P to Y, not just the chord inside the circle.
The power is a product of the distances, not a sum.
Right: PY equals PX plus XY, which is 9.
questions.explain: Both factors are distances from P, so the second one includes the first.
questions.rule: For a fixed point and circle, PX times PY is the same for every line through P that cuts the circle.

questions.q: A problem asks you to prove AB times CD = EF times GH for four segments in a diagram. According to the book, what is the natural route?
options: Equate areas, or find similar triangles, equate their ratios and cross-multiply
Angle chase until every angle in the figure is known
Place the figure in coordinates and avoid synthetic ideas
Look only for congruent triangles and equate their sides
optionExplain: Right: the book notes that a product equality leads to areas or to similar triangles with cross-multiplication.
Angle chasing gives equal angles, not products of lengths, until similar triangles enter.
Coordinates can work, but the book names areas and similar triangles as the natural first strategies.
Congruence gives equal lengths; a product of two lengths is the signature of similarity or area.
questions.explain: An equality of products points to areas, or to similar triangles with cross-multiplication.
questions.rule: For a fixed point and circle, PX times PY is the same for every line through P that cuts the circle.
questions.teaches: Faced with an equality of products, the book says to equate areas, or to produce similar triangles, equate ratios and cross-multiply.

questions.q: In a triangle, AB = 3 and AC = 6. The bisector from A meets CB, which is 9 long. Which split of CB fits?
options: CD = 3 and DB = 6
CD = 4.5 and DB = 4.5
CD = 6 and DB = 3
CD = 5 and DB = 4
optionExplain: This swaps the pieces; the longer side AC goes with the piece at C.
Equal pieces would be the case only if the two sides were equal.
Right: the pieces are in the ratio 6 to 3, like AC to AB.
No rule produces this split; the ratio must be 2 to 1.
questions.explain: The longer side next to A is matched with the longer piece. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The bisector of angle A splits the opposite side so that CD/DB = AC/AB.

questions.q: True or false: The bisector of angle A cuts the opposite side into two pieces whose ratio equals the ratio of the two sides that meet at A.
questions.explain: That is the angle bisector theorem: CD/DB = AC/AB.
questions.rule: The bisector of angle A splits the opposite side so that CD/DB = AC/AB.

questions.q: Triangle ABC has AB = 8, AC = 12 and CB = 15. The bisector of angle A meets CB at D. How long is CD?
optionExplain: This is the length of DB, the piece on the AB side.
This halves CB, as if the two sides were equal.
Right: the ratio is 12 to 8, which is 3 to 2, and 3/5 of 15 is 9.
This is a rough guess; the pieces must sum to 15 in the ratio 3 to 2, which gives 9 and 6.
questions.explain: Split the opposite side in the ratio of the neighbouring sides.
questions.rule: The bisector of angle A splits the opposite side so that CD/DB = AC/AB.

questions.q: A student writes CD/DB = AB/AC for the bisector from A. What is wrong?
options: The theorem is about medians, not bisectors
The ratio is inverted: the piece at C pairs with the side AC
The ratio should compare the angles at B and C
The equality holds only in isosceles triangles
optionExplain: A median would split the opposite side equally; the bisector gives the side ratio.
Right: CD/DB equals AC/AB, so the longer side has the longer piece.
The theorem compares side lengths, not angle measures.
The theorem holds in every triangle.
questions.explain: Check by a simple case: the longer neighbouring side must go with the longer piece.
questions.rule: The bisector of angle A splits the opposite side so that CD/DB = AC/AB.

questions.q: If AB = AC, the bisector from A cuts CB into pieces whose ratio CD/DB equals ____.
questions.explain: With equal neighbouring sides the ratio is 1, so D is the midpoint of CB.
questions.rule: The bisector of angle A splits the opposite side so that CD/DB = AC/AB.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, AC = 9 and AB = 6. A point D on CB has CD = 6 and DB = 4. What does the converse of the theorem say about AD?
options: AD is a median, because D is near the middle of CB
AD is an altitude, because the pieces have a nice ratio
Nothing, because the converse is not true
AD bisects angle CAB, because CD/DB = AC/AB
optionExplain: A median needs CD = DB, which fails here.
The ratio says nothing about perpendicularity.
The book states that the converse is true and leaves its proof as a problem.
Right: 6/4 and 9/6 both equal 3/2, so the converse applies.
questions.explain: If the pieces match the side ratio, the line through that point bisects the angle.
questions.rule: The bisector of angle A splits the opposite side so that CD/DB = AC/AB.
questions.teaches: The converse is also true: if D is placed on CB so that CD/DB = AC/AB, then AD bisects angle CAB.

questions.q: Median BD of a triangle is 15 long. The three medians meet at G. Which distance from B to G is most plausible?
optionExplain: Right: G lies two thirds of the way from the vertex.
That is the midpoint of the median; G is closer to the midpoint of the side than that.
G is not one third of the way from the vertex but closer to the far end.
That would put G on the side, but G is inside the triangle.
questions.explain: The three medians balance at a point twice as far from the vertex as from the opposite midpoint. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The medians are concurrent at the centroid, which lies two thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.

questions.q: A median is a segment from a vertex to the ____ of the opposite side.
questions.explain: That is the definition of a median.
questions.rule: The medians are concurrent at the centroid, which lies two thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.

questions.q: The medians of triangle ABC meet at G, and the median from B has length 27. How long is GD, the part from G to the midpoint D of the opposite side?
optionExplain: This is the part from B to G.
Right: BG is 18 and GD is 9, a 2 to 1 split.
This halves the median, forgetting the 2 to 1 ratio.
This divides 27 by 4.5; the median splits into thirds, so each third is 9.
questions.explain: Divide the median into three equal parts: two next to the vertex, one next to the midpoint.
questions.rule: The medians are concurrent at the centroid, which lies two thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.

questions.q: A student says the centroid divides a median 1 to 2 measured from the vertex, so AG is one third of the median. What is the error?
options: The ratio should be 1 to 1
The ratio is correct, but it applies only to the longest median
The 2 to 1 ratio starts at the vertex: AG is two thirds of the median
The centroid is not on the median at all
optionExplain: Equal parts would put G at the midpoint of the side, which is not the case.
The ratio is the same for all three medians.
Right: the centroid is closer to the midpoint of the side.
The centroid lies on every median.
questions.explain: From the vertex, the centroid is two parts out of three along the median.
questions.rule: The medians are concurrent at the centroid, which lies two thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.

questions.q: True or false: In triangle ABC with centroid G, if AG = 14 then the whole median from A has length 21.
questions.explain: AG is two thirds of the median, so the median is 14 times 3/2, which is 21.
questions.rule: The medians are concurrent at the centroid, which lies two thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.

questions.q: A triangle has vertices (0,0), (6,0) and (0,9). Where is its centroid?
optionExplain: Right: the average of the x-coordinates is 2 and of the y-coordinates is 3.
This is the midpoint of the side joining (6,0) and (0,9), where the median meets the side.
This averages the x-values wrongly as 6/2 instead of 6/3.
This swaps the roles of the coordinates.
questions.explain: The centroid of a triangle is the average of its three vertices.
questions.rule: The medians are concurrent at the centroid, which lies two thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.
questions.teaches: Later in the chapter the centroid is shown to be the centre of mass of the vertices, the point (A + B + C)/3.

questions.q: A geometry book numbers several statements. One is headed Fact; another has a number but no heading label. What does the book expect?
options: Prove both from the postulates before moving on
Assume both, since the book has already stated them
Skip the unlabelled one, since it is not important
Assume the one labelled Fact, and prove the unlabelled one yourself
optionExplain: The book grants labelled facts to save time.
The unlabelled ones are deliberately left for you to prove.
Unlabelled results are essential exercises, not optional ones.
Right: unlabelled statements are exercises for the reader.
questions.explain: The label Fact marks results you may assume; the rest are yours to prove. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Assume what is labelled Fact; prove what is unlabelled, and do not read passively.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's survival geometry, a result labelled Fact may be assumed without proof.
questions.explain: The authors give a larger stock of facts to assume, so you can start on problems quickly.
questions.rule: Assume what is labelled Fact; prove what is unlabelled, and do not read passively.

questions.q: Sort each result by how the book treats it.

items.t: Triangle inequality
Alternate interior angles cut by a transversal of parallel lines are equal
Vertical angles are equal
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two far interior angles
SAS, ASA, SSS and AAS give congruence
The angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees

questions.explain: Facts carry the label; the other results are exercises for the reader.
questions.rule: Assume what is labelled Fact; prove what is unlabelled, and do not read passively.

questions.q: A reader decides to prove every labelled Fact from the postulates before reading further. What does the book say about this plan?
options: It is not needed: the book grants these facts in the interest of time
It is required, since nothing in geometry may be assumed
It is impossible, because the facts are false in general
It is the point of the chapter and should come first
optionExplain: Right: the authors play fast and loose on purpose, to get you to real problems sooner.
The authors explicitly provide facts you can safely assume for now.
The facts are true in Euclidean geometry.
The chapter's aim is problem solving, not the foundations.
questions.explain: Use the granted facts, and spend your effort on the unlabelled exercises.
questions.rule: Assume what is labelled Fact; prove what is unlabelled, and do not read passively.

questions.q: Why does the book call its treatment of parallel lines a simplification?
options: The fact is false for triangles that are too large
The alternate-angle fact depends on a postulate independent of Euclid's others; changing it gives non-Euclidean geometries
The fact has only been proved for right angles
The fact was disproved in the nineteenth century
optionExplain: The fact is true in Euclidean geometry for lines of any size.
Right: the footnote says altering that postulate gives other consistent geometries.
It is a general statement about transversals and parallel lines.
It was not disproved; it was seen to depend on an independent postulate.
questions.explain: Facts about parallels rest on a postulate that other geometries drop.
questions.rule: Assume what is labelled Fact; prove what is unlabelled, and do not read passively.
questions.teaches: Fact 8.2.6 depends on a postulate independent of Euclid's other postulates; modifying it leads to different, mathematically consistent non-Euclidean geometries.

questions.q: In the name angle PQR, which point is the corner where the two arms meet?
options: P
R
It depends on how the figure is drawn
Q
optionExplain: The first letter names a point on one arm.
The last letter names a point on the other arm.
The convention is fixed by the middle letter.
Right: the vertex is the middle letter.
questions.explain: The middle letter of a three-letter angle name is its vertex. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The middle letter is the vertex; use three letters for an angle when a figure is crowded.

questions.q: In the name of angle ABC, the vertex is the letter in the ____ position.
questions.explain: The vertex sits between the points on the two arms.
questions.rule: The middle letter is the vertex; use three letters for an angle when a figure is crowded.

questions.q: Side BC of triangle ABC is extended beyond C to a point D. Which angle is the exterior angle at C?
options: Angle ACB
Angle BCD
Angle ACD
Angle ABC
optionExplain: This is the interior angle of the triangle at C.
B, C and D lie on one line, so this is a straight angle.
Right: it lies between side CA and the extension CD.
This is the interior angle at B.
questions.explain: The exterior angle at C is formed by one side and the extension of the other.
questions.rule: The middle letter is the vertex; use three letters for an angle when a figure is crowded.

questions.q: Match each description to its name.
pairs: Starts at A, passes through B and goes on forever
Goes on forever in both directions through A and B
Begins at A and stops at B
The number giving how far A is from B
questions.explain: The four objects built on two points differ in how far they extend and whether they are shapes or numbers.
questions.rule: The middle letter is the vertex; use three letters for an angle when a figure is crowded.

questions.q: Several lines meet at C in a crowded figure. A student writes m angle C = 80 degrees. What is the problem?
options: The measure must be written in radians
An angle can never be given a measure
A single letter is ambiguous here; three points should name the angle
The vertex should be written last
optionExplain: Degrees and radians may both be used.
Angles have measures written with an m in front.
Right: single-letter names work only in simple figures.
The vertex is the middle of a three-letter name.
questions.explain: Use three points to name an angle whenever other angles share its vertex.
questions.rule: The middle letter is the vertex; use three letters for an angle when a figure is crowded.

questions.q: A proof writes angle PQR = angle STU and later m angle PQR = 70 degrees. How does the book regard the first form?
options: As informal shorthand for the measures, acceptable when context makes this clear
As an error, since angles must always be written with m
As a statement that the two angles are the same shape and placed in the same spot
As valid only for right angles
optionExplain: Right: the authors write the angle symbol to denote the angle or its measure.
The book says the informal form is fine when clear.
Equal measures do not mean the same position.
The convention has nothing to do with right angles.
questions.explain: Context decides whether a symbol stands for the object or for its measure.
questions.rule: The middle letter is the vertex; use three letters for an angle when a figure is crowded.
questions.teaches: Informally the book writes angle ABC to denote either the angle or its measure, and sometimes just ABC, as long as context makes it clear.

questions.q: Two angles together make a straight angle. What are such angles called?
options: Complementary
Vertical
Alternate
Supplementary
optionExplain: Complementary angles add to only 90 degrees.
Vertical angles are opposite each other at a crossing; they are equal, not summing to 180.
Alternate angles come from a transversal across parallel lines.
Right: supplementary angles add to 180 degrees.
questions.explain: Supplementary means summing to a straight angle. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Complementary angles sum to 90 degrees; supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees.

questions.q: A straight angle measures ____ degrees.
questions.explain: A straight angle is the angle made by three points on a line.
questions.rule: Complementary angles sum to 90 degrees; supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees.

questions.q: An angle measures 37 degrees. What are its complement and its supplement?
options: 143 degrees and 53 degrees
53 degrees and 143 degrees
53 degrees and 53 degrees
63 degrees and 153 degrees
optionExplain: This swaps the two names.
The supplement uses 180, not 90.
This subtracts from the wrong totals, 100 and 190.
questions.explain: Subtract from 90 for the complement and from 180 for the supplement.
questions.rule: Complementary angles sum to 90 degrees; supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees.

questions.q: A student says the supplement of 65 degrees is 25 degrees. What went wrong?
options: They subtracted from 360; the supplement is 295 degrees
They subtracted from 90 instead of 180; the supplement is 115 degrees
Nothing; 25 is the supplement
They should have added 90, giving 155 degrees
optionExplain: A full turn is not the total used for supplements.
Right: 25 is the complement.
25 is the complement of 65.
Neither names a pair sum of 90 plus the angle.
questions.explain: Supplementary uses 180; complementary uses 90.
questions.rule: Complementary angles sum to 90 degrees; supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees.

questions.q: A problem gives an angle ABC = pi/2. What kind of angle is this?
options: A straight angle
An angle of 45 degrees
A right angle
It cannot be classified without degrees
optionExplain: A straight angle is pi radians, twice this.
pi/4 radians would be 45 degrees.
Right: pi radians is a straight angle, so half of it is a right angle.
Radian and degree measures can be converted either way.

A radius joins the centre to the circle.
questions.explain: A chord is a straight segment between two points of the circle. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Arcs are measured by their central angles; inscribed angles have vertices on the circle.

questions.q: A line that meets a circle in exactly one point is called a ____.
questions.explain: That is the definition of a tangent.
questions.rule: Arcs are measured by their central angles; inscribed angles have vertices on the circle.

questions.q: Central angle COB measures 110 degrees. What does the arc BC cut off by it measure?
options: 55 degrees
250 degrees
70 degrees
110 degrees
optionExplain: That is the inscribed angle on the same arc, not the arc.

questions.rule: Arcs are measured by their central angles; inscribed angles have vertices on the circle.

questions.q: A student says chord BC and arc BC are the same thing since they have the same endpoints. What is the correction?
options: A chord is a straight segment and an arc is part of the circle; they differ in shape and measure
They are the same if the arc is under 90 degrees
The arc is the straight segment and the chord is the curve
A chord is a tangent between the same points
optionExplain: Right: the arc is curved and measured in degrees.
They remain different kinds of objects.
It is the other way around.
A tangent meets the circle only once.
questions.explain: Chord is a segment; arc is a curve.
questions.rule: Arcs are measured by their central angles; inscribed angles have vertices on the circle.

questions.q: Match each term to its description.
pairs: segment joining two points of the circle
line touching the circle at exactly one point
questions.explain: Each term is defined by where its vertex or endpoints lie.
questions.rule: Arcs are measured by their central angles; inscribed angles have vertices on the circle.

questions.q: If arc BC measures 100 degrees under the book's counterclockwise reading, what does arc CB measure?
options: 100 degrees
260 degrees
80 degrees
50 degrees
optionExplain: Reading from C to B counterclockwise gives the other arc.

questions.rule: Arcs are measured by their central angles; inscribed angles have vertices on the circle.

questions.q: A chord of length 16 is drawn in a circle of radius 10. How far is the chord from the centre of the circle?

This is half of the chord.

questions.q: True or false: For a line, a circle and a chord, if the line is perpendicular to the chord and passes through the chord's midpoint, then it passes through the centre.

questions.rule: Through the centre, through the midpoint, perpendicular to the chord: any two imply the third.

questions.q: A student reasons: this line passes through the midpoint of the chord, so it passes through the centre. What is missing?
options: Nothing; the midpoint always lies on a line through the centre
The line must also be a tangent
A second condition, such as being perpendicular to the chord
The chord must be a diameter
optionExplain: Only one statement is given, which does not imply the others.

Right: two of the three statements are needed.
The theorem covers any chord.

questions.rule: Through the centre, through the midpoint, perpendicular to the chord: any two imply the third.

questions.q: True or false: A line through the centre of a circle and perpendicular to a chord also passes through the chord's midpoint.
questions.explain: Two statements (through the centre, perpendicular) give the third.
questions.rule: Through the centre, through the midpoint, perpendicular to the chord: any two imply the third.

questions.q: A circle is drawn without its centre marked. How can the chord fact locate the centre?

Draw two non-parallel chords and their perpendicular bisectors; they meet at the centre
Draw two parallel chords and join their midpoints at random
Draw a tangent and measure its length

Tangent length does not locate the centre.

questions.rule: Through the centre, through the midpoint, perpendicular to the chord: any two imply the third.
questions.teaches: The book lists finding a circle's centre with compass and ruler as one of the basic constructions (Problem 8.2.28f); the chord fact makes it work.

questions.q: A point is 13 from the centre of a circle of radius 5. How long is a tangent segment from the point to the circle?
optionExplain: Right: the radius to the touching point is perpendicular to the tangent, making a 5, 12, 13 right triangle.

This adds them.

questions.q: A tangent line is ____ to the radius at the point of tangency.
questions.explain: This is Fact 8.2.14.
questions.rule: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and tangent segments from an outside point are equal.

questions.q: A tangent segment from an outside point to a circle of radius 6 has length 8. How far is the point from the centre?
optionExplain: Right: radius 6 and tangent 8 are the legs of a right triangle, so the hypotenuse is 10.
This adds the radius and tangent.
This subtracts them.
This takes the wrong leg as the hypotenuse.

questions.rule: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and tangent segments from an outside point are equal.

questions.q: A student says the tangent at B is perpendicular to the chord BC. What is the correct statement?

The tangent at B is perpendicular to the radius OB
The tangent is parallel to the radius OB
The tangent at B is perpendicular to the arc BC

questions.rule: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and tangent segments from an outside point are equal.

questions.q: True or false: Two tangent segments drawn from the same outside point to a circle have the same length.
questions.explain: This is Problem 8.2.15: AX = AY.
questions.rule: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and tangent segments from an outside point are equal.

questions.q: A coin rests against a straight ruler, touching it at one point. A line drawn perpendicular to the ruler at that point passes through what?
options: The edge of the coin at the opposite side only
A point chosen by the angle of the ruler
Nothing special about the coin
The centre of the coin
optionExplain: It does reach the edge there, but the important point is the centre.
The ruler's angle does not change the result.
The converse of the tangent fact gives a special point.
Right: the perpendicular to a tangent at the point of tangency passes through the centre.
questions.explain: Perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact goes through the centre.
questions.rule: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and tangent segments from an outside point are equal.
questions.teaches: Conversely, the perpendicular to a tangent line at the point of tangency passes through the centre of the circle (Fact 8.2.14).

questions.q: A central angle COB measures 80 degrees. An angle CAB with A on the circle subtends the same arc. What might it measure?

160 degrees

questions.q: An inscribed angle is ____ the measure of the arc it subtends.

questions.rule: An inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc.

questions.q: True or false: If the point A moves along the circle without crossing B or C (staying on the same arc), the angle CAB stays constant.
questions.explain: Every such A gives half of the same central angle COB.
questions.rule: An inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc.

questions.q: In angle chasing, the aim is to compute many angles while keeping the number of ____ low.
questions.explain: Few variables keep the equations simple. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Compute as many angles as you can with as few variables as possible, but do not rely on angle chasing alone.

questions.q: True or false: The book recommends angle chasing as the only tool needed for geometry problems.
questions.explain: Angle chasing is powerful, but the book warns against using it to the exclusion of other tactics.
questions.rule: Compute as many angles as you can with as few variables as possible, but do not rely on angle chasing alone.

questions.q: Triangle ABC has AB = AC and angle B = 70 degrees. D lies on AC with BD = BC. Angle ABD is ____ degrees.
questions.explain: Angle A is 40 and angle C is 70; BD = BC gives angle BDC = 70 and DBC = 40, so ABD = 70 - 40 = 30.
questions.rule: Compute as many angles as you can with as few variables as possible, but do not rely on angle chasing alone.

questions.q: A solver gives every unknown angle in a crowded figure its own variable, ending with nine variables. What does the book advise?

Stop angle chasing and use a different subject
Ignore all equal angles
Keep the number of variables small by reusing relations from isosceles triangles and straight lines
optionExplain: That makes the algebra harder.
Angle chasing is useful when kept simple.
Equal angles are what reduce the variables.
Right: fewer variables make the system manageable.
questions.explain: Few variables, many angles.
questions.rule: Compute as many angles as you can with as few variables as possible, but do not rely on angle chasing alone.

questions.q: Which kind of line in a triangle gives the least useful angle information, according to the book's example?
options: An angle bisector
An altitude

A perpendicular bisector

An altitude gives right angles.

questions.explain: Medians split lengths, not angles.
questions.rule: Compute as many angles as you can with as few variables as possible, but do not rely on angle chasing alone.

questions.q: A figure features the midpoint of a side, and a solver tries angle chasing. What does the book's later example suggest?
options: Angle chasing will certainly work
Always add a circle
Abandon the problem
Expect little angular information and look for similar triangles or another structure
optionExplain: The book shows a case where it is doomed.
Circles are one tool, not a rule.
Other tactics such as similar triangles remain.
Right: angle chasing is doomed when medians are the lines of interest.
questions.explain: Know when to transcend angle chasing.
questions.rule: Compute as many angles as you can with as few variables as possible, but do not rely on angle chasing alone.
questions.teaches: In Example 8.4.4 the book says angle chasing is doomed because a median is the line of interest, and medians do not yield angular information without messy trigonometry.

questions.q: A right triangle has hypotenuse 10. A circle passes through all three of its vertices. What is the radius?

Right: the hypotenuse is a diameter of that circle.

questions.rule: A point lies on the circle with diameter AB exactly when it sees AB at a right angle.

questions.q: True or false: If AB is a diameter of a circle and C is another point on the circle, then angle ACB is a right angle.
questions.explain: This follows from the inscribed angle theorem: the central angle is 180.
questions.rule: A point lies on the circle with diameter AB exactly when it sees AB at a right angle.

questions.q: AB is a diameter of a circle, C is on the circle, and angle CAB = 35 degrees. What is angle CBA?

That equals CAB, but they are not equal here.

questions.rule: A point lies on the circle with diameter AB exactly when it sees AB at a right angle.

questions.q: A student sees angle AXB = 90 and concludes X lies on the circle through A and B with centre at any chosen point. What does the book actually say?

X lies on the circle having AB as a diameter
X lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB
X lies at the midpoint of AB

Right: that is the converse.
The right angle does not place X there.
That would make the angle straight.
questions.explain: A right angle on AB points to the circle with diameter AB.
questions.rule: A point lies on the circle with diameter AB exactly when it sees AB at a right angle.

questions.q: If angle AXB = 90 degrees, then X lies on the circle whose diameter is ____.
questions.explain: The converse of the inscribed right triangle fact.
questions.rule: A point lies on the circle with diameter AB exactly when it sees AB at a right angle.

questions.q: In acute triangle ABC, BB1 is the altitude to side AC (foot B1). Does B1 lie on the circle with diameter AB?
options: No, because B1 is on side AC
Only if the triangle is isosceles
Yes, because angle AB1B is a right angle
Only if the triangle is equilateral

No such condition is needed.

No such condition is needed.

questions.rule: A point lies on the circle with diameter AB exactly when it sees AB at a right angle.

questions.q: A quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle, with angle A = 80 degrees. What is angle C, opposite A?
options: 80 degrees
280 degrees
10 degrees
100 degrees
optionExplain: That would hold for a parallelogram, not a cyclic quadrilateral.
This subtracts from 360.
This subtracts from 90.
Right: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

questions.rule: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary; equal angles on one side of a segment put two points on a common circle.

questions.q: Points that lie on a common circle are called ____.
questions.explain: That is the term the book uses for four points on a circle.
questions.rule: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary; equal angles on one side of a segment put two points on a common circle.

questions.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, C and D lie on the same side of AB, and angle ACB = angle ADB = 38 degrees. What follows?
options: A, B, C and D lie on one circle
ABCD is a parallelogram
AB is a diameter
Nothing follows

Equal angles do not force parallel sides.
A diameter needs the angles to be 90.
The equal-angle test applies.
questions.explain: Equal angles subtended by a segment from one side mean concyclic points.
questions.rule: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary; equal angles on one side of a segment put two points on a common circle.

questions.q: A parallelogram has angles 70, 110, 70 and 110 degrees, and a student calls it cyclic because adjacent angles add to 180. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: adjacent angles summing to 180 is the cyclic test
Cyclic quadrilaterals have all angles equal
The test uses opposite angles, and here they are equal (70 and 70) so their sum is not 180
The angles must add to 180 in total
optionExplain: The test is for opposite angles.
Opposite angles are supplementary, not all equal.

questions.rule: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary; equal angles on one side of a segment put two points on a common circle.

questions.q: True or false: A rectangle is a cyclic quadrilateral.

questions.rule: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary; equal angles on one side of a segment put two points on a common circle.

questions.q: Two surveyors at C and D on the same side of segment AB each see AB under an angle of 25 degrees. What can be concluded?
options: The surveyors are equally far from AB
CD is parallel to AB
AB is a diameter
A, B, C and D lie on a common circle
optionExplain: Equal angles do not give equal distances.
Nothing here forces that.
A right angle would be needed.
Right: equal angles subtended by AB from one side.
questions.explain: Equal angles on one side of a segment give concyclic points.
questions.rule: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary; equal angles on one side of a segment put two points on a common circle.
questions.teaches: Locating or creating cyclic quadrilaterals gives circles and pairs of equal angles for free, so the book encourages the habit.

questions.q: A triangle has vertices (0,0), (10,0) and (0,24). Which point is equally far from all three vertices?
optionExplain: This is the midpoint of one leg only.
Right: it is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, 13 from each vertex.
This is the fourth corner of the rectangle.
