questions.rule: The circumcentre is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet, equidistant from the three vertices.

questions.q: True or false: The three perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle meet in a single point.
questions.explain: That point is the circumcentre, and the concurrency comes for free from the existence of the circumcircle.
questions.rule: The circumcentre is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet, equidistant from the three vertices.

questions.q: A triangle has vertices (0,0), (10,0) and (0,24). What is its circumradius?
optionExplain: Right: the circumcentre (5,12) is 13 from each vertex.
This is the y-coordinate of the circumcentre.
This is the hypotenuse, the diameter.
This is the average of 10 and 24.
questions.explain: Find the circumcentre, then measure to a vertex.
questions.rule: The circumcentre is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet, equidistant from the three vertices.

questions.q: A student says the circumcentre is the intersection of the angle bisectors. What is the correction?
options: The student is right: both give the circumcentre
The circumcentre is the intersection of the medians
The circumcentre is the intersection of the altitudes
The circumcentre comes from perpendicular bisectors of the sides; angle bisectors meet at the incentre
optionExplain: Angle bisectors meet at the incentre.
Medians meet at the centroid.
Altitudes meet at the orthocentre.
Right: two different centres.
questions.explain: Perpendicular bisectors give the circumcentre.
questions.rule: The circumcentre is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet, equidistant from the three vertices.

questions.q: A point equidistant from the three vertices of a triangle is the ____ of the triangle.
questions.explain: That point is the circumcentre.
questions.rule: The circumcentre is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet, equidistant from the three vertices.

questions.q: Three villages not on one straight line need a well equally far from each. Where should it be placed?
options: At the average position of the three villages
At the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the segments joining them
At the midpoint of the longest side
Anywhere inside the triangle
optionExplain: That is the centroid, not equidistant in general.
Right: this point is equidistant from all three, and the three bisectors meet automatically.
That is equidistant from two only, unless the triangle is right-angled.
Only one point is equidistant from all three.
questions.explain: Equidistant from three points means on all their perpendicular bisectors.
questions.rule: The circumcentre is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet, equidistant from the three vertices.
questions.teaches: Because the circumcircle exists, the three perpendicular bisectors of any triangle are concurrent, an interesting fact obtained for free.

questions.q: Which point of a triangle is equally far from all three sides?
options: The intersection of the perpendicular bisectors
The intersection of the medians
The intersection of the three angle bisectors
The intersection of the altitudes
optionExplain: That point is equally far from the vertices.
The centroid balances the triangle but is not equidistant from sides.
Right: bisectors are the lines equidistant from two sides.
The orthocentre has no equal-distance property.

questions.rule: The incentre is where the angle bisectors meet, equidistant from the three sides.

questions.q: The centre of the circle inscribed in a triangle is called the ____.
questions.explain: The incentre is the centre of the incircle.
questions.rule: The incentre is where the angle bisectors meet, equidistant from the three sides.

questions.q: In triangle ABC the incentre is I and angle BAC = 60 degrees. What is angle BAI?
options: 30 degrees
60 degrees
120 degrees
15 degrees
optionExplain: Right: AI is the bisector of angle A.
That is the whole angle A.
That is 180 - 60.
This halves the bisector angle again.

questions.rule: The incentre is where the angle bisectors meet, equidistant from the three sides.

questions.q: Match each triangle centre to the lines whose intersection defines it.
questions.explain: Each centre is a concurrency of one family of lines.
questions.rule: The incentre is where the angle bisectors meet, equidistant from the three sides.

questions.q: A student places the incentre at the point equidistant from the three vertices. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the incentre is equidistant from the vertices
The incentre is the midpoint of the longest side
The incentre is the centroid
That is the circumcentre; the incentre is equidistant from the three sides
optionExplain: It is equidistant from the sides.
It is always inside the triangle.
They coincide only in special triangles.
Right: the two centres differ.
questions.explain: Incentre: sides. Circumcentre: vertices.
questions.rule: The incentre is where the angle bisectors meet, equidistant from the three sides.

questions.q: A triangle has sides 13, 14, 15 and area 84. Its semi-perimeter is 21. What is its inradius, using area equals inradius times semi-perimeter?
optionExplain: Right: 84 divided by 21 is 4.
This divides the area by 14.
This is the area itself.
This divides by the perimeter 42.

questions.rule: The incentre is where the angle bisectors meet, equidistant from the three sides.

questions.q: To prove that a triangle has a circumscribed circle, the book's method begins by doing what?
options: Drawing a very large circle and shrinking it
Measuring the three angles
Assuming one exists and finding where its centre must lie
Proving all triangles are equilateral
optionExplain: That is a trial-and-error procedure, not the method.
Angle measures do not locate a circle.
Right: that locates the candidate point.
That is false.
questions.explain: First explore what the object would look like if it existed. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Assume the object exists, deduce where it must be, then verify that this place works.

questions.q: True or false: Showing that the centre must be an intersection of perpendicular bisectors is enough, by itself, to prove the circumcircle exists.
questions.explain: You must also check the converse: the intersection of two bisectors really is equidistant from all three vertices.
questions.rule: Assume the object exists, deduce where it must be, then verify that this place works.

questions.q: Put the steps in order for proving a triangle has a unique incircle.
items: Suppose an incircle exists and note its centre lies on the angle bisectors
Show that the intersection of any two angle bisectors is equidistant from the three sides
Conclude that this point is the centre of a circle tangent to all three sides
Observe that only one such point exists, so the circle is unique
questions.explain: Necessary properties locate the centre, the converse proves it works, and the forced location gives uniqueness.
questions.rule: Assume the object exists, deduce where it must be, then verify that this place works.

questions.q: A solver says: if the incircle exists its centre is where two angle bisectors meet, so every triangle has an incircle. What is missing?
options: Nothing is missing
The converse: that the intersection of two bisectors is the centre of a circle tangent to all three sides
A proof that all triangles are right-angled
A proof that the sides are equal
optionExplain: The argument only shows where the centre would be if the circle existed.
Right: existence has to be proved, not assumed.
That is false.
No equality of sides is needed.
questions.explain: Locate it, then verify it.
questions.rule: Assume the object exists, deduce where it must be, then verify that this place works.

questions.q: Because the incentre is forced to be one particular point, the incircle is ____.
questions.explain: The location argument shows there cannot be two such circles.
questions.rule: Assume the object exists, deduce where it must be, then verify that this place works.

questions.q: The book hints that to prove the incircle exists one should first show its centre is on two angle bisectors using which fact?
options: The triangle inequality
The law of cosines
Fact 8.2.14, that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency
The Pythagorean theorem for the hypotenuse
optionExplain: It plays no role here.
It is not used in this argument.
Right: equal distances to the sides come from perpendicular radii.
It is not the stated hint.

questions.rule: Assume the object exists, deduce where it must be, then verify that this place works.

questions.q: An altitude of a triangle is a line through a vertex ____ to the opposite side.
questions.explain: That is the definition used in the card. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Altitudes are the perpendicular bisectors of a larger triangle, so they all pass through its circumcentre.

questions.q: The point where the three altitudes of a triangle meet is called the ____.
questions.explain: The orthocentre.
questions.rule: Altitudes are the perpendicular bisectors of a larger triangle, so they all pass through its circumcentre.

questions.q: Lines through the vertices of triangle ABC parallel to the opposite sides form a larger triangle DEF. Side AC of ABC has length 7 and B is on side DE. How long is DE?
optionExplain: This is only half of DE.
Right: ADBC is a parallelogram, so BD = AC = 7, and similarly BE = 7.
This halves AC.
This squares AC.
questions.explain: The vertex B is the midpoint of DE, which has twice the length of AC.
questions.rule: Altitudes are the perpendicular bisectors of a larger triangle, so they all pass through its circumcentre.

questions.q: A student says altitudes lie inside the triangle, so in an obtuse triangle two of them cannot meet. What is the correction?

In an obtuse triangle, altitudes are not defined
They meet at the circumcentre in every triangle
Two of them are parallel

They are concurrent.

questions.rule: Altitudes are the perpendicular bisectors of a larger triangle, so they all pass through its circumcentre.

questions.q: Put the steps of the proof that the altitudes are concurrent in order.
items: Draw through each vertex a line parallel to the opposite side to make a larger triangle
Show each vertex is the midpoint of a side of the larger triangle, using parallelograms

questions.explain: The construction makes altitudes into perpendicular bisectors, whose concurrency is already known.
questions.rule: Altitudes are the perpendicular bisectors of a larger triangle, so they all pass through its circumcentre.

questions.q: Join the midpoints of the sides of triangle ABC to form its medial triangle. What are the altitudes of the medial triangle, in terms of ABC?

The angle bisectors of ABC
The altitudes of ABC
The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of ABC, so they meet at the circumcentre of ABC

Bisectors are not perpendicular to the sides.
They are not the same lines.

questions.rule: Altitudes are the perpendicular bisectors of a larger triangle, so they all pass through its circumcentre.

questions.q: Two overlapping paper rectangles have areas 20 and 15, and the overlap has area 6. What area do the two together cover?
optionExplain: This adds without correcting for the overlap, which is counted twice.
Right: 20 + 15 counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once.
This adds the overlap on top.
This subtracts 15 - 6 from 20 and loses a part.
questions.explain: Count the overlap only once. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Areas of non-overlapping parts add; for overlapping parts, subtract the overlap once.

questions.q: The area of a rectangle is its base times its ____.
questions.explain: This is the axiom that fixes how area is computed.
questions.rule: Areas of non-overlapping parts add; for overlapping parts, subtract the overlap once.

questions.q: Two tiles of areas 30 and 22 are laid so that they overlap in a region of area 8. What area is covered?
optionExplain: This ignores the overlap.
This adds 30 + 22 + 8.
This subtracts 22 - 8 from 30 only.
questions.explain: Sum minus overlap.
questions.rule: Areas of non-overlapping parts add; for overlapping parts, subtract the overlap once.

questions.q: A student finds the area of an L-shaped region by adding the areas of two rectangles that share a 2 by 3 corner square. What did they forget?
options: To subtract the area of the shared square, 6, once
To multiply by 2
To divide by 2
Nothing; area always adds
optionExplain: Right: the overlap is counted twice.
Overlap does not call for doubling.
No halving is involved.
Area adds for parts that do not overlap.
questions.explain: Sum minus overlap.
questions.rule: Areas of non-overlapping parts add; for overlapping parts, subtract the overlap once.

questions.q: True or false: Two congruent triangles placed apart on a page together have twice the area of one of them.
questions.explain: Congruent figures have equal area, and non-overlapping parts add.
questions.rule: Areas of non-overlapping parts add; for overlapping parts, subtract the overlap once.

questions.q: The rule for overlapping parts is the geometric form of which counting principle from an earlier chapter?
options: The Pigeonhole Principle
The Extremal Principle
Mathematical induction
The Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion
optionExplain: Pigeonhole is about existence, not overlaps.
That concerns best cases.
Induction is a proof method.
Right: add the sizes and subtract the overlap.
questions.explain: Area of a union uses inclusion-exclusion.
questions.rule: Areas of non-overlapping parts add; for overlapping parts, subtract the overlap once.
questions.teaches: The overlap rule for areas is the geometric version of the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion (Section 6.3), and area is a function assigning non-negative numbers to figures.

questions.q: A parallelogram has base 10 and height 6. It is pushed sideways so that it leans more, with base and height unchanged. What happens to its area?
options: It stays 60
It grows, because the slanted sides get longer
It shrinks, because the figure is less upright
It cannot be told without the angle
optionExplain: Right: only base and height matter.
Longer slanted sides do not add area when the height stays the same.
The perpendicular height is unchanged.
The base and height determine the area.
questions.explain: Shearing preserves area. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Area depends on base and height only: sliding the top of a parallelogram along its line does not change it.

questions.q: True or false: Two parallelograms with the same base and opposite sides on the same line have equal areas.
questions.explain: This is Example 8.3.1.
questions.rule: Area depends on base and height only: sliding the top of a parallelogram along its line does not change it.

questions.q: A parallelogram has base 12 and height 5. A second parallelogram with the same base lies between the same two parallel lines but leans differently. Its area is ____.
questions.explain: Same base and the same parallels give the same area, 12 times 5 = 60.
questions.rule: Area depends on base and height only: sliding the top of a parallelogram along its line does not change it.

questions.q: A student says a parallelogram with base 10 and slanted side 8 has area 80. What is wrong?
options: The area should be 10 plus 8
Height is the perpendicular distance between the bases, not the slanted side
The area should be half of 80
Nothing is wrong
optionExplain: Area is a product.
Right: the slanted side is longer than the height.
Halving applies to triangles.
The slanted side is not the height.
questions.explain: Use perpendicular height.
questions.rule: Area depends on base and height only: sliding the top of a parallelogram along its line does not change it.

questions.q: True or false: If you slide the top side of a parallelogram far to the right along its line, its area increases.
questions.explain: The area stays the same because the base and the perpendicular height are unchanged.
questions.rule: Area depends on base and height only: sliding the top of a parallelogram along its line does not change it.

questions.q: A parallelogram has sides 13 and 9, and the perpendicular distance between the sides of length 13 is 5. What is its area?
optionExplain: This multiplies the two sides.
This multiplies 9 by the height.
This adds the sides.
Right: base 13 times height 5.
questions.explain: Area of a parallelogram equals base times the perpendicular height.
questions.rule: Area depends on base and height only: sliding the top of a parallelogram along its line does not change it.
questions.teaches: The area of a parallelogram is the product of base and height, where height is the length of the perpendicular from the opposite side to the base.

questions.q: D lies on side BC of triangle ABC with BD one quarter of BC. The area of ABC is 60. What is the area of ABD?
optionExplain: This takes one third.
This takes one half.
Right: same apex A and same height, so the areas are in the ratio of the bases.
This takes one fifth.
questions.explain: Same height means areas follow the bases. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Triangles sharing a vertex with bases on one line have areas in the ratio of their bases.

questions.q: Triangles that share a vertex, with bases on one line, have areas in the same ratio as their ____.
questions.explain: Their heights are equal.
questions.rule: Triangles sharing a vertex with bases on one line have areas in the ratio of their bases.

questions.q: D lies on BC with BD = 4 and BC = 15, and [ABC] = 90. What is [ABD]?
optionExplain: This takes 4/10 of 90.
Right: 4/15 of 90.
This divides 90 by 15.
This takes 15 minus 4 of 15 as 2/3 of the area.
questions.explain: Multiply the whole area by the ratio of bases.
questions.rule: Triangles sharing a vertex with bases on one line have areas in the ratio of their bases.

questions.q: A student says triangles ABD and ACD have areas in the ratio AB : AC. What is the correction?
options: The areas are in the ratio of the bases BD : DC on the common line
The ratio is AB squared : AC squared
The areas are always equal
The ratio is the ratio of angles at A
optionExplain: Right: the shared height is from A to line BC.
Squares of sides do not appear.
They are equal only if D is the midpoint.
Angles do not decide it.
questions.explain: Compare bases on the common line.
questions.rule: Triangles sharing a vertex with bases on one line have areas in the ratio of their bases.

questions.q: True or false: A median of a triangle cuts it into two triangles of equal area.
questions.explain: The two triangles share a vertex and their bases are equal, so their areas are equal.
questions.rule: Triangles sharing a vertex with bases on one line have areas in the ratio of their bases.

questions.q: A triangle has two sides of lengths 7 and 10 with a 30 degree angle between them. What is its area?
optionExplain: This forgets the factor sin 30 = 1/2 or the half.
This is the product of the sides.
Right: half of 7 times 10 times sin 30, which is 35 over 2.
This halves twice.
questions.explain: Area equals half the product of two sides and the sine of the included angle.
questions.rule: Triangles sharing a vertex with bases on one line have areas in the ratio of their bases.
questions.teaches: Problem 8.3.32(a): if two sides of a triangle are a and b with angle theta between them, the area is one half a b sin theta.

questions.q: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. What is the hypotenuse?
optionExplain: This adds the legs.
This averages the legs.
This multiplies the legs.
questions.explain: The squares on the legs add up to the square on the hypotenuse. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Turn the equation into areas, split the hypotenuse square by the perpendicular from the right angle, and shear.

questions.q: The sum of the squares of the legs of a right triangle equals the square of the ____.
questions.explain: That is the Pythagorean theorem.
questions.rule: Turn the equation into areas, split the hypotenuse square by the perpendicular from the right angle, and shear.

questions.q: A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. A student computes the other leg as the square root of 13 squared plus 5 squared. What is the correct leg?
options: sqrt(194)
optionExplain: This adds the squares, the error in the question.
This subtracts the lengths 13 - 5.
This adds 13 and 5.
questions.explain: Subtract the square on the known leg from the square on the hypotenuse.
questions.rule: Turn the equation into areas, split the hypotenuse square by the perpendicular from the right angle, and shear.

questions.q: Put the steps of the shearing proof of the Pythagorean theorem in order.
items: Restate the equation as: the two leg squares have total area equal to the hypotenuse square
Draw through the right-angle vertex a line perpendicular to the hypotenuse, splitting its square into two rectangles
Shear each rectangle and the leg square next to it into parallelograms with a common side
Show the matching parallelograms are congruent, so the areas are equal
questions.explain: The perpendicular splits the large square, shears preserve area, and congruence completes the match.
questions.rule: Turn the equation into areas, split the hypotenuse square by the perpendicular from the right angle, and shear.

questions.q: A student says the shearing picture settles the proof because it is obvious that the parallelograms are congruent. What does the book say?
options: It is obvious and needs no further work
The picture is wrong
It is not quite obvious; it needs angle chasing to find congruent copies of the original triangle
Only algebra can prove it

The picture is fine; the congruence needs justification.

Angle chasing and congruence suffice.
questions.explain: A picture must be backed by a proof of each claimed congruence.
questions.rule: Turn the equation into areas, split the hypotenuse square by the perpendicular from the right angle, and shear.

questions.q: Why does the book recast a squared-sides equation as a statement about areas?
options: Because areas are easier to measure with a ruler
An equation of lengths times lengths can be understood so far only through area
Because the theorem is false for lengths
Because squares are not defined for lengths
optionExplain: Measuring is not the reason.
Right: area is the geometric concept that multiplies lengths.
The theorem is true for lengths.
Squares of lengths are fine; the issue is geometric meaning.
questions.explain: Products of lengths point to areas.
questions.rule: Turn the equation into areas, split the hypotenuse square by the perpendicular from the right angle, and shear.

questions.q: Two squares of side 7 each contain four right triangles with legs 3 and 4. One square also holds a square of side 3 and one of side 4. What is the area of the remaining square in the other?
optionExplain: Right: 49 - 24 = 25, matching 9 + 16.
This is the whole square.
This is the area of the four triangles.
This is the area of two triangles.

questions.rule: Equal big squares minus the same four triangles leave a squared plus b squared equal to c squared.

questions.q: The dissection proof dates from ancient ____.
questions.explain: The book credits ancient India with this cut-and-paste proof.
questions.rule: Equal big squares minus the same four triangles leave a squared plus b squared equal to c squared.

optionExplain: This is the whole big square.
This is four triangles.
Right: 289 - 4 times 30.
This is two triangles.
questions.explain: Big square minus four triangles.
questions.rule: Equal big squares minus the same four triangles leave a squared plus b squared equal to c squared.

questions.q: A student says the two big squares in the dissection proof need not be congruent. What is the correction?
options: They must have side c
One must be larger than the other
They need only be similar

questions.explain: Equal areas of the same square give the theorem.
questions.rule: Equal big squares minus the same four triangles leave a squared plus b squared equal to c squared.

questions.q: True or false: In the dissection, each big square contains four copies of the original right triangle.
questions.explain: Four triangles in each square are cut away to leave the squares on the sides.
questions.rule: Equal big squares minus the same four triangles leave a squared plus b squared equal to c squared.

questions.q: In the dissection proof, which quantity is what the equal squares allow us to compare after removing the triangles?
options: the perimeters of the two squares
a squared plus b squared on one side and c squared on the other
the angles of the triangle
the lengths of the legs only

questions.rule: Equal big squares minus the same four triangles leave a squared plus b squared equal to c squared.

questions.q: A triangle has sides 3, 4 and 5. Another has sides 6, 8 and 10. What is true about their shapes?
options: They have the same shape; one is the other enlarged by 2
They are congruent
They have different shapes
Nothing can be said without angles

Congruent triangles have equal sides.
Proportional sides give the same shape.
The side ratio is already enough.

questions.rule: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.

questions.q: Triangles that have the same shape, with equal angles and proportional sides, are called ____.

questions.rule: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.

questions.q: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF with AB = 6, DE = 9 and BC = 8. What is EF?

questions.rule: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.

options: There is no problem; any pairing is allowed
AB corresponds to EF

AB can be paired with the longest side always

questions.rule: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.

questions.q: True or false: If two triangles are similar with sides in the ratio 1 : 3, their corresponding angles are in the ratio 1 : 3.

questions.rule: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.

questions.q: A midline cuts a triangle into a small triangle and a trapezoid; the small triangle is similar to the whole with ratio 1 to 2. How does a side of the small triangle compare with its corresponding side?

It is twice as long
It is equal
It cannot be compared

questions.rule: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.

questions.q: Two triangles each have angles of 40 and 70 degrees. Are they necessarily similar?

questions.rule: Equal angles, proportional sides, or proportional sides around an equal included angle each prove similarity.

Sides 3 and 5 with a 60 degree angle not between them, and sides 6 and 10 likewise placed

The ratio 3 : 6 differs from 5 : 10

Proportional SAS is not a valid test

questions.rule: Equal angles, proportional sides, or proportional sides around an equal included angle each prove similarity.

They share a vertex, so they are congruent
Their sides are automatically proportional

questions.rule: Equal angles, proportional sides, or proportional sides around an equal included angle each prove similarity.

questions.q: A line parallel to BC meets AB at D and AC at E, with AD = 3, AB = 9 and AE = 4. What is AC?

optionExplain: DB is not a side of triangle ADE.

questions.q: If D and E are the midpoints of AB and AC, then DE is ____ as long as BC.

questions.rule: A parallel to one side cuts off a triangle similar to the whole, and proportional division implies parallelism.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, E and F are midpoints of AC and AB. What is the segment EF called, and what does it do?

questions.q: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8 and hypotenuse 10. How long is the altitude from the right angle to the hypotenuse?

a and b should both be squared with x

questions.q: A problem asks you to prove that AB/CD = EF/GH. Which tool does the book suggest first?

Counting regions

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, a problem that involves ratios almost certainly needs an investigation of similar triangles.
