questions.q: In the trisection figure a student says [FIA] : [FBI] = AI : IB. What is wrong?
options: The ratio is correct
The ratio is IA : IB squared
The triangles have no common vertex
The triangles share vertex I and have bases FA and FB on one line, so the ratio is AF : FB
optionExplain: AI and IB are not bases on a common line.
Squares do not appear.
They share vertex I.
Right: the bases must lie on the common line.
questions.explain: The ratio is of bases on the shared line.
questions.rule: Name small areas, chain base ratios through shared vertices, and read segment ratios back from area ratios.

questions.q: True or false: Points A, I, D lie on one line, and triangles CIA and CID have areas 9 and 12. Then AI : ID = 3 : 4.
questions.explain: The triangles share vertex C and have bases AI and ID on one line, so the areas are in the ratio of the bases.
questions.rule: Name small areas, chain base ratios through shared vertices, and read segment ratios back from area ratios.

questions.q: In the trisection puzzle the book writes the area as 2y instead of y. Why?
options: Because the triangle has two sides equal
To avoid fractions later in the computation
Because 2y is the area of a rectangle
Because areas must be even
optionExplain: No such fact.
Right: the book chose it for convenience.
It is a triangle.
No such rule.
questions.explain: Choose labels that keep numbers whole.
questions.rule: Name small areas, chain base ratios through shared vertices, and read segment ratios back from area ratios.
questions.teaches: The book writes [DIB] = 2y instead of y to avoid fractions later, a small piece of strategy for area bookkeeping.

questions.q: Cevians are drawn from the vertices of a triangle to first trisection points of the opposite sides, forming a small inner triangle. Which fraction of the whole is it?
optionExplain: That is too large.
A natural guess, but not it.
Right: the famous answer.
A guess from dividing each side into thirds.
questions.explain: The inner triangle has area one seventh. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The three cevians to first trisection points cut each other in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3, and the inner triangle has one seventh of the area.

questions.q: True or false: In the trisection figure each cevian is divided in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3.
questions.explain: For example FI : IH : HC = 1 : 3 : 3.
questions.rule: The three cevians to first trisection points cut each other in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3, and the inner triangle has one seventh of the area.

questions.q: The area of triangle ABC is 70 and the cevians go to first trisection points. What is the area of the small triangle GHI?
optionExplain: Right: 70 divided by 7.
This divides by 5.
This divides by 3.
This divides by 10.
questions.explain: The inner triangle is one seventh.
questions.rule: The three cevians to first trisection points cut each other in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3, and the inner triangle has one seventh of the area.

questions.q: If cevian FC has length 28, then FI, the first part, has length ____.
questions.explain: The parts are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3, so FI = 28/7.
questions.rule: The three cevians to first trisection points cut each other in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3, and the inner triangle has one seventh of the area.

questions.q: A student says the three cevians divide each other like medians, in the ratio 2 : 1, so the centre triangle is empty. What is wrong?
options: The cevians to trisection points are not concurrent; they form a small triangle and divide in ratio 1 : 3 : 3
The cevians are concurrent at a point
The ratio is 1 : 1 : 1
The inner triangle has area 1/3
optionExplain: Right: Ceva's product is 1/8 there.
They form a triangle GHI.
The ratio is 1 : 3 : 3.
It is 1/7.
questions.explain: Trisection cevians form a triangle.
questions.rule: The three cevians to first trisection points cut each other in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3, and the inner triangle has one seventh of the area.

questions.q: In a rectangle ABCD the midpoints of AB, BC, CD, DA are E, F, G, H. Lines AF, BG, CH, DE form an inner quadrilateral. If the rectangle's area is 40, what is the quadrilateral's area?
optionExplain: This is one quarter.
Right: one fifth, as in the easier problem the book poses.
This is one half.
This is one eighth.
questions.explain: The inner region has one fifth of the area.
questions.rule: The three cevians to first trisection points cut each other in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3, and the inner triangle has one seventh of the area.
questions.teaches: Problem 8.5.22 gives the easier rectangle version: lines from vertices to midpoints form an inner quadrilateral with area [ABCD]/5.

questions.q: For the three medians of a triangle, what is the product of the ratios AF/FB, BD/DC and CE/EA?
optionExplain: This confuses the ratio 2 : 1 of the centroid.
This is the trisection product.
No ratio is zero.
Right: each ratio is 1 because each foot is a midpoint.
questions.explain: Medians give ratios of 1. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Three cevians concur exactly when the product of the three ratios around the triangle equals 1.

questions.q: True or false: By Ceva's theorem, three cevians are concurrent exactly when the product of the three ratios around the triangle equals 1.
questions.explain: That is the statement of the theorem, with its converse.
questions.rule: Three cevians concur exactly when the product of the three ratios around the triangle equals 1.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, AF/FB = 2/3 and BD/DC = 3/4. For AD, BE, CF to be concurrent, CE/EA must equal ____.
questions.explain: The product must be 1, so CE/EA = 1 divided by (2/3 times 3/4) = 2.
questions.rule: Three cevians concur exactly when the product of the three ratios around the triangle equals 1.

questions.q: A student multiplies AF/FB times DC/BD times CE/EA and gets 1, concluding concurrency. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: any three ratios will do
The product should be 0
One ratio is inverted; the product must use BD/DC, going around the triangle
Ceva needs areas
optionExplain: The product must follow the theorem's pattern.
It should be 1.
Right: the order of the points matters.
It uses lengths.
questions.explain: Follow the points around the triangle.
questions.rule: Three cevians concur exactly when the product of the three ratios around the triangle equals 1.

questions.q: For the three angle bisectors, the angle bisector theorem gives AF/FB = AC/BC, BD/DC = AB/AC and CE/EA = BC/AB. What does Ceva then show?
options: The product is 2, so they are not concurrent
The product is 1, so the angle bisectors are concurrent
They are concurrent only in isosceles triangles
Nothing, since bisectors are not cevians
optionExplain: The factors cancel to 1.
Right: this is one of the concurrencies Problem 8.4.13 asks you to prove with Ceva.
They concur in every triangle.
They are cevians.
questions.explain: Ceva reproves the concurrency of bisectors, medians and altitudes.
questions.rule: Three cevians concur exactly when the product of the three ratios around the triangle equals 1.
questions.teaches: Problem 8.4.13 asks you to use Ceva's theorem to reprove that the angle bisectors, medians and altitudes of a triangle are each concurrent.

questions.q: If 3/7 equals 6/14, what is (3 + 6)/(7 + 14)?
options: 9/21 differs from 3/7
6/14 only when the numbers are equal
optionExplain: 9/21 reduces to 3/7.
A guess.
It equals 3/7.
Right: adding two equal fractions this way keeps the ratio.
questions.explain: If two ratios are equal, adding numerators and denominators keeps the ratio. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Write each ratio as a ratio of areas, add or subtract them with the proportion lemma, and the product cancels to 1.

questions.q: True or false: The lemma says that if x/y = a/b then x/y also equals (x + a)/(y + b).
questions.explain: It also equals (x - a)/(y - b).
questions.rule: Write each ratio as a ratio of areas, add or subtract them with the proportion lemma, and the product cancels to 1.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Ceva proof in order.
items: Suppose the cevians are concurrent at G and name the six small areas
Write each length ratio as a ratio of two areas
Rewrite each ratio with the proportion lemma as a ratio of sums or differences of areas
Multiply the three ratios and see that they cancel to 1
questions.explain: Concurrency makes the areas available; the lemma reshapes them so the product telescopes.
questions.rule: Write each ratio as a ratio of areas, add or subtract them with the proportion lemma, and the product cancels to 1.

questions.q: A student claims adding the same number to the numerator and the denominator leaves a fraction unchanged. What is the actual condition in the lemma?
options: The added numerator and denominator must be in the same ratio as the original fraction
It always works
It works only for fractions below 1
It works only when the numbers are equal
optionExplain: Right: x/y = a/b.
Adding 1 to 1/2 and 1/2 gives 2/3.
No such restriction.
That is a different statement.
questions.explain: The added fraction must equal the original.
questions.rule: Write each ratio as a ratio of areas, add or subtract them with the proportion lemma, and the product cancels to 1.

questions.q: How does the book suggest proving the converse of Ceva's theorem?
options: By induction on the number of cevians
By coordinates only
By contradiction, with a phantom point where the cevian through the third vertex meets the opposite side
It cannot be proved
optionExplain: Not suggested.
The hint is contradiction.
Right: the hint is proof by contradiction.
It is a stated exercise.
questions.explain: Assume the product is 1 but the cevians fail to concur, and find a phantom.
questions.rule: Write each ratio as a ratio of areas, add or subtract them with the proportion lemma, and the product cancels to 1.
questions.teaches: The converse of Ceva's theorem is left as an exercise with the hint: proof by contradiction (Problem 8.4.12).

questions.q: A light rod has weights 4 and 2 at its ends and balances on a pivot. How do the distances from the pivot to the ends compare?
options: Both are equally far
The end with weight 4 is half as far from the pivot as the end with weight 2
The heavier end is farther
The distance is the sum of the weights
optionExplain: Unequal weights give unequal distances.
Right: weight times distance is equal.
The heavier end is nearer.
Weights multiply distances.
questions.explain: Weight times distance must be equal. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Choose weights so each cevian foot balances, then read ratios along each cevian from the weights.

questions.q: At the balance point, the product of weight and ____ is equal for the two ends.
questions.explain: That is the lever rule used by the method.
questions.rule: Choose weights so each cevian foot balances, then read ratios along each cevian from the weights.

questions.q: Weights 3 at A and 5 at B balance at F on segment AB. What is AF : FB?
optionExplain: Right: 3 times AF equals 5 times FB, so AF : FB = 5 : 3.
This inverts the ratio.
Unequal weights do not balance in the middle.
No reason for this ratio.
questions.explain: The larger weight is nearer the pivot.
questions.rule: Choose weights so each cevian foot balances, then read ratios along each cevian from the weights.

questions.q: True or false: A solver places the balance point of a lever closer to the lighter weight than to the heavier one. This is correct.
questions.explain: Weight times distance must be equal, so the heavier weight sits closer to the pivot.
questions.rule: Choose weights so each cevian foot balances, then read ratios along each cevian from the weights.

questions.q: Why does the book call the method of weights seems like magic rather than giving it as a proof?
options: It gives wrong answers
It uses calculus
It only works on right triangles
It rests on informal physical intuition, and a rigorous justification is asked of the reader
optionExplain: It works on the examples.
It does not.
It works generally.
Right: Problem 8.4.21 asks you to prove it.
questions.explain: A physical analogy needs a proof.
questions.rule: Choose weights so each cevian foot balances, then read ratios along each cevian from the weights.
questions.teaches: The book finds ratios in the trisection puzzle more easily with weights than with areas, calls the method plausible, and asks for a rigorous proof and whether it can prove Ceva's theorem.

questions.q: You must prove that two lines are perpendicular and have no obvious right angle. What configuration is a good thing to aim for?
options: A triangle with the two lines as bisectors
A parallelogram with equal diagonals
A triangle with the two lines as legs, inscribed in a circle whose diameter is the third side
Two lines with equal slopes
optionExplain: That produces no right angle.
Equal diagonals give a rectangle, a different goal.
Right: an inscribed right triangle.
That gives parallel lines.
questions.explain: Inscribed right triangles give perpendicularity. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: To prove two lines perpendicular, try to make them the legs of a right triangle inscribed in a circle with a known diameter.

questions.q: True or false: In this example angle chasing alone is expected to fail because one of the lines of interest is a median.
questions.explain: Medians do not yield useful angular information without messy trigonometry.
questions.rule: To prove two lines perpendicular, try to make them the legs of a right triangle inscribed in a circle with a known diameter.

questions.q: In Example 8.4.4, why does D lie on the circle with diameter AB?
options: Because D is the midpoint of AB
Because AB equals AC
Because F is the midpoint of ED
Because triangle ADB has a right angle at D
optionExplain: D is on BC.
That gives the isosceles shape, not the circle.
F plays no role here.
Right: AD is perpendicular to BC.
questions.explain: A right angle at D means D is on the circle with diameter AB.
questions.rule: To prove two lines perpendicular, try to make them the legs of a right triangle inscribed in a circle with a known diameter.

questions.q: Put the strategic steps for proving AF perpendicular to BE in order.
items: Let G be the intersection of AF and BE
Note triangle ADB is a right triangle inscribed in the circle with diameter AB
Show A, G, D, B are concyclic by proving angle GAD = angle GBD
Conclude angle AGB is a right angle, so AF is perpendicular to BE
questions.explain: The penultimate step is concyclicity, which makes AGB an inscribed right triangle.
questions.rule: To prove two lines perpendicular, try to make them the legs of a right triangle inscribed in a circle with a known diameter.

questions.q: Where does the isosceles hypothesis AB = AC first enter the solution?
options: In the fact that D, the foot from A, is the midpoint of BC
In the fact that F is the midpoint of ED
In the fact that E is on AC
It never enters
optionExplain: Right: the first time the book uses the hypothesis.
F is a midpoint by definition.
E is a foot of a perpendicular.
It enters through D.
questions.explain: Notice where each hypothesis is used.
questions.rule: To prove two lines perpendicular, try to make them the legs of a right triangle inscribed in a circle with a known diameter.
questions.teaches: D is the midpoint of BC because ABC is isosceles, the first time the isosceles hypothesis is used; this is what makes DE a candidate midline.

questions.q: A diagram has two midpoints in a configuration that would work if a certain segment were a midline. What does wishful thinking suggest?
options: Give up on the midpoints
Measure the segment
Add a line that makes the wished-for midline exist
Replace midpoints by random points
optionExplain: They are the structure to use.
Measuring is not a proof.
Right: pretend it is there and draw what makes it true.
Random points lose the structure.
questions.explain: Draw the object you wish for. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: When a missing midline would help, draw the parallel that makes it exist; matching points in similar triangles give similar subtriangles.

questions.q: True or false: In the example the auxiliary line BH is drawn parallel to DE.
questions.explain: That makes DE a midline of triangle BHC.
questions.rule: When a missing midline would help, draw the parallel that makes it exist; matching points in similar triangles give similar subtriangles.

questions.q: Triangle ABC is similar to DEF. X on AB and Y on DE divide them in the same ratio. Then triangle AXC is similar to triangle ____.
questions.explain: Corresponding points give corresponding subtriangles.
questions.rule: When a missing midline would help, draw the parallel that makes it exist; matching points in similar triangles give similar subtriangles.

questions.q: A student claims triangle BHC is similar to AED only because both are right triangles. What is the actual reason?
options: Right triangles are always similar
The sides around the right angles are proportional, since DE is a midline and the two triangles correspond by matching points
They share a side
Their hypotenuses are equal
optionExplain: Right triangles can have different shapes.
Right: more than one right angle is needed.
They do not.
Not true here.
questions.explain: A right angle alone is not enough.
questions.rule: When a missing midline would help, draw the parallel that makes it exist; matching points in similar triangles give similar subtriangles.

questions.q: Why is the midline construction natural here?
options: It makes the triangle equilateral
D is already the midpoint of BC and F the midpoint of ED, so a midline would bring a second midpoint into play
It removes the need for a circle
Because lines through B are always parallel to DE
optionExplain: It does not.
Right: it makes both midpoints useful.
The circle is still needed.
Only the chosen line is.
questions.explain: Use the midpoints the problem gives.
questions.rule: When a missing midline would help, draw the parallel that makes it exist; matching points in similar triangles give similar subtriangles.
questions.teaches: Similar subtriangles (Problem 8.3.30): in similar triangles ABC and DEF, points X on AB and Y on DE dividing them in the same ratio give similar triangles AXC and DYF.

questions.q: A triangle has orthocentre at (0,0) and circumcentre at (3,4). Where is its centroid likely to lie?
options: At the midpoint of that segment
Off that segment, at random
At the circumcentre
On the segment joining them, two thirds of the way from the orthocentre
optionExplain: That would make the ratio 1 : 1.
The three points are collinear.
The centroid and circumcentre coincide only in special triangles.
Right: the centroid divides HK in a 2 : 1 ratio.
questions.explain: H, centroid, K are collinear. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: H, the centroid and K lie on a line, and the centroid is twice as far from H as from K.

questions.q: The line through the orthocentre, centroid and circumcentre of a triangle is called the ____ line.
questions.explain: It is named after Euler.
questions.rule: H, the centroid and K lie on a line, and the centroid is twice as far from H as from K.

questions.q: A triangle has orthocentre H = (0,0) and circumcentre K = (3,4). What is the centroid?
optionExplain: This is the midpoint.
This is one third of the way.
Right: two thirds of the way from H to K.
This is K.
questions.explain: Move two thirds of the way from H toward K.
questions.rule: H, the centroid and K lie on a line, and the centroid is twice as far from H as from K.

questions.q: True or false: A student says the centroid divides the segment HK from the orthocentre to the circumcentre so that HM : MK = 1 : 2. This is correct.
questions.explain: The centroid is nearer the circumcentre: HM : MK = 2 : 1.
questions.rule: H, the centroid and K lie on a line, and the centroid is twice as far from H as from K.

questions.q: Place the origin at the circumcentre. The orthocentre then has position A + B + C. What is the ratio HM : MK, where M = (A + B + C)/3?
optionExplain: Right: M is H/3 from K, so MK is one third and HM two thirds.
This inverts the ratio.
M is not the midpoint.
That would put M at three quarters.
questions.explain: With the circumcentre at the origin, H = 3M.
questions.rule: H, the centroid and K lie on a line, and the centroid is twice as far from H as from K.
questions.teaches: With the origin at the circumcentre, the orthocentre is the vector sum of the vertices (Problem 8.5.24a), so the centroid is H divided by 3.

questions.q: Which auxiliary triangle is the book's crux move in proving the Euler line?
options: The orthic triangle of the feet of altitudes
The medial triangle, formed by joining the midpoints of the sides
The triangle of the three vertices of the circumcircle
A right triangle on the longest side
optionExplain: That appears in a problem, not here.
Right: it connects the circumcentre and orthocentre.
That is ABC itself.
Not used.
questions.explain: The medial triangle is the crux. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The medial triangle links H and K as sister points of similar triangles; proportional SAS shows the two triangles are similar, hence collinearity.

questions.q: True or false: In the proof, K is the orthocentre of the medial triangle.
questions.explain: That is Problem 8.2.29(b).
questions.rule: The medial triangle links H and K as sister points of similar triangles; proportional SAS shows the two triangles are similar, hence collinearity.

questions.q: In the proof EK/AH = 1/2. If AH = 10, then EK = ____.
questions.explain: The medial triangle has half the size.
questions.rule: The medial triangle links H and K as sister points of similar triangles; proportional SAS shows the two triangles are similar, hence collinearity.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Euler line proof in order.
items: Draw the medial triangle and note its circumcentre K is its orthocentre and its centroid is M
Show angle HAM = angle KEM because AH and EK are parallel, and that EK/AH = 1/2 and EM/MA = 1/2
Conclude triangles HAM and KEM are similar by proportional SAS, so H, M, K are collinear
questions.explain: The angle equality and the two ratios together give proportional SAS.
questions.rule: The medial triangle links H and K as sister points of similar triangles; proportional SAS shows the two triangles are similar, hence collinearity.

questions.q: A student uses proportional SAS but the equal angle is not between the proportional sides. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: any equal angle works
The sides cannot be proportional
The triangles are congruent
The similarity is not justified; the equal angle must lie between the proportional sides
optionExplain: Only the included angle.
They can.
They are not.
Right: in the proof angle HAM lies between AH and AM.
questions.explain: Proportional SAS needs the included angle.
questions.rule: The medial triangle links H and K as sister points of similar triangles; proportional SAS shows the two triangles are similar, hence collinearity.

questions.q: What two facts about the figure give the proportional sides in triangles HAM and KEM?
options: The triangle inequality and vertical angles
The law of sines and ASA
The similarity of the medial triangle to ABC with ratio 1 : 2, and the centroid theorem EM : MA = 1 : 2
Equal medians and altitudes
optionExplain: These are not used.
Not used.
Right: EK/AH = 1/2 and EM/MA = 1/2.
Not given.
questions.explain: Two ratios of 1 : 2 give proportionality.
questions.rule: The medial triangle links H and K as sister points of similar triangles; proportional SAS shows the two triangles are similar, hence collinearity.
questions.teaches: The book calls HM and KM sister segments, each connecting the orthocentre and centroid of similar triangles, which is why proportional SAS settles the collinearity.

questions.q: Three circles overlap in pairs, so each pair has a common chord. How many of the three chords pass through one point?
options: All three
Only two, in general
None
Exactly one chord passes through the other two chords' midpoints
optionExplain: Right: the common chords are concurrent.
The third passes through the same point.
They share a point.
Midpoints play no role.
questions.explain: The three chords are concurrent. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Common chords of three pairwise intersecting circles are concurrent.

questions.q: True or false: Ceva's theorem is the obvious first tool for this problem, but the figure has no triangle and is already crowded.
questions.explain: The book sets it aside and imitates the centroid proof instead.
questions.rule: Common chords of three pairwise intersecting circles are concurrent.

questions.q: Chords AB and CD of one circle meet at X with AX = 6, XB = 2 and CX = 3. Then XD = ____.
questions.explain: Power of a Point: 6 times 2 = 12 = 3 times XD.
questions.rule: Common chords of three pairwise intersecting circles are concurrent.

questions.q: A student says the three chords must be concurrent because there are three circles. What does the book do instead?
options: It studies two chords first, finds their meeting point, then shows the third chord passes through it
It measures several drawings
It assumes the chords are medians
It shows the chords are equal in length
optionExplain: Right: the argument is built on the intersection of two chords.
A proof is required.
Chords are not medians.
Equal length is not the claim.
questions.explain: Intersect two, then test the third.
questions.rule: Common chords of three pairwise intersecting circles are concurrent.

questions.q: Define the power of P with respect to a circle with centre O and radius r as (OP + r)(OP - r). A circle has r = 5 and OP = 4. What is the power?
optionExplain: This drops the sign.
This squares 9.
This subtracts the lengths only.
Right: (4 + 5)(4 - 5) = -9; P is inside, so the power is negative.
questions.explain: Power is OP squared minus r squared.
questions.rule: Common chords of three pairwise intersecting circles are concurrent.
questions.teaches: The book generalises: the radical axis of two circles is the set of points with equal power, a line perpendicular to the line of centres; for three circles the radical axes are concurrent, coincide or are parallel (Problem 8.4.24).

questions.q: To show that three lines are concurrent after finding the meeting point X of two of them, what is the book's aim for the third line?
options: To show it is parallel to the others
To show it is perpendicular to the others
To show it passes through X
To show it is the longest
optionExplain: Parallel lines would not concur.
No perpendicularity is needed.
Right: that is what concurrency means here.
Length is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Show the third passes through X. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Assume the third chord misses X, build phantom points on a line through X, and POP forces them to coincide with the real intersection point.

questions.q: True or false: In the argument, the phantom points E1 and E2 are intersections of a false line through F and X with the two circles.
questions.explain: They stand in for E.
questions.rule: Assume the third chord misses X, build phantom points on a line through X, and POP forces them to coincide with the real intersection point.

questions.q: In the argument, FX times XE1 = 12 and FX = 4. Then XE1 = ____.
questions.explain: Divide the product by FX.
questions.rule: Assume the third chord misses X, build phantom points on a line through X, and POP forces them to coincide with the real intersection point.

questions.q: Put the steps of the phantom argument in order.
items: Let X be the intersection of chords AB and CD, which are chords of the third circle
Apply POP to find AX times XB equals CX times XD
Draw a false line through F and X meeting the two circles again at phantom points E1 and E2
Show XE1 = XE2, so the phantoms coincide with the real point E
questions.explain: Use POP twice and combine with the third chord equality.
questions.rule: Assume the third chord misses X, build phantom points on a line through X, and POP forces them to coincide with the real intersection point.

questions.q: A student draws the false line from F so that it misses X and meets AB and CD at two different points. What does the book say about this approach?
options: It always works
It produces POP equalities but no easy algebraic contradiction; the line through X is better
It proves the claim at once
It is invalid since lines cannot miss X
optionExplain: The book says it is hard.
Right: the book says it is hard to find a contradiction.
There is no contradiction yet.
It is a legitimate attempt, just harder.
questions.explain: Choose the false line that uses points you have equations for.
questions.rule: Assume the third chord misses X, build phantom points on a line through X, and POP forces them to coincide with the real intersection point.

questions.q: Why does the book say the false line is really two line segments in the computer drawing?
options: Because lines cannot be drawn on a computer
Because the circles are tangent
Because a true straight line from F through X does pass through E; the broken line is the price of accurate drawing of a false configuration
Because E1 and E2 are equal
optionExplain: They can.
The circles intersect.
Right: a genuine straight line would hit E.
They are different in the false picture.
questions.explain: A false configuration cannot be drawn straight.
questions.rule: Assume the third chord misses X, build phantom points on a line through X, and POP forces them to coincide with the real intersection point.
questions.teaches: The book notes that the dashed false line is actually two segments, since a straight line through F and X really does pass through E; that is the price of accurate computer-drawn diagrams.

questions.q: The sum 1 + 2 + ... + 100 is written with its reverse underneath. What is the sum of each column?
optionExplain: Right: for example 1 + 100, 2 + 99, and so on.
This is the last term.
This forgets the first term.
This is the total, not a column.
questions.explain: Reversal makes all columns equal. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: If a rearrangement leaves the essential data unchanged but makes the figure symmetric, solve the symmetric version.

questions.q: True or false: Rearranging the six isosceles triangles around the centre in a different order changes the radius of the circle.
questions.explain: The triangles keep their legs equal to the radius and their bases, so the circle is the same.
questions.rule: If a rearrangement leaves the essential data unchanged but makes the figure symmetric, solve the symmetric version.

questions.q: A hexagon with sides alternating 1 and 2 is inscribed in a circle. Which is the radius?
options: square root of 7, about 2.65
square root of 3, about 1.73
square root of 7/3, about 1.53
optionExplain: This is the length XZ.
This is r squared.
No step gives this.
Right: XZ squared = 7 and XZ squared = 3 r squared.
questions.explain: Law of cosines in triangle XYZ, then in the isosceles triangle XOZ.
questions.rule: If a rearrangement leaves the essential data unchanged but makes the figure symmetric, solve the symmetric version.

questions.q: A student says the alternating hexagon must have a different radius from the original because its sides sit in different places. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the sides move, so the radius moves
The six isosceles triangles are the same, so the circle is unchanged
The radius doubles
The hexagon becomes a square
optionExplain: Radius depends on the triangles, not their order.
Right: only the order of the triangles changed.
No reason.
It stays a hexagon.
questions.explain: A rearrangement of the same pieces keeps their dimensions.
questions.rule: If a rearrangement leaves the essential data unchanged but makes the figure symmetric, solve the symmetric version.

questions.q: In the rearranged hexagon, one third of it, quadrilateral XOZY, has angle XOZ equal to ____ degrees.
questions.explain: A third of the full turn of 360 degrees is 120.
questions.rule: If a rearrangement leaves the essential data unchanged but makes the figure symmetric, solve the symmetric version.

questions.q: The terms 3, 7, 11, ..., 39 are added (ten terms). Writing the sum and its reverse beneath, each column sums to 42. What is the total?
optionExplain: This forgets that the reversed sum was added as well.
This is one column.
Right: twice the sum is 10 times 42, so the sum is 210.
This adds 3 and 39 ten times.
questions.explain: Twice the sum equals the number of terms times the column sum.
questions.rule: If a rearrangement leaves the essential data unchanged but makes the figure symmetric, solve the symmetric version.
questions.teaches: The reversed sum creates a symmetry under rotation about the centre of the array, and what makes it useful is that the sums of the columns are identical.

questions.q: A transformation keeps every distance between points unchanged. What is it called?
options: A homothety
An inversion
A dilation by 2
A rigid motion
optionExplain: A homothety scales distances.
Inversion changes distances drastically.
It doubles distances.
Right: rigid motions preserve length.
questions.explain: Rigid means length-preserving. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Rigid motions keep every distance; they are translations, reflections, glide reflections and rotations.

questions.q: A transformation is a mapping from the points of the plane to ____.
questions.explain: It maps the plane to the plane.
questions.rule: Rigid motions keep every distance; they are translations, reflections, glide reflections and rotations.

questions.q: Sort each transformation by whether it is a rigid motion.

items.t: Translation
Reflection in a line
Rotation about a point
Glide reflection
Enlargement by 2 from a centre
Inversion in a circle

questions.explain: Rigid motions preserve lengths; enlargements and inversions do not.
questions.rule: Rigid motions keep every distance; they are translations, reflections, glide reflections and rotations.

questions.q: A student says a homothety with ratio 1/2 is a rigid motion because it keeps the shape. What is wrong?
options: It is rigid; shape-preserving means length-preserving
It halves distances, so it does not preserve length
It is not a transformation
It is a glide reflection
optionExplain: Shape is kept but not size.
Right: it preserves ratios of distances, not distances.
It maps the plane to itself.
Not at all.
questions.explain: Rigid means same size as well as same shape.
questions.rule: Rigid motions keep every distance; they are translations, reflections, glide reflections and rotations.

questions.q: True or false: The composition of two rigid motions, such as a rotation followed by a translation, is again one of the four types of rigid motion.
questions.explain: The book states that the composition of any two of the four types is again one of them.
questions.rule: Rigid motions keep every distance; they are translations, reflections, glide reflections and rotations.

questions.q: According to the book, how are transformations best used on a diagram with several structures?
options: Selectively: transform only the symmetric part and leave the rest alone
Transform every point of every figure
Only on figures with a centre
Only after finishing a coordinate computation
optionExplain: Right: that is how they shed light.
The point is to change some structures while others stay.
Not required.
Transformations avoid computation.
questions.explain: Apply a transformation that fixes one structure and changes the others.
questions.rule: Rigid motions keep every distance; they are translations, reflections, glide reflections and rotations.
questions.teaches: Transformations shed light on a problem when used selectively, that is, when only the symmetrical part of a diagram is transformed and the rest is left alone.

questions.q: A translation sends (x, y) to (x + 2, y - 1). Where does it send (3, 5)?
optionExplain: This subtracts 2 and adds 1.
This forgets the change in y.
Right: add 2 to x and subtract 1 from y.
This swaps coordinates.
questions.explain: Add the fixed vector. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A translation adds a fixed vector to every point; the vector from B to C is C minus B.

questions.q: True or false: A translation by a nonzero vector has no fixed point.
questions.explain: Every point moves.
questions.rule: A translation adds a fixed vector to every point; the vector from B to C is C minus B.

questions.q: B = (1, 2) and C = (4, 6). What is the motion from B to C, and how long is it?
options: (-3, -4), of length 5
(5, 8), of length sqrt(89)
(3, 4), of length 7
(3, 4), of length 5
optionExplain: This is B minus C, the motion from C to B.
This adds the points.
This adds 3 and 4 as the length.
Right: C minus B, with length sqrt(9 + 16) = 5.
questions.explain: The vector from B to C is C minus B.
questions.rule: A translation adds a fixed vector to every point; the vector from B to C is C minus B.

questions.q: A student writes the motion from B to C as B - C. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong
That gives the motion from C to B; the motion from B to C is C - B
It should be B + C
It should be BC squared
optionExplain: The order is reversed.
Right: end minus start.
That is twice the midpoint.
Squares do not appear.
questions.explain: End point minus starting point.
questions.rule: A translation adds a fixed vector to every point; the vector from B to C is C minus B.

questions.q: Translation T(z) = z + (2 - i) sends 3 + 5i to ____.
questions.explain: Add 2 to the real part and subtract 1 from the imaginary part.
questions.rule: A translation adds a fixed vector to every point; the vector from B to C is C minus B.

questions.q: A robot moves 3 east and 4 north, then the same motion is repeated from a different starting spot. What does this show about vectors?
options: A vector describes a relative motion, the same from any starting point
The two motions are different vectors
Vectors need an origin to exist
The second motion cancels the first
optionExplain: Right: vectors have no fixed starting point.
They are the same vector.
Only position vectors do.
It repeats it.
questions.explain: Vectors are relative motions.
questions.rule: A translation adds a fixed vector to every point; the vector from B to C is C minus B.
questions.teaches: Vectors have no fixed starting point; in any vector investigation one must be aware of or carefully choose the location of the origin when treating points as vectors.

questions.q: A = (1, 2) and B = (5, 6). What is the midpoint of segment AB?
optionExplain: This adds without halving.
Right: average the coordinates.
This halves the difference.
This is not the average.
questions.explain: The midpoint is the average of the two points. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A vector sum is a composition of motions; the sum around a closed polygon is zero; the midpoint of AB is (A + B)/2.

questions.q: True or false: The vector sum along the sides of a closed polygon is zero.
questions.explain: Starting at A and going round returns to A, so the net motion is zero.
questions.rule: A vector sum is a composition of motions; the sum around a closed polygon is zero; the midpoint of AB is (A + B)/2.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, you travel from A to B, then B to C. How do you describe the motion back to A?
options: It is AB + BC, doubled
It is zero already
It is the vector CA, and AB + BC + CA = 0
It is the vector AC
optionExplain: That goes further from A.
You are at C, not A.
Right: the three sides sum to zero.
AC points the other way.
questions.explain: AB + BC is AC, so CA must cancel it.
questions.rule: A vector sum is a composition of motions; the sum around a closed polygon is zero; the midpoint of AB is (A + B)/2.

questions.q: A student says the midpoint of A and B is A + B, since the diagonals of a parallelogram meet there. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: A + B is the midpoint
The midpoint is A - B
The midpoint is AB divided by 2 in length only
A + B is the far corner of the parallelogram; the midpoint is half of it, (A + B)/2
optionExplain: A + B is a full diagonal.
That is the vector between them.
The position vector is needed.
Right: the diagonals bisect each other.
questions.explain: Halve the diagonal.
questions.rule: A vector sum is a composition of motions; the sum around a closed polygon is zero; the midpoint of AB is (A + B)/2.

questions.q: For P = (0, 0) and Q = (4, 10), the midpoint has y-coordinate ____.
questions.explain: Average of 0 and 10.
questions.rule: A vector sum is a composition of motions; the sum around a closed polygon is zero; the midpoint of AB is (A + B)/2.

questions.q: Why does the midpoint of AB have position (A + B)/2?
options: The diagonals of a parallelogram with sides OA and OB bisect each other, so the midpoint of the other diagonal is half the sum
Because AB has length 2
Because the origin is at A
Because vectors always add as averages
optionExplain: Right: this uses Example 8.2.9(c).
Lengths are not assumed.
The origin may be anywhere.
Sums do not average.
questions.explain: Parallelogram diagonals bisect each other.
questions.rule: A vector sum is a composition of motions; the sum around a closed polygon is zero; the midpoint of AB is (A + B)/2.
questions.teaches: The midpoint formula comes from the parallelogram fact that the diagonals bisect each other: the diagonal from the origin is A + B, and the midpoint of AB is half of it.

questions.q: A triangle has vertices (1, 2), (5, 2) and (3, 8). Which point is the best guess for the centroid?
optionExplain: This is the midpoint of the extreme y values.
This is the midpoint of the base.
No average gives this.
Right: the average of the vertices.
questions.explain: Average the three vertices. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The centroid is the average of the vertex positions.

questions.q: True or false: The centroid of a triangle is the centre of mass of equal masses placed at its vertices.
questions.explain: That is what the vector computation shows.
questions.rule: The centroid is the average of the vertex positions.

questions.q: A triangle has vertices (0, 0), (9, 3) and (3, 9). What is its centroid?
optionExplain: This averages with 2 in the denominator.
This divides one sum by 4.
This adds without dividing.
questions.explain: Add the coordinates and divide by 3.
questions.rule: The centroid is the average of the vertex positions.

questions.q: Put the steps of the vector proof that the centroid is (A + B + C)/3 in order.
items: Let M be the midpoint of AB, so M = (A + B)/2
Use the centroid theorem: the centroid is one third of the way from M to C
Substitute M to get K = (A + B + C)/3
questions.explain: The ratio 1 : 2 from the centroid theorem turns into a one-third step.
questions.rule: The centroid is the average of the vertex positions.

questions.q: A student says K = M + (1/2)(C - M) by using the midpoint of CM. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong
It should be two thirds of the way from C
The centroid is one third of the way from the midpoint M to C, not halfway
The step uses the wrong triangle
optionExplain: Halfway would put K at the midpoint of MC.
That is the same point; the student's step is different.
Right: the ratio is 1 : 2 from M.
The triangle is right.
questions.explain: Use the 2 : 1 ratio of the centroid theorem.
questions.rule: The centroid is the average of the vertex positions.

questions.q: Three equal masses sit at (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 6). Where does the system balance?
optionExplain: Right: the centre of mass is the average of the positions.
This is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.
This is a fourth corner.
The masses are not all there.
questions.explain: Balance point of equal masses is the average.
questions.rule: The centroid is the average of the vertex positions.
questions.teaches: The centre of mass of n equal point masses is the average (X1 + ... + Xn)/n, and the centroid theorem makes the triangle's centroid exactly this for its vertices.

questions.q: The four corners of a square have a centre of symmetry at the middle of the square. Could another point also be a centre of symmetry for these four points?
options: Yes, any point on a diagonal
Yes, the midpoint of a side
No, a finite set has at most one
It depends on the size of the square
optionExplain: A point off the middle sends corners outside the set.
That does not pair every corner.
Right: the theorem excludes a second centre.
Size does not matter.
questions.explain: A finite set has at most one centre of symmetry. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: If the vectors from a centre to all points sum to zero, two centres would force n times their difference to be zero.

questions.q: True or false: A centre of symmetry of a set need not itself be a point of the set.
questions.explain: The definition says the centre is a point not necessarily in S.
questions.rule: If the vectors from a centre to all points sum to zero, two centres would force n times their difference to be zero.

questions.q: A set has centre P, and its points are A1, ..., An. What is the sum of the vectors from P to each Ak?
options: n times the vector to the farthest point
Zero
The vector to the centroid
The vector PA1 only
optionExplain: No such formula.
Right: the vectors cancel in symmetric pairs.
That is the sum divided by n.
All terms contribute.
questions.explain: Each vector is cancelled by its partner.
questions.rule: If the vectors from a centre to all points sum to zero, two centres would force n times their difference to be zero.

questions.q: A student says the integers on a number line show the theorem is false, since each half-integer is a centre. What is the response?
options: The theorem is for finite sets; the integers are infinite, and the sums used do not exist
The theorem is false
Half-integers are not centres
The integers are finite
optionExplain: Right: finiteness is needed.
It is true for finite sets.
They are, for the infinite set.
They are infinite.
questions.explain: Check the hypothesis: the set must be finite.
questions.rule: If the vectors from a centre to all points sum to zero, two centres would force n times their difference to be zero.

questions.q: Put the steps of the proof in order.
items: Suppose there were two centres P and Q
For centre P, sum the vectors from P to all the points and find zero
For centre Q, do the same and find zero
Subtract the sums to get n times the vector QP equals zero, so Q = P
questions.explain: Subtraction leaves a multiple of QP.
questions.rule: If the vectors from a centre to all points sum to zero, two centres would force n times their difference to be zero.

questions.q: In the proof, the points Bk are the images of the points Ak under symmetry about P. Why can the same set be listed as the Bk?
options: Because all points are equal
Because S has only two points
Because P lies in S
The image of a point of S is again a point of S, so the Bk are the Ak in another order
optionExplain: Points are distinct.
S is any finite set.
P need not lie in S.
Right: that is what a centre of symmetry means.
questions.explain: Symmetric partners come from the same set.
questions.rule: If the vectors from a centre to all points sum to zero, two centres would force n times their difference to be zero.
questions.teaches: In the book's proof, Bk = Aj for some j, so summing over k covers the set in a different order, and the sum of the vectors from the centre to all points is zero.

questions.q: Two vectors are perpendicular. What is special about their dot product?
options: It equals zero
It equals the product of their lengths
It equals 1
It is negative
optionExplain: Right: cos 90 is zero.
That holds when they are parallel.
No such rule.
The sign is zero.
questions.explain: Perpendicular means zero dot product. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A dot B is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular, and A dot A is the squared length.

questions.q: True or false: The dot product of a vector with itself equals the square of the vector's magnitude.
questions.explain: Because the angle is zero and cos 0 is 1.
questions.rule: A dot B is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular, and A dot A is the squared length.

questions.q: The dot product of the vectors (3, 4) and (4, -3) is ____.
questions.explain: 12 minus 12 is zero, so they are perpendicular.
questions.rule: A dot B is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular, and A dot A is the squared length.

questions.q: A student says the dot product of two vectors is another vector. What is the correction?
options: It is a vector at right angles to both
It is a point
It is a number, a scalar
It is an angle
optionExplain: That is a cross product in three dimensions.
It is a number.
Right: the product A . B is a scalar.
The angle comes from dividing by the lengths.
questions.explain: Dot product gives a number.
questions.rule: A dot B is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular, and A dot A is the squared length.

questions.q: A parallelogram has sides 5 and 7 and one diagonal of length 8. Using 2(AB squared + AD squared) = AC squared + BD squared, how long is the other diagonal squared?
optionExplain: This takes 25 + 49 once.
This is the left side.
This is the given diagonal squared.
questions.explain: Apply the parallelogram law.
questions.rule: A dot B is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular, and A dot A is the squared length.
questions.teaches: Problem 8.5.26 asks you to prove, perhaps with dot products, that for a parallelogram ABCD, 2(AB squared + AD squared) = AC squared + BD squared.

questions.q: The point (3, 1) is reflected across the x-axis. Where does it go?
optionExplain: This reflects across the y-axis.
This rotates by 180 degrees.
This reflects across the line y = x.
Right: the x-axis is the perpendicular bisector of the segment between the two points.
questions.explain: The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Reflections fix a whole line, translations and glide reflections fix no point, and a rotation fixes exactly its centre.

questions.q: Match each rigid motion to the points it fixes.
pairs: no point, though its line is mapped to itself
questions.explain: Fixed points distinguish the four types.
questions.rule: Reflections fix a whole line, translations and glide reflections fix no point, and a rotation fixes exactly its centre.

questions.q: Rotate (3, 0) counterclockwise by 90 degrees about (1, 0). What is the image?
optionExplain: This rotates clockwise.
This translates the point.
Right: the vector from the centre (2, 0) turns to (0, 2).
This rotates by 180 degrees.
questions.explain: Rotate the vector from the centre and add back the centre.
questions.rule: Reflections fix a whole line, translations and glide reflections fix no point, and a rotation fixes exactly its centre.

questions.q: A student says a glide reflection fixes every point of its line. What is wrong?
options: The translation slides each point along the line; the line is mapped to itself but no point is fixed
Nothing is wrong
A glide reflection fixes exactly one point
A glide reflection has no line
optionExplain: Right: only the line as a whole is fixed.
Each point is shifted.
It has none.
It has an axis.
questions.explain: Line fixed as a set, not point by point.
questions.rule: Reflections fix a whole line, translations and glide reflections fix no point, and a rotation fixes exactly its centre.

questions.q: True or false: A rotation by 90 degrees about C has exactly one fixed point, namely C.
questions.explain: Every other point moves around C.
questions.rule: Reflections fix a whole line, translations and glide reflections fix no point, and a rotation fixes exactly its centre.

questions.q: Footprints along a trail alternate left and right: each print is the previous one flipped across the trail's centre line and moved forward. What motion maps one print to the next?
options: A pure reflection
A rotation about the centre line
A translation
A glide reflection along the centre line
optionExplain: A reflection would not move the print forward.
A rotation has a point centre.
A translation would not flip left to right.
Right: reflect across the line then slide along it.
questions.explain: Reflect plus slide is a glide reflection.
questions.rule: Reflections fix a whole line, translations and glide reflections fix no point, and a rotation fixes exactly its centre.
questions.teaches: A glide reflection has no fixed points, but the entire line along which it glides is fixed as a set: every point of the line maps to another point of the line.

questions.q: A point is reflected in one vertical mirror, then in a parallel vertical mirror 3 units to the right. How far has it moved in total?
options: 3 units
6 units, twice the distance between the mirrors
0 units
9 units
optionExplain: That is the gap, not the total shift.
Right: the net effect is a translation.
The point does not return.
No rule gives this.
questions.explain: Twice the gap. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Two reflections make a translation if the mirrors are parallel, and a rotation by twice the angle if they cross.

questions.q: True or false: Reflecting across a line and then across the same line again gives the identity.
questions.explain: Each point returns to where it started.
questions.rule: Two reflections make a translation if the mirrors are parallel, and a rotation by twice the angle if they cross.

questions.q: Lines l1 and l2 meet at C at 25 degrees. Reflecting across l1 then l2 gives a rotation about C by ____ degrees.
questions.explain: Twice the angle between the lines.
questions.rule: Two reflections make a translation if the mirrors are parallel, and a rotation by twice the angle if they cross.

questions.q: A student says two reflections across parallel lines 3 apart give a translation of 3. What is wrong?
options: The translation is twice the distance between the lines, 6
Nothing is wrong
The result is a rotation
The result is a glide reflection
optionExplain: Right: each reflection contributes.
The shift is doubled.
Parallel lines give a translation.
No slide along a mirror arises.
questions.explain: Double the gap.
questions.rule: Two reflections make a translation if the mirrors are parallel, and a rotation by twice the angle if they cross.

questions.q: Reflecting across l1 then l2, where l1 and l2 cross at C with 40 degrees between them, what point is fixed?
options: Every point of l1
Every point of l2
No point
The point C only
optionExplain: The second reflection moves them.
The first reflection moves them.
C is fixed.
Right: C is on both lines, so each reflection fixes it.
questions.explain: The intersection is fixed.
questions.rule: Two reflections make a translation if the mirrors are parallel, and a rotation by twice the angle if they cross.

questions.q: A skater reflects a figure across a wall, then across a second wall that meets the first at a right angle. Which single motion results?
options: A translation along one wall
A reflection across a diagonal
A rotation by 180 degrees about the corner where the walls meet
The identity
optionExplain: Crossing mirrors give a rotation.
Not a mirror.
Right: twice the 90 degree angle.
The mirrors differ.
questions.explain: Crossing mirrors give a rotation by double the angle.
questions.rule: Two reflections make a translation if the mirrors are parallel, and a rotation by twice the angle if they cross.
questions.teaches: The book concludes that the composition of two reflections is either a translation (including the identity) or a rotation.

questions.q: An equilateral triangle ABC has A fixed. Rotating by 60 degrees about A sends C to which point?
options: A
B
The midpoint of BC
Nowhere in the triangle
optionExplain: A is the centre, so it stays.
Right: equal sides AB and AC with a 60 degree angle between them.
A 60 degree rotation does not do that.
It maps to B.
questions.explain: Equilateral triangles have 60 degree rotational symmetry about each vertex. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Rotate the part of the figure that must move with the triangle, here the third line, so the vertex falls on a known line.

questions.q: True or false: Rotating a line by 60 degrees makes an angle of 60 degrees between the line and its image.
questions.explain: This is Fact 8.5.6: the angle between a line and its rotated image equals the rotation angle.
questions.rule: Rotate the part of the figure that must move with the triangle, here the third line, so the vertex falls on a known line.

questions.q: Lines y = 0, 1, 2 hold A = (0, 0), B = (sqrt(3), 1), C = (0, 2). The equilateral triangle has side ____.
questions.explain: AC = 2, and AB = sqrt(3 + 1) = 2.
questions.rule: Rotate the part of the figure that must move with the triangle, here the third line, so the vertex falls on a known line.

questions.q: A solver rotates the whole figure, including l1 and l2, by 60 degrees about A. Why does the book rotate only l3?
options: Only the part that moves with C is needed; the rest of the figure stays fixed
Rotating all lines is the only valid method
l1 and l2 cannot be rotated
The triangle is not equilateral
optionExplain: Right: use transformations selectively.
The book rotates one line.
They can; it just does not help.
It is.
questions.explain: Transform only the part you need.
questions.rule: Rotate the part of the figure that must move with the triangle, here the third line, so the vertex falls on a known line.

questions.q: In the rotation solution, why must the rotated image of l3 meet l2 at B?
options: The image of l3 is parallel to l2
B is the midpoint of l2
C lies on l3, B is the image of C, so B lies on the image of l3 and also on l2
l3 and l2 are perpendicular
optionExplain: It is not parallel in general.
No such rule.
Right: the vertex sits where the two lines cross.
They are parallel.
questions.explain: A vertex on two lines is their intersection.
questions.rule: Rotate the part of the figure that must move with the triangle, here the third line, so the vertex falls on a known line.
questions.teaches: Fact 8.5.6: if a line is rotated by theta about a centre, the angle between the image line and the original is also theta.

questions.q: A figure is rotated by 90 degrees about one point and then by 150 degrees about the same point. What is the total rotation?
options: 60 degrees
240 degrees
120 degrees
13500 degrees
optionExplain: This subtracts.
Right: angles about the same centre add.
This averages.
This multiplies.
questions.explain: Angles add. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Angles of rotations add; if they total 360 degrees the result is a translation or the identity.

questions.q: True or false: A rotation of 200 degrees followed by a rotation of 160 degrees about a different centre is a translation.
questions.explain: The angles sum to 360 and the centres differ.
questions.rule: Angles of rotations add; if they total 360 degrees the result is a translation or the identity.

questions.q: Rotation by 100 degrees about A, then 80 degrees about B (different centres), is a rotation by ____ degrees.
questions.rule: Angles of rotations add; if they total 360 degrees the result is a translation or the identity.

questions.q: A student says the composition of two rotations about different centres is a rotation by the sum of the angles. What is wrong?
options: The sum should be the difference
The composition is always a translation
Nothing is wrong
If the sum is exactly 360 degrees the result is a translation
optionExplain: Angles add.
Only for a total of 360.
There is the 360 exception.
Right: that is the exception.
questions.explain: Check whether the total is 360.
questions.rule: Angles of rotations add; if they total 360 degrees the result is a translation or the identity.

questions.q: To find the centre of the rotation R(B, 120) after R(A, 60), the rays from A and B make base angles of what size with segment AB?
options: 60 degrees at A and 120 degrees at B
30 degrees at A and 60 degrees at B
30 degrees at both
90 degrees at both
optionExplain: The rotation angles are halved.
Right: half of each rotation angle.
Each uses its own half.
No rule.
questions.explain: Use half of each angle.
questions.rule: Angles of rotations add; if they total 360 degrees the result is a translation or the identity.

questions.q: A rotation by 70 degrees about A is followed by a translation. What is the result?
options: A translation
A rotation by 140 degrees
A rotation by 70 degrees about a different centre
A reflection
optionExplain: The rotation part remains.
The angle does not double.
Right: same angle, new centre.

questions.explain: Since x cubed has derivative 3x squared, it is an antiderivative of f. The integral is F(4) - F(1) = 63.
questions.rule: Subtract F at the left end from F at the right end.

questions.q: True or false: Replacing \(F\) by \(F+10\), which is also an antiderivative of \(f\), changes the value of \(F(b)-F(a)\).
questions.explain: The 10 is added at both ends and cancels: (F(b) + 10) - (F(a) + 10) = F(b) - F(a). Adding a constant does not change a derivative, so the theorem works with any antiderivative.
questions.rule: Constants cancel in F(b) - F(a).

questions.q: A student says the theorem is true because antiderivatives are often easy to compute. According to the book, what does that remark explain?
options: Why it is true, because a method that works must be correct
Nothing, because the book regards the theorem as having no practical use
Why it is true, but only for polynomial functions
What the theorem is as a method of computing, not why it is true
optionExplain: A method that is easy to use does not show that the area and the antiderivative are linked.
The book calls it an amazing algorithmic statement; it just says the algorithm is not the explanation.
The book makes no such restriction, and ease of computation is still not an explanation.
Right: the book says an easy algorithm explains what the statement is, and that understanding why needs a good interpretation of its parts.
questions.explain: The book separates what the theorem says and does from why it holds. The why comes from choosing the proper interpretation of the entities in the equation.
questions.rule: An algorithm explains what, not why.
questions.teaches: Calling the theorem an amazing algorithm explains what it is, not why it is true; the why comes from choosing the proper interpretation of the entities in the equation.

questions.q: Water flows into a tank at \(6t\) liters per minute at minute \(t\). The tank's volume is \(V(t)=3t^2\), with \(V'(t)=6t\). How many liters enter between minute 1 and minute 3?
optionExplain: This is V(3), the volume at minute 3, not the amount added after minute 1.
This is the rate at minute 3, 6 times 3, which is not an amount.
This multiplies the average of the two rates by the wrong width.
questions.explain: The rate is the derivative of the volume, so the amount added between two times is the change V(3) - V(1). Differentiation here means instantaneous rate of change, not just a tangent slope.
questions.rule: If F' = f, then f is how fast F changes.
questions.teaches: Differentiation is not just about tangent lines: it also has a dynamic interpretation as instantaneous rate of change, so F' = f says that f is how fast F is changing.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=2x\), which formula gives the area under the graph from \(x=1\) to \(x=t\), for \(t>1\)?
options: t squared minus 1
t squared
2t
2t minus 2
optionExplain: Right: the area is a trapezoid with heights 2 and 2t and width t - 1, which gives t squared - 1.
This is the area measured from 0; the region should start at 1.
This is the height at t, not an area.
This is the difference of the two heights, 2t - 2, not an area.
questions.explain: Averaging the heights gives (2 + 2t) / 2 = 1 + t, and times the width t - 1 gives t squared - 1. The card calls such a function a moving curtain.
questions.rule: Area measured from a fixed start is a function of the end.

questions.q: In \(g(t)=\int_a^t f(x)\,dx\), the variable \(t\) is the ____ limit of integration.
questions.explain: The lower limit a stays fixed. The upper limit t moves, which is what turns the integral into a function.
questions.rule: Fix the start, vary the end.

optionExplain: This is f(2), the height of the graph at 2, not the area.
This is 3 times 2, a slope-like value, not the area.
Right: g(2) = 2 cubed = 8, the area under 3x squared from 0 to 2.
This squares 2 and stops, forgetting the factor that makes g a cube.
questions.explain: g(t) gives the whole area swept up to t, so g(2) is a single number, 8. The height f(2) = 12 is a different quantity.
questions.rule: g gives area; f gives height.

questions.q: True or false: For \(f(x)=2x\), moving the start from \(a=1\) to \(a=2\) changes \(g(t)\) from \(t^2-1\) to \(t^2-4\), which lowers it by the same amount, 3, at every \(t\).
questions.explain: The difference (t squared - 1) - (t squared - 4) is 3 for every t: the area between x = 1 and x = 2. Moving the start shifts g by a constant, so g keeps the same rate of change.
questions.rule: A different start shifts g by a constant.

questions.q: At \(t=a\), the curtain has not yet moved. What is \(g(a)\)?
options: f(a), the height at the starting edge
0, since no area has been swept out
a, the starting point
It depends on f and cannot be known
optionExplain: Height is not area; a region of zero width has zero area however tall the edge is.
Right: the interval from a to a has no width, so g(a) is the integral over a single point, which is 0.
The start is a position on the x-axis, not an amount of area.
It does not depend on f: with no width there is nothing to count.
questions.explain: The book notes that g(a) = 0. The curtain starts with no area, which is how the constant gets fixed in the proof of the theorem.
questions.teaches: The book notes that g(a)=0: at t=a the curtain has not moved, so no area has accumulated.

questions.q: It rains at a constant 2 mm per hour starting at hour \(a=6\). Let \(g(t)\) be the total rain from hour 6 to hour \(t\). What is \(g(10)\)?
options: 20 mm
2 mm
8 mm
12 mm
optionExplain: This multiplies the rate by 10, counting the six hours before the rain began.
This is the rate, not the total.
Right: 2 mm per hour for 4 hours, the area of a rectangle of height 2 and width 4.
This multiplies the rate by 6, the starting hour, instead of the 4 hours of rain.
questions.explain: The total is the area under a constant rate over the 4 hours that have passed. The book names the variable t on purpose, so that g(t) is easy to picture as a function of time.
questions.rule: Read g(t) as a total that builds up over time.
questions.teaches: The book writes the variable as t on purpose, to make it easy to visualize g(t) as a function of time.

questions.q: A curtain's leading edge is 5 units tall and moves right at 1 unit per second. About how fast is the area behind it growing?
options: 5 square units per second
1 square unit per second
6 square units per second
2.5 square units per second
optionExplain: Right: each second the curtain gains a strip 1 unit wide and 5 tall.
This is the edge's speed; the area gained also depends on the height.
This adds speed and height, two quantities that should be multiplied.
This halves the height, as if the edge were a triangle.
questions.explain: Width gained times height gives 5. The card turns this into the equation g'(t) = f(t).
questions.rule: Area gain = height times width gained.

questions.q: True or false: The area of the curtain grows faster when its leading edge is tall.
questions.explain: Each small step of the edge adds a strip as tall as the edge, so a taller edge adds more area per step.
questions.rule: Tall edge, fast growth.

optionExplain: This is g(4), the area swept so far, not its rate of growth.
This is f'(4), the slope of the graph itself, not of the area function.
This is g(4) divided by 16, a number with no meaning here.
Right: g'(t) = f(t) = t squared, so g'(4) = 16.
questions.explain: Differentiating t cubed over 3 gives t squared, which is f(t). At t = 4 that is 16.
questions.rule: g' equals f, not g.

questions.q: Suppose \(f\) is positive and decreasing on \([a,b]\). Which statements about \(g(t)\) are true as \(t\) runs from \(a\) to \(b\)?
options: g is increasing
g is decreasing, since f is decreasing
The rate of growth g' is decreasing
g' stays constant
optionExplain: Right: g' = f is positive, so g rises.
A decreasing f makes g' smaller, not negative; g still gains area.
Right: g' = f, and f is falling, so g gains area more and more slowly.
g' = f, which is falling, so it is not constant.
questions.explain: The sign of f gives the direction of g, and the trend of f gives the trend of the rate of g. Confusing the two is a frequent slip.
questions.rule: f positive means g increases; f decreasing means g slows.

questions.q: In a short time \(\Delta t\), by roughly how much does the curtain's area grow when the edge is \(f(t)\) tall?
options: About f of the time step
About f(t) times the time step
About g(t) times the time step
About f'(t) times the time step
optionExplain: This evaluates f at the step size, not at the edge's position t.
Right: a thin strip of width the time step and height f(t).
g(t) is the whole area so far, not the height of the edge.
The slope of f is not the height of the strip.
questions.explain: The book argues that in a small interval of time the area grows by approximately f(t) times the step. Dividing by the step recovers g'(t) = f(t).
questions.rule: Growth in a short step is about height times step.
questions.teaches: In a small interval of time Delta t the curtain's area grows by approximately f(t) times Delta t, a strip of that width and height f(t).

questions.q: Snow falls at a rate of \(f(x)=x\) cm per hour at hour \(x\). The gauge reads the total since hour 0. Comparing the exact snow from hour 2 to 2.1 (0.205 cm) with \(f(2)\times 0.1\) (0.2 cm), what do we learn?
options: Close but not exact, because the rate changes during the step
The estimate is exact, because g'(t) = f(t) holds at every step
The estimate is wrong, so the equation g'(t) = f(t) must be false
The gauge must be inaccurate, since two correct methods should agree
optionExplain: Right: the rate rises from 2 to 2.1 inside the step, so f(t) times the step slightly underestimates.
The equation concerns the limit of the growth rate, not each finite step.
The error shrinks faster than the step, so the equation survives.
The gap is mathematical: the rate changes within the step.
questions.explain: The book points out that the curtain does not grow by exactly f(t) times the step, which is why equation (2) deserves a more careful treatment. The next idea measures the error.
questions.rule: Height times step is only approximate for a finite step.
questions.teaches: The curtain does not grow by exactly f(t) times Delta t, which is why the equation g'(t)=f(t) deserves a more careful treatment.

optionExplain: This is F(2) alone; the subtraction of F(0) is missing.
This adds F(2) and F(0).
This subtracts 5 from 8 once more, treating the constant as extra.
questions.explain: The constant 5 cancels between the two evaluations, leaving 8 - 0. The card shows why this is the area under 3x squared.
questions.rule: Constants cancel in F(b) - F(a).

questions.q: Put the steps of the curtain argument for the fundamental theorem in order.
items: Define g(t) as the area of the moving curtain from a to t
Argue that g'(t) = f(t), the edge height
Add a constant C to get F = g + C, which still has F' = f
Subtract: F(b) - F(a) = g(b) - g(a), the area from a to b
questions.explain: Each step uses the one before: the curtain gives g, its rate gives g' = f, a constant gives any antiderivative, and subtraction cancels the constant.
questions.rule: Curtain, rate, constant, subtract.

optionExplain: This is F(2) alone.
This adds the two evaluations.
This is 2 to the fourth, ignoring the interval's left end.
questions.explain: F(t) = t^4 + 8. The difference is 24 - 9 = 15, which equals g(2) - g(1) = 15 - 0, the area from 1 to 2.
questions.rule: Evaluate F at both ends and subtract.

questions.q: A student writes: \(F(b)-F(a)=(g(b)+C)-(g(a)+C)=g(b)-g(a)+2C\). What is wrong?
options: The two C's cancel in the subtraction; they do not add to 2C
Adding C changes the derivative of g, so F is not an antiderivative
The student should have used g(b) minus C
g(a) is not zero, so the formula does not apply
optionExplain: Right: (g(b) + C) - (g(a) + C) = g(b) - g(a), because minus C and plus C make zero.
A constant has derivative 0, so F' = g' = f.
Using the same C at both ends is correct; the sign handling is the issue.
g(a) = 0 does not matter here; the algebra of the C terms is the slip.
questions.explain: The slip is a sign error when distributing the minus sign. Constants cancel, which is why any C gives the same area.
questions.rule: Distribute the minus sign over the whole bracket.

questions.q: Match each fact used in the argument to its job.
pairs: Links swept area to edge height
Makes g + C an antiderivative of f
Leaves the area g(b) after subtracting
questions.explain: Each fact does one job: the first links area and height, the second keeps F' = f, the third makes g(b) the area, and the subtraction removes C.
questions.rule: Each fact has a single job in the proof.

questions.q: A car has speed \(v(t)=6t^2\) km/h and position \(s(t)=2t^3\) km, with \(s'=v\). How far does it travel from \(t=1\) to \(t=3\)?
options: 54 km
16 km
52 km
26 km
optionExplain: This is the position at t = 3, not the distance travelled from t = 1.
This is v(1) + v(3) taken as an average, which gives no distance.
Right: s(3) - s(1) = 54 - 2 = 52, the same antiderivative-difference as in the proof.
This halves the correct answer, as if finding an average position.
questions.explain: Position is an antiderivative of speed, so distance is the change in position. The book calls the crux the dynamic reading of the integral, and says that knowing many interpretations of differentiation and integration is critically important.
questions.rule: Choose the interpretation that makes the link visible.
questions.teaches: The crux move was to interpret the definite integral dynamically; the book stresses the critical importance of knowing many alternate interpretations of both differentiation and integration.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x\), the exact area from \(x=2\) to \(x=2.1\) is 0.205. By how much does it exceed the rectangle \(f(2)\times 0.1=0.2\)?
optionExplain: This moves the decimal point one place.
The graph rises across the step, so the rectangle misses a small triangle.
This is the width of the step, not the missing area.
questions.explain: The rectangle lies below the rising graph and misses a thin triangle of area 0.005. The card calls the missing piece the error E(t).
questions.rule: The rectangle misses a thin sliver.

questions.q: True or false: To prove \(g'(t)=f(t)\), it is enough to show that \(E(t)\) itself tends to 0 as \(\Delta t\) tends to 0.
questions.explain: Even the rectangle f(t) times the step tends to 0, so E tending to 0 says nothing. What matters is E divided by the step.
questions.rule: Compare the error with the step, not with 0.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^2\), \(t=1\) and \(\Delta t=0.1\), the exact growth is 0.11033. What is \(E/\Delta t\), to three places?
optionExplain: This is E itself, not E divided by the step.
This is the difference quotient 0.11033 / 0.1, which includes f(t) = 1.
This is 3 times 0.11033, a number with no meaning here.
questions.explain: The difference quotient is f(t) + E/step = 1.103, so the error ratio is the 0.103 that sits above f(t).
questions.rule: Error ratio = difference quotient minus f(t).

questions.q: With \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(t=1\), halving the step from 0.1 to 0.05 changes \(E/\Delta t\) from 0.103 to about ____ (two decimal places).
questions.explain: The exact value is 0.05 + 0.05 squared / 3 = 0.0508. For this f the error ratio is close to the step itself, so halving the step halves it, and it tends to 0.
questions.rule: A good error ratio shrinks with the step.

questions.q: In the book's picture, \(E(t)\) is negative. On which kind of interval does that happen?
options: Where f is increasing, so the curve is above the rectangle
Where f is constant, so the rectangle matches the curve exactly
Where f is negative, so the region lies below the x-axis
Where f is decreasing, so the rectangle overshoots the curve
optionExplain: That makes the true area larger, so E is positive.
Then the rectangle matches the curve and E is 0.
The sign of E depends on how f changes, not on the sign of f.
Right: the rectangle is taller than the curve over the step, so the true area is less than f(t) times the step.
questions.explain: E(t) is a signed area. It is negative when the rectangle overshoots, positive when it undershoots, and 0 for a constant f.
questions.rule: E is a signed quantity.
questions.teaches: E(t) is a signed area: in the book's picture it is negative, because the rectangle f(t) times Delta t overshoots the true area.

questions.q: The book defers the proof that \(E(t)/\Delta t\to 0\) to its section on continuity. What does that suggest about the property doing the work?
options: How smoothly f varies, that is, f being continuous
How easily an antiderivative of f can be written down
The fact that f is a polynomial
The size of the interval from a to b
optionExplain: Right: the book says this step requires an understanding of continuity and proves it in its section on uniform continuity.
Antiderivatives are not needed to show the error is small.
The theorem is stated for continuous functions, not polynomials only.
The proof concerns tiny steps, not the length of the whole interval.
questions.explain: The error sliver is small only if f cannot change much over a tiny step. That is what continuity of f provides.
questions.rule: A small step is only enough if f cannot jump.
questions.teaches: Showing that E(t)/Delta t tends to 0 requires an understanding of continuity; the book proves it in its discussion of uniform continuity.

questions.q: The derivative of a function at a point is a limit of what?
options: Slopes of secant lines as the step shrinks
Areas under the graph as the interval grows
Values of f at larger and larger x
Second derivatives of f
optionExplain: Right: the quotients (f(a + h) - f(a)) / h approach the derivative as h shrinks.
That describes an integral, not a derivative.
That is the behaviour at infinity, not a rate of change.
Higher derivatives are built on first derivatives, not the other way round.
questions.explain: A derivative is built from secant slopes. The card names the idea behind all such constructions.
questions.rule: A derivative is a limit of difference quotients.

questions.q: The book calls convergence of ____ the theoretical foundation of calculus.
questions.explain: Limits, continuity, derivatives and integrals can all be reduced to the convergence of sequences.
questions.rule: Sequences first.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^2\), what number do the quotients \(\frac{f(3+1/n)-f(3)}{1/n}\) approach as \(n\) grows?
optionExplain: This is f(3), not the slope there.
The numerator and denominator both shrink, but their ratio does not.
Right: the quotient simplifies to 6 + 1/n, which settles at 6.
This is the point itself, not the derivative of x squared.
questions.explain: Expanding gives (9 + 6/n + 1/n squared - 9) / (1/n) = 6 + 1/n. The sequence of slopes tends to f'(3) = 6.
