questions.rule: Compute the sequence, then its limit.

questions.q: Match each notion to the sequence whose limit it is.
pairs: Difference quotients as the step shrinks
Sums over n thin strips as n grows
Partial sums with more and more terms
questions.explain: Each notion is a limit of a sequence of simpler numbers: slopes of secants, sums of strips, or partial sums.
questions.rule: Name the sequence behind the notion.

questions.q: For the series \(\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\cdots\), the partial sums are \(\frac12,\frac34,\frac78,\ldots\). Using the book's definition of an infinite series, what is the sum?
options: Infinity, since there are infinitely many positive terms
1, the limit of the partial sums
It has no sum, because an infinite process never ends
1/2, the first term
optionExplain: Infinitely many terms can still have a finite sum when the partial sums settle.
Right: the n-th partial sum is 1 - 1/2^n, which tends to 1.
The sum is defined as a limit, so an unfinished process can still have a value.
The first term is only the first partial sum.
questions.explain: The sum of an infinite series is defined as the limit of the sequence of partial sums, if that limit exists.
questions.rule: Series sum = limit of partial sums, if it exists.
questions.teaches: An infinite series is defined as the limit, if it exists, of the sequence of its partial sums.

questions.q: A friend applies the chapter's convergence ideas to a sequence of points in a plane. What does the chapter assume about functions?
options: Nothing; convergence is defined for any objects, so the chapter covers that case
Only polynomial functions are covered, so the plane case is excluded here
Domains may be complex, but ranges must be real, so only half the case fits
Functions are taken to be real-valued, so the plane case is outside its scope
optionExplain: The chapter fixes real numbers as its setting.
The chapter treats many kinds of functions, all real-valued.
Both domain and range are taken to be real.
Right: the book states this convention at the start of the chapter.
questions.explain: Our reading is that the same idea of closeness carries over to other settings, but the chapter itself only treats real-valued sequences and functions.
questions.rule: Check the setting before applying a definition.
questions.teaches: The chapter assumes that the domain and range of all functions are subsets of the real numbers.

questions.q: The terms are 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and so on. From which term on are all terms below 0.01?
options: The 10th term
The 100th term
The 1000th term
The 101st term
optionExplain: The 10th term is 0.1, which is still ten times too large.
The 100th term is exactly 0.01, so it is not below 0.01.
This works, but it is not the first term from which all later terms are below 0.01.
Right: the 100th term equals 0.01 exactly, which is not below it, and every term from the 101st on is smaller.
questions.explain: We need 1/n < 0.01, so n > 100. The card names this 'getting in and staying in'.
questions.rule: Strictly below needs n greater than the boundary.

questions.q: In the definition, every term after index \(N\) lies within \(\varepsilon\) of ____.
questions.explain: The distance is measured from the limit L. The index N is where the terms get in and stay in.
questions.rule: Within epsilon of L.

questions.q: For \(a_n=\frac{n+1}{n}\) with limit 1, what is the smallest \(N\) such that \(|a_n-1|<0.05\) for all \(n\ge N\)?
optionExplain: At n = 20 the distance is exactly 0.05, which is not less than 0.05.
Right: |a_n - 1| = 1/n, and 1/n < 0.05 exactly when n > 20.
This is too early: 1/19 is greater than 0.05.
This works but is not the smallest N.
questions.explain: The distance from the limit is 1/n. Solving 1/n < 0.05 gives n > 20, so the smallest N is 21.
questions.rule: Solve the inequality, then take the next integer.

questions.q: True or false: A student reasons: \((-1)^n\) equals 1 for every even \(n\), so the sequence converges to 1. The reasoning is correct.
questions.explain: The odd terms equal -1, at distance 2 from 1. For epsilon = 1, no index N keeps all later terms within epsilon of 1. Convergence needs all later terms close, not just infinitely many of them.
questions.rule: All later terms, not just some.

questions.q: For \(a_n=1/n\) with limit 0, the tolerance shrinks from \(\varepsilon=0.01\) (where \(N=101\)) to \(\varepsilon=0.001\). What happens to the smallest \(N\)?
options: It grows to 1001, as a stricter tolerance needs a later start
It stays at 101, since the sequence itself has not changed
It shrinks, since a smaller epsilon means smaller numbers
It becomes infinite, which would mean the sequence diverges
optionExplain: Right: 1/n < 0.001 needs n > 1000, so N = 1001.
The sequence is the same, but the demand is stricter.
A smaller epsilon is a harder test, so more terms must be skipped.
N stays a finite integer for every epsilon.
questions.explain: N depends on epsilon: a stricter tolerance needs a later N. The book asks you to picture epsilon as tiny and N as a huge number that depends on it.
questions.rule: N depends on epsilon.
questions.teaches: The integer N depends on epsilon; the tinier the tolerance, the huger the N.

questions.q: A thermostat's error shrinks as \(|d_n|=8/2^n\) degrees at minute \(n\). From which minute on is the error below 0.1 degrees?
options: Minute 6
Minute 5
Minute 80
Minute 7
optionExplain: At minute 6 the error is 0.125, which is above 0.1.
At minute 5 the error is 0.25.
The error is already below 0.1 long before minute 80.
questions.explain: This is the epsilon-N game with a different sequence. The book notes that in practice there are several methods for showing convergence, and the next ideas present them.
questions.rule: The definition is the benchmark; use it with a tolerance.
questions.teaches: In practice there are several methods of showing that a sequence converges, such as pictures, guessing the limit, the Cauchy property, bounded monotonic sequences, the squeeze principle and big-Oh analysis.

questions.q: A table shows a_n creeping toward 2 for n up to 1000. What does a proof still need?
options: Another 1000 terms, to be on the safe side of the guess
A check that every single term is below 2, from the first onward
Nothing more; a clear trend in a table of values is already a proof
Proof that the terms get arbitrarily close to 2 for all large n
optionExplain: More terms are still finitely many.
Terms may approach 2 from above, below or both sides.
A trend is a reason to guess, not a reason to be certain.
Right: 1000 terms cannot cover the infinitely many later ones.
questions.explain: The guess is the first step; the second step must cover all large n. The card shows the two steps.
questions.rule: A guess needs a proof.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, pictures rarely supply rigor, but they often supply the key ideas of an argument.
questions.explain: The book uses pictures all through the chapter, as sources of ideas, while saying that rigor has to come from the argument itself.
questions.rule: Pictures give ideas, arguments give rigor.

questions.q: For \(a_n=\frac{3n+1}{n}\) and the guess \(L=3\), what is the smallest \(N\) so that \(|a_n-3|<0.002\) for all \(n\ge N\)?
optionExplain: Right: |a_n - 3| = 1/n, and 1/n < 0.002 exactly when n > 500.
At n = 500 the distance is exactly 0.002, which is not below 0.002.
At n = 499 the distance is slightly above 0.002.
This works but is not the smallest N.
questions.explain: After simplifying a_n - 3 to 1/n, the question becomes solving an inequality in n.
questions.rule: Simplify the distance first.

questions.q: A student tabulates \(a_n=\sin n\) for 1000 terms, sees values between -1 and 1, and writes: the sequence converges to 0, proved. What is wrong?
options: The student should have used 2000 terms or more before concluding
The limit must be 1, the largest value that appears in the table
A finite table cannot show that later terms stay near 0, and these do not
Sequences with negative terms cannot converge, so the table rules out any limit
optionExplain: More terms would show the same swinging.
No single value is approached.
Right: the terms keep swinging between about -1 and 1 and never settle.
Negative terms are fine; these terms just do not settle.
questions.explain: A guess has to be checked against the definition. Here the check fails for every guess, so the sequence does not converge.
questions.rule: Test every guess against the definition.

questions.q: For \(a_n=1/n\), a student guesses \(L=0.1\). For large \(n\) the distance \(|a_n-0.1|\) tends to ____, so the guess fails the check.
questions.explain: The terms approach 0, so the distance to 0.1 settles near 0.1 instead of shrinking to 0. The check rejects bad guesses, and 0 is the only limit.
questions.rule: A wrong guess fails the distance check.

questions.q: A staircase picture suggests that a sequence zigzags in toward the crossing point of two graphs. Why is that not yet a proof of convergence?
options: Pictures can never be used in mathematics, because only algebraic arguments are allowed in proofs
A staircase can only end at the origin, wherever the graphs cross
The graphs would have to be drawn on graph paper to be trusted
Nothing in the picture rules out bouncing away from the crossing; that needs an argument
optionExplain: The book uses pictures to find the key ideas.
The staircase ends at the crossing point it spirals toward, which can be anywhere.
Accuracy of the drawing is not the issue; rigor is.
Right: the book says that such a picture would need an argument showing we never bounce away.
questions.explain: In the book's square-root example, the staircase picture suggests the limit, but the convergence is shown algebraically.
questions.rule: Picture first, argument second.
questions.teaches: To show convergence from a staircase picture you would need to argue carefully why the sequence never bounces away from the convergence point; the book changes gears to an algebraic analysis instead.

questions.q: The terms of a sequence eventually stay within 0.001 of each other, and within any smaller tolerance later still. What would you expect?
options: The terms settle toward a single value
The terms must be constant from some point
The terms must grow without bound
Nothing can be said
optionExplain: Right: terms that crowd together ever more closely are heading toward one number.
They can keep changing by tiny amounts.
Crowding together rules out growth without bound.
The pattern forces convergence for real numbers.
questions.explain: This is the idea behind the Cauchy property. The card states it exactly.
questions.rule: Terms that crowd together settle.

questions.q: True or false: A real sequence whose terms eventually get arbitrarily close to one another, in the Cauchy sense, converges.
questions.explain: That is the content of the Cauchy property for real sequences: terms that crowd together settle at a limit.
questions.rule: Cauchy means crowding together.

questions.q: Which sequence has the Cauchy property, so that it must converge?
options: \(a_n = \ln n\)
optionExplain: Terms n and n + 1 are always 1 apart, so they never crowd together.
Right: later terms are all within 1/2^N of each other.
Terms 1 and -1 stay 2 apart forever.
Neighbouring terms get close, but terms far apart do not: ln n grows without bound.
questions.explain: Only the first sequence has all later terms close to each other. The others fail for pairs of terms at the right distance apart.
questions.rule: Check every pair of late terms.

questions.q: A student argues that \(a_n=\ln n\) has the Cauchy property because \(|a_{n+1}-a_n|=\ln(1+1/n)\to 0\). What is wrong?
options: The difference |a_{n+1} - a_n| does not tend to 0 as n grows
Logarithms are only defined at integers, so n cannot be used here
The Cauchy property is a property of series of numbers rather than of sequences
Cauchy needs |a_m - a_n| small for all later m and n, not only neighbours
optionExplain: It does tend to 0, so that step is correct.
ln n is defined for all positive reals, and the issue lies elsewhere.
It is a property of sequences.
Right: ln 1000000 - ln 1000 is about 6.9, however large N is.
questions.explain: Small steps can add up to a large distance. Only a bound on every pair works.
questions.rule: Neighbours close does not mean all late terms close.

questions.q: The Cauchy property is often fairly easy to verify, but it gives no information about the actual ____ of the sequence.
questions.explain: It proves that a limit exists without saying what it is. Use it when you cannot guess the limit and only want to know that one exists.
questions.rule: Cauchy proves existence, not value.
questions.teaches: The Cauchy property is often fairly easy to verify, but it gives no information about the actual limiting value of the sequence.

questions.q: Cumulative readings do not decrease and stay at or below 500. A colleague argues by contradiction that they converge. Which property would non-convergence make them lack?
options: The Cauchy property
Boundedness
Monotonicity
Continuity
optionExplain: Right: the book starts its argument for bounded monotonic sequences with: if it did not converge, it would not have the Cauchy property.
The readings are given to be bounded by 500.
The readings are given to be non-decreasing.
Continuity is a property of functions, not of this sequence.
questions.explain: The Cauchy property is the link between terms crowding together and a limit existing, which makes it the natural thing to contradict.
questions.rule: Not converging means failing the Cauchy property.
questions.teaches: The book proves that bounded monotonic sequences converge by contradiction: if the sequence did not converge, it would not have the Cauchy property.

questions.q: Which sequence is guaranteed to converge?
options: \(a_n=\sin n\)
optionExplain: It is bounded but jumps between 1 and -1 forever.
Right: it increases and is below 1.
It increases but is unbounded.
It is bounded but oscillates without settling.
questions.explain: Moving one way and staying bounded guarantee convergence. The card states this as a theorem.
questions.rule: One-way and bounded implies convergent.

questions.q: True or false: Every bounded monotonic real sequence converges.
questions.explain: A bounded monotonic sequence cannot oscillate and cannot escape, so it must settle.
questions.rule: Bounded and monotonic implies convergent.

questions.q: Which of these sequences are bounded and monotonic, so the theorem says they converge?
options: \(a_n = 2-\frac1n\)
\(a_n = n+\frac1n\)
optionExplain: Right: it increases and stays below 2.
It is bounded, but it alternates in sign, so it is not monotonic. (It does converge, but the theorem does not say so.)
It increases but is unbounded.
Right: it decreases and stays above 5.
questions.explain: Check both hypotheses. The second sequence converges for other reasons, but the theorem is silent about it.
questions.rule: Check both hypotheses before using the theorem.

questions.q: Match each sequence to what the theorem says about it.
questions.explain: The theorem applies only when both hypotheses hold, which is the case for the last sequence.
questions.rule: Both hypotheses are needed.

questions.q: A sequence is increasing and bounded by \(B=5\), for example \(a_n=1-\frac1n\). What can be said about its limit?
options: It equals the bound 5
It equals the first term
It exists, but need not equal the bound 5
It may not exist, because the bound is not the limit
optionExplain: A bound is only an upper limit; the sequence can stay well below it.
An increasing sequence leaves its first term.
Right: this sequence has limit 1, which is far below 5.
The theorem guarantees a limit exists.
questions.explain: The book warns that the limit of the sequence need not be the bound B, and invites you to construct an example.
questions.rule: A bound is not a limit.
questions.teaches: The limit of a bounded monotonic sequence need not be the bound B; the book asks the reader to construct an example to be sure of that.

questions.q: A cooling pot's temperatures decrease every minute and stay above the 20 degree room temperature. What does the theorem tell you about the sequence?
options: It converges to exactly 20, the room temperature, by the same theorem
It converges only if all of the temperatures are whole numbers
Nothing can be said, since a list of temperatures is not a sequence of numbers
It converges to some limit; the theorem does not give the value
optionExplain: That would need extra information about the cooling, such as the physical law.
Whole numbers play no part in the theorem.
A list of readings is a sequence of numbers.
Right: the limit exists and is at least 20, and finding it needs further information.
questions.explain: Knowing that a limit exists is separate from finding it. The book later shows how to find a limit once existence is known.
questions.rule: Existence first, then the value.
questions.teaches: Knowing that a bounded monotonic sequence converges does not give its value; the limit still has to be found, which the book does later by guessing it or by solving an equation.

questions.q: A sequence satisfies \(0<a_n<\frac1n\) for every \(n\). What is its limit?
options: It has no limit
optionExplain: Right: it is trapped between 0 and a sequence that tends to 0.
Nothing pushes the terms toward 1; the bound 1/n is at most 1 and shrinks.
A sequence trapped between two sequences with the same limit cannot wander.
Terms below 1/n for n at least 2 are below 1/2, but they keep shrinking.
questions.explain: Both bounds have limit 0, so the terms in between must too. The card calls this the squeeze principle.
questions.rule: Trapped between equals means equal.

questions.q: True or false: The squeeze principle needs the two bounding sequences to converge to the same limit.
questions.explain: If the bounds had different limits, the trapped sequence would have room to move.
questions.rule: Same limit on both sides.

questions.q: What is \(\lim \frac{\sin n}{n}\)?
options: It does not exist, since sin n does not settle
optionExplain: This confuses the ratio with sin x / x as x tends to 0.
The numerator oscillates, but it is divided by n, which squeezes the quotient.
Right: |sin n / n| is at most 1/n, which tends to 0.
The terms never settle at 1/2; they shrink toward 0.
questions.explain: Bounding by 1/n squeezes the quotient to 0 whatever sin n does.
questions.rule: Use the bounds of the oscillating part.

questions.q: Sort each pair of bounds by whether the squeeze principle gives the limit of the sequence between them.

items.t: \(-\frac1n\le a_n\le\frac1n\)
\(2-\frac1n\le a_n\le 2+\frac1n\)
\(0\le a_n\le 1\)
\(1\le a_n\le 3\)
\(0\le a_n\le n\)

questions.explain: The principle works only when both bounds converge to the same number. Constant gaps, or an unbounded upper bound, give no conclusion.
questions.rule: Both bounds must close in on one value.

questions.q: A student says: since \(\frac1n\le a_n\le 2\) for all \(n\) and \(\frac1n\to 0\), the squeeze principle gives \(a_n\to 0\). What is wrong?
options: The lower bound 1/n does not tend to 0, so it cannot be used here
The upper bound 2 does not tend to 0, so nothing squeezes the sequence
A squeeze needs at least three sequences, not only two bounding ones, to trap a term
The inequality should be strict everywhere for a squeeze to work
optionExplain: It does tend to 0, so this part is fine.
Right: both bounds must tend to the same limit.
Two bounding sequences are enough.
Strict or not, the bounds' limits are what matter.
questions.explain: A squeeze needs both sides. Here the sequence could, for example, equal 1 forever.
questions.rule: Check both bounds.

questions.q: The cost of the \(n\)th batch is \(c_n\ge 10n\) dollars. According to the book's converse, what follows about the sequence \(c_n\)?
options: It converges to 10, the coefficient of n in the bound
It converges, since costs are positive numbers
Nothing can be said, because a squeeze needs an upper bound and this is a lower bound
It diverges, since its terms exceed those of a sequence tending to infinity
optionExplain: A lower bound of 10n gives no limit of 10.
Positive terms can still grow without bound.
A lower bound that diverges is enough here.
Right: the terms are at least as large as 10n, which grows without bound.
questions.explain: The book states a converse of the squeeze: if the terms are larger in absolute value than those of a sequence that diverges, the sequence also diverges.
questions.rule: A lower bound that diverges forces divergence.
questions.teaches: Conversely, if the terms of a sequence are greater in absolute value than the corresponding terms of a sequence that diverges (has an infinite limit), then the sequence also diverges.

questions.q: For large \(x\), which single power of \(x\) best describes how \(4x^3+50x^2\) grows?
options: \(4x^3+50x^2\) must be kept in full
optionExplain: Right: for large x the cubic term dominates.
The x squared term is eventually dwarfed by the cubic.
Adding exponents has no meaning here.
The point of the notation is to drop the unimportant part.
questions.explain: The leading term sets the growth rate. The card gives this idea a name and a precise definition.
questions.rule: The biggest term sets the growth.

questions.q: True or false: \(f(x)=o(g(x))\) means that \(f(x)/g(x)\) tends to 0 as \(x\) tends to infinity.
questions.explain: That is the definition of little-oh: f grows fundamentally slower than g.
questions.rule: o means the ratio tends to 0.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=5x^3+100x^2\), which statements are true as \(x\to\infty\)?
optionExplain: Right: f is at most 105 x cubed for x of at least 1.
The ratio f / x cubed tends to 5, not 0.
Right: f / x to the fourth tends to 0.
No constant multiple of x squared bounds f, because the cubic term outgrows it.
This repeats the false claim that the ratio tends to 0.
questions.explain: Compare the ratio with the target. The ratio with x cubed tends to 5, so only O holds; the ratio with x to the fourth tends to 0.
questions.rule: Compute the ratio to test o.

questions.q: A student reads \(x^2=O(x^3)\) as 'x squared is about as large as x cubed for large x'. What is wrong?
options: The statement is false, since x squared is smaller than x cubed
Big-Oh is only an upper bound; x squared is far smaller, in fact o(x cubed)
O means equal up to a constant, so the student is right and nothing is wrong
It holds only for x below 1, and the student ignored that
optionExplain: The statement is true; smaller functions are still bounded by larger ones.
Right: x squared over x cubed is 1/x, which tends to 0.
That is the claim of the student, not of the definition.
It holds for all sufficiently large x.
questions.explain: Read big-Oh as at most this order. To say that two functions grow at the same rate you need bounds both ways.
questions.rule: O is an upper bound, not an equality of growth.

questions.q: The notation also works near zero. As \(x\to 0\), which statement is true?
options: \(x=o(x^2)\), since x is smaller than 1
\(x^2=O(x)\) is false
Near zero the notation is undefined
optionExplain: Near 0, x squared is smaller than x, so the ratio x / x squared = 1/x grows.
It is true: x squared is at most |x| times x for small x.
The book defines it for x tending to 0, with bounds for small nonzero x.
Right: near 0, the higher power is the smaller one, the reverse of the situation at infinity.
questions.explain: Near 0 the roles of the powers swap. The book defines O(g) as x tends to 0 as a bound by a constant multiple of g for sufficiently small, nonzero x.
questions.rule: State which way x is going.
questions.teaches: The notation also describes behaviour as x tends to 0: f = O(g) there means f is bounded by a constant multiple of g for sufficiently small but nonzero x.

questions.q: A sorting step costs \(T(n)=O(n^2)\) operations per item, and a loop runs it \(n\) times, one for each size. What can be said about the total \(n\cdot T(n)\)?
optionExplain: Right: multiplying a function that is O(n squared) by n gives O(n cubed).
The extra factor n is not absorbed by the constant.
The total is at most of order n cubed and can be larger than n squared.
The bound cannot shrink when multiplied by n.
questions.explain: Simple algebra works with these symbols: the book notes that if a function is O of a power of x, multiplying it by x raises the power by one.
questions.rule: Oh-bounds multiply like powers.
questions.teaches: One can do simple algebra with the 'oh' functions: if f is big-Oh of a power of x, then x times f is big-Oh of the next power.

questions.q: What is the value of \(\left(1+\frac12\right)\left(1+\frac14\right)\left(1+\frac18\right)\), to the nearest tenth?
optionExplain: Right: 1.5 times 1.25 is 1.875, and times 1.125 is 2.109.
This stops after the second factor.
This adds the three fractions to 1 and multiplies the integer parts, overshooting.
This adds the three fractions and halves them, which does not match a product.
questions.explain: Products of numbers just above 1 climb slowly. The card asks how far an endless product can climb.
questions.rule: Each extra factor adds a little.

questions.q: True or false: The lower bound \(\frac1{1-x}\) comes from multiplying out the product and keeping the terms \(1, x, x^2,\ldots\)
questions.explain: Every power of x occurs at least once in the expansion, and the other terms are positive, so the product is at least the geometric series.
questions.rule: Multiply out for a lower bound.

questions.q: For \(x=\frac13\), the bounds are \(\frac1{1-x}<S(x)<e^{x/(1-x)}\). Which interval does this give for \(S(1/3)\), to three places?
optionExplain: This uses e to the power 1, the exponent for x = 1/2.
Right: 1/(1 - 1/3) = 1.5 and e to the power (1/3)/(2/3) = e to the 0.5 = 1.649.
This uses 1/(1 + x) for the lower bound, which is not the geometric sum.
This swaps the two bounds and changes the upper one.
questions.explain: Substitute x = 1/3 in both bounds. The true value, about 1.565, lies between them.
questions.rule: Substitute x into both bounds.

questions.q: As \(x\) increases toward 1, what happens to the two bounds \(\frac1{1-x}\) and \(e^{x/(1-x)}\)?
options: Both bounds tend to 1, so they pinch together at the value
The lower bound blows up, but the upper bound stays bounded near the number e
They become equal, and so give the exact value of the product
Both grow without bound, so the method gives no finite bound near 1
optionExplain: Neither bound tends to 1; both blow up.
The upper bound's exponent also blows up.
They separate more and more.
Right: the denominator 1 - x tends to 0 in both.
questions.explain: Both bounds rely on the geometric series, which needs x well below 1.
questions.rule: Geometric bounds fail as x nears 1.

questions.q: Put the steps in order that show \(\left(1+\frac1m\right)^m<e\).
items: Expand (1 + 1/m) to the power m with the binomial theorem
Compare each term with the matching term of 1 + 1 + 1/2! + 1/3! + ...
Note that the comparison series adds up to e
Conclude that (1 + 1/m) to the power m is less than e
questions.explain: Each binomial term is at most 1/k!, and the series of those terms sums to e. This is the inequality the upper bound uses.
questions.rule: Bound each binomial term by 1/k!.
questions.teaches: The inequality (1+1/m)^m < e follows from the binomial theorem: each term of the expansion is less than the matching term of 1+1+1/2!+1/3!+..., whose sum is e.

questions.q: For \(x=\frac12\), a student reports: 'the infinite product equals \(e\), because \(e\) is the upper bound.' What is the flaw?
options: The upper bound should be 2, not e, since 2 is the better estimate
The product diverges, so it has no value
A bound is not the value; the product is about 2.38, below e
The student should have used the lower bound 2 instead
optionExplain: 2 is the lower bound for x = 1/2.
It converges, being bounded and increasing.
Right: the method only locates the limit between 2 and e, and the book asks whether the bounds can be improved.
Neither bound is the value.
questions.explain: The task in the book was only to find upper and lower bounds a and b with a at most the limit at most b. It then asks whether better bounds exist.
questions.rule: Report a bound as a bound.
questions.teaches: The example only asks for upper and lower bounds on the limit, and the book then asks whether these bounds can be improved: bounds are not the value.

questions.q: Start with \(x_0=5\) and apply \(x_{n+1}=\frac12\left(x_n+\frac5{x_n}\right)\). What is \(x_1\)?
optionExplain: This leaves the starting value unchanged.
Right: half of (5 + 1) is 3.
This adds 5 and 1 without halving.
This halves only the starting value.
questions.explain: Each new term averages the old term with 5 divided by it. The card follows this sequence.
questions.rule: Average x_n with a / x_n.

questions.q: True or false: Each term x_{n+1} of the sequence is the average of x_n and a/x_n.
questions.explain: That is the defining recurrence: add the two numbers and halve.
questions.rule: Each term averages x_n and a over x_n.

questions.q: With \(a=5\) and \(x_1=3\), the next term is \(x_2=\) ____ (give a fraction).
questions.explain: The average of 3 and 5/3 is half of 14/3, which is 7/3, closer to the root of 5 (2.236) than 3 was.
questions.rule: Average the two numbers.

questions.q: A student shows \(x_{n+1}\le x_n\) for every \(n\) and concludes that the sequence converges. What is missing?
options: A lower bound, because a decreasing sequence can fall without limit
A proof that the sequence is increasing as well as decreasing
Nothing is missing, since every decreasing sequence of numbers converges
A proof that every term of the sequence is a whole number
optionExplain: Right: the book's argument adds that every term is at least the root of a.
It would then not be decreasing.
A sequence such as -1, -2, -3, ... decreases and does not converge.
The terms are not integers (3, 7/3, 47/21, ...).
questions.explain: Both hypotheses of the bounded monotonic theorem are needed. The lower bound comes from the AM-GM inequality.
questions.rule: Monotone needs a bound.

questions.q: The book notes that \(x_{n+1}\le x_n\) could be checked another way. Which check works for positive terms?
options: Showing that the ratio x_n / x_{n+1} is at most 1
Showing that the ratio x_{n+1} / x_n is at most 1
Showing that the sum x_n + x_{n+1} is at most twice a number
Showing that x_n is an integer
optionExplain: That would show the sequence increases.
Right: for positive terms, a ratio at most 1 means the sequence does not grow.
A sum bound does not compare consecutive terms.
Integrality is irrelevant.
questions.explain: The book's footnote says that the ratio is just as easy to study as the difference, and is at most 1 given that x_n is at least the root of a.
questions.rule: Ratio at most 1 or difference at least 0.
questions.teaches: Instead of the difference x_n - x_{n+1}, one can study the ratio x_{n+1}/x_n, which is at most 1 for the same reason.

questions.q: To estimate \(\sqrt{10}\), a spreadsheet starts at \(x_0=1\), below the root, and applies the averaging rule with \(a=10\). What happens at the first step?
options: x_1 is 5.5, above the root; afterwards the terms decrease
x_1 stays below the root, so the sequence increases toward it
x_1 is 10, the same as a, so the sequence is constant afterwards
The rule fails, because x_0 is below the root of a
optionExplain: Right: the average of 1 and 10 is 5.5, and every term after that is at least the root.
The average of x and a/x is never below the root.
10 is a/x_0, not the average.
The rule works for any positive start.
questions.explain: The bound x_{n+1} is at least the root of a holds no matter what x_n is. Only the first term can be below the root.
questions.rule: After one step the terms are at least the root.
questions.teaches: Since x_{n+1} is at least the square root of a no matter what x_n is, every term after the first is above the root.

questions.q: Each error is less than half the previous one, and the first error is 8. What is the best upper bound for the third error, three steps later?
optionExplain: Right: 8 times (1/2) three times is 1, so the third error is less than 1.
This halves only once.
This halves only twice.
The error shrinks but is not yet 0.
questions.explain: Halving three times divides by 8. The card uses this kind of geometric shrinking to prove convergence.
questions.rule: Repeated halving divides by powers of 2.

questions.q: The error ratio \(E_{n+1}/E_n\) is positive and less than ____.
questions.explain: The ratio is E_n / (2 x_n), and E_n is less than x_n, so the ratio is below one half.
questions.rule: Ratio below one half.

questions.q: For \(a=5\) the errors are \(E_2\approx0.0973\) and \(E_3\approx0.00203\). What is \(E_3/E_2\), to two places?
optionExplain: This is the bound, not the actual ratio.
This is 10 times too large.
This inverts the ratio.
questions.explain: The actual ratio is far below the guaranteed 1/2, since E_n is tiny compared with 2 x_n.
questions.rule: The bound is a ceiling, not the value.

questions.q: True or false: Near the end, \(x_n\approx2.236\) and \(E_n=0.001\). By \(E_{n+1}=E_n^2/(2x_n)\), the next error is about 0.0005.
questions.explain: Squaring gives 10^-6, and dividing by 2 x_n, about 4.47, gives about 2 x 10^-7. The factor-of-one-half bound is very pessimistic once the error is small.
questions.rule: Squaring a small error makes it tiny.

questions.q: In the algebra for \(E_{n+1}\), the numerator is \(x_n^2-2x_n\sqrt a+a\). What does it factor as?
options: It does not factor
optionExplain: That factorization has the wrong middle term.
The middle term is minus, not plus.
Right: it is a perfect square, which is why the new error is the old error squared over 2 x_n.
It factors as a perfect square.
questions.explain: The book remarks, 'aren't you glad you studied factoring': the numerator is exactly (x_n minus the root) squared.
questions.rule: Look for perfect squares.
questions.teaches: The numerator x_n^2 - 2 x_n sqrt(a) + a is a perfect square, (x_n - sqrt(a))^2, which is what makes E_{n+1} equal E_n^2 / (2 x_n).

questions.q: A thermostat reads r_n degrees, the setpoint is 21, and each error r_n - 21 is positive and less than a third of the previous error. Which sequence should you prove tends to 0?
options: The errors e_n = r_n - 21, so the target becomes 0
The readings r_n themselves, which tend to 21
The ratios r_{n+1} / r_n of consecutive readings, taken one by one
The setpoints 21, 21, 21, ... of the thermostat
optionExplain: Right: the book defines errors because 0 is an easier number to work with than the target.
Their limit is 21, which is the harder number to work with.
The ratios tend to 1, not 0.
The setpoint is a constant, not a sequence.
questions.explain: Proving the errors tend to 0 shows the readings tend to 21. This is the strategy of the square-root example.
questions.rule: Convert 'tends to the target' into 'error tends to 0'.
questions.teaches: The book defines the error sequence E_n = x_n - sqrt(a) because 0 is a much easier number to work with than the limit itself.

questions.q: A sequence satisfies \(x_{n+1}=\frac12x_n+3\) and converges to \(L\). What is \(L\)?
optionExplain: Right: L = L/2 + 3 gives L = 6.
This is the constant term alone.
The constant 3 keeps pushing the sequence upward.
This doubles the correct answer.
questions.explain: If the terms settle at L, the rule leaves L unchanged. The card turns that into a general tool.
questions.rule: At the limit, the rule leaves L unchanged.

questions.q: True or false: The solve-for-the-limit tool proves that the limit of the sequence exists.
questions.explain: It only shows what the limit must equal if it exists. Existence needs a separate argument.
questions.rule: The tool gives candidates, not proofs.

questions.q: Positive terms satisfy \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+x_n}\). If the sequence converges, its limit is ____.
questions.explain: L = sqrt(2 + L) gives L squared - L - 2 = 0, so (L - 2)(L + 1) = 0. The root -1 cannot be the limit of positive terms, so L = 2.
questions.rule: Reject roots that contradict the terms.

questions.q: For \(x_{n+1}=2x_n\) with \(x_0=1\), a student solves \(L=2L\), gets \(L=0\), and concludes that \(x_n\to0\). What is wrong?
options: The equation should be L = 2L + 1, with an added constant
The terms 1, 2, 4, 8, ... diverge, so there is no limit to find
The solution should be L = 1, since the first term is 1
L = 0 is correct, since 0 satisfies the equation L = 2L, and equations decide limits
optionExplain: The recurrence has no added constant.
Right: the tool gives the limit only if one exists.
The first term does not satisfy L = 2L.
A solution of the equation is a candidate, not a limit.
questions.explain: The solution L = 0 is a fixed point of the rule, but these terms move away from it.
questions.rule: Check that the limit exists.

questions.q: In the square-root example, the book calls one part the trickiest. Which part?
options: Proving that the sequence is decreasing at each step
Computing the first few terms of the sequence by hand
Drawing the graphs of y = x and y = 5/x
Guessing that the limit was the square root of a
optionExplain: The book describes that step as easy.
That is routine arithmetic.
The graphs are drawn for the picture; the guess is the hard part.
Right: the tool is offered as a way to find the guess when you do not have a nice picture.
questions.explain: With a picture the limit was easy to guess; without one, the tool gives the guess by algebra.
questions.rule: The tool is the fallback when no picture helps.
questions.teaches: The trickiest part of the square-root example was guessing that the limit was sqrt(a); the solve-for-the-limit tool answers the question of what to do without a nice picture.

questions.q: Define \(a_1=1\) and \(a_{n+1}=1+\frac1{a_n}\), whose terms are positive. If it converges, what does it converge to?
options: \(\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\approx1.618\)
\(\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}\approx -0.618\)
optionExplain: This is the first term, which does not satisfy L = 1 + 1/L.
Right: L = 1 + 1/L gives L squared - L - 1 = 0, and the positive root is (1 + root 5)/2.
This is a_2 = 1 + 1/1, the second term.
It solves the equation, but the terms are positive.
questions.explain: The equation only gives candidates. Positivity of the terms rules out the negative root. A separate argument would still be needed to show that the sequence converges.
questions.rule: Solve, then use what you know to pick the root.
questions.teaches: The tool applies to any recursively defined sequence, and it gives a candidate for the limit without any picture.

questions.q: Which is smaller: \(\sqrt[3]{1001}-\sqrt[3]{1000}\) or \(\sqrt[3]{2}-\sqrt[3]{1}\)?
options: Cube roots of 1001 and 1000, about 0.0033
Cube roots of 2 and 1, about 0.26
They are equal, since both pairs of numbers differ by 1
Neither can be compared
optionExplain: Right: cube roots of large numbers are packed more tightly.
This difference is the larger one.
Equal gaps between inputs do not give equal gaps between cube roots.
The graph of the cube root flattens, which settles the question.
questions.explain: The cube root flattens as its input grows, so a unit step in n moves it less and less.
questions.rule: Cube roots crowd together as n grows.

questions.q: As \(n\) grows, the difference \(\sqrt[3]{n+1}-\sqrt[3]{n}\) tends to ____.
questions.explain: It behaves like n to the power -2/3, which shrinks to 0.
questions.rule: Gaps between cube roots shrink to 0.

questions.q: What is \(\sqrt[3]{1001}-10\), to four decimal places?
optionExplain: This is 10 times too large.
This is 10 times too small.
This is 1/3, the wrong order of magnitude.
Right: 10.0033 cubed is about 1001.
questions.explain: The cube of 10 + d is about 1000 + 300 d, so 300 d = 1 and d is about 0.0033.
questions.rule: Estimate with a linear approximation.

questions.q: True or false: Moving from \(m=10^3\) to \(m=10^6\) makes the first step of the ladder \(\sqrt[3]{n}-\sqrt[3]{m}\) about 100 times smaller.
questions.explain: The gap scales like n to the minus two thirds. A thousand times larger n gives steps a hundred times smaller (0.0033 against 0.000033).
questions.rule: Gap scales as n^(-2/3).

questions.q: The book rewrites the starting value 3 as \(\sqrt[3]{1000}-\sqrt[3]{343}\). How does that choice sharpen the approximation?
options: It makes the difference exactly 3, so the search is over
It replaces the cube root by a square root, which is smoother
It starts the ladder from a larger cube, so rungs are closer
It removes the need for any estimate of the gap
optionExplain: The value 3 is only the starting rung; it does not reach the target.
The function stays the cube root.
Right: starting from 10 cubed minus 7 cubed uses larger inputs, so the rungs \(\sqrt[3]{1001}-7,\ \sqrt[3]{1002}-7,\dots\) are more finely spaced than a ladder built near \(\sqrt[3]{28}\).
The O-estimate is still needed.
questions.explain: The ladder now starts at 3 written with larger cubes, so the steps are finer than those of the sequence built near the cube root of 28.
questions.rule: Larger inputs give finer ladders.
questions.teaches: To get closer to a target, the book restarts the ladder at 3 written as the cube root of 1000 minus the cube root of 343, giving the more finely spaced sequence cube root of 1001 minus 7, cube root of 1002 minus 7, and so on.

questions.q: Is every positive real number a limit of numbers of the form k/2^j, where k and j are non-negative integers?
options: No, since these fractions allow only powers of two as denominators, a far too sparse set
Yes, but only for numbers between 0 and 1
No, because there are only countably many such fractions
Yes: round down to a multiple of 1/2^j, which errs by at most 1/2^j
optionExplain: Few denominators still allow arbitrarily fine grids.
The same rounding works for any positive real.
Countably many points can still approximate every real number, as the rationals do.
Right: such a set is dense, meaning it has elements arbitrarily close to every real number.
questions.explain: A set is dense when each real number has members of the set arbitrarily close to it. The rationals are the standard example, and so are fractions with powers of two below.
questions.rule: Show that a set gets arbitrarily close.
questions.teaches: A set S of reals is dense if, given any real x, there are elements of S arbitrarily close to x; the rationals are dense, since decimal approximations come arbitrarily close to any real number.

questions.q: Let \(f(x)=0\) for \(x<1\) and \(f(x)=1\) for \(x\ge1\). For \(x_n=1-\frac1n\), what do the values \(f(x_n)\) approach?
options: They have no limit
optionExplain: Right: every x_n is below 1, so f(x_n) = 0 for all n.
This is f(1), the value at the limit point, not the values along the sequence.
The function takes only the values 0 and 1.
A constant sequence of zeros has limit 0.
questions.explain: The values along the sequence approach 0 while f(1) = 1. The card calls this a failure of continuity.
questions.rule: Compare the limit of f(x_n) with f(a).

questions.q: f is continuous at \(a\) if \(f(x_n)\) tends to ____ for every sequence \(x_n\) tending to \(a\).
accept: the value of f at a
questions.explain: The outputs must approach the value of f at the limit point.
questions.rule: Outputs approach f(a).

questions.q: For \(f(x)=3x+1\) and \(x_n=2+\frac1n\), what is \(\lim f(x_n)\)?
options: The limit does not exist
optionExplain: This is f(2) minus 1, a slip in evaluating 3 times 2 plus 1.
Right: f(x_n) = 7 + 3/n, which tends to 7 = f(2).
This is the constant term only.
The values 7 + 3/n clearly settle down.
questions.explain: Since f(2) = 7 and the sequence of values tends to 7, the test passes for this sequence, as it does for all sequences.
questions.rule: Compute f(x_n), then take the limit.

questions.q: True or false: A student tests the step function above (0 for \(x<1\), 1 for \(x\ge1\)) only with \(x_n=1+\frac1n\), finds \(f(x_n)=1=f(1)\), and concludes that \(f\) is continuous at 1. The conclusion is justified.
questions.explain: The test must pass for every sequence. The sequence 1 - 1/n gives f(x_n) = 0, not 1, so the function is not continuous at 1.
questions.rule: One failing sequence is enough.

questions.q: Why might the book choose the sequence form of continuity over the other equivalent definitions?
options: It is the only definition that is correct, so the others are wrong
It avoids the need for any limits, by using only inequalities
It is easy to use and builds on convergence of sequences
It applies only to polynomial functions and similar formulas
optionExplain: The book says there are many equivalent definitions.
The definition is stated using a limit of a sequence.
Right: the book says that of the many equivalent formal definitions, this is one of the easiest to use.
It applies to any function with a domain D.
questions.explain: The sequence form lets all the earlier methods for convergence be reused.
questions.rule: Choose the definition that is easiest to use.
questions.teaches: Of the many equivalent formal definitions of continuity, the sequence form is one of the easiest to use, so the book adopts it.

questions.q: A taxi fare is 3 for any trip up to and including 1 km, and 5 for trips above 1 km up to 2 km. Which sequence of trip lengths shows the fare is not continuous at 1 km?
options: 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, ... approaching 1 from below
1.5, 1.5, 1.5, ... a constant sequence
Any sequence works equally well
optionExplain: Right: the fares are 5, 5, 5, ... but the fare at 1 km is 3.
These fares are all 3, which equals the fare at 1 km, so this sequence passes the test.
This sequence does not approach 1, so it says nothing about continuity at 1.
Only a sequence approaching 1 from above fails.
questions.explain: A function fails to be continuous as soon as one sequence breaks the rule. Here the sequence from the right does, even though the one from the left passes.
questions.rule: Look for one sequence that breaks the rule.
questions.teaches: Since the definition requires the property for all sequences, a single sequence that approaches the point but whose function values do not approach f(a) shows the function is not continuous there.

questions.q: Which of these functions is NOT continuous at \(x=2\)?
options: x squared plus 1, a polynomial with no breaks
the square root of x, a radical defined from 0
2 to the power x, an exponential function
the floor of x, the greatest integer at most x
optionExplain: A polynomial is continuous everywhere.
The square root is continuous at every point where it is defined, and 2 is such a point.
Exponential functions are continuous.
Right: it jumps from 1 to 2 as x passes 2, so x_n = 2 - 1/n gives values 1, not 2.
questions.explain: A step-like function breaks the pencil rule. The card lists the functions that do not.
questions.rule: Jumps break continuity.

questions.q: True or false: A polynomial is continuous at every real number.
questions.explain: Polynomials are elementary functions, and elementary functions are continuous at all points of their domains, which here is every real number.
questions.rule: Elementary means continuous on its domain.

questions.q: Sort each function by whether it is continuous at every point of its domain, according to the card.
groups: Continuous at all points of its domain
Not covered by the card's statement

items.t: \(\sin x\)
\(\dfrac1x\) for \(x\ne0\)
\(\lfloor x\rfloor\)
\(\lceil x\rceil\)

questions.explain: The first four are elementary functions. The floor and ceiling functions are not covered by the statement; they are the notable exceptions.
questions.rule: Check whether the function is a finite combination of elementary ones.

questions.q: A student says: 1/x is not continuous, because it has no value at 0. What is wrong?
options: Continuity concerns points of the domain; 0 is not in it
1/x is continuous at 0 because its limit exists there
A rational function can never be continuous at all
The student should have tested the sequence 1/n at 0, which would settle it
optionExplain: Right: 1/x is continuous at every point where it is defined.
The function is not defined at 0, and its values are unbounded near it.
Rational functions are continuous where defined.
A sequence that tends to the excluded point is not covered by the definition.
questions.explain: A discontinuity needs a point of the domain where a sequence fails. A point outside the domain does not count.
questions.rule: Test points in the domain only.

questions.q: Take \(f(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor\), which is 2 for \(2\le x<3\). Restrict it to the interval \([2,3)\). What happens to continuity?
options: It is still discontinuous at 2, because the jump is still there
It is discontinuous at every point of the interval
Continuous, since it is constant on that interval
It becomes undefined on the restricted interval
optionExplain: The jump at 2 came from points below 2, which have been removed.
A constant function is continuous.
Right: on [2, 3) every sequence has f(x_n) = 2 = f(a).
The floor function is defined for every real number.
questions.explain: Continuity depends on the domain. Removing the points where the jump occurs removes the failing sequences.
questions.rule: Continuity is relative to the domain.

questions.q: Which everyday quantity is a problem if we take continuity for granted, as the book says we usually do?
options: The temperature in a room over the course of a day
Postage cost by weight, which jumps at each weight limit
The height of a falling ball over time in free fall
The area of a square as its side length grows smoothly from 0
optionExplain: Temperature changes smoothly, with no jumps.
Right: step pricing is a floor-type function and it is not continuous.
The height varies continuously.
The area is the polynomial s squared.
questions.explain: The book notes that most functions given by simple formulas are continuous, and gives the floor and ceiling functions as notable exceptions. Step functions of weight or time fit that pattern.
questions.rule: Prices and counts often jump.
questions.teaches: Virtually every function that can be written with a simple formula is continuous; the floor and ceiling functions are notable exceptions, which is why the book concentrates on the good properties continuous functions have.

questions.q: A function f is continuous on [0, 10], with f(0) = -3 and f(10) = 4. Which value must f take somewhere on [0, 10]?
optionExplain: 5 lies above both end values, so f need not reach it.
-5 lies below both end values.
Right: 0 lies between -3 and 4.
Nothing forces such a large value.
questions.explain: A continuous graph that starts below 0 and ends above 0 must cross the axis. The card states this as a theorem.
questions.rule: Between the end values, every value is taken.

questions.q: If f is continuous on [a, b], it takes every value between f(a) and f(b). This is the ____ value theorem.
questions.explain: The intermediate value theorem is named for the values in between.
questions.rule: Intermediate means in between.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^3-x-1\), \(f(1)=-1\) and \(f(2)=5\). Evaluating at the midpoint 1.5 gives 0.875. In which interval does a zero lie?
options: There is no zero, since f(1.5) is positive
optionExplain: f(1.5) = 0.875 and f(2) = 5 are both positive, so no sign change is guaranteed there.
This lies outside the interval being searched.
A sign change occurs between 1 and 1.5.
Right: f changes sign from -1 to 0.875 on [1, 1.5].
questions.explain: Keep the half-interval whose ends have opposite signs. This is the repeated-bisection idea behind a rigorous proof.
questions.rule: Keep the half with the sign change.

questions.q: A student argues: for \(f(x)=1/x\) on \([-1,1]\), \(f(-1)=-1\) and \(f(1)=1\), so by the intermediate value theorem \(f\) has a zero. What fails?
options: The values -1 and 1 are not on either side of 0
The function is not continuous on [-1, 1], undefined at 0
The theorem works only for increasing functions, which 1/x is not
The interval must be open
optionExplain: The value 0 lies between -1 and 1; the issue is the hypothesis.
Right: the hypothesis of continuity on the whole interval is missing.
It applies to any continuous function.
The theorem uses a closed interval.
questions.explain: A theorem applies only when its hypotheses are met. Here the graph has a break at 0 that lets it skip over 0.
questions.rule: Check every hypothesis.

questions.q: Put the steps of finding a zero by bisection in order.
items: Check that f has opposite signs at the two ends of the interval
Evaluate f at the midpoint
Keep the half whose ends have opposite signs
Repeat, so that the interval shrinks toward one point
questions.explain: Each pass halves the interval while keeping a sign change inside it. The book's problem uses this to prove the theorem.
questions.rule: Halve the interval and keep the sign change.
questions.teaches: The book suggests proving the intermediate value theorem by repeated bisection, like trapping the square root of 2 between a too-small and a too-big approximation that improve each time.

questions.q: Let \(p(x)=x^3-4x+1\), so \(p(0)=1\) and \(p(1)=-2\). What does the intermediate value theorem give?
options: A zero of p between 0 and 1
A zero of p at 0.5
No information, since the end values are not equal
A maximum of p between 0 and 1
optionExplain: Right: p is a polynomial, hence continuous, and p changes sign.
The theorem gives existence, not the location.
Equal end values are not needed.
The theorem says nothing about extreme values.
questions.explain: The book calls the theorem obvious, yet it has many immediate applications such as proving that an equation has a solution.
questions.rule: Use sign changes to prove a solution exists.
questions.teaches: Although the intermediate value theorem is 'obvious', it has many immediate applications, such as showing that an equation has a solution.

questions.q: Does \(f(x)=x\) have a largest value on the open interval \((0,1)\)?
options: No: the values approach 1 but never reach it
Yes, the largest value is 1, at the right end
Yes, the largest value is 0.99, near the right end
Yes, it is 0, at the left end of the interval
optionExplain: Right: for any value x below 1, a larger value lies between x and 1.
1 is not in the interval.
Then 0.999 would be larger.
0 is the smallest candidate, not the largest.
questions.explain: An open interval can leave out the point where the extreme would occur. The card says closed intervals do not.
questions.rule: Open intervals can miss the extremes.

questions.q: True or false: A continuous function on a closed interval [a, b] attains a minimum and a maximum value.
questions.explain: That is the extreme value theorem. Both extremes are attained at points of the interval.
questions.rule: Closed and continuous gives attained extremes.

questions.q: What are the maximum and minimum of \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) on \([-2,2]\)?
options: Maximum 8, minimum -8
Maximum 2, minimum -2
Maximum 2, minimum 0
Maximum 4, minimum -4
optionExplain: This evaluates x cubed at the ends and forgets the -3x term.
The function dips to -2 at both x = 1 and x = -2.
No point of the interval produces values of +4 or -4.
questions.explain: Compare the values at the endpoints and at the turning points x = -1 and x = 1. The largest is 2 and the smallest is -2.
questions.rule: Compare endpoints and turning points.

questions.q: Sort each case by whether the extreme value theorem guarantees a maximum and a minimum.

items.t: \(\tan x\) on \([0,\frac\pi2]\)

questions.explain: The theorem needs a continuous function on a closed interval. The last case fails because tan is undefined at pi/2, so it is not continuous on the whole interval.
questions.rule: Check closed interval and continuity.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^2\), the interval \([-1,2]\) is changed to \((-1,2)\). What happens to the extremes?
options: Both extremes are lost, since the interval is now open
Both extremes are still attained, since f is continuous
The minimum is lost and the maximum remains attained
The minimum 0 survives, but the maximum 4 is lost
optionExplain: The minimum is at x = 0, which is still inside.
The values approach 4 near x = 2 but never reach it.
The maximum was at the removed endpoint, so it is the one lost.
Right: the maximum was at x = 2, which has been removed.
questions.explain: Dropping an endpoint can remove an extreme that sits there. Closedness is a hypothesis that does real work.
questions.rule: Endpoints can hold the extremes.

questions.q: The function \(g(x)=x^2\) is continuous on the open interval \((0,3)\). Does it attain a maximum there?
options: Yes, the maximum 9 is attained at x = 3
Yes, because g is continuous on the interval
No: values approach 9 without reaching it
Yes, the maximum is 0, attained at x = 0
optionExplain: 3 is not in the open interval.
Continuity is not enough on a non-closed interval.
Right: the book gives the same kind of example, 1/x on (0, 5), continuous but attaining neither a maximum nor a minimum.
0 is not in the interval and is the smaller value in any case.
questions.explain: The book's own example for dropping the closed interval is 1/x on (0, 5): continuous there, yet it reaches neither a maximum nor a minimum. The function g above shows the same failure.
questions.rule: Without a closed interval, extremes can escape.
questions.teaches: The book's example of failure: f(x)=1/x is continuous on (0,5) but achieves neither a maximum nor a minimum value on that interval.

questions.q: A continuous function \(f\) maps \([0,1]\) into \([0,1]\). Must the graphs of \(y=f(x)\) and \(y=x\) cross?
options: Yes: at some point they meet
No: f could stay above the line y = x throughout
Only if f is increasing
Only if f is a polynomial
optionExplain: Right: the graph of f starts at or above the line and ends at or below it.
At x = 1, f(1) is at most 1, so f cannot be above the line there.
Monotonicity is not needed.
Continuity is enough.
questions.explain: At x = 0 the graph of f is at or above the line, and at x = 1 it is at or below it. The card turns this into a proof.
questions.rule: Start above, end below, so cross.

questions.q: The proof defines a new function g(x) = f(x) - ____.
questions.explain: The difference between f and the identity function is zero exactly at the fixed points.
questions.rule: Fixed points are zeros of f(x) - x.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=1-x^2\) on \([0,1]\), what is the fixed point, to three places?
optionExplain: This solves x squared = 1/2, a different equation.
Right: x = 1 - x squared gives x squared + x - 1 = 0, whose positive root is 0.618.
questions.explain: Setting g(x) = 0 gives the quadratic x squared + x - 1 = 0. Its root in [0, 1] is (root 5 - 1)/2.
questions.rule: Solve f(x) = x.

questions.q: A student writes: g(0) = f(0) is at least 0 and g(1) = f(1) - 1 is at least 0, so g has a zero by the intermediate value theorem. What is wrong?
options: g(0) must be negative, not at least 0, since f(0) is small
g is not continuous, since f(x) - x has a corner
The theorem needs three points, not only two end values
g(1) = f(1) - 1 is at most 0, so there is no sign change
optionExplain: g(0) = f(0) is at least 0.
g is the difference of two continuous functions.
Two end values with a value between them are enough.
Right: f(1) is at most 1, so g(1) is at most 0.
questions.explain: A sign change needs opposite signs at the two ends. The inequality for g(1) points the other way from the one claimed.
questions.rule: Check the sign at each end.

questions.q: True or false: For \(f(x)=x+1\) on \([0,1]\), which maps outside \([0,1]\), the proof breaks because \(g(1)\) is positive; indeed \(f\) has no fixed point.
questions.explain: Here g(x) = 1 for every x, so there is no sign change, and x + 1 = x has no solution. Mapping [0, 1] into itself is a hypothesis of the theorem.
questions.rule: The map must stay inside the interval.

questions.q: A hiker walks up a trail from 8:00 to 18:00 on Monday and back down the same trail over the same hours on Tuesday. Which new function shows there is a time of day when she is at the same spot on both days?
options: The sum of the up and down positions at each time
The difference between the up and down positions
The product of the up and down positions at each time
The average speed over the two days of walking
optionExplain: A sum being zero says nothing about the positions being equal.
Right: it is positive at one end of the day and negative at the other, so it vanishes somewhere.
The product has no sign change that matters.
A single number is not a function of time.
questions.explain: The book calls defining a new function the crux move and says it is a typical tactic in problems of this kind. Here the difference of positions plays the role of f(x) - x.
questions.rule: Define a function that is zero where you want it.
questions.teaches: The crux move, defining a new function, is a typical tactic in problems of this kind.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=2x+1\), two inputs differ by less than 0.05. By how much can the outputs differ, at most?
options: Less than 0.1
Less than 0.05
Less than 0.2
It depends on where the inputs are
optionExplain: Right: the outputs differ by 2 times the input difference.
This forgets the factor 2 in the slope.
This doubles the factor twice.
For a line, the answer is the same everywhere.
questions.explain: A line has the same slope everywhere, so one rule works everywhere. The card names this uniform behaviour.
questions.rule: A line has one slope everywhere.

questions.q: In uniform continuity, δ depends only on ε and not on the ____.
questions.explain: The same δ must serve every pair of points in the domain.
questions.rule: One δ for all points.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=3x\), what δ guarantees \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|<0.06\) whenever \(|x_1-x_2|<\delta\)?
optionExplain: This ignores the factor 3, so outputs may differ by 0.18.
This multiplies by 3 instead of dividing.
This divides in the wrong direction, by 0.3.
questions.explain: The slope 3 multiplies input differences, so dividing the tolerance by 3 gives δ = ε/3.
questions.rule: Divide the tolerance by the slope.

questions.q: A student shows that near a given \(x_1\), the value \(\delta=\varepsilon/(2|x_1|+1)\) works for \(f(x)=x^2\), and concludes that \(f\) is uniformly continuous on all of \(\mathbb R\). What is wrong?
options: The delta is too large to work for any choice of x_1
The function x squared is not continuous at points far from 0
The student should have used epsilon in place of delta
This delta depends on x_1, so no single delta serves the whole domain
optionExplain: The issue is not its size but its dependence on x_1.
It is continuous at every point.
The roles of ε and δ are correct.
Right: uniform continuity needs a δ that depends on ε alone.
questions.explain: A δ that changes with the location is the signature of ordinary continuity. Uniformity demands one δ for all locations.
questions.rule: δ must not depend on x.

questions.q: True or false: If f is uniformly continuous on a set A, then f is uniformly continuous on every subset B of A.
questions.explain: The same δ that works for all pairs in A works for all pairs in B, since B's pairs are among A's pairs.
questions.rule: Smaller domain, same δ works.

questions.q: The book says every continuous function on a closed interval is uniformly continuous. How does it treat this fact, and why?
options: It accepts it on faith, since the proof is difficult
It proves it in full in the chapter, using bisection
It denies it, giving a counterexample on [0, 1]
It applies it only to linear functions
optionExplain: Right: for this reason uniform continuity is not often introduced in elementary calculus classes.
The book skips the proof.
The statement is true, and the book relies on it.
The statement covers all continuous functions on closed intervals.
questions.explain: The book calls uniform continuity such a useful idea that it accepts the theorem for now, and later uses it to complete the proof of the fundamental theorem.
questions.rule: Use a hard theorem on faith while its use is clear.
questions.teaches: It is rather difficult to prove that all continuous functions on closed intervals are uniformly continuous, so uniform continuity is not often introduced in elementary calculus classes, and the book accepts the fact on faith.

questions.q: If \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) both lie in \([-3,3]\), what is the largest possible value of \(|x_1+x_2|\)?
optionExplain: This takes one number at its end and the other at 0.
Right: it occurs when both equal 3 or both equal -3.
This squares an endpoint, as if finding f(3).
This is the smallest value, attained when x_1 = -x_2.
questions.explain: The sum is largest when both inputs are at the same end. The card uses this bound in the factorization.
questions.rule: Bound the sum at the ends.

questions.q: True or false: The factorization \(x_1^2-x_2^2=(x_1+x_2)(x_1-x_2)\) is what lets the output difference be bounded by a constant times the input difference.
questions.explain: The second factor is the input difference, and on [-3, 3] the first factor is at most 6 in absolute value.
questions.rule: Difference of squares.

questions.q: On \([-3,3]\), what δ does the card's method give for \(\varepsilon=0.3\)?
optionExplain: This takes δ equal to ε, ignoring the factor |x_1 + x_2| of up to 6.
This multiplies ε by 6 instead of dividing.
This uses 3 in place of 6, bounding only one input.
Right: delta = epsilon / 6 = 0.3 / 6 = 0.05.
questions.explain: The output difference is at most 6 times the input difference, so δ = ε/6.
questions.rule: δ = ε divided by the bound.

questions.q: The interval is widened to \([-10,10]\). With \(\varepsilon=0.3\), the same method gives \(\delta=\) ____ (decimal).
questions.explain: Now |x_1 + x_2| is at most 20, so delta = 0.3 / 20 = 0.015. Widening the domain raises the bound and makes delta smaller.
questions.rule: A bigger domain may need a smaller delta.

questions.q: A student writes: \(|x_1^2-x_2^2|\le|x_1-x_2|\), so \(\delta=\varepsilon\) works on \([-3,3]\). What is wrong?
options: The factor |x_1 + x_2|, up to 6, was dropped
The student used absolute values of the differences
Delta should be larger than epsilon in this case
The function is not defined at 0, so no delta exists
optionExplain: Right: for x_1 = 3 and x_2 = 2.9, the left side is 0.59, much larger than 0.1.
Absolute values are needed here.
The problem is the missing factor, not the size of δ alone.
x squared is defined at 0.
questions.explain: Check an example. With x_1 = 3 and x_2 = 2.9, the inputs differ by 0.1 and the outputs by 0.59.
questions.rule: Test a bound on a sample pair.

questions.q: Square tiles have a side s measured between 0 and 3 cm, with area s squared. Each side may be wrongly measured by at most 0.01 cm. What is the largest error in area the method guarantees?
options: 0.01 square cm
0.06 square cm
0.03 square cm
0.6 square cm
optionExplain: This ignores the factor from |s_1 + s_2|.
Right: the bound is 6 times 0.01.
This uses 3 instead of 6.
This is 60 times the side error.
questions.explain: In the book's language, the ε challenge (a tolerance on the output) gets a δ response (a tolerance on the input) that depends only on ε. Here the roles are reversed: a given δ = 0.01 gives ε = 0.06.
questions.rule: Translate between input and output tolerance.
questions.teaches: The book describes uniform continuity as a game: an epsilon challenge (a tolerance on the function values) is answered by a delta response, and the point of the definition is that the delta response does not depend on x.

questions.q: For f(x) = 1/x, compare two pairs of inputs, each 0.01 apart: (0.01, 0.02) and (2, 2.01). Where do the outputs differ more?
options: (0.01, 0.02): the outputs are 100 and 50
(2, 2.01): the outputs differ by about 0.0025
They differ equally, since the inputs are 0.01 apart
They cannot be compared
optionExplain: Right: the outputs differ by 50, against about 0.0025 for the other pair.
That is the smaller difference.
The function is much steeper near 0.
Both are easily computed.
questions.explain: The same input gap gives very different output gaps. The card explains why this rules out one δ for the whole domain.
questions.rule: Steep regions need smaller δ.

questions.q: True or false: On the interval [2, 1000], the function 1/x is uniformly continuous.
questions.explain: On a closed interval away from 0, the product x_1 x_2 stays at least 4, so one δ works.
questions.rule: Stay away from 0.

questions.q: On \([2,1000]\) the card gives \(\delta=4\varepsilon\). For \(\varepsilon=0.02\) this is \(\delta=\) ____ (decimal).
questions.explain: The output difference is at most a quarter of the input difference, so inputs within 4 epsilon give outputs within epsilon: 4 times 0.02 = 0.08.
questions.rule: delta = 4 epsilon on [2, 1000].

questions.q: A student says: 1/x is continuous at every point of \((0,\infty)\), so it is uniformly continuous there. What is wrong?
options: 1/x is not continuous at points of (0, infinity), only at 0
Pointwise continuity lets delta vary with the point; no single delta serves all
Uniform continuity is a weaker property than ordinary continuity everywhere
The interval should be written as (0, 1000) rather than (0, infinity)
optionExplain: It is continuous at each of them.
Right: near 0 the needed δ shrinks without limit.
It is the stronger property.
The length of the interval is not the issue.
questions.explain: Uniform continuity asks for more than continuity at each point: one δ per ε for the whole domain.
questions.rule: Pointwise is weaker than uniform.

questions.q: The interval is changed from \([2,1000]\) to \([0.5,1000]\). With \(\varepsilon=0.4\), what \(\delta\) does the same method give?
optionExplain: This keeps δ = 4ε, which assumed the product is at least 4.
This takes δ equal to ε.
This divides by 16.
Right: now x_1 x_2 is at least 0.25, so the output difference is at most 4 times the input difference, and δ = ε/4 = 0.1.
questions.explain: Moving the left end closer to 0 makes the function steeper, so δ shrinks. The smallest product is 0.5 times 0.5.
questions.rule: Closer to 0 means smaller δ.

questions.q: A gas has pressure P = 12/V. Which range of volumes lets one volume tolerance guarantee a given pressure tolerance everywhere?
options: The closed range [0.1, 10], which stays away from 0
The range (0, 10], which includes volumes arbitrarily close to 0
Any range, since P is continuous
No range, since P changes with V
optionExplain: Right: on a closed interval away from 0, 1/V is uniformly continuous.
Near 0 the pressure changes too fast for any single volume tolerance.
Continuity at each point does not give a single tolerance.
Every function changes; closed ranges still work here.
questions.explain: The book notes that on any closed interval, 1/x is uniformly continuous: the trouble comes only from approaching 0.
questions.rule: Keep the domain away from the trouble spot.
questions.teaches: The book notes that on any closed interval within its domain, f(x)=1/x is uniformly continuous; the failure comes only from x-values close to 0.

questions.q: The strip has width 0.1, and the curve differs from the rectangle's height by at most 0.02 anywhere in the strip. What is the largest the error area can be?
optionExplain: Right: height at most 0.02 times width 0.1.
This forgets to multiply by the width.
This adds the height and width.
This divides the height by the width.
questions.explain: Area is at most height times width. The card uses exactly this bound with an arbitrary tolerance.
questions.rule: Area is at most height times width.

questions.q: With the height bounded by ε, the error satisfies \(|E(t)|\le\varepsilon\cdot\) ____.
questions.explain: The error is a region of width Δt and height at most ε, so its area is at most ε times Δt.
questions.rule: Error area is at most ε times the step.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,1]\), the card shows \(|E|/\Delta t\le2\Delta t\). Which \(\Delta t\) guarantees \(|E|/\Delta t<0.04\)?
options: Any step below 0.04
Any step below 0.2
Any step below 0.02
Any step below 0.002
optionExplain: Then 2 Δt could be 0.08, which exceeds 0.04.
That allows ratios up to 0.4.
Right: 2 times 0.02 is 0.04.
This works but is far stricter than necessary, so it is not the sharpest answer.
questions.explain: Solve 2Δt < 0.04. The bound is a guarantee for steps below 0.02.
questions.rule: Solve the bound for the step.

questions.q: Put the steps of the proof that E(t)/Δt tends to 0 in order.
items: Note that f is continuous on a closed interval, so it is uniformly continuous
Given epsilon, choose a step small enough that function values within it differ by less than epsilon, for every t
Bound the error area by epsilon times the step
Divide by the step to get an error ratio below epsilon, so the limit is 0
questions.explain: The order is: hypothesis, choice of step, bound, conclusion. The choice of step is the only place where uniform continuity is used.
questions.rule: Hypothesis, step, bound, conclusion.

questions.q: Which part of the proof is the part that uses uniform continuity, rather than ordinary continuity?
options: Writing the error area as an integral over the step
Dividing the error by the step
Taking the limit as the step tends to 0
Choosing one step that works for every t at once
optionExplain: That is definition, not continuity.
That is algebra.
The limit is the goal of the argument, not a use of the hypothesis.
Right: the same δ response serves all positions of the curtain.
questions.explain: Uniform continuity supplies a single step size valid at every position t, which is exactly the single-δ property.
questions.rule: Uniform means one step for every t.

questions.q: A reader recalls the proof of the fundamental theorem after a year, and has forgotten all the epsilon details. According to the book, what should she keep?
options: Only the algebra of the error bound, since the picture cannot be trusted
The moving curtain picture, which leads back to the proof and its details
Nothing, because the proof cannot be rebuilt once the details are lost
The statement that every continuous function is uniformly continuous on any set
optionExplain: The book calls the picture the crux idea.
Right: the details are important but the picture, or the idea behind it, is fundamental.
The picture is easy to remember and leads back to the proof.
That is false for many functions.
questions.explain: The book calls the moving curtain the crux idea: a simple picture that gives a short proof without technical details. The details matter, but the picture is easier to carry in the head.
questions.rule: Remember the picture; rebuild the details.
questions.teaches: The crux idea of the proof was to picture a moving curtain; this simple picture is easy to remember and leads to a one-sentence proof lacking technical details. The details are important, but the picture, or the idea behind it, is fundamental.

questions.q: If f(x) gives the temperature of a cup of coffee at time x, what does f'(x) tell you?
options: The temperature itself, measured at time x
The highest temperature reached so far
How fast the temperature is changing then
The average temperature over the whole day
optionExplain: That is f(x) itself.
That is a maximum value.
Right: a derivative is a rate of change.
An average is an integral-type quantity.
questions.explain: The derivative measures speed of change, not the value. The card adds the geometric reading.
questions.rule: Derivative equals rate of change.

questions.q: The second derivative measures how fast the ____ is changing.
questions.explain: The second derivative is the derivative of the derivative.
questions.rule: The second derivative is the rate of change of the first.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\), \(f'(1)=0\) and \(f''(1)=6\). What does this suggest at \(x=1\)?
options: A local minimum
A local maximum
An inflection point
A vertical tangent
optionExplain: Right: the slope is zero and increasing, so the graph bottoms out.
A maximum would need the slope to be decreasing, f'' < 0.
That needs f'' to change sign, and f'' = 6 is positive.
f' = 0 means a horizontal tangent.
questions.explain: Zero slope with positive f'' means the slope goes from negative to positive: the bottom of a valley.
questions.rule: f' = 0 and f'' > 0 gives a local minimum.

questions.q: Match each sign condition at a point to what it says about the graph.
pairs: The slope is increasing; the graph curves upward
The slope is decreasing; the graph curves downward
questions.explain: The first derivative tells direction, and the second tells how the direction is changing.
questions.rule: f' gives direction; f'' gives bending.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=-x^2\), \(f''\) is negative everywhere. What does the graph look like, and what is at \(x=0\)?
options: It curves upward, with a minimum at 0
It is a straight line through the origin
It has no extreme value
It curves downward, with a peak at 0
optionExplain: That is the shape of x squared, with f'' > 0.
A line has f'' = 0.
The top of the hill is a maximum.
Right: f'(0) = 0 and f'' < 0, so the slope falls from positive to negative.
questions.explain: A negative second derivative bends the graph downward, so a horizontal tangent sits at a peak.
questions.rule: f'' < 0 bends the graph down.

questions.q: An investment's value V(t) has V' > 0 and V'' < 0 at a given time. Which describes it?
options: Shrinking, but at a slowing pace
Growing, but at a slowing pace
Growing at an increasing pace
Constant
optionExplain: V' > 0 means growth, not shrinking.
Right: the value rises while its rate of increase falls.
That needs V'' > 0.
A constant value has V' = 0.
questions.explain: Sometimes the book finds that simple analysis of the signs of f' and f'' is enough to solve fairly complicated problems; the next example does exactly that.
questions.rule: Read the two signs together.
questions.teaches: Sometimes just a simple analysis of the signs of f' and f'' is enough to solve fairly complicated problems.

questions.q: At a relative minimum of a twice-differentiable function, what can be said about the second derivative?
options: It is at least 0
It is negative
It must be exactly 0
It does not exist
optionExplain: Right: the slope is moving from negative to positive, so it is not decreasing.
A negative second derivative bends the graph down, as at a maximum.
At the bottom of x squared, the second derivative is 2.
A twice-differentiable function has one.
questions.explain: The second derivative cannot be negative at a minimum. The card uses this for a contradiction.
questions.rule: Minimum means second derivative at least 0.

questions.q: An even-degree polynomial with positive leading coefficient tends to ____ as \(x\to\pm\infty\).
questions.explain: The leading term dominates, and for even degree it is positive at both ends.
questions.rule: The leading term decides the ends.

questions.q: For \(p(x)=x^2+2\), compare \(p(0)\) and \(p''(0)\) at the minimum point 0.
options: p(0) = 0 and p''(0) = 2, so p(0) is below p''(0)
p(0) = 2 and p''(0) = 2, with equality
p(0) = 2 and p''(0) = 0, so p(0) is above p''(0)
p(0) = 2 and p''(0) = -2, so p(0) is well above
optionExplain: p(0) = 0 squared plus 2 = 2.
Right: this is consistent with the hypothesis, with equality.
The second derivative of x squared plus 2 is the constant 2.
The second derivative is positive.
