questions.explain: Differentiating twice gives p'' = 2. At the minimum point 0, both p and p'' equal 2.
questions.rule: Evaluate p and p'' at the minimum.

questions.q: A student argues: take the minimum value \(p(a)<0\); at a minimum the second derivative at \(a\) is at most 0; this agrees with the hypothesis, so no contradiction arises. What is wrong?
options: A minimum value of a polynomial is never allowed to be negative, by definition
The hypothesis should read p plus its second derivative, not p minus it
The second derivative is not defined for polynomials of even degree
At a minimum the second derivative is at least 0, which with the hypothesis forces p(a) to be at least 0
optionExplain: A minimum can be negative; the argument shows it is not, under the hypothesis.
The hypothesis p minus p'' at least 0 is the one the example uses.
Polynomials can be differentiated any number of times.
Right: the direction of the second-derivative inequality is the key.
questions.explain: The sign of the second derivative at a minimum drives the whole contradiction. Reversing it removes the contradiction.
questions.rule: Check the direction of each inequality.

questions.q: True or false: If the leading coefficient were negative, the polynomial would tend to minus infinity at both ends and have no minimum point, so the argument could not get started.
questions.explain: The proof needs a finite minimum value. Even degree and a positive leading coefficient are there to guarantee that one exists.
questions.rule: Check that the minimum exists.

questions.q: Let \(h(x)=x^4-4x^2+5\). To show \(h(x)>0\) for all \(x\), find its smallest value. What is it?
options: 1, at x = plus or minus root 2
5, at x = 0, where the graph has a peak
0, at x = plus or minus 2, where h vanishes
-3, at x = 1, between the turning points
optionExplain: That is a local maximum, since h(0) = 5 exceeds h(sqrt 2) = 1.
questions.explain: The book uses the fact that a polynomial only blows up as x tends to plus or minus infinity, so its minimum value is finite and can be found where the derivative is zero.
questions.rule: Find the finite minimum at a critical point.
questions.teaches: Since a polynomial only blows up as x tends to plus or minus infinity, a polynomial with both ends going to plus infinity has a finite minimum value.

questions.q: The roots of \(x^3-6x^2+9x-2\) are \(2-\sqrt3,\ 2,\ 2+\sqrt3\). What is their sum?
optionExplain: Right: the roots add to 6, the negative of the x-squared coefficient.
This is the coefficient itself, without the sign change.
This is the pairwise-product sum, not the sum of roots.
This is the constant term, which is the product of the roots.
questions.explain: The sums of the roots and of their pairwise products appear as coefficients. The card uses this to build the cubic.
questions.rule: Coefficients encode root sums.

questions.explain: The quadratic 3x squared - 12x + 9 factors as 3(x - 1)(x - 3).
questions.rule: Factor the derivative.

questions.q: For \(k=2\), the roots of \(x^3-6x^2+9x-2\) are \(2-\sqrt3,\ 2,\ 2+\sqrt3\). What is the smallest root \(a\), to three places?
optionExplain: This is root 3 minus 1, a slip in the subtraction.
This is 3 minus root 3.
Right: 2 - 1.732 = 0.268, which lies between 0 and 1.
No step produces this value.
questions.explain: The root lies in (0, 1), as the method predicts for 0 < k < 4. Here k = 2.
questions.rule: Check the answer against the predicted interval.

questions.q: For \(k=5\), outside \(0<k<4\), \(P(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x-5\). How many real roots does it have?
options: Three, as in the problem, since cubics can have three
Two, one of them a double root at x = 1 or 3
None, since k is too large for a cubic
One: the maximum value P(1) = -1 is below the axis
optionExplain: The three-root picture needs P(1) positive.
A double root would need P(1) = 0.
A cubic always has a real root.
Right: the local maximum value is below 0, so only one real root remains, beyond 3.
questions.explain: The condition 0 < k < 4 is exactly what makes the relative maximum positive and the relative minimum negative.
questions.rule: Three real roots need a positive maximum and negative minimum.

questions.q: Put the steps of the argument in order.
items: Build the cubic whose zeros are a, b, c from the sums
Differentiate to find the turning points 1 and 3
Deduce a < 1 < b < 3 < c from the shape of the graph
Use P(1) > 0 and P(3) < 0 to get 0 < k < 4
Evaluate P(0) and P(4) to show a > 0 and c < 4
questions.explain: Each step needs the one before: the shape gives the ordering, the ordering gives the signs, the signs bound k, and k fixes the sign of P at 0 and 4.
questions.rule: Shape, then signs, then bounds.

questions.q: Three real numbers \(a<b<c\) have \(a+b+c=9\) and \(ab+bc+ca=24\). Where are the turning points of the cubic with these zeros, whatever the product \(abc\) is?
options: At x = 2 and x = 4
At x = 3 and x = 8
At x = 1 and x = 3
They depend on the product, so they cannot be found
optionExplain: Right: P(x) = x^3 - 9x^2 + 24x - k has P'(x) = 3(x - 2)(x - 4), and k vanishes in the derivative.
These come from mixing up the coefficients.
These belong to the cubic of the card, with sums 6 and 9.
The constant term disappears on differentiating.
questions.explain: The unknown constant k disappears when differentiating, so the turning points are known even though k is not. That is why the sketch method works.
questions.rule: Constants vanish under differentiation.
questions.teaches: The unknown product k drops out of P'(x), so the turning points 1 and 3 are known even though k is not; this lets the sketch of the cubic be used before the signs of a, b, c are known.

questions.q: A function has f(3) = 2 and f'(3) = 4. Roughly what is f(3.1)?
optionExplain: This adds only the step.
Right: moving 0.1 along a slope of 4 adds about 0.4.
This adds the slope to f(3).
This adds f'(3) and the step.
questions.explain: A slope of 4 means that a step of 0.1 changes the value by about 0.4. The card makes this a rule.
questions.rule: Change is about slope times step.

questions.q: The tangent-line approximation is \(f(a+h)\approx f(a)+h\cdot\) ____.
questions.explain: The slope of the tangent line at a is f'(a).
questions.rule: Slope times step.

questions.q: Use \(f(x)=\sqrt x\) at \(a=25\) to estimate \(\sqrt{25.5}\).
optionExplain: This adds the step to 5 without using the slope.
This uses a step of 0.05 instead of 0.5.
This adds the correction to 25, the input, instead of 5.
Right: f'(25) = 1/10, so the estimate is 5 + 0.5 times 0.1 = 5.05.
questions.explain: The derivative of the square root at 25 is 1/10. The step 0.5 changes the root by about 0.05.
questions.rule: Estimate f(a + h) by f(a) + h f'(a).

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^2\) at \(a=3\), the tangent estimate of \(f(3.1)\) is 9.6. How does it compare with the true value?
options: Slightly below the true value 9.61, as the graph curves upward
Slightly above the true value, as the graph curves downward
Exactly right, since a tangent line is exact at the point
Far off, because a step of 0.1 is large for a function like x squared
optionExplain: Right: for a graph that curves upward, the tangent line lies below it.
Above would need the graph to curve downward.
The error is 0.01, which is h squared.
The error is only 0.01.
questions.explain: A positive second derivative means the graph bends away from its tangent line, upward. The error is of the order of h squared.
questions.rule: Convex graphs lie above their tangent lines.

questions.q: True or false: A student estimates f(3 + h) by f(3) + f'(3), leaving out the factor h. This gives a good approximation for small h.
questions.explain: The slope must be multiplied by the step h. With f(3) = 2, f'(3) = 4 and h = 0.1 the correct estimate is 2.4, while the student's gives 6.
questions.rule: Remember the factor h.

questions.q: A thermometer reads 20 degrees at noon and rises at 2 degrees per hour. With \(T(h)\) the reading \(h\) hours after noon, which line \(\ell(h)\) satisfies \(\frac{T(h)-\ell(h)}{h}\to0\) as \(h\to0\)?
options: Every line through (0, 20) works
optionExplain: Right: it is the only linear function with that property, since T' is 2.
The error T(h) - ℓ(h) is then about 0.5h, and divided by h it does not tend to 0.
A constant has the wrong slope.
Only the line with the right slope does.
questions.explain: The book calls the tangent line the best linear approximation in just this sense: it is the only linear function whose error is small compared with h.
questions.rule: Only the tangent line has an error small compared to h.
questions.teaches: The function ℓ(h)=f(a)+h f'(a) is the best linear approximation in the sense that it is the only linear function with lim (f(a+h)-ℓ(h))/h = 0 as h tends to 0.

questions.q: Which is larger: 1.1 cubed, or 1 plus 3 times 0.1?
options: 1.1 cubed, which is 1.331
They are equal
It depends on the calculator
optionExplain: Right: 1.1^3 = 1.331, against 1.3.
This is the smaller one, from the linear estimate.
They differ by 0.031.
Exact arithmetic settles it.
questions.explain: Powers grow faster than their linear estimates. The card gives the reason.
questions.rule: Powers exceed their tangent-line estimates.

questions.q: True or false: For \(x>-1\) and \(\alpha\ge1\), Bernoulli's inequality says \((1+x)^\alpha\ge1+\alpha x\).
questions.explain: That is the statement, with equality at x = 0.
questions.rule: Power at least tangent-line value.

questions.q: Bernoulli's inequality gives a lower bound for \((0.9)^4\). What is it?
optionExplain: This is close to the true value but not what the inequality gives.
Right: 1 + 4(-0.1) = 0.6, and the true value 0.6561 is above it.
This takes 1 - 4(0.15), a wrong x.
This ignores the exponent.
questions.explain: Setting x = -0.1 and alpha = 4 in 1 + alpha x gives 0.6. The inequality says 0.9 to the fourth is at least 0.6.
questions.rule: Plug x and α into 1 + αx.

questions.q: For an exponent \(\alpha\) between 0 and 1, the graph of \(u^\alpha\) curves ____, so the tangent line lies above it and Bernoulli's inequality reverses.
questions.explain: For example, with alpha = 1/2 and x = 0.44, sqrt(1.44) = 1.2 is below 1 + 0.22 = 1.22. This is our reading of why the book requires alpha at least 1.
questions.rule: The exponent condition matters.

questions.q: For integer \(\alpha\), the inequality can be proved by induction. Why does that not settle the case \(\alpha=2.5\)?
options: 2.5 is less than 1, so the inequality does not apply
Induction only works for negative exponents, not positive ones
Induction moves through integers and never reaches 2.5
The inequality is false for 2.5
optionExplain: 2.5 is greater than 1.
Induction can prove the integer case.
Right: the book says induction will not work for arbitrary real α.
It holds for all real α at least 1.
questions.explain: The convexity proof works for all real α at least 1, which is its advantage over induction.
questions.rule: Convexity covers real exponents.
questions.teaches: For integer exponents Bernoulli's inequality can be proved by induction, but induction will not work for an arbitrary real exponent, which is why the convexity argument is used.

questions.q: An account grows by a factor \(1+r\) each year, \(r=0.05\). Compound growth over 10 years is \((1.05)^{10}\). What does Bernoulli's inequality say about it?
options: At least 1 + 10(0.05) = 1.5, the simple-interest value
At most 1.5, since compounding cannot beat simple interest
Equal to 1.5, since the rate is small
Nothing, since the exponent 10 is not a real number
optionExplain: Right: compounding is at least as large as simple interest; here (1.05)^10 = 1.629.
The inequality gives a lower bound.
Equality holds only for x = 0.
The exponent 10 is an integer, which is a real number.
questions.explain: The book says that analysing f(a + h) with its tangent-line approximation is very useful, especially when combined with other geometric information such as convexity. Bernoulli's inequality is the example.
questions.rule: Compound growth beats simple growth.
questions.teaches: Analyzing f(a+h) by its tangent-line approximation is very useful, especially when combined with other geometric information such as convexity.

questions.q: A differentiable function on a closed interval has the same value at both endpoints. What must be true?
options: The function is constant on the interval
Some point strictly inside has a horizontal tangent
The derivative is zero at both endpoints
The function is increasing and then decreasing
optionExplain: Many functions return to their starting height without being constant.
Right: a high or low point inside gives a zero derivative.
Nothing is said about the derivative at the endpoints.
It could dip first and then rise; either way a turning point exists, but the order is not fixed.
questions.explain: The turning point is the key: where the graph turns, the slope is zero.
questions.rule: Look for the highest or lowest point inside.

questions.q: True or false: Rolle's theorem requires that \(f(a)=f(b)\).
questions.explain: The equal endpoint values are what force a turning point inside the interval.
questions.rule: Equal endpoint values are a hypothesis.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^2-4x+3\) on \([1,3]\), the point \(u\) in the theorem has \(u=\)____.
questions.explain: Since \(f'(x)=2x-4\), setting it to zero gives \(x=2\). The endpoint values are f(1)=0 and f(3)=0.
questions.rule: Solve f'(u)=0 inside the interval.

questions.q: A student says: for \(f(x)=|x|\) on \([-1,1]\), the endpoint values are equal, so Rolle's theorem gives a point where \(f'=0\). What is the flaw?
options: The function has a corner at 0, so it is not differentiable on the open interval
The endpoint values are not equal, since the function takes different values at the two ends
The function is not continuous on the closed interval, because it has a jump near 0
The interval is too short for the theorem to apply to a function of this kind
optionExplain: Right: a hypothesis fails, and indeed no horizontal tangent exists.
Both endpoint values equal 1.
The absolute value function is continuous everywhere.
The theorem applies to any interval a to b with a less than b.
questions.explain: The graph is a V shape. Its slope is -1 on the left, 1 on the right, and undefined at 0.
questions.rule: Check each hypothesis, including differentiability.

questions.q: Put the book's picture argument for Rolle's theorem in order.
items: The function is continuous on the closed interval, so it reaches a highest and a lowest value
If both are at the endpoints, the function is constant, and any inside point works
Otherwise an extreme value occurs at an inside point
At that inside point the tangent line is horizontal, so the derivative is 0
questions.explain: The argument goes from existence of extremes, to their location, to the slope there.
questions.rule: A turning point inside carries a zero derivative.
questions.teaches: Rolle's theorem rests on a continuous function reaching an extreme value inside the interval, where the derivative must be zero.

questions.q: A function is differentiable everywhere and has four distinct zeros. At least how many zeros must its derivative have?
optionExplain: The zeros of f give only 3 gaps between consecutive zeros.
Three gaps each contain a zero of the derivative, so at least 3 are guaranteed.
Right: apply Rolle's theorem once to each of the 3 gaps between consecutive zeros.
One gap alone would give 1, but there are 3 gaps.
questions.explain: Between two zeros of f the endpoint values are equal (both 0), so Rolle's theorem applies on each gap.
questions.rule: Count the gaps between consecutive zeros.
questions.teaches: Between any two zeros of a differentiable function there lies a zero of its derivative, which counts zeros.

questions.q: A car covers 120 km in 2 hours, and its position is a smooth function of time. What must be true?
options: It drives at 60 km/h for the whole trip
Its speed is below 60 km/h at the halfway time
Its top speed is exactly 60 km/h
At some moment its speed is exactly 60 km/h
optionExplain: The speed can vary; only one moment is guaranteed.
The halfway speed is not determined.
The top speed is at least 60 km/h and could be much more.
Right: the average speed is realized at some instant.
questions.explain: The mean value theorem links average speed with speed at one instant.
questions.rule: Average slope equals some instantaneous slope.

questions.q: True or false: The secant slope of \(f(x)=x^2\) between \(x=1\) and \(x=3\) is 4.
questions.explain: The slope is (9 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 4.
questions.rule: Rise over run between the endpoints.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^3\) on \([0,3]\), the point \(u\) from the theorem is \(u=\)____ (give an exact value).
questions.explain: The secant slope is 9, and f'(u)=3u^2=9 gives u=sqrt(3), approximately 1.732, which lies in (0,3).
questions.rule: Set the derivative equal to the secant slope.

questions.q: Take \(f(x)=|x|\) on \([-1,2]\). The secant slope is \(1/3\). Predict what happens to the conclusion.
options: The point u = 1/3 works
No point has derivative 1/3; the derivative is -1, 1, or undefined
The point u = 0 works because that is the middle
Some point works because the function is continuous
optionExplain: The derivative at 1/3 is 1, not 1/3.
Right: differentiability fails at 0, and the conclusion fails with it.
The derivative does not exist at 0.
Continuity alone is not enough.
questions.explain: Away from 0 the slope is -1 or 1. A value of 1/3 is never taken.
questions.rule: Check differentiability first.

questions.q: A differentiable function has \(|f'(x)|\le3\) for all x, and \(f(0)=1\). What is the largest value \(f(2)\) can have?
optionExplain: This would use slope 2, but the bound allows slope up to 3.
The interval length is 2, not 1, so the increase is up to 6, giving 7.
Right: f(2) - f(0) = 2 f'(u), and |f'(u)| at most 3, so f(2) is at most 1 + 6.
This is the bound on the slope, not on the value of f(2).
questions.explain: The theorem turns a bound on derivatives into a bound on how much f can change.
questions.rule: Write f(2) - f(0) as 2 f'(u).
questions.teaches: A bound on the derivative bounds the change in the function, since the change equals the interval length times a derivative value.

questions.q: Two cameras 30 km apart on a road record a car 15 minutes apart, and the speed limit is 100 km/h. What can be said?
options: The car's speed was exactly 120 km/h at some instant, so it broke the limit
The car may have kept below 100 km/h the whole time
The speed is above 100 km/h at every instant
Nothing, because the cameras do not see the road between them
optionExplain: Right: the average speed is 120 km/h.
Then the average speed could not reach 120 km/h.
Only one instant is guaranteed.
The theorem covers the unobserved stretch.
questions.explain: Average speed is 30 km in 0.25 hours, which is 120 km/h. The theorem produces an instant of exactly that speed.
questions.rule: Compute the average speed first.
questions.teaches: Average speed over a stretch of road equals the speed at some instant, so a recorded average above a limit proves the limit was exceeded at some moment.

questions.q: Which function is guaranteed a fixed point by the theorem in the card?
optionExplain: The slope is 1, which is not below a constant k less than 1; indeed f(x) is always above x.
The slope 2 is larger than 1.
Right: the slope is 1/2 everywhere, and the fixed point is 2.
The slope is 1 and the graph never meets y = x.
questions.explain: Only the first has a slope bounded by a constant less than 1.
questions.rule: Find the one with slope bounded below 1.

questions.q: The fixed point of \(f(x)=x/2+1\) is \(x=\)____.
questions.explain: Solving x/2 + 1 = x gives x = 2.
questions.rule: Set f(x) = x.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=\cos(x)/2\), let \(g(x)=f(x)-x\). Which interval must contain a fixed point?
optionExplain: On [1,2] g is negative at both ends.
Right: g(0)=1/2 is positive, g(1)=cos(1)/2 - 1 is negative, so the IVT gives a zero.
On this interval g is positive at both ends, so no sign change.
On [2,3] g is negative at both ends.
questions.explain: A sign change of g on [0,1] gives a root by the IVT; the numerical root is about 0.45.
questions.rule: Find where g changes sign.

questions.q: A student says: \(f(x)=x+\dfrac1{1+e^x}\) has \(f'(x)<1\) for every x, so by the theorem it has a fixed point. What is wrong?
options: The slope must be bounded by one constant k below 1; here it approaches 1 far from 0
The function is not differentiable, so the mean value theorem cannot be applied at all
The slope is above 1 at some points, which breaks the hypothesis of the theorem
A fixed point exists, so the claim is correct although the proof given is incomplete
optionExplain: Right: the slope is between 3/4 and 1, never reaching 1 but getting arbitrarily close, and f(x) is always greater than x.
It is differentiable everywhere.
The slope is always below 1.
Since 1/(1+e^x) is positive, f(x) is always greater than x.
questions.explain: Slope below 1 at each point is weaker than slope at most k for a fixed k below 1. The proof needs the stronger condition.
questions.rule: Does a single k work?

questions.q: In the proof, why does the mean value theorem on [0, b] with large b lead to a contradiction?
options: It shows the derivative equals zero somewhere
It shows f is continuous on [0, b]
It shows f(b) equals b
Some derivative value is at least 1 - v/b, which approaches 1, exceeding k
optionExplain: That would be Rolle's theorem, with equal endpoint values.
Continuity was already given by differentiability.
The proof assumes f(b) is not b, to reach a contradiction.
Right: f(b) is above b, so the average slope is close to 1 for large b.
questions.explain: The mean value theorem guarantees a derivative value equal to an average slope, and the average slope is nearly 1.
questions.rule: Bound the average slope from below.
questions.teaches: The mean value theorem converts a fact about the average slope on a long interval into a fact about a single derivative value.

questions.q: True or false: A function with \(|f'(x)|\le1/3\) everywhere has exactly one fixed point.
questions.explain: Existence comes from the theorem. Two fixed points p and q would give an average slope of 1 between them, so a derivative value of 1, contradicting the bound.
questions.rule: Suppose there were two fixed points.
questions.teaches: A slope bound below 1 gives not only existence but also uniqueness of the fixed point, since two fixed points would force an average slope of 1.

questions.q: How does the book handle proofs of basic calculus facts such as Rolle's theorem?
options: It gives a hand-waving argument and focuses on using the tool
It proves every fact from the construction of the real numbers
It refuses to use these facts at all
It treats them as false unless checked by computer
optionExplain: Right: the book says it is not a real analysis textbook.
The book says it will not attempt all proofs.
It uses them repeatedly, for example in the fixed point example.
No computer checking is involved.
questions.explain: The book wants you to think more rigorously without becoming an analysis text.
questions.rule: It is a problem-solving book.

questions.q: True or false: The book says that some obvious statements about differentiable functions rely on deep properties of the real numbers.
questions.explain: That is why a full proof is beyond its scope.
questions.rule: Obvious does not mean easy to prove.

questions.q: In the fixed point example, sort each step by whether it is quoted as a known tool or proved in the example.

items.t: The intermediate value theorem
The mean value theorem
The average slope on [0, b] is near 1 for large b
The contradiction with the slope bound

questions.explain: The two big theorems are quoted. The estimate and the contradiction are the new work.
questions.rule: Tools are quoted; the problem-specific argument is proved.

questions.q: A student rejects the mean value theorem in a solution because its proof in the book is only a hand-waving proof. What is the flaw?
options: Pictures are always enough for a proof
The theorem is false for most functions
Theorems can be used as tools once their hypotheses are checked, whatever the book's proof
The book forbids using it
optionExplain: The book calls its argument hand-waving, not a full proof.
It holds for every function meeting its hypotheses.
Right: the statement is a true theorem.
The book uses it in examples.
questions.explain: A theorem stands on its own proof, which is given in analysis courses.
questions.rule: Separate the statement from the book's sketch.

questions.q: Which of these are good habits when using a named theorem in a solution?
options: State the hypotheses and check them
Say which theorem is used and where
Re-derive the real numbers first
Check that the conclusion is what is needed
optionExplain: Each use needs its hypotheses.
Naming the tool makes the argument checkable.
Not needed; that is the job of analysis courses.
The conclusion must match the goal.
questions.explain: Checking hypotheses and conclusions guards against misuse such as the absolute value example.
questions.rule: Use tools with care, not with reconstruction.
questions.teaches: Using a theorem well means naming it, checking its hypotheses, and confirming that its conclusion serves the goal.

questions.q: You want to use Rolle's theorem on a function with a corner inside the interval. What should you do?
options: Use it anyway, since the endpoint values are equal
Notice differentiability fails, and look at a smaller interval or another method
Replace the corner by a smooth curve in the picture
Conclude the function is constant
optionExplain: The theorem needs differentiability inside.
Right: a corner violates a hypothesis.
Changing the function changes the problem.
A corner does not make the function constant.
questions.explain: A tool is safe only when its hypotheses hold.
questions.rule: Check the hypotheses before using the tool.
questions.teaches: A theorem is safe to use only when its hypotheses hold, so a corner inside the interval blocks Rolle's theorem.

questions.q: Why is it not enough to say that \(f(x)=1/(x^2+1)\) because \(f(1/n)=n^2/(n^2+1)\)?
options: The formula is false at x = 1
The function is not continuous
The values n^2/(n^2+1) are not defined
The formula is known only at the points 1/n, not at every x
optionExplain: At x = 1 it gives 1/2, which is the given value.
It is infinitely differentiable, hence continuous.
They are defined for every positive integer n.
Right: infinitely many other values of x are unconstrained.
questions.explain: The data are given at a sequence of points only.
questions.rule: Count the points where the data hold.

questions.q: True or false: The points \(1, 1/2, 1/3, \dots\) form a sequence with limit 0.
questions.explain: The terms 1/n shrink to 0 as n grows.
questions.rule: Limit of 1/n.

questions.q: A continuous function h satisfies \(h(1/n)=n/(n+1)\) for all n. Then \(h(0)=\)____.
questions.explain: The limit of n/(n+1) = 1/(1+1/n) is 1, and continuity gives h(0) = lim h(1/n) = 1.
questions.rule: Use the sequence form of continuity.

questions.q: A function g has \(g(1/n)=(-1)^n\) for all n. Can g be continuous at 0?
options: No, because the values alternate between -1 and 1 and have no limit
Yes, with g(0) = 0, the average of the two values that the sequence takes
Yes, with g(0) = 1, matching the values at the even terms of the sequence
Yes, with g(0) = -1, matching the values at the odd terms of the sequence
optionExplain: Right: g(0) would have to equal the limit of g(1/n).
Continuity requires the limit of g(1/n) to exist and equal g(0).
The odd terms are -1, so 1 fails.
The even terms are 1, so -1 fails.
questions.explain: If the values along 1/n do not settle, no value at 0 can match all of them.
questions.rule: Look at the limit of g(1/n).

questions.q: If v is continuous and \(v(1/n)=0\) for all n, what follows about v?
options: \(v(x)=0\) for all x
\(v'(0)=0\) from this alone
optionExplain: Only the point 0 is determined by continuity.
A derivative needs further argument, such as Rolle's theorem.
Right: v(0) equals the limit of v(1/n), which is 0.
In fact v(1/2) = 0 by hypothesis.
questions.explain: Agreement on a sequence reaches only its limit point.
questions.rule: Apply the sequence definition of continuity.
questions.teaches: If a continuous function vanishes on a sequence converging to a point, it vanishes at that point.

questions.q: A continuous function h satisfies \(h(1/n)=7+1/n\) for all n. What is \(h(0)\)?
options: Cannot be determined
optionExplain: This is h(1), the first term; the limit is smaller.
Right: the limit of 7 + 1/n is 7.
The constant 7 does not vanish.
Continuity pins down h(0) as the limit.
questions.explain: h(0) must equal the limit of h(1/n) as n grows.
questions.rule: Take the limit as n grows.
questions.teaches: To find the value at 0 of a continuous function known along 1/n, take the limit of the known values.

questions.q: The function v is zero at \(1, 1/2, 1/3, \dots\). Where does Rolle's theorem place zeros of \(v'\)?
options: Exactly at the points 1/n
Only at 0
In each gap between consecutive points 1/(n+1) and 1/n
Nowhere, since v is not constant
optionExplain: Those are zeros of v, not of v'.
Rolle gives points inside the gaps; 0 comes from a limit.
Right: v has equal endpoint values (both 0) on each gap.
Rolle needs only equal endpoint values.
questions.explain: Equal endpoint values on each gap give a horizontal tangent inside it.
questions.rule: Apply Rolle to each gap.

questions.explain: The expansion 1 - x^2 + x^4 - ... gives w''(0) = 2 times the coefficient of x^2, which is -2.
questions.rule: Second derivative is 2 times the x^2 coefficient.

questions.explain: The coefficient of x^4 is 1 and the fourth derivative at 0 is 4! = 24.
questions.rule: k-th derivative at 0 is k! times the coefficient of x^k.

questions.q: Predict \(f^{(6)}(0)\) for the Putnam function, using \(w=1-x^2+x^4-x^6+\cdots\).
optionExplain: The sign of the x^6 term is negative.
Right: the coefficient of x^6 is -1 and 6! = 720.
The factorial 6! = 720 multiplies the coefficient.
Odd orders vanish, but 6 is even.
questions.explain: Even-order derivatives alternate in sign: -2, 24, -720.
questions.rule: Use the coefficient times k!.

questions.q: True or false: The zeros of \(v'\) are at the points \(1, 1/2, 1/3, \dots\), because v vanishes there.
questions.explain: Zeros of v are at those points. Rolle's theorem places zeros of the derivative strictly inside each gap between consecutive points.
questions.rule: Zeros of v and of v' are different points.

questions.q: Why can the argument be repeated for \(v'\), \(v''\), and so on?
options: Each derivative is continuous and vanishes along a new sequence tending to 0
Each derivative equals v at the points 1/n, so the same zeros are reused each time
The function v is a polynomial, so the zeros can be counted at every order
The derivatives are all zero everywhere, so there is nothing further to prove
optionExplain: Right: this is the same situation as for v.
Derivatives are different functions.
Nothing says v is a polynomial.
Only their values at 0 are shown to vanish.
questions.explain: The inductive step has the same shape each time: zeros of the derivative, new zeros by Rolle, limit 0.
questions.rule: Check what each step needs.
questions.teaches: An argument that reproduces its own hypotheses for the derivative can be repeated infinitely often.

questions.q: If \(f(1/n)=\dfrac{n}{n+1}\) for all n and f is infinitely differentiable, what is \(f'(0)\)?
optionExplain: The derivative of 1/(1+x) at 0 is -1.
The function is not flat at 0.
Right: w(x)=1/(1+x) matches f at 1/n, and w'(0) = -1.
That is w''(0).
questions.explain: The matching function is 1/(1+x), with derivatives -1, 2, -6, ... at 0.
questions.rule: Find the matching function first.
questions.teaches: To find derivatives at 0 of a function known on 1/n, find a nice function that agrees on the sequence and read its derivatives.

questions.q: What is the derivative of \(\log f(x)\)?
options: \(f'(x)\cdot f(x)\)
optionExplain: That would be half the derivative of f squared.
Right: this is the chain rule applied to the logarithm.
The factor f'(x) is missing.
The logarithm is not applied to the derivative.
questions.explain: Derivative of log of f is f' divided by f.
questions.rule: Chain rule.

questions.q: True or false: Taking logarithms turns a product into a sum.
questions.explain: log(ab) = log a + log b, which is the point of the method.
questions.rule: Product to sum.

questions.explain: f(1) = 6 and f'/f at 1 is 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 = 11/6, so f'(1) = 6 times 11/6 = 11. Expanding x^3+3x^2+2x confirms 3+6+2=11.
questions.rule: Multiply the sum by f(1).
Multiply f(1) by the sum of reciprocals.

questions.q: A student computes \(f'(1)\) for \(f(x)=x(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)\) as \(1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14=\frac{25}{12}\). What is the flaw?
options: That is f'/f; it must be multiplied by f(1)=24
The sum should have only three terms
The value is correct
The reciprocals should be squared
optionExplain: Right: the answer is 50.
There are four factors, so four terms.
The sum gives f'(1)/f(1), not f'(1).
No squares appear.
questions.explain: Logarithmic differentiation gives the ratio f'/f.
questions.rule: Undo the logarithm at the end.

questions.q: Use the same method for \(f(x)=x^2(x+1)^3\). What is \(f'(1)\)?
optionExplain: That is 2 times 7, not 8 times 7/2.
This is f'/f; multiply by f(1) = 8.
Check the multiplication: 8 times 7/2 is 28.
questions.explain: Powers become multiples of logarithms: 2 log x + 3 log(x+1).
questions.rule: Write log f, then differentiate.
questions.teaches: Logarithmic differentiation handles repeated factors: an exponent multiplies the corresponding term in f'/f.

optionExplain: The constants are swapped.
Then f'/f would not be constant.
Right: log f = 3x + c, and f(0) = 2 gives f = 2e^{3x}.
This has f(0)=1, not 2.
questions.explain: Antidifferentiate f'/f to get log f.
questions.rule: f'/f is the derivative of log f.

questions.q: True or false: The derivative of \(f(x)^2\) is \(2f(x)f'(x)\).
questions.explain: This is the chain rule applied to a square.
questions.rule: Power rule with the chain rule.

questions.q: If \(f'(x)=2xf(x)\) and \(f(0)=1\), then \(f(1)=\)____ (give an exact value).
questions.explain: Since (log f)' = 2x, log f = x^2, so f(1) = e.
questions.rule: Divide by f and antidifferentiate.

questions.q: A student writes \((f^2+f'^2)'=2f'+2f''\). What is the flaw?
options: Nothing is wrong
The answer should be \(f'^2+f''^2\)
The answer should be \(2f+2f'\)
The correct result is \(2ff'+2f'f''=2f'(f+f'')\)
optionExplain: The factors f and f' are missing from the student's formula.
That treats squares as if they were first powers.
The derivative of each term needs the chain rule.
Right: the chain rule brings the inner function and its derivative.
questions.explain: The derivative of f^2 is 2ff' and of f'^2 is 2f'f''.
questions.rule: Apply the chain rule to each square.

questions.q: A function satisfies \(f''+f=0\). What does the bank suggest about \(f^2+f'^2\)?
options: It grows without bound
Its derivative is 2f'(f+f'') = 0, so it is constant
It equals zero
Nothing can be said
optionExplain: Its derivative is zero.
Right: the equation makes the factor in brackets vanish.
It is constant, not necessarily zero.
The identity gives a conserved quantity.
questions.explain: Recognizing the combination in the equation yields a quantity that does not change.
questions.rule: Compute its derivative.
questions.teaches: If an equation makes the derivative of a combination of f and f' vanish, that combination is constant.

questions.q: You are given a problem containing the ratio f'(x)/f(x). What is a sensible first move?
options: Antidifferentiate to get log f(x) and use it to analyze f
Differentiate again to remove the ratio, since derivatives of quotients simplify
Set f equal to zero, which makes the ratio disappear from the problem
Replace f' by f'' in the ratio, which changes the order but not the form
optionExplain: Right: f'/f is the derivative of log f.
That makes the expression more complicated.
The ratio requires f nonzero.
Nothing justifies changing the order.
questions.explain: A ratio of a function's derivative to the function is a logarithmic derivative.
questions.rule: Match the expression to a known derivative.
questions.teaches: A ratio f'/f in a problem is the derivative of log f, so antidifferentiating it gives information about f.

questions.q: Why does the solution multiply both sides of the equation by the derivative of f?
options: To make the equation linear
To cancel g
To solve for f exactly
The left side then becomes half the derivative of f squared plus f' squared
optionExplain: Multiplying by f' makes it more nonlinear.
g remains on the right side.
The text says the equation cannot be solved for f easily.
questions.explain: The goal is to recognize a derivative on the left.
questions.rule: Look for a derivative on the left.

questions.q: True or false: If a function E has \(E'\le0\) for \(x\ge0\), then \(E(x)\le E(0)\) for \(x\ge0\).
questions.explain: A function with nonpositive derivative does not increase.
questions.rule: Monotonicity from the sign of the derivative.

questions.q: With \(f(0)=3\) and \(f'(0)=4\), the bound \(C\) is ____.
questions.rule: C is the square root of E(0).

questions.q: A student concludes \(|f(x)|\le f(0)^2+f'(0)^2\). Test with \(f(0)=1/2\) and \(f'(0)=0\). What is wrong?
options: The bound for f squared is E(0); the bound for |f| is its square root
The student should use f'(0) alone, since the derivative controls the size of f
Nothing; the student's claim is right whenever f(0) and f'(0) are both nonzero
The bound should be f(0) + f'(0), the sum of the two starting values
optionExplain: Right: here E(0) = 1/4 is less than 1/2, so the student's bound would fail at x = 0.
The quantity E(0) uses both values.
At x = 0 it would say |f(0)| is at most 1/4, but |f(0)| = 1/2.
That is not what E gives.
questions.explain: E bounds f squared, not |f|.
questions.rule: Take a square root.

questions.q: For \(x\le0\) the factor \(-xg(x)f'^2\) is at least 0. What does that say about E on negative x?
options: E is unbounded for negative x
E is constant
E does not decrease as x rises toward 0, so E(x) is at most E(0)
The argument cannot be used
optionExplain: E increases only up to the value E(0) at x = 0.
Its derivative is nonnegative, not zero.
Right: the same bound holds for negative x.
It works with the inequality reversed.
questions.explain: On the left of 0, E rises toward E(0), so its values are below E(0).
questions.rule: Track the sign of E' for negative x.
questions.teaches: A monotone quantity gives a bound in both directions from the starting point once the sign of its derivative on each side is known.

questions.q: Suppose \(f^{\prime\prime}+f=-xf^{\prime}\) (so \(g=1\)). Which quantity does not increase for \(x\ge0\)?
options: \(f'\) alone
optionExplain: Its derivative is f' + f'', not signed by the equation.
Right: its derivative is -2x f'^2, which is at most 0 for x at least 0.
Its derivative is 2f'(f-f''), which the equation does not control.
The equation does not give a sign for f''.
questions.explain: Multiply the equation by 2f' to get the derivative of f^2 + f'^2.
questions.rule: Multiply by f'.
questions.teaches: Multiplying an equation by f' can reveal a combination of f and f' with a definite sign for its derivative.

questions.q: What does \(\frac1n\left(f(\tfrac1n)+f(\tfrac2n)+\cdots+f(\tfrac nn)\right)\) approach as n grows?
options: \(\int_0^n f(x)\,dx\)
optionExplain: The sum has n terms, each weighted 1/n, so it averages many values.
The factor 1/n is balanced by the n terms.
Right: the points k/n fill [0, 1] with step 1/n.
The points k/n only reach 1.
questions.explain: The sum is a Riemann sum with step 1/n on [0, 1].
questions.rule: Identify the step and the interval.

questions.q: For \(a=0\), \(b=1\) and \(n=4\), the step \(\Delta\) is ____.
questions.rule: Interval length over n.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,1]\) with \(n=4\), \(S_4=\)____ (give a fraction).
questions.rule: Use the points 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4.

questions.q: True or false: The book's sum \(S_n\) has \(n+1\) terms, because it uses both \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\).
questions.explain: It runs from f(a) to f(b - Delta), which is n terms; the value f(b) is not included.
questions.rule: Count the terms.

questions.q: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on [0, 1] with \(n=4\), including \(f(1)\) instead of \(f(0)\) gives \(15/32\). Why do both versions have the same limit?
options: The two sums are always equal
Their difference is \(\Delta(f(b)-f(a))\), which tends to 0
Both sums use the same points
The function is constant
optionExplain: At n = 4 they are 7/32 and 15/32.
Right: here it is 1/4 and shrinks as n grows.
One uses the point 0 and the other the point 1.
The function x^2 is not constant.
questions.explain: Shifting the endpoint term changes the sum by Delta times a bounded difference.
questions.rule: Subtract the two sums.
questions.teaches: Sums that include the left end or the right end of the interval have the same limit, because they differ by a term of size Δ.

questions.q: The sum \(\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac kn\) equals \(\frac{n+1}{2n}\). What is its limit?
options: \(\infty\)
optionExplain: The limit of (n+1)/(2n) is 1/2.
The sum does not vanish.
The sum is at most 1.
Right: this matches the integral of x on [0, 1].
questions.explain: Both the formula and the integral give 1/2.
questions.rule: Compare with the integral of x.
questions.teaches: A limit computed from a closed form for the sum can be checked against the integral it represents.

questions.q: What is the first move for finding \(\lim\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{n}{k^2+n^2}\)?
options: Pull out a factor 1/n so that the rest depends on k/n
Show each term goes to 0 and conclude that the whole sum does too
Compute the exact sum of the n terms in closed form and take the limit
Replace n by 1 and read off the value of the first term of the sum
optionExplain: Right: divide numerator and denominator by n^2.
The number of terms grows, so the sum need not vanish.
No closed form is available.
The limit is taken as n grows.
questions.explain: The book calls this the crux move: extract the step.
questions.rule: Look for Δ = 1/n.

questions.q: True or false: The term \(\dfrac{n}{k^2+n^2}\) equals \(\dfrac1n\cdot\dfrac1{(k/n)^2+1}\).
questions.explain: Divide the numerator and denominator by n^2.
questions.rule: Algebra check.

questions.q: The limit of \(\sum_{k=1}^n\frac n{k^2+n^2}\) is ____ (give an exact value).
questions.explain: The sum becomes the integral of 1/(1+x^2) over [0, 1], which is arctan 1 = pi/4.
questions.rule: Evaluate the integral you found.

questions.q: The limit of \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1{n+k}\) is \(\ln\)____ (a whole number).
questions.explain: Write the term as (1/n) times 1/(1 + k/n). The integral of 1/(1+x) on [0, 1] is ln 2. With n = 100000 the sum is 0.693145, close to ln 2 = 0.693147.
questions.rule: Pull out 1/n again.

questions.q: A student says the limit of \(\sum_{k=1}^n\frac n{k^2+n^2}\) is 0, because every term goes to 0. What is the flaw?
options: The terms do not go to 0
The sum has more and more terms, so the total need not go to 0
The limit equals 1
The limit does not exist
optionExplain: Each term is at most 1/n, so it does go to 0.
Right: the limit is pi/4, not 0.
The integral is pi/4, about 0.785.
The sum converges.
questions.explain: Many tiny terms can add up to a definite amount.
questions.rule: Count the terms as well as their size.

questions.q: What is the limit of \(\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\frac1{n+k}\)?
optionExplain: This would be the limit with only n terms.
The integral of 1/(1+x) on [0, 2] is ln 3, not 2 ln 2.
Right: the points k/n now fill [0, 2], and the integral of 1/(1+x) there is ln 3.
No factor of 6 appears.
questions.explain: With 2n terms and step 1/n, the interval is [0, 2]. The numerical value at n = 100000 is 1.098609.
questions.rule: Find the interval from the largest k/n.
questions.teaches: The upper limit of the interval is the largest value of k/n, so doubling the number of terms doubles the interval.

questions.q: Why does the Putnam 1996 problem (a product of odd numbers compared with powers involving e) suggest taking logarithms?
options: The exponents and the base e become a sum of logs compared with expressions in x log x
Logarithms make every inequality into an equality, so the exponents can be ignored
Taking logarithms removes the odd numbers, which leaves a simpler product to bound
It converts the problem into a limit as n goes to 0, where the bounds are easier
optionExplain: Right: a product becomes a sum, and the sum can be compared with an integral.
They preserve the inequality; they do not remove it.
The odd numbers remain as arguments of the log.
The positive integer n stays fixed.
questions.explain: The book sees ugly exponents as a hint to take logarithms.
questions.rule: Turn the product into a sum.

questions.q: True or false: If f is increasing, a rectangle of width 2 whose height is the value of f at the left end of an interval lies under the graph on that interval.
questions.explain: The graph rises from the left end, so it is above the left-end height.
questions.rule: Increasing means values rise to the right.

questions.q: For \(1\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9\), half of the integral of \(\log x\) from 1 to 11 is the upper bound for \(\log 945\). Its value to two decimals is ____.
questions.explain: The integral is 11 ln 11 - 11 + 1 = 16.38, and half of it is 8.19. The lower bound from 1 to 9 is 5.89, and log 945 = 6.85 lies between.
questions.rule: Evaluate x log x - x from 1 to 11.

questions.q: A student bounds \(\sum_{k=1}^{10}\sin(k)\) by integrals using the same rectangle idea. What is the flaw?
options: Sums cannot be compared with integrals
The sine function is not monotone, so the rectangles are not all above or all below
The sum has too few terms
Sine has no antiderivative
optionExplain: They can, for monotone functions.
Right: monotonicity is needed.
The number of terms is not the issue.
Its antiderivative is -cos.
questions.explain: The comparison relies on f rising throughout.
questions.rule: Check monotonicity.

questions.q: For \(\log(10!)=15.10\), which integral bounds are correct?
options: Only the upper bound is valid
optionExplain: The upper bound must exceed 15.10.
The lower bound must be below 15.10.
Right: with step 1, the sum of log k lies between these.
Both the upper and lower rectangles are valid for increasing log.
questions.explain: The same sandwich works with step 1 instead of step 2.
questions.rule: Use rectangles of width 1.
questions.teaches: The sandwich between two integrals works for any equally spaced sum of an increasing function, here giving bounds for log(n!).

questions.q: A sum \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} f(k)\) has decreasing f. Which comparison holds?
options: \(\sum f(k)\le\int_1^{n+1} f\)
\(\int_1^{n+1}f(x)\,dx\le\sum_{k=1}^n f(k)\le\int_0^{n}f(x)\,dx\) when f is defined and decreasing there
No integral comparison is possible
\(\sum f(k)=\int_1^{n}f\)
optionExplain: For decreasing f the left-end rectangles lie above the graph.
Right: the inequalities reverse for decreasing functions.
A decreasing function is monotone too.
A sum is not equal to the integral.
questions.explain: For a decreasing function the rectangle heights at the left ends are larger than the graph on that interval.
questions.rule: Reverse the inequalities.
questions.teaches: For a decreasing function the inequalities between a sum and its integrals reverse, because left-end rectangles lie above the graph.

questions.q: The function \(f(x)=1/(1+\tan^\alpha x)\) goes from 1 at x = 0 to 0 at x = π/2, with \(f(\pi/4)=1/2\). What does this suggest?
options: The graph is symmetric about the center point (π/4, 1/2)
The integral is 0, because the function takes both large and small values
The exponent matters a lot, so each exponent needs its own separate argument
The function is constant on the interval, since it starts and ends at fixed values
optionExplain: Right: this points to the transformation x → π/2 − x.
The function is positive on the interval.
The result does not depend on the exponent.
It changes from 1 to 0.
questions.explain: Values at the ends add to 1 and the middle value is 1/2.
questions.rule: Look for a central symmetry.

questions.q: True or false: The identity \(\tan(\pi/2-x)=1/\tan x\) holds for x in (0, π/2).
questions.explain: Tangent of the complementary angle is the cotangent.
questions.rule: Trigonometric identity.

questions.q: With \(f(x)+g(x)=1\) and \(\int f=\int g\) on \([0,\pi/2]\), the integral \(\int_0^{\pi/2}f(x)\,dx=\)____ (exact).
questions.explain: Twice the integral equals the integral of 1, which is pi/2.
questions.rule: Add the two integrals.

questions.q: Predict the value of \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\tan^{7}x}\).
optionExplain: The exponent is irrelevant.
The exponent does not divide the result.
Right: the exponent does not change the argument.
That is the sum of the two integrals.
questions.explain: Any positive exponent gives f + g = 1.
questions.rule: Redo the argument for the new exponent.

questions.q: A student says: \(\int f=\int g\) because f and g are equal functions. What is the flaw?
options: The integrals are not equal
They are not equal; the integrals match because of the substitution x → π/2 − x
f and g are equal at every point
g is the derivative of f
optionExplain: They are equal.
Right: g(x) = f(π/2 - x), a reflected copy.
They add to 1; they agree only where both are 1/2.
No derivative relation is involved.
questions.explain: A change of variable preserves the integral when the interval maps onto itself.
questions.rule: Name the reason for equality.

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int_0^{1}\dfrac{x^2}{x^2+(1-x)^2}\,dx\) using the symmetry \(x\to1-x\).
optionExplain: That would be the integral of x^2.
That is the sum of the two integrals.
The sum of the pair is 1, so each is 1/2.
Right: the integrand and its mirror image add to 1, so each integral is 1/2 (numerically 0.5).
questions.explain: Call the integrand f(x); then f(1-x) = (1-x)^2/((1-x)^2 + x^2), and f(x) + f(1-x) = 1.
questions.rule: Find the mirror image and add.
questions.teaches: The substitution x → a + b − x maps [a, b] onto itself; if f(x) + f(a + b − x) is constant, the integral is half of that constant times the length.

questions.q: Which transformation maps the interval [2, 5] onto itself and swaps its ends?
options: \(x\to-x\)
\(x\to2x\)
optionExplain: This maps [2, 5] to [-5, -2].
Right: a + b - x with a = 2, b = 5.
It maps [2, 5] to [4, 10].
It moves the interval to [5, 8].
questions.explain: The reflection of [a, b] is x → a + b − x.
questions.rule: Check where the ends go.

questions.q: True or false: A substitution that maps the interval of integration onto itself leaves the value of the definite integral of a function unchanged when the integrand is replaced by its transformed version.
questions.explain: That is the change-of-variables principle used for x → π/2 − x.
questions.rule: Invariance of the integral.

questions.q: Sort each integral by whether the reflection x → 1 − x gives the mirror integrand on the same interval.
groups: Reflection x → 1 − x keeps the interval [0, 1]

items.t: \(\int_2^5 \frac{dx}{x}\)

questions.explain: The first two are over [0, 1], which is mapped to itself. The third needs x → π/2 − x and the fourth needs x → 7 − x.
questions.rule: Look at the interval.

questions.q: A student applies \(x\to1-x\) to \(\int_0^{2}f(x)\,dx\) and says the interval is unchanged. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the map keeps [0, 2]
The interval should be [0, 1]
The map should be x → 1/x
The map sends [0, 2] to [-1, 1]; the reflection should be x → 2 − x
optionExplain: The ends 0 and 2 go to 1 and -1.
The interval is given.
That map is not a reflection of the interval.
Right: the ends must add to a + b = 2.
questions.explain: The correct reflection sends a to b and b to a.
questions.rule: Check the images of the ends.

questions.q: Which statement best summarizes how the book generalizes the tan integral's trick?
options: Search for natural transformations and the invariants they preserve
Always replace x by pi/2 - x, whatever the integral looks like
Use trigonometric identities to evaluate every integral that arises
Avoid integrals that look hard, since few of them have a trick
optionExplain: Right: symmetry comes in many forms.
That transformation fits only this integral.
The point is the symmetry, not the identities.
The book shows that hard ones often have a symmetry.
questions.explain: The book also mentions circle inversion as a valid kind of symmetry.
questions.rule: Think of the moral of the story.
questions.teaches: Transformations that are invariant for integration, such as reflections, can simplify an integrand; look for them by asking which maps preserve the interval.

questions.q: Which pairing of an integral with a useful transformation is the best?
options: \(\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x^2}\) with \(x\to x+1\)
\(\int_0^1 x\,dx\) with \(x\to\sin x\)
\(\int_0^{\infty}\frac{dx}{1+x^2}\) with \(x\to1/x\), which swaps [0, 1] and [1, ∞)
\(\int_0^1 e^x\,dx\) with \(x\to2x\)
optionExplain: This translation moves the interval and does not help.
This makes the integral harder.
Right: the integrand keeps its form under this map, so the two halves of the integral are equal.
It stretches the interval and has no invariant.
questions.explain: For 1/(1 + x^2), x → 1/x gives 1/(1 + 1/x^2) times 1/x^2 = 1/(1 + x^2) in absolute value, so it is an invariant.
questions.rule: Look for the map that preserves the integrand.
questions.teaches: A map is natural when it preserves the integrand up to a simple factor, as x → 1/x does for 1/(1 + x²).

questions.q: Start at \(x=1/2\) and apply \(\tau(x)=1/(1-x)\) repeatedly. Which sequence appears?
optionExplain: The map does not add 1.
1/2 is not a fixed point.
Check: tau(1/2) = 2, not -2.
Right: the orbit has length 3.
questions.rule: Apply the map step by step.
Substitute into 1/(1 − x).

questions.q: The value \(f(1/2)\) for \(f(x)=\frac{x^2-x}{x^3-3x+1}\) is ____ (a fraction).
questions.explain: Numerator: 1/4 - 1/2 = -1/4. Denominator: 1/8 - 3/2 + 1 = -3/8. The ratio is 2/3. The same value occurs at 2 and -1.
questions.rule: Evaluate numerator and denominator separately.

questions.q: True or false: If \(f(\tau(x))=f(x)\) and \(f(1/2)=2/3\), then \(f(-1)=2/3\).
questions.explain: Under tau, 1/2 goes to 2 and 2 goes to -1, so -1 lies in the orbit of 1/2 and f takes the same value there.
questions.rule: Follow the orbit.

questions.q: A student claims \(\tau(\tau(x))=x\), because \(\tau\) looks like a reflection. Test at \(x=3\). What is the correct statement?
options: \(\tau(\tau(3))=2/3\), not 3; in general \(\tau\circ\tau(x)=(x-1)/x\)
\(\tau(\tau(3))=3\), because applying a map twice returns the starting point
\(\tau(\tau(3))=-1/2\), which is the value after the first application
\(\tau(\tau(3))=1/3\), the reciprocal of the starting point
optionExplain: Right: it is a cycle of length 3 and not a reflection.
Compute tau(3) = -1/2 and tau(-1/2) = 2/3.
That is tau(3); apply tau again.
A slip: the second step gives 2/3.
questions.explain: A reflection has order 2, but tau has order 3.
questions.rule: Compute at a sample value.

questions.q: Why does having \(\tau^3=\text{identity}\) help in combining three integrals?
options: It makes each integral equal to zero
It makes the integrand constant
Three substitutions cycle the three ranges back to the first range
It lets us avoid computing derivatives
optionExplain: The integrals are not zero.
The integrand is not constant.
Right: all three integrals can be moved to one range.
The derivatives of tau and tau∘tau appear in the combined integrand.
questions.explain: The cycle brings each integral back to the first range, where they are added.
questions.rule: Follow the cycle of ranges.
questions.teaches: A transformation of order n that preserves the integrand lets n integrals over cyclically related ranges be added into one over a single range.

optionExplain: The denominator is 2, not 1.
That is a_2(1).
The term is below 1.
questions.explain: Substitute x = 1 and n = 1.
questions.rule: Substitute.

questions.q: True or false: In the definition of S(x), the limit of the partial sums is taken with x held fixed.
questions.explain: Each x gives its own series of constants.
questions.rule: Fix x first.

questions.q: For \(x=1\), the partial sum \(S_3(1)=\frac12+\frac14+\frac18=\)____ (a fraction).
questions.explain: The sum is 4/8 + 2/8 + 1/8 = 7/8, which also equals 1 - 1/2^3.
questions.rule: Add the three terms.

questions.q: Predict \(S(2)\) for the series with \(a_n(x)=x^2/(1+x^2)^n\).
options: The series diverges at x = 2
optionExplain: Right: S_n(2) = 1 - 5^{-n}, which tends to 1.
That is the value at x = 0 only.
This is the first term, not the sum.
The terms form a geometric series with ratio 1/5.
questions.explain: Any nonzero x gives S_n(x) = 1 - (1+x^2)^{-n}, which approaches 1.
questions.rule: Use the closed form.

questions.q: A student says \(S(0)=1\), because \(S(x)=1\) for every x near 0. What is the flaw?
options: S(0) is undefined
S(x) is not 1 near 0
Each a_n(0) is 0, so the partial sums at 0 are all 0 and S(0) = 0
The sum should be taken as x goes to 0 first
optionExplain: The partial sums at 0 are all 0, so it is defined.
It is 1 for every nonzero x.
Right: the sum is defined point by point.
The definition fixes x first.
questions.explain: The value at x = 0 is determined by the terms at 0 alone.
questions.rule: Evaluate at the point itself.

questions.q: Treat \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} x^k\) as partial sums. What is \(S_3(1/2)\), and what does \(S(1/2)\) equal?
options: 7/8 and 1
optionExplain: The limit is the sum of all terms, not the partial sum.
Right: the partial sum is (1 - x^4)/(1 - x) = 15/8, and the limit is 1/(1 - 1/2) = 2.
This pattern belongs to the other series.
The roles are reversed.
questions.explain: A power series is a series of functions of x with terms x^k.
questions.rule: Use the geometric sum formula.
questions.teaches: A power series is a series of functions, and its partial sums can be written in closed form by the geometric sum formula.

questions.q: Every partial sum of a series is a continuous function. What can be said about the sum function?
options: It must be continuous
It must be differentiable
It may be discontinuous
It must be zero
optionExplain: The example in the book has a jump.
Not even continuity is guaranteed.
Right: an infinite sum involves another limit.
Nothing forces the sum to be zero.
questions.explain: The book calls this a warning about infinite series of functions.
questions.rule: Think of the order of two limits.

questions.q: True or false: A finite sum of continuous functions is continuous.
questions.explain: This is a standard property; the problem comes only with infinite sums.
questions.rule: Finite versus infinite.

questions.q: For the series in the card, \(\lim_{x\to0}S(x)=\)____.
questions.explain: S(x) = 1 for every x not equal to 0, so the limit as x approaches 0 is 1, even though S(0) = 0.
questions.rule: Look at nonzero x.

questions.q: At \(x=0.1\), predict \(S_n(0.1)\) for large n such as 1000.
options: About 0.1
About 0
About 0.095
About 0.99995, very close to 1
optionExplain: The first term is 0.0099; the sum is much bigger.
Only x = 0 gives 0.
That is S_10; many more terms add more.
questions.explain: The partial sum is 1 - (1.01)^{-n}.
questions.rule: Use the closed form.

questions.q: A student says S is continuous, because it is a sum of continuous functions. What is wrong?
options: The terms are not continuous
The rule holds for finite sums, but an infinite sum adds a limit
S is continuous only at 0
S is not a function
optionExplain: Each a_n is continuous, even differentiable.
Right: S has a jump at 0.
S is discontinuous at 0.
It is a function, equal to 1 off 0 and 0 at 0.
questions.explain: Check the claim against the actual sum.
questions.rule: Distinguish finite from infinite.

questions.q: Which interchange is safe, according to the book's footnote, when summing and integrating?
options: Integrating a finite sum term by term
Integrating an infinite sum term by term, without further conditions
Taking a limit inside an infinite sum without conditions
Differentiating any infinite sum term by term
optionExplain: Right: a finite sum with an integral commutes.
That needs extra care, such as uniform convergence.
Two limit operations need proof.
This can fail.
questions.explain: Interchanging a limit operation with a finite sum is always safe.
questions.rule: Finite versus infinite again.
questions.teaches: Interchanging two limit operations needs justification, while interchanging a limit with a finite sum is always safe.

questions.q: How does uniform convergence differ from pointwise convergence?
options: Uniform convergence needs the limit function to be zero
Pointwise convergence requires more terms
In uniform convergence, one N serves all x
They are the same for continuous functions
optionExplain: The limit can be any function.
It is the weaker notion.
Right: N does not depend on x.
The book's example shows they differ.
questions.explain: The book compares it to uniform continuity.
questions.rule: Which quantity is independent of x?

questions.q: True or false: In uniform convergence, the number N may depend on the point x.
questions.explain: That is pointwise convergence. In uniform convergence N is chosen once for all x.
questions.rule: N is independent of x.

questions.q: For n = 10, the error \((1+x^2)^{-10}\) equals 1/2 when \(x^2=2^{1/10}-1\). Give \(x^2\) to two decimals: ____.
questions.explain: 2^{0.1} = 1.0718, so x^2 = 0.0718, which is 0.07 to two decimals.
questions.rule: Compute 2 to the power 1/10 minus 1.

questions.q: Is the convergence of \(S_n\) to S uniform on the set \(|x|\ge1/2\)?
options: No, because it fails at x = 0
Yes, since the error is at most (1.25)^(-n) there, which tends to 0
Yes, because S is continuous
No, uniform convergence never holds for series
optionExplain: The point 0 is not in the set.
Right: the trouble point 0 is excluded.
Continuity is not the reason.
Many series converge uniformly.
questions.explain: Away from 0 the error is bounded by a quantity independent of x.
questions.rule: Bound the error uniformly.

questions.q: A student says convergence is uniform, because the error \((1+x^2)^{-n}\) tends to 0 at every x. What is wrong?
options: The error does not tend to 0 at any x
The error is negative
The student needed to check x = 0 only
That shows pointwise convergence; one N must work for all x together
optionExplain: At each nonzero x it does.
It is positive.
A single point is not enough.
Right: near 0 the error stays near 1/2 for the matching points.
questions.explain: Pointwise is weaker than uniform.
questions.rule: Ask whether N depends on x.

questions.q: Let \(f_n(x)=x^n\) on \([0,1]\). Each \(f_n\) is continuous but the pointwise limit is 0 for x < 1 and 1 at x = 1. What follows?
options: The convergence is not uniform on [0, 1]
The convergence is uniform
The functions are not continuous
The limit is continuous
optionExplain: Right: a uniform limit of continuous functions would be continuous.
The limit is discontinuous, so it cannot be uniform.
Each power of x is continuous.
It jumps at x = 1.
questions.explain: A discontinuous limit of continuous functions rules out uniform convergence.
questions.rule: Use the continuity result.
questions.teaches: A discontinuous pointwise limit of continuous functions proves that the convergence is not uniform.

questions.q: What does the book recommend about the technical issues of uniform convergence?
options: Not to worry: power series converge uniformly in a smaller disc, so term-by-term work is safe
Check uniform convergence for every series by hand before using it in any argument
Avoid power series altogether, since their convergence is hard to control
Never differentiate series, since the derivative of a sum may differ from the sum
optionExplain: Right: the punch line is Don't worry.
The book says not to dwell on it.
Power series are the safe case.
Uniformly convergent power series can be differentiated.
questions.explain: The section is titled Don't Worry!.
questions.rule: Recall the section title.

questions.q: True or false: If a sequence of continuous functions converges uniformly, the limit function is continuous.
questions.explain: This is the first of the book's three consequences.
questions.rule: Uniform limits preserve continuity.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether uniform convergence of the sequence makes it safe.

items.t: The limit of continuous functions is continuous
The integrals of f_n converge to the integral of f
Term-by-term integration of a power series inside its radius
An infinite sum of continuous functions is continuous
The derivative of the limit is the limit of the derivatives

questions.explain: The first three are the book's results. For pointwise convergence the book gives continuity as a failure, and for derivatives it mentions that the derivative of a sum can differ from the sum of the derivatives.
questions.rule: Match each with the book's list.

questions.q: On \([0,1/2]\), \(\int_0^{1/2}x^n\,dx\) for n = 3 is 1/64. What do these integrals do as n grows?
options: They tend to 1
They grow without bound
They tend to 0, the integral of the limit function
They stay at 1/64
optionExplain: The limit function is 0.
They shrink geometrically.
Right: (1/2)^(n+1)/(n+1) tends to 0.
The expression decreases.
questions.explain: The convergence of x^n to 0 on [0, 1/2] is uniform.
questions.rule: Evaluate the formula.

questions.q: A student says the series \(\sum x^2/(1+x^2)^n\) converges uniformly on the whole real line, because every term is continuous. What is wrong?
options: Continuous terms always give a discontinuous sum
The sum S has a jump at 0, so uniform convergence on the whole line is impossible
The terms are not continuous
Uniform convergence needs differentiability
optionExplain: Not always; the claim here is about this series.
Right: uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous.
Each term is continuous.
It does not.
questions.explain: Use the contrapositive of the continuity result.
questions.rule: S is discontinuous.

questions.q: Which gives the strongest reason to differentiate a power series term by term inside its radius of convergence?
options: The terms are polynomials
The series is geometric
Every series can be differentiated term by term
The series converges uniformly there, in the sense the book states
optionExplain: Polynomial terms alone do not decide it.
Not every power series is geometric.
The example with a jump contradicts that.
Right: this is the third result.
questions.explain: The book states that uniformly convergent power series can be differentiated and integrated term by term.
questions.rule: Name the hypothesis.
questions.teaches: Term-by-term differentiation of a power series is justified by uniform convergence inside the radius of convergence.

questions.q: For \(1+x+x^2+\cdots=1/(1-x)\) valid for \(|x|\lt1\), what is the radius of convergence?
options: Infinity
optionExplain: The series converges for many x.
Right: it converges within 1 unit of the center 0.
At x = 1 the series diverges.
The series converges at x = 0.9.
questions.explain: Radius is the distance from the center within which it converges.
questions.rule: Find the distance to the first failure.

questions.q: True or false: The center of convergence of \(\sum a_n(x-3)^n\) is 3.
questions.explain: The center is the value c in (x - c).
questions.rule: Read the center from the form.

questions.q: For \(\sum x^n\) on \(|x|\le0.9\), the smallest n for which the error bound \(0.9^{n+1}/0.1\) drops below 0.01 is ____.
questions.explain: At n = 64 the bound is 0.01061; at n = 65 it is 0.00955.

questions.q: Predict whether the geometric series converges uniformly on the whole interval \((-1,1)\).
options: No, the needed n grows without bound as |x| approaches 1
Yes, because it converges at every point
Yes, since the radius is 1
No, because it diverges at 0
optionExplain: Right: the error x^(n+1)/(1-x) is large near x = 1.
Pointwise convergence is not uniform convergence.
Uniform convergence holds on smaller closed discs only.
At 0 it converges.
questions.explain: The error x^(n+1)/(1 - x) tends to infinity as x approaches 1 for any fixed n.
questions.rule: Check what happens near 1.

questions.q: A student says: \(\sum x^n\) converges uniformly on \(|x|\le0.9999\), but needs about 138,000 terms for error 0.01, so it is not uniform. What is wrong?
options: The number 138,000 is wrong
Uniform convergence needs N under 100
A large N that works for all x in the set still shows uniform convergence
The set should be larger
optionExplain: The estimate is about 138,148.
No bound on N is needed.
Right: uniform means one N for all x, however large.
It is a closed set strictly inside the radius.
questions.explain: Uniformity is about independence of x, not the size of N.
questions.rule: What does uniform require?

questions.q: The series for \(\sin x\) converges for all real x. What is its radius of convergence?
options: π
Infinite
optionExplain: That belongs to the geometric series.
The sine function is periodic but the series is not limited by that.
It converges for all x.
Right: the series converges everywhere.
questions.explain: Convergence for all x means no finite radius.
questions.rule: Find where it fails.
questions.teaches: A power series that converges for every real x has an infinite radius of convergence, as for sine.

questions.q: What fact about integrals makes it valid to integrate an inequality between functions?
options: Integrals of different functions are always equal
The integral of a bound is always zero
If u ≤ v on the interval, the integral of u is at most the integral of v
Every function is its own integral
optionExplain: Inequalities are the point.
Integrating a constant bound M gives M times the length.
Right: integration preserves order.
That holds only for the exponential function.
questions.explain: The book cites this in a footnote.
questions.rule: Integration preserves order.

questions.q: True or false: Integrating \(-M_3\le f'''(t)\le M_3\) from a to x gives \(-M_3(x-a)\le f''(x)-f''(a)\le M_3(x-a)\) for x above a.
questions.explain: The integral of f''' is f'' minus f''(a) by the fundamental theorem.
questions.rule: Apply the fundamental theorem.

questions.q: For \(\sin x\) at 0, the degree-3 Taylor polynomial at \(x=0.5\) is \(0.5-0.5^3/6=0.479167\). The error bound \(M_4|x|^4/4!\) with \(M_4=1\) is ____ (three decimals).
questions.explain: 0.5^4 = 0.0625 and 4! = 24, so the bound is 0.0625/24 = 0.0026, which is 0.003 to three decimals.
questions.rule: Divide 0.0625 by 24.

questions.q: The true error of the degree-3 polynomial for sin at 0.5 is 0.000259. Predict how this compares with the bound 0.0026.
options: The error is smaller than the bound, as guaranteed
The error exceeds the bound, since the bound uses only the fourth derivative
The error equals the bound, because the bound is exact for sine at 0.5
No comparison is possible, because the bound holds only at the point 0
optionExplain: Right: the bound is a guarantee, not an exact value.
The remainder formula forbids this.
The bound is rarely exact.
The bound holds for every x in the interval.
questions.explain: The bound uses a worst-case derivative size.
questions.rule: Compare the numbers.

questions.q: A student bounds the degree-3 remainder at distance h by \(M_3h^3/3!\), where \(M_3\) bounds the third derivative. What is the flaw?
options: There is no flaw
The remainder after degree 3 involves the fourth derivative: M_4 h^4/4!
The bound should have no factorial
The distance h should be squared
optionExplain: After a degree-3 polynomial the next derivative is the fourth.
Right: the orders must match n + 1 = 4.
The factorial is part of the formula.
The power of h equals n + 1.
questions.explain: For R_{n+1} the formula is M_{n+1} times |x-a|^(n+1) over (n+1) factorial.
questions.rule: Match the orders.

questions.q: If \(|f^{(5)}|\le2\) everywhere, which bound holds for the degree-4 Taylor remainder at distance \(h=|x-a|\)?
optionExplain: The exponent and factorial must be 5.
The factorial 5! is missing.
The factor M_5 = 2 is missing.
Right: M_5 = 2 and (n+1)! = 120.
questions.explain: Degree 4 means n = 4 and the remainder involves the fifth derivative.
questions.rule: Use n + 1 = 5.
questions.teaches: The remainder after a degree-n polynomial is controlled by the bound on the next derivative, M_{n+1}, divided by (n+1)! with the power of the distance.

questions.q: The Taylor series of sine at 0 uses only values of sine and its derivatives at 0. What does the book say about its convergence?
options: It converges only near 0
It converges for all real x, so local data give global information
It converges only for x between -1 and 1
It does not converge
optionExplain: It converges everywhere.
Right: this is worth pondering.
That is the geometric series.
The remainder tends to 0.
questions.explain: The remainder is at most |x|^(n+1)/(n+1)! for all x.
questions.rule: Look at the remainder.

questions.q: True or false: For each fixed x, \(|x|^{n}/n!\) tends to 0 as n grows.
questions.explain: The factorial grows faster than any power.
questions.rule: Factorial beats power.

questions.q: For \(x=10\), the largest term \(10^k/k!\) over all k is about ____ (nearest whole number).
questions.explain: The maximum is at k = 9 or k = 10 where the value is 2755.7, about 2756.
questions.rule: Compare consecutive terms.

questions.q: At \(x=10\), what happens to the terms \(10^k/k!\) as k grows past 40?
options: They keep growing
They stay near 2756
They alternate in sign
They are already below 1.3e-8 at k = 40 and keep shrinking
optionExplain: Eventually the factorial dominates.
They peak near k = 10 and then fall.
The terms of the exponential-like bound are positive.
Right: 10^40/40! is about 1.2e-8.
questions.explain: The growth stops when k exceeds x.
questions.rule: Compare the factorial with the power.

questions.q: A student says: the sine series cannot converge at x = 10, because its first terms grow to over 2000. What is wrong?
options: Convergence depends on the tail; the terms eventually shrink
The terms never reach 2000, so the student's premise about large terms is wrong
The series diverges, so the student's conclusion is correct for this series
Early terms are zero, so the large values quoted never occur at all
optionExplain: Right: early terms can be large.
They do reach about 2756.
It converges.
They are not.
questions.explain: Only the behavior as n grows decides convergence.
questions.rule: Look at the tail.

questions.q: Suppose \(f\) has derivative bounds \(M_k=3^k\) at all orders. Does the Taylor remainder at distance h tend to 0?
options: No, since M_k grows
Only if h is less than 1
Yes, because (3h)^(n+1)/(n+1)! tends to 0
It depends on a
optionExplain: The factorial grows faster than any exponential.
It tends to 0 for every h.
Right: even exponential growth of M is beaten by the factorial.
The bound does not depend on a.
questions.explain: The book offers non-exponential growth as an example of reasonable bounds; the factorial also handles a bound of the form c^k.
questions.rule: Compare (3h)^n with n!.
questions.teaches: A derivative bound of the form c^k, which is an exponential in k, still gives a remainder that tends to 0 because k! outgrows c^k.

questions.q: Which series for \(1/(1+x^2)\) comes from the geometric series?
optionExplain: That is 1/(1 - x^2).
That is 1/(1 + x).
Right: replace x by -x^2 in 1/(1 - x).
The constant term is missing.
questions.rule: Substitute.

questions.q: True or false: Substituting \(t=x^2\) into the series \(e^t=1+t+t^2/2!+\cdots\) gives a valid series for \(e^{x^2}\).
questions.explain: The series for the exponential holds for every t, so any substitution works.
questions.rule: Substitution.

questions.q: The fourth derivative of \(e^{x^2}\) at 0 is ____.
questions.explain: The coefficient of x^4 is 1/2, and the fourth derivative equals 4! = 24 times it, so 12.
questions.rule: Fourth derivative = 4! times the coefficient.

questions.q: For \(f=e^x\), predict the limit of \((f(x)-Q(x))/x^2\) as x goes to 0, where \(Q=1+x+x^2\).
optionExplain: Right: f(x) - Q(x) is about -x^2/2 for small x (numerically -0.498 at x = 0.01).
That is for the Taylor quadratic, not for Q.
The sign is negative.
The coefficient of x^2 in e^x is 1/2, so the difference is -1/2.
questions.explain: Compare the coefficient of x^2 in Q with that in e^x.
questions.rule: Compare x^2 coefficients.

questions.q: A student says: the series I found for \(1/(1+x^2)\) by the geometric series may differ from the Taylor series. What is the flaw?
options: The two series agree only to degree 2
Power series expansions are unique, so they agree
The geometric series has no x terms
Taylor series exist only for polynomials
optionExplain: Uniqueness holds at every degree.
Right: the geometric series form gives the Taylor series.
It does.
They exist for many functions.
questions.explain: The best-approximation argument holds at each degree.
questions.rule: Use uniqueness.

questions.q: Which statement describes why the Taylor quadratic is the best quadratic approximation near a?
options: It has the largest leading coefficient
It passes through the most points
It equals f at every x
It is the only quadratic for which \((f-P)/(x-a)^2\) tends to 0
optionExplain: Size of the coefficient is not the criterion.
It matches f, f', f'' at a only.
It is an approximation near a.
Right: any other quadratic leaves a nonzero limit.
questions.explain: The book generalizes the best linear approximation idea.
questions.rule: Recall the limit test.
questions.teaches: The Taylor polynomial of degree n is the unique polynomial of degree n whose difference from f is small compared with (x − a)^n, which explains uniqueness of power series.

questions.q: How does the book define Eulerian mathematics?
options: Non-rigorous reasoning that leads to an interesting truth
Any proof written by Euler, whether or not it is fully rigorous
Reasoning that is rigorous and complete in every step of the argument
A method for avoiding all proof and checking in mathematics
optionExplain: Right: it may even be incorrect in some sense.
The term covers a style of argument, not authorship.
It is non-rigorous by definition.
The aim is to reach truths that can then be confirmed.
questions.explain: It is named in honor of the eighteenth-century mathematician.
questions.rule: Recall the definition.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, a lack of rigor is the same as nonsense.
questions.explain: The book says lack of rigor is not the same as nonsense, although a fine line separates the two.
questions.rule: Not the same.

questions.q: Sort each step by whether it is Eulerian (non-rigorous inspiration) or a rigorous check.

items.t: Treat the difference of a sequence as a derivative and solve the differential equation
Pretend an infinite product of series can be expanded as if it were finite
Confirm the guessed quadratic satisfies every condition in the problem
Replace the infinite sums by partial sums and show the limits exist
