media.alt: A small circle omega with centre O and a larger circle gamma through O cross at A (top) and B (bottom), joined by a dashed vertical line. X is on gamma, outside omega, far to the upper right. Lines from X reach C and D on omega; segment CD is crossed at X' by line OX. A dashed circle passes through O, C, X and D.

questions.q: The four circles are inverted in the dashed circle centred at C. Why do c2 and c3 become circles rather than lines?
options: Neither c2 nor c3 passes through C, so each maps to a circle
Both are tangent to a circle through C, which forces a circular image
Both are smaller than c4, and smaller circles keep their shape
Every circle maps to a circle, and lines come only from straight objects
optionExplain: Right: only circles through the centre of inversion turn into lines, and c2 and c3 do not pass through C.
Being tangent to a circle through C does not matter; what counts is whether the circle itself passes through C.
Size is not the test; a small circle through the centre would still become a line.
A circle through the centre of inversion does become a line, as c1 and c4 do here.
questions.explain: A circle through the centre of inversion maps to a line; one that misses the centre maps to a circle. c1 and c4 pass through C and become lines, while c2 and c3 miss it and stay circles.
questions.rule: Circles through the centre of inversion become lines; all other circles become circles.

media.alt: Four circles in a ring, each touching the next: c1 (upper left) touches c2 (left) at D, c2 touches c3 (bottom) at A, c3 touches c4 (large, right) at B, and c4 touches c1 at C. A dashed circle omega, centred at C, overlaps c1 and c4 and passes near B.

questions.q: A student says the staircase picture of A, B, C, D, E proves the sequence converges to the square root of 5. According to the authors, what is wrong?
options: The picture is an aid; one must still argue the points never bounce away from the crossing
The picture is exact, but it only works for the starting value 5
The picture proves convergence, but not that the limit is the square root of 5
The picture cannot be used, because averaging is not shown in it
optionExplain: Right: the authors call the picture an aid to reasoning and say a careful argument is needed, which they then give algebraically.
The authors do not say the picture is exact, and nothing limits it to one starting value.
The authors do not say the picture proves convergence; they say it only suggests it.
The picture does show averaging: the midpoint of A and B gives the next value.
questions.explain: The authors use the picture to guess that the sequence settles at the crossing of y = x and y = 5/x. They then say it is not a rigorous proof and switch to an algebraic argument showing the terms decrease and stay above the square root.
questions.rule: A picture suggests the limit; a proof must rule out the terms moving away from it.

media.alt: Graph with a rising straight line y equals x and a falling curve y equals 5 over x, which cross near the lower left. Vertical axis ticks at 1, 4 and 6. A on the curve and B on the line share one x-value. Dashed arrows lead left from B's height to C on the line, down to D on the curve, then left to E near the crossing. Dashed verticals from B, C and E end in three dots on the x-axis.

questions.q: In the diagram, f(u) equals u to the power alpha, with alpha above 1, touches its tangent line at (1,1). Which statements follow?
options: Away from u = 1 the curve lies strictly above the tangent line
With u = 1 + x, equality in (1+x)^alpha >= 1 + alpha x occurs only at x = 0
The curve lies below its tangent line for every u less than 1
For large u the tangent line overtakes the curve, so the inequality reverses
optionExplain: Right: the curve bends upward, so it stays above the tangent line except at the touching point.
Right: the line and curve meet only at (1,1), which is x = 0, so the inequality is strict elsewhere.
On both sides of (1,1) the curve is above the line; it does not cross it there.
The curve keeps bending upward, so it pulls further above the line for large u; the inequality does not reverse for alpha at least 1.
questions.explain: Because the graph bends upward, it lies above its tangent line everywhere except where they touch, at (1,1). In terms of x = u - 1, this is the strict form of Bernoulli's inequality for x other than 0.
questions.rule: A graph that bends upward stays above its tangent line, touching it only at the point of tangency.

media.alt: Graph of the curve f of x, flat near the horizontal axis on the left and bending steeply upward on the right, through the marked point (1,1). A straight line touches the curve at that point; on both sides the curve stays on or above the line, pulling away to the right. Ticks labelled 1 on each axis.

questions.q: In the diagram, each rectangle's top-left corner touches the curve. On a stretch where the curve is falling, how does each rectangle compare with the curve?
options: It sticks out above the curve, because the left corner is the highest point on that strip
It sits entirely below the curve, because the left corner is the lowest point on that strip
It matches the area under the curve exactly on each strip
It sticks out above the curve only on the very last strip
optionExplain: Right: on a falling stretch the curve is highest at the left end of a strip, so a rectangle of that height overshoots the curve.
That would hold on a rising stretch, where the left end is the lowest point of the strip.
Equality on each strip would need the curve to be flat there, which a falling stretch is not.
Nothing special happens on the last strip; the overshoot occurs on every strip where the curve falls.
questions.explain: The rectangle's height is the curve's value at the left end of the strip. Where the curve falls, that value is the largest on the strip, so each rectangle overshoots; where the curve rises, it undershoots.
questions.rule: A left-endpoint rectangle overshoots on a falling curve and undershoots on a rising one.

media.alt: Graph of a smooth curve that rises from the vertical axis to a peak and then falls gradually to the right. Beneath it stand six thin adjacent rectangles of equal width, with a double arrow labelled delta for that width. Each rectangle's top-left corner touches the curve. An integral sign from a to b is written above.

questions.q: In the diagram, which integrand gives the area of the black region above the line y = c, between the two crossings?
questions.explain: Between the two crossings the curve lies above the line, so the height of the region at each x is the curve minus the line, \(2x-3x^3-c\).
optionExplain: This is the height of the left black region, where the line is above the curve, not the hump.
Right: above the line the thickness is curve minus line.
This would measure the area down to the x-axis, which includes the white part below the line.
This is the height of a rectangle up to the line, not of the region between line and curve.
questions.rule: Area between two graphs is the integral of upper minus lower.

media.alt: A graph with axes and the curve y = 2x - 3x cubed, which rises from near the y-axis, peaks, then falls to cross the x-axis on the right. A horizontal line y = c cuts the curve twice. Two regions are shaded black: one at the left between the y-axis, the line above it and the curve below, and one above the line under the hump between the two crossings.

questions.q: In the picture, taking the logarithm of the expression inside the limit turns it into which sum?
options: \(\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}\ln(1+k/n)\)
\(\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}\ln(k/n)\)
questions.explain: The log of a product is a sum of logs, and the power 1/n becomes a factor 1/n. That is a Riemann sum for \(\ln(1+x)\) on [0, 1].
optionExplain: The factor 1/n from the root is lost, so this sum grows instead of settling.
The logarithm is dropped, so this is a sum of the factors themselves, not of their logs.
Right: the factor 1/n times a function of k/n is a Riemann sum.
The factor 1 + is lost inside the log, which changes the function being integrated.
questions.rule: A product with an n-th root becomes a Riemann sum after taking logs.

media.alt: A displayed limit as n tends to infinity of the n-th root of a product: the product runs over k from 1 to n of the factor one plus k over n, all raised to the power one over n.

questions.q: Suppose x counts equal parts of a fixed total S, so each part has size S/x. In the picture's function, how big is each part at the maximum?
questions.explain: Logarithmic differentiation of \((S/x)^x\) gives \(\ln(S/x)=1\), so the part size S/x is e, and the number of parts is S/e.
optionExplain: S/e is the number of parts at the maximum, not the size of each part.
2 is a good integer choice near e, but it is not where the continuous maximum sits.
S would be a single part, which gives the product S and not the maximum.
Right: S/x equals e at the maximum.
questions.rule: Calculus points to parts of size near e; integers then decide.

media.alt: A displayed definition: f of x is defined to equal the quantity S divided by x, raised to the power x, followed by a comma. Here S is a constant.

questions.section: Beauty, Simplicity, and Symmetry: The Quest for a Moving Curtain
questions.q: In the picture, for n = 2, what does the binomial theorem make the sum inside the integral?
questions.explain: Each term is \(\binom nk(px)^k(1-p)^{n-k}\), so the sum over k is the binomial expansion of \((px+(1-p))^n\).
optionExplain: Right: the sum is the binomial expansion of the sum of px and 1 - p to the power n.
The power 2 is applied only to one term, so the middle term of the expansion is missing.
The exponent 2 on x is wrong: x carries the index k, not n.
Only the k = 0 and k = 2 terms are kept, so the k = 1 term is missing.
questions.rule: The binomial theorem collapses the sum to one power.

media.alt: A displayed formula: f of x equals the integral from 0 to 1, with respect to p, of a sum over k from 0 to n of n choose k times p to the k times x to the k times the quantity one minus p raised to the power n minus k.

questions.q: In the picture, which substitution swaps the two square-root terms in the denominator and keeps the interval from 2 to 4 in place?
questions.explain: Under \(x\to6-x\), \(9-x\) becomes \(x+3\) and vice versa, and 2 and 4 swap. The integrand and its mirror add to 1, so the integral is 1.
optionExplain: Right: it swaps 9 - x with x + 3 and sends 2 to 4.
This maps 9 - x to x, not to x + 3, and sends the interval [2, 4] to [5, 7].
This sends the interval [2, 4] to [-1, 1], so it does not preserve the limits.
This does not map [2, 4] onto itself and does not turn 9 - x into x + 3.
questions.rule: Use a + b - x for an integral on [a, b].

media.alt: A displayed integral from 2 to 4. The integrand is a fraction: the numerator is the square root of the natural log of 9 minus x, times dx; the denominator is that same square root plus the square root of the natural log of x plus 3.

questions.q: In the picture, the first integral runs from 1/101 to 1/11 and the second from 101/100 to 11/10. Which map sends the first limits to the second?
questions.explain: Check: \(\tau(1/101)=101/100\) and \(\tau(1/11)=11/10\). So the substitution \(x\to\tau(x)\) carries the first range onto the second.
optionExplain: 1 - x sends 1/101 to 100/101, which is not 101/100.
1/x sends 1/101 to 101, which is not 101/100.
x + 1 sends 1/101 to 102/101, which is not 101/100.
Right: both pairs of limits match.
questions.rule: Find the map by testing it on the limits.

media.alt: Cropped formula piece: an integral sign with lower limit the fraction 1 over 101 and upper limit the fraction 1 over 11, then an opening parenthesis and a fraction bar. The integrand itself is cut off.

Cropped formula piece: an integral sign with lower limit the fraction 101 over 100 and upper limit the fraction 11 over 10, then an opening parenthesis and a fraction bar. The integrand itself is cut off.

questions.section: Beauty, Simplicity, and Symmetry: The Quest for a Moving Curtain
questions.q: In the grid, columns A to E hold five random numbers: A is the dial setting and each other column one toss. The number of tosses is ____.
questions.explain: Five columns minus the dial column leaves four tosses, which are ranked together with A among five numbers, giving five equally likely head counts.
questions.rule: n tosses need n + 1 uniform numbers.

media.alt: A spreadsheet-style grid with column headers A to E and row numbers 1 to 3. Only cell A1 shows a visible entry, the letter p in bold; the other cells in rows 1 to 3 are blank or too faint to read.

cover.alt: Book cover: The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, Second Edition, by Paul Zeitz, showing two cyclists on a rocky cliff edge above a wide canyon landscape.
